Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 1:

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light.﴾

The phrase ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ indicates that Allah alone deserves praise, to the exclusion of any other, because it conveys restriction (al-hasr). The lam is for the definition of the genus (lam al-jins), so it indicates that the entitlement to this kind of praise belongs exclusively to Allah, the Exalted. The explanation of this has already been given in full at the beginning of Surah al-Fatihah.

Furthermore, the phrase ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ here is a declarative statement (khabar) both in form and in meaning, since there is nothing here that turns it toward the intention of creating praise (insha'), unlike in Surah al-Fatihah, because there it is followed by ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5] through to the end of the surah. Whoever permits that this phrase here be an expression of praise (inshā' ma'na) has not reflected carefully.

The meaning here is that all praise is deserved by none but Allah. This is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), to refute the polytheists who praised the idols for what they imagined of their bestowing blessings, victory and the relief of distresses upon them. Abu Sufyan, when he and his party prevailed on the day of Uhud, said: "Exalt Hubal! We have al-'Uzza and you have no 'Uzza." It is also permissible that it be an absolute restriction (qasr haqiqi) in the sense of perfection, and that praising others than Allah among the benefactors is a figure of speech (tasamuh), because in reality they are a formal intermediary through which Allah's blessing flows by their hands. The intended purpose is still the same, namely the refutation of the polytheists, since the idols do not deserve formal praise, let alone real praise, as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, nor avails you anything?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. For this reason, after the praise for Allah's great act of creation, the statement follows: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the position of an attribute to the Name of Majesty conveys, together with its relative clause, a reminder of the great attribute of creation, which encompasses the heavens, the earth, and what is in them of substances and accidents. This is the most concise expression for evoking the greatness of Allah's power. Defining by means of the relative pronoun here does not indicate that the preceding sentence is being given a reason, since the sentence is not an expressive one (inshā'i), as you know. A declarative sentence is not given a reason, because a declarative statement is a report of what is in reality, so there is no need to justify it. Thus the purpose of the attributes is to prepare for His saying afterwards: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

He used the plural for "heavens" because they are many worlds, since each star among them is an independent world distinct from the others, and among them are the seven well-known planets, referred to in the Qur'an as "the seven heavens," as far as we see. He used the singular for "earth" because it is one world, and for this reason the word "earth" does not occur in the plural in the Qur'an.

As for His saying: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, al-Kashshaf indicated that (ja'ala), when it takes one object, means "originated" and "brought into being," approaching the synonymy of the meaning of (khalaqa, created). The difference between them is that in khalq (creation) there is consideration of the meaning of measuring and determining, while in ja'l (making) there is consideration of the meaning of attribution, meaning that the made thing is created for the sake of something else or is attributed to something else, and the one to which it is attributed is known by the aid of the context. So since darkness and light are accidents, their creation is a formation so that the existing things of the heavens and the earth are qualified by them. This is known from mentioning ﴿the darknesses and the light﴾ after mentioning ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾, and from choosing the word "created" for the heavens and the earth and the word "made" for the darknesses and the light, and from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate﴾ [al-A'raf: 189]. The mate, who is the female, is considered in her existence as a completion of the creation of the male, and for this reason He followed it with: ﴿so that he might find rest in her﴾ [al-A'raf: 189]. Creation (khalq) is more general in usage, and for this reason He said in another verse: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], because every formation is not free of measure and order.

He singled out from among substances and accidents two great accidents, namely the darknesses and the light, saying: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, because all people are equal in perceiving them and being aware of them. By mentioning these four matters, reference is made to both kinds of created things, substances and accidents. Therefore the distinction between the verb (khalaqa) and the verb (ja'ala) here is counted among the eloquence of the words. Each word has its own position alongside its companion, which is what the men of letters call the grace (rashaqa) of the word: the verb (khalaqa) is more fitting for bringing essences into being, and the verb (ja'ala) is more fitting for bringing into being the accidents of essences, their states, and their order.

Limiting the mention of created things to these four is an allusion (ta'rid) that refutes the beliefs of the disbelievers among the Arabs, for they were among polytheists, Sabians, Magians, and Christians, and all of them affirmed gods other than Allah. The polytheists affirmed gods from the earth; the Sabians affirmed gods from the heavenly bodies; the Christians affirmed the divinity of 'Isa, or 'Isa and Maryam, and both of them are earthly existents; and the Magians, namely the Manichaeans, deified light and darkness, so that light is in their view the god of good and darkness the god of evil.

So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, that is, of what is in them, and the Creator of the darknesses and the light.

Furthermore, in choosing to mention the darknesses and the light specifically, rather than other accidents, there is an indication and allusion to the condition of those addressed by the verse, with the disbelief of one group and the faith of another group. For disbelief resembles darkness, since it is immersion in ignorance and bewilderment, and faith resembles light, since it is the clarifying of guidance and truth. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. He placed the mention of the darknesses first in observance of the order of existence, because darkness precedes light, for light came into being after the creation of luminous essences, and darkness was general.

He used the plural for "darknesses" and the singular for "light" in conformity with usage, because the word "darknesses" in the plural is lighter, and the word "light" in the singular is lighter. For this reason the word "darknesses" does not occur in the Qur'an except in the plural, and the word "light" does not occur except in the singular. Both of them indicate the genus, and the generic definite article is equal in respect of the singular and the plural, so there remains no cause for the difference that would require following usage, contrary to what is in al-Kashshaf.

﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

The clause ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens﴾. Here "thumma" (then/yet) indicates gradation of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), signifying that what follows it includes a meaning of the same kind as what precedes it, but is more important in its domain. This is the function of "thumma" when it conjoins one clause to another, for the deviation of the polytheists from worshipping Allah, while knowing that He is the Creator of things, is a strange matter among them, more astonishing than their knowledge of that.

The argument is decisive against those who disbelieve, for all of them, except the Manichaeans, acknowledge that Allah is the Creator and the Governor of the universe, and for this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17].

The statement is used in the sense of wonder by way of metonymy (kinaya), by the indication of the position of "thumma" and the denotation of the present tense on renewal. The wonder at the condition of the polytheists is evident, and as for the Manichaeans, the wonder at their condition is that they did not find guidance to the Creator, and worshipped some of His creatures. Thus what is meant by ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ [al-An'am: 7] is everyone who disbelieved by affirming a god other than Allah, exalted is He, whether he is one who made a partner for Him, like the polytheists of the Arabs and the Sabians, or one who assigned divinity to other than Allah, like the Manichaeans. This meaning is indicated by the context, although the customary usage of the Qur'an is to apply "those who disbelieve" to the polytheists.

The meaning of "ya'dilun" is "they equate." Al-'adl means equalization. One says: "I made so-and-so equal to so-and-so (adaltu fulanan bi-fulan)," when you make him equal to him, as was mentioned previously in His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. So His saying "bi-rabbihim" (with their Lord) is connected to "ya'dilun," and it is not correct to connect it to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ [al-An'am: 7], since there is no need for that.

The object of "ya'dilun" is omitted, meaning they equate with their Lord something other than Him, and every party knows what they equated with Allah. What is meant is that they equate it with Allah in divinity, even though some of them acknowledge that Allah is greater, as the polytheists of the Arabs used to say: "Here I am, with no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours, whom You own and what he owns." And as the Sabians said concerning the spirits, and the Christians concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The meaning of the wonder is general concerning the condition of those who claimed divinity for other than Allah, exalted is He, whether among them is one who was capable of inference and reflection upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, or one who was not capable of that, because the object of wonder is that He creates them and creates their objects of worship, yet they do not find guidance to Him, but rather invent the divinity of other than Him. It is known that the wonder at their condition varies according to the degree of variation in their disbelief and error.

This is a resumption (istinaf) for another purpose: to express wonder at the state of the polytheists who denied the Resurrection. He first reminded them of the creation of the heavens and the earth, and then wondered at their state in equating with God, in divinity, those who did not create the heavens or the earth. Then He reminded them of their first creation, and wondered at their state: how do they combine acknowledging that God is the One who created them in the first creation with doubting the second creation?

The pronoun (huwa) in His words ﴿He is the One who created you﴾ is used so that both the predicate and the subject are defined together. Thus the sentence conveys restriction (qasr) in both pillars of the predication and in its complement, meaning: He is your Creator and no other; from clay and not from anything else; and He is the One who decreed a term, and with Him is a specified term. The ruling of restriction therefore extends to what is conjoined to the restricted element. The situation that required the restriction is their denial of resurrection. Since they denied it, which is the second creation, they were placed in the position of one who denies the first creation, for there is no difference between the two creations. Rather, in the common understanding of craftsmen, repetition is easier, as God said: ﴿And He it is who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], and He said: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Nay, they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15]. The restriction conveys the negation of all these acts of creation from anyone other than God, including their idols. It is like His words: ﴿God is He who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will give you life. Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ [al-Rum: 40].

The address in His words ﴿created you﴾ is directed to those who disbelieved, so there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person, for the purpose of rebuke.

He mentioned the substance from which creation came, by His words ﴿from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], to show the invalidity of their reasoning for denying the second creation, because they deemed it unlikely that a human be recreated after having become dust. This report about them is repeated in the Qur'an. They acknowledged that they will become dust after death, and they acknowledge that they were created from dust, because this is established among people in all ages. So they argued for the denial of resurrection with something that is actually fit to be an argument for the possibility of resurrection, because their return to dust brings the re-creation closer, since they return to the substance of the first creation. Therefore God said here: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾, and in the verses of reflection on His wondrous formation He said: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid﴾ [al-Insan: 2], and similar things.

This critique of their argument is called in the terminology of the science of disputation (ilm al-jadal) al-qawl bil-muwjib (the argument of turning the premise against its user), and the indication of the error in their reasoning is called fasad al-wad' (the invalidity of the premise's structure).

The meaning of ﴿created you from clay﴾ is that He created the origin of mankind, namely the first human, from clay, so all humanity traces back to the creation from clay. Therefore He said: ﴿created you from clay﴾. In another place He said: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid﴾ [al-Insan: 2], meaning man as he reproduces from the origin of humanity.

Thumma (then) denotes sequence and interval, and it conjoins the verb qada (decreed) to the verb khalaqa (created). So it is the conjunction of a verb with a verb, not the conjunction of a sentence with a sentence. The interval here is considered with respect to distribution: He created each individual of mankind, then decreed for him his term, that is, fulfilled it for him. So qada here does not mean "measured," because the measuring of the term is either concurrent with creation or prior to it, not subsequent to it. Rather, qada here means "completed" (awfa), the term of every created being, as in His words: ﴿Then when We decreed death for him﴾ [Saba': 14], meaning, We caused him to die. You may also take thumma to denote a rank-based delay.

The reason that what indicates the ending of the term of every created being from clay was chosen here, rather than saying "until a term," is that the indication that the term ends points more clearly to the possibility of the second creation, which is resurrection, than the indication of the decreeing of the term. This is because the decreeing is hidden, whereas what people know is the end of the term of life; and because the end of the term of life is a prelude to the second life.

The clause ﴿and with Him is a specified term﴾ is an interjected clause between the clause ﴿then decreed a term﴾ and the clause ﴿then you doubt﴾. The purpose of this interjection is to inform the creatures that God knows the terms of people, in response to the words of the polytheists: ﴿And nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24].

[p. 130]

The common usage has been departed from in placing the adverbial predicate before an indefinite qualified subject, as in His words: ﴿I have one ewe﴾ [Sad: 23]. So much so that the author of al-Kashshaf said that it is the commonly circulating expression. Here He did not place the adverbial phrase first in order to show concern with the subject, since the commonly used form delays it; thus by this fronting its indefiniteness conveys the meaning of magnification, meaning: and a great specified term is with Him.

[p. 131]

The meaning of musamma (specified) is determined, because the root sima is the mark by which the marked item is determined. The determination here is the determination of the limit and the time.

The "with" in His words ﴿with Him﴾ is the "with" of knowledge, meaning: it is known to Him alone, not to anyone else. So what is meant by His words ﴿and a specified term﴾ is the term of the raising of people to the gathering. Repeating an indefinite noun after an indefinite noun indicates that the second is other than the first. So the meaning becomes: then He decreed for you two terms: a term whose duration you know by the death of its owner, and a term whose duration is fixed in God's knowledge. So what is meant by the first term is the lifespan of each person, for people know it at the death of its owner, and say: he lived so many years. Although its knowledge is not certain until its end, it is nonetheless knowledge attained by many people through inference. And the known term, although it has ended, was in origin an extended term.

What is meant by the second term is what lies between each person's death and the Day of Resurrection on which all people will be raised, for no one in this world knows it, nor do they know it on the Day of Resurrection. God said: ﴿And the Day We gather them, it will seem as though they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another﴾ [Yunus: 45], and He said: ﴿And the Day the Hour will be established, the criminals will swear that they had not remained but an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55].

His words ﴿then you doubt﴾ are conjoined to the clause ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾, so the particle thumma here denotes a rank-based delay, as is its usual function in conjoining sentences, for a shift from one report to something more wondrous than it, as was previously mentioned in His words: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. That is, the wonder is indeed directed at those who doubt the matter of resurrection while knowing about the first creation and about death.

The addressees in His words ﴿you doubt﴾ are the polytheists. The subject is brought as an explicit pronoun for rebuke.

Imtira' means doubt and hesitation about a matter. It follows the pattern of ifti'al, derived from al-miryah, with a kasra on the mim, which is a noun for doubt. Its verb form occurs only with the added taa', and no bare verb form has been heard for it.

The complement of tamtarun is omitted because it is clear from the context: you doubt the possibility of resurrection and the re-creation. What indicates that this is the thing they doubt is His words: ﴿created you from clay, then decreed a term, and with Him is a specified term﴾, for without the intent of reminding them, by way of evidence for the possibility of resurrection, there would be no reason to mention the creation from clay, the first term, and the second term, which would favor the specification by mention.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 3:

﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying ﴿He it is Who created you from clay﴾ [al-An'am: 2], meaning: He created you and did not neglect to watch over you, so He knows all your conditions.

The pronoun (ḍamīr) is a subject (mubtada') referring back to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala) in His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and it is not a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), since the pronoun of separation does not occur after a conjunctive particle (ḥarf al-ʿaṭf). His saying "Allah" is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. Since the subject is a pronoun referring back to the Name of Allah, the intended purpose of the predication that "He is Allah" cannot be to inform that the One who created and decreed is Allah, since that is already known from the return of the pronoun. Therefore the intended purpose of informing that He is Allah must be a meaning that the context conveys, namely that it serves as a conclusion to the preceding statements beginning from His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who created﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. It draws attention to the corruption of the belief of those who ascribed divinity to other than Allah and praised their gods by saying that they are the Creator of the cosmos, the Creator of man and the One who restores him. Then it declares that He alone is the Deity in the heavens and on the earth, since there is no creator other than Him, as has been established just above. And since He knows the secret and the open, while others have no perception at all, let alone intellect, let alone being knowing.

Since the Name of Majesty is well known among them and is not confused with anything else, His saying ﴿And He is Allah﴾ has the sense of: the one described by these attributes is the bearer of this name and no other.

His saying ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ is connected either to the being (kawn) implied by the restrictive sentence (jumlat al-qaṣr), or to what is implied in ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 1] of the meaning of sole divinity (infirad bil-ilahiyya), as one who mentions a generous man and then says: "He is Hatim among the Arabs." This is for the purpose of explicitly stating that none shares His attributes in all existents.

His saying ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾ is a sentence that confirms the meaning of the sentence ﴿And He is Allah﴾; for this reason it is separated (fuṣilat), because it stands in relation to it in the position of emphasis, since His sole divinity in the heavens and on the earth requires His knowledge of the conditions of some earthly existents.

It is not permissible to attach ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ to the verb in His saying ﴿He knows your secret﴾, because the secret, the open and the earning of people occur on the earth specifically and not in the heavens. Whoever estimates that has erred a hidden error.

He mentioned the secret because knowledge of the secret is evidence of the generality of knowledge, and He mentioned the open to encompass both kinds of speech. By ﴿what you earn﴾ is meant all beliefs and deeds, good and bad, so it is an allusion to promise and threat.

The address is to all listeners, so it includes the disbelievers, who are the primary intended audience of this address, because it is instruction and awakening with respect to them, and reminder with respect to the believers.

This is a transition to the disbelief of the polytheists in their denial of the Messenger of Muhammad (ﷺ), after the proof had been established against the falsity of their disbelief concerning the associating of others with God in divinity. It is conjoined (by "و") because both matters are among the conditions of their disbelief, and because what moved them to deny the Messenger (ﷺ) was his call to them to monotheism (tawhid). From this call arose the dispute between them and him, so they denied him and demanded from him signs as proof of his truthfulness.

The pronouns of the third-person plural refer to the polytheists, who are among those addressed by the pronouns of address in the preceding verse. Thus the shift from address (khitab) to the third person regarding them is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) that was required by the desire to publicly expose them with this blameworthy condition, to specify it explicitly, to turn away from addressing them, and to devote the address exclusively to the believers. This is among the finest kinds of iltifat, because what makes an iltifat good is that it has an additional purpose beyond shifting the speech from one style to another, namely renewing the listener's attentiveness. The waw is then resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and what follows it is a fresh, independent statement.

He used the present tense in His saying ﴿تَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (there comes to them) to indicate recurrence, although this coming is also past, as indicated by the past tense in His saying ﴿كانُوا﴾ (they were).

By "its coming to them" is meant its reaching them and their being challenged by it. The reaching is likened to the arrival of one who comes, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

It reached me, may you not be cursed, that you blamed me.

He omitted what would indicate the source from which it comes, because it is evident from His saying ﴿مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (of the signs of their Lord). That is: no sign from among His signs comes to them from their Lord except that they turn away from it.

The ﴿مِن﴾ in His saying ﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ (any sign) serves to emphasize the negation, with the aim of generality over all kinds of signs that have come and that come. The ﴿مِن﴾ in His saying ﴿مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ is partitive. By ﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ is meant every indication that points to God Most High's being alone in divinity. Among these are the verses of the Qur'an, which, by their inimitability to them, were proofs of the Messenger's (ﷺ) truthfulness in what he reported of God's oneness. Likewise the miracles of the Messenger (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, such as the splitting of the moon. The meaning of the verse has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَكَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ (And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs) [al-Baqarah: 39], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The attribution of the Lord to the pronoun (them) is for the purpose of recording against them the ingratitude owed to the right of servanthood. For it is the servant's right to attend to what comes to him from his Lord, and to the one who comes to him saying: "I am sent to you from your Lord." Then he should reflect and consider. It is not his right to turn away from this, since perhaps he would be turning away from something which, had he reflected upon it, he would have known to be from his Lord.

The exception (al-istithna') is a mufarragh (exception with the element omitted) from omitted circumstances.

The clause ﴿كانُوا عَنْها مُعْرِضِينَ﴾ (they were turning away from it) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The coming is expressed in the form of the active participle in the predicate of kana, to indicate that this turning away is established by the meaning of the verb "to be" and renewed by the meaning of the participial form, because derived forms have the force of the present tense. The exception indicates that they had no state except turning away.

Turning away arises only from the belief that reflection and consideration are of no use. Therefore it is an indication that the one who turns away denies the informant from whose report he turns away.

The root meaning of i'rad (turning away) is turning the face away from looking at a thing. Here it is used metaphorically for refusing to know, so it includes the literal sense with regard to visible signs such as the splitting of the moon, and includes abandoning listening to the Qur'an, and includes obstinate refusal to acknowledge its inimitability and its being true, regarding those who listen to the Qur'an and are obstinate, as occurs in His saying: ﴿وَمِنْهُم مَّن يَسْتَمِعُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (And among them are those who listen to you) [al-An'am: 25]. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 5:

﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them, so there will come to them the news of what they used to mock.﴾ The fa' here is, according to the most apparent view, *fa' fasiha* (the "eloquent" fa', which indicates an omitted premise). It makes explicit a statement implied by His words: ﴿except that they turned away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 4]. That is, once this turning away is established, it is confirmed that they denied the truth when it came to them from Allah, since turning away is a sign of denial, as I mentioned just before. Thus what follows the fa' of explicitness is the consequence (*jaza'*). Its meaning is that it is known to the nations that the outcome of those who denied the truth that comes from Allah is evil. Since the preceding verse established that they turned away from the signs of Allah, it is confirmed that they denied the truth sent down from Allah. Therefore He built on this His words: ﴿so there will come to them the news of what they used to mock﴾, as a confirmation of the promise to the believers of victory and of making Islam prevail over all religion, and as a warning to the polytheists that there will befall them what befell the nations who denied their messengers, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and the People of the Rass, whom they knew of.

With this interpretation there is no need to make the fa' purely a fa' of consequence and to make what follows it the cause (*'illah*) of an omitted apodosis, understood from its cause, as the apparent reading of the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) has it, namely the content of ﴿they have denied﴾, so that one would supply: "Do not be surprised, for they have denied the Qur'an." For whoever supplies this is led to think that their denial meant is their denial of the signs they turned away from other than the sign of the Qur'an. This is a restriction of the generality of His words ﴿any sign﴾ [al-A'raf: 132] without any specifying evidence, since the Qur'an is among the signs, indeed it is the primary intended one. You have known that ﴿they have denied﴾ is the apodosis, and that it has a great position within the eloquence of conciseness. Moreover, that supposition requires that the signs meant in His words ﴿of the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4] be other than the Qur'an, and this is a restriction that does not suit the situation of the Qur'an being the greatest of them.

The fa' in His words "fa-sawfa" is the fa' of causation (*tasabbub*) upon His words ﴿they have denied the truth﴾, meaning: as a result of that, there follows their being struck by what Allah has threatened them with.

The particle of futurity (*harf al-taswif*) here serves to emphasize that this occurs in the future. The verb "come" (*al-ityan*) is used here, metaphorically, for befalling and occurrence. *Al-anba'* is the plural of *naba'*, which is news that has importance. The word *naba'* is used here for the realization of the content of the news, as in His words ﴿and you will surely know its news after a time﴾ [Sad: 88], meaning the realization of its news, because the news itself was already known beforehand.

﴿What they used to mock﴾ [al-An'am: 10] is the Qur'an, as in His words ﴿That is because you took the signs of Allah in mockery﴾. The Qur'an includes their threat of punishment in this world by the sword, and the punishment of the Hereafter. So these are news that He informed them of, and they denied it and mocked it, and so Allah threatened them that the content of that news would befall them. When He said to them ﴿what they used to mock﴾ [al-An'am: 10], they knew that these were the news of the Qur'an, because they knew that they were mocking the Qur'an, and the listeners knew that these people had been mocking the Qur'an. The meaning of *al-istihza'* (mockery) was already explained at His words, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

[Page 136]

[Page 137]

This sentence explains the statement, ﴿So the news will certainly reach them of that which they used to mock﴾ [6:5]. It does so in the form of a rebuking interrogative about their failure to see the many generations whom sudden events, contrary to the normal course of things, destroyed. Their condition indicates that these events were imposed on them by God as punishment for their denial.

The verb "to see" (ruʾya) may be cognitive, meaning: "Do they not know how many generations We destroyed?" It may also be visual, with the implied meaning: "Have they not seen the remains of the generations We destroyed, such as the dwellings of ʿAd and the Hijr of Thamud?" Many of the polytheists saw these in their travels and related accounts of them to people, until these accounts became widely transmitted among them, so that they were like things seen, and their souls affirmed them.

On both readings, the verb "they saw" (yarawā) is suspended from acting on its two objects, or its one object, by the interrogative word, which is *kam* (how many).

*Kam* is a noun used to ask about an indefinite number, so it must be followed by a specifier, which is its *tamyīz* (specification, a noun in the accusative or genitive that clarifies the vagueness). This was mentioned earlier in God's words: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [2:211] in Surat al-Baqarah. *Kam* may also be declarative, in which case it indicates a large, indefinite number, and it must still have a specifier that clarifies the vagueness. The specifier of the interrogative *kam* is in the accusative or genitive, while the specifier of the declarative *kam* is always in the genitive. Since *kam* is a noun in both cases, it has the grammatical position of nouns according to the governing words, nominative, accusative or genitive. Here it is in the position of one object or two objects of *yarawā*. The *min* in God's words ﴿from before them﴾ is for the starting point, to emphasise priority. As for the *min* in God's words ﴿from a generation (qarn)﴾, it is an extra preposition governing the specifier of the declarative *kam*, because the separation between *kam* and its specifier requires that it be in the genitive with *min*, as we explained at God's words ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [2:211] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Qarn* (generation) originally means a long period of time, and its use came to refer to a nation that endured for a long time. God said: ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [28:43]. The word *qarn* was explained as a perished nation. It is also used for a generation of people, as in the hadith: "The best generation is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them." It is also used for a period of time, commonly said to be one hundred years, though other views exist.

The clause ﴿We established them in the land﴾ is a descriptive clause modifying *qarn*. The pronoun was made to agree with the meaning of *qarn*, because it refers to a collective.

The meaning of ﴿We established them in the land﴾ is: We firmly established them and gave them sovereignty. The root of this verb derives from *makān* (place). Thus *makkanahu* and *makkana lahu* mean: he placed him in a place. God said: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ [28:57]. Similar is the expression "land for him" (arḍun lahu). *Tamkīn* (establishment) is used as a metonym (kināya) for empowerment and free disposal, because the owner of a place disposes of his place and house freely.

Then it is used for firm establishment, strengthening, and independence in affairs. One says: "He is *makīn*," meaning "*mumakkan*" (one who has been established), where the form *faʿīl* carries the sense of *mafʿūl*. God said: ﴿Indeed, today you are with Us established and trusted﴾ [12:54]. This is also a metonym at a second level, or it is a figurative metonymy (majāz mursal) built on the metonymic meaning. The establishment in the land is the strengthening of disposal over the land's resources and reliance on worldly means, by being secure from enemies, having abundance of provision and good circumstances. God said: ﴿Indeed We established him in the land﴾ [18:84], and He said: ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer﴾ [22:41], and the verse goes on. So *makkanahu* means: He made him one who is established, and *makkana lahu* means: He made him established for his sake, that is, for his benefit, as in *ḥamidahu* and *ḥamida lahu*. The preposition *lām* and its object add nothing except an indication that the agent did the action out of desire for the benefit of the object. But usage removed the distinction between them and made *makkanahu* and *makkana lahu* have one meaning, so the *lām* became extra, as Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said. The evidence for this is God's statement here: ﴿We established them in the land as We have not established you﴾. The two verbs here refer to one thing, since it is necessary that the meanings of the two verbs be equal, so that the superiority of the earlier generations' establishment over the establishment of those addressed becomes clear. Differences appear only in one thing. Also, because the earlier generations were more firmly established than those addressed, the verb with the *lām* of purpose should have been on their side, not on the side of those addressed. Here it has been reversed. By this explanation we reconcile al-Rāghib's statement that *makkanahu* and *makkana lahu* are equal in meaning, with al-Zamakhsharī's statement that *makkana lahu* means "made a place for him" and *makkanahu* means "established him." Al-Rāghib's view is more acceptable in Arabic. Lexicographical books have neglected to point out these two opinions. The use of *tamkīn* for firm establishment and strengthening, as metonymy or figurative metonymy, is because it implies strengthening. This usage has spread until it became like a plain term or like a literal meaning.

*Mā* is a relative pronoun whose meaning is the establishment. It stands in place of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: an establishment We did not give to you. So *mā* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) specifying the type. The intended meaning is: We established them with an establishment We did not give to you. That is, it was stronger than your establishment in the land.

The address in God's words ﴿to you﴾ is an *iltifāt* (shift of address) directed to those who disbelieved, because they were the ones established in the land at the time the verse was revealed. The Muslims at that time had no establishment. This *iltifāt* is the reverse of the *iltifāt* in God's words: ﴿until, when you were in the ships and they sailed with them﴾ [10:22]. The meaning is that the bygone nations of the extinct Arabs were stronger and more numerous than the Arabs addressed by the Qur'an, and greater than them in traces of civilisation and power. It is enough that the Arabs used to coin proverbs about great matters, saying they were "ʿĀdī" (of ʿĀd), or "Thamūdī" (of Thamud), or "Sabaʾī" (of Sheba). God said: ﴿and they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [30:9], that is, those before the present people cultivated the earth more than the people of this age have cultivated it.

*Samāʾ* (sky) is also one of the names of rain, as in the Muwatta' hadith, from the words of Zayd ibn Khālid: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in prayer following a *samāʾ*," meaning after a rain. This is the meaning intended here, because it fits His words "We sent down," unlike God's words: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky﴾ [23:18]. *Midrār* is an intensive form, like *mindār* (one who slaughters often for guests) and *midhkār* (one who often begets males), from "the she-camel gave milk" and "the udder gave milk" when its udder yielded milk freely. For this reason milk is called *darr*. Describing the rain as *midrār* is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), since the *midrār* is really the cloud. This form is used equally for masculine and feminine.

The intended meaning is the sending of rain at times when people need it, so that it did not fail them in its seasons. A consequence of this is the abundance of rivers and valleys, through the abundance of springs gushing forth from the plentiful water in the layers of the earth. The condition of most of the lands of the Arabs was in this fertility and abundance, as God knew, and as evidenced by the traces of their dams and dykes and the migration of peoples to them. Then circumstances changed through events from heaven, such as the drought that struck ʿĀd for years, or from the earth, so that most of it became barren, and its peoples perished, and they were scattered as "the hands of Sheba" (*ayādī Sabaʾ*).

The explanation of the meaning of ﴿rivers flowing beneath them﴾ has already been given in its parallel, which is God's words: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [9:89], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The *fāʾ* in God's words ﴿so We destroyed them﴾ is for sequence, coordinating with ﴿We established them﴾ and what follows. Since His words ﴿for their sins﴾ are attached to ﴿so We destroyed them﴾, this shows that the sequence of establishment and what accompanies it with destruction occurred after they sinned. The implied meaning is: "They sinned, so We destroyed them for their sins," or "They were ungrateful for the blessing, so We destroyed them." This includes an economy of ellipsis, like God's words: ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ [2:60], and the verse goes on, meaning: "He struck, and it gushed forth," and so on. You may also make the *fāʾ* explanatory, detailing the first "We destroyed," like God's words: ﴿How many a town We destroyed, and Our punishment came to it by night﴾ [7:4] in Surat al-Aʿraf.

[Page 140]

Destruction (*ihlāk*) means annihilation. It is a punishment for a nation, indicating God's wrath upon it, because the extinction of nations occurs only through what their own bad conduct brings upon them. This differs from the death of individuals, which is an inevitable end even if a person lived upright his whole life, because the constitution of living beings necessarily ends in death when the vital organs can no longer supply the body with the materials of life. Thus it is not punishment except as accompanied by circumstances of disgrace for the one destroyed.

The sins here are disbelief, denial of the messengers, and similar things, as indicated by the comparison with the condition of those about whom God said here: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [6:1], ﴿Yet you still doubt﴾ [6:2], ﴿and no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it﴾ [6:4], ﴿they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾ [6:5], and what He said after that: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a written scroll on paper﴾ [6:7], and the verse goes on.

His words: ﴿and We produced after them other generations﴾. *Inshāʾ* means bringing into existence in a novel way. God said: ﴿Indeed We produced them a [new] production﴾ [56:35]. What is meant is their production with those same qualities which the earlier generation had, namely establishment in the land and being provided with abundance. Thus they replaced the generations that perished, whether their production was in the dwellings of the people who were destroyed, as He produced Quraysh in the dwellings of Jurhum, or in other dwellings, as God produced Thamud after ʿAd in other dwellings. The purpose of this is an allusion to the polytheists: God will destroy them and produce after them a generation of Muslims in their dwellings. In it there is a warning of the conquest of Mecca and of all the lands of the Arabs at the hands of the Muslims. The meaning of *inshāʾ* is not birth and creation, because that is a continuous matter among humans that does not end, and it contains no admonition or threat to the arrogant polytheists. The word *qarn* is singular while the verb governing it is restricted by "after the generations" (plural), by way of an implied genitive construction: "We produced after each generation of those destroyed a different generation."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 7:

﴿And had We sent down to you a written scroll on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would surely have said, "This is nothing but evident magic."﴾

It is possible that the *waw* is conjunctive (*ʿaṭf*), with the conjoined element being the clause ﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4], etc., and what lies between them consists of clauses connected to the first clause by way of *iʿtirāḍ* (parenthetical insertion, a clause placed between parts of a sentence). When the first clause mentioned the signs in general terms, here he mentions the supposition of a sign that would be the clearest in indicating the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ): that God would send down to him a book from heaven in the form of the familiar books, which they would see with their eyes and touch with their hands. Even then, they would not have believed, and they would have claimed that this book was magic.

It is also possible that the *waw* is circumstantial (*ḥāl*), referring to the pronoun in *kadhdhabū* in His words: ﴿Indeed they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 5], meaning they denied that the Qur'an is from God and that it is a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger. They claimed that if it were from God, it would have descended in the form of a book from heaven. For they said: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32], and they said: ﴿Until you send down to us a book that we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. Thus His words ﴿Indeed they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 5] comprised, in summary form, their statements, so it was correct for the circumstantial clause to come from it. What lies between them is also a parenthetical insertion.

On the first reading, *kitāb* means "a written thing," whether a volume or a letter. On the second reading, the meaning of *kitāb* is a volume, i.e., like the Torah.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) without doubt, because every speech that descends from the Qur'an is directed to him, since he is the one who conveys it. The shift of address to him after speaking about people referred to by other pronouns does not require a justification for the shift. It is not necessary that the intended book be one that contains his confirmation; rather, the meaning is more general than that.

His words *fī qirṭās* ("on paper") are a description of *kitāb*, and the locative sense is metaphorical, from the locative relation of the name of a thing to the name of its part. *Qirṭās* with a kasra on the *qāf* is the eloquent form; a damma on the *qāf* has been reported, but it is weak. It is the name of the sheet on which one writes, and it may be of parchment (*riqq*), of papyrus (*bardī*), or of paper (*kāghad*). It is not restricted to what is made of paper; rather, what is made of parchment is also called *qirṭās*. Some people claimed that *qirṭās* is only said of what has been written on, and otherwise it is called *ṭirs*, but this is not correct. The Arabs also called the leather that is set up as a target for one learning archery a *qirṭās*, and they said *saddada al-qirṭās*, meaning he aimed his shot correctly. Al-Jawaliqi said: "The Arabs spoke this word in ancient times, and it is said that its origin is not Arabic." Al-Raghib did not mention this, nor did *Lisan al-ʿArab* or *al-Qamus*, but al-Khafaji affirmed it in *Shifa' al-Ghalil*, and he said: it is the white horse. Al-Alusi said: its origin is *kurrasa* (notebook). They did not mention from which language it is arabized; if it is arabized, perhaps it is arabized from Greek (*Rūmiyya*), and for this reason the name of the sheet of paper in the language of some people today is (*kārta*).

His words *falamasūhu* ("and they touched it") are a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on *nazzalnā* ("We sent down"). *Lams* (touching) is placing the hand on a thing in order to know its existence, or to know the description of its outer surface, such as smoothness or roughness, coldness or heat, or the like. So His words *bi-aydīhim* ("with their hands") are an emphasis on the meaning of touching, to remove the possibility that it is metaphorical for contemplation, as in His words: ﴿And we touched the heaven, and we found it filled with fierce guards and flaming meteors﴾ [al-Jinn: 8]. It is also to make explicit the extreme of their habitual arrogance and impudence in denial and rejection, and to prepare for His words ﴿those who disbelieved would surely have said, "This is nothing but evident magic"﴾, because the apparent magical phenomena are imaginings that cannot be touched.

His words ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ came in place of "they would have said," as He said "and they touched it," as an explicit mention in the place of a pronoun, for the purpose of recording that what drove them to this obstinacy is disbelief, because the relative construction indicates causation.

The meaning of ﴿This is nothing but evident magic﴾ is that they deceive themselves and deceive their people in order to conceal their arrogance and to push away what has become apparent of their defeat. This is the way of the defeated one, who has been refuted, to cling to false excuses.

*Mubīn* means clear and evident, derived from *abāna*, a synonym of *bāna*. The meaning of magic (*siḥr*) has already been discussed at His words ﴿They taught people magic﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 8–9:

﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved.﴾ ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered over for them what they cover over.﴾

This is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book﴾ [al-An'am: 7], because this is a report of their obstinacy and their stubbornness, while what precedes it is an explanation that attempting to remove their obstinacy is futile. Thus the supposition is of sending down a book to them from heaven in which the Prophet ﷺ is confirmed. This is a report of a demand from them for a sign by which they would confirm him.

In the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq it is related that this statement actually occurred, and that among those who said this were Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, 'Abdah ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; and Ubayy

صفحة ١٤٣
ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and those with them, who sent to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ask your Lord to send an angel with you who will confirm what you say and will debate us on your behalf."

So His saying, ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ means: why has an angel not been sent down to him whom we would see and who would inform us of his truthfulness, for that is what the obstinate one seeks. As for the descent of an angel whom they do not see, that is a matter that has occurred, and His saying in another verse explains it: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him, so that he might be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] in Surat al-Furqan.

The pronoun refers to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ [al-An'am: 25], even though some of them said it, because all of them are speakers of this statement and agree with it.

Law (lawla) here is for urging (tahdid) in the sense of "why not" (halla). Urging is used here for making them incapable (ta'jiz) according to their own belief. The pronoun in ("'alayhi") refers to the Prophet ﷺ. The referent of the pronoun is known from the context, for when a third-person pronoun appears in speech without a prior referent, and among the people there is one who is the subject of a report or a story that people talk about, it becomes determined that he is the intended referent of the pronoun. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when he asked his permission to kill Ibn Sayyad: "If he is he, you will not be given power over him; and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him." He means, from the first three third-person pronouns, al-Dajjal, because people were saying that Ibn Sayyad was al-Dajjal. Like the pronoun is the demonstrative when no noun is mentioned in the speech to which it points, as is reported in the hadith of Abu Dharr that he said to his brother when Muhammad ﷺ was sent: "Go and find out for us the knowledge of this man." And in the hadith about the questioning in the grave: "It is said to him (i.e., the one in the grave): what made you know about this man," meaning that this is what they said among themselves, or what they said to the one they had sent to the Prophet to ask God to send an angel with him. They also addressed him with it once more, as God related about them, when they said: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad!﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7] For "lawma" is a sister of "lawla" in conveying urging.

His saying: ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved﴾ means: if We had sent down an angel in the form they demanded, speaking to them, the matter would have been decided, that is, their affair; so the lam is a substitute for the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi) by the indication of the context. That is, the matter of their punishment with which he threatens them would have been decided.

صفحة ١٤٤
The meaning of "qudiya" is "completed," as His saying indicates: ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾. That is because no angels descend except those whom God has subjected to ordinary affairs, such as the guardian angels, the angel of death, and the angel who brings revelation; except angels who descend to support the messengers with victory over those who deny them, like the angels who descended to aid the believers at Badr. Angels do not descend among a people upon whom wrath has fallen except to bring punishment upon them, as the angels descended upon the people of Lot. So when the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet to show them an angel with him, they thought their proposal was a challenge; so God informed them that they had proposed a matter which, if they were answered in it, would be a cause of hastening their destruction, which He had given them respite until, out of mercy from Him.

Perhaps the wisdom of this is that God created the angels with firmness and anger for the truth without leniency, and made the angelic nature swift in executing recompense in accordance with deeds, as His saying indicates: ﴿And they intercede only for whom He is pleased with﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. Therefore God restrained them from connecting with any but the honored servants whose human souls resembled angelic souls; and for this reason God barred them from descending to the earth except in special circumstances, as He said of them: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and as He said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 8]. So if God had sent angels into the human midst, they would not have given respite to the people of error and corruption, but would have immediately carried out the punishment. Do you not see that the angels whom God sent to the people of Lot, when they met Lot, ﴿said, "O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a portion of the night"﴾ [Hud: 81]. And when Abraham argued with them about the people of Lot after they had given him good tidings and he had become at ease with them, ﴿they said, "O Abraham, turn away from this; the command of your Lord has come"﴾ [Hud: 75], which is the descent of the angels; for angels are not diverted to other than what they were sent for.

So the meaning of the verse is that what they proposed, if it had occurred, would have been of evil outcome for them in ways they do not perceive. The intended meaning is not that the reason for not sending down an angel is mercy toward them, but rather that God would not display His signs in response to the proposal of the misguided, since the Messenger ﷺ is not in the business of catering to people's desires as a craftsman or merchant does; and if the desires of some proposers were answered, every one to whom the call is presented would seek to have a sign appear to him according to his proposal, and the Messenger ﷺ would be wasting the period of guidance, and the people would crowd around him as they crowd around charlatans. That would contradict the sanctity of prophethood. Rather, signs come by pure choice from God, the Exalted, without request. God answered the disciples' proposal to send down a table (al-ma'idah) only because they were righteous people who desired nothing but good. Yet God informed them that answering them in that was for another wisdom, which would entail a benefit for them in ways they do not perceive, so they were worthy of thanking God's blessing upon them in what preserved them, had they been granted success. The further explanation of this will come at His saying: ﴿And they say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed God is able to send down a sign"﴾ [al-An'am: 37].

Some exegetes interpreted ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41] to mean their destruction from the terror of seeing the angel in his original form; but this is not necessary, because they did not ask for that. The realization of his angelic nature in their sight does not depend on seeing a form that breaks habit; rather, it is sufficient that they see him descending from heaven, for example, while he accompanies the Prophet, peace be upon him, when he calls them to Islam, as His later saying indicates: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man.﴾

His saying: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾. So it is a second answer to their proposal, containing an escalation in the answer. Their proposal entails dispensing with the sending of a human messenger, because if the call of a human messenger is not acceptable to them unless an angel accompanies him as a warner, as they said and as is related of them in other than this verse, then the coming of a human messenger to them would be useless, since they could dispense with him in favor of the angel who accompanies him. Moreover, they explicitly stated this necessary implication in what is related of them in other than this verse, His saying: ﴿They said, "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾ [Fussilat: 14]. So this second answer came suitable for refuting both proposals; but in the composition of its words it was observed what fits the necessary meaning of their speech, so the verb "ja'alna" was used, which implies making something else into something or substituting it with it. The pronoun in "ja'alnahu" refers to the Messenger to whom the pronoun of "lawla unzila 'alayhi malak" refers, meaning: and if We had dispensed with sending a messenger from the human kind and made the messenger to them an angel, it would have been necessary that We depict that angel in the form of a man, because there is no escape from his taking a shape, so that their eyes can encompass him and he is contained in a place. When he takes a form, he takes the form of a man so that they can endure seeing him and being addressed by him; and then his affair would become confused for them, just as the affair of Muhammad ﷺ became confused for them.

صفحة ١٤٦
So the clause ﴿and We would have covered over for them what they cover over﴾ is part of the proof and argument against them that sending an angel would be of no benefit.

Confusion (al-labs) is a mixing that occurs in attributes and meanings such that it becomes difficult to distinguish some of them from others. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it is transitive with the particle "'ala" because what is meant is a confusion that overpowers their minds.

The meaning: "and We would have confused their minds, so they would doubt that he is an angel and would reject him, since their habit was to seek extraordinary acts as evidence of truthfulness and to neglect exercising the reasoning by which the truthfulness of the truthful is known."

The "ma" in His saying ﴿what they cover over﴾ is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle stripped of temporal meaning, and the meaning is by way of comparison: "and We would have covered over for them the confusion that befell them when they said, 'Why has an angel not been sent down to him?'", that is, like their earlier confusion that befell them regarding the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

In the speech there is ihtibak, because both confusions are by God's decree, since He withheld success from them. The sense is: "and We would have confused them regarding the matter of the angel, so they would be confused in themselves regarding his matter, as We confused them regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, when they are confused in themselves regarding his matter." All this is viewed in terms of taking their proposal at its apparent state, that they intended to seek evidence; therefore they were answered in their speech by way of giving rein. Otherwise they only intended by their speech incapacitation and mockery, and for this reason He follows it with His saying: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked﴾ [al-An'am: 10], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 8–9:

﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved.﴾ ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered over for them what they cover over.﴾

This is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book﴾ [al-An'am: 7], because this is a report of their obstinacy and their stubbornness, while what precedes it is an explanation that attempting to remove their obstinacy is futile. Thus the supposition is of sending down a book to them from heaven in which the Prophet ﷺ is confirmed. This is a report of a demand from them for a sign by which they would confirm him.

In the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq it is related that this statement actually occurred, and that among those who said this were Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, 'Abdah ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; and Ubayy

صفحة ١٤٣
ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and those with them, who sent to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ask your Lord to send an angel with you who will confirm what you say and will debate us on your behalf."

So His saying, ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ means: why has an angel not been sent down to him whom we would see and who would inform us of his truthfulness, for that is what the obstinate one seeks. As for the descent of an angel whom they do not see, that is a matter that has occurred, and His saying in another verse explains it: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him, so that he might be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] in Surat al-Furqan.

The pronoun refers to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ [al-An'am: 25], even though some of them said it, because all of them are speakers of this statement and agree with it.

Law (lawla) here is for urging (tahdid) in the sense of "why not" (halla). Urging is used here for making them incapable (ta'jiz) according to their own belief. The pronoun in ("'alayhi") refers to the Prophet ﷺ. The referent of the pronoun is known from the context, for when a third-person pronoun appears in speech without a prior referent, and among the people there is one who is the subject of a report or a story that people talk about, it becomes determined that he is the intended referent of the pronoun. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when he asked his permission to kill Ibn Sayyad: "If he is he, you will not be given power over him; and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him." He means, from the first three third-person pronouns, al-Dajjal, because people were saying that Ibn Sayyad was al-Dajjal. Like the pronoun is the demonstrative when no noun is mentioned in the speech to which it points, as is reported in the hadith of Abu Dharr that he said to his brother when Muhammad ﷺ was sent: "Go and find out for us the knowledge of this man." And in the hadith about the questioning in the grave: "It is said to him (i.e., the one in the grave): what made you know about this man," meaning that this is what they said among themselves, or what they said to the one they had sent to the Prophet to ask God to send an angel with him. They also addressed him with it once more, as God related about them, when they said: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad!﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7] For "lawma" is a sister of "lawla" in conveying urging.

His saying: ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved﴾ means: if We had sent down an angel in the form they demanded, speaking to them, the matter would have been decided, that is, their affair; so the lam is a substitute for the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi) by the indication of the context. That is, the matter of their punishment with which he threatens them would have been decided.

صفحة ١٤٤
The meaning of "qudiya" is "completed," as His saying indicates: ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾. That is because no angels descend except those whom God has subjected to ordinary affairs, such as the guardian angels, the angel of death, and the angel who brings revelation; except angels who descend to support the messengers with victory over those who deny them, like the angels who descended to aid the believers at Badr. Angels do not descend among a people upon whom wrath has fallen except to bring punishment upon them, as the angels descended upon the people of Lot. So when the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet to show them an angel with him, they thought their proposal was a challenge; so God informed them that they had proposed a matter which, if they were answered in it, would be a cause of hastening their destruction, which He had given them respite until, out of mercy from Him.

Perhaps the wisdom of this is that God created the angels with firmness and anger for the truth without leniency, and made the angelic nature swift in executing recompense in accordance with deeds, as His saying indicates: ﴿And they intercede only for whom He is pleased with﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. Therefore God restrained them from connecting with any but the honored servants whose human souls resembled angelic souls; and for this reason God barred them from descending to the earth except in special circumstances, as He said of them: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and as He said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 8]. So if God had sent angels into the human midst, they would not have given respite to the people of error and corruption, but would have immediately carried out the punishment. Do you not see that the angels whom God sent to the people of Lot, when they met Lot, ﴿said, "O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a portion of the night"﴾ [Hud: 81]. And when Abraham argued with them about the people of Lot after they had given him good tidings and he had become at ease with them, ﴿they said, "O Abraham, turn away from this; the command of your Lord has come"﴾ [Hud: 75], which is the descent of the angels; for angels are not diverted to other than what they were sent for.

So the meaning of the verse is that what they proposed, if it had occurred, would have been of evil outcome for them in ways they do not perceive. The intended meaning is not that the reason for not sending down an angel is mercy toward them, but rather that God would not display His signs in response to the proposal of the misguided, since the Messenger ﷺ is not in the business of catering to people's desires as a craftsman or merchant does; and if the desires of some proposers were answered, every one to whom the call is presented would seek to have a sign appear to him according to his proposal, and the Messenger ﷺ would be wasting the period of guidance, and the people would crowd around him as they crowd around charlatans. That would contradict the sanctity of prophethood. Rather, signs come by pure choice from God, the Exalted, without request. God answered the disciples' proposal to send down a table (al-ma'idah) only because they were righteous people who desired nothing but good. Yet God informed them that answering them in that was for another wisdom, which would entail a benefit for them in ways they do not perceive, so they were worthy of thanking God's blessing upon them in what preserved them, had they been granted success. The further explanation of this will come at His saying: ﴿And they say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed God is able to send down a sign"﴾ [al-An'am: 37].

Some exegetes interpreted ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41] to mean their destruction from the terror of seeing the angel in his original form; but this is not necessary, because they did not ask for that. The realization of his angelic nature in their sight does not depend on seeing a form that breaks habit; rather, it is sufficient that they see him descending from heaven, for example, while he accompanies the Prophet, peace be upon him, when he calls them to Islam, as His later saying indicates: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man.﴾

His saying: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾. So it is a second answer to their proposal, containing an escalation in the answer. Their proposal entails dispensing with the sending of a human messenger, because if the call of a human messenger is not acceptable to them unless an angel accompanies him as a warner, as they said and as is related of them in other than this verse, then the coming of a human messenger to them would be useless, since they could dispense with him in favor of the angel who accompanies him. Moreover, they explicitly stated this necessary implication in what is related of them in other than this verse, His saying: ﴿They said, "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾ [Fussilat: 14]. So this second answer came suitable for refuting both proposals; but in the composition of its words it was observed what fits the necessary meaning of their speech, so the verb "ja'alna" was used, which implies making something else into something or substituting it with it. The pronoun in "ja'alnahu" refers to the Messenger to whom the pronoun of "lawla unzila 'alayhi malak" refers, meaning: and if We had dispensed with sending a messenger from the human kind and made the messenger to them an angel, it would have been necessary that We depict that angel in the form of a man, because there is no escape from his taking a shape, so that their eyes can encompass him and he is contained in a place. When he takes a form, he takes the form of a man so that they can endure seeing him and being addressed by him; and then his affair would become confused for them, just as the affair of Muhammad ﷺ became confused for them.

صفحة ١٤٦
So the clause ﴿and We would have covered over for them what they cover over﴾ is part of the proof and argument against them that sending an angel would be of no benefit.

Confusion (al-labs) is a mixing that occurs in attributes and meanings such that it becomes difficult to distinguish some of them from others. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it is transitive with the particle "'ala" because what is meant is a confusion that overpowers their minds.

The meaning: "and We would have confused their minds, so they would doubt that he is an angel and would reject him, since their habit was to seek extraordinary acts as evidence of truthfulness and to neglect exercising the reasoning by which the truthfulness of the truthful is known."

The "ma" in His saying ﴿what they cover over﴾ is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle stripped of temporal meaning, and the meaning is by way of comparison: "and We would have covered over for them the confusion that befell them when they said, 'Why has an angel not been sent down to him?'", that is, like their earlier confusion that befell them regarding the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

In the speech there is ihtibak, because both confusions are by God's decree, since He withheld success from them. The sense is: "and We would have confused them regarding the matter of the angel, so they would be confused in themselves regarding his matter, as We confused them regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, when they are confused in themselves regarding his matter." All this is viewed in terms of taking their proposal at its apparent state, that they intended to seek evidence; therefore they were answered in their speech by way of giving rein. Otherwise they only intended by their speech incapacitation and mockery, and for this reason He follows it with His saying: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked﴾ [al-An'am: 10], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 10:

﴿And certainly, messengers before you were mocked, but those who mocked them were encompassed by what they used to mock at.﴾

This is coordinated with the statement ﴿And they say: Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8], to show the variety of their obstinacy and defiance, their firmness in polytheism and their persistence in it. They leave no means of repelling people from accepting the call of Islam without employing it. The reason for coordinating this statement with their saying ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8] is

page 147
that in saying that they intended both to challenge (ta'jiz) and to mock, because they said it only out of certainty on their part that such would not happen. So the reply begins by refuting the apparent meaning of their statement with His saying ﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. Then He followed it with a threat against them for what they intended of mockery. The purpose, together with that, is to threaten them that the punishment will surely encompass them, and that this is the custom of God toward every nation that mocked a messenger sent to it.

So His saying ﴿And certainly, messengers before you were mocked﴾ indicates an omitted sentence by way of brevity; its estimated form is: "And they mocked you, and certainly nations mocked messengers before you," because His saying ﴿before you﴾ implies that he too was mocked; otherwise there would be no benefit in describing the messengers as being before him, since that is known. He omitted the agent of the mocking and made the verb passive, because the purpose here is the consequence of the mocking, not identifying the mockers.

The lam is for oath, and (qad) is for emphasis; both indicate the emphasis of the report. What is intended by stressing it is in view of what branches from it, namely His saying ﴿so those who mocked were encompassed﴾ etc., because the situation of the polytheists is that of one who hesitates over whether the cause of the destruction of earlier nations was mockery of the messengers. Had it not been for their hesitation in this, they would have taken precaution for themselves with the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, who came to them, and they would have looked into the evidences of his truthfulness, and not turned away, in order to clear themselves of an expected punishment; or they were placed in the position of one who hesitates, if they knew that, by not acting according to what their knowledge required. Their mockery of him takes many forms, among them their saying "Why has not an angel been sent down to him?"

The meaning of mockery (istihza') was explained at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is synonymous with sukhriyya (ridicule) in the speech of the lexicographers. He mentioned istuhzi'a first because it is more well known; when it was repeated he expressed it with sakhiru, and when it was repeated a third time he returned to the verb yastahziu, because it is lighter than (yaskharun). This is among the wondrous eloquence of the Qur'an, its miraculous character.

Sakhiru means hazi'u, and it takes its object with (min). It was said: it does not take any other preposition. And it was said: it takes the ba'. The same disagreement applies to the transitivity of hazi'a and istahza'a. The more correct view is that both verbs take the particles min and ba', and that the more common usage for hazi'a is with ba', and for sakhira is with min. The root sakhara indicates that the agent took the object as subjected, disposing of it as he wishes without restraint, because of the close relation of the root sakhira, a lightened form of the root of taskhir, i.e. subjugation; so it is as if he turned him away from his right of inherent dignity and took from him a source of ridicule for himself.

page 148
Scholars of the language differed over the meaning of the verb haqa. Al-Zajjaj said: it means ahata (to encompass), and al-Zamakhshari followed him; al-Farra' explained it as "returned upon him" ('ada 'alayhi). Al-Raghib said: its root is haqqa, meaning wajaba (to be due), then one of the two doubled letters was replaced by a weak letter for lightness, just as they said tazanna becoming tazanna... and as they said taqadda al-bazi, meaning taqadqada. The more evident view is that of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj.

The verb of encompassing was chosen to indicate the firm settling of that upon them and that none of them escapes it.

The relative pronoun was used in His saying ﴿those who mocked﴾ and not "the mockers," to hint at the cause of the ruling, which is His saying: "so there encompassed."

The pronoun "from them" is connected to "mocked," and the pronominal suffix refers to the messengers, to reinforce that the punishment is on account of them, elevating their status.

The "ma" in His saying ﴿what they used to mock at﴾ is a relative pronoun. The ba' in "bihi" is for transitivity of the verb of mocking. The presence of the ba' prevents making "ma" non-relative. This is a matter over which writers have dwelt at length.

What is meant by ﴿what they used to mock at﴾ is what the messengers warned them of, of evil consequence and the descent of punishment upon them.
