Thereby another benefit is achieved: the mockers used to mock the messengers, especially for what they warned them of, of the descent of punishment if they persisted in not believing what they brought. So their mockery of what they were warned of makes what they were warned of like the person mocked, if we take the ba' as transitive; or their mockery of the messengers because of what they warned them of, if the ba' is taken as causal.

The placement of the prepositional phrase before the verb is for the sake of maintaining the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 11:

﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of those who denied."﴾

This sentence stands in the same relation to the sentence before it as an elaboration (bayan) stands to what it elaborates upon, and for that reason it is disconnected from it (fusilat). The sentence before it informs us that those who mocked the Messengers have been overtaken by the consequences of their mockery, and this sentence urges them to look upon the abodes of those mockers. The opening of this sentence with an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) does not contradict its being an elaboration, because he was addressed to say that elaboration. So the intended meaning lies in what follows "say".

Its opening with the command to "say" is because it comes as a response within a dialogue to their words: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. This is a series of replies and answers to their reported statement mentioned just before, since it contains their determination upon polytheism and their denial of the Message. It was resolvable into many doubts which were intended to be refuted and disproved, so all these replies were opened with the word "say" ten times.

As for "thumma" (then), it indicates a graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usual function in conjoining sentences, since observing the end of the deniers is the purpose of travelling, so it is something ascended to after the command to travel. And because this observation requires reflection and tracing of traces, it is more important than the travel.

The word "nazar" (observing) may be sighted (basari) or of the heart (qalbi), and on both possibilities the interrogative "kayfa" has suspended its object or objects from taking effect. And "kayfa" is the predicate of "kana" (was), placed before it obligatorily.

"Al-'aqibah" is the last part of a thing, its outcome, and what follows it of its consequences. It is said: 'aqibah and 'uqba, and it is a noun like al-'afiyah and al-khatimah.

They were described as "the deniers" rather than "the mockers" to indicate that denial and mockery were two of their traits, and that either one of these two traits is sufficient for deserving that consequence, since in the preceding verse He said: ﴿So there befell those who mocked them what they used to mock at,﴾ and in this verse He said: ﴿how was the end of the deniers.﴾

This is a comprehensive reply to refute their misguidance, which follows the same course as the misguidance of their counterparts among the earlier deniing nations.

[p. 150]

The clause ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ is a repetition in a context of argumentation (istidlal). This argument includes a rhetorical question of affirmation (istifham taqriri), and affirmation is one of the requirements of repetition. For this reason the clause is not joined with a conjunction. It is also possible to take the opening of this statement as an imperative, that he should say it with the intention of drawing attention to what follows the verb of saying, in the manner that we will explain at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you﴾ [Al-An'am: 40] in this surah. The interrogative is used figuratively for affirmation. The affirmation here is intended in its implied meaning (lazim ma'nahu), namely the rebuke (tabkit) of the polytheists and compelling them to acknowledge what necessarily leads to the invalidation of their belief in association (shirk). Thus it is used in its figurative meaning (kinaya) together with its literal meaning, and the intended meaning is the figurative one.

Because it is intended to compel acknowledgment, the answer to it is one that the questioner wants, namely the acknowledgment of the one questioned, which is established and unavoidable, since there is no way to deny it or to evade it. Therefore the questioner did not wait for their answer, but anticipated the answer himself by saying ﴿To God﴾, as a rebuke to them, because the speech is directed toward conveying the proof, with an implied dialogue within it, though it is not an actual dialogue. This is a stylistic feature of speech issuing from a single speaker. So these people, who are presumed to be compelled to answer, whether they are fair and acknowledge the correctness of the answer, or they deny and obstinately refuse, the aim of crushing them with the proof has been achieved. This is a method followed in the Qur'an: sometimes no answer from them is mentioned, as here, and as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: God﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 16], and His saying: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ [Al-An'am: 91] up to His saying: ﴿Say: God﴾ [Al-An'am: 91]. And sometimes it mentions what they will answer after mentioning the question, attributing to them that they answer with it, and then moves on to what follows from it of reproach or the like, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 84] ﴿They will say: To God. Say: Will you not then remember?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 85] up to His saying: ﴿Say: Then how are you deluded?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 89].

It begins with the invalidation of their greatest error, which is the error of associating partners with God. Joined to it is the error of their denial of resurrection, which the surah began with, after it had moved from that to the warning arising from their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ). For this reason, when the evidence of God's oneness previously mentioned indicated, explicitly, the creation of the heavens and the earth and their conditions, and implicitly indicated the servitude of the existing things they encompass, He mentioned that servitude explicitly in this verse, saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God.﴾

[p. 151]

His saying "To God" is the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ and so on. The subject is presumed to be postponed after the predicate, in the pattern of the question, because the intended purpose is to convey restriction (hasr).

The lam in His saying "To God" is the lam of ownership (milk). It indicates that people are servants of God alone and not of anyone else, and it implies that the servant will inevitably return to his owner. In this there is an affirmation of the earlier proof of resurrection, which is based on establishing servitude by the right of creation. There is no cause for servitude more worthy and greater than creatorship. This argument is followed by the warning of His anger against whoever associates others with Him.

This is an argument against the polytheists that someone other than God is not worthy of divinity, because what is other than God does not own what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, since ownership of these belongs to the Creator of these. It is also a preparation for His saying after it: ﴿that He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾, because the owner of things does not neglect to call them to account.

The clause ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and it is part of what was said (al-maqul) that the Messenger was commanded to say.

In this parenthetical insertion there are several meanings. The first is that since what follows it suggests a warning of a threat, He first mentioned to them that He is merciful to His servants, perhaps they will repent and turn away from their obstinacy, in the manner of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, then indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Al-An'am: 54]. And associating partners with God is a greater evil and more deeply tainted with ignorance.

The second is that the statement that ﴿to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 284] raises the question of a questioner about the non-hastening of their punishment for their association, since they are His possession. The disbeliever says: If what you say were true, He would have hastened punishment for us, and the believer longs for the delay of their punishment. So His saying ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ was an answer to both groups, that it is a bestowal of mercy. Of it there is a complete mercy, and this is His mercy to His righteous servants, and of it there is a temporary mercy, which is the mercy of respite and giving time to the disobedient and the astray.

The third is that what is in His saying ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ is a preparation for what is in the clause ﴿that He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection, there is no doubt in it﴾ [An-Nisa': 87] of threat and promise.

The mercy of God was mentioned as an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to good tidings for the believers and a threat to the polytheists.

[p. 152]

The fourth is that it contains an allusion (ima') that God has saved the community of the Muhammadan call from the punishment of total annihilation (isti'sal) by which He punished the nations that denied their messengers before them. This is by the blessing of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), since He made him a mercy to the worlds in all his conditions, by the ruling of the Exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 107]. And since he desired to increase his followers, He did not decree a swift judgment against his deniers, but gave them respite and gave them time, so that from among them there would come forth those who believe in him, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) hoped. For this reason, when they said: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Anfal: 32], God the Exalted said: ﴿But God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [Al-Anfal: 33]. What the Messenger of God hoped for was fulfilled, and those among the polytheists who remained did not delay in believing in God and His Messenger after the conquest of Mecca, and they entered the religion of God in multitudes. God then strengthened His religion and His Messenger through them, and they spread the word of Islam throughout the horizons of the earth. Since God the Exalted had decreed that this religion should be the seal of religions, it was wise to give respite to those who obstinately opposed it and denied it, because if God had annihilated them at the first appearance of the religion, it would have destroyed whoever Mecca contained, both polytheist and Muslim, and then they would be resurrected according to their intentions, as it occurred in the hadith: "When Umm Salamah said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): Shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us? He said: Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread." Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions. So if that had occurred at the time when Islam appeared, this religion would have been eliminated, and the purpose of making it the seal of religions would not have been achieved. And "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sought refuge when there was revealed to him: ﴿Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet﴾ [Al-An'am: 65], and he said: I seek refuge in the splendours of Your noble Face."

The meaning of "prescribed" (katab) is that His will has been directed, by making His mercy, with which He is attributed in His essence, connected in a general and uniform manner to created beings, even though it is specific with regard to times and directions. Since this is uniform, His will has been likened to obligation, and the verb "prescribed," which is literally used for obligation, has been borrowed for it, and the indication is the station of divinity. Or it is taken to mean that He prescribed it upon Himself, because no one obliges himself to something except by choice, since otherwise another would oblige him. The intended meaning is that this does not fail, like a decreed obligatory matter. For when they wanted to confirm a promise or a covenant, they would write it down, as al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

"Remember the alliance of the one of al-Majaz, and what was put forward in it of covenants and guarantors,
out of fear of oppression and of injustice, and can desires overturn what is written in the scrolls?"

[p. 153]

So "mercy" here is a verbal noun, meaning He prescribed for Himself that He should show mercy, and the intended meaning is not the attribute, i.e., that He prescribed for Himself the attribute of mercy, that is, being merciful, because mercy is an essential attribute of God the Exalted, necessary for Him. The necessary rational thing is not the object of will, except if we take "prescribed" as used in another figurative sense, namely likening the essential obligation to a fixed and imposed command, while the indication remains the same. Nonetheless, the first meaning is more apparent in terms of favour and of the intended purpose of the mercy's inclusion of the servants who turn away from their due gratitude and the polytheists who associate others with Him in His dominion.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God the Exalted had finished the creation, He wrote a book which He placed with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy has preceded My wrath."

The clause ﴿that He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾ stands in the position of the conclusion of the argument and the effect of the cause. For when their deities' fitness for divinity was invalidated and the oneness of God with divinity was made pure, their claim that resurrection is impossible on the pretext of the scattering of the parts of bodies or their annihilation was also invalidated.

The oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) together convey the certainty of the threat. The meaning of "gathering" is the complete collection of the scattered parts of all people, individuals and dispersed portions. Its construction with "to" (ila) is because it implies the sense of driving (suq). The discussion of its counterpart has already been given at His saying the Exalted: ﴿God, there is no god but He; He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection, there is no doubt in it﴾ [An-Nisa': 87] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The pronoun of address in His saying "will gather you" is intended to refer specifically to the polytheists who were confronted with the proof, since they are the direct target of this statement from its beginning. Thus it is a warning to them, a threat, and an answer to the least that may be suspected as an objection arising from His saying ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾, as has already been explained.

The clause ﴿Those who have lost their souls, so they do not believe﴾: In my view, the most apparent is that it is consequent upon the clause ﴿that He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾, and that the fa' in His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is for consequence and causation. The original structure is: "So you do not believe, because you have lost your souls on the Day of Resurrection." He turned from the pronoun to the relative construction in order to convey, through the relative clause, that they lost their souls because of their non-belief.

[p. 154]

And ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: "You are those who have lost your souls, so they do not believe." The arrangement of the speech in this way is more effective in making them hear it, and with this estimate one is spared the question raised by al-Kashshaf about the correctness of the consequence of non-belief from the loss of their souls, while in fact the matter is the reverse. It has also been said that ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is its predicate, and it is joined by fa' because the relative pronoun contains the sense of a conditional, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you﴾ [An-Nisa': 15]. The relative has taken on the sense of a condition so as to convey that it includes everyone who is characterized by the content of the relative clause, and it conveys that the attachment of the content of the predicate clause, which occupies the position of the apodosis, is conditional upon the realization of the content of the relative clause, which occupies the position of the protasis. Thus it conveys that this connection and causation is continuous throughout all future times in which the meaning of the relative clause is realized. In this clause there is, in terms of rhetorical features, what is not found in the like of any speech other than the inimitable Word.

The meaning of "they have lost their souls" (﴿خَسِرُوا أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾) is that they wasted them, as a merchant wastes his capital. Thus "loss" (al-khusran) is used figuratively for the squandering of that which by nature should be a means of gain. So the meaning of ﴿they have lost their souls﴾ is that they lost the benefit of using what people benefit from in themselves, namely the intellect (al-'aql) and reflection (al-tafakkur), for it is the movement of the soul among intelligible things in order to know the realities of matters. That is because, when they turned away from reflecting on the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), they wasted from themselves the most beneficial means of success in this world and the next. This was the cause of their not believing in God, the Messenger, and the Last Day. Thus non-belief is the consequence of their being deprived of the benefit of the most excellent of benefits. Another loss follows from non-belief, namely the loss of success in this world through safety from punishment, and in the Hereafter through deliverance from the Fire. This is called loss, but it is not called the loss of souls. The Exalted's saying indicates both losses: ﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed from them﴾ [Hud: 21]. Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers (al-akhsarun).

[Page 155]

It is a clause conjoined (*ma'tufah*) to "to Allah" in His saying ﴿Say: To Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 12], which is in the sense of a clause. That is: whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and to Him belongs whatever rests (*sakana*).

*Sukun* (rest, stillness) is the settling of a body in a place, that is, a space it does not move from for a period. It is the opposite of motion, and it is one of the causes of concealment, because the one who hides remains still and does not spread out. In my view, the best reading here is that it is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for concealment, while the literal meaning is also intended. The reason it is a *kinaya* is that the speech is directed at reminding the listeners of Allah's knowledge, that nothing of their deeds is hidden from Him, and that He will call them to account for them on the Day when He gathers them until the Day of Resurrection. It is like His saying: ﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], up to His saying: ﴿and one who hides by night﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10]. So what rests by night and day is part of what is in the heavens and the earth. When He informed them that He owns what is in the heavens and the earth, He followed it with the information that He owns what rests of that, because it is such that people may overlook it among what is included in the heavens and the earth. For it is customary among people, when they speak of things, to mean the familiar and well-known things. This is the mention of the specific after the general, to establish the generality of Allah's dominion, that His dominion encompasses both the apparent and the hidden. In this there is an invitation to direct rational reflection toward hidden existents, and to what their concealment indicates of the breadth of power and the workings of divine wisdom.

*Fi* is for temporal containment (*zarfiyyah zamaniyyah*), and it is a stable adverbial (*zarf mustaqarr*), because the verb *sukun* does not transitively reach time in the way that the loose adverbial (*zarf laghw*) does, as it reaches place. This would be the case if it meant *halla wa-istaqarra* (alighted and settled), which does not suit interpreting the verse in that way. The speech is a preparation for the breadth of knowledge, because it is the nature of an owner to know what he owns. The night is singled out for mention because the one who rests at that time becomes more hidden, as in His saying: ﴿nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. He conjoined the day to it in order to increase comprehensiveness, because the night, being the place where concealment is expected, might lead one to think that the Knower intends to know the resting things in it with particular concern, and does not intend to know the resting things in the day. So He mentioned the day to establish complete encompassing of the known things.

Fronting the prepositional phrase (*lahu*) indicates restriction (*hasr*), restricting the resting things to being His and not to anyone else's. That is, their complete ownership belongs to Him, as was stated previously in His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 12].

His saying ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ comes as the conclusion of the premise, because the purpose of informing that Allah owns the resting things is to prepare for establishing the generality of His knowledge. Otherwise, ownership of moving, active things is stronger than ownership of things that show no motion. Thus the fitting effect of His saying ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ immediately after this becomes evident.

*Al-Sami'* (the All-Hearing) is the All-Knowing, the Great, with regard to heard things or sensed things. *Al-'Alim* (the All-Knowing) is the Intensely Knowing, the Knower of every known thing.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Surah 6, verse 14:**

﴿Say: Shall I take as a protector other than God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed?﴾

This is another resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence that follows on from a preceding one) arising from the statement ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-Anʿām: 12].

The command "say" is repeated to draw attention to what is being said, because its purpose differs from the purpose for which the first "say" was commanded. When it was established by the previous statement that everything in the heavens and the earth is in servitude to God, and that the final return of all of it is to Him, the discourse moved on to establishing the obligation of worshipping Him alone, since that is a necessary consequence of His being the owner of everything that the heavens and the earth contain. This statement therefore proceeds by way of *taʿrīḍ* (indirect allusion), since the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to disavow worshipping anyone other than God. The intended meaning is a rebuke of those who worshipped other than Him and took them as protectors, in the way that a speaker in the presence of a stubborn disputant may say, "I do not deny the truth," the context making clear that the Messenger ﷺ would never do such a thing. How could he, when they knew that he had called them to the Oneness of God from the very beginning of his mission? This surah was revealed only many years after the mission began, as we have deduced from what preceded in the opening of the surah.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from some exegetes that this statement was commanded to the Messenger ﷺ so that he might answer the polytheists who called him to worship their idols. That is, it is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Is it other than God that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64]. By my life, the style of the speech does indicate this, although Ibn ʿAṭiyya said that the apparent meaning of the verse does not include it. How could it not, when the *istiʾnāf* must have a purpose (*nukta*, a subtle point)?

The interrogative is for denial. He placed the first object of *attakhidh* (take) before the verb and its subject so that it would immediately follow the interrogative particle, because it is precisely this that is the object of denial, not the mere act of taking a protector. The rule for the interrogative hamza, in all its uses, is that it is followed by the part of the sentence about which the question is asked, as here with the denied element. So the fronting is for emphasis on it. This is one of the instances of emphasis that ʿAbd al-Qāhir said must have a stated reason. It does not signify restriction in such a case, since it is evident that the motive for the fronting is to specify what the interrogation is about, and so it need not be for any other purpose. Therefore, whoever makes the fronting here signify restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), meaning that the denial of taking a protector is confined to taking other than God, as some commentators on the *Kashshāf* inclined to, has burdened the text with what usage and taste do not support. The *Kashshāf* itself is free of this. Rather, the truth is that the fronting here serves only to give importance to what is fronted, so that it comes directly after the interrogative particle, and thus it is known that the locus of denial is the taking of other than God as a protector. As for anything beyond that, the speaker does not intend it. Perhaps what led them to this view is that the object in this verse and its parallels, such as ﴿Is it other than God that you order me to worship?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64] and ﴿Is it other than God that you call upon?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 40], is the word *ghayr* (other than) when attached to the Name of Majesty (God), and it is general to everything other than God. Thus God is implicitly contained within the object. So the denial of taking God as a protector is implied, because denying the taking of anyone other than Him as a protector entails not denying the taking of God as a protector, since once the taking of other than God is denied, only the taking of God remains. Thus this construction carries the meaning of restriction and leads to it, but it does not explicitly signify restriction, nor does it convey what explicit restriction (*qaṣr idāfī*) conveys, namely reversing a belief, specifying the individual, or determining the choice. Do you not see that if the object were something other than the word *ghayr*, restriction could not be considered? For example, if you said, "Do you take Zayd as a friend?", it would convey only the denial of taking Zayd as a friend, without any reference to taking anyone else. That is because you see him as unfit for friendship, so there is no difference between this and your saying, "Do you take Zayd as a friend?" except that you intended the denial to be directed at the one taking, not at the act of taking, for emphasis on him. The difference between the two is subtle, so apply your mind carefully to it.

Furthermore, if the polytheists had asked the Prophet ﷺ to take their idols as protectors, the fronting of the object would carry a second emphatic purpose, namely that it is a response to a statement which is itself the intended object of the discourse, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Is it other than God that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], and His words: ﴿They said: O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 138] up to His words: ﴿He said: Shall I seek for you a god other than God?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 140]. The author of the *Kashshāf*, in commenting on His words ﴿Shall I seek a lord other than God?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 164], which comes later at the end of the surah, indicated that the fronting of ﴿other than God﴾ [al-Anʿām: 164] before "I seek" is because it is a response to their call to him to worship their gods. Al-Ṭībī said: "Because every fronting is either for emphasis or in response to a denial."

*Al-walī* (the protector) is the helper who manages affairs, so it contains the meanings of knowledge and power. One says *tawallā fulānan*, meaning he took him as a helper. An ally is called a *walī* because the purpose of an alliance is support. Since the god is the one to whom the worshipper returns, he is called *walī* for this reason. Among the Names of God, the Exalted, is *al-Walī* (the Protector).

*Al-fāṭir* (the Originator) means the one who innovates and creates. Its root is from *al-faṭr*, which is splitting. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "I did not know the meaning of *al-fāṭir* until two Bedouins came to me disputing about a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who *faṭartuhā*' (I originated it, i.e. dug it)." The attachment of this attribute to the Name of Majesty, rather than another attribute, is an argument that no one else deserves to be taken as a protector. It refers back to His words at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made darknesses and light; yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-Anʿām: 1]. The statement before it, ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-Anʿām: 12], does not make this redundant, because that was an argument against them by means of servitude to God, whereas this is an argument by means of their dependence on God for the means of their survival until a term.

His words ﴿while He feeds﴾ form a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*), meaning: He gives people what they eat from what He brings forth for them from the earth: grains, fruits, pasture, and game. This is an argument against the polytheists based on something they already accept, because they acknowledge that the Provider is God, and that He is the Creator of created things; they only made the other gods partners in deserving worship. The Qurʾān often argues against the polytheists in this manner, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 63] ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the causer of growth?﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 64].

As for His words ﴿and is not fed﴾, with the *yāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma* and the *ʿayn* with a *fatḥa* (*yuṭʿam*, passive), this is a completing addition that signifies absolute self-sufficiency, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿I do not want them to feed Me﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 57]. It has no bearing on the argument, since the gods of the Arabs were not things that people fed with food. It is possible, however, that it is meant as an allusion to them regarding what they offer to their idols of sacrifices and the blood they pour over them, since their act does not escape the belief that the idols are gratified by this.

* * *

﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists.﴾

This is a repeated resumptive sentence, of the same form as the one before it. The source of both resumptions is the same, but their purposes differ. What came before revolves around establishing, by the proof of reason, the nullity of polytheism, whereas this is an argument by the proof of revelation, in which there is a command to follow the religion of Islam and what is built upon the name Islam, namely directing the face toward God. As He said in another verse: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 20]. So this is a refutation of their criticism of the religion brought by the one called by the name Islam, whose emblem is the declaration of Oneness, which nullifies association.

The verb *ummirtu* (I have been commanded) is in the passive, because the one who issues this command is known from the repeated attribution of revelation to God.

The meaning of ﴿the first of those who submit﴾ is that he is the first to be characterised by the submission that God sent him with. This is the specific Islam brought by the Qurʾān, which is an addition to what the prophets before him believed, through its clarity of exposition and its tolerance. It does not conflict with the fact that some prophets were described as "Muslims," as in the words of the Exalted, relating of Abraham and Jacob: ﴿O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqara: 132]. This was explained earlier when that verse was mentioned in Surah al-Baqara.

It is also possible that the meaning is "the first of those who submitted among those who were called to Islam."

It is also possible that "the first" is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the strongest and most steadfast in Islam, because the first in every deed is the most eager for it and the most attached to it. Priority thus implies eagerness and strength in the deed, as God related of Moses: ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 143]. Moses' being the first of them is known, and what he meant was: "I am now, after the swoon, the strongest of people in faith." In a ḥadīth: "We are the last and the first on the Day of Resurrection." Something of this was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 41] in Surah al-Baqara.

The purpose of all this, in all its aspects, is to make the polytheists despair of his returning to their religion. For they may have thought, whenever they saw him showing them mercy and gentleness of speech, that he might return to their religion, and said that it is the religion of his fathers.

His words ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ are coordinated with "say," meaning: say this to them so that they may despair. The statement is a prohibition from God to His Messenger, intended to emphasise the command to submit, because a command to do something implies a prohibition of its opposite. Mentioning the prohibition of the opposite after the command is therefore an emphasis on it, and this emphasis is so that the root of polytheism may be cut from this religion.

The *min* here is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*), so the meaning of "among the polytheists" is "from the body of those who associate partners." It is also possible that the prohibition is against affiliation with the polytheists, meaning that this is a command to disavow them. In that case *min* is "connective" (*ittiṣāliyya*, indicating connection or belonging), and "the polytheists" is used in its nominal sense (*laqabī*), that is, those who became known by this name. The sense is: let nothing in you have any connection with the polytheists, as in the verse of al-Nābigha:

*For I am not of you, and you are not of me.*

The despair in this sense is stronger and more forceful.

From this verse one may derive an argument for the position transmitted from al-Ashʿarī: that belief in God alone is not obligatory by the proof of reason, but accountability for it depends on the sending of a Messenger. This is because God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to deny that he would take anyone other than God as a protector, since He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. Then He commanded him to say ﴿Indeed I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾, and then commanded him with what indicates accountability, in His words ﴿Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a terrible day﴾ [al-Anʿām: 15], up to His words ﴿on that day, whoever is spared it, He has shown him mercy﴾ [al-Anʿām: 16].

This is a continuation of the commentary on the preceding verses. It repeats what came before and develops the shared theme: whoever associates partners with God is warned of punishment, and whoever abandons that is promised mercy. The verse "Shall I take other than God as a protector?" (al-An'am 6:14) is a rejection of shirk by rational proof.

His saying, "Say: Indeed I was commanded to be the first of those who submit" (al-An'am 6:14), is a rejection of shirk in compliance with God's command and majesty.

His saying here, "Say: Indeed I fear..." is an avoidance of shirk out of fear of punishment and hope for mercy. These verses come in an order that corresponds to their order in reality.

Page 161

From His saying, "if I disobey my Lord," it is understood that the One who commanded him to be the first to submit and who forbade him from being among the polytheists is God, exalted is He.

In the shift from the Name of Majesty (Allah) to "my Lord," there is an allusion that disobeying Him is an ugly matter, since He is his Lord, so how could he disobey Him?

The punishment is attributed to "a great day" to convey its terror, because it is customary among the Arabs to refer to a day as the day of victory of one party and the defeat of another among combatants. The day then becomes a calamity for the defeated, as killing and capture become widespread among them and the vanquished suffer the worst torment. Mentioning a day thus stirs up familiar fears in the imagination. This is why God, exalted is He, said: "So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a great day" (al-Shu'ara' 26:189), and He did not say "the punishment of the Canopy; indeed, it was a great punishment." The explanation of this will come in detail at His saying, "The Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering, that is the Day of Mutual Loss" (al-Taghabun 64:9), in the chapter of al-Taghabun. On this basis, it is fitting to make the attribution of the punishment to the great day a metonymy for the greatness of that punishment, because the greatness of a great day customarily entails the greatness of what occurs in it.

His saying, "Whoever is turned away from it that day, He has indeed shown him mercy" is a conditional sentence (shart and jaza') occupying the position of a qualifier for "punishment" ('adhab).

"Yuṣraf" is in the passive voice in the reading of the majority, its subject being either the pronoun referring to the punishment or the pronoun referring to "man" (whoever), as a substitute for the agent. The pronoun governed by "'an" refers to "man," meaning the punishment is turned away from him; or it refers to the punishment, meaning whoever is turned away from it (the punishment). The reverse of this reference would apply to the hidden pronoun in his saying "yuṣraf."

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Ya'qub and Khalaf read "yaṣrif" in the active voice, its subject being the pronoun referring to "my Lord," as the agent.

As for the hidden pronoun in "raḥimahu," it refers to "my Lord," and the attached pronoun refers to "man," in both readings.

The meaning of describing the punishment by the content of the conditional clause is: whoever God has enabled to avoid the causes of that punishment, God has decreed mercy for him and facilitated for him its causes.

The intent of this statement is to affirm the counterpart of His saying: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day." It is as if he said: I hope, if I obey Him, that my Lord will have mercy on me, for whoever is spared the punishment has mercy established for him. This meaning is conveyed through the method of the theological school, which is mentioning the proof so that the thing proven becomes known. This is a kind of metonymy and an elegant style, whereby the one to whom the ruling applies enters under it by virtue of being one of the individuals of the general category to whom the ruling has been established.

For this reason, he followed it with His saying: "And that is the manifest triumph." The demonstrative refers either to the turning away derived from "whoever is turned away from it," or to what was mentioned. Being spared the punishment is a triumph because whoever is spared the punishment on that day has entered into bliss on that day. God, exalted is He, said: "So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed" (Al 'Imran 3:185).
