The meaning of describing the punishment by the content of the conditional clause is: whoever God has enabled to avoid the causes of that punishment, God has decreed mercy for him and facilitated for him its causes.

Page 162

The intent of this statement is to affirm the counterpart of His saying: "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day." It is as if he said: I hope, if I obey Him, that my Lord will have mercy on me, for whoever is spared the punishment has mercy established for him. This meaning is conveyed through the method of the theological school, which is mentioning the proof so that the thing proven becomes known. This is a kind of metonymy and an elegant style, whereby the one to whom the ruling applies enters under it by virtue of being one of the individuals of the general category to whom the ruling has been established.

For this reason, he followed it with His saying: "And that is the manifest triumph." The demonstrative refers either to the turning away derived from "whoever is turned away from it," or to what was mentioned. Being spared the punishment is a triumph because whoever is spared the punishment on that day has entered into bliss on that day. God, exalted is He, said: "So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed" (Al 'Imran 3:185). "Al-Mubin" is an active participle from abana, meaning bana (to be clear/manifest).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 17:

﴿If Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿatf) of the sentences that begin with the verb "Say" (qul), so the address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

This indicates that the polytheists had threatened the Prophet ﷺ, or had made allusion to him, with their determination to inflict harm and injury upon him. So Allah addressed him with that which strengthens his soul and which despairs his enemies of making him slip. This is like what is related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down to you no authority?﴾ [al-An'am: 81]. Behind this is the affirmation that the absolute disposer of the states of all existent things is Allah the Exalted, after He had established, through the preceding sentences, that He is the originator of all existent things in the heavens and the earth. He made this in the style of a reassurance to the Messenger ﷺ against fear of the might, threats and menaces of the polytheists, and a promise to him of the attainment of good as a result of the pleasure of his Lord alone with him, and a challenge to the polytheists that they are unable to harm him or bring him benefit. It also results in a rebuttal of the polytheists who, when reminded that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them, acknowledged this, yet claimed that their gods intercede with Allah and that they bring good and ward off evil. When the preceding verses nullified the claim of the idols to divinity, because they create nothing, and made worship obligatory only for the one truly deserving of divinity, this verse nullified their claim to be worshipped, because they possess neither harm nor benefit for people, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76], and He said concerning Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿He said: Do they hear you when you call, or do they benefit you or harm you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 72].

The preceding sentences have prepared a place for this sentence, for when it is established that the Creator of existent things is Allah alone, it necessarily follows that He decrees their states and their actions, because His being within the sphere of His power is more fitting and more worthy, after the things that befall existent things are created by Him. The accidents that befall existent things occur by the decree of Allah, since He the Exalted is the decreer of their causes, the establisher of the order of their occurrence and attainment, and the creator of the means of the psychological motives toward them or the deterrents from them.

The root meaning of al-massu (touching) is placing the hand upon a thing. It may be direct or by means of an instrument, and it is used metaphorically for the conveying of one thing to another, so it is borrowed in the sense of conveying, and it is frequent that there is mentioned along with it that which is borrowed for the instrument. The instrumental particle, which is the bāʾ (with), enters upon it as here, so there are in it two dependent metaphors (istiʿaratān tabaʿiyyatān), one in the verb and the other in the meaning of the particle, as in His saying: ﴿And do not touch them with harm﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]. The meaning is: "If Allah afflicts you with harm," or "If there reaches you from Allah some harm."

Al-ḍurr, with a dammed ḍād, is the state that pains a person; it is of the category of evil (sharr), and it is what is repugnant to the person. Its opposite is al-nafʿ (benefit), which is of the category of good (khayr), and it is what is agreeable. The meaning is: If Allah decrees for you harm, then no one can remove it from you except Him, if He wills that, because His decrees are bound and enclosed by laws and orders, and none can reach changing them except the power of their Creator.

He placed His saying "And if Allah touches you with harm" in correspondence with His saying "And if He touches you with good," a correspondence by the more general term, because khayr includes benefit, which is the agreeable, and includes safety from the repugnant, to indicate that what is meant by ḍurr is what is more general. It is as if it were said: "If He touches you with harm and evil, and if He touches you with benefit and good," so in the verse there is ihtibak (interlocking omission). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The term ḍurr in this verse takes the place of sharr, and sharr is more general and is the counterpart of khayr." This is from eloquence, a deviation from the rule of artifice and contrivance, for it is of the rule of artifice that a thing be paired with that which is specific to it. He compared this to His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] to you that you will not hunger therein nor go naked, and that you will not thirst therein nor be exposed to the sun﴾ [Taha: 118]. End quote.

His saying ﴿and He is over all things competent﴾ is made the answer to the condition, because it is the reason for the omitted answer and for the answer mentioned before it, since the estimate is: "And if He touches you with good, then there is no preventer for it, because He is over all things competent, in harm and benefit." He made this generality a preparation for His saying after it: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 18:

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

This sentence is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the sentence ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾ [al-An'am: 17], and the connection between them is that the meaning of both nullifies the idols' entitlement to worship. The first verse nullified that by negating that the idols have any control over the conditions of creatures, and this verse nullifies that anyone other than Allah could be a subduer over anyone, or all-aware, or one who gives every creature what suits it. Undoubtedly, the God must possess power and knowledge, and these two are the summation of the attributes of perfection, just as He must possess the attributes of action, such as benefit, harm, giving life and causing death. These are connections (ta'alluqat) of power, which those other than al-Ash'ari called "attributes" (sifat) according to common usage, while al-Ash'ari included them under the attribute of power because they are connections of it, and this is the verified view (al-tahqiq).

For this reason, this verse stands in relation to the preceding one as generalization after specification, because the preceding verse mentioned His perfect control over creatures and came in the form of strengthening the Messenger (ﷺ), as we have mentioned. This verse encompasses His power over everything and His knowledge of everything, and that is the root of all action and making.

Al-qahir is the one who overcomes, compels, and from whom nothing escapes His power, the one to whom the act of subduing is attributed.

The definite form of both components (ta'rif al-juz'ayn) conveys restriction (qasr), meaning there is no subduer except Him, because the subjugation of Allah the Exalted is the true subjugation from which the one subdued finds no refuge, since it is a subjugation through causes that no one can create anything to repel. Among what is continually observed of these are sleep, and likewise death. Glory be to Him who subdued the servants by death.

"Fawq" (above) is a adverbial of place related to "al-qahir," and it is a metaphorical representation (isti'ara tamthiliyya) of the state of the subduer as one who seizes the vanquished from above, so that he finds no way to resist or move. This is a wonderful representation, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿And indeed we are above them, subduers﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

It should not be understood from this that there is a direction that is high, as may be imagined, so this verse is not counted among the ambiguous (mutashabihat) verses.

"Al-'ibad" (the servants) are the created rational beings, so the beasts are not called "servants of Allah." It is in origin the plural of "'abd," but usage has restricted it to creatures, and it restricted "'abid" (slaves) to the plural of "'abd" in the sense of owned.

The meaning of "subduing above the servants" is that He is the creator of what does not fall within their capacities, such that He brings into existence what they do not want to exist, like death, and prevents what they want to attain, like a child for the barren, and ignorance of many things, such that everyone finds within himself matters he is able to do, matters he is unable to do, and matters he does sometimes and cannot do other times, like walking for one whose leg has gone numb. Thus everyone knows that Allah is the creator of capacities and abilities, since He may prevent them, and since He creates what lies beyond human capacity. Then reason measures the worlds of the unseen by the world of the witnessed. Allah has created the elements and forces and has given power to some over others, so none can repel except what Allah has empowered.

"Al-Hakim" (the Wise) is the one who perfects and makes firm the created things; it is fa'il in the sense of muf'il. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿Know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209] in Surat al-Baqarah and in many other places.

"Al-Khabir" is an intensive form of the active participle from "khabara" in its transitive sense, meaning "'alima" (knew). It is said: "khabara al-amr" when he knew it and tested it. It has also been said that it is derived from "khabar" (news), because when a thing is known, it becomes possible to inform about it.

[Page 166]

This is a shift from the argument for establishing the attributes that befit God to establishing the truthfulness of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and to making God the judge between him and those who denied him. The sentence is therefore a fresh beginning (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes), and its connection to the preceding passage is clear.

Al-Wahidi related in *Asbab al-Nuzul* (Occasions of Revelation), on the authority of al-Kalbi, that the leaders of Mecca said: "O Muhammad, we do not see anyone confirming what you say. We have asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that they have no mention of you and no description of you in their scriptures. So show us someone who testifies that you are the Messenger of God." Then this verse was revealed.

The dialogue opens with a question used in the sense of affirmation (*taqrir*), as I explained at the words of God Most High: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-An'am: 12]. This style serves to prepare the listeners to receive what comes after the question.

*Ayy* (which) is an interrogative noun by which one seeks to specify one of the items shared within what this interrogation is joined to. The noun it is joined to here is *shay'* (thing), which is explained as being of the category of testimony.

*Shay'* (thing) is a general term, one of the highest genera with very broad scope. It has been said that it means "the existent," and it has been said that it means "that which can be known and whose existence is possible." The more apparent definition is that it is "a matter that can be known, about which one can make statements, whether it is an existent, an attribute of an existent, or a meaning that can be conceived and discussed." From this usage is God's saying: ﴿So the disbelievers said: "This is a strange thing."﴾ [Qaf: 2] ﴿"When we have died and become dust, that is a far-off return."﴾ [Qaf: 3]

I have already discussed the contexts in which the word *shay'* is well used and those in which it is weak, at God's words: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155], in Surah al-Baqarah.

*Akbar* (greatest) here means stronger and more just within the category of testimonies. It is an instance of applying a term whose literal meaning is the greatness of a physical entity to the greatness of a non-physical meaning, as in God's saying: ﴿But the pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], and His saying: ﴿Say: Fighting therein is grave﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. This was discussed previously in Surah al-Baqarah.

The strength of a testimony is measured by the soul's tranquillity in it and its acceptance of what it affirms.

His saying *shahadatan* (as testimony) is a specification (*tamyiz*) for the relation of greatness to the thing, so that what the "thing" refers to, through this specification, becomes testimony. The meaning is: "What testimony is the truest of testimonies?" The item asked about with *ayy* is one individual of the category of testimonies, and one seeks to know which individual of its kind is the truest.

[Page 167]

The concept of testimony has already been explained at God's words: ﴿the testimony between you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106], in Surah al-Ma'idah.

Since God's testimony to the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) was not known to those being addressed who denied that he is the Messenger of God, God's testimony against them takes on the sense of an oath, in the manner of God's saying: ﴿And it will avert the punishment from her if she testifies four times by God that he is surely among the liars﴾ [al-Nur: 8]. That is, she would make God a witness to the husband's lying, meaning she would swear by God's name to that effect. The expression ﴿I call God to witness﴾ [Hud: 54] is among the formulas of oath. However, if it does not carry the meaning of calling to witness, it is a figurative usage by metonymy (*majaz mursal*). If it carries the meaning of calling to witness, as here, then it is a figure of speech (*kinayah*) indicating an oath, with the intended meaning of making God a witness against them. By this, the position of His saying becomes clear: ﴿God is a witness between me and you﴾, that is, "I call Him to witness against you." Close to this is what God related from Hud: ﴿He said: "I call God to witness."﴾ [Hud: 54]

His saying: ﴿Say: God is a witness between me and you﴾ is an answer to the question, which is why its sentence, introduced by *qul* (say), is separated from what precedes. This is an answer that the one addressed by the question is commanded to give, in the sense that he asks and then himself promptly gives the answer, because the question's purpose is affirmation (*taqrir*), and the answer is something the one being asked cannot deny. This is in the manner I explained at His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-An'am: 12].

The statement ﴿God is a witness between me and you﴾ occurs as an answer on their tongues, because it follows from the question and is what the question aims at. The estimated meaning is: "Say: God's testimony is the greatest testimony. Therefore God is a witness between me and you." The consequence was omitted, since the consequence is indicated by what follows it, out of concision, as is required by the eloquence of a style of compelling argument and debate. The meaning is: "I call God to witness, whose testimony is the greatest testimony, that I have conveyed to you that He does not accept that you associate anything with Him, and that I have warned you."

This verse implies the permissibility of applying the name *shay'* (thing) to God Most High, because His saying "God is a witness" was given as an answer to the saying "What thing is greatest," so it required applying the name *shay'* as a predicate concerning God Most High, even if this is not explicitly stated. Accordingly, if a believer applied it to God Most High, there would be no transgression of proper manners in it and no sin. This is the view of the Ash'arites, contrary to Jahm ibn Safwan and his followers.

The meaning of ﴿God is a witness between me and you﴾ is that, since the signs and warnings did not benefit them so that they would turn back from denial and obstinacy, nothing remained but to leave them to God's reckoning. The aim is to warn them of God's punishment in this world and the next. The reason for mentioning "between me and you" is that God is a witness on his behalf, as the context requires. So the meaning of "between" is that God bears witness to the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), to refute their denial of his mission, as is the role of a witness in disputes.

[Page 168]

His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿God is a witness between me and you﴾, and it is the most important element of what he swore to regarding the establishment of the mission. It includes all that the Messenger (ﷺ) conveyed to them and all the proofs he established. So the conjunction of ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ is a conjunction of the particular to the general (*'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm*). The agent of the revelation is omitted and the verb is put in the passive, because the one who revealed it to him is known, namely God Most High.

The demonstrative ﴿this Qur'an﴾ refers to what is in the mind of both speaker and listener. An explicative apposition (*'atf al-bayan*) after the demonstrative clarifies the intended referent of the demonstrative.

He limited the reason for the Qur'an's revelation to warning, without mentioning good news, because those addressed, in their state of obstinacy which is the context of the speech, are only suited to warning. So the ultimate purpose of the Qur'an in relation to their condition is warning. For this reason He said ﴿that I may warn you thereby﴾, explicitly using the pronoun of those addressed. He did not say "that I may warn with it," although they are the primary intended audience of this address, even though what is coordinated with their pronoun warns and gives good news. Moreover, the particle of purpose (*lam al-'illah*) does not imply that the purpose is restricted to what follows it, since a verb transitive by means of it may have many purposes.

﴿And whomever it reaches﴾ is coordinated with the pronoun of those addressed, meaning: "and that I may warn thereby whoever the Qur'an reaches and hears, even if I did not address him directly with the call." The object pronoun that links the relative clause was omitted, because its omission is frequent and good, as Abu 'Ali al-Fari­si said.

The generality of *man* (whoever) and its relative clause includes everyone whom the Qur'an reaches in all eras.

* * *

﴿Do you really testify that there are other gods along with God?﴾ ﴿Say: I do not testify.﴾ ﴿Say: He is only one God, and I am innocent of what you associate.﴾

This is a sentence resumed (*mustanifah*) from the statement of the speech that he was commanded to say to them.

[Page 169]

It is a resumption after the clause ﴿What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ This was singled out for mention because denying a partner to God in divinity is the very foundation of the Islamic call. So, after he had established for them that God's testimony is the greatest testimony and had made God a witness concerning what he conveyed, and against them concerning what they turned away from and obstinately denied, he resumed with a question in the form of denial, to exhaust the case against them. He said: "Do you testify, regarding what you persist in, that there are other gods along with God, just as I have testified to what I have called you to?" The matter being affirmed here is one they deny, as indicated by the context.

The reason he made the interrogation used for denial follow a statement emphasized by *inna* (indeed) and the lam of emphasis is so that it conveys that this testimony of theirs is something listeners can hardly believe they would give, because it is so hard to imagine such a thing coming from sensible people. Hence the one reporting it about them needs to emphasize his statement with two emphatic devices, saying: "Indeed they testify that there are other gods along with God." At that point, the one addressing them with denial needs to introduce the interrogative particle of denial into the sentence through which their statement is to be reported. Such a construction therefore conveys two denials: one explicit, by the particle of denial, and the other implicit, through the implication of the emphasis on the report, because this claim is so strange that a listener doubts it could have come from them.

The meaning of ﴿you testify﴾ is "you make claims which you verify with a certainty resembling testimony regarding a matter that is certainly established." So the use of "you testify" is in agreement with His saying: ﴿Say: God is a witness between me and you﴾.

*Al-alihah* (the gods) is the plural of *ilah* (god). The feminine adjective is applied to it to draw attention to the fact that they do not understand, because the plural of non-rational things takes the adjective like that of a single feminine item.

His saying ﴿Say: I do not testify﴾ is an answer to the interrogation in His saying ﴿Do you really testify?﴾, since it is in the sense of: "Say: Do you really...?" The answer was made quickly by the speaker's disassociation from testifying to that. This is because the answer of those addressed to this question is known from their condition, that they acknowledge it. So He turned away from them after their question, as if saying: "Leave aside your testimony and take my testimony, for I do not testify to that."

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150].

[Page 170]

The sentence ﴿Say: He is only one God﴾ is an explanation (*bayan*) of the sentence ﴿I do not testify﴾. That is why it is separated from it, because it is in the position of explicative apposition, since the meaning of "I do not testify that there are gods with Him" is the meaning of "He is one God." The verb "say" is repeated to emphasize the conveying of the message.

The particle *innama* (only) conveys restriction, meaning: He alone is the one specified with oneness. Then he stressed this by disowning its opposite in His saying: ﴿and I am innocent of what you associate.﴾ This contains a cutting off of the argument with them, in the manner of disengagement.

The *ma* in His saying ﴿of what you associate﴾ may be a verbal-noun particle, meaning "of your association." It may also be a relative pronoun, which is the more apparent reading, meaning "of your idols which you associate." Here the relative pronoun's returning pronoun, which is in the prepositional phrase, is omitted, since the omitted preposition together with the returning pronoun is determined to be the one estimated without ambiguity. This is the criterion for permissibility of omitting a returning pronoun governed by a preposition, as in His saying: ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 60], meaning "to glorify it," and His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 94], meaning "by proclaiming it aloud." The apparent sense of Ibn Malik's *al-Tashil* is that this is prohibited, and that is an oversight by its author, which some commentators of his books have been deceived by.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (*jumlah mustanfa'ah*), by which the mode of speech shifts from addressing the polytheists on the tongue of the Messenger ﷺ to a general report, like the other reports of the Qur'an. God presented evidence for the truthfulness of the Messenger in what he brought, after the testimony of God mentioned in His words: ﴿Say: "God is witness between me and you"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. When the mention of the Qur'an occurred there, this shift took place in order to call on the truthfulness of the Qur'an, which includes the truthfulness of the one who brought it, because it is the general, lasting, miraculous sign. You have already learned that al-Wahidi reported that the chiefs of the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We have asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that they have no mention of you nor description of you," and so on. If that is the case, then the reference to the People of the Book here is a refutation of what they had said, namely that they do not have mention of the Prophet nor his description. That is, they [i.e., the People of the Book] are [one with] you in denying the truth.

[p. 171]

If you do not take the verse as alluding to what is mentioned in the occasions of revelation (*asbab al-nuzul*, the circumstances in which a verse was revealed), it becomes necessary to take the intended meaning of ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾ as some of the People of the Book, namely the fair-minded among them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq. The polytheists used to esteem the People of the Book and trust their knowledge, and some of the polytheists followed the religion of the People of the Book and turned away from polytheism, such as Waraqa ibn Nawfal. Therefore their testimony concerning the knowledge of the soundness of the religion was trusted by them, when they gave it and did not conceal it. In this there is also a recording against the People of the Book of the obligation to convey this testimony to the people.

The pronoun in the accusative in His words *yaʻrifūnahu* ("they recognize it") refers to the Qur'an mentioned in His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. The meaning is that they recognize that it is from God, and they recognize what it contains of what their books have reported, including the mission of the one who brought it, Muhammad ﷺ, because of what their books contain of good tidings of him. The intended meaning of "those given the Book" is the scholars of the Jews and the Christians, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "God suffices as witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

The comparison in His words ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾ is a comparison of recognition with recognition. The point of resemblance is certainty and firm conviction that this is the Book that was promised. The reason that the recognition of one's sons was chosen as the thing compared is that a man does not go astray in recognizing the person and identity of his son when he meets him, and that he is his known son. This is because sons are customarily in constant company with their fathers.

It has been said that the pronoun in (*yaʻrifūnahu*) refers to the monotheism derived from His words ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ [al-An'am: 19], but this is far-fetched. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ, although no mention of him has occurred in what precedes, either explicitly or by interpretation. It also requires that the addressee be other than the Messenger ﷺ, which is not appropriate. Moreover, returning the pronoun to the Qur'an is sufficient without this, and it also adds the establishment of the matter by the proof, which is the Qur'an itself.

His words ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 12] are a resumptive statement to add clarification of the obstinacy and persistence of the polytheists. Thus they are the intended meaning of "those who have lost their souls," just as they were intended by its earlier counterpart, which came after His words ﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-An'am: 12]. This is part of the repetition for the sake of recording, establishing the proof, and cutting off excuses, and [it shows] that they persist in disbelief even if the People of the Book testify to the truthfulness of the Messenger.

[p. 172]

As in His words: ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If it is from God and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel testifies to its like and believes, while you are arrogant…?"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10]. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the People of the Book, namely those who concealed the testimony, so that ﴿those who have lost﴾ [al-An'am: 12] is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 21:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿those who have lost their souls﴾ [al-An'am: 20]. The ones meant here are the polytheists, like His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114]. Its like has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. By their fabrication is meant the creed of polytheism (shirk) in the period of ignorance (jahiliyyah), with what it contains of falsehoods, and by their denial of the signs is meant their denial of the Qur'an after the mission (al-ba'thah). He has made the one who commits either of these two traits the most unjust of people, so how about those who combined both of them?

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil), and that is why it is separated (from what precedes) without a conjunction. That is, once it is established that there is no one more unjust than them, they are certainly not successful, because the wrongdoers do not succeed; so how about one whose injustice has reached its utmost limit? Thus, mention of the cause (ʿillah) has sufficed in place of mention of the effect (maʿlul).

The placement of (inna) in this context conveys the meaning of giving a reason (taʿlil) for the omitted clause, as has been established in the words of ʿAbd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani). The placement of the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-shan) with it conveys attention to this news (al-ihtimam bi-hadha al-khabar) with the attention of affirmation, so that the clause that serves as its explanation settles firmly in the mind of the listener.

Al-Iftira' (fabrication) is deliberate lying. His saying kadhiban (a lie) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing it, and it is more general than fabrication. Emphasis may be achieved with a more general term, as we have previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-Ma'idah. He has negated their success, so it encompasses every success in this world and the Hereafter, for the success that is esteemed in the view of religion in this world is faith and righteous action, and that is the cause of success in the Hereafter.

[Page 173]

This is connected (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21], or to the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21], because the content of these coordinated clauses has a relevance to the content of the clause ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21] and to the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21]. This is because the content of these clauses is among the consequences of wrongdoing and the consequences of failing to succeed. Also, the content of the verse encompasses a threat regarding association of partners with Allah (shirk) and denial (takdhīb), an affirmation of the Gathering (ḥashr), and a refutation of shirk.

The word ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (yawma, "the Day") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and its governing verb is omitted. The most apparent view is that it is to be understood from what the coordinated elements indicate, namely: ﴿نَقُولُ﴾ (naqūlu, "We shall say"), or ﴿قالُوا﴾ (qālū, "they said"), or ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ (kadhdhabū, "they lied"), or ﴿ضَلَّ﴾ (ḍalla, "has gone astray"). All of these are suitable to indicate the omitted element. Those verbs are not the thing the adverb of time depends on; rather, they are an indication of the omitted dependent element, because the intent is to convey the terror of what will happen to them on the Day of Gathering, of the trial and turmoil that arise from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, to them: ﴿Where are your partners?﴾, and to introduce that dreadful situation.

Al-Zamakhsharī (in his commentary, al-Kashshāf) estimated the response (jawāb) from what the whole narration indicates. His estimate is: "Whatever happened happened." He held that its omission is intended to convey vagueness, which is part of the intimidation. In this he followed what the leading scholars of eloquence (balāgha) habitually did in estimating omitted responses and dependents. In my view, the better approach is that one resorts to this only when there is no evidence in the speech that specifies the omitted element. Otherwise, intimidation and terror through detail may be stronger than through vagueness, when each part of the detail itself conveys intimidation. Some exegetes estimated: "Remember the Day when We gather them." There is no particular point in this. There are other estimates by some of them that should not be dwelt upon.

The object pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ (naḥshuruhum, "We gather them") refers either to ﴿مِمَّنِ افْتَرى عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21] or to (the wrongdoers). Since the intended group is the polytheists, it implies both polytheists and those with whom they associated. To draw attention to the fact that the pronoun refers to the polytheists and their idols, the word ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (jamīʿan, "all") was included, to indicate the intention of comprehensiveness. The inclusion of the pronoun for all the polytheists is not something the hearer would doubt, so as to require emphasis by a word of encompassment and totality. Therefore, it is established that the mention of ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ was intended as an alert, that the pronoun refers to the polytheists and their idols. This is like His saying: ﴿And the Day We gather them all, then We shall say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners"﴾ [Yūnus: 28], and His saying: ﴿And the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ [al-Furqān: 17]. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ is here in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun.

The intent of gathering their idols with them is to display the humiliation of the idols and their uselessness, just as a victor gathers captives of a tribe along with those they used to rely upon for victory. This is because, if the idols were absent, they would think that if they had come, they would have interceded. Or, they would be occupied with their own glory and bliss, away from their worshippers. Captives would often hope for the presence of their intercessors or those who could ransom them. The poet al-Nābigha said:

*They hope for the journey of Naṣr and Ibn Sayyār.*

The verb ﴿نَقُولُ﴾ (naqūlu, "We shall say") is coordinated with ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ (thumma, "then"), because the saying is delayed in time after their gathering, by an interval. This is because the share of the criminal in waiting for what will befall him is more severe upon him, and because neglecting attention to them is a humiliation of them. Along with this, ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ conveys the sequence of rank (tartīb rutbī), meaning a movement from one report to a greater one.

He specified ﴿الَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا﴾ (alladhīna ashrakū, "those who associated others with Allah") because they are a part of what the pronoun included, that is: "Then We shall say to those who associated others with Allah from among that gathering."

The original use of ﴿أيْنَ﴾ (ayna, "where") in a question is as an inquiry about the place where the subject of the predication is located, as in: "Where is your house?" and "Where are you going?" It may also be used to ask about a thing that has no place, so that the inquiry is about the cause of its absence. Such is the statement of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam when he went out on the day of the festival and headed for the pulpit before the prayer: "Where is the advancing of the prayer?" It may also be used with ﴿أيْنَ﴾ about the action of someone from whom something was expected; when its time arrives and it has not occurred from him, he is asked about it with ﴿أيْنَ﴾, as if the questioner is searching for his place, treating him as an absent one whose location is unknown. So the question with ﴿أيْنَ﴾ here is about the supposed partners, while they are present, as other verses indicate. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship besides Allah﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 22].

The question is reproachful (tawbīkhī) regarding what the polytheists used to claim about them, that they would intercede for them with Allah, or that they would support them in times of need. So when they saw that these had no use, it was said to them: "Where are your partners?", that is, "Where is their work?", as if they had been made absent from them.

The partners are attributed to the second-person pronoun (the addressees) by an attribution of particularization (iḍāfat ikhtiṣāṣ), because they are the ones who claimed partnership with Allah in divinity for them. So they were not partners except in the belief of the polytheists. For this reason it was said: ﴿your partners﴾. This is like the saying of one of the champions of the Arabs to ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, when ʿAmr narrated in a gathering that he had killed him, while he himself was present in that gathering. He said to him: "Gently, Abā Thawr, your slain one is listening", that is, the one supposed to be your slain.

They were described as ﴿الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ (alladhīna kuntum tazʿumūn, "whom you used to claim") as a denial of them. The second object of ﴿تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ (tazʿumūn, "you claim") was omitted so that it would generalize to all that they used to claim for them of divinity, victory, and intercession. As for the first object, it was omitted following the manner of omitting the returning pronoun of a relative clause that is in the accusative.

Al-zaʿm (claim) is an assumption that inclines toward falsehood or error, or because of its strangeness its holder is accused. One says: ﴿zaʿama﴾ (he claimed), meaning that the responsibility for the report falls upon him, not upon the transmitter. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 60], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. A further clarification of the meaning of al-zaʿm will come at His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghābun: 7], in Sūrat al-Taghābun.

His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتَهُمْ﴾ (thumma lam takun fitnatahum, "Then their trial was not...") is coordinated with the clause ﴿ثُمَّ نَقُولُ﴾ (thumma naqūlu, "then We shall say"), and ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ here is for the sequence of rank, which is a movement from one report to another greater than it.

The root meaning of fitna is testing, from the expression: "fatana al-dhahab" when one tests the purity of gold from its impurities. It is also used for the disturbance of opinion due to the occurrence of a fear that cannot be endured, because such a thing indicates the measure of steadfastness of the one who experiences it. This may happen in a state of life, or in hatred and love, or in belief and reflection and confusion of affairs. The discussion of it was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqara: 102], in Sūrat al-Baqara.

Here, ﴿فِتْنَتُهم﴾ (fitnatuhum, "their trial") is followed by an exception from it: ﴿أنْ قالُوا واللَّهِ رَبِّنا ما كُنّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (an qālū wallāhi rabbanā mā kunnā mushrikīn, "except that they said: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'"). That saying is either of the type of what the exception excludes from, the omitted element in the exception being emptied out (tafrīgh al-istithnāʾ), so the excluded item is from the sayings described as a trial. The estimate is: "They had no saying that was a trial for them except their saying: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.'"

Or the excepted saying indicates their trial, meaning that they were in a trial when they said it. In either case, their saying ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ implies that they were tried at that time.

On this basis, the word fitna may mean the disturbance of opinion and bewilderment in the matter, and the speech would then be concise (ījāz). The estimate is: "They were tested regarding what to answer, so their answer was ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾." He deviated from the estimated expression to this structure because it is known that their answer was their trial, since it was its effect and its manifestation.

It is also possible that by fitna is meant their false answer, because it leads to the trial of its speaker, that is, the testing of the state of his own soul.

It is also possible that the word was used in its original meaning, which is testing, and what is meant by it is the question, because a question is a test of what the one questioned has of knowledge, or of truthfulness or its opposite. Then it is necessary to estimate an added word, meaning: "Their answer (jawāb) to their trial, that is, their being questioned about the state of their polytheism, was nothing but ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾."

Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read ﴿لَمْ تَكُنْ﴾ (lam takun) with the feminine marker of the imperfect verb. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Yaʿqūb read it with the yāʾ of the imperfect for the feminine third person, considering that ﴿أنْ قالُوا﴾ (an qālū) is the subject (ism) of kāna.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿فِتْنَتَهم﴾ (fitnatahum) in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of kāna, so kāna is a defective verb whose subject is ﴿إلّا أنْ قالُوا﴾ (illā an qālū). It was placed after the predicate because it is restricted by exception.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read it in the nominative, as the subject of kāna, with ﴿أنْ قالُوا﴾ as the predicate of kāna, so kāna is made complete (tāmma). The meaning is: "No trial occurred for them except their saying: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'", that is, their trial did not happen except by their denying that they associated partners.

The reason the verb is joined with the feminine imperfect marker, according to the reading in which fitnatahum is in the accusative, is that its subject is feminine by estimate, because the saying formed from ﴿أنْ﴾ and its clause is part of the trial, according to one of the two interpretations. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is like the feminine form of the numeral in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-Anʿām: 160], because the "likes" (amthāl) were in the sense of the good deeds, so the numeral was made feminine.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿رَبِّنا﴾ (rabbinā, "our Lord") in the genitive, as an adjective of the divine name (ism al-jalāla). Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it in the accusative, as a vocative with the particle of address omitted.

Their mention of the Lord with the attribution to their own pronoun is an exaggeration in disavowing polytheism, meaning: "We have no lord other than Him." They lied and swore falsely, following their habit that they had in life, because a person is gathered upon what he lived upon. Also, the bewilderment and astonishment that afflicted them made them imagine that they could deceive Allah, the Exalted, and thereby escape punishment. There is no obstacle to the occurrence of a lie together with the manifestation of the truth on that day, because the realities will appear to them while they think that they will not appear to others. Also, this is a report from them about a matter absent from that day, since they were informed about their affairs in this world.

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: a man said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "I find in the Qur'an things that contradict one another for me," and he mentioned among them His saying: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 42], and His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. He said: "They have concealed in this verse." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Indeed, Allah forgives the sins of the people of sincerity. The polytheists will say: 'Come, let us say: we were not polytheists.' Then their mouths will be sealed and their hands will speak. At that point they will know that Allah does not conceal any statement."

His saying: ﴿انْظُرْ كَيْفَ كَذَبُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (unẓur kayfa kadhabū ʿalā anfusihim, "Look how they lied against themselves") makes their state, which is being spoken about, as if it were witnessed, because it comes from one about whose reporting there is no dispute. Therefore He commanded the hearer, or commanded the Messenger ﷺ, with what indicates looking at it, as if it were present and witnessed.

The most apparent view is that ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (kayfa, "how") is merely for the state and does not indicate a question. Looking at the state is looking at its people at the time they take on that state. Similar instances of this have preceded, among them His saying: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 50], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Many exegetes made the looking here a mental looking (naẓar qalbī), because it comes as the verb of seeing comes, so that it is suspended from acting by the interrogative, meaning: "Consider the answer to the saying of the speaker ('how they invent lies against Allah' [al-Nisāʾ: 50]); you will find it a clear and evident answer."

Because of this certainty regarding the report of their gathering, He expressed their lying that occurs on the Day of Gathering in the past tense, in His saying: ﴿They lied against themselves﴾. Likewise, His saying: ﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾.

The verb kadhaba is construed with the preposition ʿalā ("upon") when it governs the one about whom the liar tells a lie, as in this verse and in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." As for its construction with the person to whom the liar tells a false report, it takes the object directly, without a preposition, as in the expression kadhabaka, meaning "he told you a lie."

Ḍalla in the sense of "to be absent, to be lost from view" is as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Shall we, when we have gone astray in the earth?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning: when we have been hidden within it by burial. The "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) and "yaftarūna" (they fabricate) is its relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "that which they used to fabricate." What was affirmed to be false is "their associates" (shurakāʾuhum). The intended meaning is the absence of their intercession and their support, because that is what was expected of them. When nothing of that appeared, their presence was treated as though it were absence, just as one says: "You have been seized, and your helper has vanished," while he is present.

Or the excepted saying indicates their trial, meaning that they were in a trial when they said it. In either case, their saying ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ implies that they were tried at that time.

On this basis, the word fitna may mean the disturbance of opinion and bewilderment in the matter, and the speech would then be concise (ījāz). The estimate is: "They were tested regarding what to answer, so their answer was ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾." He deviated from the estimated expression to this structure because it is known that their answer was their trial, since it was its effect and its manifestation.

It is also possible that by fitna is meant their false answer, because it leads to the trial of its speaker, that is, the testing of the state of his own soul.

It is also possible that the word was used in its original meaning, which is testing, and what is meant by it is the question, because a question is a test of what the one questioned has of knowledge, or of truthfulness or its opposite. Then it is necessary to estimate an added word, meaning: "Their answer (jawāb) to their trial, that is, their being questioned about the state of their polytheism, was nothing but ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾."

Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read ﴿لَمْ تَكُنْ﴾ (lam takun) with the feminine marker of the imperfect verb. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Yaʿqūb read it with the yāʾ of the imperfect for the feminine third person, considering that ﴿أنْ قالُوا﴾ (an qālū) is the subject (ism) of kāna.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿فِتْنَتَهم﴾ (fitnatahum) in the accusative, as the predicate (khabar) of kāna, so kāna is a defective verb whose subject is ﴿إلّا أنْ قالُوا﴾ (illā an qālū). It was placed after the predicate because it is restricted by exception.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read it in the nominative, as the subject of kāna, with ﴿أنْ قالُوا﴾ as the predicate of kāna, so kāna is made complete (tāmma). The meaning is: "No trial occurred for them except their saying: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'", that is, their trial did not happen except by their denying that they associated partners.

The reason the verb is joined with the feminine imperfect marker, according to the reading in which fitnatahum is in the accusative, is that its subject is feminine by estimate, because the saying formed from ﴿أنْ﴾ and its clause is part of the trial, according to one of the two interpretations. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is like the feminine form of the numeral in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-Anʿām: 160], because the "likes" (amthāl) were in the sense of the good deeds, so the numeral was made feminine.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿رَبِّنا﴾ (rabbinā, "our Lord") in the genitive, as an adjective of the divine name (ism al-jalāla). Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it in the accusative, as a vocative with the particle of address omitted.

Their mention of the Lord with the attribution to their own pronoun is an exaggeration in disavowing polytheism, meaning: "We have no lord other than Him." They lied and swore falsely, following their habit that they had in life, because a person is gathered upon what he lived upon. Also, the bewilderment and astonishment that afflicted them made them imagine that they could deceive Allah, the Exalted, and thereby escape punishment. There is no obstacle to the occurrence of a lie together with the manifestation of the truth on that day, because the realities will appear to them while they think that they will not appear to others. Also, this is a report from them about a matter absent from that day, since they were informed about their affairs in this world.

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: a man said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "I find in the Qur'an things that contradict one another for me," and he mentioned among them His saying: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 42], and His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. He said: "They have concealed in this verse." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Indeed, Allah forgives the sins of the people of sincerity. The polytheists will say: 'Come, let us say: we were not polytheists.' Then their mouths will be sealed and their hands will speak. At that point they will know that Allah does not conceal any statement."

His saying: ﴿انْظُرْ كَيْفَ كَذَبُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (unẓur kayfa kadhabū ʿalā anfusihim, "Look how they lied against themselves") makes their state, which is being spoken about, as if it were witnessed, because it comes from one about whose reporting there is no dispute. Therefore He commanded the hearer, or commanded the Messenger ﷺ, with what indicates looking at it, as if it were present and witnessed.

The most apparent view is that ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (kayfa, "how") is merely for the state and does not indicate a question. Looking at the state is looking at its people at the time they take on that state. Similar instances of this have preceded, among them His saying: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 50], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Many exegetes made the looking here a mental looking (naẓar qalbī), because it comes as the verb of seeing comes, so that it is suspended from acting by the interrogative, meaning: "Consider the answer to the saying of the speaker ('how they invent lies against Allah' [al-Nisāʾ: 50]); you will find it a clear and evident answer."

Because of this certainty regarding the report of their gathering, He expressed their lying that occurs on the Day of Gathering in the past tense, in His saying: ﴿They lied against themselves﴾. Likewise, His saying: ﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾.

The verb kadhaba is construed with the preposition ʿalā ("upon") when it governs the one about whom the liar tells a lie, as in this verse and in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." As for its construction with the person to whom the liar tells a false report, it takes the object directly, without a preposition, as in the expression kadhabaka, meaning "he told you a lie."

Ḍalla in the sense of "to be absent, to be lost from view" is as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Shall we, when we have gone astray in the earth?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning: when we have been hidden within it by burial. The "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) and "yaftarūna" (they fabricate) is its relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "that which they used to fabricate." What was affirmed to be false is "their associates" (shurakāʾuhum). The intended meaning is the absence of their intercession and their support, because that is what was expected of them. When nothing of that appeared, their presence was treated as though it were absence, just as one says: "You have been seized, and your helper has vanished," while he is present.

[Page 173]

This is connected (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21], or to the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21], because the content of these coordinated clauses has a relevance to the content of the clause ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21] and to the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21]. This is because the content of these clauses is among the consequences of wrongdoing and the consequences of failing to succeed. Also, the content of the verse encompasses a threat regarding association of partners with Allah (shirk) and denial (takdhīb), an affirmation of the Gathering (ḥashr), and a refutation of shirk.

The word ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (yawma, "the Day") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and its governing verb is omitted. The most apparent view is that it is to be understood from what the coordinated elements indicate, namely: ﴿نَقُولُ﴾ (naqūlu, "We shall say"), or ﴿قالُوا﴾ (qālū, "they said"), or ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ (kadhdhabū, "they lied"), or ﴿ضَلَّ﴾ (ḍalla, "has gone astray"). All of these are suitable to indicate the omitted element. Those verbs are not the thing the adverb of time depends on; rather, they are an indication of the omitted dependent element, because the intent is to convey the terror of what will happen to them on the Day of Gathering, of the trial and turmoil that arise from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, to them: ﴿Where are your partners?﴾, and to introduce that dreadful situation.

Al-Zamakhsharī (in his commentary, al-Kashshāf) estimated the response (jawāb) from what the whole narration indicates. His estimate is: "Whatever happened happened." He held that its omission is intended to convey vagueness, which is part of the intimidation. In this he followed what the leading scholars of eloquence (balāgha) habitually did in estimating omitted responses and dependents. In my view, the better approach is that one resorts to this only when there is no evidence in the speech that specifies the omitted element. Otherwise, intimidation and terror through detail may be stronger than through vagueness, when each part of the detail itself conveys intimidation. Some exegetes estimated: "Remember the Day when We gather them." There is no particular point in this. There are other estimates by some of them that should not be dwelt upon.

The object pronoun in ﴿نَحْشُرُهم﴾ (naḥshuruhum, "We gather them") refers either to ﴿مِمَّنِ افْتَرى عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾ [al-Anʿām: 21] or to (the wrongdoers). Since the intended group is the polytheists, it implies both polytheists and those with whom they associated. To draw attention to the fact that the pronoun refers to the polytheists and their idols, the word ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (jamīʿan, "all") was included, to indicate the intention of comprehensiveness. The inclusion of the pronoun for all the polytheists is not something the hearer would doubt, so as to require emphasis by a word of encompassment and totality. Therefore, it is established that the mention of ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ was intended as an alert, that the pronoun refers to the polytheists and their idols. This is like His saying: ﴿And the Day We gather them all, then We shall say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners"﴾ [Yūnus: 28], and His saying: ﴿And the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ [al-Furqān: 17]. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ is here in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun.

The intent of gathering their idols with them is to display the humiliation of the idols and their uselessness, just as a victor gathers captives of a tribe along with those they used to rely upon for victory. This is because, if the idols were absent, they would think that if they had come, they would have interceded. Or, they would be occupied with their own glory and bliss, away from their worshippers. Captives would often hope for the presence of their intercessors or those who could ransom them. The poet al-Nābigha said:

*They hope for the journey of Naṣr and Ibn Sayyār.*

The verb ﴿نَقُولُ﴾ (naqūlu, "We shall say") is coordinated with ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ (thumma, "then"), because the saying is delayed in time after their gathering, by an interval. This is because the share of the criminal in waiting for what will befall him is more severe upon him, and because neglecting attention to them is a humiliation of them. Along with this, ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ conveys the sequence of rank (tartīb rutbī), meaning a movement from one report to a greater one.

He specified ﴿الَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا﴾ (alladhīna ashrakū, "those who associated others with Allah") because they are a part of what the pronoun included, that is: "Then We shall say to those who associated others with Allah from among that gathering."

The original use of ﴿أيْنَ﴾ (ayna, "where") in a question is as an inquiry about the place where the subject of the predication is located, as in: "Where is your house?" and "Where are you going?" It may also be used to ask about a thing that has no place, so that the inquiry is about the cause of its absence. Such is the statement of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam when he went out on the day of the festival and headed for the pulpit before the prayer: "Where is the advancing of the prayer?" It may also be used with ﴿أيْنَ﴾ about the action of someone from whom something was expected; when its time arrives and it has not occurred from him, he is asked about it with ﴿أيْنَ﴾, as if the questioner is searching for his place, treating him as an absent one whose location is unknown. So the question with ﴿أيْنَ﴾ here is about the supposed partners, while they are present, as other verses indicate. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship besides Allah﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 22].

The question is reproachful (tawbīkhī) regarding what the polytheists used to claim about them, that they would intercede for them with Allah, or that they would support them in times of need. So when they saw that these had no use, it was said to them: "Where are your partners?", that is, "Where is their work?", as if they had been made absent from them.

The partners are attributed to the second-person pronoun (the addressees) by an attribution of particularization (iḍāfat ikhtiṣāṣ), because they are the ones who claimed partnership with Allah in divinity for them. So they were not partners except in the belief of the polytheists. For this reason it was said: ﴿your partners﴾. This is like the saying of one of the champions of the Arabs to ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, when ʿAmr narrated in a gathering that he had killed him, while he himself was present in that gathering. He said to him: "Gently, Abā Thawr, your slain one is listening", that is, the one supposed to be your slain.

They were described as ﴿الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ (alladhīna kuntum tazʿumūn, "whom you used to claim") as a denial of them. The second object of ﴿تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ (tazʿumūn, "you claim") was omitted so that it would generalize to all that they used to claim for them of divinity, victory, and intercession. As for the first object, it was omitted following the manner of omitting the returning pronoun of a relative clause that is in the accusative.

Al-zaʿm (claim) is an assumption that inclines toward falsehood or error, or because of its strangeness its holder is accused. One says: ﴿zaʿama﴾ (he claimed), meaning that the responsibility for the report falls upon him, not upon the transmitter. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 60], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. A further clarification of the meaning of al-zaʿm will come at His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghābun: 7], in Sūrat al-Taghābun.

His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتَهُمْ﴾ (thumma lam takun fitnatahum, "Then their trial was not...") is coordinated with the clause ﴿ثُمَّ نَقُولُ﴾ (thumma naqūlu, "then We shall say"), and ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ here is for the sequence of rank, which is a movement from one report to another greater than it.

The root meaning of fitna is testing, from the expression: "fatana al-dhahab" when one tests the purity of gold from its impurities. It is also used for the disturbance of opinion due to the occurrence of a fear that cannot be endured, because such a thing indicates the measure of steadfastness of the one who experiences it. This may happen in a state of life, or in hatred and love, or in belief and reflection and confusion of affairs. The discussion of it was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqara: 102], in Sūrat al-Baqara.

Here, ﴿فِتْنَتُهم﴾ (fitnatuhum, "their trial") is followed by an exception from it: ﴿أنْ قالُوا واللَّهِ رَبِّنا ما كُنّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (an qālū wallāhi rabbanā mā kunnā mushrikīn, "except that they said: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'"). That saying is either of the type of what the exception excludes from, the omitted element in the exception being emptied out (tafrīgh al-istithnāʾ), so the excluded item is from the sayings described as a trial. The estimate is: "They had no saying that was a trial for them except their saying: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.'"

Or the excepted saying indicates their trial, meaning that they were in a trial when they said it. In either case, their saying ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ implies that they were tried at that time.

On this basis, the word fitna may mean the disturbance of opinion and bewilderment in the matter, and the speech would then be concise (ījāz). The estimate is: "They were tested regarding what to answer, so their answer was ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾." He deviated from the estimated expression to this structure because it is known that their answer was their trial, since it was its effect and its manifestation.

It is also possible that by fitna is meant their false answer, because it leads to the trial of its speaker, that is, the testing of the state of his own soul.

It is also possible that the word was used in its original meaning, which is testing, and what is meant by it is the question, because a question is a test of what the one questioned has of knowledge, or of truthfulness or its opposite. Then it is necessary to estimate an added word, meaning: "Their answer (jawāb) to their trial, that is, their being questioned about the state of their polytheism, was nothing but ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾."
