Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 25:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾

It is a new independent sentence coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the preceding independent sentences, from His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls—they do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 20].

The pronoun governed by "min" (partitive "some of") refers to the polytheists with whom and about whom the discourse has been conducted from the beginning, from His saying: ﴿Then those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals [to Him]﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. That is, "and among the polytheists are those who listen to you." The discourse has shifted to the conditions of their particular intellectuals, who held themselves aloof from meeting the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) with the total aversion that their foolish ones displayed, and from their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against that to which you invite us, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. But these intellectuals feigned forbearance, deliberation and fairness, and they gave the masses the impression that they were able to dispute with the Messenger (peace be upon him) and to nullify his proofs, and then they would forbid people from believing.

Al-Wahidi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he named some of these: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and Umayya and Ubayy, the two sons of Khalaf. They gathered before the Prophet (ﷺ) listening to the Qur'an. When they heard it, they said to al-Nadr: "What is Muhammad saying?" He said: "By the One who made it His house" (meaning the Kaaba), "I do not know what he is saying, except that I see the movement of his lips. He says nothing but the fables of the ancients, like what I used to tell you about the past generations." This means that he said that out of arrogance toward the truth and envy of the Messenger (peace be upon him). al-Nadr was one who often narrated about the ancient generations, and he would tell the Quraysh tales of the non-Arabs, such as the stories of (Rustam) and (Isfandiyar), and they would find his narration pleasing. He was a man who travelled to the lands of Persia. al-Nadr was intensely hostile to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he is the one whose blood the Messenger (peace be upon him) declared lawful to shed; he was killed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah.

It is reported that Abu Sufyan said to them: "I truly think it is true." Abu Jahl said to him: "No!" So God described their condition with this verse. God benefited Abu Sufyan ibn Harb by this word of his, for he alone among them embraced Islam on the night of the Conquest of Makkah, and he gained the merit of companionship and the in-law relationship with the Prophet (ﷺ), through his wife Hind bint ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa.

Al-Akinna (the coverings) is the plural of kinan, with the kasra on the kaf. The pattern afʿila is specifically required for fiʿal with a kasra on the first radical when its second and third radicals are identical. Al-kinan means a covering, because it conceals (yakunn) the thing, that is, shields it. Here it is figurative: the hearts are likened, in that the truth does not reach them, to things hidden from something, and "coverings" is attributed to them figuratively, though there is nothing in a person's heart resembling a kinan.

The attribution of making this condition in their hearts to God Most High is because He created them with this blameworthy trait and a deviated reasoning. They have intellects and perception, because they are like the rest of mankind, but their desires chose for them the prevention from following the truth. Therefore they were addressed with belief, even though God knows that they will not believe, given that they were of that attribute. Moreover, the address of obligation is general, with no specification for particular people and no exception for particular people in it. So "making" (jaʿl) here means "creating," and it is not for transformation from one state to another. All those named died in polytheism except Abu Sufyan, for he at that time testified that what he had heard was true, and his testimony indicated the soundness of his heart from the coverings.

The object pronoun in "an yafqahuhu" (that they understand it) refers to the Qur'an, understood from His saying "listens to you." The preposition has been omitted; the estimate is "min an yafqahuhu" (from their understanding it), and it is connected to "akinna" because of the sense of prevention in it, meaning coverings that prevent them from understanding the Qur'an.

Al-waqr, with a fatha on the waw, is severe deafness. Its verb, like waʿada and wajada, is used intransitively, as one says waqarat udhunuhu (his ear became deaf), and transitively, as one says waqara Allah udhunahu fa-waqarat (God made his ear deaf, so it became deaf). Al-waqr is a non-analogical verbal noun for the intransitive waqarat udhunuhu, since the analogical form of its verbal noun is with a moved qaf; it is analogical for the transitive waqara. It is used metaphorically for failing to understand what is heard. The failure to understand is made equivalent to deafness, and no complement is mentioned for al-waqr indicating what is prevented, namely, "by the deafness of their ears," because it is evident that it is from their hearing it, since the waqr implies that, and because the intended hearing is figurative, which is knowledge of what the heard thing contains.

His saying "over their hearts" and His saying "in their ears" are both connected to "We have placed." Each of them is placed before the object of "We have placed," to draw attention to its connection to it from the outset.

If you say: could this verse be evidence for those of our scholars who said that the inimitability of the Qur'an is by *ṣarfa* (divine diversion), that is, God made the polytheists unable to oppose it by diverting them from attempting to oppose it, so that the proof would be established against them, and the diversion would be among the coverings that God placed over their hearts? I say: the proponents of that view did not argue with this verse, for you have known that the coverings are figurative, that the deafness is a metaphor, and that al-Nadr's saying "I do not know what I should say" is calumny and arrogance. Therefore God Most High said: ﴿And even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it.﴾

The word "kull" (every) here is used figuratively for abundance, because the literal meaning is impossible, whether the impossibility is rational, as in this verse and in His saying: ﴿So do not incline with complete inclination﴾ [al-Nisa': 129], since the individual signs are limited, being determined individuals that become manifest when they come into existence, as they are of a general genus; or the impossibility is customary, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Over it is every dhayyal and khansa' that grazes toward every rajjaf of the sand, a lone one."

For custom makes it impossible for all the oryxes of the wild to gather in this place. So it is impossible for the people to see every individual of what could be a sign; therefore "kull" here means a great abundance, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if you brought those who were given the Book every sign﴾ [al-Baqara: 145] in Surat al-Baqara.

"Hatta" (until) is a particle set to indicate the limit, that is, what follows it is the limit of what precedes it. The original use of "hatta" is as a preposition like "ila" (to), so that a singular noun whose meaning is the limit of what precedes "hatta" comes after it. It may depart from this, and a sentence comes after "hatta," so that "hatta" is initial (ibtidaʾiyya), meaning it signals the beginning of a speech whose content is the limit of a speech before "hatta." Therefore Ibn al-Hajib said in al-Kafiya that it indicates causality. So the meaning is not that their listening extends to the time of their coming, nor that the placing of coverings on their hearts and deafness in their ears extends to the time of their coming; rather, the meaning is that their listening without understanding causes [their coming and disputing]. And the deafness in their ears and the coverings on their hearts [are such that] when they come to you, they dispute with you.

"Hatta" is called initial because what follows it is in the position of a new, independently begun speech. Something close to this comes up at His saying: ﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have lost, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 31] in this surah, and a further clarification of the meaning of initial "hatta" comes at His saying: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie?﴾ [al-An'am: 144] up to His saying: ﴿until when Our messengers come to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 37], etc., in Surat al-A'raf.

"Idha" (when) is a conditional temporal particle. "Jaʾuka" (they come to you) is its condition, and it is the governing element for it. The clause "yujadilunaka" (they dispute with you) is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the pronoun of "jaʾuka," meaning they come to you disputing, that is, intending the dispute with you, showing their people that they are equal to this dispute.

The clause "yaqulu" (says) is the answer to "idha." The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun in His saying ﴿those who disbelieve say﴾

to add emphasis on them with disbelief, and that they did not come seeking the truth as they claim, but they entered with disbelief and left with it. So they say: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, and thus they turned from disputation to bewilderment and arrogance.

"Asatir" is the plural of "usṭura," with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the sin, and it means a story and a report about the past. The more evident view is that "usṭura" is a word Arabicized from Roman (Greek), its origin being "isṭuriya" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning a story. What indicates this is the variation of the Arabs in it: they said usṭura, usṭīra, usṭūr and usṭīr, all with a damma on the hamza, and isṭāra and isṭār with a kasra on the hamza. Variation in the vowels of a single word is among the signs of arabicization. Among their sayings: "A foreigner—so play with it as you wish." The best of the forms for it is usṭura, because it matches a pattern that conveys the meaning of the passive participle, that is, "the story that has been written down" (al-qiṣṣa al-masṭūra), and it conveys fame in the meaning of its root, like al-uʿjūba (the marvel), al-uḥdūtha (the tale), and al-ukrūma (the honor). It was also said: "asatir" is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) with no singular, like ababil, ʿabadid and shamatit. The Arabs used it for what people chat about with stories and reports of various kinds, true or false. They did not distinguish between histories, stories and fables, so all of that is charged with falsehood and exaggeration. So their saying ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ may mean that they intended to attribute the reports of the Qur'an to falsehood according to what they had come to believe about fables. It may also mean that the Qur'an does not go beyond being a collection of stories and fables, meaning that it does not deserve to be from God, since, due to the deficiency of their understanding or their ignorance, they turn away from the lesson intended by those stories and take them as the fables with which people pass the time to shorten the hours. It will come in Surat al-Anfal that the one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and that he used to compare the Qur'an to the reports of (Rustam) and (Isfandiyar).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 26:

﴿And they forbid others from it, and keep away from it themselves; and they destroy none but themselves, though they perceive it not.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [al-An'am: 25], and the two pronouns in the genitive refer to the Qur'an, indicated by the demonstrative in their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. The meaning of "forbidding from it" is forbidding from listening to it. This is from attaching the judgment to the essence (min taʿlīq al-ḥukm bi-l-dhāt), and what is meant is one of its states, which the context specifies.

Page 183

Likewise, "keeping away from it" means keeping away from listening to it, that is, they forbid the people from listening to it and distance themselves from listening to it. Al-Nabigha said:

"Indeed I forbade the Banu Dhubyan from Uqur, and from their pasturing in every season of spring."

He means: I forbade them from grazing in Dhu Uqur, which is the protected pasture (ḥimā) of the king al-Nuʿman ibn al-Ḥarith al-Ghassani. Between his saying "yanhawna" and "yanʾawna" there is a near-complete paronomasia (al-jinas al-qarīb min al-tamām).

The restriction (al-qaṣr) in His saying ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ is a relative restriction (qaṣr idāfī), which serves to reverse their belief, because they assume that by forbidding and keeping away from the Qur'an they harm the Prophet ﷺ, so that people will not follow him and they will not follow him. In fact, they destroy only themselves by persisting in misguidance and by misleading the people, so they bear their own burdens and the burdens of the people. In this sentence there is also consolation for the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and that whatever they intended as harm to him, they are only harming themselves by it.

The origin of destruction (halāk) is death, and it is applied to severe harm, because the common view among people is that death is the greatest harm. So what is meant by destruction here is what they encounter in this world of killing and humiliation when Islam prevails, and in the Hereafter of punishment.

Al-nay' means distance. It is intransitive and does not take a direct object except with a preposition; what occurs as transitive without a preposition is by way of omission and transitivization under poetic necessity.

He follows His saying ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ with His saying "though they perceive it not", as an addition in confirming the error in their belief, and to display the weakness of their minds, even though they used to count themselves leaders of the people. Therefore the best view is that the waw in His saying "wa-mā yashʿurūna" is for coordination (ʿatf), not for circumstance (ḥāl), so that this indicates that what follows it is intended as an independent statement, because people regard them as the greatest of their wise men.

[Page 184]

The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), because the report that follows contains consolation for him regarding what was implied in His saying: ﴿and they forbid others from it, and keep away from it themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 26]. He began with that, then followed it with ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 26], and then added a depiction of their condition on the Day of Resurrection. Every person who hears this report shares this address with the Messenger.

"Law" (لَوْ) is conditional, meaning "if you were to see now." "Idh" (إذْ) is temporal. The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, indicated by the pronoun in "waqafu," meaning "if you were to see them." "Waqafu" is past in form, but its meaning is future, i.e., "when they will be made to stand." The past form is used to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, since it comes from One whose report is beyond dispute.

The meaning of ﴿they were made to stand over the Fire﴾ is that they were brought to it after being driven toward it. The verb takes "ʿalā" (over/upon). The sense of elevation conveyed by "ʿalā" is figurative, meaning the strength of connection with the place. Therefore "ʿalā" does not indicate that their standing over the Fire was from its upper part. God, Exalted, has said: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 30]. The origin of this usage is from the Arabic saying: "I stopped my mount at Zayd," meaning I reached him and held back my camel from moving. Dhu al-Rummah said:

I stopped my camel at the abode of Mayya, and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it.

They omitted the object of "waqaftu" because of its frequent use. It is said: "waqafahu fa-waqafa" (he stopped him, and he stopped), but one does not say "awqafahu" with the hamzah.

The verb "fa-qalu" (then they said) is joined to it with "fa" (then), which indicates sequence, because they had already recognized, from the terror they witnessed, that it was the recompense for their denial, either through an inspiration that God placed in their hearts or through the report of the angels of punishment. So they hastened and wished that they might be returned.

The vocative particle in their saying ﴿O would that we were returned﴾ is used to express lamentation, because the vocative implies the distance of the one addressed. It is therefore used for lamentation, since the object of their wish has become far from them, that is, no longer beneficial to them, like God's saying: ﴿lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected regarding God's side"﴾ [al-Zumar: 56].

The meaning of "nuradd" (we are returned) is "we return to the worldly life." It is joined to it by ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers﴾. In the reading of the majority, both verbs are in the indicative after the negating "la," as a conjunction to "nuradd." Thus it is part of what they wished for. For this reason it is not put in the subjunctive as the answer to a wish, since the intended meaning is not a condition. Also, treating it as a conditional answer with "wa" (and) is not well known, unlike with "fa" (then), because "fa" is fundamentally indicative of causation. Return is not intended for its own sake; they wished for it only because of the faith and the abandonment of denial that would accompany it. The mention of abandoning denial before faith is because it is the basis for attaining what is wished for, on the reading that "wa" carries the sense of accompaniment, standing in the place of the causal "fa" in the answer to the wish.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and not deny and be﴾ with both verbs in the subjunctive, as they are governed in the answer to the wish. Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿and not deny﴾ in the indicative like the majority, meaning that the absence of denial is present at the time of their speech, so it is not future, and therefore it does not require the implied "an" (that), which indicates the future. He read "wa-nakuna" (and be) in the subjunctive as an answer to the wish, meaning "that we might be among the people known as believers." The meaning does not differ.

God's saying ﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from their saying ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers﴾. The meaning of "bal" (nay) is that there is no longer any hope left for them of deliverance. "Bada al-shay'" means it appeared. It is said: "bada lahu al-shay'," when it appeared to him directly. Here it is figurative for the removal of doubt about something, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

It has become clear to me that I will not overtake what has passed, nor precede anything that is coming.

Since "bada lahum" (there appeared to them) in this verse is paired with ﴿what they used to conceal﴾, we know that the appearance is the manifestation of a matter in their souls which they used to conceal in the worldly life. That is, the thought that they used to conceal came to them at that time, that is, it occurred to their minds that it would happen, and they did not declare it. Then it appeared to them now, so they declared it and confessed to it openly. In the speech there is ihtibak, a rhetorical device in which one element is omitted from each of two parts that correspond to each other. Its estimated form is: "Nay, there appeared to them what used to appear to them in the world, so they now showed it, and they used to conceal it." The reason is that faith would occur to them because of the proofs they saw or the victory of the believers, but stubbornness held them back from it, along with the desire to preserve leadership, the aversion to acknowledging the virtue of the Messenger, and the believers' precedence in good deeds before them. Among the believers were the weak of the people and their servants, as we have mentioned at God's saying ﴿and do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52] in this surah. This meaning was indicated by God's saying: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieve will wish they had been Muslims﴾ [al-Hijr: 2] in Surat al-Hijr. This explanation makes unnecessary the many possibilities over which the exegetes became perplexed, which do not suit the arrangement of the verse. Some of them are supported by its beginning, some by its end, and none is supported by all of it.

God's saying ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden﴾ is an escalation in refuting their claim, to the point that it stands as a dialectical concession in debate. That is: even if their wish were granted and they were returned to the world, they would revert to the matter the Prophet had forbidden them, which is denial and rejection of the Resurrection. This is because their souls, which denied in the past out of obstinacy after the clear signs had come, are the same souls that will be returned to them on the Day of Resurrection. So the intellect is the same intellect and the reasoning is the same reasoning. They only wished what they wished because of the intensity of the terror, and imagined that they would escape it by this wish. But if their wish were fulfilled and they were returned and relieved of that terror, their desires would overcome their right guidance, so they would forget what had befallen them and return to what they had become accustomed to of denial and obstinacy.

In this there is evidence that thoughts arising from the influences of the senses, rather than from reflection and proof, have no stability in the soul and do not act upon their demands except for as long as that sensation lasts. When it ceases, its effect ceases. So being moved by it resembles the reaction of dumb animals to reproof, the whip, and the like. It disappears with its disappearance, until a similar stimulus returns.

God's saying ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding affirmation) to what precedes it. It is expressed in a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and stability, meaning: lying is their disposition, to which they became habituated in the world. So it is no wonder that they wish to be returned in order to believe. But if they were returned, they would revert to what they were upon, for lying is their nature. Their wish has included a promise, so it is correct to include it under their lying, as a specific falls under a general, because the tadhyil indicates that what it concludes includes that and more. Therefore, describing them as liars does not refer back to the wish alone, but to what it contains of a promise of belief and of not denying God's signs.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 6, verse 29:

﴿And they say, "There is only our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected."﴾

It is permissible for this to be coordinated ('atf) with His saying ﴿and [if they were returned] they would return to what they were forbidden﴾, in which case it is the answer to "law" (jawab law), meaning: [Page 187] "Even if they were returned, they would deny the Qur'an as well, and they would deny the resurrection just as they did during their first life." It is also permissible that this sentence is coordinated with the sentence ﴿those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the myths of the ancients"﴾, and that what lies between the two sentences is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) relating to the denial of the Qur'an.

As for His saying إنْ هي, the إنْ is negating the genus (nafiyah li-l-jins), and the pronoun after it is ambiguous (mubham), explained by what follows the exceptive particle in the "incomplete" construction (al-istithna' al-mufarragh). Its ambiguity was intended for brevity (al-ijaz), relying on the explanation that follows it. Since the pronoun is explained by an indefinite noun (nakirah), it has the status of an indefinite noun. It is not the pronoun of the matter and situation (damir al-qissah wa al-sha'n), because the meaning of the exceptive construction does not hold with it. The meaning is: "The life for us is nothing but our life of this world," that is, the genus of our life is restricted to our life of this world, so there is no life for us other than it, and thus life after death is nullified. Accordingly, the noun that comes after إلّا has the status of a substitute (badal) for the pronoun.

The clause ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾ is a negation of the resurrection, and this necessarily entails the emphatic negation of any life other than the life of this world, because resurrection cannot occur except with life. It was coordinated rather than separated, so that it would serve as an emphasis for the preceding clause, because their intention was to nullify the statement of the Messenger (ﷺ), "They will live a second life," and his other statement, "They will be resurrected after death." So they intended to nullify each of them independently.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 30:

﴿Had you but seen when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say: "Is this not the truth?" They will say: "Yes, by our Lord!" He will say: "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾

When he (Allah) mentioned their denial of the Resurrection (al-ba'th), He followed it with a description of their state when they are gathered (yuhsharun) to Allah, which is the very state of the Resurrection they denied.

The discussion regarding the address (al-khitab), the meaning of "they were made to stand" (wuqifu), and the answer to "law" (law, "had you but seen") has already passed in its theory (nazariyyatiha) a moment ago. The linking of "before their Lord" (ʿala rabbihim) to "were made to stand" (wuqifu) is a figurative expression (tamthil) for their presence at the place of gathering at the time of the Resurrection. Their state of being present for reckoning is likened to the state of a servant who has committed a wrong, was seized, and was made to stand before his Lord. By this, the distinctive value of expressing it with the word "their Lord" (rabbihim) rather than the name of majesty (Allah) becomes apparent.

The clause "He will say: 'Is this not the truth?'" (qala alaysa hadha bil-haqq) is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because His saying "Had you but seen when they were made to stand" has already announced a great and awe-inspiring scene, so it is fitting that the listener asks: "What did they encounter from their Lord?" And the answer is given: "He said: 'Is this not the truth?'" – the verse.

The indication is to the Resurrection which they witnessed and saw with their own eyes. The interrogative here is confirmatory (taqriri), entering upon the negation of a matter that is being affirmed, in order to test the extent of the one questioned in acknowledging it. Therefore, one asks about the negation of what is actually occurring, because if he had any hope of denying it, he would resort to the negation contained in a question that confirms. The intended meaning is: "Is this the truth?", since they used to claim that it was falsehood. For this reason, they answered with the particle designed to nullify what precedes it, which is "bala" (yes/indeed). It negates the negation, so it is an affirmation that the matter has occurred, i.e., "Yes, it is the truth." They reinforced this with an oath, to confirm their acknowledgment of what they were acknowledging, since it is known to Allah, the Exalted; that is, "We affirm it and have no doubt about it, and therefore we swear to it."

This is from the use of an oath to emphasize a necessary implication of the information conveyed.

The phrase "He said: 'Then taste the punishment'" (qala fadhuqu al-adhab) is separated (fasl) in the manner of the separation of dialogues. The fa' (then) is either for consequence upon their speech, or a fa' of eloquence (fa' fasihah), meaning: "Since this is the truth, then taste the punishment for your disbelief," i.e., in the Resurrection.

The ba' (bi-) is causal (sababiyyah), and ma (ma) is verbal-masdarian (masdariyyah), meaning: "because of your disbelief," i.e., in this. The tasting of punishment is a metaphor (isti'arah) for feeling it, because tasting is the strongest of the direct senses of the body, so the sensation of the skin is likened to it.

This is a new continuation with a new commentary section.

It is a resumptive statement that expresses wonder at their condition when, on the Day of Resurrection, they fall into punishment for persisting in the disbelief that their belief in the denial of resurrection emboldened them to sustain. So they taste the punishment for this. That is a state by which they deserve to be described as: ﴿they have lost and failed﴾.

As for loss (khusran), its discussion was already presented at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 20] in this surah.

[Page 189]

The loss here is the deprivation of the goods of the Hereafter, not of this world. Those who denied the meeting with God are those about whom He related, saying: ﴿And they said, "There is only our life of this world"﴾ [al-An'am: 29]. So the apparent requirement would be the pronoun, following His saying ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-An'am: 27] and what follows it, saying: "They have lost." But He shifted to the explicit noun so that the statement would be self-standing, and so that upon it would be built the detail contained in the relative clause, with His saying ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ and so on.

The meeting with God is the manifestation of the effects of His pleasure and His anger without delay, without respite, and without protection by the customary means of the order of this worldly life. Since the otherworldly realm, which is what follows resurrection, is the realm of the manifestation of realities through their effects without impediments, and those realities are the supreme purpose of God, which He made the realm of the perfection of realities, He made the arrival there analogous to the meeting of the possessor of right after a long absence and independence from him. For this reason resurrection is called the encountering of God, the meeting with God, and the going to God and coming to Him, in many verses and prophetic expressions. Otherwise, people in this world are in the grip of God's disposal; if He willed, He would take them to Himself and hasten their recompense to them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they hasten for good, their term would have been decreed for them﴾ [Yunus: 11]. But when He gave them respite and led them on gradually in this worldly realm, and encouraged and warned, promised and threatened, the condition of people in it became like the condition of slaves to whom a command comes from their master, who is absent from them, encouraging them and warning them. Some of them comply and some of them disobey, and at that time they receive neither recompense for obedience nor punishment for disobedience, because He gives them respite and delays them. So when this world is folded up and the second life comes, people enter another order, the order of the manifestation of effects without delay. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. So they are like slaves who meet their Lord after they had been absent and given respite. Thus "meeting" is a metaphorical allegory (isti'ara tamthiliyya): it likens the state of creation at the arrival at the execution of God's promise and threat to the state of slaves at the presence of their master after an absence, so that He may recompense them for what they did during the period of absence. This allegory became common in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ), as he said: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him." And in the Qur'an: ﴿to warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [Ghafir: 15].

As for His saying ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾: "until" (hatta) here is ibtida'iyya (introductory, a "hatta" that introduces a new clause, not expressing a limit), and it does not express a terminus but expresses causation, as Ibn al-Hajib explicitly stated. That is, "so when the Hour comes upon them suddenly." Some exegetes made the arrival of the Hour a terminus for the loss, and that is invalid, because the loss intended here is their loss on the Day of Resurrection; as for in this world, there are some of them who have lost nothing. A discussion of the introductory "hatta" was already presented at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it, until, when they come to you, they dispute with you﴾ [al-An'am: 25] in this surah. An explanation of the meaning of "hatta" will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God or denies His signs?﴾ [al-A'raf: 37] up to His saying ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 37] in Surat al-A'raf.

"As-Sa'ah" (the Hour) is a proper name by predominance for the hour of resurrection and gathering.

"Al-Badhta" (suddenness) is a form (fa'la) from "al-bagt," which is a verbal noun. "Baghathahu al-amr" means when a matter befalls him suddenly, without anticipation, without notice, and without the appearance of a figure or the like. So in "al-bagt" there is the meaning of arrival without warning. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), because a verbal noun comes as a circumstantial state when its interpretation as an active participle is apparent, and this returns to the reporting of the verbal noun for the purpose of emphasis.

His saying "they said" (qalu) is the answer to "idha" (when). "Ya hasratana" (O our regret!) is a vocative used for the purpose of wonder and lamentation. In its original form it is a call to regret, by treating it as a person who hears and is called to be present, as if he says: "O regret, be present! For this is the time of your presence." From it come the expressions "Would that I had done such-and-such" and "Alas for me" (ya asafi or ya asafa), as was mentioned just before.

They attributed the regret to themselves so that their lamentation would be on account of themselves; they are both the lamenting ones and the ones over whom lament is made. This differs from the speaker's saying "O regret!", for that is generally a lament on account of others, so he laments over the condition of others. For this reason "'ala" (over) comes with it, the particle that enters upon the object for which one laments, entering here upon what indicates something other than lamentation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30]. But with "ya hasrati" or "ya hasrata," "'ala" comes only to enter upon the matter that was the cause of the lamentation, as here: "over what we neglected concerning it." Similar to this are the expressions "O woe is me!" and "O woe is my condition!" He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they say, "O woe to us!"﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. But when the speaker wants that the woe is for another, he says "Woe to you," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Woe to you! Believe﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17], and they say "Woe is to you."

[Page 191]

"Al-Hasrah" is intense regret, which is anguish, and it is a form (fa'la) from "hasira yahsaru hasaran," of the pattern "fariha," and it is said "tahassara tahassuran." The Arabs treat the noun of the single instance as if it were the general verbal noun, not considering the meaning of the single instance in it, but they regard the verbal noun as included in a single individual, like the referent of the generic definite article. For this reason this consideration is fitting in the context of the vocative, because the verbal noun is a name for what is achieved by the act, unlike the noun of the single instance, which is a name for one individual of the verbal noun, so it stands in place of the quiddity.

"Farrata-na" (we neglected) means we wasted. It is said "farrata fi al-amr" when one is careless about a thing and does not guard it, or in acquiring it until it escapes him and slips away from him. It is transitive to its object directly, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. Most often it is transitive with the particle "fi," so one says "farrata fi malihi" (he neglected his wealth) when he wasted it.

"Ma" is a relative pronoun whose referent is the good deeds. The object of "farrata-na" is omitted and refers back to "ma." Its estimated form is "ma farratanahu" (what we neglected of it), and the pronoun "hum," as an antecedent of general reference like its counterpart, means: we regret wasting everything that by its nature would have benefited us, so we neglected it. The pronoun in "fiha" refers to the Hour. The "fi" is causal (ta'lilliyya), meaning: what we let slip of beneficial deeds for the sake of the benefit of this Hour. It is also possible that "fi" is for transitivity, with an omitted noun governing the pronoun, meaning: in its goods. The meaning would be "over what we neglected in the Hour," meaning what they witnessed of the salvation and bliss of the people of success. It is also possible that the pronoun of "fiha" refers back to the worldly life, so that "fi" is for true locative sense (zarfiyya haqiqiyya).

The clause ﴿and they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of "qalu" (they said), meaning they said that in a state in which they bear their burdens. So they are between anguish over neglecting good deeds and faith, and between suffering the punishment for the sins they committed. That is, they were not merely deprived of the good of that day; rather, they were additionally exhausted and burdened with punishment.

"Al-awzar" is the plural of "wizr" with a kasra on the waw, which is a heavy load, and its verb is "wazara yazir," meaning he carried. From it is His saying here: ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾. And His saying: ﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. "Wizr" has been applied to sin and crime because of the heaviness of its consequence on its perpetrator.

His saying ﴿and they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ is an allegory for the form of their distress because of their sins, by the condition of one who carries a heavy load. The mention of "upon their backs" here is for intensification in depicting the state, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. He mentioned the hands because earning is done by the hand, so it resembles imaginative (takhyil) metaphor, but imaginative depiction cannot occur in the allegory, because what is mentioned in it is suitable for being considered part of the whole form, since carrying on the back indicates the utmost heaviness of the load on the carrier.

Among the subtle points of this wording is the placement of the term "awzar" in this allegory, for it is shared between heavy loads and sins. They fell into this hardship only because of their sins, so it is as if they carry them, since they suffer the severity of their pains.

The clause ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil).

"Ala" is a particle of opening that indicates attention to draw attention to the news. "Sa'a ma yazirun" is an expression of blame. "Yazirun" means "yahmilun" (they carry), meaning: evil is what their condition is depicted as being, by carrying. "Ma yazirun" is the subject of "sa'a." The object of blame is omitted, its estimated form being: their load.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 32:

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but amusement and diversion. But the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then reason?﴾.

When the mention of the Hour was made, and of what the polytheists would suffer in it of regret over what they neglected (ma farraṭū), it was fitting to remind people that the life of this world is transient and that they must prepare themselves for the life to come. It is therefore possible that this verse is a response to the words of the polytheists, ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-An'am: 29]. In that case the wāw is for the circumstantial (li'l-ḥāl), meaning: you say, "There is nothing but our life of this world," whereas if you looked with true looking, you would find the life of this world to be amusement and diversion, and there is nothing lasting in it. Then you would know that behind it is another life, containing good things greater than those of this world, which only the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn), i.e. the believers, attain. Thus the verse is a renewal of their call to faith and piety, and the address in ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is a shift (iltifāt) from speaking about them in the third person to addressing them directly in the call.

It is also possible that it is an interjected concluding clause (i'tirāḍ bi'l-tadhyīl) appended to the account of their state in the Hereafter. For when He related their saying, ﴿Alas for us, that we neglected it in it﴾, the listener knows that they neglected the beneficial matters for the Hereafter because of their absorption in the adornments of this world. So this is appended with an address to the believers, to define the worth of the adornments of this world and to give them good news that the Hereafter is the abode of goodness for the believers. Thus the wāw conjoins the clause of glad tidings to the account of warning. The connecting factor (munāsabah) is antithesis. Also, in this there is a rebuke of the foolishness of their minds, for the world deceived them, so that they came to regard the call of Allah to the truth lightly. Accordingly, his saying ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ may be taken as a new address to the believers, warning them lest the adornments of this world deceive them and distract them from working for the Hereafter.

This judgment is general over the kind of the life of this world; the definite article in "al-ḥayāh" is the definite article of genus (ta'rīf al-jins), meaning the life which every person lives, known as "the worldly" (al-dunyā), i.e. the first and nearest to people. The expression "the life of this world" is applied to its conditions, or to its duration.

Al-la'ib (play): an action or speech carried out with lightness, haste and frivolity, having no beneficial aim; rather its aim is relaxing the mind, shortening time, and attracting minds in a state of weakness, like the mind of a child or of one who is exhausted. Most of it is the activity of children. They said that for this reason it is derived from al-lu'āb, which is the child's saliva flowing. The opposite of play is seriousness (al-jidd).

Al-lahw (diversion): what a person occupies himself with, of which his soul finds comfort and whose occupation does not tire his mind. It is therefore applied only to that which contains enjoyment, pleasure, and agreeableness to desire.

Between lahw and la'ib there is a partial general-and-specific relationship (al-'umūm wa'l-khuṣūṣ al-wajhī). They meet in an activity that is agreeable and accompanied by some lightness and frivolity, such as merriment and diversion with women. Play is found exclusively in children's play; diversion is found exclusively in things like gambling and hunting.

The construction ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and diversion﴾ conveys a restriction (qaṣr) of life to play and diversion, a restriction qualified by an attribute. What is meant by "life" is the actions for which a person loves life, because life is a duration and time, which does not accept description except by time-attributes such as long or short,

Page 194
limited or its opposite; so it is determined that what is meant by "life" is the actions contained within it. "Play" and "diversion" are in the force of an adjective, since they are verbal nouns used to denote the attribute for emphasis, like the saying of al-Khansā':

"Indeed it is only advance and retreat."

This restriction is claimed (qaṣr idd'ā'ī), intended for emphasis, because the actions occurring in life are many, among them diversion and play, and among them other things. God, exalted, said: ﴿The life of this world is only play and diversion, adornment and boasting among yourselves, and rivalry in wealth and children﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 20]. Life includes many conditions, among them the agreeable such as eating and pleasures, and among them the painful such as illnesses and griefs. As for the painful, no account is taken of them here nor any attention paid to them, because they are not what the desirers desire; the intended meaning of mentioning life here is what occurs in it that people love it for, and that is the agreeable things.

As for the agreeable things, they are many, and among them are some that are not play or diversion, such as food and drink, warming oneself in winter, cooling oneself in summer, gathering wealth for one who is devoted to it, hospitality to the guest, striking the enemy, and giving good to the needy. However, since most of these require the exertion of resolve and work, they involve some weariness, which is repugnant. Thus most of what people love life for is diversion and play, since that predominates over the actions of people in the early part of life and prevails over them afterwards. From play come joking and flirting with women; from diversion come wine, gambling, singing-girls, tales, riding horses, and hunting.

As for their actions in acts of devotion such as the Hajj, the 'Umrah, vows, circumambulating the idols, the 'atīrah sacrifice and the like, these are joined to play because, since no account is taken of them without faith, they are classed with play, as God, exalted, said: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ [al-Anfāl: 35], and He said: ﴿Those who took their religion as diversion and play, and whom the life of this world deceived﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51].

Therefore it is inevitable that the predominant character of the polytheists, and of people generally, was play and diversion, except those who believed and did righteous deeds. Hence the claimed restriction occurs in his saying: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and diversion﴾.

He followed it with his saying: ﴿But the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah﴾, from which it is known that the actions of the God-fearing in

Page 195
this world are the opposite of play and diversion, because a different abode has been prepared for them which is better; and it is known that success therein is attained only through action in this world. So it follows that their action in this world is not diversion and play, and that the life of others is the one restricted to diversion and play.

Al-dār is the place where people dwell, being the land on which people's dwellings stand, whether of building, tents, or domes. Al-ākhirah is the feminine of the adjective al-ākhir (with kasrah on the kh), the opposite of al-awwal, meaning the final resting place of people, after which there is no further transfer.

The majority of the ten readers read (wa-li'l-dāru) with two lams, the lam of inception and the lam of definition, and they read (al-ākhirah) in the nominative. Ibn 'Āmir read (wa-la-dāru al-ākhirah) with the lam of inception only, and with the noun (dār) indefinite in annexation to (al-ākhirah); it is thus an annexation of the modified to the modifier, like the saying "masjid al-jāmi'," or it is on the assumption of an omitted noun, so that (al-ākhirah) is an adjective of it. The estimated phrase is: dār al-ḥayāh al-ākhirah.

(Khayr) is a comparative in respect of the world, considering the immediate, transient bliss of this world, most of which is followed by reckoning and punishment.

His saying ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ is an allusion to the polytheists that they will indeed go to the Hereafter, but it will not be better for them than what they had in this world. What is meant by "those who fear Allah" is the believers who follow what Allah commanded, as in His saying: ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], for the Hereafter is pure goodness for them. As for believers who are subject to reckoning for their evil deeds, since their final destination is ultimately Paradise, the Hereafter is better for them than the world.

His saying ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ is a conjunction with the fā' upon the clause ﴿And the life of this world...﴾ to its end, since the content of the conjoined clause follows from it. The interrogation about their not reasoning is used as reproach if the address is to the polytheists, or as warning if the address is to the believers. Yet since its use in either of these is by way of metonymy (kināyah), it is valid that both meanings be intended with respect to both groups, since metonymic implications may be multiple and their multiplicity does not entail homonymy, as their signification is by implication; moreover, we hold to the use of the homonym in both its senses.

Page 196
Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥafs, Abū Ja'far, and Ya'qūb read (﴿Will you not then reason?﴾) with the taa' of address, in the manner of iltifāt. The rest read it with the yā' of the third person, so on this reading it refers back to the third-person pronouns preceding it, and the interrogation then serves to express wonder at their state.

In his saying ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ there is a discouragement (ta'yīs) of the polytheists.

[p. 197]

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), whose purpose is to console the Messenger (ﷺ), to command him to be patient, to promise him victory, and to make him despair of the faith of the most stubborn among the disbelievers. It also promises him the faith of some of them, by His saying: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35], up to His saying "they hear." The context has been made ready for this purpose after the completion of the argument against the polytheists, refuting their polytheism and their denial of the Messenger's mission, and after the completion of the warning to them and the exposure of their obstinacy, beginning from His saying: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4] up to here.

The particle (*qad*) is a confirmation of the verbal statement. In confirming a verbal sentence, it has the same role as (*inna*) in confirming a nominal sentence. The particle (*qad*) is specific to entering upon inflected verbs that are declarative, affirmative, and free of a governing particle, a jussive particle, or the future particle (*sawf/sa-*), and the meaning of confirmation is always attached to it. The more correct view is that it is so whether the verb it governs is in the past or the present tense, and the meaning of (*qad*) does not differ with respect to the two verbs. It has spread among many grammarians that (*qad*) when it enters upon the present tense conveys the diminishing of the occurrence of the action. Some of them said that this is derived from the words of Sibawayh, and from the apparent sense of al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) in this verse. The verified position is that the words of Sibawayh indicate only that (*qad*) may be used to express diminution, but through a contextual indicator, and this is not its original signification. This is what I have deduced from their statements, and it is what I rely upon. Therefore there is no difference between (*qad*) entering upon the past tense and its entering upon the present tense in conveying the confirmation of occurrence, as al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated in his commentary on His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿He certainly knows what you are upon﴾ [al-Nur: 64] in Surat al-Nur. So the confirmation is considered in the past tense if the verb after (*qad*) is a past verb, and in the present or future time if the verb after (*qad*) is a present verb, together with what the context adds to the confirmation by way of indication, such as bringing the past time close to the present, as in the phrase: *qad qamati al-salat* ("the prayer has indeed been established"). This is a metonymy arising from addressing the confirmation of an action which the hearer would not normally doubt will occur. Also (*qad*) conveys frequency with the present tense, following what the present tense implies of continuity, as in the verse attributed by Sibawayh to al-Hudhali, which Ibn Barri verified belongs to 'Abid ibn al-Abras, and it is:

*Indeed I leave the foe with his fingertips yellowed,*
*as if his garments were stained with safflower dye.*

And the verse of Zuhayr:

*A trustworthy brother whom wine does not ruin of his wealth,*
*but whose gifts indeed do ruin wealth.*

And (*qad*) conveys the evoking of an image, as in the words of Ka'b:

*Indeed I stand in a station where, if the elephant were to stand in it,*
*I would see and hear what the elephant would not see or hear,*

*it would keep trembling, unless there were for it*
*a gift from the Messenger by God's permission.*

He intended the confirmation of his presence before the Messenger (ﷺ), together with evoking that wondrous state of awe mixed with hope.

The verified position is that the words of Sibawayh are free of what they attributed to him, and the confusion in the statements of the grammarians arose only from Ibn Malik's understanding of Sibawayh's words. Abu Hayyan refuted him with a sound refutation.

So the meaning of the verse is: "We know that what they say grieves you, confirmed, so be patient." I have previously made a statement on this question at His saying ﴿We indeed see the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144] in Surat al-Baqarah, but it was brief, and I referred to the commentary of the verse in Surat al-An'am. This is what my view has settled upon.

The verb (*na'lamu*, "We know") is suspended from operating upon two objects by the presence of the (*lam*) of confirmation.

By (*alladhi yaqulun*, "that which they say") is meant their statements which indicate their non-acceptance of the Messenger (ﷺ), as His saying after it indicates: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you﴾. He turned away from mentioning the word "denial" or the like, to the relative pronoun and its clause, to exalt the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, from mentioning this ugly word in relation to him, out of gentleness toward him.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read *layuhzinuka* with a dammah on the *ya'* and a kasrah on the *zay*. The rest read it with a fathah on the *ya'* and a dammah on the *zay*. It is said: *ahzantu al-rajul*, with the hamzah of transitivity to the verb *hazana*, and it is also said: *hazantuhu*. From al-Khalil: that *hazantuhu* means "I caused grief in him," just as it is said *dahantuhu* ("I anointed him"). As for transitivity, it is only by the hamzah. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: *hazantu al-rajul* is more frequently used, and *ahzantuhu* is more analogical. (*Alladhi yaqulun*) is their saying: "sorcerer," "madman," "liar," "poet." He turned away from detailing their saying to a general reference, for brevity, or out of reticence about stating it explicitly in regard to the one who is exalted above it.

The pronoun made the subject of (*inna*) is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), the (*lam*) is the lam of oath, the verb (*yuhzinuka*) is the verb of oath, and (*alladhi yaqulun*) is its subject. The (*lam*) in (*layuhzinuka*) is the lam of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*), and the clause (*yuhzinuka*) is the predicate of *inna*. The pronouns of the third person refer to those who disbelieved in His saying: ﴿Then those who disbelieved in their Lord make equals [with Him]﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

The *fa'* in His saying (*fa-innahum*) may be causal, the thing caused being omitted and indicated by His saying (*qad na'lamu*), meaning: "So do not grieve, for they do not deny you," that is, because they do not deny you. It may also be the *fa'* of the explanatory clause (*fasiha*), and the estimate is: "If that grieves you because of the denial, then they do not deny you." So God has consoled His Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, by informing him that the polytheists do not deny him, but rather they are people of rejection and obstinacy. That suffices as consolation. It may also be the *fa'* of consequence upon "We know," meaning: our knowledge of that entails that We establish your heart and expand your breast by informing you that they do not deny you, and by reminding you of the custom of the messengers before you, and reminding you that the outcome is your victory, as has preceded in the knowledge of God.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Ja'far read (﴿*la yukdhibunaka*﴾, "they do not discredit you"), with a sukun on the *kaf* and a lightening of the *dhal*. The majority read it with a fathah on the *kaf* and a shaddah on the *dhal*. Some of the masters of the language have said that *akdhaba* and *kadhdhaba* have one meaning, that is, to attribute lying to him. Some said: *akdhabahu* means "he found him to be a liar," just as it is said *ahmadahu* means "he found him praiseworthy." As for *kadhdhaba* with the shaddah, it is for attributing lying to the object. From al-Kisa'i: that *akdhabahu* has the meaning of *kadhdhaba* regarding what he brought, without attributing the object to lying, while *kadhdhabahu* means he attributed it to lying. This is the meaning of what is transmitted from al-Zajjaj: the meaning of *kadhdhabtuhu* is "I said to him: you lie," and the meaning of *akdhabtuhu* is "I showed him that what he brought is a lie."

His saying: ﴿But the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ is a *istidrak* (a corrective contrast), to prevent the misunderstanding that might arise from His saying ﴿they do not deny you﴾ according to the reading of Nafi' and those who agree with him, that they confirmed and believed; and according to the reading of the rest, ﴿they do not discredit you﴾, that the original act of denial did not proceed from them at all, though the reality is contrary to that. So it corrects this by stating that they deny the signs of God, so their state appears like that of one who attributes lying to the bearer of the signs, though they are not, in their souls, deniers.

The *jahd* and *juhud* mean denial of a known matter, that is, denial while knowing the occurrence of what is denied. So it is the negation of what the negator knows to be established, and so it is denial out of obstinacy.

He turned away from the pronoun to His saying: ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾, as a censure of them and an announcement that the nature of the wrongdoer is denial of the proof, and as a recording against them that wrongdoing is their disposition.

The verb *yajhadun* is transitive with the *ba'* just as it is in His saying: ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were certain of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14], to emphasize the connection of the denial to the object denied, like the *ba'* in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and in His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former ones denied them﴾ [al-Isra': 59], and in the saying of al-Nabigha:

*For you is goodness, if the earth covers you as one alone,*
*and the people's majority becomes lame, stumbling.*

Then, the denial of the signs of God is meant to refer to the denial of what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of the signs. And denying them is denying that they are from God's signs, that is, discrediting the one who brings them in His saying that they are from God. This ends in their denying the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace. How then can this be combined with His saying ﴿so they do not discredit you﴾ according to the reading of the majority? What is derived from the context of the verse is that the meaning is: they do not believe that you are a liar, because the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, was known among them for truthfulness, and he was called among them "the Trustworthy." Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said when Quraysh consulted about the affair of the Messenger: "O assembly of Quraysh, Muhammad was among you a youth most pleasing to you, and most truthful in speech among you, until when you saw grey hairs at his temples, you said: he is a sorcerer, and you said: he is a soothsayer, and you said: he is a poet, and you said: he is a madman. By God, he is not any of those." And because the signs he brought are not doubted by anyone to be from God, and because the indications of his truthfulness are clear and manifest, but you are wrongdoers.

The wrongdoer is the one who acts contrary to the truth without any doubt. So they deny the truth while knowing that it is the truth, and that is denial. God has informed about them of this, and He knows best their inner secrets. A parallel to it is His saying, related about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿and they denied them, wrongfully and arrogantly, though their souls were certain of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. So in the verse there is *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device of interlocking omission). The estimate is: "So they do not discredit you, nor do they discredit the signs, but they deny the signs and deny your truthfulness," so it omitted from each one because of the indication of the other.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Najiyah ibn Ka'b, a Successor (*tabi'i*), that Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We do not discredit you, but we discredit what you have brought." So God revealed: ﴿they do not discredit you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾.

I do not think this is the occasion of revelation of the verse, because if Abu Jahl did say that, he intended mockery, as Ibn al-'Arabi said in *al-'Aridah*: "That is because denying what he brought is necessarily denial of him. So his saying 'we do not discredit you' is mockery, with the hope of assent (*ibtam al-tasdiq*)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 34:

﴿And messengers were certainly denied before you, but they endured patiently what they were denied and were harmed, until Our help reached them. There is none who can alter the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you [some] news of the messengers.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿So they do not deny you﴾ [al-Anʿam: 33], or upon the clause ﴿but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Anʿam: 33]. It is also permissible that the waw be the waw of the circumstantial clause (wāw al-ḥāl) from the omitted speech before the fāʾ, meaning: "So do not grieve," or "If that grieves you, then they do not deny you, while [the situation is that] messengers were denied before you." The discourse, under every interpretation, is consolation, reassurance and honouring, in that the harm done by the people of polytheism to Muḥammad (ﷺ) is less than what the nations inflicted upon the messengers before him; for they denied [their messengers] both by speech and by belief, whereas his people denied only by speech alone. The discourse also contains an exhortation for the Messenger (ﷺ) to follow the example of the messengers who preceded him.

The oath particle (lām al-qasam) serves to emphasise the report, by treating the Messenger (ﷺ) as one who had long been oblivious to the denial of the messengers, because the words of his people had grieved him so much that he was as one whose knowledge of that had grown distant.

"Min qablika" (from before you) is a descriptive qualifier (waṣf kāshif) of "rusulun" (messengers), brought to establish the meaning of consolation: that this is the practice (sunnah) of the messengers.

The placement of this verse after the one preceding it contains an indication of the superiority of the intellects of the Arabs over those of the nations that came before them: for the nations denied their messengers through belief and the utterance of their tongues, whereas the Arabs denied with the tongue alone, and they were certain of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) through their intellects, in which counterfeit does not pass.

"Mā" is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyyah), meaning: they endured patiently the denial. It is permissible that his saying "wa-ūdhū" (and were harmed) be a conjunction upon "kudhdhibū" (were denied), with the clause "fa-ṣabarū" (so they endured) being parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah); the sense being: "And messengers were certainly denied and harmed, so they endured." Thus a pause is not observed at his saying "ʿalā mā kudhdhibū," but the speech is connected to his saying "naṣrunā." It may also be a conjunction upon "kudhdhibat rusulun," meaning: they were denied and were harmed. The patience under harm is understood from the patience under denial, because denial is a harm; hence a pause at his saying "ʿalā mā kudhdhibū" is appropriate.

He attached the verb "kudhdhibat" to the feminine marker, because when the subject of the verb is a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr), it is preferred to attach the verb to the feminine marker, in view of interpreting it as a group (jamāʿah). Hence the verbs "fa-ṣabarū" and "kudhdhibū" came with the plural waw, because their subjects are concealed pronouns, and so the consideration of the masculine was preferred.

He conjoined "wa-ūdhū" to "kudhdhibat" by the conjunction of the more general to the more specific (ʿaṭf al-aʿamm ʿalā al-akhaṣṣ), for harm is more general than denial, since harm is that which causes distress, even if it is some slight distress. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They will not harm you except with some minor harm﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 111], and it is also applied to its severe form. Thus "adhan" (harm) is a noun derived from "ādhā" when one makes harm for someone and attaches it to him; the hamzah in it is for making or causing. The verbal nouns of this verb are adhan, adhāh and adhiyyah, all of which are nouns of verbal action (asmāʾ maṣādir) and not verbal nouns in the strict sense. The regular verbal noun would be "īdhāʾ," but it has not been heard in the speech of the Arabs. Therefore the author of al-Qāmūs said: "It is not said: īdhāʾ." And al-Rāghib said: "It is said: īdhāʾ." Perhaps the disagreement is based on the disagreement over whether a regular (qiyāsī) form may be used even if it has not been heard in their speech, or whether its use depends upon hearing its type from its root. Whoever objected to the author of al-Qāmūs has wronged him. In any case, "al-īdhāʾ" is a word not eloquent, due to its strangeness. Indeed, the use of it here by the author of al-Kashshāf is counted against him, given his standing in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-balāghah).

"Ḥattā" is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), conveying the endpoint of what precedes it, namely the denial, the harm and the patience under them; for the help came by the destruction of the deniers and harmers, so it was an endpoint for the denial and the harm, and an endpoint for the specific patience, which is patience under denial and harm. The patience of the messengers over other matters that they were commanded to endure remains.

The coming in his saying "atāhum naṣrunā" (Our help came to them) is a metaphor for the help occurring after it was awaited; its occurrence is likened to arrival from a distant place, as the awaited caller arrives. The explanation of this has already been given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾ [al-Anʿam: 4] in this surah.

The clause ﴿and there is none who can alter﴾ is a conjunction upon the clause ﴿Our help came to them﴾.

"Kalimāt Allāh" (the words of Allah) is His revelation to the messengers, which indicates His promise to them of help, as the attribution of "naṣr" (help) to the divine pronoun also indicates. Thus what is meant is words of a particular kind, so it is not objected that some of the words of Allah in legislation may be altered by abrogation (naskh). Moreover, the negated alteration is a metaphor for annulment (naqḍ), as has been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 181] in Surat al-Baqarah. The verification of this meaning will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice; none can alter His words﴾ [al-Anʿam: 115] in this surah.

This is reassurance to the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah will help him just as He helped the messengers before him. It is also permissible that "kalimāt Allāh" refers to what He has written in His eternal knowledge and decreed of His ways among the nations, meaning that the destruction of the deniers occurs as the destruction of those before them occurred.

The negation of "al-mubaddil" is a metonymy for the negation of alteration, meaning: there is no alteration, because alteration only occurs from an alterer. Its meaning is that other than Allah is incapable of altering the will of Allah, and that Allah has willed that He not alter His words in this matter.

His saying ﴿And there has certainly come to you [some] news of the messengers﴾ is a conjunction upon the clause ﴿there is none who can alter the words of Allah﴾,

which is a comprehensive statement encompassing the details of what befell the deniers, and how the help of Allah came to His messengers. That is within the contents of what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning that.

The discussion of "jāʾaka" is like the discussion of "atāhum naṣrunā": it is a metaphor for the reaching of that and the informing of the Prophet (ﷺ) of it.

As for "min" in his saying "min naba'" (some news), it is either a noun meaning "some" (baʿḍ), in which case it is the subject, annexed to "naba'" (news), and it looks to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Of them are those We have related to you and of them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghāfir: 78]. The better view is to make it a qualifier of an omitted noun, whose implied sense is: "There has certainly come to you a news from the news of the messengers." And "naba'" is information about a great matter, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2], and He says: ﴿Say: It is a great news, from which you turn away﴾ [Ṣād: 67], and He says in this surah: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know﴾ [al-Anʿam: 67].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 35:

﴿And if their aversion is great to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign, [then do so]. And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿We know that what they say grieves you﴾ [al-Anʿam: 33], for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was grieved by what they said concerning him of denial of him and of the Qur'an: grief over the ignorance of his people regarding the worth of counsel and their rejection of the virtue of its bearer, and grief stemming from sorrow over them because of the continuation of their misguidance, out of compassion for them. Allah the Exalted consoled him regarding the first grief with His saying ﴿for they do not deny you﴾ [al-Anʿam: 33], and consoled him regarding the second with His saying ﴿And if their aversion is great to you﴾, to the end of the verse.

And (kabura) is like (karuma), kibaran like ʿinab: its body became large. The meaning of kabura here is "it was hard upon you." Its origin is largeness of body, then it was used figuratively for great and heavy matters, because largeness of body entails heaviness, then it was used figuratively in the sense of (shaqqa, "was difficult"), because a heavy thing is difficult to carry. So it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) with two connections.

In this conditional is used the particle (in), which is frequently used with a condition whose occurrence is not expected, to indicate that the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, is not one to whom that is likely, but it is by way of supposition.

Page 204

And (kana) was added after the conditional (in) between it and what is in meaning the verb of the condition, so that the verb of the condition retains the sense of the past; the conditional (in) does not bring it into the future, as is the case with verbs of conditions after (in). For (kana), because of the strength of its indication of the past, is not accepted by the conditional particle into the future.

The aversion defined by the annexation (iḍāfa) is that which was mentioned in His saying: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign of the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾ [al-Anʿam: 4]. It is another state distinct from the state of denial, and both are among the causes of the continuation of their disbelief.

His saying ﴿then if you are able﴾ is the response (jawab) of ﴿if their aversion is great﴾ [Yunus: 71], and it is a second condition that came as a response to the first condition. Istiṭāʿa (ability) is qudra (power). The sīn and tāʾ in it are for emphasis in ṭāʿa, i.e., submitted.

Ibtighāʾ (seeking) is ṭalab (request). It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 83] in Surat Āl ʿImrān; that is, that you seek a tunnel or a ladder so as to reach the hidden treasures of the earth and its wonders, and the hidden things of the sky. The meaning of seeking here is: searching.

Nafaqan and sullaman are in the accusative as the two objects of (tabtaghī).

The nafaq is a deep passage in the earth.

The sullam, with a damma then a fatḥa and a doubled lām, is an instrument for climbing, made of two thick parallel ropes between which are joined sticks or other scattered ropes across the breadth of the space between the two ropes, at the measure by which the climber raises one of his feet to the stick above that; these sticks are called rungs (darajāt). The length of the two ropes is made equal to the height to which one wishes to climb. The sullam is also called mirqāh and midraja.

They also called the stirrup by which the rider mounts onto the saddle of his camel a sullam. They used to climb with the sullam to the palm trees for harvesting dates. Perhaps the ladders in houses were made of wood, and they were called mirqāh. As for the stone stairs built in upper rooms, they are called sullam, and the step is called darajah, as in the ḥadīth of the killing of Abū Rāfiʿ, the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAtīk in one of the narrations: "until I reached a step of his," and in another narration: "until I came to the ladder, intending to descend, and I fell from it."

His saying "in the earth" is a qualifier of nafaq, i.e., penetrating, i.e., deep. He mentioned this prepositional phrase to convey exaggeration in depth together with evoking the state and depicting the state of ability, since it is known that a tunnel can only be in the earth.

As for His saying "in the sky," it qualifies sullam, i.e., existing in the sky, i.e., reaching to the sky. The meaning is: you reach by it to the sky, as in the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"And I ascended the causes of the sky by a ladder."

The meaning: if you are able to seek a sign from all directions for the creatures. Perhaps the choice of seeking in the earth and the sky is because the polytheists asked the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, for signs of the kind found on the earth, as in their saying ﴿until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 90], and of the kind found in the sky, as in their saying ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 93].

His saying (with a sign), i.e., with a sign by which they would submit, so there is an omitted qualifier indicated by His saying "their aversion," i.e., from the signs which you brought them.

The answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by the verb of the condition, which is "you are able."

The condition and its answer are used figuratively to express despair of their faith and their being persuaded, because Allah placed coverings upon their hearts and deafness in their ears, and even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it.

It is necessary to estimate the answer of the condition from what the preceding speech indicates, i.e., "then bring them a sign, for they will not believe in it," as one says to someone eager to satisfy a persistent person: "If you are able to bring what is in your house," i.e., he will not be content with what is beyond your ability, let alone what is within it. This is a common usage, and there is nothing in it of reproach or rebuke, as many commentators have imagined.

Page 206

His saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ is a counterfactual conditional (sharṭ imtināʿī) which indicates that Allah did not will that; that is, if Allah had willed to gather them upon guidance, He would have gathered them upon it. The object of the will is omitted for the purpose of clarification after ambiguity, following the established manner with the verb of will when its connection to its object is not strange and it is the condition for one of the conditional particles, as here, and as in His saying ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 133].

The meaning of ﴿gathered them upon guidance﴾ is: He would have guided them all. A variation in the style of expression occurred, so it became a particular construction, departing from the well-known construction as in His saying ﴿Then if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-Anʿam: 149], to indicate the distinction of those of the people of Makkah who believed from those among them who remained polytheists; that is, if He had willed, He would have gathered them together with the believers upon what He guided the believers of their people to.

The meaning: if Allah had willed to create them with intellects receptive to the truth, He would have created them with them, and they would have accepted guidance. But He created them according to what He described in His saying ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾ [al-Anʿam: 25], to the end of the verse, as its explanation has already passed. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾ [Hud: 118]. By this you know that this is a comprehensive, creative will, so there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying at the end of this surah: ﴿Those who associated will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers"﴾ [al-Anʿam: 148], to the end of the verse.
