For that is of the will related to creation and bringing into being, not of the will related to command and legislation. Between them is a great gulf, into which whoever was not granted protection has fallen.

His saying ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) branching from what preceded.

The intended meaning of "the ignorant" may be from ignorance which is the opposite of knowledge, as in His saying addressed to Noah: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46], and this is what the commentators have taken here. It may also be from ignorance which is the opposite of forbearance (ḥilm), i.e., do not constrict your chest over their aversion. This is more suitable to His saying ﴿And if their aversion is great to you﴾. Intending both meanings harmonizes with the implication of the two clauses: the clause ﴿And if their aversion is great to you﴾ and the clause ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾. Although this clause is a concluding clause to the preceding speech, the meaning is: let their aversion not be great to you, nor constrict your chest over it; and also, be aware that if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance. This is an informing from Allah the Exalted to His Messenger (ﷺ) of a matter from the knowledge of reality, which pertains to a particular situation, and so it is not generalized to other than that from positions of legislation.

He turned away from the command to knowledge because the prohibition against ignorance includes it, so it becomes firmly established in the mind twice; and because in the prohibition against ignorance of this there is an exhortation to keep knowledge of it present, as one says to a student: "Do not forget this issue." There is no prohibition in the speech concerning something the Messenger (ﷺ) was engaged in, as a group of commentators have imagined, and they went in it in directions that are not clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 36:

﴿Only those who listen respond. As for the dead, Allah will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.﴾

This is a reason (ta'lil) for what was conveyed by His saying, ﴿And if their aversion has been hard on you...﴾ [al-An'am: 35] up to His saying, ﴿so do not be among the ignorant﴾ [al-An'am: 35], by way of despairing of the call entering their souls. That is: only those who listen, apart from these whom He has deprived of the benefit of hearing and of understanding what is heard, respond.

The implication of the restriction (mafhum al-hasr) signals the activation of its explicit meaning, which hints at a deferral after despair: that Allah has given other people hearts with which they understand and ears with which they hear, so those will respond.

His saying yastajibu means yujibu (responds). The sin and the ta' are additional for emphasis. The discussion of this verb has already preceded at His saying, ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], in the surah of Al 'Imran. The object of yastajibu is omitted because it is clear from the context, since the context is the call to monotheism and the confirmation of the Messenger.

As for the meaning of yasma'un (they hear): they comprehend what is directed to them of guidance, because the misguided are like one who does not hear. The intended hearing is therefore a particular hearing, namely the hearing of reflection (sama' al-i'tibar).

As for His saying, ﴿and the dead, Allah will raise them﴾, the preferred view is that it stands in contrast to ﴿those who hear﴾. For this reason, the coordination of this clause upon the clause ﴿Only those who hear respond﴾ is apt. So the meaning of the speech is: as for those who turn away from you, they are like the dead, so they do not respond,

Page 208

like His saying, ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80]. The speech has omitted what the context indicates, for the one who does not hear may have lost his hearing due to an ailment such as deafness, and may also lack hearing due to not being alive, as 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam al-Thaqafi said:

"You would have made them hear, had you called out to a living one, but there is no life for one you call."

Thus the coordination of ﴿and the dead, Allah will raise them﴾ includes an allusion that these are like the dead, from whom no response is to be hoped. He then proceeds to their threat, that He will raise them after their death, that is: no return to the truth is to be hoped from them until they are raised, and then they will meet the recompense of their disbelief. "The dead" is a metaphor for those who do not benefit from their minds and faculties in the most important matters, which is what pleases Allah the Exalted. "Will raise them" on this reading is literal, and it is a tarshih (nurturing) for the metaphor, since raising is among the features that suit the likened-to (mushabbah bihi) in custom, although the living may be described as being raised, i.e. after his death; but custom mentions raising only in terms of describing the one raised as dead.

It is also permissible that the raising is itself a metaphor for guidance after misguidance, following the metaphor of death for the non-acceptance of guidance, according to the two well-known types of tarshih in the science of rhetoric (fann al-bayan): that it sometimes remains in its literal sense, its only purpose being to strengthen the metaphor; and sometimes it is borrowed from a feature suited to the likened-to into a counterpart suited to the likener, as in His saying, ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah all together﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. On this reading, the speech contains a promise to the Messenger ﷺ that some of these misguided deniers Allah the Exalted will guide to Islam, namely those whose deprivation of faith did not precede in His knowledge.

On the first reading, His saying ﴿then to Him they will be returned﴾ is an increase in threat and warning. On the second reading, it is an exhortation for them to believe, so that they may meet its reward when they are returned to Allah. It is also permissible that the pause be at His saying "Allah will raise them," and the illustration is complete there, and His saying ﴿then to Him they will be returned﴾ is a digression (istitrad) by which he moves on to rousing them regarding the gathering that takes place after the literal raising, so that "raising" in His saying "Allah will raise them" is used in both its literal and figurative senses. Close to this in transition is His saying, ﴿So We said: strike him with part of it; thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 73] in the surah of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 37:

[p. 209]
﴿They say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾
This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿And if their aversion has been grievous to you…﴾ [al-An'am: 35] and so on. This returns to what came at the beginning of the surah concerning their aversion to the signs of Allah, in His saying ﴿And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them but they turn away from it﴾ [al-An'am: 4]. Then He mentioned the excuses they varied in, from their saying ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8] and His saying ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. That is: they said, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him?", i.e., in accordance with their demand, and they had proposed various signs in many disputes. For this reason Allah the Exalted summarised them here, relying on their being known to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, so He said ﴿They say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾.

The clause ﴿They say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ has its conjunction placed as an interruption between the clause ﴿And the dead—Allah raises them, then to Him they will be returned﴾ [al-An'am: 36] and the clause ﴿And there is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies on its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38] etc. In the use of the verb "nuzzila" (was sent down) there is an indication that the sign requested is of the kind that comes from the sky, like their saying ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8], and their saying ﴿And we will not believe in your ascending until you send down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93], and what resembles that.

The verb "nuzzila" is left without the feminine marker because the feminine noun whose feminine marking is purely lexical permits stripping its verb of the feminine marker. When a separator falls between the verb and its subject, two justifications for stripping the verb of the feminine marker combine, since the separation alone justifies stripping the verb of the marker. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) explicitly stated that stripping the verb of the feminine marker is then good.

"Law" (لَوْلا) is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ) in the sense of "hallā" (why not). The urging here is for silencing the opponent and rendering him incapable, as was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And they say: "Why has not an angel been sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am: 8].

The derivation of "āya" (sign) was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[p. 210]
The verb "qul" (say) is separated and not conjoined, because it occupies the place of a dialogue, and so it follows the manner of separation (al-fasl) which we explained in many places, the first of which is His saying ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah commanded His Messenger to answer them with what makes known that if Allah had willed, He would have sent down a sign in accordance with their demand, by which the proof would be established against them concerning the affirmation of the Messenger; but Allah did not will that for a wisdom He knows. So He expressed this meaning by His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is able to send down a sign﴾, and they do not deny that Allah is able, which is why they asked for a sign; but they claim that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, is not established as truthful unless Allah supports him with a sign in accordance with their demand. Thus His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is able to send down a sign﴾ is used in its metaphorical (kinaʾi) meaning, namely the negation that Allah the Exalted wills to answer their demand, since when He sent His Messenger with clear signs, the purpose of establishing proof against those who disbelieved was achieved; so if He willed, He would have increased them in signs, because He is able.

In this manner of answer there is an affirmation of refutation by evidence, and with this the position of the istidrak (the corrective "but") in His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ becomes clear, for it refers to the implicit consequential meaning: that is, but most of the obstinate do not know that if Allah willed, He would have done it, and they suppose that not answering their demand is a sign of the untruthfulness of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace; and that is from the darkness of their minds, for there has come to them of the signs that which is sufficient to deter.

Thus the meaning conveyed by this refutation differs from the meaning conveyed by His saying ﴿And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, then they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-An'am: 8], for in that they were alerted that not answering them has a benefit for them, namely their being spared; whereas in this they were alerted to the bad consideration in their reasoning.

The explanation of that is that Allah the Exalted set up the signs as proofs suited to the matter being argued for, as the logicians say: the premises and the conclusion point by reason to the thing sought to be proven, and the conclusion is in reality the very thing sought, though it is other in consideration. Therefore we find the Qur'an mentions arguments for the great power of Allah to create great matters, such as bringing the living out of the dead and bringing the dead out of the living, in the context of arguing for the occurrence of resurrection and gathering. It calls those arguments "signs," as in His saying ﴿And He it is who produced you from a single soul, then there is a place of rest and a place of storage; We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-An'am: 98], and as will come at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. He also mentioned in the course of that the detailing of the signs up to His saying ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5]. Likewise is the mention of proofs for the oneness of Allah by His independence in creation, as in His saying ﴿And He created every thing, and He is knowing of all things﴾ [al-An'am: 101], ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him﴾ [al-An'am: 102], up to His saying ﴿Thus We vary the signs, and that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ [al-An'am: 105], etc.; and as His saying, in arguing for His sole right to the kinds of guidance, ﴿And He it is who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea; We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. And since the descent of the Qur'an upon the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, was a proof of his truthfulness in his report that it was sent down from Allah—because of what it contains of knowledge, detailed admonitions, the circumstances of the prophets and nations, and the legislation of rulings, together with the fact that the one who brought it was known among them to be unlettered, having spent his youth among them—He made it a sign of the Messenger's truthfulness, upon him be blessings and peace, in what he reported about Allah the Exalted; so He called it "signs" in His saying ﴿And when Our signs are recited to them as clear proofs, you recognise in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial; they nearly assault those who recite Our signs to them﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. Allah did not will to make the indications of things other than what suits them.

As for the ignorant and the astray, they seek signs of the wondrous transformations that break the order of the world, wishing that these be a token between them and Allah in accordance with their proposal, by His answering them with it as an indication from Him that he (the Messenger) told the truth in what he conveyed from Him. This is not of the kind of reasoning, but of the kind of gamble, so that they may claim that their not being answered in what they proposed is a sign that Allah did not confirm the Messenger ﷺ in his claim to prophethood. And whence do they have that Allah is pleased to descend with them into this arena? For this reason Allah the Exalted said ﴿Say: "Indeed Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know,"﴾ that is, they do not know what the connection is between the indication of the sign and what it indicates. For this reason He said in answering them in Surat al-Ra'd ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]; they made their faith contingent upon a sign being sent down from the sky. They mean that a sign is sent down from the sky all at once. They said ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32] and they said

[p. 212]
﴿And we will not believe in your ascending until you send down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. Allah answered them with His saying "You are only a warner," that is, there is no connection between warning and the condition that the warning be in a book sent down from the sky, because the warning is achieved by its being a detailed, eloquent warning indicating that the one warned of was not invented by the warner from his own self; for this reason He answered them with what makes this clear, in His saying ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48], up to His saying ﴿And they say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 50], ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51], that is, what is the benefit of its being sent down on a parchment from the sky, when the content is one and the same?

He also said, in answering their saying ﴿until you send down to us a book we can read﴾, "Say: Glory be to my Lord! Was I anything but a human messenger?" [al-Isra': 93]. Yes, Allah may establish signs of this kind by His own choice, without a demand made upon Him, and this is what is called a miracle, just as He called some of that "signs" in His saying ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [al-Naml: 12]; that is a matter newly originated from Allah, which no one proposed to Him. He has given our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ much of that outside the context of a demand from those who turn away, such as the splitting of the moon, the gushing of water from between his fingers, the multiplying of little food, and the water gushing from the earth by an arrow he shot into the ground. This is the explanation I promised at His saying ﴿And they say: "Why has not an angel been sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am: 8] in this surah.

Some exegetes took the meaning of His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ to be that they do not know that sending down a sign in accordance with their demand would be followed by annihilation if they do not believe, and they, due to their obstinacy, do not believe. However, what I have explained it by is more preferable, so that its meaning is not a repetition of the meaning of the preceding verse, and with it the hesitation about the correspondence of the answer to the requirement of the question is removed, as al-Taftazani hesitated over it in his exposition of the words of al-Kashshaf.

His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ is an alert that among them are some who know that, but who act arrogantly and make it appear that the argument is not complete for them except in the manner they proposed.

The repetition of the word "āya" in the indefinite in His saying "that He send down a sign" is repetition of an indefinite noun as an indefinite, while it is the very same as the first. This nullifies the rule current among grammarians that if an indefinite word is repeated in speech as indefinite, the second is other than the first. Ibn Hisham mentioned it in Mughni al-Labib in the sixth chapter and refuted it. Among what he cited as an example of repeating an indefinite as an indefinite, being the very same and not something else, is His saying ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. This was already discussed at His saying ﴿There is no blame upon them if they make a settlement between themselves, a settlement, and settlement is best﴾ [al-Nisa': 128] in Surat al-Nisa'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 38 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies on its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then unto their Lord they will be gathered.﴾

The meaning of this verse is obscure at the beginning, its conclusion is even more obscure, and its placement in this context has a hidden relevance. Know that the meaning of His saying ﴿There is no creature on the earth﴾ up to His saying ﴿but they are communities like you﴾ is that they have characteristics for every genus and species among them, just as the nations of mankind have their characteristics. That is, God has given each species that by which its existence is sustained, and has inspired it to follow its order, and that they have a life that is appointed, without doubt.

So the meaning of "like you" (amthalukum) is the similarity in animal life and in being bound to its order.

As for the meaning of His saying ﴿Then unto their Lord they will be gathered﴾, it is that they are destined for death. This is supported by what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "The gathering (hashr) of beasts is their death." That is, the term "gathering" is used in a metaphor close to its linguistic reality, as in His exalted saying ﴿And his hosts were gathered for Solomon﴾ [al-Naml: 17]. The placement of this verse, according to some exegetes, is that it serves as evidence for the content of His exalted saying ﴿Say: Indeed, God is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-An'am: 37]. So it is permissible that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, God is able to send down a sign﴾ [al-An'am: 37], as being part of what the Prophet was commanded to say to them; and it is permissible that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿Say: Indeed, God is able﴾ [al-An'am: 37], as being part of God's address to them. That is, the One who created all kinds of living beings and made them, like nations, possessing comprehensive characteristics for the individuals of each kind, their creation is
Page 214
a sign of His great power—nothing prevents Him from bringing a sign according to your proposal, but you do not know the wisdom in His not answering what you asked.

Its being followed by His exalted saying ﴿And those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb﴾ [al-An'am: 39] and what follows is of clear relevance, that is, they do not come to guide themselves to what lies in the worlds of beasts and birds of the indications of God's oneness.

As for His saying ﴿Then unto their Lord they will be gathered﴾, if we consider it taken on its own wording, disregarding the transmitted reports attached to its interpretation, the first thing that appears to the observer is that the pronouns in (their Lord) and (they will be gathered) refer to (creature) and (bird), by virtue of their indication of the groups of beasts and birds, since they fall within the scope of the particle (min), which conveys generality in a negative context. So the observer asks about this, since the two pronouns are designated for rational beings. The scholars have interpreted the use of these two pronouns for non-rational beings in two ways: first, that it is based on the predominance of the rational (taghlib), since after it comes (except that they are communities like you). The second way is that the two pronouns refer to ﴿communities like you﴾, that is, all nations are gathered to God, exalted is He.

A more excellent interpretation than this is that the two pronouns refer to what the pronouns of absence in these verses refer to, the last of which is the pronoun in ﴿They say: Why has no sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ [al-An'am: 37]. Then the clause ﴿Then unto their Lord they will be gathered﴾ holds the position of insertion and digression, confronting the polytheists with the fact that they will certainly be gathered to God, even if they deny it.

When the reports transmitted concerning the verse are considered, the matter becomes problematic. Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The rights will certainly be rendered to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, even to the hornless sheep (al-shatu al-jal'a, the one without horns; in another narration, from others: al-jamma') from the horned sheep." Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in their Musnads from Abu Dharr who said: "Two sheep or two she-goats butted each other in the presence of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know why they butted each other?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'But God knows, and He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.'" This requires the affirmation of the gathering of beasts for the Day of Reckoning, so its meaning is obscure in wisdom, since it is established that beasts and birds are not charged with obligation, following the absence of intellect in them. Its placement is of clear relevance by what al-Fakhr said, quoting 'Abd al-Jabbar, that when God had stated that the disbelievers return to Him and are gathered, He then made clear that beasts and birds are communities like them in that they too are gathered. The intent is to make clear that gathering and resurrection, as they occur among people, occur among animals too. This is the apparent sense of His saying (they will be gathered), because the general usage of "gathering" (hashr) in the Qur'an is for the gathering to reckoning. So it is fitting that the clause ﴿There is no creature on the earth﴾ and what follows be conjoined to the clause ﴿And the dead—God raises them﴾ [al-An'am: 36], for the polytheists deny resurrection and make the Messenger's (peace be upon him) report of it one of the grounds for accusing him regarding what he brought. So when God threatened them with the previous verse, that they will be returned to Him, He added that He recorded their ignorance upon them, informing them of what is more astonishing than what they denied, namely, informing them that gathering is not restricted to humans but encompasses every living thing among beasts and birds. The purpose of this report is His saying ﴿Then unto their Lord they will be gathered﴾. As for what precedes it, it holds the position of a preface to it and proof for it. That is, beasts and birds are resurrected like humans, and all their individuals are present on the Day of Gathering, and that necessarily entails that retribution be made for them, so the wisdom of their gathering may be a consequence of the earth casting out what is in it and the restoration of the parts of animals.

And if the intent of these two hadiths is their apparent meaning, then this is a manifestation of the manifestations of truth on the Day of Resurrection, to rectify what was neglected in the world of annihilation of the circulation of falsehood and the rule of force over justice. Retribution will be by enabling the wronged among the beasts to retaliate against his wrongdoer, so that falsehood does not remain established. This is of the kind of the consequences following their causes, resembling the address of legal causation (khitab al-wad'), and there is in that no reward nor punishment, since obligation is absent. Then on that day the beasts will become dust, as is reported in a narration from Abu Hurayrah concerning His exalted saying ﴿And the disbeliever will say: Would that I were dust﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Al-Mazari said in al-Mu'allim: The scholars have differed concerning the resurrection of beasts. The strongest thing on which those who say they are resurrected rely is His exalted saying ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [al-Takwir: 5]. It has been said: all of this is an allegory for justice. Al-Mazari attributed this to some of his teachers, saying: It is a striking of a parable, to inform creation that no right will remain with anyone.

And "dabba" (creature) is derived from "dabba," meaning he walked on the earth, and it is a name for everything that crawls upon the earth. His saying "on the earth" is a qualifier intended to convey generality and comprehensiveness by mentioning the name of the place that contains all creatures, which is the earth. Likewise the description of (bird) by His saying ﴿that flies on its two wings﴾ is intended for comprehensiveness and encompassment, because it is a description that returns to the meaning of emphasis, since the import of ﴿that flies on its two wings﴾ is that it is a bird; as if it were said: nor any bird, nor any bird. The emphasis here reinforces the meaning of comprehensiveness conveyed by the (min) that is superfluous in a negative context, so from these two descriptions there results the affirmation of the meaning of comprehensiveness arising from the negation of the two generic nouns. The point of the emphasis is that the report, because of its strangeness to them and its being a likely object of their denial, is fit to be emphasized.

It occurs in al-Miftah, in the discussion of following the predicate with clarification, that these two descriptions in this verse are for indicating that the intent of the two words is the genus, not some of the individuals, and this is other than what is in al-Kashshaf. How can it be imagined that the intent is some of the individuals when the presence of (min) in the negation is an explicit statement negating the genus rather than the unity?

By this you know that the description ﴿that flies on its two wings﴾ is not given to remove the possibility of metaphor in "bird," as many exegetes have inclined to, although removing the possibility of metaphor is among the points of verbal emphasis, yet it is not consistent; and because considering the emphasis of generality is preferable, unlike such expressions as: "I saw him with my own eyes and heard him with my own ears," and the verse of Sakhr:

"And she took for her shirt of hair,"

since it is known that a shirt (sidar) is only of hair.

"Umam" is the plural of "ummah." The ummah's original sense is a group of people sharing essential attributes, whether of lineage, language, custom, genus or species. It has been said: it was called ummah because its members aim at one ummam (model/exemplar), which is what gathers its constituents. I reckon that the word ummah is specific to a great group of humans, so it is not said in the language "the ummah of the angels" or "the ummah of beasts of prey." As for the application of "umam" to beasts and birds in this verse, it is a metaphor, meaning "like the nations," because each kind has its individuals gathered in uniform attributes, which is what unites them as one nation; and I reckon the term is specific to humans.

"Dabba" and "tair" in a negative context are intended to include all individuals of the two kinds, as is the nature of generalization. So the predication about them with the word "umam," which is plural, is according to its interpretation as their groups, that is, except that their groups are nations, or except that individuals are of nations.

The earth includes the sea, because it is part of the earth, and because its creatures are also called "dabba," as in the report of the expedition of Sayf al-Bahr, where Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "The sea cast up to us a creature called al-'anbar."

The similarity in His saying "like you" is the resemblance in the essential divisions of realities and the properties that distinguish each kind from others, which are the innate orders with which God originated the kinds of creatures. So beasts and birds resemble humans in that they were created upon a nature in which the individuals of their kinds share, and that they are created by God, given a determined life along with the determination of their sustenance, birth, youth and old age, and they have orders which they cannot change. The similarity does not refer to all attributes, for they do not resemble humans in thought and acquired civilization which is the faculty peculiar to humans. Therefore it is not valid that non-humans have a system of state, nor laws, nor messengers sent to them, for the absence of the intellect of obligation in them; and likewise it is not valid that they be described as knowing God, exalted is He. As for His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], that is by the tongue of state in the dumb creatures, when we see them joyful upon the arrival of what suits them, so we see them exuberant and elated. And that is only through the bounty God has sent to them, which they do not comprehend in its origin, but they sense its effect and so rejoice. Also, in each kind there are characteristics that indicate God's great power and knowledge, differing from the rest of the kinds of its genus; and the purpose of this is to turn minds toward reflection upon the order of creation which God deposited in each kind. The address in His saying "like you" is directed to the polytheists.

The clause ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ is parenthetical, to show the breadth of God's knowledge and the greatness of His power. Here "the Book" means the written, which is what is alluded to by the Pen, meaning what preceded in God's knowledge and His will flowing in accordance with it, as already discussed in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 12].

It has been said that "the Book" means the Qur'an. This is far-fetched, since there is no connection to the purpose on this interpretation, for it raises the question of how the Qur'an could contain everything. Fakhr al-Din expounded this explanation in choosing this view, and likewise Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi in al-Muwafaqat.

"Tafrit" means neglect and omission, and its explanation has been given just before, at His saying: ﴿They say: Alas for us over what we neglected concerning it﴾ [al-An'am: 31].

"Shay'" (thing) is that which exists. What is meant by it here is the states of created beings, as the context indicates, so it includes the states of beasts and birds, for these are known to God, exalted is He, determined by Him with the wisdom of His creation, exalted is He.

Page 218
His saying ﴿Then unto their Lord they will be gathered﴾ has had its explanation given just before, at the beginning of the explanation of this verse.

In the verse there is a reminder to Muslims to be gentle with animals. The report that they are "communities like you" is an alert to their sharing in createdness and in all the attributes of animality. And in His saying ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ there is a casting of fear of transgressing against them by doing what the Law has forbidden of torturing them. And if retaliation is taken for some of them against others, though they are not legally responsible, then taking retaliation for them from a human being is more fitting in justice.

It is established in the sound hadith: "That Allah thanked the one who gave water to the thirsty dog," and "That Allah caused a woman to enter the Fire because of a cat that she confined, so it died of hunger."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 39:

﴿والَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا صُمٌّ وبُكْمٌ في الظُّلُماتِ مِن يَشَأِ اللَّهُ يُضْلِلْهُ ومَن يَشَأْ يَجْعَلْهُ عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ .

It is permissible for the *waw* to be conjunctive (*li-l-'atf*), with the thing conjoined being the clause "Only those who listen respond" (*innama yastajibu alladhina yasma'un*). The meaning is: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾ and did not listen to them, meaning they do not respond, being in the position of deaf and mute people in darkness who are not guided.

It is also permissible for the clause to be a new beginning (*mustaN'afa*) and the *waw* to be resumptive (*isti'nafiyya*), meaning that it introduces an independent statement that is not linked to a particular clause of the preceding discourse, but arises from the whole of the preceding discourse. For when God mentioned, among His creatures and the traces of His power, what is suited to make people know His oneness and guide them to His signs and to the truthfulness of His Messenger, He followed it with an explanation that the deniers are in manifest error, turning away from being guided by that and from reflecting and contemplating upon it. On both readings, the connection of this clause after the clause ﴿And there is no creature moving on the earth﴾ (verse 38) is as we have already discussed above.

The intended referents of "those who denied" are the polytheists, whose conditions have been discussed earlier, in general and in particular.

His saying ﴿deaf and mute in darkness﴾ is an allegory (*tamthil*) for their state in the error of their beliefs and their remoteness from guidance, by way of the state of a people who are deaf and mute in darkness. Deafness prevents them from receiving the guidance of one who would guide them; muteness prevents them from seeking direction from one who passes by them; and darkness prevents them from seeing clearly the path or the exit that would bring them out of their predicament.

It was said "in darkness" and they were not described as blind, as in His saying ﴿blind, dumb and deaf﴾ [al-Isra': 97], so that some parts of the image used as the comparison would have something corresponding to some parts of the image being compared. For the disbelief in which they are, and which has brought them to the continuance of error, resembles darkness in that it intervenes between the one who is within it and the attainment of guidance to the path of salvation. In a hadith: "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." Thus this allegory comes in the most complete form of the conditions of allegory, namely that it admits of being broken down into individual comparisons, as in the verse of Bashshar:

*As if the dust raised above our heads and our swords were a night whose stars are falling.*

The plural *al-zulumat* ("darknesses") is in accordance with the eloquent usage of not using *al-zulma* in the singular; this was discussed earlier at the beginning of the surah. It has also been said that the plural points to the darkness of disbelief, the darkness of ignorance, and the darkness of obstinacy.

His saying ﴿deaf and mute﴾ is a predicate and a conjoined predicate, and His saying "in darkness" is a third predicate, since in multiple predicates what is permissible with multiple adjectives is permissible, namely conjoining or not conjoining.

His saying ﴿whomever God wills to lead astray, He leads him astray﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because their astonishing condition provokes a question, namely that someone might say: what is wrong with them that they are not guided despite the clarity of these manifest proofs? So it was answered that God has led them astray, so they are not guided, and that God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. The words ﴿whomever God wills to lead astray, He leads him astray﴾ indicate that these deniers who are in error are among those whom God willed to lead astray, by way of conciseness (*ijaz*) through omission, since the omitted element is evident. This is connected with His earlier saying: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35].

The meaning of God's leading astray is His decreeing error for them: that He creates the one who errs with an intellect capable of error, persisting in his error and obstinately clinging to it. When he begins the early stages of error, as occurs to many people, and a preacher admonishes him, or a thought comes to his mind that he is in error, his persistence prevents him from giving it up, and he continues to be pushed by it into the abysses of error until it brings him to the point of being characterized by error, so that he no longer refrains from it. This is among the matters indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] ﴿then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5]. It is also indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man continues to be truthful until he becomes a *siddiq* (a person of great truthfulness), and a man continues to lie until he is recorded with God as a great liar." All of this is among the workings of God, the Exalted, through creation and bringing into being, and it is the working of divine decree (*qadar*). It is also connected to the law of succession (*namus al-tasalsul*, i.e., the chain of causes) in the development of human conditions through their minds and habits. This is a far-reaching chain, required by the wisdom of God, the Exalted, in governing the order of this world, and none knows its reality except God, the Exalted. This leading astray is not a command to error, for God does not command indecency, nor does He instill it, urge it, or facilitate it, since that is the act of Satan. Likewise, God has deprived of His favor the one whom He wills to lead astray, from being rescued and from His kindness toward him, because that is grace bestowed by the One who knows best those who deserve it.

The object of (*yasha'*) is omitted, because the answer of the conditional clause indicates it, as is common with the object of the verb of willing when it occurs as a condition.

The *sirat* is the clear road. The meaning of "straight" (*mustaqim*) is that there is no crookedness in it, because travelling on a straight road is easier for the traveller and brings him more quickly to his destination.

The meaning of ﴿upon﴾ (*'ala*) is elevation, namely the traveller's being elevated upon the road. Thus the discourse is an allegory for the state of the one whom God created and graced with an intellect that restrains him from his misguidance and makes him listen to counsel, so that he does not fall into corruption and follows the true religion, by way of the state of a traveller on a road that is clear, so that he does not wander or miss his aim, and is straight, so that it does not throw him off course over a long journey. This allegory is also suitable for comparing each part of the image being compared with a part of the image used as comparison, as was discussed in a similar case. Something of this has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6]. Thus the religion resembles the road that delivers one to the destination without hardship, and being guided to it resembles being placed upon the road.

[Page 221]

This is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i) that contains a warning of threat, to drive away the earlier aims. Woven into it is an indirect exhortation to renounce polytheism, since their associates have no benefit in their hands. They are reminded of states that may come upon them, in which they turn to Allah, and a question is put to them: Will they persist in associating others with Allah in that state? And will they, from now until the punishment reaches them or the Resurrection comes upon them, persist in polytheism, when they will turn to belief in His oneness, though it will be too late for belief?

This threat is introduced with the command to speak, for the sake of emphasis on it. Otherwise, most of what is in the Qur'an is something the Messenger (ﷺ) is commanded to say to them. The command to speak continues in the verses after this, up to His words, ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ (6:67), twelve times. A similar passage occurs in Surah Yunus.

His words, "Have you considered" (أرَأيْتَكم), are a widely used construction, with which a statement that is meant to be affirmed and emphasized is opened. The interrogative hamzah in it is for the interrogative of confirmation (istifham taqriri) (a question that seeks the listener's affirmation).

The verb "ra'a" (رَأى) here has the meaning of "think/judge" (zann). It is attached to a second-person feminine-form suffix ta' (تاء خطاب) that always stays in one fixed state, with one fixed vowel, the fatha, not varying with the number or gender of the addressee, whether singular or otherwise, masculine or otherwise. In this construction the first object is usually the second-person pronoun referring back to the subject of the mental seeing, and it is sufficient in itself to specify who is addressed by the ta' of address. The meaning is that the addressee knows himself to be in the stated state, which follows the pronoun of address. So the addressee is both subject and object, depending on the viewpoint. Among the characteristics of verbs of the class of "thinking" (باب الظن) is that their subject and object may be one and the same. Two verbs are attached to the knowledge verbs: "faqada" and "adima" in supplication, as in "faqadtuni." After the attached pronoun in the accusative, a clause comes in the position of its second object. Sometimes in that clause there is something that suspends the verb of seeing from operating.

This is the correct way of analyzing this construction. Some grammarians make that clause fill the place of both objects, out of concern for consistency in analysis, since they treat the pronouns of address as mere markers of address without any place in i'rab (grammatical inflection). They do this to preserve the commonly known rules of grammar in the original usage. However, rare usages have special conditions which should not be ignored, except when the aim is to clarify the basis of the speech or to avoid confusing learners. It is not hidden that what they proposed is more unusual, namely combining two markers of address that differ in form while their referent is one and the same. According to the view we have chosen, the second object of this construction is the clause "Other than Allah do you call upon?"

The ta' was left in one fixed state because, when the subject's identity was made the object's identity in grammatical terms, and they wanted to make this construction work like a proverb in having few words and abundant meaning, they avoided the heaviness that results from combining two pronouns of address, one nominative and one accusative, as in "a-ra'aytumaka-ma" (أرَأيْتُماكُما), "a-ra'aytumukum" (أرَأيْتُمْكم), "a-ra'aytunnakunna" (أرَيْتُنَّكُنَّ), and similar forms. They adopted this unusual method, relying on the variation of the second pronoun's state instead of varying the first pronoun's state, for brevity and lightness. By this, this construction could function like a proverb, because of its conciseness, to facilitate its widespread use as a specific usage that is not changed. For this reason that ta' is not pronounced with a kasra when addressing a feminine, nor with a damma when addressing a dual or plural.

From al-Akhfash: The Arabs removed this expression entirely from its meaning and restricted it to address, and they moved it away from its original subject to the meaning of "amma" (أمّا, "as for") with an opening hamzah. So they placed the fa' after it in some of its uses, as in His words, ﴿Have you considered, when we took refuge at the rock, I indeed forgot the fish?﴾ (18:63). The fa' only enters when "ara'ayta" has been removed to mean "as for." It is also removed to mean "inform me," and then after it there must be the name of the one about whom information is sought. It is followed by a clause after the interrogative. It may also come out with this meaning and be followed by a conditional and a time expression. End of quote.

In al-Kashshaf: The object of the inquiry is omitted; its estimate is: "If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom do you call upon?" Then He rebukes them with His words, "Other than Allah do you call upon?" That is: Do you single out your gods for supplication, or do you call upon Allah apart from them? "Rather, it is Him you call upon." End of quote.

The clause "Other than Allah do you call upon?" is the second object of the verb of "Have you considered."

Know that this is a usage specific to this particular construction, which functions like a proverb. But when the verb of knowledge-seeing is meant to operate in its basic form, it follows the common practice of transitivity of the verb to its subject and its two objects. So if someone says to you, "I see myself knowing so-and-so," and you want to verify this, you say, "Have you considered yourself knowing so-and-so?" To the dual you say, "A-ra'aytumaka-ma 'alimayni bi-fulan" (أرَأيْتُماكُما عالِمَيْنِ بِفُلانٍ); to the plural, "a-ra'aytumukum" (أرَأيْتُمُوكم); to the feminine, "a-ra'ayti-ki" (أرَأيْتِكِ) with a kasra on the ta'.

Nafi', in the well-known reading, pronounced the hamzah as an alif (softening it). A transmission from him has it in between the hamzah and the alif. al-Kisa'i read it with the omission of the hamzah which is the root letter of the word, so he says "ara'yta" (أرَيْتَ), and this is a dialect form. The rest read it with the hamzah fully pronounced.

The clause "If the punishment of Allah comes upon you..." etc. is an intervening clause between the two objects of the verb of seeing. It is a conditional clause whose apodosis (jawab) is omitted, because the second object clause indicates it.

The arrival of the punishment means its descent and occurrence. It is therefore a metaphor, because the literal sense of "coming" (ityan) is arriving, which is moving from a distant place to the place where the object of the coming settles. So it is used metaphorically for the occurrence of something that had not been occurring. The same applies to the arrival of the Hour.

As for repeating the verb "the Hour came upon you" (أتَتْكُمُ السّاعَةُ) when the conjunction particle could serve without repeating the governing verb, as in "If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour," the reason for it is what is called the appearance of the noun in place of a pronoun, namely the desire to emphasize the noun that appears, so that it is repeated in its explicit form, because it is more firmly settled in the mind of the listener.

The emphasis here is motivated by the desire to inspire awe and to bring fear into the listener's heart, by explicitly attributing this arrival to the noun denoting something terrifying, so that the connection of this verb to its object indicates its terror and dread.

Shaykh Muhammad ibn Arafa sensed the need to justify repeating the verb here in the lesson of his tafsir. He justified it by saying: when the two governing verbs differ in meaning, because one of them is more intense, the governing verb is repeated after the conjunction, to indicate the difference. For the punishment of Allah is more intense than the arrival of the Hour, meaning on the basis that the punishment of Allah means the punishment of the Hereafter. Or, if the two governing verbs are distant from each other: if by the Hour is meant the Resurrection and by the punishment of Allah is meant destruction and calamities in this world, then one is followed by a complete interval. If by the Hour is meant a period of time, then worldly destruction is numerous, some of it earlier and some later, up to death, so the earlier is evident. End of quote. But there is a problem with this justification, since usage does not support it.

[Page 222]

The attribution of the punishment to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is to magnify it, because it comes from the most powerful of the powerful. The intended meaning is a punishment that occurs in this world, when they plead to Allah to lift it from them, as evidenced by His words, ﴿Other than Allah do you call upon?﴾, since supplication does not mean asking to lift the punishment of recompense (in the Hereafter). This is a threat and a warning.

The "Hour" (al-sa'ah) is a proper name by dominance for the hour of the end of this world. That is: if the Hour overtakes you.

Placing "Other than Allah" before its governing verb "do you call upon" serves to make the question-clause a clause of restriction (qasr): that is, do you turn away from calling upon Allah and call upon other than Him, as is your habit now? So the restriction is to describe their state, not to refute others. The speech indicates astonishment, that is, you continue in this state. The speech is an increase in warning.

The clause "If you are truthful" is an independent clause, and its apodosis is omitted, indicated by His words, "Have you considered" (أرَأيْتَكُمُ), which has the meaning of confirmation. So the estimated apodosis is: "If you are truthful, then you are affirming that you do not call upon other than Allah." In this verse He reminded them and drove them to reflection, so that they would know that if Allah wills their punishment, their gods cannot repel it from them. If they sincerely speak the truth about this future matter and reflect again, they will have no choice but to acknowledge that when Allah wills something, no one can repel it except by His will. For they acknowledge that the idols only bring them closer to Allah, so if they are truthful and say, "We call upon Allah," then the proof has been established against them now. For one who does not help in some hardships should not be relied upon in others.

For this reason, the position of "Rather, it is Him you call upon" immediately after this question is that of a conclusion to the argument. The particle "bal" (بَلْ, "rather") serves to nullify the call to other than Allah. That is: I answer on your behalf that you call upon none but Allah. The reason the questioner himself takes over the answer for them is that since this answer cannot be anything but what the questioned party must affirm, it is correct for the questioner to give the answer himself, as was previously mentioned in His words, ﴿Say: To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ (6:12) in this surah.

The fronting of the object before "you call upon" is for restriction, and it is a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad), to refute the polytheists in their claim that they call upon Allah and call upon their idols. Although they did not claim this in the state of the punishment of Allah or the Hour coming upon them, yet since they claimed it in other states, they were treated as those who carry this claim over into that state as well.

[Page 223]

[Page 224] — (continuing from the text)

His words "so He removes" (فَيَكْشِفُ) are conjoined to "you call upon." This is an encouragement to hope in Allah's mercy, so that perhaps they will be mindful. For the sake of hastening this, He fronted "and you forget what you associate," although its proper place was later. It is like hastening good news. The object of "you call upon" is omitted, and it is the pronoun of the Name of Majesty, that is, "what you call upon Him for." The pronoun governed by "ila" (إلى, "to") refers back to "ma" (ما) in "ma tad'una" (what you call upon): that is, He removes that which you call upon Him to remove.

He restricted the removal of harm from them by His will only because it is an encouragement, not a promise.

The verb "tad'una" (تَدْعُونَ) is transitive with the particle "ila" because the basis of supplication is calling, so the one called is as if he is required to come to the place of despair.

The object of "shaa'a" (شاءَ) is omitted, following the manner of omitting the object of the verb of will when it occurs as a condition, as previously mentioned.

In His words "if He wills" there is an indication of its opposite: if He does not will, He does not remove it. This applies to the punishment of this world. As for the arrival of the Hour, it is not removed, unless by the arrival of it is meant what accompanies it of calamities and disasters, such as collapse and the like, in which case its removal from some people is possible. Among what Allah removed from them of worldly punishment is the punishment of hunger, which is in His words, ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a visible smoke that envelops people. This is a painful punishment﴾ (44:10), up to His words, ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return. On the day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution﴾ (44:15). The "greatest seizure" was interpreted as the Day of Badr.

The clause "so He removes" etc. is an intervening clause between the two conjoined elements. His words, "and you forget what you associate," are conjoined to "Rather, it is Him you call upon," that is: indeed you, at that time, will forget what you associate with Allah, which are the idols.

His words "and you forget what you associate" may be taken literally: that is, you will be distracted from the idols because of the terror of the punishment you see, and because of what occurs in their souls that it has been sent down upon them by Allah. So their minds will be occupied with the One who sent the punishment, and they will forget the idols that they used to seek intercession through.

This may be a figurative usage meaning abandonment and turning away, i.e., "and you will abandon the idols," since perhaps in that moment they will be inspired or will reason that other than God cannot remove from them any of that punishment. The use of "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning" (tark) is common in Arabic speech, as in His saying, ﴿Today We shall forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your day﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 34], meaning, "We shall neglect you just as you denied the meeting with God on this day." Of the same kind is His saying, ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

In His saying ﴿then He will remove that which you call upon Him for, if He wills﴾ there is evidence that God, exalted is He, may answer the supplication of the disbeliever in this world, following from the continuation of God's blessings upon the disbelievers. The disagreement on this matter between the Ash'ari and the Maturidi (schools of kalam) ultimately leads to a verbal disagreement.

His words "so He removes" (فَيَكْشِفُ) are conjoined to "you call upon." This is an encouragement to hope in Allah's mercy, so that perhaps they will be mindful. For the sake of hastening this, He fronted "and you forget what you associate," although its proper place was later. It is like hastening good news. The object of "you call upon" is omitted, and it is the pronoun of the Name of Majesty, that is, "what you call upon Him for." The pronoun governed by "ila" (إلى, "to") refers back to "ma" (ما) in "ma tad'una" (what you call upon): that is, He removes that which you call upon Him to remove.

He restricted the removal of harm from them by His will only because it is an encouragement, not a promise.

The verb "tad'una" (تَدْعُونَ) is transitive with the particle "ila" because the basis of supplication is calling, so the one called is as if he is required to come to the place of despair.

The object of "shaa'a" (شاءَ) is omitted, following the manner of omitting the object of the verb of will when it occurs as a condition, as previously mentioned.

In His words "if He wills" there is an indication of its opposite: if He does not will, He does not remove it. This applies to the punishment of this world. As for the arrival of the Hour, it is not removed, unless by the arrival of it is meant what accompanies it of calamities and disasters, such as collapse and the like, in which case its removal from some people is possible. Among what Allah removed from them of worldly punishment is the punishment of hunger, which is in His words, ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a visible smoke that envelops people. This is a painful punishment﴾ (44:10), up to His words, ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return. On the day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution﴾ (44:15). The "greatest seizure" was interpreted as the Day of Badr.

The clause "so He removes" etc. is an intervening clause between the two conjoined elements. His words, "and you forget what you associate," are conjoined to "Rather, it is Him you call upon," that is: indeed you, at that time, will forget what you associate with Allah, which are the idols.

His words "and you forget what you associate" may be taken literally: that is, you will be distracted from the idols because of the terror of the punishment you see, and because of what occurs in their souls that it has been sent down upon them by Allah. So their minds will be occupied with the One who sent the punishment, and they will forget the idols that they used to seek intercession through.

This may be a figurative usage meaning abandonment and turning away, i.e., "and you will abandon the idols," since perhaps in that moment they will be inspired or will reason that other than God cannot remove from them any of that punishment. The use of "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning" (tark) is common in Arabic speech, as in His saying, ﴿Today We shall forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your day﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 34], meaning, "We shall neglect you just as you denied the meeting with God on this day." Of the same kind is His saying, ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

In His saying ﴿then He will remove that which you call upon Him for, if He wills﴾ there is evidence that God, exalted is He, may answer the supplication of the disbeliever in this world, following from the continuation of God's blessings upon the disbelievers. The disagreement on this matter between the Ash'ari and the Maturidi (schools of kalam) ultimately leads to a verbal disagreement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 42–45 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿So why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing.﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ ﴿So the people who had wronged were cut off at the root. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

When He warned them of the expectation of punishment, He followed this with evidence of the occurrence of punishment upon nations before them, so that these people would know that this is the custom of Allah concerning those who wronged by associating partners with Him.

This report is used to warn the listening polytheists by way of allusion (ta'rid), and they are the ones addressed by the speech commanded in the sentence before it.

So the clause "Wa-laqad arsalna" (And We certainly sent) is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "Qul ara'aytakum" (Say: Have you seen...), and the waw is for coordinating clauses, so it is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), since the clause it is coordinated with was itself resumptive. This clause opens with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and "qad" (certainly), to emphasize the content of the clause, which is what is derived with the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ (so We seized them with adversity and hardship). The listeners who were alluded to in the warning are treated as those who deny that what befell the nations before them was a punishment from Allah Most High for their turning away.

His saying "fa-akhadhnahum" (so We seized them) is coordinated with "arsalna" (We sent) in view of what the description "min qablika" (before you) implies of their nations' treatment of them with the same treatment your people gave you; the coordination therefore indicates an omitted element whose estimation is: "fa-kadhdhabuhum" (so they denied them).

Since their being seized with adversity and hardship coincided with the time of their messengers' presence among them, the position of the fa' of coordination indicates that this occurred in the sight of their messengers and before their extinction, so as to be a sign that Allah supported His messengers and aided them during their lifetimes. For the seizing of nations with punishment has two wisdoms: first, restraining them from denial; second, honouring the messengers by support in the sight of the deniers. In this there is an honour for the Prophet ﷺ, by informing him that Allah is his helper against his deniers.

The meaning of "akhadhnahum" is "asabnahum" (We struck them) with a striking that is firmly established. The explanation of "al-akhdh" has already passed at His saying ﴿akhadhat-hu al-'izzatu bil-ithm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The object of the seizing has been mentioned here because it is a seizing with a specific thing, unlike what comes shortly after this.

"Al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'" have already been discussed at His saying ﴿wal-sabirina fil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah. It has been explained that "al-ba'sa'" is hunger and "al-darra'" is sickness, but this is a specification with no basis, since what befell the nations of punishment was of many kinds. Perhaps whoever explained it this way considered what befell Quraysh through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ.

"La'alla" (perhaps) is for hope. It is made a cause for the beginning of their being seized with adversity and hardship before the uprooting.

The meaning of "yatadarra'un" is "yatadhallalun" (they humble themselves), because "al-dara'a" is humility and submission, and here it is a metonymy for acknowledging the sin and repenting from it, which is faith in the messengers.

The intended meaning is that Allah placed before them a light punishment before the greater punishment, as He said ﴿wa-lanudhiqannahum min al-'adhabi al-adna duna al-'adhabi al-akbar la'allahum yarji'un﴾ (And We will surely make them taste a punishment nearer than the greater punishment, perhaps they will return). This is from the abundance of His mercy mixed with what His wisdom requires. In it is a warning to Quraysh that adversity and hardship will befall them before the uprooting, which is the uprooting by the sword. Allah chose that their uprooting be by the sword to show that the victory of the Messenger, upon him blessings and peace, over them was by his hand and the hands of those who believed in him. That is more effective upon the Arabs, and for this reason the condition of those addressed by the warning was observed while they were present. So He placed all nations in their station, and said ﴿fa-lawla idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ (So why, when Our might came to them, did they not humble themselves?). Here "lawla" is a particle of rebuke, since it precedes a single past verbal clause, so "lawla" is not a particle of prohibition due to existence.

Rebuke is only fitting for those present, not for those who have passed away, since the purpose would be lost. So in this placement there is an indication of the equality of the two situations, and a rebuke of those present with the important lesson, because the time for remedy remains, cutting off their excuse.

It is permissible to take "lawla" here as expressing wishing (tamanni), by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), and the wishing would be a metonymy for informing that Allah loves the desired matter, so this is building a metaphor upon a metaphor. This love is what was expressed by "rejoicing" in the hadith: "Allah rejoices more at the repentance of His servant", the hadith. And the fronting of the temporal adverbial with its clause before its governing verb in His saying ﴿idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ is for emphasis on the content of its clause, and that it is a time that rightly should prompt hastening to humility because of the might that occurred in it.

"Al-ba's" has already been discussed at His saying ﴿wa-hina al-ba's﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it means severity against the enemy and overpowering him. The arrival of the might is the arrival of its effect, since what befell them of adversity and hardship is one of the effects of the strength of Allah Most High's power and His dominance over them. "Arrival" is used metaphorically for occurrence and taking place after not being, as a likening of a thing's occurrence to the arrival of one coming from another place through the movement of steps.

Since rebuke or wishing indicates the negation of the occurrence of the matter, he coordinated after it with "lakin" (but), as coordination according to the meaning of the speech, because humility arises from softness of heart. So its negation, conveyed by the particle of rebuke, arose from the opposite of softness, which is hardness, so he coordinated with "lakin".

The meaning: "But there came upon them what was in their creation of stubbornness and not turning back from falsehood, as if their hearts were not affected, so they were likened to a hard thing." Hardness (al-qaswa) is firmness.

Satan found in their dispositions an aid for casting his purpose into them, so he made that hardness attractive to them and incited them to persist in their sins and deeds. From here it becomes clear that misguidance arises from the readiness that Allah placed in the constitution of the soul.

Tazyin (making attractive) is making a thing an adornment. It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿zuyyina lil-nasi hubbu al-shahawat﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying ﴿fa-lamma nasu ma dhukkiru bihi﴾ (So when they forgot what they had been reminded of) is coordinated with the clause "qasat qulubuhum wa-zayyana lahumu al-shaytan" (their hearts became hard and Satan made attractive to them). Here "nisyan" (forgetting) means turning away, as already passed just before at His saying ﴿wa-tansawna ma tushrikun﴾. The apparent meaning is that abandonment is a consequence of the hardness of hearts and Satan's making their deeds attractive to them. "Ma" is a relative pronoun whose referent is "al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'", meaning: when they turned away from understanding through that and did not reach to remedy their situation. The meaning of "dhukkiru bihi" is that Allah reminded them of His great punishment through what He had previously sent to them of adversity and hardship. "Lamma" is a conditional particle indicating that the occurrence of its response coincides with the occurrence of its condition, and it does not carry the meaning of causation as the rest of the conditional particles do.

His saying ﴿fa-fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ is the response of "lamma". "Al-fath" is the opposite of "al-ghalq" (closing). "Al-ghalq" is blocking the opening through which one can pass to what is beyond it, with a door or the like; this is unlike erecting a wall, which is not called closing.

"Al-fath" is making the barrier that blocks not blocking and capable of being blocked, like a door when it is opened. Because the meanings of opening and closing are relative to one another, the instrument by which the barrier is held and opened is called "miftah" (key) and "miglaq" (bolt). Opening is only conceived after conceiving closing, and therefore His saying ﴿fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ implies that the doors intended here were closed at the time they were seized with adversity and hardship, so it is known that they are the doors of good, since these are what cannot coexist with adversity and hardship.

So "al-fath" here is a metaphor for removing what pains and distresses, as in His saying ﴿wa-law anna ahla al-qura amanu wattaqaw lafatahna 'alayhim barakatin min al-sama' wal-ard﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. From it is the naming of victory as "fath," because it is the removal of the distress of subjugation.

He made their turning away from what they had been reminded of the time for opening the doors of good, because the meaning is that when they turned away from taking admonition from the warnings of punishment, We lifted punishment from them and opened to them the doors of good, as He explicitly stated in His saying ﴿wa-ma arsalna fi qaryatin min nabiyyin illa akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'i la'allahum yadarra'un﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] ﴿thumma baddalna makana al-sayyi'ati al-hasanata hatta 'afaw wa-qalu qad massa aba'ana al-darra'u wal-sarra'u fa-akhadhnahum baghtatan wa-hum la yash'urun﴾ [al-A'raf: 95].

Al-Jumhur read "fatahna" with the second letter (the tā') lightened. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the tā' doubled, for intensification of the opening through its abundance, as indicated by His saying "abwaba kulli shay'" (the doors of everything).

The word "kull" (all) here is used in the meaning of abundance, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

Upon them every long-tailed one and every Khansa' inclines toward every trembling one of the sand, a wide one.

Or it is used in its literal meaning, as a general term with specification, meaning the doors of every thing they seek. It is known that by "kull shay'" is meant all things of good specifically, by the context of His saying "hatta idha farihu" (until when they rejoiced), and by the contrast of this with His saying "akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'" (We seized its people with adversity and hardship). So there is an implied qualifier, meaning every good thing, like His saying ﴿ya'khudhu kulla safinatin ghasban﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound boat.

"Hatta" in His saying ﴿hatta idha farihu﴾ is for the beginning (ibtida'iyyah). The meaning of "farah" here is exultation and arrogance over a blessing and forgetfulness of the Benefactor, as in His saying ﴿idh qala lahu qawmuhu la tafrah inna Allaha la yuhibbu al-farihin﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. Al-Raghib said: "Rejoicing was not permitted except in His saying ﴿qul bi-fadli Allahi wa-bi-rahmatihi fa-bidhalika falyafrahu﴾ [Yunus: 58]." "Idha" is a temporal adverb for the past.

What Allah intends by this is respite for them, so that they might remember Allah and affirm His oneness, and thus their souls would be purified. So Allah tested them with harm and good, so that He might exhaust for them the two causes of remembrance and fear, because among souls there are souls led by hardship and souls led by gentleness.

The meaning of "akhdh" here is destruction. For this reason no object was mentioned for it, as was mentioned in His saying earlier ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾, to indicate that it is a seizing without leniency.

"Al-baghtah" is a form from "al-baght", which is suddenness, meaning the occurrence of a thing unexpectedly to the one to whom it happens, and it entails concealment. Therefore it is contrasted with "al-jahrah" (open manifestation) in the following verse. Here it may be construed as an active participle in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the nominative, meaning "surprising them", or construed as a passive participle as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the accusative, meaning "taken by surprise". ﴿Wa-kadhalika akhdhu rabbika idha akhadha al-qura wa-hiya zalimatun﴾ [Hud: 102].

His saying ﴿fa-idha hum mublisun﴾ — "idha" is "fuja'iyyah" (sudden). It is a place adverb according to Sibawayh, and a particle according to the grammarians of Kufa.

"Al-mublisun" are those despairing of good, bewildered, from "al-iblas", which is stupefaction and silence when seeking pardon, out of despair of being answered.

The clause ﴿fa-quti'a dabira al-qawm﴾ is coordinated with the clause "akhadhnahum", meaning: so We seized them with a seizing of uprooting. So He left none of them.

"Al-dabir" is an active participle from "dabarahu", from the pattern of "kataba", meaning he walked behind him. The verbal noun is "al-dubur" with the dal dammed, and "dabir al-nas" means their last ones. This is derived from "al-dubur", which is behind. Allah Most High said ﴿wa-ittabi' adbarahum﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. Cutting off the "dabir" is a metonymy for the destruction of all, because the one who uproots begins with what is nearest to him and goes on uprooting until he reaches its last, which is its "dabir." This has become like a proverb, and it is repeated in the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿inna dabira ha'ula'i maqtu'un musbihin﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

By "alladhina zalamu" (those who wronged) are meant the polytheists, since associating partners with Allah is the greatest wrong, because it is a transgression upon the right of Allah Most High over His servants, that they acknowledge His lordship alone, and because association entails many injustices, as those who associate do not believe in a law that restrains people from wrongdoing.

The sentence ﴿والحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ may be coordinated with the sentence ﴿ولَقَدْ أرْسَلْنا إلى أُمَمٍ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾ together with what is connected to it, as a coordination of one purpose with another. It may also be a concluding parenthetical sentence (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī), in which case the waw is a waw of parenthesis (wāw i'tirāḍiyya). Whatever its position, there are three considerations regarding its meaning:

The first: it is an instruction to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers to praise God for His granting victory to His messengers and their allies and for destroying the wrongdoers, because that victory is a blessing, since it removes a corruption that had been on the earth. Moreover, in God's reminding people of it there is an indication that they should expect the example of what happened to those before them, that they should expect God's victory as He gave victory to the believers before them. Thus "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a substitute (badal) for a verbal action, and it has been shifted from the accusative and indefiniteness to the nominative and definiteness to indicate the meaning of continuity and permanence, as was already explained in His saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh" in Surat al-Fātiḥa.

The second: "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a metonymy (kināya) for the fact that what was mentioned before it is one of God's blessings, because it is among the necessary implications of praise (ḥamd) that it be for a blessing. It is as if it were said: "So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off." And that is one of God's blessings, which calls for praising Him.

The third: the utterance "al-ḥamdu lillāh" comes from His Majesty as an expression of praise, used to express wonder at God's treatment of them and His gradual granting of respite to them in degrees, until the punishment became due upon them.

It may also be that God's utterance is a praise of Himself, with an allusion to the favour bestowed upon the Messenger and the Muslims. The lām in "al-ḥamdu" is for the genus, meaning: and the whole genus of praise, of which is the praise for the blessing of destroying the wrongdoers.

In all of this there is an alert that praise is due to God at the destruction of the oppressors, because their destruction is a benefit to people, and benefit is among the greatest blessings, and gratitude for a blessing is obligatory. This praise is a form of gratitude because it is a return for a blessing. Their destruction was a benefit because wrongdoing is an alteration of rights and a nullification of acting by the Sharia; when the right and the benefit are altered, ruin and chaos come, and people are afflicted in their lives. When the wrongdoers are destroyed, justice returns, and it is the balance by which the world is sustained.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you see God giving the servant of the worldly life what he loves despite his disobedience, then it is only a gradual leading on (istidrāj)." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of every thing, until when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾
