Here "nisyan" (forgetting) means turning away, as already passed just before at His saying ﴿wa-tansawna ma tushrikun﴾. The apparent meaning is that abandonment is a consequence of the hardness of hearts and Satan's making their deeds attractive to them. "Ma" is a relative pronoun whose referent is "al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'", meaning: when they turned away from understanding through that and did not reach to remedy their situation. The meaning of "dhukkiru bihi" is that Allah reminded them of His great punishment through what He had previously sent to them of adversity and hardship. "Lamma" is a conditional particle indicating that the occurrence of its response coincides with the occurrence of its condition, and it does not carry the meaning of causation as the rest of the conditional particles do.

His saying ﴿fa-fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ is the response of "lamma". "Al-fath" is the opposite of "al-ghalq" (closing). "Al-ghalq" is blocking the opening through which one can pass to what is beyond it, with a door or the like; this is unlike erecting a wall, which is not called closing.

"Al-fath" is making the barrier that blocks not blocking and capable of being blocked, like a door when it is opened. Because the meanings of opening and closing are relative to one another, the instrument by which the barrier is held and opened is called "miftah" (key) and "miglaq" (bolt). Opening is only conceived after conceiving closing, and therefore His saying ﴿fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ implies that the doors intended here were closed at the time they were seized with adversity and hardship, so it is known that they are the doors of good, since these are what cannot coexist with adversity and hardship.

So "al-fath" here is a metaphor for removing what pains and distresses, as in His saying ﴿wa-law anna ahla al-qura amanu wattaqaw lafatahna 'alayhim barakatin min al-sama' wal-ard﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. From it is the naming of victory as "fath," because it is the removal of the distress of subjugation.

He made their turning away from what they had been reminded of the time for opening the doors of good, because the meaning is that when they turned away from taking admonition from the warnings of punishment, We lifted punishment from them and opened to them the doors of good, as He explicitly stated in His saying ﴿wa-ma arsalna fi qaryatin min nabiyyin illa akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'i la'allahum yadarra'un﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] ﴿thumma baddalna makana al-sayyi'ati al-hasanata hatta 'afaw wa-qalu qad massa aba'ana al-darra'u wal-sarra'u fa-akhadhnahum baghtatan wa-hum la yash'urun﴾ [al-A'raf: 95].

Al-Jumhur read "fatahna" with the second letter (the tā') lightened. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the tā' doubled, for intensification of the opening through its abundance, as indicated by His saying "abwaba kulli shay'" (the doors of everything).

The word "kull" (all) here is used in the meaning of abundance, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

Upon them every long-tailed one and every Khansa' inclines toward every trembling one of the sand, a wide one.

Or it is used in its literal meaning, as a general term with specification, meaning the doors of every thing they seek. It is known that by "kull shay'" is meant all things of good specifically, by the context of His saying "hatta idha farihu" (until when they rejoiced), and by the contrast of this with His saying "akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'" (We seized its people with adversity and hardship). So there is an implied qualifier, meaning every good thing, like His saying ﴿ya'khudhu kulla safinatin ghasban﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound boat.

"Hatta" in His saying ﴿hatta idha farihu﴾ is for the beginning (ibtida'iyyah). The meaning of "farah" here is exultation and arrogance over a blessing and forgetfulness of the Benefactor, as in His saying ﴿idh qala lahu qawmuhu la tafrah inna Allaha la yuhibbu al-farihin﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. Al-Raghib said: "Rejoicing was not permitted except in His saying ﴿qul bi-fadli Allahi wa-bi-rahmatihi fa-bidhalika falyafrahu﴾ [Yunus: 58]." "Idha" is a temporal adverb for the past.

What Allah intends by this is respite for them, so that they might remember Allah and affirm His oneness, and thus their souls would be purified. So Allah tested them with harm and good, so that He might exhaust for them the two causes of remembrance and fear, because among souls there are souls led by hardship and souls led by gentleness.

The meaning of "akhdh" here is destruction. For this reason no object was mentioned for it, as was mentioned in His saying earlier ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾, to indicate that it is a seizing without leniency.

"Al-baghtah" is a form from "al-baght", which is suddenness, meaning the occurrence of a thing unexpectedly to the one to whom it happens, and it entails concealment. Therefore it is contrasted with "al-jahrah" (open manifestation) in the following verse. Here it may be construed as an active participle in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the nominative, meaning "surprising them", or construed as a passive participle as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the accusative, meaning "taken by surprise". ﴿Wa-kadhalika akhdhu rabbika idha akhadha al-qura wa-hiya zalimatun﴾ [Hud: 102].

His saying ﴿fa-idha hum mublisun﴾ — "idha" is "fuja'iyyah" (sudden). It is a place adverb according to Sibawayh, and a particle according to the grammarians of Kufa.

"Al-mublisun" are those despairing of good, bewildered, from "al-iblas", which is stupefaction and silence when seeking pardon, out of despair of being answered.

The clause ﴿fa-quti'a dabira al-qawm﴾ is coordinated with the clause "akhadhnahum", meaning: so We seized them with a seizing of uprooting. So He left none of them.

"Al-dabir" is an active participle from "dabarahu", from the pattern of "kataba", meaning he walked behind him. The verbal noun is "al-dubur" with the dal dammed, and "dabir al-nas" means their last ones. This is derived from "al-dubur", which is behind. Allah Most High said ﴿wa-ittabi' adbarahum﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. Cutting off the "dabir" is a metonymy for the destruction of all, because the one who uproots begins with what is nearest to him and goes on uprooting until he reaches its last, which is its "dabir." This has become like a proverb, and it is repeated in the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿inna dabira ha'ula'i maqtu'un musbihin﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

By "alladhina zalamu" (those who wronged) are meant the polytheists, since associating partners with Allah is the greatest wrong, because it is a transgression upon the right of Allah Most High over His servants, that they acknowledge His lordship alone, and because association entails many injustices, as those who associate do not believe in a law that restrains people from wrongdoing.

The sentence ﴿والحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ may be coordinated with the sentence ﴿ولَقَدْ أرْسَلْنا إلى أُمَمٍ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾ together with what is connected to it, as a coordination of one purpose with another. It may also be a concluding parenthetical sentence (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī), in which case the waw is a waw of parenthesis (wāw i'tirāḍiyya). Whatever its position, there are three considerations regarding its meaning:

The first: it is an instruction to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers to praise God for His granting victory to His messengers and their allies and for destroying the wrongdoers, because that victory is a blessing, since it removes a corruption that had been on the earth. Moreover, in God's reminding people of it there is an indication that they should expect the example of what happened to those before them, that they should expect God's victory as He gave victory to the believers before them. Thus "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a substitute (badal) for a verbal action, and it has been shifted from the accusative and indefiniteness to the nominative and definiteness to indicate the meaning of continuity and permanence, as was already explained in His saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh" in Surat al-Fātiḥa.

The second: "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a metonymy (kināya) for the fact that what was mentioned before it is one of God's blessings, because it is among the necessary implications of praise (ḥamd) that it be for a blessing. It is as if it were said: "So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off." And that is one of God's blessings, which calls for praising Him.

The third: the utterance "al-ḥamdu lillāh" comes from His Majesty as an expression of praise, used to express wonder at God's treatment of them and His gradual granting of respite to them in degrees, until the punishment became due upon them.

It may also be that God's utterance is a praise of Himself, with an allusion to the favour bestowed upon the Messenger and the Muslims. The lām in "al-ḥamdu" is for the genus, meaning: and the whole genus of praise, of which is the praise for the blessing of destroying the wrongdoers.

In all of this there is an alert that praise is due to God at the destruction of the oppressors, because their destruction is a benefit to people, and benefit is among the greatest blessings, and gratitude for a blessing is obligatory. This praise is a form of gratitude because it is a return for a blessing. Their destruction was a benefit because wrongdoing is an alteration of rights and a nullification of acting by the Sharia; when the right and the benefit are altered, ruin and chaos come, and people are afflicted in their lives. When the wrongdoers are destroyed, justice returns, and it is the balance by which the world is sustained.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you see God giving the servant of the worldly life what he loves despite his disobedience, then it is only a gradual leading on (istidrāj)." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of every thing, until when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 42–45 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿So why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing.﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ ﴿So the people who had wronged were cut off at the root. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

When He warned them of the expectation of punishment, He followed this with evidence of the occurrence of punishment upon nations before them, so that these people would know that this is the custom of Allah concerning those who wronged by associating partners with Him.

This report is used to warn the listening polytheists by way of allusion (ta'rid), and they are the ones addressed by the speech commanded in the sentence before it.

So the clause "Wa-laqad arsalna" (And We certainly sent) is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "Qul ara'aytakum" (Say: Have you seen...), and the waw is for coordinating clauses, so it is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), since the clause it is coordinated with was itself resumptive. This clause opens with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and "qad" (certainly), to emphasize the content of the clause, which is what is derived with the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ (so We seized them with adversity and hardship). The listeners who were alluded to in the warning are treated as those who deny that what befell the nations before them was a punishment from Allah Most High for their turning away.

His saying "fa-akhadhnahum" (so We seized them) is coordinated with "arsalna" (We sent) in view of what the description "min qablika" (before you) implies of their nations' treatment of them with the same treatment your people gave you; the coordination therefore indicates an omitted element whose estimation is: "fa-kadhdhabuhum" (so they denied them).

Since their being seized with adversity and hardship coincided with the time of their messengers' presence among them, the position of the fa' of coordination indicates that this occurred in the sight of their messengers and before their extinction, so as to be a sign that Allah supported His messengers and aided them during their lifetimes. For the seizing of nations with punishment has two wisdoms: first, restraining them from denial; second, honouring the messengers by support in the sight of the deniers. In this there is an honour for the Prophet ﷺ, by informing him that Allah is his helper against his deniers.

The meaning of "akhadhnahum" is "asabnahum" (We struck them) with a striking that is firmly established. The explanation of "al-akhdh" has already passed at His saying ﴿akhadhat-hu al-'izzatu bil-ithm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The object of the seizing has been mentioned here because it is a seizing with a specific thing, unlike what comes shortly after this.

"Al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'" have already been discussed at His saying ﴿wal-sabirina fil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah. It has been explained that "al-ba'sa'" is hunger and "al-darra'" is sickness, but this is a specification with no basis, since what befell the nations of punishment was of many kinds. Perhaps whoever explained it this way considered what befell Quraysh through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ.

"La'alla" (perhaps) is for hope. It is made a cause for the beginning of their being seized with adversity and hardship before the uprooting.

The meaning of "yatadarra'un" is "yatadhallalun" (they humble themselves), because "al-dara'a" is humility and submission, and here it is a metonymy for acknowledging the sin and repenting from it, which is faith in the messengers.

The intended meaning is that Allah placed before them a light punishment before the greater punishment, as He said ﴿wa-lanudhiqannahum min al-'adhabi al-adna duna al-'adhabi al-akbar la'allahum yarji'un﴾ (And We will surely make them taste a punishment nearer than the greater punishment, perhaps they will return). This is from the abundance of His mercy mixed with what His wisdom requires. In it is a warning to Quraysh that adversity and hardship will befall them before the uprooting, which is the uprooting by the sword. Allah chose that their uprooting be by the sword to show that the victory of the Messenger, upon him blessings and peace, over them was by his hand and the hands of those who believed in him. That is more effective upon the Arabs, and for this reason the condition of those addressed by the warning was observed while they were present. So He placed all nations in their station, and said ﴿fa-lawla idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ (So why, when Our might came to them, did they not humble themselves?). Here "lawla" is a particle of rebuke, since it precedes a single past verbal clause, so "lawla" is not a particle of prohibition due to existence.

Rebuke is only fitting for those present, not for those who have passed away, since the purpose would be lost. So in this placement there is an indication of the equality of the two situations, and a rebuke of those present with the important lesson, because the time for remedy remains, cutting off their excuse.

It is permissible to take "lawla" here as expressing wishing (tamanni), by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), and the wishing would be a metonymy for informing that Allah loves the desired matter, so this is building a metaphor upon a metaphor. This love is what was expressed by "rejoicing" in the hadith: "Allah rejoices more at the repentance of His servant", the hadith. And the fronting of the temporal adverbial with its clause before its governing verb in His saying ﴿idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ is for emphasis on the content of its clause, and that it is a time that rightly should prompt hastening to humility because of the might that occurred in it.

"Al-ba's" has already been discussed at His saying ﴿wa-hina al-ba's﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it means severity against the enemy and overpowering him. The arrival of the might is the arrival of its effect, since what befell them of adversity and hardship is one of the effects of the strength of Allah Most High's power and His dominance over them. "Arrival" is used metaphorically for occurrence and taking place after not being, as a likening of a thing's occurrence to the arrival of one coming from another place through the movement of steps.

Since rebuke or wishing indicates the negation of the occurrence of the matter, he coordinated after it with "lakin" (but), as coordination according to the meaning of the speech, because humility arises from softness of heart. So its negation, conveyed by the particle of rebuke, arose from the opposite of softness, which is hardness, so he coordinated with "lakin".

The meaning: "But there came upon them what was in their creation of stubbornness and not turning back from falsehood, as if their hearts were not affected, so they were likened to a hard thing." Hardness (al-qaswa) is firmness.

Satan found in their dispositions an aid for casting his purpose into them, so he made that hardness attractive to them and incited them to persist in their sins and deeds. From here it becomes clear that misguidance arises from the readiness that Allah placed in the constitution of the soul.

When the wrongdoers are destroyed, justice returns, and it is the balance by which the world is sustained.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you see God giving the servant of the worldly life what he loves despite his disobedience, then it is only a gradual leading on (istidrāj)." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of every thing, until when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 42–45 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿So why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing.﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ ﴿So the people who had wronged were cut off at the root. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

When He warned them of the expectation of punishment, He followed this with evidence of the occurrence of punishment upon nations before them, so that these people would know that this is the custom of Allah concerning those who wronged by associating partners with Him.

This report is used to warn the listening polytheists by way of allusion (ta'rid), and they are the ones addressed by the speech commanded in the sentence before it.

So the clause "Wa-laqad arsalna" (And We certainly sent) is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "Qul ara'aytakum" (Say: Have you seen...), and the waw is for coordinating clauses, so it is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), since the clause it is coordinated with was itself resumptive. This clause opens with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and "qad" (certainly), to emphasize the content of the clause, which is what is derived with the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ (so We seized them with adversity and hardship). The listeners who were alluded to in the warning are treated as those who deny that what befell the nations before them was a punishment from Allah Most High for their turning away.

His saying "fa-akhadhnahum" (so We seized them) is coordinated with "arsalna" (We sent) in view of what the description "min qablika" (before you) implies of their nations' treatment of them with the same treatment your people gave you; the coordination therefore indicates an omitted element whose estimation is: "fa-kadhdhabuhum" (so they denied them).

Since their being seized with adversity and hardship coincided with the time of their messengers' presence among them, the position of the fa' of coordination indicates that this occurred in the sight of their messengers and before their extinction, so as to be a sign that Allah supported His messengers and aided them during their lifetimes. For the seizing of nations with punishment has two wisdoms: first, restraining them from denial; second, honouring the messengers by support in the sight of the deniers. In this there is an honour for the Prophet ﷺ, by informing him that Allah is his helper against his deniers.

The meaning of "akhadhnahum" is "asabnahum" (We struck them) with a striking that is firmly established. The explanation of "al-akhdh" has already passed at His saying ﴿akhadhat-hu al-'izzatu bil-ithm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The object of the seizing has been mentioned here because it is a seizing with a specific thing, unlike what comes shortly after this.

"Al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'" have already been discussed at His saying ﴿wal-sabirina fil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah. It has been explained that "al-ba'sa'" is hunger and "al-darra'" is sickness, but this is a specification with no basis, since what befell the nations of punishment was of many kinds. Perhaps whoever explained it this way considered what befell Quraysh through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ.

"La'alla" (perhaps) is for hope. It is made a cause for the beginning of their being seized with adversity and hardship before the uprooting.

The meaning of "yatadarra'un" is "yatadhallalun" (they humble themselves), because "al-dara'a" is humility and submission, and here it is a metonymy for acknowledging the sin and repenting from it, which is faith in the messengers.

The intended meaning is that Allah placed before them a light punishment before the greater punishment, as He said ﴿wa-lanudhiqannahum min al-'adhabi al-adna duna al-'adhabi al-akbar la'allahum yarji'un﴾ (And We will surely make them taste a punishment nearer than the greater punishment, perhaps they will return). This is from the abundance of His mercy mixed with what His wisdom requires. In it is a warning to Quraysh that adversity and hardship will befall them before the uprooting, which is the uprooting by the sword. Allah chose that their uprooting be by the sword to show that the victory of the Messenger, upon him blessings and peace, over them was by his hand and the hands of those who believed in him. That is more effective upon the Arabs, and for this reason the condition of those addressed by the warning was observed while they were present. So He placed all nations in their station, and said ﴿fa-lawla idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ (So why, when Our might came to them, did they not humble themselves?). Here "lawla" is a particle of rebuke, since it precedes a single past verbal clause, so "lawla" is not a particle of prohibition due to existence.

Rebuke is only fitting for those present, not for those who have passed away, since the purpose would be lost. So in this placement there is an indication of the equality of the two situations, and a rebuke of those present with the important lesson, because the time for remedy remains, cutting off their excuse.

It is permissible to take "lawla" here as expressing wishing (tamanni), by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), and the wishing would be a metonymy for informing that Allah loves the desired matter, so this is building a metaphor upon a metaphor. This love is what was expressed by "rejoicing" in the hadith: "Allah rejoices more at the repentance of His servant", the hadith. And the fronting of the temporal adverbial with its clause before its governing verb in His saying ﴿idh ja'ahum ba'suna tadarra'u﴾ is for emphasis on the content of its clause, and that it is a time that rightly should prompt hastening to humility because of the might that occurred in it.

"Al-ba's" has already been discussed at His saying ﴿wa-hina al-ba's﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it means severity against the enemy and overpowering him. The arrival of the might is the arrival of its effect, since what befell them of adversity and hardship is one of the effects of the strength of Allah Most High's power and His dominance over them. "Arrival" is used metaphorically for occurrence and taking place after not being, as a likening of a thing's occurrence to the arrival of one coming from another place through the movement of steps.

Since rebuke or wishing indicates the negation of the occurrence of the matter, he coordinated after it with "lakin" (but), as coordination according to the meaning of the speech, because humility arises from softness of heart. So its negation, conveyed by the particle of rebuke, arose from the opposite of softness, which is hardness, so he coordinated with "lakin".

The meaning: "But there came upon them what was in their creation of stubbornness and not turning back from falsehood, as if their hearts were not affected, so they were likened to a hard thing." Hardness (al-qaswa) is firmness.

Satan found in their dispositions an aid for casting his purpose into them, so he made that hardness attractive to them and incited them to persist in their sins and deeds. From here it becomes clear that misguidance arises from the readiness that Allah placed in the constitution of the soul.

Tazyin (making attractive) is making a thing an adornment. It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿zuyyina lil-nasi hubbu al-shahawat﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying ﴿fa-lamma nasu ma dhukkiru bihi﴾ (So when they forgot what they had been reminded of) is coordinated with the clause "qasat qulubuhum wa-zayyana lahumu al-shaytan" (their hearts became hard and Satan made attractive to them). Here "nisyan" (forgetting) means turning away, as already passed just before at His saying ﴿wa-tansawna ma tushrikun﴾. The apparent meaning is that abandonment is a consequence of the hardness of hearts and Satan's making their deeds attractive to them. "Ma" is a relative pronoun whose referent is "al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'", meaning: when they turned away from understanding through that and did not reach to remedy their situation. The meaning of "dhukkiru bihi" is that Allah reminded them of His great punishment through what He had previously sent to them of adversity and hardship. "Lamma" is a conditional particle indicating that the occurrence of its response coincides with the occurrence of its condition, and it does not carry the meaning of causation as the rest of the conditional particles do.

His saying ﴿fa-fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ is the response of "lamma". "Al-fath" is the opposite of "al-ghalq" (closing). "Al-ghalq" is blocking the opening through which one can pass to what is beyond it, with a door or the like; this is unlike erecting a wall, which is not called closing.

"Al-fath" is making the barrier that blocks not blocking and capable of being blocked, like a door when it is opened. Because the meanings of opening and closing are relative to one another, the instrument by which the barrier is held and opened is called "miftah" (key) and "miglaq" (bolt). Opening is only conceived after conceiving closing, and therefore His saying ﴿fatahna 'alayhim abwaba kulli shay'﴾ implies that the doors intended here were closed at the time they were seized with adversity and hardship, so it is known that they are the doors of good, since these are what cannot coexist with adversity and hardship.

So "al-fath" here is a metaphor for removing what pains and distresses, as in His saying ﴿wa-law anna ahla al-qura amanu wattaqaw lafatahna 'alayhim barakatin min al-sama' wal-ard﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. From it is the naming of victory as "fath," because it is the removal of the distress of subjugation.

He made their turning away from what they had been reminded of the time for opening the doors of good, because the meaning is that when they turned away from taking admonition from the warnings of punishment, We lifted punishment from them and opened to them the doors of good, as He explicitly stated in His saying ﴿wa-ma arsalna fi qaryatin min nabiyyin illa akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'i la'allahum yadarra'un﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] ﴿thumma baddalna makana al-sayyi'ati al-hasanata hatta 'afaw wa-qalu qad massa aba'ana al-darra'u wal-sarra'u fa-akhadhnahum baghtatan wa-hum la yash'urun﴾ [al-A'raf: 95].

Al-Jumhur read "fatahna" with the second letter (the tā') lightened. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the tā' doubled, for intensification of the opening through its abundance, as indicated by His saying "abwaba kulli shay'" (the doors of everything).

The word "kull" (all) here is used in the meaning of abundance, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

Upon them every long-tailed one and every Khansa' inclines toward every trembling one of the sand, a wide one.

Or it is used in its literal meaning, as a general term with specification, meaning the doors of every thing they seek. It is known that by "kull shay'" is meant all things of good specifically, by the context of His saying "hatta idha farihu" (until when they rejoiced), and by the contrast of this with His saying "akhadhna ahlaha bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'" (We seized its people with adversity and hardship). So there is an implied qualifier, meaning every good thing, like His saying ﴿ya'khudhu kulla safinatin ghasban﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound boat.

"Hatta" in His saying ﴿hatta idha farihu﴾ is for the beginning (ibtida'iyyah). The meaning of "farah" here is exultation and arrogance over a blessing and forgetfulness of the Benefactor, as in His saying ﴿idh qala lahu qawmuhu la tafrah inna Allaha la yuhibbu al-farihin﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. Al-Raghib said: "Rejoicing was not permitted except in His saying ﴿qul bi-fadli Allahi wa-bi-rahmatihi fa-bidhalika falyafrahu﴾ [Yunus: 58]." "Idha" is a temporal adverb for the past.

What Allah intends by this is respite for them, so that they might remember Allah and affirm His oneness, and thus their souls would be purified. So Allah tested them with harm and good, so that He might exhaust for them the two causes of remembrance and fear, because among souls there are souls led by hardship and souls led by gentleness.

The meaning of "akhdh" here is destruction. For this reason no object was mentioned for it, as was mentioned in His saying earlier ﴿fa-akhadhnahum bil-ba'sa'i wal-darra'﴾, to indicate that it is a seizing without leniency.

"Al-baghtah" is a form from "al-baght", which is suddenness, meaning the occurrence of a thing unexpectedly to the one to whom it happens, and it entails concealment. Therefore it is contrasted with "al-jahrah" (open manifestation) in the following verse. Here it may be construed as an active participle in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the nominative, meaning "surprising them", or construed as a passive participle as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the accusative, meaning "taken by surprise". ﴿Wa-kadhalika akhdhu rabbika idha akhadha al-qura wa-hiya zalimatun﴾ [Hud: 102].

His saying ﴿fa-idha hum mublisun﴾ — "idha" is "fuja'iyyah" (sudden). It is a place adverb according to Sibawayh, and a particle according to the grammarians of Kufa.

"Al-mublisun" are those despairing of good, bewildered, from "al-iblas", which is stupefaction and silence when seeking pardon, out of despair of being answered.

The clause ﴿fa-quti'a dabira al-qawm﴾ is coordinated with the clause "akhadhnahum", meaning: so We seized them with a seizing of uprooting. So He left none of them.

"Al-dabir" is an active participle from "dabarahu", from the pattern of "kataba", meaning he walked behind him. The verbal noun is "al-dubur" with the dal dammed, and "dabir al-nas" means their last ones. This is derived from "al-dubur", which is behind. Allah Most High said ﴿wa-ittabi' adbarahum﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. Cutting off the "dabir" is a metonymy for the destruction of all, because the one who uproots begins with what is nearest to him and goes on uprooting until he reaches its last, which is its "dabir." This has become like a proverb, and it is repeated in the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿inna dabira ha'ula'i maqtu'un musbihin﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

By "alladhina zalamu" (those who wronged) are meant the polytheists, since associating partners with Allah is the greatest wrong, because it is a transgression upon the right of Allah Most High over His servants, that they acknowledge His lordship alone, and because association entails many injustices, as those who associate do not believe in a law that restrains people from wrongdoing.

The sentence ﴿والحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ may be coordinated with the sentence ﴿ولَقَدْ أرْسَلْنا إلى أُمَمٍ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾ together with what is connected to it, as a coordination of one purpose with another. It may also be a concluding parenthetical sentence (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī), in which case the waw is a waw of parenthesis (wāw i'tirāḍiyya). Whatever its position, there are three considerations regarding its meaning:

The first: it is an instruction to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers to praise God for His granting victory to His messengers and their allies and for destroying the wrongdoers, because that victory is a blessing, since it removes a corruption that had been on the earth. Moreover, in God's reminding people of it there is an indication that they should expect the example of what happened to those before them, that they should expect God's victory as He gave victory to the believers before them. Thus "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a substitute (badal) for a verbal action, and it has been shifted from the accusative and indefiniteness to the nominative and definiteness to indicate the meaning of continuity and permanence, as was already explained in His saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh" in Surat al-Fātiḥa.

The second: "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a metonymy (kināya) for the fact that what was mentioned before it is one of God's blessings, because it is among the necessary implications of praise (ḥamd) that it be for a blessing. It is as if it were said: "So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off." And that is one of God's blessings, which calls for praising Him.

The third: the utterance "al-ḥamdu lillāh" comes from His Majesty as an expression of praise, used to express wonder at God's treatment of them and His gradual granting of respite to them in degrees, until the punishment became due upon them.

It may also be that God's utterance is a praise of Himself, with an allusion to the favour bestowed upon the Messenger and the Muslims. The lām in "al-ḥamdu" is for the genus, meaning: and the whole genus of praise, of which is the praise for the blessing of destroying the wrongdoers.

In all of this there is an alert that praise is due to God at the destruction of the oppressors, because their destruction is a benefit to people, and benefit is among the greatest blessings, and gratitude for a blessing is obligatory. This praise is a form of gratitude because it is a return for a blessing. Their destruction was a benefit because wrongdoing is an alteration of rights and a nullification of acting by the Sharia; when the right and the benefit are altered, ruin and chaos come, and people are afflicted in their lives. When the wrongdoers are destroyed, justice returns, and it is the balance by which the world is sustained.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you see God giving the servant of the worldly life what he loves despite his disobedience, then it is only a gradual leading on (istidrāj)." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of every thing, until when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 6, verse 46:**

﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts, what deity other than Allah could bring them back to you? Look how We vary the signs, yet they turn away.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), which returns the discourse to the argument with them about their associating others with Allah, the Exalted. The speech had moved away from this specific subject after His words: "Say: What thing is greatest in testimony?" Afterward it varied its treatment, covering the affirmation of resurrection, the affirmation of the truthfulness of the Messenger, the mention of calamities and threats, up to His words: "Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you?" [al-An'am: 40], and the verses that follow.

The repetition of the command to "say" to the one addressed is the same as what came just before, at His words: "Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you?" [al-An'am: 40], and so on.

The verb *ra'aytum* (have you considered) here is a heart-verb (ru'ya qalbiyya, used of mental perception) that takes two objects. This is not the same usage as the one mentioned just before in His words: "Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you or the Hour comes upon you?" [al-An'am: 40].

The readers' variant readings on *ara'aytum* are the same as their variants on the similar form in His words: "Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you?" [al-An'am: 40].

*Al-akhdh* (taking) means seizing a thing and removing it from its place. Here it is a metaphor for deprivation and annihilation, because deprivation is a necessary consequence of taking, with respect to the thing taken from. So it is a metonymy (majaz mursal, a figure where a related meaning stands in for the intended one). You may also take it as a figurative representation (tamthil), because Allah is the Giver of hearing and sight. When He removes them, that removal is like the situation of taking back what had been given, so the state of the Creator annihilating some of the faculties of His creature is likened to the state of a person seizing something from its place. Thus the likened state here is intellectual and not perceptible, while the state it is likened to is perceptible.

The sealing over the hearts was explained earlier in Surah al-Baqarah, at His words: "Allah has sealed over their hearts" [al-Baqarah: 7]. By "hearts" is meant the intellects by which intelligible things are perceived.

*Al-sam'* (hearing) is a verbal noun that denotes a kind, so it has the force of a plural. By its being made a construct with the pronoun of the addressees, it covers them all, and there is no need to pluralize it.

*Al-absar* is the plural of *basar*, which in lexical usage strictly means the eye. It has been said that *al-basar* is used for the faculty of sight, and for this reason it was pluralized so that, by its attachment to the pronoun, it would cover all the sights of the addressees. Perhaps the singular *sam'* and plural *absar* follow what complete eloquence requires: when two words are paired, one is light in the singular and the other in the plural. There is a wondrous secret in the arrangement of letters, vowels and pauses in the movement of the tongue, which is part of the eloquence of the Qur'an's speech, expressed by its composition. Similarly we see their placement in the Qur'an. He, the Exalted, said: "And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing and their sight and their hearts availed them nothing" [al-Ahqaf: 26].

In Arabic usage, *al-qulub* (hearts) is used to mean the intellects, because the heart is the source that supplies the intellect with the power of perception.

His words *man ilah* (what deity) are a suspension of the verb of seeing, because it is an interrogative. That is: do you know the answer to this question, or are you in doubt? This interrogative is used for affirmation (taqrir, a question that compels the hearer to affirm a truth), and its purpose is to force the listeners to consider its answer, so that they become certain that there is no deity other than Allah who could bring these back to them. For He is the Creator of hearing, sight and intellects, and they do not deny that the idols do not create. For this reason the Qur'an said to them: "Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not remember?" [al-Nahl: 17].

*Man* is in the nominative position as the subject. *Ilah* is the predicate of *man*. *Ghayr Allah* (other than Allah) is an attribute of *ilah*. *Ya'tikum* (brings to you) is a clause in the position of an attribute too. The thing being asked about is *ilah*, meaning: there is no deity other than Allah who brings these back. This indicates the unity of God (wahdaniyya). The meaning of *ya'tikum bihi* is "returns it to you," because the original sense of *ata bihi* is "came with it." Since a deprived thing, when a rescuer retrieves it, brings it back to its place, the bringing of the thing was used for returning it, as a metonymy or an allusion (kinaya, indirect expression).

[Page 235]

The pronoun governed by the preposition *ba'* (with) refers to hearing, sight and hearts, taken as referring to what was mentioned. For this reason it did not say *bihā* (with them, feminine). This usage of the pronoun is rare, but it is eloquent. It was discussed earlier in the interpretation of His words: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it to ransom themselves thereby" [al-Ma'idah: 36] in Surah al-Ma'idah, and at His words: "And give the women their dowries as a gift; but if they give you something of it willingly" [al-Nisa': 4] in Surah al-Nisa'. Its choice here over saying *ya'tikum bihā* is to avoid the supposition that the pronoun refers specifically to the hearts.

The speech runs in the manner of a threat and a warning. In it, the threat chosen is the seizing of their hearing and sight and the removal of perception from their hearts, because they did not give thanks for the blessing of these gifts but rather lost the benefit of them. This is what His earlier words indicate: "And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness; and if they should see every sign, they will not believe in it" [al-An'am: 25]. So this was a warning to them that these gifts are of no benefit to them, though they are fit to be used. It fits here that they be threatened with their total loss, if they persist in leaving these gifts unused in what their Creator commanded.

His words *unzur* (look) are a presentation of a rationally understood matter as if it were observed. That matter is the varying of the signs together with turning away from them, to the extent that the one looking can see them. As for the imperative form, it is used to express wonder at the state of their turning away.

The clause is a new resumptive sentence (istina' ibtida'i), functioning as a concluding statement (tadhyil, a closing remark that sums up what precedes). When He overwhelmed them with proofs of the unity of God and the truthfulness of the Messenger, and refuted their doubts, He followed all of that with a marvel at the strength of the proofs together with their continued turning away and obstinacy. Something close to this appeared earlier at His words: "Look how they invent lies against Allah" [al-Nisa': 50] in Surah al-Nisa'. This is a reminder to them that Allah is the Creator of their hearing, sight and minds, so that none other than Him is fit to be worshipped. *Tasrif al-ayat* (varying the signs) means the diversity of their kinds: sometimes signs come as proofs from observations in the heavens and the earth, sometimes as proofs from indications in human souls, and sometimes as proofs from the conditions of the earlier nations that Allah brought into being. So the signs here are the indications of the unity of God. They are united in purpose but differ in their methods, and vary in how closely they approach the understanding of people, both general and specific. They also differ in how the indications are composed, from the side of rational premises and otherwise, and from the side of encouragement and warning, and of admonition and reminder, so that they comprehensively reach understanding across the differing capacities of minds.

The definiteness of *al-ayat* (the signs) is anaphoric (li al-'ahd, referring back to something already known), and they are the signs known in this surah from the beginning, starting from His words: "He who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light" [al-An'am: 1].

*Thumma* (then) indicates a sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), because it conjoins one clause to another. It signals that the conjoined clause is more central to the purpose the speech is directed toward, which here is wonder at the strength of the proofs, and that the continuation of turning away and obstinacy despite them is even more worthy of wonder.

The predicate in *hum yasdifun* (they turn away) is a verb in the present tense, to indicate that their turning away is renewed. The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate serves to strengthen the judgment.

*Yasdifun* means they turn away intensely. It is said: *sadafa sadfan wa sududan*, when one inclines to a side and turns away from a thing. It is most often used intransitively, taking its object with *'an* (from). It is also sometimes used transitively, as al-Qamus explicitly states. Lexicographers rarely address this, but al-Zamakhshari, in his interpretation of His words near the end of this surah: "Who does greater wrong than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them?" [al-An'am: 157], supposed the sense "and turned people away from them," although he did not discuss this in al-Asas, nor did his commentators annotate his supposition. Since the signs were mentioned earlier, the object of *yasdifun* is omitted because it is evident, meaning: they turn away from the signs.

[Page 237]

This is a resumed sentence (*istinaf*) serving as a threat and warning, and as a notice to them that their turning away returns only evil upon themselves and does not harm anyone else, as in His saying: ﴿While they forbid others from it and keep away from it themselves; and they destroy none but themselves, though they perceive it not﴾ (6:26).

The discussion of ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly﴾ and the rest of the verse is the same as the discussion of its two preceding parallels.

In this verse and its preceding parallel, the *kaf* of address is used with the pronoun of address, unlike His saying ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight﴾ (6:46), and what follows it. This is because this verse and its parallel are more emphatic in rebuke, since they are more evident in establishing that the polytheists are within the power of Allah's capability. The coming of punishment is more likely to occur than the removal of sight, hearing and intellect, since such removal is rare. Therefore, rebuke for neglecting caution against the coming of Allah's punishment is stronger than rebuke for feeling secure against the taking of their hearing and sight. Thus the *kaf* of address is used here, its purpose being to alert, not to refer to specific persons addressed.

"Suddenly" (*baghta*) has already been explained above.

"Openly" (*jahra*) means open, the opposite of concealment and the opposite of secrecy. Its use in His saying ﴿And when you said: O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ (2:55) has been discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqara.

Here "openly" is placed in opposition to "suddenly." One would expect "suddenly" to be opposed by "gradually" (*nazra*, lit. "waiting"), or "openly" to be opposed by "secretly" (*khufya*). However, since "suddenly" means that a thing occurs without awareness of it, its occurrence is hidden, so it is good to oppose it with "openly." Thus the punishment that comes suddenly is that which is not preceded by any sign or announcement. The punishment that comes openly is that which is preceded by a sign, such as the cloud described in His saying ﴿So when they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ (46:24), or which is preceded by an announcement, as in His saying ﴿Then they hamstrung her, so he said: Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾ (11:65). Thus applying "openly" to what is preceded by something that indicates the occurrence of a thing is a metaphorical usage. The meaning of "suddenly" is not what occurs at night, nor the meaning of "openly" what occurs by day.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿will any be destroyed﴾ is used in the sense of denial, which is why an exception follows it. The meaning is: none will be destroyed by that punishment except the disbelievers.

By "the wrongdoing people" is meant those addressed themselves. The expression is stated explicitly in place of a pronoun so that they may be described as wrongdoers, that is, polytheists, because they wrong themselves and wrong the Messenger and the believers.

[Page 238]

This includes a promise from Allah, exalted is He, that He will save the believers. For this reason He permitted His Messenger to emigrate from Makkah together with the believers, lest the punishment descend upon them, as an honour to them, just as He honoured Lut and his family, and just as He honoured Nuh and those who believed with him. This is indicated by His saying ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ (8:33), then His saying ﴿And why should Allah not punish them?﴾ (8:34).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 48–49:

﴿We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners. So whoever believes and makes amends, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve. But those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them for their defiance.﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause ﴿Observe how We diversify the signs, yet they turn away﴾ [al-An'am: 46]. The connection is that their turning away and aversion were accompanied by pretexts: they claimed to seek signs according to their own proposals, and that they were not satisfied with the signs of the Divine Oneness. Do you not see their saying ﴿We will not believe you until you make a spring gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], up to the end of what is related of them in that verse? So God informed them that the sending of messengers is for conveying (tabligh), giving good news and warning, and not for amusing themselves with them by proposing signs.

He expressed it with (nursilu) rather than (arsalna) to indicate the renewal of sending, occurring concurrently with these two states, i.e., "We did not send and We do not send except...". So the phrase ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥālān), which are potential with respect to the future and realized with respect to the past.

The exception (istithnā') is from omitted circumstances, i.e., We did not send them except in the state of being bearers of good news and warners.

The restriction (qaṣr) is relative (idafi), in response to those who claimed that if he did not bring them a sign as they proposed, then he is not a messenger from God. It is thus a qaṣr qalb (restriction by reversal): i.e., We did not send the Messenger to be admired for displaying extraordinary feats. He used "good news and warning" as a metonymy (kināya) for conveying the message, because conveying it entails both matters, namely encouragement (targhib) and admonition (tarhib). Thus this metonymy achieves brevity (ījāz), since mentioning the necessary implication suffices without combining it with the thing implied.

The fa' in His saying ﴿so whoever believes﴾ is for consequence (tafrī'), i.e., so whoever among those addressed believes, then there is no fear for them, etc.

﴿Min﴾ is most apparently a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), as the conjunction of ﴿those who denied﴾ upon it supports. It is permissible for it to be conditional (sharṭiyya), especially since it carries the sense of elaboration (tafṣīl) of His saying ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾. If it is conditional, the coupling of ﴿there is no fear﴾ with the fa' is clear; if it is made relative, the fa' is for treating the relative as a conditional, and the two usages are close.

The meaning of (aṣlaḥa) is he did righteousness (al-ṣalāḥ), which is obedience to God in what He commanded and forbade, because God did not intend by His law anything but the reform of people, as He related of Shu'ayb: ﴿I intend only reform as far as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88].

The root meaning of (massa) is direct contact of a body with the hand, and it is synonymous with (lamasa) and (jassa). It is figuratively used for one body striking another, as in this verse. It has been discussed earlier in His saying ﴿A painful punishment will touch those among them who disbelieved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73] in Surat al-Ma'idah. It is also used figuratively for being affected by states, as one says: "he has a touch of madness." He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are conscious of God, when a passing impulse from Satan touches them, remember, and at once they see clearly﴾ [al-A'raf: 201].

He gathered the pronouns referring back to (min) in observance of its meaning, while singularizing the verbs (āmana) and (aṣlaḥa) in observance of its wording.

The ba' is causal (sababiyya), and (mā) is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyya), i.e., because of their defiance. Fisq is in its root meaning departure from the limit of good. Its usage became widespread in the Qur'an in the sense of disbelief and transgressing the limits of God, exalted. Its detailed treatment was given earlier at His saying ﴿And He leads astray thereby none but the defiant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The predicate of (kāna) was brought as a present-tense clause to indicate that their defiance was renewed and repeated; moreover, the use of (kāna) itself indicates continuity, because when (kāna) is not intended to denote the cessation of its predicate in the past, it indicates the continuation of the predicate through context, as in His saying: ﴿And God was ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 50:

﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.﴾

Page 240

When the argument with the polytheists had run its course, refuting their idolatry and dismantling their pretexts for denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, on the grounds that they would believe in his prophethood only if he brought a sign according to their own desires, and their doubt had been answered by the words ﴿And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-An'am: 48], and Muhammad ﷺ was among those included in the word "messengers", the discourse moved on to dismantling their excuses. Allah informed them of the true nature of prophethood and its connection with signs. He made clear to them that the Messenger is the one who challenges the community, because he is a deputy of Allah in conveying His will to His creation, and it is not the community that challenges the Messenger. The sign of the Messenger's truthfulness comes in accordance with his claim to be a messenger. Had he claimed to be an angel, or that he had been sent to rescue people from the calamities of this world and bring its good things close to them, it would have been a valid excuse for them to ask him for signs confirming that. But since the Messenger is sent for guidance, his sign is that what he brings is guidance itself, and that his miracle is what accompanies his call of things that human beings are incapable of producing the like of in their own time.

So His words ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾ form an initial, independent resumption (istiʼnaf ibtida'i), by which the discourse moved from one purpose to another.

The opening of the speech with the command to "say" is for emphasis on conveying it, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 40].

The command to "say" recurs from here up to His words ﴿For every news there is a settled time﴾ [al-An'am: 67], twelve times.

The restriction to denying these three claims mentioned in the verse looks back to the signs they had asked for, from His words ﴿And they say: Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8], and His words ﴿And if We had sent down to you a written scroll on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and His words ﴿If you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 35], and so on.

He opened the speech with the negation of saying in order to show that this saying was not joined with a claim to prophethood, so there is no basis for demanding those matters whose claim is negated for the Messenger, because a miracle by its nature comes in accordance with the claim to prophethood.

The lam in "lakum" is the lam of conveyance (lam al-tabligh), and it serves to strengthen the verb "to say" when there is no need to mention the one addressed by the speech, as here, since it is evident that those addressed by the speech are the deniers. For this reason His words ﴿and I do not say that I am an angel﴾ [Hud: 31] came without the lam of conveyance. When the purpose is to mention the one addressed by the speech, the lam is then called the lam of transitivity (lam ta'diyat fi'l al-qawl). What required the bringing in of this lam here is this saying itself, such that if a speaker said it, it would be fitting for it to have the lam of conveyance.

"Khaza'in" is the plural of "khizana", with a kasra on the kha', and it is the room or chest that contains what souls yearn for and what is beneficial in times of hardship and need. The meaning is that I have no authority with Allah, and I do not claim to be a keeper of the knowledge of Allah or His provisions.

And "khaza'in Allah" is used metaphorically for the connection of Allah's power with bestowing favours and giving beneficial goods to people in this world. Those potential and immediate connections, in their being concealed from people's eyes and their reach while benefiting them, are likened to the treasuries of the wealthy, which gather wealth, provisions, garments and food, just as that term is applied to them in His words ﴿And to Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7], meaning what is deposited in the higher and lower worlds of what benefits people. Likewise is His words ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

Fronting the predicate, which is His words "ʻindi" (with me), is for emphasis on it, because of the strangeness and good tidings it contains for those to whom it is announced, had he said it.

His words ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾ are conjoined to ﴿with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾, so it falls within the scope of the negated saying. The negation particle is repeated in the manner of conjoining negated items to one another, since it is customary to repeat the negation particle with them, to make explicit that all of those conjoined items are intended by the negation individually, lest it be supposed that what is negated is the combination of the two matters. The meaning is: I do not say "I know the unseen", that is, with a continuous knowledge constantly accompanying the attribute of messengerhood. As for his informing about some of the unseen matters, that happens when Allah wills to inform him of it by a special revelation, as He said ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not reveal His unseen to anyone except a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], and this falls under His words ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾.

The conjoining of ﴿and I do not say that I am an angel﴾ to ﴿I do not say that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾ has the verb "to say" expressed in it, unlike His words ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾. Perhaps this is to avoid the heaviness of two particles meeting: "lā" and "inna", which the context of emphasis requires, because claiming the like of this is something that should be emphasised. That is: I did not claim that I am of the angels, so that you would say ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. The negation of his being an angel is an answer to their proposal that an angel be sent down to them, or that an angel be with him as a warner. The intended meaning is the negation that the Messenger should be of the kind of angels, such that he would be accompanied by another angel in a relation of necessary association, as is the case with individuals of one kind. They imagined that messengerhood requires that the Messenger be of a species other than human, and for that reason they said ﴿What is this messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. So the meaning is the negation of the quiddity of angelhood from him, because the kind of angel has distinctive properties different from the properties of human beings. This is like a person who says to someone who is imposing hardship on him: "I am not made of iron."

Among the forced reasoning is that al-Jubba'i argues from this verse in support of the view of his companions, the Mu'tazila, regarding the superiority of angels over prophets, despite how far that is from the course of the verse. Al-Zamakhshari followed him in this, and such is his habit: he often compels the meanings of the Qur'an to accord with his school, so that his partisanship shrinks and his brilliance shrinks. This is a question we will discuss in its proper place.

The clause ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ is a resumed clause by way of explanatory resumption (istiʼnaf bayani), because when he denied that he says these statements, the context prompted the question of one asking: "Then what do you claim with regard to messengerhood, and what is its substance?" Since the ignorant imagine that the meaning of prophethood is those things disavowed in His words ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries...﴾ etc., it is answered by His words ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾, that is: messengerhood is nothing but conveying from Allah, the Exalted, through the medium of revelation.

So the meaning of "atabi'u" (I follow) is a figurative metonymy (majaz mursal) in restricting oneself to a thing and adhering to it alone, to the exclusion of other things, because that is among the necessary implications of the true meaning of following, which is walking behind the one followed (al-muttabi'), with a fatha on the mim... [Note: the original reads "bi-fathi al-muwahhadah", i.e., with a fatha on the letter ba' of al-muttaba'] that is: I do not deviate from conveying what is revealed to me to answering your proposals, whether by displaying extraordinary wonders, or by adding provisions, or by informing about the unseen. So receiving and conveying is the meaning of following, and it is the very essence of messengerhood from Allah, the Exalted. The restriction (qasr) derived here is relative (idafi), that is: rather than occupying oneself with displaying what you propose of the wonders that go beyond custom. The purpose of the restriction is to reverse their belief that the Messenger is not a messenger until he brings them the marvels they demand. Through this, the explanation of the true nature of messengerhood was achieved, that reality which the obstinate went astray from comprehending. This is the meaning of His words ﴿And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-An'am: 48].

Since the restriction is relative, it necessarily looks to reversing their belief with respect to their demands for following their proposals, that is: in conveying to you I follow only what is revealed to me. There is nothing in this statement that requires confining the Messenger's conduct, peace and blessings be upon him, to acting upon revelation alone, such that someone who denies, among our scholars, the permissibility of ijtihad for the Prophet ﷺ in matters of religion would take it as proof. That is a separate question with evidence on both sides, and it has no connection with this restriction. Whoever imagines it has misinterpreted.

* * *

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not then reflect?﴾

This is the conclusion of the argument with them and a tailpiece to the speech that opened with His words ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾, that is: say to them this tailpiece after that reasoning.

The state of one who does not comprehend the proofs and does not distinguish between similar meanings is likened to the state of the blind man who does not know where to aim or where to place his foot. And the state of one who discerns realities, and in whom no part of them is confused with another, is likened to the state of the one of strong sight, to whom shapes are not mixed up. This is an illustration of the state of the polytheists in the corruption of the arrangement of their proofs and the barrenness of their analogies, and of the state of the believers who were guided and put things in their proper places. Or it is an illustration of the state of the polytheists in which they are entangled, and the state demanded of them, from which they fled, so that they may know which of the two states is more fitting to adopt.

His words ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ are an interrogation of denial. It is conjoined by the fa' to the first interrogation, because it is consequent upon it, since the non-equality of the blind and the seeing is self-evident, and they can do nothing but acknowledge that they are not equal. Therefore it is inevitable that the denial of their failure to reflect should follow from it, as to which of the two they more resemble. The discussion of the command to "say" is like what was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 40].

Page 244

Tafakkur (reflection): the roaming of the intellect along the path of acquiring sound knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 51:

﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having besides Him no protector and no intercessor, that they may become righteous.﴾

The more apparent view is that it is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to His saying ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ [al-An'am: 50], because that is an introduction to the mention of those whose state is likened to the state of the seeing, and they are the believers.

The pronoun in (bihi) refers to ﴿what is revealed to me﴾ [al-An'am: 50], which is the Qur'an. What is revealed to the Messenger ﷺ is not intended by it as a miracle (iʿjaz).

And ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ are the believers, who are likened to the state of the seeing. They are defined by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) because of what the relative clause indicates of praise, and of the causal reasoning in directing his warning to them specifically and not others, because warning those who fear that they will be gathered is a beneficial warning, unlike the state of those who deny the gathering, who do not fear it, let alone feel the need for intercessors.

﴿That they will be gathered﴾ is the object (mafʿul) of "they fear", meaning they fear the gathering to their Lord, so they advance righteous deeds and refrain from what He has forbidden, out of fear that they will meet Allah while He is not pleased with them. Fear of the gathering entails belief in its occurrence. Thus there is in the speech an allusion that the polytheists are not benefited by warning, because they do not believe in the gathering, so how would they fear it? Therefore He said of them ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is alike to them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6].

The clause ﴿having besides Him no protector and no intercessor﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿that they will be gathered﴾, meaning they will be gathered in this state, so this state falls within the scope of fear. The content of the circumstance is something they believe, meaning they are not among those who claim that they have intercessors with Allah whose intercession will not be rejected; they are thus unlike the polytheists who claimed their idols were intercessors for them with Allah.

And His saying ﴿besides Him﴾ is a circumstantial phrase from (waliyy) and (shafiʿ), and the governing element of the circumstance is the verb "fear",

Page 245
meaning: they have no protector apart from Allah and no intercessor apart from Allah, because Allah is the Protector of those who believe. This is an allusion to the polytheists who took intercessors and protectors other than Allah.

In the verse there is evidence for the establishment of intercession by Allah's permission, as He said ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. Al-Zamakhshari (Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf) here has far-fetched interpretations regarding the meaning of ﴿they fear that they will be gathered﴾ and in making the circumstance from the pronoun in "yuḥsharu" a necessary (lazima) circumstance, and perhaps he aims by that at the root of his school's denial of intercession.

His saying ﴿that they may become righteous﴾ is a hoped-for outcome presented as the reason for the command to warn the believers, because their piety is hoped for, unlike those who do not believe in the resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 52 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. You are not accountable for their reckoning in anything, nor are they accountable for yours in anything, so that you would drive them away and thereby be among the wrongdoers.﴾

It is coordinated with His saying ﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 51], because it carries the meaning of "warn them and keep company with them," even though the arrogant among the polytheists disliked this. Here another attribute is applied to them, one more fitting to this ruling than the attribute mentioned before it, just as that attribute is more fitting to the ruling with which it was joined. For this reason the speech did not take the form of a pronoun, saying "and do not drive them away," since the Prophet ﷺ came calling to God, and the people most deserving of his companionship are those whose constant concern is calling upon God Most High with sincerity. How, then, would he drive them away, when they are most deserving of that gathering? As God Most High said, ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68].

Muslim related on the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "We were with the Prophet, six men. The polytheists said to the Prophet: 'Drive these away; they will not dare against us.' He said: 'I was there, and Ibn Mas'ud, a man from Hudhayl, Bilal, and two men whose names I will not mention. What God willed to occur occurred in the soul of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so he spoke to himself, and God Most High revealed ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾.'" End of quotation. Al-Wahidi named the rest of the six: they were Suhayb, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and al-Miqdad

صفحة ٢٤٦

ibn al-Aswad, and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt. In Ibn Mas'ud's words, "What God willed to occur occurred in the soul of the Messenger of God," there is a generality that is clarified by what al-Bayhaqi related: "The chiefs of Quraysh said to the Messenger of God: 'If you drove away these slaves and the smell of their woollen cloaks — the plural of jubbah — we would sit with you and converse with you.' He said: 'I am not one to drive away the believers.' They said: 'Then set them aside from us when we come, and when we rise, seat them with you if you wish.' He said: 'Yes,' hoping for their faith." Then God revealed this verse. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Khabbab, it occurs that the one who said this to the Prophet ﷺ was al-Aqra' ibn Habis and 'Uyayna ibn Hisn, and that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is remote, because the verse is Meccan, and 'Uyayna and al-Aqra' came to Medina only with the delegation of Banu Tamim in the Year of Delegations." End of quotation. I say: perhaps it did come from the two of them, and the Messenger of God ﷺ answered them with this verse, which was revealed concerning a similar proposal of theirs.

Its chain contains Asbat ibn Nasr, or Nadr, who was not strong, and in it is al-Suddi, who is weak. A similar report is mentioned in some tafsirs from Salman al-Farisi, but its chain is not known. Ibn Ishaq named those meant as the weak among the believers: Khabbab, 'Ammar, Abu Fukayha Yasar, mawla of Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Muharrith, Suhayb, and their likes, and that Quraysh said: "Are these the ones whom God has favoured among us?"

Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul that this verse was revealed during the lifetime of Abu Talib. On the authority of 'Ikrima, he said: "'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Mut'im ibn 'Adi, and al-Harith ibn Nawfal came, among the nobles of Banu 'Abd Manaf, to Abu Talib and said: 'If your nephew Muhammad would drive away from himself our clients, our slaves, and our freed men, it would be greater in our hearts, more hopeful for him with us, more inducing to our following him and our believing in him.' Abu Talib came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of what they had said to him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'If you did that, so that we might see what they want and where their words lead,' and God revealed these verses. When they were revealed, 'Umar came apologising." The meaning is that the Messenger of God ﷺ, out of eagerness for the faith of the great men of Quraysh so that they might be an example to their people, and knowing that his companions shared his eagerness and would not be troubled to be asked to rise from the assembly when the great men of Quraysh attended, since they had believed seeking the countenance of God and not for show or reputation; but God forbade him from that, and called it "driving away" to emphasise the meaning of the prohibition. That was for a wisdom, which outweighed the hope for the faith of those people, because God had perceived their inner states and knew that they would not believe; and God willed to show the self-sufficiency of His religion and His Messenger from relying on those tyrants and hard-hearted ones, and to show them that those weak ones were better than them, and that eagerness for nearness to the Messenger ﷺ is more deserving than eagerness for nearness to the polytheists, and that people are drawn to the religion, not that it is drawn to people, as God Most High said: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me; rather God has conferred a favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

The meaning of ﴿call upon their Lord﴾ is that they declare their faith in Him, apart from idols, by speech; and this entails that the speaker believes what he says, since at that time there was no hypocrisy, the hypocrites having appeared only in Medina.

Al-ghadah is the beginning of the day, and al-'ashi is from midday to morning. The ba' is for time (zarfiyya), and the definite article in both is the definite of genus. The meaning is that they call upon God all day long. So "morning and evening" is intended to encompass time and days, as "east and west" is intended to encompass places, and as one says: "Praise be to God, at dawn and at dusk." It was also said: what is meant by the calling is prayer, and by "morning and evening" is the general time of the five prayers. The meaning, then, is: do not drive away those who pray, that is, the believers.

Al-Jumhur read bil-ghadati with a fatha on the ghayn and an alif after the dal. Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ghayn, a sukun on the dal, and a silent waw after the dal, and this is a dialect form of al-ghada.

The clause ﴿seeking His countenance﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the raised pronoun in yad'una, meaning they call upon Him sincerely, seeking the countenance of God, that is, they do not seek any worldly gain.

Al-wajh is literally the part of the head in which are the two eyes, the nose, and the mouth. The word wajh is also used metonymically, by sending metaphor, for the whole essence. Here wajh is used metaphorically for the essence, on the reckoning of an elided noun: they seek the pleasure of God, that is, they seek to please Him rather than another. From this is His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the countenance of God; we desire no reward from you, nor thanks﴾ [al-Insan: 9], and His saying: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the countenance of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], which has been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. So the meaning of ﴿seeking His countenance﴾ is that they believed and called upon God, not seeking by that any worldly object. It has been said that Quraysh slandered the faith of the weak and attributed hypocrisy to them, but no sound report has come with this; so the more apparent view is that His saying

صفحة ٢٤٨

﴿seeking His countenance﴾ is praise of them for the completeness of their faith, and a testimony that they are free of all worldly aims; and it is not intended as a rebuttal of the polytheists.

The clause ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning in anything﴾ is a justification for the prohibition against driving them away, or a nullifying of the cause of the concern about driving them away, or of the cause of the request to drive them away. For nullifying the cause of the forbidden act amounts to its being a justification for the prohibition; and for this reason this clause is separated.

Al-hisab is counting the individual units of a thing that has units, and it is also used for exercising judgement to distinguish some states from others when they are confused, by way of metaphor, likening the tracing of states to the counting of units. From it comes the meaning of al-hisba, with a kasra on the ha', which is inquiry into distinguishing the conditions of the market people, between uprightness and its opposite.
