One says: "He reckoned with so-and-so over his deeds" when he examined and traced them. Al-Nabigha said:

He reckons with himself over how much he bought it for.

So hisab here is the verbal noun of hasaba, and what is meant by it is tracing the deeds and states and considering what they are to be recompensed with.

The plural pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ and in ﴿your reckoning for them﴾ may refer back to ﴿those who call upon their Lord﴾, which is an explicit antecedent, and this suits the consistency of the pronouns with ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾. The meaning is that they are the people of truth in your assembly, because they are believers, so they are not driven from it; and it is no concern of yours to reckon whatever else attaches to them by the claim of the polytheists, nor that their presence in your assembly turns the chiefs of the polytheists away from faith; that is, that claim is rejected in the face of the right of the believers to be in the assembly of their Messenger and to hear his guidance.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning﴾ is that the polytheists slandered the sincerity of these men. They said: "O Muhammad, these only gathered around you and accepted your religion because they find food and clothing with you." God Most High said: What is incumbent on you is only to consider their outward state, even if they have an inward state that contradicts it; their reckoning is with God, that is, the taking account of their states and calling them to account for them, in the manner of Noah's saying: ﴿Their reckoning is only with my Lord, if you were aware﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. So the meaning of their reckoning in this sense is the scrutiny of their intentions and inner states. The purpose of this is to rebuke the polytheists by the method of letting them run on, and it is not intended to weaken the certainty of the believers. Their reckoning in this sense is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object.

It is also possible that the two pronouns refer to something not mentioned in the speech but known from the context indicated by the occasion of revelation, so the two pronouns refer to the polytheists who asked for the weak believers to be driven from the Prophet's ﷺ assembly, and the pronoun in ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾ refers to the believers. The reference of the two pronouns differs according to what the context of the speech means, as in His saying: ﴿And they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [al-Rum: 9], and the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas concerning the battle of Hunayn:

We returned, and had it not been for us, their host would have surrounded the Muslims and seized what they had gathered.

That is, the polytheists seized what the Muslims had gathered of the spoils.

The meaning: you are not accountable for the reckoning of the polytheists, whether for faith in you or for not believing, anything at all; for that is committed to Me. So do not wrong the believers by depriving them of a right for the sake of obtaining the faith of the polytheists. This is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿If he is rich or poor, God is closer to both of them; so do not follow your desire, lest you deviate﴾ [al-Nisa': 135].

On this reading the idafa of their reckoning may be from the verbal noun to its object, that is, your calling them to account; and it may be from the verbal noun to its subject, that is, the reckoning of the polytheists concerning these believers, their poverty and weakness.

Alayka is a predicate placed first, and 'ala in it indicates the meaning of obligation and necessity, because the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, was concerned, or was in a state where he was concerned, with answering the chiefs of Quraysh when they asked him; so this is an alert that that interest is rejected.

The min in ﴿min shay'in﴾ is superfluous, for emphasising the negation, to make explicit the generality within the context of negation; and it is the particle whose implicit presence is the reason the noun following la is built on fatha, to indicate the intent of negating the genus.

The fronting of the two predicates before the subjects they are attached to in ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning in anything, nor are they accountable for yours in anything﴾ is not obligatory fronting, since there is a justification for starting with the two indefinite nouns here, namely that they occur in a context of negation; so the fronting of the two prepositional phrases is optional, and it must therefore have a purpose. The purpose may be mere concern, and it may be restriction. Since the meaning of restriction is attainable here, adopting it is more fitting to the most eloquent speech, and for this reason al-Kashshaf's discussion follows it. On this reading the meaning of the speech is the restriction of the negation of their reckoning to the Prophet ﷺ, to convey that their reckoning is with someone else, namely God Most High. This is the meaning conveyed by restriction arising from fronting when it occurs within a negation, and it is a meaning that is hidden from many because restriction by fronting within negation is rarely found. A famous example is His saying: ﴿No intoxication is in it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]; they explained it as meaning that the absence of intoxication is restricted to being the attribute of the wine of Paradise, so the restriction is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 52 (part 2 of 2):

Five emphatic devices have come together in this statement: (min) al-bayaniyyah (the explanatory min), (min) al-za'idah (the superfluous min), the fronting of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul), the exclusive construction in His words ﴿ma 'alayka min hisabihim min shay'﴾, and the emphasis by completion through negating the counterpart in His words ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾, for it resembles lafzi emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi). All of this serves to specify the utmost degree of disavowal of any attempt to answer their demand.

This statement also implies an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to the leaders of Quraysh who asked that the poor be distanced from the gathering of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, whenever they attend. They gave the impression that this was what prevented them from attending the gathering of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, from believing in him, and from being among his companions. So God addressed His Messenger with this statement, since the Messenger was the one being asked to push away his companions from his gathering. This was so that the askers would know that they had requested something that would not happen, and so that they would know that God had informed His Messenger ﷺ of their lying, and that, had they truly been desirous of faith, the reckoning of people's conditions would not have been incumbent upon them, and they would have occupied themselves with reforming their own selves. Thus the address is in the manner of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Lain ashraqta layahbatanna 'amaluka﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. He has explicitly stated this in His later words ﴿wa li-tastabina sabila al-mujrimin﴾ [al-An'am: 55]. Since the exclusive construction resolves into two relations, affirmation and negation, the relation implied along with the exclusion, namely the affirmation, is evident from the combination of the pronoun of the addressee and the pronoun of the absent parties: that is, the non-reckoning of them is restricted to you, so their reckoning falls upon themselves, since every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.

This is also indicated by His saying after it ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾, for it was mentioned to complete the justification, and for this reason it was coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the cause, because the combined meaning of the two clauses is the cause: that is, their reckoning is not upon you just as your reckoning is not upon them, but upon yourself, since every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, ﴿wa la taziru waziratun wizra ukhra﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. Just as you look only at their being believers, so too they are not required to fall short in any right of the believers in order to fulfill a desire of yours in something that does not concern them, or to attain the desire of others for their faith. The fronting of the predicate before the subject here is like its fronting in its earlier parallel.

In His words ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾ there is an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists, in that they displayed that by expelling the weak among the believers from the gathering of the Messenger ﷺ they wanted to give him counsel, so that he would gain the favor of the polytheists and the hope that they would believe, and thus his followers would increase.

Then, by this it becomes clear that the meaning is not: "Rather their reckoning is upon God and your reckoning is upon God," because this is not suitable to the context of the verse, and because then His words ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾ would become superfluous in this setting. For this reason the parallel of this second clause did not recur with the parallel of the first clause in what God related of Noah: ﴿in hisabuhum illa 'ala rabbi﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113] in Surat al-Shu'ara', because that was related as what had proceeded from Noah, whereas here what is related is the speech of God, exalted is He, to His Messenger. So be attentive.

It is also possible that the fronting of the predicate in both places of the verse is merely for the sake of emphasizing the negation of the obligation and duty indicated by the particle (ʿala) in both places, especially since considering the meaning of exclusivity in His words ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾ is not clear. For if we grant that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, had something like a belief that it was obligatory to follow up on their conditions, and that this belief was reversed by the exclusion, we do not find that regarding ﴿alladhina yad'una rabbahum bil-ghadati wal-'ashiyy﴾, since they have no such belief in this matter.

He placed the explanatory element before what it explains in His words ﴿wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾, because what is more important in both contexts is what concerns the addressee, in whom the allusion is made to those who asked him to drive them away, since he is the primary intended one. The second clause was only introduced to complete the justification, as has preceded.

His words ﴿fa-tatrudahum﴾ are in the accusative as the answer to the prohibition in His words ﴿wa la tatrudi alladhina yad'una rabbahum﴾. The repetition of the verb of driving away, rather than being limited to His words ﴿fa-takuna min al-zalimin﴾, is to convey the emphasis of that prohibition, and so that His words ﴿fa-takuna min al-zalimin﴾ may be built upon it, because of the long separation between the consequence and what it follows. Thus two aims were achieved by repeating the verb ﴿fa-tatrudahum﴾: a verbal one and a semantic one. Moreover, it is permissible to make ﴿fa-tatrudahum﴾ accusative as the answer to the negation in His words ﴿ma 'alayka min hisabihim min shay' wa ma min hisabika 'alayhim min shay'﴾, meaning: do not drive them away in response to the desire of their enemies.

His words ﴿fa-takuna min al-zalimin﴾ are coordinated upon ﴿fa-tatrudahum﴾ and consequent upon it, meaning: you would be among the wrongdoers by driving them away. That is, his being among the wrongdoers is negated, following the negation of its cause, which is the driving away.

He made their driving away an injustice because, when the obligation to reckon for them was removed from him, driving them away in order to please others became an injustice to them. In this there is an indirect allusion to those who asked for their expulsion in order to satisfy their arrogance, that they are wrongdoers who excessively commit injustice. It is also permissible to make His words ﴿fa-takuna min al-zalimin﴾ accusative as the answer to the prohibition, and to take His words ﴿fa-tatrudahum﴾, which was brought in this style to renew the connection of the speech because of the long separation between the prohibition and its answer by the adverbial phrase, the circumstantial clause and the justification, as being like an introduction to His words ﴿fa-takuna min al-zalimin﴾, and not intended in itself as the answer. The sense is: "you would be among the wrongdoers by driving them away."

[Page 253]

The waw is resumptive, as it is in its counterparts. The sentence is resumed as an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī, a resumption that clarifies), because the listener, having sensed a story alluded to by His saying, ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52], is struck with wonder at the arrogance of the great men of polytheism: how do they accept remaining in error out of pride, refusing to sit in a gathering that includes the weak among the righteous? So it is answered that this strange disposition is a trial (fitna) for them, which God created in their souls because of their bad character.

This sentence falls as a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the two conjoined sentences, to hasten the explanation. It is joined with the waw to alert the reader to the insertion, and this is the iʿtirāḍ waw, which is also called the istiʾnāf waw. God thus shows that the motive behind their demand to drive them away is contempt born of envy. Envy is at its greatest when the envious person sees himself as more deserving of the blessing envied. So that motive became a great trial in the souls of the polytheists, since it combined pride, self-admiration and delusion about what they did not possess, with contempt for the excellent and envy of them, and oppression of the people of truth. It also came between them and faith, and between them and benefiting from nearness to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The comparison is intended to express wonder at what is compared, namely that it has reached the utmost point of self-admiration.

The demonstrative refers back to the trial (futūn) derived from "fatannā" (We tried), just as a pronoun may refer back to a verbal noun in such a case as ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Maʾida: 8]. The meaning is: We tried some of them by means of others, a trial that makes the hearer desire to compare it and to picture it, so as to bring its reality near. When the speaker wants to bring it near by way of comparison, he finds no likeness to it in its strangeness and enormity, except to compare it with itself, since nothing is more wondrous than it, in the manner of their saying: "Foolishness is like its name."

There is no reference here to anything preceding that differs from what is compared. The demonstrative for the distant is used to indicate the greatness of what is pointed to. The detailed treatment of this type of comparison was given earlier, at His saying, ﴿And thus We made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], in Surat al-Baqara.

By "some" in the accusative (al-baʿḍ al-manṣūb) is meant the polytheists, who are the ones tried. By "some" in the genitive after the bāʾ (al-baʿḍ al-majrūr bi-l-bāʾ) are meant the believers. That is, We tried the great men of the polytheists, in the persistence of their polytheism and that of their followers, by means of the state of the poor believers who were sincere. This is shown by His saying, ﴿So that they say: "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾, for such a statement can only be made by polytheists. It is also confirmed by His saying at its conclusion, ﴿Is not God best aware of the grateful?﴾.

The saying may be a statement they make to themselves, or words they spoke among their chiefs. Whichever it is, they only say it while believing its content. So those who say, ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour?﴾ are the polytheists.

The lām in His saying "li-yaqūlū" (so that they say) is the lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl). What follows it is the effect of the cause, which indicates the cause after it has been omitted, in the manner of concision. The estimate is: We tried them so that they would see in themselves distinction and a right to precedence in virtues, deluded by the state of luxury, and so they would marvel how it is claimed that God bestows guidance and grace upon people whom they see as lower than themselves, and how they could be counted inferior to them before God. This is part of delusion and false self-admiration. A parallel, in omitting the cause and mentioning only its effect, is the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Taʾi:

*And I advanced while the spear was swaying between us, so that I might know which of them was the coward and which the brave.*

That is: so that the coward and the brave would be made manifest, and so that I would know them.

The interrogative is used for wonder and denial, as in ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25]. The demonstrative is used for belittling or wondering, as in His saying, relating the words of the polytheists, ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 36], in Surat al-Anbiyaʾ.

Placing the subject before a verbal predicate is for the purpose of strengthening the predicate.

Their saying, ﴿God has bestowed favour upon them﴾, was said in the manner of mockery and of going along with the opponent. That is, given that the believers believed God had favoured them with knowledge of the truth and had deprived the leaders of Quraysh of it, the polytheists marvelled at this belief: how can it be supposed that God bestows favour on poor people and slaves, and leaves aside the masters of the valley? This is like what God relates of them: ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. This is a well-known trait of the arrogant and tyrants. Something similar happened in Medina. Al-Bukhari narrated that al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Only the thieves of the pilgrims from Aslam, Ghifar, Muzayna and Juhayna have pledged allegiance to you." The Messenger of God said to him: "Tell me: if Aslam, Ghifar, Muzayna and Juhayna are better than Tamim, Amir, Asad and Ghatafan, have they failed and lost?" (that is, have the Banu Tamim and those joined with them failed?) He said: "Yes." He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they are indeed better than them."

There is another meaning in the verse: that the saying is hidden within the soul, and the pronoun in "li-yaqūlū" refers to the poor believers, so they are the ones tried, and the "some" in the genitive after the bāʾ refers to those of the polytheists who enjoy blessings. The demonstrative "these" then refers to the great men of the polytheists. By "favour" is meant the giving of wealth and good living. The interrogative is used for bewilderment, by way of metonymy (kināya). The reference to the polytheists takes into account what they were known for: their association of partners with God and their bad belief about Him. The meaning is: Likewise is the trial that befalls the great men of the polytheists, namely the trial of self-admiration and pride, when they disdained to enter into what the weak and the slaves entered into, of believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and keeping his company, out of arrogance at being equal to them. Likewise was the trial of another group, namely some of the believers, when they witnessed the good living of the great men of the polytheists in this world, despite their association of partners with their Lord. They then marvelled how God gives abundant provision to those who deny Him, and does not bestow such favour upon His friends, who are more deserving of their Lord's blessing.

The Qur'an has refrained from explicitly declaring the corruption of this inner suggestion, being content with calling it a trial. Thus it is known that it is an untrue thought. Also, His saying, ﴿Is not God best aware of the grateful?﴾, points to the refutation of this doubt. That is because it is a doubt that confused two matters that differ in their causes: the reward for faith and what God has prepared for its people of eternal bliss in the Hereafter, which follows from it as an effect follows its cause ordained by God's wisdom, and provision in this world, which follows from worldly causes such as trade, raiding, inheritance and gifts. Worldly provision has no causal connection with inner states of the heart, but is one of the effects of material circumstances. So God is best aware of the thanks of the grateful, and has prepared for them the reward of their thanks, and He is best aware of the causes of the provision of those who are provided for and given good fortune. Confusing the two domains results from the weakness of thought that afflicts human suggestions, arising from poor reasoning and neglect of reflection on realities, on causes and their effects. Many doubts and errors on this matter have befallen Muslims and others, diverting them from seeking things from their proper sources, keeping them from mending their deficiencies in the present life, or deceiving them into neglecting what they must prepare for. All of this results from confusing the religious states of the Hereafter with the worldly regularities of created existence. This happened to Ibn al-Rawandi, through bewildering ignorance, in his saying:

*How many a learned man whose doctrines have baffled him, and how many an ignorant man you find provided for!*

*This is what left the thoughts bewildered, and made the eminent scholar a heretic.*

There is no doubt that those who listened to the Qur'an from the one upon whom it was revealed (ﷺ) were guided and awakened, and for this reason they became fit to possess knowledge and to meet it.

The "min" in His saying, ﴿from among us﴾, is the min of origin (ibtidāʾiyya). "Bayn" is a noun of place indicating the middle. The meaning is: God favoured them by choosing them from our midst, that is, He favoured them and left us, so it returns to the meaning of "from other than us."

His saying, ﴿Is not God best aware of the grateful?﴾, is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) for the whole sentence. It is therefore part of the speech of God, Most High, and not part of what was said. For this reason it is separated. The interrogative is affirmative (taqrīrī). "Aʿlam" is made transitive with the bāʾ because, in the form of the comparative, it has become intransitive. The meaning is that God is best aware of the grateful among His servants, and for this reason He bestowed the favour of faith and success upon those who pointed to them with their saying, ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour?﴾.

The meaning of God's knowledge of the grateful is that He is best aware of those who came to the Messenger (ﷺ) responding to his call with sincerity, seeking deliverance from unbelief and desiring a good end. He is gentle with them, facilitates faith for them, makes it beloved to them, adorns it in their hearts, and increases them day by day in firmness, success and righteousness. He is therefore more aware of their hearts and their sincerity than the people who suppose that the shabbiness of the condition of some believers corresponds to the state of their hearts in faith, and so judge people by their outward garb rather than their intentions. This concluding remark therefore looks back to His saying, ﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾ [al-Anʿam: 36].

It is also known from His saying, ﴿Is not God best aware of the grateful?﴾, that He is likewise best aware of their opposites. The opposite of thanks is disbelief, as He, Most High, said: ﴿If you give thanks, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. He is therefore best aware of those who come to the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, mocking and arrogant, with no concern except to belittle Islam and the Muslims, having exhausted their strength and their reason in disputing with the Messenger (ﷺ) and misleading the common people about the reality of the religion. So there is an allusion in the speech to the polytheists.

[Page 257]

It is coordinated with His saying ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am 6:52], and it is an ascent in honouring those who call upon their Lord morning and evening. They are the ones meant by His saying ﴿those who believe in Our signs﴾.

The meaning of ﴿they believe in Our signs﴾ is that they are certain that God is able to send down many signs. They believe in what has been sent down of the signs, and especially in the signs of the Qur'an, which is among the signs. God the Exalted says ﴿Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:51].

As for His saying ﴿so say: Peace be upon you﴾, it has been said that its meaning is: greet them with the greeting of Islam, which is the phrase "Peace be upon you." It has also been said: convey to them peace from God the Exalted, as an honouring of them, in opposition to the polytheists' demand that they be driven away.

God has honoured them with two honours. The first is that the Prophet ﷺ greets them with peace first when they enter upon him, and this is a distinction for them, because it is the custom of peace that the one who enters begins it. Then it is possible that this is a ruling that holds continually with them whenever they are admitted to the Messenger of God ﷺ. And it is possible that it refers to the occasion on which he conveys to them this good news, so he is regarded as one who comes to them, because he brings them this glad tidings.

The second honour is the good news to them of God's pleasure with them, in that He forgives them what evil they do if they repent after it and make amends. Although this report includes all Muslims, perhaps it was not known, so the good news of it was given to the faces of the believers on that day as an honouring of them, so that they would be blessed in their stance toward the rest of their brethren and those who come after them.

As for al-salam (peace): it means security. It is a word the Arabs used when a man met another, to show that he was at peace and not at war. This was because the Arabs had bloodshed and vendettas among them, and they would take revenge for themselves even on someone other than the aggressor from his tribe. So when a man met someone he did not know, he could not feel safe that there was not between himself and that person's tribe some enmity and resentment, so one of them would grant the other security by saying "Peace be upon you," or "Peace," or something similar. God the Exalted has related this of Abraham, peace be upon him. Then this expression spread and became used as an honour. The verbal noun of sallama is taslim. Al-salam is a noun of action (ism masdar), and in usage it occurs indefinite, in the nominative and accusative, and definite with the article only in the nominative. As for its being indefinite with the nominative, as in this verse, it is on the basis that it is treated as a noun meaning security, and beginning with it is permissible because the intended sense is the category, not a particular individual. The predicate was not put first in order to express the visitor's concern to bring reassurance into the heart of the one visited, that he is the bearer of good, not the bearer of evil. So this is a case of placing what would normally come later first, as a kind of optimism (tafa'ul).

As for its being definite with the nominative, it is because the definite article of the genus (lam al-jins) has entered upon it.

[Page 258]

The word 'ala (upon) in both cases serves to indicate the firm establishment of being clothed in security, i.e., security is settled upon you and enveloping you, meaning: do not fear.

If they put it in the accusative with indefiniteness, then on this basis it is like the verbal noun of sallama, so it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) that stands in place of its verb. Its implied sense is: "I greet you with a greeting (sallamtu salaman)." Therefore it is not used with 'ala. Then they also put it in the nominative on this basis, so they do not use 'ala with it, for the purpose of indicating permanence and stability through the nominal sentence in the nominative, because this cuts off the consideration of its substitution for the verb. For this reason it is necessary to assume an inchoative subject (mubtada'), i.e., "your affair is peace," on the pattern of ﴿so patience is fitting﴾ [Yusuf 12:18]. The nominative is stronger, and for this reason it has been said that Abraham returned a greeting better than the greeting of the angels, as is related by His saying ﴿They said: Peace. He said: Peace﴾ [Hud 11:69]. It has been reported concerning the return of greeting that it should be with the same expression of the first greeting, as in His saying ﴿except the saying: Peace, peace﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:26]. It has also been reported both with the definite and the indefinite, so it is fitting to make the return the better in indication. As for the definite and the indefinite, they are equal, because the definite is the definiteness of the genus. For this reason the Qur'an mentions Jesus: ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born﴾ [Maryam 19:15], and it is related that he said ﴿And peace be upon me the day I was born﴾ [Maryam 19:33].

The clause ﴿Your Lord has prescribed upon Himself mercy﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), a fresh beginning, and it is the first thing intended from what is said, whereas peace is a preface to the speech. Some have permitted that it be a second speech.

Its counterpart has already been explained in His saying ﴿He has prescribed upon Himself mercy; He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-An'am 6:12] in this surah.

So His saying here ﴿Your Lord has prescribed upon Himself mercy﴾ is a preparation for His saying ﴿that whoever among you does evil out of ignorance﴾, and so on.

His saying ﴿that whoever among you does evil out of ignorance﴾ was read by Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub with the hamza opened (annahu), as an apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from "mercy," because the general mercy includes forgiveness for one who commits a sin and then repents and makes amends. The rest read it with the hamza kasra (innahu), as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) answering an expected question about the extent of the mercy.

[Page 259]

("Man," in "whoever," is conditional, and it is more indicative of generality than the relative pronoun.) The preposition ba' in His saying "bi-jahalah" (out of ignorance) is for accompaniment (mulabasah), i.e., "accompanied by ignorance." The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "'amila" (did).

Jahalah is used for the absence of knowledge of something, and it is also used for what is opposite to forbearance (hilm). It has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon God for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:17], in the surah of al-Nisa'. The fitting meaning here is the second: whoever does evil out of folly from his own self and foolishness, because the believer does not commit misdeeds except through his desire overcoming his right guidance and restraint. This is the sense that suits the realisation of the meaning of mercy. As for taking jahalah to mean lack of knowledge, on the basis that one ignorant of a sin is not held accountable, then there is no strength in linking His saying ﴿then he repents after it and makes amends﴾ to it, unless it is meant to be: then he realises that he has done evil.

The pronoun in His saying "min ba'dih" (after it) refers to "evil," i.e., after the evil, after his doing it. It is also possible to make it refer to the verbal noun implied in "'amila," as in the pattern of ﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:8].

The meaning of "aslaha" (made amends) is that he made his self righteous, or he made his deed righteous after having done evil. It has already been mentioned at His saying ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed God will turn to him﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:39], in the surah of al-Ma'idah, and at His saying ﴿except those who repent, make amends and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:160], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is the answer-indicator of the conditional clause (dalil jawab al-shart); that is, He is intensely forgiving and merciful. This is a metonymy (kinaya) for forgiveness of this penitent who makes amends.

It was read by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf with the hamza of "fa-innahu ghafur rahim" kasra, on the basis that the clause is emphasised with inna. Thus it is known that the meaning is that God has forgiven whoever repents, because He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy. It was read by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub as "fa-annahu" with the hamza opened, on the basis that it is the opened "anna," sister of "inna," so what follows it is interpreted as a verbal noun. The implied sense is: "then His forgiveness and His mercy." This is part of a sentence that necessarily requires an implied predicate, i.e., "for Him," meaning: it is established for whoever does evil and then repents.

[Page 260]

The conjunction *waw* is resumptive (*isti'nafiyyah*), as stated earlier in His words ﴿And thus We test some of them by means of others﴾ [al-An'am: 53]. The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for the discourse that began with His words, exalted is He, ﴿And warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 51].

*Tafsil* (detailing) means clarification and elucidation. It is derived from *fasl*, which is the separation of one thing from another. Since mixed things, when they are detailed, become distinguished from one another, *tafsil* was applied to clarification through the relation of necessary association (*'alaqat al-luzum*), and this usage became so common that it became a literal meaning. Of the same kind is the naming of explanation as *tabyin* and *ibanah*, since the root meaning of *ibanah* is severing. The intended meaning of *tafsil* here is elucidation, that is, bringing clear signs that indicate the purpose behind them.

The *ayat* (signs) are the signs of the Qur'an. The meaning is: We detail the signs and make them clear with a detailing like this detailing, above which there is no other detailing, and it is a detailing through which knowledge of their intended meaning is attained clearly.

His words ﴿and so that you may come to know﴾ (*wa-li-tastabin*) are coordinated with a deleted cause (*'illah muqaddarah*), which is indicated by His words ﴿And thus We detail the signs﴾. This is because what is referred to by the demonstrative is a detailing that reaches the utmost degree of clarity, so it is understood from the reference to it that its purpose is the manifestation of knowledge to the Messenger. Since that detailing is of this standing, it is known that it is a cause for something that suits it, namely the Messenger's grasp of that detailing. Thus it is valid for another cause from the knowledge of the Messenger ﷺ to be coordinated with it, namely his clarifying for himself the way of the criminals. The estimated meaning, for example, is: "And thus, by this detailing, We detail the signs so that you may know their reality through their detailing, and so that the way of the criminals may become clear to you." Thus the sentence contains concision through ellipsis (*ijaz al-hadhf*).

Likewise, whenever the use of "*kadhalika naf'alu*" (thus do We do) follows the mention of great acts, and the verb mentioned after the demonstrative is suitable to be a cause for a matter that is of a kind to be caused by something similar, it is valid to coordinate another cause with it, as here, and as in His words ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. This is unlike cases where it is not suitable. For this reason, when a cause is intended to be mentioned after it, it is mentioned without coordination, as in His words ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced nation, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

*Sabil al-mujrimin* (the way of the criminals) means their path and their conduct in wrongdoing, envy, arrogance, contempt for people, and obstinacy in disbelief.

[Page 261]

The criminals are the polytheists. The noun in apparent form was placed in the position of the pronoun, in order to specify that they are the intended people, and to apply to them the description of criminality.

He singled out the criminals because they are the ultimate aim of all these signs, for the clarification of the hidden conditions of their state to the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read it with a *ta'* (t) with a dot above at the beginning of the verb, taking it as the *ta'* of address (*ta' al-khitab*). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with a *ya'* of the third-person absent. Furthermore, Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read *sabil* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, taking it as the object (*maf'ul*) of *tastabin*; in that case the *sin* and the *ta'* are for requesting (*talab*). The rest read it with a *damma* on the *lam*, taking it as the subject (*fa'il*) of *yastabin* or *tastabin*; in that case the *sin* and the *ta'* are not for requesting but for intensification (*mubalaghah*), like *istajaba*.

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read *sabilu* with a *damma*, taking the *ta'* of the present tense as the *ta'* of the feminine, because *sabil* is feminine in the dialect of the Hijaz. And it is taken as from *istabana*, which is intransitive, with the meaning of *ban* (to become evident), so that *sabilu* is the subject of *tastabin*, meaning: so that their way may become clear to you and to the believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 56:

﴿Say: "Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God." Say: "I will not follow your desires; for then I would have strayed, and I would not be among the guided."﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the discourse returns to refuting polytheism through disavowing the worship of their idols. After he had refuted the divinity of the idols by way of argument, from His saying ﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 14], and His saying ﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you..."﴾ [al-An'am: 40], and His saying ﴿Say: "Tell me, if God takes away your hearing and your sight..."﴾ [al-An'am: 46], this verse comes with another method for refuting the worship of idols, namely that God forbade His Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, from worshipping them and from following the desires of their worshippers.

Page 262

The verb nuhitu ("I have been forbidden") is in the passive form, to dispense with mentioning the agent, since the intended meaning is clear, i.e., "God forbade me." It takes the preposition ('an), so the preposition is elided before (an) in the regular manner.

The relative pronoun used for the idols is alladhina, which is designated for rational beings, because they treated them as rational beings, so He brought for them what expresses their belief; or because they worshipped jinn and some humans, so the rational ones among their objects of worship were given precedence.

The meaning of tad'una ("you invoke") is "you worship and turn to them in matters of great concern," i.e., you call upon them. The phrase ﴿min dun Allah﴾ ("besides God") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the omitted object, and its governing element is tad'una. It is a description of what came to dominate the polytheists, namely their preoccupation with worshipping idols and calling upon them instead of worshipping and calling upon God, to the extent that it is as if they worshipped them besides God, even though they only associated them in worship with God, even if only at some times. In this there is a rebuke against them for the disorder of their belief, since they associated in worship with God those who do not deserve it, while they themselves maintain that God is the owner of the idols and the one who made them intercessors. But that is as nothing, because every act of worship they directed toward the idols was a transgression upon the right of God to have it directed to Him alone.

The clause ﴿Say: "I will not follow your desires"﴾ is another independent resumptive sentence. The conjunction was avoided in favor of resumption so that it would be an independent purpose. The command "say" is repeated for additional emphasis on the resumption and its independence, so that this negation includes following them in the worship of idols and in other aspects of their misguidance, such as seeking to drive away the believers from his assembly.

Al-ahwa' ("desires") is the plural of hawa, which is excessive love. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120] in Surat al-Baqarah. The reason He said ﴿I will not follow your desires﴾ rather than "I will not follow you" is to indicate that they, in their religion, follow desire and reject the proof of reason. In this there is a declaration of their ignorance in establishing their religion on a foundation that is not firm.

The clause ﴿for then I would have strayed﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, i.e., "If I were to follow your desires, then I would have strayed." Similarly, the position of "idhan" (then) when it enters upon a non-future verb is that it is then the answer to an implied condition stated by (inna, "if") or (law, "if") in some cases, as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

If 'Abd al-'Aziz returns to me with the like of it, and enables me to it, then I will not forgive it.

and implied in other cases, like this verse and His saying ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

The placement of the answer of idhan before idhan in this verse is for emphasis on the answer. For this emphasis it is reinforced with "qad," although it is hypothetical and not actual, to indicate that its occurrence is certain if the implied condition, indicated by idha, were to be realized.

His saying ﴿and I am not among the guided﴾ is conjoined to ﴿I have strayed﴾; it is conjoined to it to indicate that it is another consequence of the implied condition. It indicates that if he did that, he would move out of his present state, in which he is among those guided, into the state of straying. In addition, it provides the emphasis of the content of the clause ﴿I have strayed﴾, because he negated of himself the opposite of straying, so the reality of straying is established by supposition and assumption.

Emphasizing a thing by negating its opposite is an Arabic method, which I have discovered and pointed out at His saying ﴿They have indeed strayed and were not guided﴾ [al-An'am: 140] in this surah. Its parallel is His saying ﴿Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 79].

The predicate has been given as a prepositional phrase: "min al-muhtadin" ("among the guided"), and it was not said "wa ma ana muhtad" ("and I am not guided"), because the intended meaning is the negation of the category of which the predicate is "among the guided." The definite article in al-muhtadin is the definite article of the class (ta'rif al-jins). So the speaker's report about himself that he is among the guided indicates that he is one of the group known among people as the group of the guided, and so it conveys that he is guided by a method resembling the method of inference. It is thus of the type of kinaya (allusion), which is establishing a thing by establishing its necessary concomitant, and it is more eloquent than explicit statement. In the Kashshaf, on His saying ﴿He said: "Indeed, I am of those who do your deed" from among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 168], it is said: "Your saying 'So-and-so is among the scholars' is more eloquent than your saying 'So-and-so is a scholar,' because you bear witness for him that he is counted in their company and that his participation with them in knowledge is well known." And at His saying ﴿They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 136] in Surat al-Shu'ara', it says: "If you say: if it were said, 'Whether you admonish or do not admonish,' it would be more concise, and the meaning would be the same. I say: The meaning is not the same, and there is a difference between them, because what is intended is 'It is all the same to us whether you performed this act, which is admonition, or you were not at all of its people and not engaged in it.' So it is more eloquent in showing little regard for his admonition than the saying 'or you did not admonish.'" Al-Khafaji said the origin of this is from Ibn Jinni.

For this reason, the negation of this predicate conveys the negation of this allusive attribution, so its eloquence in negation is like its eloquence in affirmation, because the allusive meaning is the same. Therefore, the Kashshaf explained it with the phrase: "And I am not in anything of guidance." Some of those who examined it did not perceive this subtlety; al-Tibi transmitted it from him and said: since your saying "He is among the guided" conveys in affirmation that the one spoken of has great shares of guidance, then in negation it necessitates that many shares be negated from him, and that is compatible with his retaining a small share. This is a sophistry that was hidden from its speaker, because the negation conveys that only if the affirmation's indication were through explicit lexical restrictions; but when it is by way of allusion, it is necessarily tied to the expression, in affirmation and negation alike, because it is an intellectual, not a lexical, indication. For this reason al-Taftazani said: it is of the type of emphasizing the negation, not negating the emphasis. It conveys that he has departed from this group of which he was counted, and this is more severe than merely being characterized by the absence of guidance, because a person's separation from his group after having been of it is more grievous to him than being characterized by what opposes their attributes before joining them.

The saying of God ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] has already occurred in Surat al-Baqarah, and we deferred its full exposition to this place.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 57:

﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it. What you seek to hasten is not with me. The judgment belongs only to Allah. He relates the truth, and He is the best of deciders.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a resumptive sentence that opens a new topic). The discourse moves from refuting shirk, through the proof of divine revelation which confirms the earlier proofs, to establishing the truthfulness of the Message by a proof from Allah that likewise confirms the earlier proofs. The aim is that the disbelievers should despair of trying to turn the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, away from his call to Islam, and of casting doubt on his revelation by saying: "He is a sorcerer, a madman, a poet, and these are the fables of the ancients." And that they should also despair of

[Page 265]

introducing doubt about the sincerity of the faith of his companions, and of sowing estrangement between him and them, through their attempts to drive his companions away from his gathering when his opponents were present. So Allah commanded him to tell them that he is upon certainty regarding the affair of his Lord, which does not waver. Joined to this is a response to the doubt raised by their argument for denying the threat, based on what befell the nations before them: that if it were true, the punishment would have been hastened upon them. They used to say: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and they would say: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our portion before the Day of Reckoning﴾ (Sad: 16). So Allah said to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Say: If I had what you seek to hasten, the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾ (al-An'am: 58). He emphasized the sentence with a particle of emphasis because they deny that he is upon a clear proof from his Lord.

The repetition of the command "say" is for renewing the attention already explained at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you﴾ (al-An'am: 40).

Al-bayyinah (the clear proof) is, originally, a feminine adjective from *bayyin*, meaning "clear." It is therefore a qualifier applied to an elided noun, known from the context, i.e., a clear indication or a clear proof. Then the use of this adjective became common, so that it became a noun for the proof that establishes the truth and to which no doubt attaches, and for a clear indication, and also for a miracle. Here it may mean a clear indication, i.e., certainty. This is more fitting with *'ala* ("upon"), which indicates firm establishment, as in their saying: "So-and-so is upon insight (*'ala basirah*)," meaning: I am firmly established in certainty regarding the matter of revelation.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of al-bayyinah is the Qur'an, and that *'ala* is used in the sense of adherence, as a figurative metonymy, because being "upon" something implies adherence, meaning: I do not oppose what the Qur'an has brought.

The phrase "from my Lord" (*min Rabbi*) is a qualifier of *bayyinah*, which conveys its exaltation and perfection. The *min* is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*), meaning a clear proof coming to me from my Lord, namely the indications which Allah revealed to him and which the Qur'an and other than it brought. It is also possible that the *min* is for connection (*ittisaliyyah*), meaning: upon a certainty connected to my Lord, i.e., through knowledge of His Oneness. That is, I do not waver in this, so do not hope to turn me away from it. That is, I believe in one God whose existence and oneness are indicated by the signs of His creation and power; so I am certain of what I have believed, and no doubt reaches me. This is then presented in a manner that implicitly censures the polytheists, in that they are in confusion regarding the affair of their gods and are without insight.

The clause ﴿and you have denied it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to *bayyinah*. It conveys wonder at them, that they denied what the clear proof indicates. It is also possible that it is coordinated with the clause ﴿I am upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾, meaning: I am upon a clear proof, while you have denied what the clear proofs indicate, so there is a vast difference between me and you.

The pronoun in His words "it" (*bihi*) refers to the clear proof, considering its interpretation as clarification, or considering that what confirms it is certainty or the Qur'an, in a way that makes *min* for origin, meaning: you have denied certainty out of obstinacy and stubbornness. It may also refer to "my Lord," in a way that makes *min* for connection, meaning: I was upon certainty regarding my Lord, and you have denied Him although the indications of His Oneness are clear and manifest. It may also refer to something not mentioned in the speech, namely the Qur'an, because of its common circulation among them regarding its affair; when the pronoun of the absent is used without antecedent, it is understood to refer to it by context.

The *ba'* with which the verb *kadhdhabtum* is transitive is for emphasizing the adherence of the verb's meaning to its object, as in His words: ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 6). Therefore, the verb "to deny" when transitive with *ba'* indicates the sense of rejection, i.e., strong denial. Perhaps the usage is that they do not make the verb of denial transitive with *ba'* except when what is meant is the denial of a proof or evidence that is regarded as a cause of belief. So one does not say *kadhdhabtu bi-fulan* ("I denied so-and-so"), but rather *kadhdhabtu fulanan* ("I called so-and-so a liar"). Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿When they denied the Messengers﴾ (al-Furqan: 37), and He says: ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ (al-Qamar: 23).

The indirect implication regarding them with respect to their belief about their gods remains as we have explained.

His words ﴿What you seek to hasten is not with me﴾ form an explanatory resumptive sentence (*istinaf bayani*), because their condition, in persisting in denial, is something that increases their obstinacy when they hear the foolishness of their opinions and the disparagement of their beliefs. So they would say: If your statement were true, where is the threat you have threatened us with? They said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and they said: ﴿Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ (al-Isra': 92). So he was commanded to answer by saying: ﴿What you seek to hasten is not with me﴾.

*Al-isti'jal* means seeking that something be hastened. It is transitive to one object, which is the one from whom the hastening of something is sought. When one wishes to mention the thing that is hastened, it is transitive to it with *ba'*. The *ba'* here is for transitivity. The object here is elided, indicated by His words ﴿with me﴾. The estimated meaning is: you seek to hasten me with it (i.e., the punishment). As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (al-Nahl: 1), the more apparent view is that the pronoun of the absent refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah), and this will come at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl.

The meaning of ﴿with me﴾ is that it is not within my power, as one says: "such-and-such is not in my hand." So "being with" is a figurative expression for disposal through knowledge and capability. The meaning is: I am not the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful; that is, I am not a god, but I am a sent servant who stops at what I was sent with.

The literal meaning of *'inda* ("with, at") is a noun of place denoting nearness. It is used figuratively for a thing's being stable with something and its ownership of it, as in His words: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ (al-An'am: 59). It is also used figuratively for keeping hold of a thing, as in His words: ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 85), and ﴿Their scheming is with Allah﴾ (Ibrahim: 46). It does not suit any other meaning. The intended meaning of ﴿what you seek to hasten﴾ is the threatened punishment. It is expressed in the form of a relative clause, because of what the relative clause indicates: that it is deferred and stored up for them, that they seek to hasten it, and that it will certainly befall them, since hastening and delaying are two states of an event that will occur. So His words "you seek to hasten" were in themselves a threat.

It indicates that it is in Allah's hand, and that Allah is the One who determines the time at which it descends upon them, because placing the predicate adverbial (*zarf*) first conveys restriction by reversal (*qasr al-qalb*). For they supposed, from the Prophet's ﷺ threat to them, that he had threatened them with a punishment within his power. So they took its delay as a failure of his threat. He therefore answered them that the threat is in Allah's hand, as He will state explicitly in His words: ﴿The judgment belongs only to Allah﴾. So His words ﴿The judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ are an explicit statement of the implication of restriction, and an emphasis of it.

On the reading where the pronoun of (*bihi*) refers to the Qur'an, the meaning is: you denied the Qur'an, which is a great clear proof, and you asked for the punishment to be hastened in order to put me in a position of incapacity, but that is not in my hand.

The clause ﴿He relates the truth﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the Name of Majesty, or a resumptive sentence, meaning: He is most knowing of the wisdom in delaying or hastening.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read *yaqussu* with a *damma* on the *qaf* and with the unpointed *sad*, so it is from *al-iqtisas*, which is following a trace, meaning: He carries out His decree in accordance with the truth, i.e., in conformity with it. Or it is from *al-qasas*, which is narration, meaning: He narrates with the truth, i.e., His promise is certain to occur, so He reports only the truth. The word *al-haqq* is in the accusative as the object in both interpretations.

The rest read (*yaqdi*) with a sukun on the *qaf* and with a pointed *dad* that is kissed, as the present tense of *qada* ("to decide"). In the Mushaf it is written without a *ya'*. This is explained by the fact that the *ya'* was dropped in the orthography in accordance with its dropping in pronunciation in connected speech, since this is not a place of pause. This is among those cases where the script was adjusted to the connected reading in a rare way, as *sanad'u al-zabaniyah* ("we will call the guards") was written (al-'Alaq: 18). Makki said: the reading with the unpointed *sad* is more beloved to me, because the two Harams (Nafi' and Ibn Kathir) agree upon it, and because if it were from *qada* the single *ba'* would have been required in it, meaning that one would say *yaqdi bi-al-haqq*. Its interpretation as accusative by removal of the preposition is rare. Al-Zajjaj answered that *al-haqq* is in the accusative as an absolute object, meaning "the decision is the truth." On this reading, one should not pause on it, so that the reader is not forced to pronounce the *ya'* and thus contradict the Mushaf script.

The clause ﴿and He is the best of deciders﴾ means: He relates and informs with the truth, and He is the best of those who separate between people; or He decides with the truth, and He is the best of those who decide judgment.

Separation (*al-fasl*) is used in the sense of judgment. 'Umar said in his letter to Abu Musa: "Indeed, decisive judgment (*fasl al-qada'*) produces resentments." It is also used in the sense of a speech that separates truth from falsehood and correct from mistaken, and from it is His words: ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾ (Sad: 20), and His words: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ (al-Tariq: 13). So the meaning of ﴿the best of deciders﴾ encompasses both the true speech and the just judgment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 58:

﴿Say: "If I had what you are hastening for, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And God knows best the wrongdoers."﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*, a sentence that answers a question the listener is expected to ask). His saying ﴿I do not have what you are hastening for﴾ [al-An'am: 57] prompts a question in the listener's mind: "If the sending down of the punishment upon them were in your hand, what would you do?" The answer is given by his saying ﴿If I had what you are hastening for﴾, and so on. Since his saying ﴿If I had﴾ etc. is an explanatory resumption, the command that he say it has the force of an explanatory resumption as well. The whole discourse is built on the Messenger being instructed in what to say to them, so the listener seeks from the one giving the instruction what his Messenger is to be instructed to say to them. The meaning of ﴿what you are hastening for﴾ [al-An'am: 57] has been explained above, namely: if the wisdom of it were within my knowledge and the act of it within my power. This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the meaning: "I am not a god, but I am a servant who follows what is revealed to me."

His saying ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾ is the answer to (*law*, "if"). The meaning of *qudiya* ("was decided") is "was completed and ended." "The matter" (*al-amr*) is meant to refer to the dispute and the disagreement. The definite article in it is for a known reference (*al-'ahd*). The verb *qudiya al-amr* is put in the passive voice because it is evident that the one who decides it is the one who holds what they are hastening for.

The construction *qudiya al-amr* became widespread and came to function as a proverb (*mathal*). Therefore the subject is omitted so that it can be used as a proverb in every context. From this usage come His saying ﴿The matter about which you two sought a ruling has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41], His saying ﴿Had it not been for a prior word of decision, the matter would have been decided between them﴾ [al-Shura: 21], and His saying ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided﴾ [Maryam: 39]. For this reason, when it occurs outside the proverbial usage, its subject is stated explicitly, as in the Exalted's saying ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

That decision may involve several matters: that He brings them the proposed sign so that they believe; or that He becomes angry and destroys them; or that He turns their hearts away from seeking what He does not grant them, so that they repent and return.

Page 270

His saying ﴿And God knows best the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*), meaning: God knows better than I, and better than anyone, the wisdom behind delaying the punishment and the time of its descent, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, in whose possession is what you are hastening for. The expression "the wrongdoers" is an explicit noun used in place of the pronoun of address, to make them aware that they are wrongdoers in their polytheism, since they have transgressed against the right of God; that they are wrongdoers in their denial, since they have transgressed against the right of God and His Messenger; and that they are wrongdoers in their treatment of the Messenger (ﷺ).

[Page 271]

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And God knows best the wrongdoers﴾ [al-An'am: 58] by way of *takhallus* (transition to a new topic). The link in this transition is the information that God knows best the state of the wrongdoers, since it is hidden from people's observation. So God knows what suits their condition, whether hastening or delaying the threat. This is a move to explain His exclusive possession of the knowledge of the unseen, the breadth of His knowledge, then the breadth of His power, and that all creation is in the grip of His power.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase serves to confer exclusivity: "with Him," not with anyone else. The "withness" here is a withness of knowledge and exclusive possession, not a withness of place.

*Al-mafatih* is the plural of *miftah*, with a kasra on the mim, which is the instrument by which a locked thing is opened, and is called *al-miftah*. It has been said that *mifteh* (with fatha) is more eloquent than *miftah*. God, exalted is He, says ﴿And We gave him of the treasures what its keys would weigh down a band of strong men﴾ [al-Qasas: 76].

*Al-ghayb* is what is hidden from people's knowledge such that they have no way to know it. This includes hidden entities such as angels and jinn, hidden accidents, and the appointed times of things.

﴿Mafatih al-ghayb﴾ here is an imaginative metaphor (*istiara takhyiliyya*) built upon an implicit metaphor (*makniyya*), in that the hidden matters from people are likened to precious goods stored in storerooms and treasuries secured with locks, such that no one knows what is inside except the one who holds their keys. Keys are attributed to them by way of imaginative representation. The indicator (*qarina*) is the annexation of the keys to the unseen. So His saying ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ is equivalent to saying: "With Him is the knowledge of the unseen which no other knows."

*Mafatih al-ghayb* is a definite plural annexed form that encompasses all unseen things, because the knowledge of all of them is specific to God, exalted is He. As for matters that have signs, such as the signs of storms and the symptoms of illnesses known to the physician, these are not from the unseen but from the obscure matters of the visible. Their obscurity varies, people differ in arriving at them, and their knowledge of them belongs to the category of conjecture, not certainty, so it is not called knowledge. It has also been said that *mafatih* is the plural of *mafter* (with fatha on the mim), which is the house or storeroom that is locked over what is in it and then opened when there is need of what is in it. This is reported from al-Suddi. In that case it is an explicit metaphor (*istiara musarraha*), and the likened element is the knowledge of the unseen, likened in its encompassing and concealing of the hidden things to a storehouse, a likening of an intelligible thing to a sensible thing.

The clause ﴿None knows them except He﴾ explains the meaning of "with Him," so it is an elucidation of the preceding clause, and it also confers emphasis on the first clause, to remove the possibility that the fronting of the adverbial phrase is merely for emphasis; the element that is definitively for restriction (*qasr*) is therefore repeated.

The pronoun in *ya'lamuha* ("knows them") refers to *mafatih al-ghayb* by an omitted modifier, by implied meaning (*dalalat al-iqtida'*). Its estimated form is: "None knows their place except He," because knowledge does not relate to the essences of the keys. This is a supporting element (*tarshih*) for the metaphor of "keys of the unseen" as knowledge of the hidden things. The negation of others' knowledge of them is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the negation of knowledge of what the keys lock up of the knowledge of hidden things.

The meaning of ﴿None knows them except He﴾ is: knowledge possessed independently. As for what He reveals of His unseen to some of His chosen servants, as God, exalted is He, says, ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone except whom He has approved of the messengers﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], that is knowledge that is acquired by one whom He informs by way of His own information, so it returns to His knowledge. Knowledge (*'ilm*) is the apprehension of things in the manner of certainty.

In the Sahih, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Umar, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The keys of the unseen are five: ﴿Indeed, God has with Him knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs, and no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, God is Knowing and Acquainted﴾ [Luqman: 34]."

The clause ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾ is conjoined either to the clause ﴿None knows them except He﴾ or to the clause ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾, because both clauses include affirmation of knowledge to God and negation of knowledge from others. So this clause, which affirms God's knowledge without negating others' knowledge, is conjoined to them. This is the knowledge of apparent matters, some of which people may come to know in part. Thus conjoining this clause to ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ serves to convey the generalization of His knowledge to visible things, which vary in visibility, after having conveyed His knowledge of what is not apparent to people.

The visibility of what is on land to people, in general, is stronger than the visibility of what is in the sea. The mention of land and sea is for the purpose of encompassing everything this sphere contains, because land is the surface of the earth on which animals walk without swimming, and sea is the abundant water that covers a part of the earth, whether the water is salty or sweet. The Arabs call a river a sea, as with the Euphrates and the Tigris.

The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) is general, so it includes all essences and meanings.

The clause ﴿And not a leaf falls﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾, for the purpose of adding further generalization to minute particulars. Encompassing knowledge of hidden things, despite their being among the weakest particulars, indicates encompassing knowledge of what is greater and more deserving of it. This is one of the miracles of the Qur'an, for God knew what the philosophers believe and knew that someone among the followers of Islam who has no firm grounding in religion would adopt their view. So He left no room for interpretation regarding the reality of His knowledge, when He said ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth﴾, as we will explain the preferred view regarding its grammatical construction.

By "leaf" is meant a leaf of a tree. The particle *min* (in "from a leaf") is superfluous, to emphasize the negation so that it conveys generality explicitly. The clause ﴿He knows it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the leaf, which lies within the scope of negation, and is independent of a qualifier through generality. This is because the exception is an exception from circumstances (*istithna' mufraragh min ahwal*), and this circumstance is a necessary circumstance after the negation, by which, together with the negated verb, the exception from the generality of circumstances is conveyed. That is: "Not a leaf falls in any state except in a state in which He knows it."

The more evident analysis of the construction of ﴿And not a leaf falls﴾ is that *waraqa* ("leaf") is in the position of the subject, governed by the superfluous *min*, and the clause *tasqutu* ("falls") is a qualifier of *waraqa* placed before it, so it is parsed as a circumstantial clause. The clause ﴿but He knows it﴾ is a predicate with the exceptive particle. ﴿Nor a grain﴾ is conjoined to the subject by repeating the negative particle, and ﴿in the darknesses of the earth﴾ is a qualifier of *habba* ("grain"), meaning: nor a grain of seeds lodged in the layers of the earth to the deepest depth possible. So *habba* is not an object of the verb *tasqutu*, because a grain that falls does not, by its falling, reach the darknesses of the earth. ﴿Nor moist nor dry﴾ are conjoined to the subject governed by *min*. The predicate for these three subjects is the statement ﴿except in a clear Book﴾, because it comes after the three, which is evident from the predicate being stated about all three; and the first predicate refers back to the phrase "from a leaf."

By "the clear Book" is meant the established knowledge that does not change. As for whatever traces of knowledge may exist with God, such as writing or otherwise, He has not informed us of their reality.

It has also been said: the genitive case of *habba* is conjoined to *waraqa*, with the negative particle repeated, and ﴿in the darknesses of the earth﴾ is a descriptive phrase for *habba*. Similarly, the statement ﴿nor moist nor dry﴾ in the genitive case is conjoined to *habba* and *waraqa*, which requires that they are objects of the verb *tasqutu*, meaning: no moist or dry thing falls, and it is restricted by the circumstance in His saying ﴿but He knows it﴾.

His saying ﴿except in a clear Book﴾ is an emphasis of His saying ﴿but He knows it﴾, because by the clear Book is meant the knowledge of God, exalted is He, whether the Book is literal or figurative for precision and the absence of alteration. This emphasis was made good by renewing the meaning, since the first statement was distanced by the conjoined elements and their qualifiers, and it was repeated in another expression for variety.

The discussion of the reason for the plural *zulumat* ("darknesses") has already been given at His saying ﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1] in this sura. *Mubin* ("clear") is either from *abana*, the transitive form, meaning one that makes clear for some of His creation what He wants, such as the angels; or from *aban*, the intransitive form, which has the meaning of *bana*, meaning clear, that is, detailed in a way that admits no ambiguity or hesitation.

It is known from these verses that God, exalted is He, has general knowledge of universals and particulars. This is agreed upon among the people of the religions, without explicit statement in the earlier books; and it was only the Qur'an that declared it explicitly, as in His saying ﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾ [al-An'am: 101]. In this there is a refutation of the view of the majority of the philosophers that God knows universals only and does not know particulars, on the claim that they exalt the supreme knowledge above divisibility. They affirmed the attribute of knowledge to God, exalted is He, but denied that His knowledge relates to the particulars of existing things. This is what is transmitted from them according to the scholars. Ibn Rushd al-Hafid and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi interpreted their view in this way. Al-Imam al-Razi said in al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyya: "It is necessary to specify the doctrine of the philosophers, for what is fitting to their principles is that it be said: matters are of four kinds. They are either neither formed nor changing; or formed but not changing; or changing but not formed; or both formed and changing. As for what is neither formed nor changing, He, exalted is He, knows it, whether it is universal or particular. How can it be said that He, exalted is He, does not know the particulars of these, when most of them agree that He knows His own specific essence and the intellects?

As for what is formed but not changing, which is the celestial bodies, these are not known to Him, exalted is He, in their individual persons according to them, because the perception of corporeal things can only occur through corporeal instruments.

As for what is changing but not formed, that is like forms, accidents that come into being, and rational souls; these are not known to Him, because their relation requires a corporeal instrument, but also because, since they are changing, their change entails knowledge.

As for what is both formed and changing, these are the corruptible bodies that come into being. It is impossible that they be perceived by Him, exalted is He, for the two reasons mentioned in the second and third categories." End of quotation.

The denial by the philosophers that God knows particulars has been counted among three principles of theirs that contradict what is known necessarily from the religion of Islam. They are: the denial of God's knowledge of particulars; the denial of the resurrection of bodies; and the claim that the world is eternal. This was mentioned by al-Ghazali in Tahafut al-Falasifa. Whoever among the Muslims agrees with them in that is considered to have uttered unbelief, but it is unbelief by necessary implication (*kufr bi-l-lazim*), so its speaker is not considered an apostate unless he is made aware of what his statement entails and refuses to retract it. Then he is asked to repent three times; if he repents, well and good; otherwise he is judged an apostate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 60:

﴿It is He who takes you in death by night, and knows what you have earned by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a decreed term may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

He conjoined the clause ﴿It is He who takes you in death﴾ to the clause ﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59], shifting from the demonstration of the breadth of His knowledge to the demonstration of the magnitude of His power, because all of that is among the proofs of divinity, as instruction for His allies and as a reproach to the polytheists, His enemies. The custom of the Qur'an has been to mention the proofs of divine oneness within the souls of people immediately after mentioning them in the horizons, so these were gathered here in a wondrous manner that signals the teaching of His attributes within the context of the proof of His oneness. In this there is also an approximation to resurrection after death.

So His saying ﴿It is He who takes you in death﴾ is a form of restriction (qasr) defining both parts of the sentence, meaning: it is He who takes souls, not the idols, for they possess neither death nor life.

The address is directed to the polytheists, as the preceding context requires, namely His saying ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾ [al-An'am: 58], and the following context, His saying ﴿then you associate partners [with Him]﴾ [al-An'am: 64], and as the mode of restriction requires. Since this state is not specific to the polytheists, it is understood from it that people are equal in it.

Al-tawaffi (taking in full) is literally "causing to die," since it is literally the seizing of a thing in full. Its application to sleep is metaphorical, due to the resemblance of sleep to death in the cessation of perception and action. Do you not see His Exalted saying ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die in their sleep; so He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back until a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]? Its detailed treatment has already preceded at His saying ﴿When God said: "O Jesus, I will take you in full (mutawaffika)"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Page 276
The meaning of His saying ﴿takes you﴾ is "puts you to sleep," as indicated by the context of His saying ﴿then raises you up therein﴾, that is, during the day. Thus by tawaffi here He means sleep, by way of comparison. Its benefit is that it is an approximation to the manner of resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, and for this reason raising up (al-ba'th) is borrowed for waking from sleep, so that the approximation is complete in His saying ﴿then raises you up therein﴾.

The meaning of "jaraḥtum" is "you earned." The original sense of jarh (wounding) is tearing the skin of a living being with a pointed object such as a knife, a sword, a claw, or a fang. It was discussed at His saying ﴿and for wounds, retaliation﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], in Surat al-'Uqud. The term jawarih (the hunting animals) is applied to hunting dogs, falcons and the like, because they wound the game so that the hunter may seize it. He Exalted said ﴿and what you have taught of the trained hunting beasts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], which was discussed in Surat al-'Uqud. They were also called kawasib (earners), as in the words of Labid:

Ghudfan kawasib ma yumannu ta'amuha
(Floppy-eared, earning hunters whose food is not bestowed as a favour)

Thus the word jawarih became synonymous with kawasib, and this became widespread, so the name of wounding (jarh) was applied to earning (kasb), and this is what is meant here. He Exalted said ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21].

The clause ﴿and He knows what you have wounded by day﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah) for the purpose of reminding of the blessing of respite.
