That is: were it not for His grace, He would not have raised you up during the day, while He knows that you earn during the day the worship of other than Him, and that some of you commit what He has forbidden them, like the believers do.

The statement is restricted to informing of His knowledge of what people earn during the day, rather than the night, in deference to what is predominant, since the day is the time of most action and earning. So in the information that He knows what occurs therein there is a warning against earning what God does not approve of earning, with respect to the believers, and a threat to the polytheists.

The clause ﴿then He raises you up therein﴾ is conjoined to ﴿takes you by night﴾, so "then" (thumma) denotes real temporal interval, and this is the more apparent reading. You may also take "then" to denote graded sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), conjoining it to the clause ﴿and He knows what you have wounded﴾, meaning: and He knows what you earn of prohibited deeds, then He returns you and grants you respite. This is more fitting for the group of polytheists.

"Fi" here denotes location in time. The pronoun refers to the day. The raising up (al-ba'th) is a metaphor for waking from sleep, because ba'th became widespread for bringing the dead to life, especially in the Qur'anic usage: ﴿They say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised up?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82]. What makes this metaphor good is that it is built upon the metaphor of tawaffi for sleep, approximating the manner of resurrection, over which their minds were perplexed. Thus each of the two metaphors supports the other.

The lam in ﴿that a decreed term may be fulfilled﴾ is the lam of causation, because among the wisdoms and causes for which God established the system of wakefulness and sleep is that it be a division of the life-span of the living being, and this is his term (ajal), which was set for his life on the day of his creation, as has come in the hadith: "He is commanded to write down his provision, his term, and his deeds." So the term is measured in days and nights, which are the time of sleeping and waking. A cause that means wisdom need not be single, for God's act may have many wisdoms. So there is no difficulty in taking the lam as denoting causation.

The fulfilment (qada') of the term is its ending. Its being "specified" (musamma) means that it is determined and fixed. The marji' (return) is a mimi verbal noun, so it may mean return by death, because souls come under God's control and their former disposal by their own will is nullified. It may also mean the gathering (hashr) on the Day of Resurrection, and this is more apparent.

His saying ﴿then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ means: He will call you to account for your deeds after death, and in that case the interval in "then" is evident; or after the gathering, in which case the interval is because there is a period between the gathering and the beginning of reckoning, as occurs in the hadith of intercession.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 61–62:**

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾.

It is conjoined to the clause ﴿And He is the One who takes you back in death﴾ [al-An'am 6:60], and the explanation of its counterpart has already preceded. The connection here is that God created sleep and death, and they overcome human strength however great it becomes. So, right after mentioning them, He declares that God is the Mighty, the Victorious, to the exclusion of the idols. Sleep is a form of subjugation, because a person may wish not to sleep, yet sleep overcomes him. Death is a subjugation too, and it is more evident. Among the true words is the saying: "Glory be to the One who subdued His servants by death."

* * *

﴿And He sends over you guardians, until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect [their duty]. Then they are returned to God, their true Master. Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾.

*Wa-yursilu* is conjoined to *al-qahir* (the Subduer). Accordingly, the subject is treated as placed before the verbal predicate, which indicates restriction (*takhsis*) also, by the context: that is, He is the One who sends over you guardians, to the exclusion of any other. The restriction here is real (*haqiqi*), so it does not call for the rejection of a contrary belief. The purpose is to inform of this true report, so that the listeners may beware of committing sins.

The meaning of *ʿalā* in His saying *ʿalaykum* ("over you") is figurative elevation (*isti'la' majazi*), that is, the sending of subjugation and obligation, like His saying ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ [al-Isra' 17:5]. This is because the context of the discourse is addressed to the polytheists, as you know. Similar is His exalted saying ﴿No! Rather, you deny the Religion. And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar 82:9–10].

*ʿAlaykum* is connected to *yursilu*. Thus it is known that the intended meaning of the guardians' *hifz* (guarding) is counting and recording, from the expression "I preserved his such-and-such deed against him" (*hafiztu ʿalayhi fiʿlahu kadha*), which is the opposite of forgetting. From this is His exalted saying ﴿And with Us is a Book that preserves﴾ [Qaf 50:4]. It is not the *hifz* of protection and care, like His exalted saying ﴿The righteous women are guarding in the unseen what God has guarded﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:34].

The guardians are angels whose function is to count the deeds of the servants, good and bad. And there is reported in the authentic hadith: "Angels succeed one another among you, by night and by day," and the hadith continues.

His saying ﴿when death comes to one of you﴾ is the limit (*ghaya*) of what the designation "guardians" indicates of the meaning of counting. That is, the counting ends with death. When the time arrives at which the term of life ends, the angels sent for seizing the souls take him in death.

His saying *rusulunā* ("Our messengers") is in the sense of an indefinite noun, because the genitive-attached word is a derived noun, so it has the sense of the passive participle, and attachment does not make it definite. For this reason, the intended "messengers" who take him are messengers other than the guardians sent over the servants, based on the general pattern that when an indefinite noun follows an indefinite noun, the second is other than the first. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿Our messengers take him﴾ is that a number of angels undertake the taking of each individual person.

In the other verse ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:11], he is named in the reports as ʿAzrail. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Angel of Death has helpers. Thus the reconciliation of the two verses is evident.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 61–62:**

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾.

It is conjoined to the clause ﴿And He is the One who takes you back in death﴾ [al-An'am 6:60], and the explanation of its counterpart has already preceded. The connection here is that God created sleep and death, and they overcome human strength however great it becomes. So, right after mentioning them, He declares that God is the Mighty, the Victorious, to the exclusion of the idols. Sleep is a form of subjugation, because a person may wish not to sleep, yet sleep overcomes him. Death is a subjugation too, and it is more evident. Among the true words is the saying: "Glory be to the One who subdued His servants by death."

* * *

﴿And He sends over you guardians, until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect [their duty]. Then they are returned to God, their true Master. Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾.

*Wa-yursilu* is conjoined to *al-qahir* (the Subduer). Accordingly, the subject is treated as placed before the verbal predicate, which indicates restriction (*takhsis*) also, by the context: that is, He is the One who sends over you guardians, to the exclusion of any other. The restriction here is real (*haqiqi*), so it does not call for the rejection of a contrary belief. The purpose is to inform of this true report, so that the listeners may beware of committing sins.

The meaning of *ʿalā* in His saying *ʿalaykum* ("over you") is figurative elevation (*isti'la' majazi*), that is, the sending of subjugation and obligation, like His saying ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ [al-Isra' 17:5]. This is because the context of the discourse is addressed to the polytheists, as you know. Similar is His exalted saying ﴿No! Rather, you deny the Religion. And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar 82:9–10].

*ʿAlaykum* is connected to *yursilu*. Thus it is known that the intended meaning of the guardians' *hifz* (guarding) is counting and recording, from the expression "I preserved his such-and-such deed against him" (*hafiztu ʿalayhi fiʿlahu kadha*), which is the opposite of forgetting. From this is His exalted saying ﴿And with Us is a Book that preserves﴾ [Qaf 50:4]. It is not the *hifz* of protection and care, like His exalted saying ﴿The righteous women are guarding in the unseen what God has guarded﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:34].

The guardians are angels whose function is to count the deeds of the servants, good and bad. And there is reported in the authentic hadith: "Angels succeed one another among you, by night and by day," and the hadith continues.

His saying ﴿when death comes to one of you﴾ is the limit (*ghaya*) of what the designation "guardians" indicates of the meaning of counting. That is, the counting ends with death. When the time arrives at which the term of life ends, the angels sent for seizing the souls take him in death.

His saying *rusulunā* ("Our messengers") is in the sense of an indefinite noun, because the genitive-attached word is a derived noun, so it has the sense of the passive participle, and attachment does not make it definite. For this reason, the intended "messengers" who take him are messengers other than the guardians sent over the servants, based on the general pattern that when an indefinite noun follows an indefinite noun, the second is other than the first. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿Our messengers take him﴾ is that a number of angels undertake the taking of each individual person.

Initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*). Since this statement is a threat and opens with an interrogative of affirmation (*istifham taqriri*), it is established that the second-person pronouns refer to the polytheists and not to the Muslims. Even clearer is His saying ﴿then you ascribe partners﴾.

The repetition of the command "say" is for emphasis, as was explained earlier at His saying ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you...﴾ [al-An'am: 40].

The interrogative is used for affirmation (*taqrir*) and compulsion (*ilja'*), because they do not dispute this according to their polytheistic beliefs.

It is said that *al-zulumat* (the darknesses) is meant literally, so a omitted noun must be understood: "from the harms of the darknesses of land and sea." The darknesses of the land are the darkness of night in which the traveller may lose the way and in which the enemy is feared, that is, what befalls one in the darknesses of the land of calamities, for both the traveller and the one who stays put. The darknesses of the sea are those in which drowning, going astray, and the enemy are feared. It is also said that the darknesses are used figuratively for the terrors arising on land and sea, as one says, "a day is dark" when hardships occur in it. Among the proverbs of the Arabs is "he saw the stars at noon" (*ra'a al-kawakib muzhiran*), meaning that his day grew dark before his eyes because of the hardships he met, until it became as if it were night in which the stars are seen. The plural, in both interpretations, takes into account the multiplicity of the kinds of darknesses that may occur. Moreover, we noted at the beginning of the surah that the use of the plural in the word *zulumat* follows the rules of eloquence.

The clause ﴿you call upon Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in the accusative in ﴿yunajjikum﴾.

It is read ﴿man yunajjikum﴾ with the doubled letter (*tashdid*) by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf. Ya'qub read it without doubling (*takhfif*).

*Tadarru'* (humility, supplication) means self-abasement, as was explained in His saying ﴿so that they may humble themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 42] in this surah. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, interpreted as an active participle. *Khufyah* (secrecy, quietness), with a *damma* or *kasra* on the *kha'*, is the opposite of *jahr* (loudness). The majority read it with a *damma* on the *kha'*. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a *kasra* on the *kha'*, which is a dialect form like *uswah* and *iswah*. The coordination of *khufyah* with *tadarru'* is either coordination of circumstantial clause with circumstantial clause, as attributes are coordinated, in which case it is a verbal noun interpreted as an active participle; or it is coordination of the absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) with the circumstantial clause, in which case it specifies the type of calling, meaning: you call upon Him in the darknesses, concealing your voices for fear that the enemy among people or wild beasts will notice.

The clause ﴿if He delivers us﴾ is in a position of accusative by an omitted verb of saying, meaning "saying." The omission of the verb of saying is frequent in the Qur'an when the context indicates it. The *lam* in *la'in* is the *lam* of preparation for an oath, and the *lam* in *latakunanna* is the *lam* of the answer to the oath. The plural pronoun is used either because the intent is to narrate their gathering in supplication, such that each one calls for himself and for his companions; or because the plural is intended to express the group in terms of distribution, like: "the people mounted their horses," while each one mounted a single horse.

The majority read *anjaytana* with a *ya'* after the *jim* and a *ta'* after the *ya'*. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *anjana* with an *alif* after the *jim*, and the pronoun refers to *man* in His saying ﴿Say: Who delivers you﴾.

The demonstrative ﴿this﴾ refers to the darkness witnessed by the speaker, in consideration of what arises from it, or in consideration of the figurative meaning, which is hardship; or to a state expressed by a feminine noun, such as *al-shiddah* (hardship), *al-warṭah* (predicament), or *al-ribqah* (snare).

The *shakir* (thankful) is the one who observes the favour of the benefactor and treats him well whenever he finds a way to do so. The Arabs regarded gratitude as a great right and reproached whoever denies a favour.

Their saying ﴿among the thankful﴾ is more emphatic than saying "we will surely be thankful," as was explained earlier at His saying ﴿then I would have gone astray and I would not be among the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56].

The clause ﴿Say: God delivers you from them﴾ is a prompting of the answer to the interrogative in His saying ﴿who delivers you﴾, so that they answer the questions. For this reason the clause ﴿say﴾ is separated, since it functions as speech in dialogue, as was explained earlier in this surah. He Himself gave the answer on their behalf, because this answer leaves them no option but to acknowledge it.

The subject is placed before the verbal predicate for the sake of exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), meaning: God alone delivers you, not another. For this reason He stated the verb that is being asked about explicitly; otherwise He would have limited Himself to "Say: God." The pronoun in ﴿from them﴾ refers to the darknesses or to the event.

He added ﴿and from every distress﴾ to express generality, and to indicate that limiting it to the darknesses of land and sea, in both senses, is merely an example.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub read ﴿yunjikum﴾ with a sukun on the *nun* and a light *jim* (*takhfif*), as being from *anjahu*. The verse thus combines the two usages, which is a kind of variety (*tafannun*) to avoid repetition. A parallel is His saying ﴿so give respite to the disbelievers, give them respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17].

Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, Khalaf, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yunajjikum﴾ with doubling, like the first.

The *thumma* (then) in His saying ﴿then you ascribe partners﴾ is for graduated order (*tartib rutbi*), because the intent is that their ascribing partners, despite their acknowledgement that they turn only to God in hardships, is a strange matter; so the intent is not a delay in time.

Placing the subject before the verbal predicate is merely for emphasis on the report of their ascribing partners, meaning: it is you who humble yourselves to God, and yet by your own acknowledgement you ascribe partners to Him before and after. It is of the type of ﴿then you are those who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], and of the type: "Had another than you said it, or had a woman with bracelets slapped me..."

The predicate is expressed as an imperfect verb to indicate the renewal of their polytheism, and that this renewal and persistence in it is more wondrous.

The meaning is: God delivered you, so you promised to be among the thankful, and then, behold, you ascribe partners. Between *al-shakirin* (the thankful) and *tushrikun* (you ascribe partners) there is a *jinas muharraf* (near-paronomasia).

This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic). It follows the blessing mentioned in His words ﴿Say: Who delivers you...﴾ [al-An'am: 63], and mentions power to inflict punishment, as a warning to the polytheists. Repeating the verb of command "Say" is like its repetition in similar passages, for emphasis, as is made clear at His words ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you...﴾ [al-An'am: 40]. The meaning is: "Say to the polytheists." The second-person pronouns address the polytheists. The purpose of the statement is not to inform them of God's power, since that is already known, but to threaten them by reminding them that the One who has power is one whose might should be feared. The statement is therefore used indirectly, as a figurative allusion (*ta'rid*), either as a compound metonymy (*majaz mursal murakkab*) or as a compositional implicature (*kinaya tarkibiyya*). This is a threat to them, in response to their saying: "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?"

The definiteness of the predicate and the subject yields restriction (*qasr*), which establishes that God alone has power to send punishment upon them, and that no other can do so. Therefore they should not fear the idols. Had they wanted good for themselves, they would have feared God, and singled Him out for worship to seek His good pleasure. The restriction is relative (*idafi*). The definite article in (*al-qadir*, "the Able") is the definite article of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), since no one other than God can bring about this kind of punishment.

The punishment from above is like thunderbolts and wind; the punishment from beneath the feet is like earthquakes, landslides and floods.

*Yalbisakum* is the imperfect of *labasahu* (with a vowel on the middle letter), meaning "he mixed it." The transitive use of the verb *yalbisakum* with the pronoun referring to people implies the confusion, disturbance and disorder of their affairs. The soundness of affairs resembles the orderliness of a string of beads, which is why the soundness of people's affairs is called *nizam* (order). The opposite, the disruption of affairs and chaos, resembles the mixing of things, which is why it is called *marj* (confusion) and *labs* (mixing up). This happens with the loss of security and the entry of corruption into the affairs of the community. For this reason *al-harj* (killing) is linked with *al-marj* (mixing), and people say: "They are in *harj* and *marj*." The sukun on the *ra'* in the second word is for rhyme (*muzawaja*).

*Shiya'an* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the object pronoun in *yalbisakum*. *Shiya'* is the plural of *shi'a* (with a kasra on the *shin*), meaning a group united in an aim, a belief or a desire, so that they agree on it. God, Most High, said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you have nothing to do with them﴾ [al-An'am: 159]. The *shi'a* of a man are his followers and those who imitate him. God, Most High, said: ﴿And indeed, among his *shi'a* was Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 83], meaning among the followers of Noah.

The scattering of sects and the multiplicity of opinions creates greater confusion and mixing, because a confusion of this kind is one after which no order can be hoped for.

He joined to it ﴿or make some of you taste the violence of others﴾, because one of the consequences of such confusion is mutual killing. *Ba's* means killing and evil. God, Most High, said: ﴿and coats of mail that protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. *Idhaqa* (to make taste) is a metaphor for pain.

As we have said, this is a threat to the polytheists, by way of metaphor or implicature. The last of these has indeed happened, for the polytheists tasted the violence of the Muslims at Badr and in many battles.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you punishment from above you﴾, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I seek refuge in Your face.' He said ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾, and he said: 'I seek refuge in Your face.' He said ﴿or to confuse you in sects and make some of you taste the violence of others﴾, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'This is easier, or this is lighter.'" [End of quotation.]

The Prophet's (ﷺ) seeking refuge from these is out of fear that the punishment, if it descended upon the disbelievers, might encompass those among the Muslims who are near them, as in God's words ﴿And beware of a trial which will not afflict those who wronged among you exclusively﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. In a hadith: "They said: 'O Messenger of God, will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?' He said: 'Yes, when wickedness increases.'" In another hadith: "Then they will be gathered according to their intentions." The meaning of his saying "this is easier" is that if killing befalls the polytheists, it is at the hands of the Muslims, so harm, great harm, reaches the Muslims from it. But it is easier, because there is no annihilation or cutting off of the word of the religion. It is a punishment for the polytheists and a testimony and support for the Muslims.

In a hadith: "Do not wish to meet the enemy, but ask God for well-being." Some scholars explained the hadith as meaning that he sought refuge from such a thing happening among the Muslims themselves. It may be objected: why did the Messenger (ﷺ) not seek refuge from such a thing happening among the Muslims? Perhaps this is because it was revealed to him that such a thing would happen among the Muslims, but God promised him that He would not give power over them to an enemy from outside themselves. His seeking refuge is not indicative that the verse is intended as address to the Muslims, as some commentators hold, nor that it is a threat to the polytheists and believers together, as some of the early scholars held, except in the sense that its meaning, which is not explicit, is suitable for both groups, because God's power to do this applies to both groups. But the threatening meaning is not appropriate to the Muslims here. This interpretation suits the statement being used in its basic sense of information together with its implication, so it is both explicit and implicative, and does not suit the compound metonymy explained earlier.

* * *

﴿Look how We vary the signs, that perhaps they may understand﴾.

This is a resumptive sentence that came after the two preceding interrogatives.

In the command to look there is the treatment of the intelligible as if it were perceptible, for the purpose of wonder at it. This has already been discussed in the commentary on His words ﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾ [al-Nisa': 50] in Surat al-Nisa'.

[Page 286]

*Tasrif al-ayat* means varying the signs by encouragement at times and warning at others. The signs here means the signs of the Qur'an. The meaning of *tasrif* was previously explained at His words ﴿Look how We vary the signs, then they turn away﴾ [al-An'am: 46] in this surah.

﴿That perhaps they may understand﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*istinaf bayani*), an answer to a questioner asking about the benefit of varying the signs. It expresses hope that they will attain understanding, because, due to their obstinacy, they were in need of clarification that surrounds their understanding, so that it might perhaps remember and draw back.

The meaning of *la'alla* ("perhaps") was discussed at His words ﴿that perhaps you may be mindful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of *fiqh* (understanding) was discussed at His words ﴿What is the matter with these people that they hardly understand any statement?﴾ [al-Nisa': 78] in Surat al-Nisa'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 6, verses 66–67:**

﴿Your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you.﴾ ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) with ﴿Look how We vary the signs﴾ [al-An'am: 65], meaning: "Perhaps they will understand," but they did not understand and they denied. The pronoun in *bihi* ("it") refers to the punishment in His words ﴿that He may send upon you a punishment﴾ [al-An'am: 65]. Their denial of it means their denial that God would punish them because of their turning away.

The expression "your people" (*qawmuka*) is a way of recording against them their evil treatment of one who is from among themselves, as in God's words ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. Tarafa said:

*"The wrong done by close kin is more painful to a man than the stroke of a well-tempered sword."*

The way the verb *kadhdhaba* ("to deny") takes *bi* (with) has already been explained at God's words ﴿and you have denied it﴾ [al-An'am: 57] in this surah.

The clause ﴿and it is the truth﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) intended to affirm the power to send upon them a punishment, etc.

Some of this was fulfilled: a punishment from above them, which is the punishment of drought, and their being made to taste the might of the Muslims on the day of Badr.

[p. 287]

It is also possible that the pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Qur'an. Then God's words ﴿and he denied it﴾ would be a return of the speech to His words ﴿Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it﴾ [al-An'am: 57], meaning: you denied the Qur'an. This is on the understanding that *min* in "from my Lord" is a *min* of origin (*ibtida'iyya*), as explained before. That is: you denied the sign of the Qur'an and demanded the descent of punishment as a test of the truth of my message, though that is not in my hands. Then the speech was interrupted by many clauses. The first of them is ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 59], followed by what comes after it of allusion to threat. Then on this he built His words ﴿Your people have denied it, though it is the truth.﴾ It is as if it was said: "Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you."

God's words ﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾ are a humbling (*irghām*) of them, because they imagined that, since they had denied him and turned away from his call, they had angered him. So God informed them that this does not anger him, and that his duty is only to call. If they are angry, they can only harm themselves.

The word *wakil* here means one who defends and supports, that is, the protector. It was explained at God's words ﴿They said: God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in the surah of Al 'Imran.

Its construction with *'ala* ("over") is because it implies the meaning of dominance and authority: I am not a keeper over you who prevents you from denying, like God's words ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a watcher over them. Your duty is only to deliver the message﴾ [al-Shura: 48].

The clause ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because His words ﴿and it is the truth﴾ raise the question in them of asking: "When will the punishment descend?" So they were answered with ﴿For every news there is a fixed time.﴾

*Naba'* means an important report, and it was mentioned earlier in this surah. It may be taken in its literal sense: for every report among the reports of the Qur'an. It may also be that the verbal noun is used in the sense of the object (*ism al-maf'ul*): for every thing reported, that is, what they were informed of, namely His words ﴿that He may send upon you a punishment from above you﴾ [al-An'am: 65] and the verse that follows.

*Al-mustaqarr* is the time of settling, so it is the noun of its time, and for this reason it is formed on the pattern of the passive participle, as is the regular pattern for forming the noun of time from a derived form other than the triliteral. *Istiqrar* means occurrence, that is, for every promised thing there is a time in which it occurs. This is a confirmation of the threat and the entrusting of its time to the knowledge of God, exalted is He. It is possible that *al-mustaqarr* here is used metaphorically for the end and the limit, as in God's words ﴿And the sun runs on to a fixed place for it﴾ [Ya Sin: 38]. It includes both the threat of the Hereafter and the threat of this world, and for every one there is a fixed time. It is reported from al-Suddi: "On the day of Badr, what He had promised them of punishment occurred."

The conjunction of ﴿you will come to know﴾ to the clause ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ means: you will know it. That is, it is now not known to you, and you will know it in the future when it befalls you. This is more apparent as a threat of punishment in this world.

[p. 289]

It is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause ﴿And your people denied it﴾ [al-Anʿam: 66].

The shift from using a pronoun to using the explicit noun, the relative pronoun (ism al-mawṣūl), is significant. He did not say, "And when you see them, turn away from them." This shows that "those who engage in discourse about Our signs" are a specific group among the people who denied the Qur'an or the punishment. The general body of the people rejected and denied without engaging in discussion of the Qur'anic signs. Those are one category. Those who engage in discourse about the signs are another category, which was more vulgar, more abusive, more disbelieving, and more shameful. They were the ones who took it upon themselves to attack the Qur'an. The Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to turn away from disputing with them and to abandon sitting with them until they desisted from that. Had the Messenger (ﷺ) been commanded to turn away from all the deniers, the call and the conveying of the message would have been brought to a standstill.

The meaning of ﴿when you see those who engage in discourse﴾ is: when you see them in the state of their engagement.

These people are identified by the relative construction rather than by saying "the ones engaged in discourse" (al-khāʾiḍīn) or "a people engaged in discourse," because the relative clause contains an indication of the reason for the command to turn away. It is a strange command, since the Messenger's (ﷺ) normal course was to mix with people in order to present the call of the religion. Therefore God's command to him to turn away from a group among them requires guidance and reassurance. This is achieved through the causal sense conveyed by the relative clause and its complement, meaning: "turn away from them because they engage in discourse about Our signs."

[p. 289 continues]

This verse is the best example for illustrating how the relative clause indicates the causal explanation of what is built upon it, whether a statement or a directive. Do you not see that the command to turn away is limited by the end point of the opposite of the relative clause's content having occurred? It is also the strongest evidence for the correctness of the interpretation given by al-Qutb al-Shirazi in his commentary on Miftāḥ al-ʿUlūm of the phrase of al-Sakkākī: "or that you indicate by it the reason for the construction of the statement, namely that the reason for the construction of the statement is its cause and its motive," even though al-Taftazānī rejected that interpretation.

The root meaning of khawḍ (engaging in discourse / wading) is entering water by walking with the legs, without swimming. It was then borrowed for any activity that involves hardship or difficulty, just as taʿassuf (wandering aimlessly) was borrowed, which is walking on sand, for the same purpose. Khawḍ was also borrowed for speech that involves the contrived fabrication of falsehood and vanity, because its speaker labors at it. Al-Rāghib said: "Most of what occurs in the Qur'an with this term concerns something whose beginning is blameworthy. God says: ﴿they engage in discourse about Our signs﴾, ﴿we engage in discourse and play﴾ [al-Tawba: 65], ﴿you engaged in discourse as those before you engaged in discourse﴾ [al-Tawba: 69], and ﴿leave them to their discourse, playing﴾ [al-Anʿam: 91]." Therefore the meaning of ﴿they engage in discourse about Our signs﴾ is that they speak about them with falsehood and mockery.

The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) directly, and the ruling for the rest of the Muslims is the same as his ruling, as He said in mentioning the hypocrites in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ: ﴿do not sit with them until they engage in discourse about something other than it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 140].

The meaning of turning away (iʿrāḍ) was already explained at His words ﴿turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 63] in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

Turning away from them here is abandoning sitting in their gatherings. This is a metaphor close to the literal meaning, since it generally entails actual turning away. If they overwhelm the Messenger's (ﷺ) gathering, then turning away from them means that he rises up and leaves them. From Ibn Jurayj: "Whenever they mocked, he would get up. They were warned and told, 'Do not mock, or he will rise up.'" The benefit of this turning away is to rebuke them and to cut off the argument with them, perhaps they will return from their obstinacy.

"Until" (ḥattā) is the endpoint of the turning away, because it is a turning away that involves suspending the call to them for a period of time, required by the preservation of another interest that is itself of the category of the call. Therefore suspending the call for a time does no harm. When the reason for that ceases, the attempt to guide them returns to its original state, because it has become purely for the sake of that interest.

[p. 290]

He expressed their moving to another topic of speech by the term "discourse" only because they do not speak except about what has no benefit, namely matters of polytheism and matters of the Age of Ignorance.

"Other" (ghayrihi) is an adjective of "speech" (ḥadīth). The pronoun attached to it refers back to "discourse" (khawḍ), in consideration of its being a speech, as the description of "speech" as "other than it" requires.

His words ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ are a conjunction of the state of forgetting, as an added emphasis on the command to turn away. He attributed the causing of forgetting to Satan, which indicates to us that forgetting is one of the effects of the creation in which God has placed a share for Satan's activity. Similarly, it is related that "yawning is from Satan." This is not from Satan's whispering (waswasa) into human actions, because the Messenger (ﷺ) is protected from Satan's whispering in that respect. Forgetting is therefore among the human accidents permissible for the prophets in matters other than conveying what they were commanded to convey, according to the majority of the scholars of the Sunna, including the Ashʿarites and others. Ibn al-ʿArabī said in al-Aḥkām: "The major Rāfiḍa are those who held that the Prophet (ﷺ) is exempt from forgetting." This is the view of some Ashʿarites, and it is attributed to the Master Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī, as reported by Nūr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī in his commentary on the Nūniyya poem of his shaykh Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī.

It must be determined that his meaning there is what pertains to conveying, as is clear from what al-Qurṭubī reported from him: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forgot and concluded the prayer after two rak'ahs in a four-rak'ah prayer, and forgot verses from some sūrahs, remembering them when he heard a man reciting in the night prayer," as in the Ṣaḥīḥ. And in the authentic hadith: "I am only a human being; I forget just as you forget, so when I forget, remind me." That is forgetting the recollection of it after he had conveyed it. Our concern here is not the permissibility of that, but the attribution of it to Satan, for that requires that Satan has a share that has an effect on the soul of the Messenger. It is therefore possible that some of the human accidents permissible for the prophets were placed by God in the original creation as the work of the devils, just as He placed some accidents in the charge of the angels. Forgetting may be among the accidents entrusted to the devils, as its attribution to Satan has recurred in many verses, among them. This is like yawning being from Satan, and like ḏāt al-janb (pleurisy) being from Satan. Ayyūb said: ﴿Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment﴾ [Ṣād: 41]. In that case, the correct view is that the human accidents permissible for the prophets, which do not impair conveying and do not lead to disobedience, may in some cases be from the effect of Satan's work, and that God protected them from Satan in other respects.

[p. 291]

It is possible that Muḥammad (ﷺ) was singled out from among the prophets in that no power of satanic work has authority over him, even if that is among the permissible accidents for the station of prophethood. Those accidents that touch him are only those in which Satan has no effect. This may be indicated by what is related in the hadith of the splitting of the chest: "When Gabriel extracted the clot he said, 'This is Satan's portion from you,'" meaning the center of his activities. So Satan can reach nothing that occurs in the soul of our Prophet (ﷺ) except through the arrangement of something that occupies the Prophet, to the point that he forgets, like what occurs in the hadith of the Muwaṭṭaʾ when "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) slept and entrusted Bilāl to watch over them for the dawn, and Bilāl slept until the sun rose. The Prophet said, 'Satan came to Bilāl and kept soothing him as a child is soothed, until he slept.'" As for the sleep of the Prophet and the Muslims other than Bilāl, it was ordinary sleep and not the work of Satan. ʿIyāḍ indicated this view in al-Shifāʾ. Close to this is what is related: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Laylat al-Qadr, then went out to inform the people, but two men argued, and it was lifted." The quarrelling is from the work of Satan, and he could not lift the Night of Power by himself, so he whispered quarrelling.

The conclusion is that the Messenger (ﷺ) is protected from whispering, but things below it, such as forgetting and nazgh (slight incitement), do not necessarily require that he be protected from them. The two matters may be distinguished: whispering has positive effects, while forgetting and nazgh have negative effects, namely distraction, preoccupation, and the like.

So the meaning is: if Satan causes you to forget turning away from them, then when you remember, do not sit with them. This forgetting moves the Messenger (ﷺ) from one act of worship to another, and from one method of call to another. Satan's causing him to forget is therefore not an inducement to disobedience, since there is no corruption in committing that, and it does not achieve any aim of Satan's scheme in misguidance. God has lifted the blame for forgetting, and for this reason He said ﴿then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning: after you remember the command to turn away. "Reminder" (dhikrā) is the name for remembering, which is the opposite of forgetting. It is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar): if you were negligent after this and sat with them, then when you remember, do not sit. This is the opposite of "turn away," since commanding a thing is a prohibition of its opposite.

Al-Jumhūr read yunsiyannaka with a sukūn on the nūn and a light sīn. Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a fatḥa on the nūn and a shadda on the sīn, from tansiya, which is an intensification of ansāhu (caused him to forget).

[p. 292]

Some scholars interpreted this verse as something addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is his community, like His words ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī said: "If we excuse our companions for their statement about ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], because association is impossible for him, then they have no excuse regarding this verse, since forgetting is permissible for him."

The wrongdoing people are those who engage in discourse about the signs of God. This is an explicit noun used in place of a pronoun, to increase the benefit of describing them with wrongdoing. Thus it is known that their engaging in discourse about God's signs is wrongdoing, and it is therefore known that it is discourse of denial of the truth and obstinacy in the face of what is evident.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 69:

﴿And upon those who are mindful of God there is no account of theirs at all, but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may be mindful of God.﴾

When turning away from the assemblies of those who engage in mockery of the verses could not, in some cases, prevent the words of those people on this subject from reaching the ears of the believers without intention, God followed the earlier prohibition with a pardon for what the ears of the believers accidentally pick up of that. Thus the verse serves as an excuse for what reaches the ears of the believers without their sitting with those who revile.

By ﴿those who are mindful﴾ is meant the believers. The Prophet (ﷺ) is the foremost of the mindful, so the relative pronoun functions as a generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), and it includes all Muslims, just as His saying ﴿so turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68] carries its ruling to the rest of the Muslims by way of following (bi-hukm al-taba'). A group of exegetes said: the verse ﴿And when you see those who engage in mockery of Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68] was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And upon those who are mindful of God there is no account of theirs at all﴾ came as a concession (rukhsah) for other than the Prophet among the Muslims to be present in those assemblies, because the polytheists would be angered by the Prophet's rising from their gatherings. This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jubayr, so the generality of the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿those who are mindful﴾ is restricted by what the preceding verse requires.

Al-Baghawi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: When ﴿And when you see those who engage in mockery of Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68] was revealed, the Muslims said: How can we sit in the Sacred Mosque and circumambulate the House while they are constantly engaged in mockery? Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed ﴿And upon those who are mindful of God there is no account of theirs at all﴾, meaning: when you rise from them, you bear no responsibility for what they say while you keep away from them, since the matter is not your doing, and it is not incumbent upon you to stop them.

His saying ﴿And upon those who are mindful of God there is no account of theirs at all﴾ has had its like explained earlier, namely His saying ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾ [al-An'am: 52].

Then the word "reckoning" (al-hisab) here is a verbal noun (masdar) added to the pronoun of those who engage in mockery of the verses. This verbal noun is in the position of a passive verb, so its subject may be ﴿those who are mindful﴾, in the same pattern as what preceded in His saying ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾ [al-An'am: 52], meaning: the mindful are not obliged to call the mockers to account, that is, to prevent them from mockery, since God has not charged them with that, because they are unable to restrain the polytheists. It may also be that its subject is God, exalted is He, as in His saying ﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 26], meaning: the mindful bear no burden of the reckoning of the polytheists, that is, they have no share in the sin of that mockery if they hear it.

His saying ﴿but it is a reminder﴾: the conjunction "wa" connects the exceptive (istidrak) to the negation, meaning: there is nothing upon them of their reckoning, but upon them is a reminder. "Al-dhikra" is a verbal noun of dhakkara (with doubled letter), meaning "admonished," as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back [to God]﴾ [Qaf: 8]. That is, if they hear them mocking, it is incumbent upon them to admonish them and warn them of God's wrath. Thus "dhikra" may be parsed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) which replaces its verb, the implied sense being: "but they remind them with a reminder." It may also be parsed as nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), the implied sense being: "but upon them is a reminder."

The pronoun in ﴿that perhaps they may be mindful of God﴾ refers back to what the pronoun of "their reckoning" refers to, meaning: perhaps those who engage in mockery of the verses will be mindful, that is, will abandon the mockery. On this reading, "taqwa" is used in its linguistic sense and not its legal sense. It may also be that the pronoun refers to ﴿those who are mindful﴾, meaning: but upon them is a reminder, perhaps they will be mindful by fulfilling the duty of forbidding evil, or perhaps they will continue in their mindfulness.

From al-Kisa'i: the meaning is "but this is a reminder," that is, His saying ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-An'am: 68] is a reminder to you, and it is not a censure for forgetfulness, since there is no responsibility upon the mindful for hearing the mockery of the mockers; rather, We have reminded them of turning away from them, that perhaps they may be mindful of hearing them.

The majority hold that this verse is not abrogated. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi held that it is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they enter into a conversation other than it; indeed, you would then be like them﴾ [al-Nisa': 140], on the basis of their opinion that His saying ﴿And upon those who are mindful of God there is no account of theirs at all﴾ permitted the believers to sit, and only forbade it for the Prophet (ﷺ) by His saying ﴿And when you see those who engage in mockery of Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68], as was mentioned earlier.

[Page 295]

Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat al-Anʿām, verse 70:

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, and whom the life of this world has deceived. And admonish with it, lest a soul be given over to destruction for what it has earned. It shall have, besides God, no protector and no intercessor. And if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it. Those are the ones who have been given over to destruction for what they earned. For them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause ﴿So turn away from them﴾ [al-Anʿām: 68], or on the clause ﴿Nor is anything of their reckoning upon those who are mindful of God﴾ [al-Anʿām: 69]. This is a separate ruling, different from the ruling to turn away from those who engage in vain discourse about the signs of God, and for this reason it is conjoined to it. The relative pronoun and the other relative clause are used here, and this is not an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun.

"Dhar" is an imperative verb. It is said: no past tense, verbal noun, active participle, or passive participle of it is attested. Its forms are thus replaced in usage by their equivalents from the root *taraka* (to leave), out of avoidance of heaviness, and they used its present tense and imperative from the root. The grammarians of morphology (ʿulamāʾ al-taṣrīf) treated it as a weak-initial (*mithāl wāwī*) verb, because they found that one of its radicals had been elided, and they found it operating like *yaʿidu* and *yarithu*. They therefore determined that the elided radical is the first, and that it is a *wāw*. It was elided in forms like *dhar* and *daʿ* even though the middle radical is fatha-vowelled, in conformity with usage. This is elision for lightness (*ḥadhf takhfīf*), not elision to remove heaviness (*ḥadhf daf ʿthiql*), unlike the elision in *yaʿidu* and *yarithu*.

The meaning of *dhar* is "leave," that is, do not mix with them. Here it is a metaphor for not caring about them and paying little attention to their mockery, as in His saying, ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], and His saying, ﴿So leave me with those who deny this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44], and the verse of Ṭarafa:

*So leave me with my nature, for I am grateful to you,*
*Even if my house is situated far away near Ḍarghad.*

That is: do not be concerned with them, do not care about their persistent misguidance, and do not occupy your heart with them. The admonition with the Qur'an is then inclusive of them. Or: do not heed them, but admonish them with it, that is, the poor quality of their response should not deter you from repeating the admonition to them.

The word "religion" in His saying ﴿who have taken their religion﴾ may mean "creed" (*milla*), that is, what they adhere to, profess, and use to draw near to God, as in the saying of al-Nābigha:

*Their assembly is the sanctuary of God, and their religion*
*Is upright; they hope for nothing but the outcome.*

That is: they took it as play and amusement, that is, they made religion a collection of matters that belong to play and amusement, that is, frivolity and amusement at the idols during their festivals, and whistling and clapping at the Kaʿba, according to one of the two interpretations of His saying ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ [al-Anfāl: 35].

He did not say "they took play and amusement as a religion" because of the word "took." They did not make everything that belongs to play and amusement into a religion for themselves. Rather, they deliberately adopted a religion, gathered for it matters from play and amusement, and named them a religion.

It is also possible that "religion" here means custom (*ʿāda*), as in the saying of al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī:

*She says, when I had pushed away her camel's halter cord:*
*"Is this his custom forever, and is mine?"*

That is: those whose habit is play and amusement, who turn away from the truth; this concerns their treatment of the Messenger (ﷺ).

[Page 296]

The meanings of play (*laʿib*) and amusement (*lahw*) were explained earlier, in His saying ﴿The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾ [al-Anʿām: 32] in this sūra.

Those who have taken their religion as play and amusement are a group identified by the condition of this relative clause, and it is specific to them. Thus they are not the same as those who engage in vain discourse about the signs; rather, there is a difference between them and those who engage in vain discourse about the signs. It is possible that the intended referents are all the polytheists, based on interpreting "religion" as creed and sect. In that case they are more general than those who engage in vain discourse, and the relation between them is general and specific (*ʿumūm wa khuṣūṣ muṭlaq*). This suits the interpretation of *dhar* as not caring about them or their religion, either to avoid despairing of their faith or to increase the admonition against them. That is: admonish them with the Qur'an. It is possible that the intended referents are a group of foolish polytheists who made play and amusement their habit, based on interpreting "religion" as custom. In that case the relation between them and those who engage in vain discourse is general and specific in both directions (*ʿumūm wa khuṣūṣ wajhī*).

"And whom the life of this world has deceived": that is, the life of this world has deceived them, and they thought that there is no life after it, and that its bliss will last for them, out of arrogance on their part. The meaning of "deception" (*ghurūr*) was explained earlier at His saying ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the lands deceive you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 196] in the sūra of Āl ʿImrān.

The mention of "life" here has a great significance: their concern regarding this world is life in it, not what is gained in it of good things through which there is happiness in the Hereafter. That is: the life of this world deceived them, so it made them imagine there is no life after it, and they said, ﴿It is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-Anʿām: 29].

The pronoun in the genitive in ﴿And admonish with it﴾ refers back to the Qur'an, because admonition is admonition about God, the resurrection, bliss, and punishment. This can only happen through the Qur'an. Thus the listener knows that the third-person pronoun refers to what is in the mind of the addressee from the context. This is supported by His saying ﴿So admonish with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qāf: 45]. He omitted the object of *dhakkir* because of the indication of His saying ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾; that is, "And admonish them with it."

His saying ﴿lest a soul be given over to destruction (*an tubsala nafs*)﴾ may be a second object of *dhakkir*, and this is the more apparent,

[Page 297]

that is: admonish them with it about a soul being given over to destruction for what it has earned. The verb of admonition is transitive to two objects in the pattern of *aʿṭā* (to give), because the basic unaugmented form of the verb is transitive to one object, so with the doubling (*taḍʿīf*) it becomes transitive to two: *hum* (them) and *an tubsala nafs*. This verbal noun was singled out among the events to be admonished about because of the terror it contains. It is also possible that *an tubsala* is, with an assumed genitive particle, a causal clause for the admonition, and so it functions as an accusative of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*). Then the negative particle *lā* must be assumed after the omitted causal *lām*. The sense would be: "lest a soul be given over to destruction," as in His saying ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 176], which was discussed at the end of the sūra of al-Nisāʾ. Other interpretations of this have been allowed, but I am not certain about them.

The word *nafs* ("soul") occurs as an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, and it is intended in a general sense, by the indication of the context of exhortation, as in His saying ﴿A soul will know what it has put forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infiṭār: 5]; that is, every soul knows the soul's deeds that it has brought forward, that is, every soul.

*Ibsāl* means handing over to punishment; it is said it also means imprisonment and pledging (*irtihān*). Both meanings occur in their speech, and both are suitable here. Its root is *basl*, which means prevention and what is forbidden. Ḍamra al-Nahshalī said:

*She came in the morning blaming you, after weakness in generosity;*
*Forbidden to you is my blame and my reproach.*

As for *ibsāl* in the sense of handing over, the words of ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ al-Kilābī occur in it:

*And my handing over my sons, without any crime,*
*We have not appeased him, nor with blood poured out.*

The meaning of ﴿for what it has earned﴾ is "for what it has committed." This is the earning of evil, by the indication of *tubsala*.

The clause ﴿It shall have, besides God, no ...﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) regarding *nafs*, because of the generality of "nafs," or in the position of a descriptive clause (*ṣifa*), considering that its wording is singular.

*Walī* means helper. *Shafīʿ* means one who seeks pardon for a wrongdoer because of a position he holds with the one who holds punishment in his hand. *Walī* was explained earlier at His saying ﴿Say: Shall I take other than God as a protector?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 14] in this sūra, and intercession was explained at His saying ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqara: 48] in the sūra of al-Baqara.

The clause ﴿And if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿It shall have, besides God, no protector and no intercessor﴾.

[Page 298]

*Taʿdilu* is the present tense of *ʿadala*, when one ransoms something with something and equates it with it. Ransom is called *ʿadl*, as was explained earlier at His saying ﴿nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqara: 48] in the sūra of al-Baqara. The particle *in* ("if") is used in the conditional, which indicates that the fulfilment of the condition is not realized, because this condition is hypothetical, just as an impossibility is supposed.

The word *ʿadl* in "every ʿadl" is the verbal noun of *ʿadala*, mentioned before. This is its regular verbal noun, so *kull* ("every") is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), as in *al-Kashshāf*. That is: "And if you give every gift as ransom, its gift will not be accepted." It cannot be the direct object of *taʿdil*, because the verb *ʿadala* is transitive to the thing exchanged by means of *bi* (with), and it is transitive directly only to the thing compensated, and that is not the intended meaning here. For this reason *al-Kashshāf* forbade "every ʿadl" from being a direct object, and this is a subtle point.

*Kull* here is metaphorical for abundance, since *ʿadl*, that is, ransom, has no limit that would encompass all of it. The use of *kull* in the sense of abundance was mentioned earlier, at His saying ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign﴾ [al-Baqara: 145] in the sūra of al-Baqara; it is a common metaphor.

His saying ﴿it will not be taken from it﴾ means: what it would ransom itself with will not be taken from it. Thus "from it" is the deputy subject of *yu'khadhu*. There is no pronoun of *ʿadl* in *yu'khadhu*, because you already know that *ʿadl* here means the verbal noun, so the act of taking is not attributed to it, as in *al-Kashshāf*. The verb of taking is treated as intransitive, and no object is assumed for it, as if it were said: "No taking is taken from it." The meaning is: nothing is taken from it. This verse has gathered all that people commonly use to escape from subjugation and domination: the helper, the intercessor, and the ransom. It is thus like His saying ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqara: 48] in the sūra of al-Baqara.

The clause ﴿Those are the ones who have been given over to destruction for what they earned﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) of the explanatory kind (*bayānī*), because the discourse provokes the question of a questioner who says: "What then is the state of those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, compared with the state of the souls that are given over to destruction for what they have earned?" So the answer is given that "those are the ones who were given over to destruction for what they earned." The demonstrative therefore refers to the relative pronoun together with its relative clause, and the definiteness of both parts conveys restriction (*qaṣr*): "those are the ones given over to destruction and no others." This is a restriction of emphasis (*qaṣr mubālagha*), because their being given over is the most severe handing over that people undergo, so everything else is treated as if non-existent.

[Page 299]

It is also possible that the demonstrative refers to the soul in His saying ﴿lest a soul be given over to destruction﴾, by considering that the indefinite noun indicates generality. That is: those who are given over to destruction, who have no protector or intercessor and whose ransom is not accepted, are the ones who were given over to destruction for what they earned. That is: this is the true handing over, not the handing over that you know in your crimes and wars, such as the handing over of the sons of ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ mentioned earlier in his poem. This is like His saying ﴿That is the day of mutual loss and gain﴾ [al-Taghābun: 9].

The clause ﴿For them is a drink of boiling water﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of handing over, or a comprehensive substitute (*badal ishtimāl*) for the meaning of handing over, and for this reason it is separated.

*Ḥamīm* means water of extreme heat. From it comes *ḥamma* (with a fatha on the ḥāʾ), a spring of hot water with which one seeks healing from pains of the limbs and boils. In a hadith: "The likeness of the scholar is like the hot spring: the distant come to it, and the close ones leave it." The drink of boiling water is singled out from among the other kinds of punishment mentioned, to indicate that they become thirsty, and so they drink only water that increases their heat above the heat of thirst.

The *bi* in ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾ is causal, and *mā* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*).

The verb *kāna* ("used to") is added to indicate that disbelief has taken firm hold of them and that they persist in it, because the verb of the root *kawn* indicates existence. Reporting it about something that is itself reported about, or described by something else, adds nothing to the function of descriptions except that it indicates existence in the past; and that is used to express firm establishment.

[Page 300]

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verses 71–73 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?﴾

This is a resumptive (*istinaf*) sentence beginning a new clause, intended to make the polytheists despair of some Muslims apostatizing from the religion. The polytheists would try to turn back some of their relatives or those with whom they had some connection, as is related in the report about Sa'id ibn Zayd and what he suffered from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is also narrated that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq invited his father to worship idols, and that the verse was revealed concerning that. The meaning of this is that the verse was revealed [pointing] to that and to other things, since Surah al-An'am was revealed all at once. The polytheists also tried to divert the Prophet (ﷺ) from calling to Islam, while they offered to please him with whatever he loved, as is related in the report about Abu Talib.

The interrogative is a denial and an expression of despair. The first-person plural pronoun "we" (*nun al-mutakallim*) is used along with others because the speech is from the Messenger (ﷺ) about himself and all the Muslims. The phrase ﴿besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 70] is connected to "call upon." What is meant by "that which neither benefits nor harms" is the idols, for they are stones, and their lack of benefit and their inability to inflict harm are evident. Had they been able to inflict harm, they would have harmed the Muslims, because the Muslims had renounced their worship, scorned their adherents, and declared their worthlessness. So when they made the lack of benefit and harm the reason for negating the worship of idols, they thereby alluded, by means of this, to the worship of the One who benefits and harms, which is Allah, glorified is He.

His saying ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ is conjoined to "call upon," so it falls within the scope of the denial. *Radd* (returning) means sending back to the place from which one came, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ [Sad: 33].

*A'qab* is the plural of *'aqib*, which is the back part of the foot. The *'aqib* of anything is its end and its last part. One says: "He returned on his heel" (*raja'a 'ala 'aqibihi*) and "he turned back on his two heels" (*nakasa 'ala 'aqibayhi*), meaning he returned to the place from which he came, because he had been placing it behind him, and so he went back.

The preposition *'ala* here indicates elevation, meaning he returned along the path of his heel, just as one says "he returned behind him." Then it became a common figurative expression for being engaged in a blameworthy state that its possessor had left and then returned to and became engaged in again. The one who sets out on a journey or for a need goes walking toward a goal he intends; if he turns back before reaching his goal, he has wasted his walking. So his condition is represented by the condition of one who turned back on his heels. In the hadith: "O Allah, make the emigration of my companions complete, and do not turn them back on their heels." So in the verse it is likewise a representation of the state of one who apostatizes to polytheism after having embraced Islam, by the condition of one who set out on an important matter and turned back on his heels without accomplishing what he had set out for. This is more eloquent in depicting the evil state than to say: "and we return to disbelief after faith."

The word *ba'da* (after) is annexed to ﴿idh hadana﴾ (when He guided us), and both are nouns of time. *Ba'da* indicates a time subsequent to something, as in His saying ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [Al-Nur: 58]. When *idh* indicates a time defined by something, then *idh* is a noun of time that is inflected and is intended to denote time, and it is not an adverbial object. The meaning is: after the time at which Allah guided us. Its parallel is ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], in Surah Al 'Imran.

* * *

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered; he has companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us."﴾

He advanced, in depicting their state supposing their return on their heels, to another, more precise representation, by His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth﴾. This is a representation by an imagined image founded on the belief of the addressees concerning the conditions of those possessed. The *kaf* (like) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾, meaning: in a state of our being like the one whom the devils have enticed. So this circumstance emphasizes what is contained in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ of the meaning of representing the apostate by one who turns back on his heels.

*Istihwa'* is of the form *istif'al*, meaning seeking the desire and love of a person, that is, drawing a person's desire toward something that the one drawing him is attempting. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi brought it close to the meaning of the transitivizing hamza, saying: *istahwahu* means *ahwahu*, like *istazalla* means *azalla*. In the *Kashshaf* it occurs that it is of the form *istif'al* from *hawa fi al-ard* when one goes in the earth; but this meaning is not known from the speech of the leading lexicographers, and he himself did not mention it in the *Asas*, although he mentioned ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed﴾, and no one who came after him pointed this out.

The Arabs say "the devils have enticed him" when the jinn snatch away his intellect and direct him as they wish. This is close to their saying "he has been bewitched" (*saharathu*), and they believe that the *ghilan* are the sorcerers of the jinn, also called *sa'ala*, whose singular is *si'lah*. They also say: "the jinn have made him wander" (*istahamathu al-jinnu*) when they seek his wandering in obedience to them.

His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ is connected to *istahwathu*, because it implies the meaning of "they carried him away and he went astray in the earth." This is because the condition that the Arabs imagine as the jinn's enticement is accompanied by savagery and the madman's going off on his face in the earth, riding his head, not accepting advice from anyone, as happened with many of their madmen, and those whom they claim the jinn had snatched. Among the most famous of them is 'Amr ibn 'Udayy al-Iyadi al-Lakhmi, son of the sister of Judhayma ibn Malik, king of al-Hira. Some have allowed that "in the earth" be connected to *hayran* (bewildered), but this is far-fetched, since there is no requirement for fronting the complement.

*Hayran* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the one whom the devils have enticed," and it is a description derived from *hayra*, which is the failure to find the way. One says *har yahar* when one wanders in the earth and does not know the road. It is used figuratively for hesitation in a matter such that its way out is not known. *Hayran* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of "the one."

The clause ﴿he has companions﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, meaning he has a company with him at the time the enticement of the jinn befell him. The clause ﴿who call him﴾ is a qualifier of "companions."

*Du'a'* (calling) is speech that indicates a request for an action from the addressee. *Huda* (guidance) is the opposite of misguidance. That is, they call him to what contains his guidance. The choice of the word *huda* here is because of its suitability to the condition being compared. In this word there is an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the representation (*tamthiliyyah*), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 17], in Surah al-Baqarah. Therefore, its being followed by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ has a wonderful effect. In the *Kashshaf* it is permitted that *huda* be a metaphor for the straight path.

The clause ﴿Come to us﴾ is an explanation of ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, because calling has in it the sense of speech. So it is correct that it be explained by what they say when they call him. Because it is an explanation, it is separated from what precedes it. The explanation of the calling to guidance was needed only to fix the representation in the mind of the hearer, since a madman is not addressed with a plain purpose, and so he is not called to guidance in words that would show him to be astray, because stubbornness and obstinacy are part of the nature of madmen. Therefore they call him with what conveys their desire for his company and their love for him, so they say "Come to us," until, once they have gained control of him, they bind him and return with him to his house.

This wondrous representation has been used to illustrate the condition of one who is supposed to have apostatized to the error of polytheism after the guidance of Islam, under the calls of the polytheists to him and his abandonment of his Muslim companions who try to keep him from them. He is like one whose intellect has been corrupted by the enticement of the devils and the jinn, so that he wanders in the earth after having been sane and knowing its paths, and he has left his sane company calling him to agree with them. This wondrous composition is suitable for analysis, so that each part of the image being compared is likened to a part of the image used as the comparison: the apostasy after faith is likened to the loss of the madman's reason, disbelief is likened to wandering in the earth, the polytheists who invite him to apostasy are likened to the devils, and God's calling of people to faith and the descent of the angels with His revelation are likened to the companions who call to guidance. According to this interpretation, the one referred to ("the one whom") applies to an unspecified individual, so it is like a definite noun with the generic article (*al-jins*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq when he was a disbeliever, and his father and mother were calling him to Islam, but he refused. He later embraced Islam at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his Islam was good.

* * *

﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And (we have been commanded): establish prayer and fear Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth; and the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth, and His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾

The clause ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ is a resumptive clause, restating what he was commanded to say to the polytheists when they were called to return to what they had been upon in the time of ignorance. It is narrated that they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Worship our gods for a time, and we will worship your God for a time." During that time they claimed that their religion was guidance, so they were addressed with a restrictive form (*qasr*). That form is ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾, in which both constituents are defined, the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) and the particle of emphasis are used, so four emphases gathered in the clause, because restriction is equivalent to two emphases, since restriction is nothing but emphasis upon emphasis. The separating pronoun is an emphasis, and *inna* is an emphasis. So this was in keeping with the condition of the denying polytheists, who denied that Islam is guidance.

The definition of the predicate (*musnad ilayhi*) by annexation indicates the guidance coming from Allah, exalted is He, which is the religion prescribed, and here it is Islam, by the indication of His saying ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾. He described Islam as the guidance of Allah in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Jews will not be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 120], in Surah al-Baqarah, meaning the Qur'an is the guidance, not their books.

The definition of the predicate by the generic article (*lam al-jins*) indicates the restriction of the genus of guidance to the religion of Islam, as is the usual case with the definition of the predicate by the generic article. This is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), because the context is to refute the polytheists' call to them to return to their religion, which implies their belief that it is guidance. So the restriction is for correction of belief (*qasr li al-qalb*), since they are not upon any guidance. Therefore the restriction of guidance to the guidance of the Qur'an does not mean "complete guidance," unlike what occurs in Surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿and we have been commanded to submit﴾ is conjoined to what is said. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 56], and His saying ﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah...﴾, the verse.

The *lam* in *li-nuslima* was originally for causation, but the sense of causation has been effaced from it, so it became merely for emphasis. This is the *lam* that frequently occurs after the verb of command and the verb of will. Some called it *lam anna*, with the hamza vowelled with a fatha and the nun sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs say: "I commanded you to do" (*amartuka bi-an taf'ala*), "I commanded you that you do" (*amartuka an taf'ala*), and "I commanded you in order that you do" (*amartuka li-taf'ala*). So the *ba'* is for attachment, and if they omit it, it is implied together with *an*. As for "I commanded you in order that you do," the *lam* is for causation, since he has informed of the cause for which the command occurred. This means that the cause has sufficed in place of mentioning what is caused.

It was also said: the *lam* means *ba'*, and it was said: it is superfluous. In every case, *an* is implied after it, meaning "for the sake of our submitting." The meaning is: "and we have been commanded to Islam," that is, we have been commanded that we submit. The discussion of this *lam* was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [Al-Nisa': 26], in Surah al-Nisa'.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ is connected to *nuslima*, because it carries the sense of devotion to Him, as He said ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]. The discussion of the meaning of Islam was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 131], in Surah al-Baqarah.

In the mention of the name of Allah, exalted is He, with the attribute of lordship over all creation, rather than His proper name, there is an indication of the reason for the command and its rightfulness.

[Page 306]

As for His saying ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾: if you take (*an*) in it to be a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle according to the view of Sībawayh, since the verbal *an* may come before an imperative verb and then conveys both the imperative sense and the verbal sense together, because the imperative form is not used in vain. The statement of the grammarians that it is stripped of the imperative sense means that it has been stripped of the meaning of the imperative verb and given the meaning of the verbal particle, so it falls under the coordination of single words. It is either coordinated with *li-nuslima* (﴿that we may submit﴾) by supposing a deleted preposition before *an*, which is the *bāʾ*, and the deleted particle is indicated by the meaning of the sentence. Or it is coordinated on the meaning of *li-nuslima*, because it occupies the position of *bi-an nuslima* (﴿that we should submit﴾), as has been mentioned earlier from al-Zajjāj. So the sense is: "We were commanded to submit, and then coordinated upon it, *wa-an aqīmū*," meaning, "and we were commanded that we should establish [the prayer]."
