Coordination upon the meaning and position of the wording is a well-known Arabic usage, as in His saying, ﴿Why did You not defer me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous?﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 10], since the meaning is: "If You defer me, I will give charity and be among the righteous."

If you take *an* in it to be an explanatory particle (*tafsīriyya*), then it is coordination of sentences. The statement "we were commanded, li-nuslima" is then supposed to be "we were commanded, *an aslimū* (be submissive), li-nuslima," and ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾ means "li-nuqīma" (so that we may establish). Thus there is *iḥtibāk* (an ellipsis in which one part of a parallel pair is omitted while the other remains, so that each is understood from its counterpart) in the sentence.

More evident than this is that *an* is explanatory. It explains what the coordinating *wāw* indicates of a supposed governing verb coordinated with, namely *"wa-umirnā"* (and we were commanded), since *umirnā* carries the sense of saying without its letters, so the position of the explanatory *an* fits.

The meaning of establishing the prayer has been mentioned at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara.

﴿And fear Him﴾ is coordinated upon *aqīmū* (establish), and what was established concerning His saying ﴿and that you establish﴾ applies to it.

The object pronoun refers to the Lord of the worlds, and it is part of the speech that they were commanded to act upon, by God saying to the believers: "Submit to the Lord of the worlds, establish the prayer, and fear Him." It is also permissible that it be reported in meaning, so that God said, "Fear Me," and it was reported in a form that agrees with the words of the Prophet, who was commanded to say it, through His saying, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, as in the report of the statement of Jesus: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 117].

[Page 306]

His saying ﴿and fear Him﴾ encompasses all the affairs of the religion, and singling out the establishment of the prayer for mention is for emphasis.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ is either coordinated upon the sentence *ittaqūhu* (fear Him), as coordination of a report upon a directive, so it is part of the speech commanded by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, meaning: "Say to them, 'And it is He to whom you will be gathered.'" Or it is coordinated upon *qul* (say), so it is not part of the speech. In this is an affirmation of the gathering for those who deny it, and a reminder of it for the believers in it, as an encouragement to establish the prayer and to piety.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ contains several emphasizers: the form of restriction (*ḥaṣr*) by definiteness of both parts; and the fronting of the object of *tuḥsharūn* (you will be gathered), which conveys emphasis, because the purpose is to confirm the occurrence of the gathering for those among the polytheists who denied it, and to confirm the promise and threat for the believers. The restriction here is real, since they did not deny that the gathering is to God, but they denied that the gathering would occur. So [the Qur'an] took, in affirming it, the path of metonymy (*kināya*), restricting it to God Most High, which implies its occurrence and that it cannot be except toward God, as an allusion that their gods will not avail them anything.

The sentence ﴿And it is He who created the heavens﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾, and the restriction is real, since there is no rejection of a belief here, because the polytheists acknowledge that God is the Creator of the things in the heavens and the earth, as we mentioned at the beginning of the sūra. So the purpose is to argue, through the restriction, that He is the one deserving of worship, because the creatures are His servants, as in His saying, ﴿Then is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17].

The *bāʾ* in His saying *bi-l-ḥaqq* (with truth) is for accompaniment (*mulābasa*), and the phrase it governs is connected to *khalaqa* (created), or it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun.

*Al-ḥaqq* (truth) originally is a verbal noun of *ḥaqqa* when it is established, then it became a noun for the established matter that is not denied, by the usage of the verbal noun meaning the agent noun, like "Fulān is just" (*ʿadl*). *Al-ḥaqq* is the opposite of *al-bāṭil* (falsehood). So *al-bāṭil* is a name for the opposite of what *al-ḥaqq* is called. *Al-ḥaqq* is commonly applied to an action or speech that is just and the giving of what is deserved to its deserver, and in that sense it is synonymous with justice, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with injustice and oppression. *Al-ḥaqq* is also applied to an action or speech that is sound, right, and reaching the limit of perfection and correctness, and it is synonymous with wisdom and reality, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with frivolity and play. *Al-ḥaqq* in this verse is in the second sense, as in His saying, ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhān: 39], after His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhān: 38], and as in His saying, ﴿They reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191].

So God Most High brought the heavens and the earth and what is in them from nonexistence into existence for great wisdoms, and He deposited in all created things powers and properties by which the effects proceed that belong to them, and He arranged them in wondrous orders that preserve their kinds and bring forth that for which they were created. The greatest of these is the creation of man, and the creation of reason in him, and knowledge. In this there is a preparation for affirming the recompense, since if the actions of the accountable were neglected, that would be a deficiency in the truth with which the heavens and the earth were created, so He followed it with His saying, ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾.

The sentence ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ is coordinated upon the one preceding it, because of the connection of truth to His actions, Exalted is He, so it explains the connection of truth to His command, Exalted is He, indicated by *yaqūlu* (He says). By ﴿the day He says "Be"﴾ is meant the Day of Resurrection, due to His saying after it, ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾.

The construction of His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ has been problematic, and the commentators took various approaches to it. The correct view is that His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is﴾ is an adverbial phrase whose predicate has been fronted for emphasis, and the subject is His saying *wa-yakūnu al-ḥaqq*, and the word *al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of the subject. The original structure is: "His word is the truth, the day He says, 'Be,' and it is." The point of fronting the adverbial phrase is to refute the polytheists who deny that this formation occurs after non-existence.

The description of the word as being the truth is also to refute the polytheists. This word is the very thing said by the verb *yaqūlu* (He says) "Be," and the omission of what is said to *kun* (Be) is because it is evident from the context, meaning: He says to the non-existent thing that is to be: "Be." And His saying *fa-yakūnu* (and it is) is a parenthetical clause, meaning: He says to what He intends to form: "Be," and so the thing addressed by "Be" exists immediately after the command of formation.

The meaning is that He originated the creation of the heavens and the earth with truth, and that He will restore the creation that He began with a true word, so that nothing is free from His first formation or His second formation of the truth. It implies that this is a future word, which is the second creation, in contrast to the first creation, and for this reason the word "day" (*yawm*) is used to indicate that it is a specific formation with a determined appointed day.

In His saying ﴿His word is the truth﴾ there is a form of restriction for emphasis, meaning: He is the complete Truth, because the speech of others, although much of it is true, is exposed to error; and whatever in it is not exposed to error is from the revelation of God or from His favor through reason and correctness. This is a recognition that it returns to the grace of God. A parallel to this is the Prophet's saying in his supplication: "Your word is the truth, and Your promise is the truth."

By *al-qawl* (the word) is meant everything that indicates the will and decree of God Most High on the Day of Gathering, which is the day of "Be," whether it is a command of formation, or a command of reward or punishment, or a report of what people have earned of righteous deeds and their opposites. All of that is from the word of God on that day, and it is truth. He singled out from among the words the command of formation because of what the fronting necessitated by singling it out for mention, as you have come to know.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of this verse and the establishment of its meaning from it, the commentators have other paths that do not follow the clear ways.

His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ is an independent sentence, and its arrangement is like the arrangement of the sentence ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾, except that in fronting the predicate over the subject there is a restriction of the predicate to the subject, meaning: the dominion is restricted to belonging to Him and to no other, to refute what the polytheists might hope for regarding their idols sharing in disposal and judgment on that day. The purpose of this adverbial phrase is to magnify the terror of that day.

The blowing of the Trumpet is an example struck for the formative command with the life of the dead, which encompasses all the dead, so they come to life through it and attend the gathering, just as an army attends at the blowing of horns and the beating of drums. *Al-ṣūr* means the horn. It is reported in a hadith that "the angel charged with blowing the Trumpet is Isrāfīl," and none knows the true nature of this blowing except God Most High. The day of the blowing of the Trumpet is the day of "He says, Be, and it is," but it is expressed here as ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ to convey this awe-inspiring state, and because the day, when it was made an adverbial for the word, was defined by its attachment to the sentence ﴿He says, Be, and it is﴾. And when the day was made an adverbial for the dominion, it was appropriate to define the day by what is among the emblems of dominion and armies.

[Page 309]

The phrase *yawma yunfakhu* (the day it is blown) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and its governing element is the stability (*istiqrār*) in His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾. It is also permissible to make it a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿the day He says "Be," and it is﴾. And ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾ may be made a coordination upon ﴿His word is the truth﴾, on the basis that the whole is one sentence.

From Ibn ʿAbbās: *al-ṣūr* here is the plural of *ṣūra* (form), meaning that it is blown into the forms of existing things.

When the intended purpose of reporting about matters pertaining to God Most High was complete, it was followed by attributes that point to accountability for every great and subtle matter, outward and inward, through His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The style of the speech came in the manner of omitting the subject of the predicate in a context where its attributes precede. So the omission of the subject in such a case follows the customary usage of following reports with a greater report in which the subject of the report is made the predicated element and its omission is required. This has been explained earlier at His saying ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān. Therefore here He said "Knower of the unseen," omitting the subject, and then did not omit the subject in His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾.

*Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is that which is absent. Its explanation has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3] in Sūrat al-Baqara, and at His saying ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-Anʿām: 59] in this sūra.

*Al-shahāda* (the witnessed) is the opposite of the unseen, and it is the matters that people witness and reach by means of their doing. It is said *shahida*, meaning "attended," and its opposite is *ghāba* (was absent). Existing things do not go outside of being described by these two attributes, so it is as if it were said: "The Knower of the states of all existing things." The definite article in *al-ghayb* and *al-shahāda* is for comprehensiveness, meaning: Knower of every unseen and every witnessed.

His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾ is coordinated upon His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾.

The attribute *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise) combines perfection of workmanship, and so it indicates the greatness of power together with the connection of knowledge to what is made. The attribute *al-Khabīr* (the Acquainted) combines knowledge of the known things, both the apparent and the hidden. Thus the two attributes are like a summation (*fadhlaka*) of His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ and of His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

[Page 310]

[Page 300]

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verses 71–73 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?﴾

This is a resumptive (*istinaf*) sentence beginning a new clause, intended to make the polytheists despair of some Muslims apostatizing from the religion. The polytheists would try to turn back some of their relatives or those with whom they had some connection, as is related in the report about Sa'id ibn Zayd and what he suffered from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is also narrated that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq invited his father to worship idols, and that the verse was revealed concerning that. The meaning of this is that the verse was revealed [pointing] to that and to other things, since Surah al-An'am was revealed all at once. The polytheists also tried to divert the Prophet (ﷺ) from calling to Islam, while they offered to please him with whatever he loved, as is related in the report about Abu Talib.

The interrogative is a denial and an expression of despair. The first-person plural pronoun "we" (*nun al-mutakallim*) is used along with others because the speech is from the Messenger (ﷺ) about himself and all the Muslims. The phrase ﴿besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 70] is connected to "call upon." What is meant by "that which neither benefits nor harms" is the idols, for they are stones, and their lack of benefit and their inability to inflict harm are evident. Had they been able to inflict harm, they would have harmed the Muslims, because the Muslims had renounced their worship, scorned their adherents, and declared their worthlessness. So when they made the lack of benefit and harm the reason for negating the worship of idols, they thereby alluded, by means of this, to the worship of the One who benefits and harms, which is Allah, glorified is He.

His saying ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ is conjoined to "call upon," so it falls within the scope of the denial. *Radd* (returning) means sending back to the place from which one came, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ [Sad: 33].

*A'qab* is the plural of *'aqib*, which is the back part of the foot. The *'aqib* of anything is its end and its last part. One says: "He returned on his heel" (*raja'a 'ala 'aqibihi*) and "he turned back on his two heels" (*nakasa 'ala 'aqibayhi*), meaning he returned to the place from which he came, because he had been placing it behind him, and so he went back.

The preposition *'ala* here indicates elevation, meaning he returned along the path of his heel, just as one says "he returned behind him." Then it became a common figurative expression for being engaged in a blameworthy state that its possessor had left and then returned to and became engaged in again. The one who sets out on a journey or for a need goes walking toward a goal he intends; if he turns back before reaching his goal, he has wasted his walking. So his condition is represented by the condition of one who turned back on his heels. In the hadith: "O Allah, make the emigration of my companions complete, and do not turn them back on their heels." So in the verse it is likewise a representation of the state of one who apostatizes to polytheism after having embraced Islam, by the condition of one who set out on an important matter and turned back on his heels without accomplishing what he had set out for. This is more eloquent in depicting the evil state than to say: "and we return to disbelief after faith."

The word *ba'da* (after) is annexed to ﴿idh hadana﴾ (when He guided us), and both are nouns of time. *Ba'da* indicates a time subsequent to something, as in His saying ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [Al-Nur: 58]. When *idh* indicates a time defined by something, then *idh* is a noun of time that is inflected and is intended to denote time, and it is not an adverbial object. The meaning is: after the time at which Allah guided us. Its parallel is ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], in Surah Al 'Imran.

* * *

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered; he has companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us."﴾

He advanced, in depicting their state supposing their return on their heels, to another, more precise representation, by His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth﴾. This is a representation by an imagined image founded on the belief of the addressees concerning the conditions of those possessed. The *kaf* (like) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾, meaning: in a state of our being like the one whom the devils have enticed. So this circumstance emphasizes what is contained in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ of the meaning of representing the apostate by one who turns back on his heels.

*Istihwa'* is of the form *istif'al*, meaning seeking the desire and love of a person, that is, drawing a person's desire toward something that the one drawing him is attempting. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi brought it close to the meaning of the transitivizing hamza, saying: *istahwahu* means *ahwahu*, like *istazalla* means *azalla*. In the *Kashshaf* it occurs that it is of the form *istif'al* from *hawa fi al-ard* when one goes in the earth; but this meaning is not known from the speech of the leading lexicographers, and he himself did not mention it in the *Asas*, although he mentioned ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed﴾, and no one who came after him pointed this out.

The Arabs say "the devils have enticed him" when the jinn snatch away his intellect and direct him as they wish. This is close to their saying "he has been bewitched" (*saharathu*), and they believe that the *ghilan* are the sorcerers of the jinn, also called *sa'ala*, whose singular is *si'lah*. They also say: "the jinn have made him wander" (*istahamathu al-jinnu*) when they seek his wandering in obedience to them.

His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ is connected to *istahwathu*, because it implies the meaning of "they carried him away and he went astray in the earth." This is because the condition that the Arabs imagine as the jinn's enticement is accompanied by savagery and the madman's going off on his face in the earth, riding his head, not accepting advice from anyone, as happened with many of their madmen, and those whom they claim the jinn had snatched. Among the most famous of them is 'Amr ibn 'Udayy al-Iyadi al-Lakhmi, son of the sister of Judhayma ibn Malik, king of al-Hira. Some have allowed that "in the earth" be connected to *hayran* (bewildered), but this is far-fetched, since there is no requirement for fronting the complement.

*Hayran* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the one whom the devils have enticed," and it is a description derived from *hayra*, which is the failure to find the way. One says *har yahar* when one wanders in the earth and does not know the road. It is used figuratively for hesitation in a matter such that its way out is not known. *Hayran* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of "the one."

The clause ﴿he has companions﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, meaning he has a company with him at the time the enticement of the jinn befell him. The clause ﴿who call him﴾ is a qualifier of "companions."

*Du'a'* (calling) is speech that indicates a request for an action from the addressee. *Huda* (guidance) is the opposite of misguidance. That is, they call him to what contains his guidance. The choice of the word *huda* here is because of its suitability to the condition being compared. In this word there is an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the representation (*tamthiliyyah*), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 17], in Surah al-Baqarah. Therefore, its being followed by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ has a wonderful effect. In the *Kashshaf* it is permitted that *huda* be a metaphor for the straight path.

The clause ﴿Come to us﴾ is an explanation of ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, because calling has in it the sense of speech. So it is correct that it be explained by what they say when they call him. Because it is an explanation, it is separated from what precedes it. The explanation of the calling to guidance was needed only to fix the representation in the mind of the hearer, since a madman is not addressed with a plain purpose, and so he is not called to guidance in words that would show him to be astray, because stubbornness and obstinacy are part of the nature of madmen. Therefore they call him with what conveys their desire for his company and their love for him, so they say "Come to us," until, once they have gained control of him, they bind him and return with him to his house.

This wondrous representation has been used to illustrate the condition of one who is supposed to have apostatized to the error of polytheism after the guidance of Islam, under the calls of the polytheists to him and his abandonment of his Muslim companions who try to keep him from them. He is like one whose intellect has been corrupted by the enticement of the devils and the jinn, so that he wanders in the earth after having been sane and knowing its paths, and he has left his sane company calling him to agree with them. This wondrous composition is suitable for analysis, so that each part of the image being compared is likened to a part of the image used as the comparison: the apostasy after faith is likened to the loss of the madman's reason, disbelief is likened to wandering in the earth, the polytheists who invite him to apostasy are likened to the devils, and God's calling of people to faith and the descent of the angels with His revelation are likened to the companions who call to guidance. According to this interpretation, the one referred to ("the one whom") applies to an unspecified individual, so it is like a definite noun with the generic article (*al-jins*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq when he was a disbeliever, and his father and mother were calling him to Islam, but he refused. He later embraced Islam at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his Islam was good.

* * *

﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And (we have been commanded): establish prayer and fear Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth; and the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth, and His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾

The clause ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ is a resumptive clause, restating what he was commanded to say to the polytheists when they were called to return to what they had been upon in the time of ignorance. It is narrated that they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Worship our gods for a time, and we will worship your God for a time." During that time they claimed that their religion was guidance, so they were addressed with a restrictive form (*qasr*). That form is ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾, in which both constituents are defined, the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) and the particle of emphasis are used, so four emphases gathered in the clause, because restriction is equivalent to two emphases, since restriction is nothing but emphasis upon emphasis. The separating pronoun is an emphasis, and *inna* is an emphasis. So this was in keeping with the condition of the denying polytheists, who denied that Islam is guidance.

The definition of the predicate (*musnad ilayhi*) by annexation indicates the guidance coming from Allah, exalted is He, which is the religion prescribed, and here it is Islam, by the indication of His saying ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾. He described Islam as the guidance of Allah in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Jews will not be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 120], in Surah al-Baqarah, meaning the Qur'an is the guidance, not their books.

The definition of the predicate by the generic article (*lam al-jins*) indicates the restriction of the genus of guidance to the religion of Islam, as is the usual case with the definition of the predicate by the generic article. This is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), because the context is to refute the polytheists' call to them to return to their religion, which implies their belief that it is guidance. So the restriction is for correction of belief (*qasr li al-qalb*), since they are not upon any guidance. Therefore the restriction of guidance to the guidance of the Qur'an does not mean "complete guidance," unlike what occurs in Surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿and we have been commanded to submit﴾ is conjoined to what is said. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 56], and His saying ﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah...﴾, the verse.

The *lam* in *li-nuslima* was originally for causation, but the sense of causation has been effaced from it, so it became merely for emphasis. This is the *lam* that frequently occurs after the verb of command and the verb of will. Some called it *lam anna*, with the hamza vowelled with a fatha and the nun sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs say: "I commanded you to do" (*amartuka bi-an taf'ala*), "I commanded you that you do" (*amartuka an taf'ala*), and "I commanded you in order that you do" (*amartuka li-taf'ala*). So the *ba'* is for attachment, and if they omit it, it is implied together with *an*. As for "I commanded you in order that you do," the *lam* is for causation, since he has informed of the cause for which the command occurred. This means that the cause has sufficed in place of mentioning what is caused.

It was also said: the *lam* means *ba'*, and it was said: it is superfluous. In every case, *an* is implied after it, meaning "for the sake of our submitting." The meaning is: "and we have been commanded to Islam," that is, we have been commanded that we submit. The discussion of this *lam* was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [Al-Nisa': 26], in Surah al-Nisa'.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ is connected to *nuslima*, because it carries the sense of devotion to Him, as He said ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]. The discussion of the meaning of Islam was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 131], in Surah al-Baqarah.

In the mention of the name of Allah, exalted is He, with the attribute of lordship over all creation, rather than His proper name, there is an indication of the reason for the command and its rightfulness.

[Page 306]

As for His saying ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾: if you take (*an*) in it to be a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle according to the view of Sībawayh, since the verbal *an* may come before an imperative verb and then conveys both the imperative sense and the verbal sense together, because the imperative form is not used in vain. The statement of the grammarians that it is stripped of the imperative sense means that it has been stripped of the meaning of the imperative verb and given the meaning of the verbal particle, so it falls under the coordination of single words. It is either coordinated with *li-nuslima* (﴿that we may submit﴾) by supposing a deleted preposition before *an*, which is the *bāʾ*, and the deleted particle is indicated by the meaning of the sentence. Or it is coordinated on the meaning of *li-nuslima*, because it occupies the position of *bi-an nuslima* (﴿that we should submit﴾), as has been mentioned earlier from al-Zajjāj. So the sense is: "We were commanded to submit, and then coordinated upon it, *wa-an aqīmū*," meaning, "and we were commanded that we should establish [the prayer]." Coordination upon the meaning and position of the wording is a well-known Arabic usage, as in His saying, ﴿Why did You not defer me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous?﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 10], since the meaning is: "If You defer me, I will give charity and be among the righteous."

If you take *an* in it to be an explanatory particle (*tafsīriyya*), then it is coordination of sentences. The statement "we were commanded, li-nuslima" is then supposed to be "we were commanded, *an aslimū* (be submissive), li-nuslima," and ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾ means "li-nuqīma" (so that we may establish). Thus there is *iḥtibāk* (an ellipsis in which one part of a parallel pair is omitted while the other remains, so that each is understood from its counterpart) in the sentence.

More evident than this is that *an* is explanatory. It explains what the coordinating *wāw* indicates of a supposed governing verb coordinated with, namely *"wa-umirnā"* (and we were commanded), since *umirnā* carries the sense of saying without its letters, so the position of the explanatory *an* fits.

The meaning of establishing the prayer has been mentioned at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara.

﴿And fear Him﴾ is coordinated upon *aqīmū* (establish), and what was established concerning His saying ﴿and that you establish﴾ applies to it.

The object pronoun refers to the Lord of the worlds, and it is part of the speech that they were commanded to act upon, by God saying to the believers: "Submit to the Lord of the worlds, establish the prayer, and fear Him." It is also permissible that it be reported in meaning, so that God said, "Fear Me," and it was reported in a form that agrees with the words of the Prophet, who was commanded to say it, through His saying, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, as in the report of the statement of Jesus: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 117].

[Page 306]

His saying ﴿and fear Him﴾ encompasses all the affairs of the religion, and singling out the establishment of the prayer for mention is for emphasis.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ is either coordinated upon the sentence *ittaqūhu* (fear Him), as coordination of a report upon a directive, so it is part of the speech commanded by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, meaning: "Say to them, 'And it is He to whom you will be gathered.'" Or it is coordinated upon *qul* (say), so it is not part of the speech. In this is an affirmation of the gathering for those who deny it, and a reminder of it for the believers in it, as an encouragement to establish the prayer and to piety.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ contains several emphasizers: the form of restriction (*ḥaṣr*) by definiteness of both parts; and the fronting of the object of *tuḥsharūn* (you will be gathered), which conveys emphasis, because the purpose is to confirm the occurrence of the gathering for those among the polytheists who denied it, and to confirm the promise and threat for the believers. The restriction here is real, since they did not deny that the gathering is to God, but they denied that the gathering would occur. So [the Qur'an] took, in affirming it, the path of metonymy (*kināya*), restricting it to God Most High, which implies its occurrence and that it cannot be except toward God, as an allusion that their gods will not avail them anything.

The sentence ﴿And it is He who created the heavens﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾, and the restriction is real, since there is no rejection of a belief here, because the polytheists acknowledge that God is the Creator of the things in the heavens and the earth, as we mentioned at the beginning of the sūra. So the purpose is to argue, through the restriction, that He is the one deserving of worship, because the creatures are His servants, as in His saying, ﴿Then is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17].

The *bāʾ* in His saying *bi-l-ḥaqq* (with truth) is for accompaniment (*mulābasa*), and the phrase it governs is connected to *khalaqa* (created), or it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun.

*Al-ḥaqq* (truth) originally is a verbal noun of *ḥaqqa* when it is established, then it became a noun for the established matter that is not denied, by the usage of the verbal noun meaning the agent noun, like "Fulān is just" (*ʿadl*). *Al-ḥaqq* is the opposite of *al-bāṭil* (falsehood). So *al-bāṭil* is a name for the opposite of what *al-ḥaqq* is called. *Al-ḥaqq* is commonly applied to an action or speech that is just and the giving of what is deserved to its deserver, and in that sense it is synonymous with justice, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with injustice and oppression. *Al-ḥaqq* is also applied to an action or speech that is sound, right, and reaching the limit of perfection and correctness, and it is synonymous with wisdom and reality, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with frivolity and play. *Al-ḥaqq* in this verse is in the second sense, as in His saying, ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhān: 39], after His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhān: 38], and as in His saying, ﴿They reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191].

So God Most High brought the heavens and the earth and what is in them from nonexistence into existence for great wisdoms, and He deposited in all created things powers and properties by which the effects proceed that belong to them, and He arranged them in wondrous orders that preserve their kinds and bring forth that for which they were created. The greatest of these is the creation of man, and the creation of reason in him, and knowledge. In this there is a preparation for affirming the recompense, since if the actions of the accountable were neglected, that would be a deficiency in the truth with which the heavens and the earth were created, so He followed it with His saying, ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾.

The sentence ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ is coordinated upon the one preceding it, because of the connection of truth to His actions, Exalted is He, so it explains the connection of truth to His command, Exalted is He, indicated by *yaqūlu* (He says). By ﴿the day He says "Be"﴾ is meant the Day of Resurrection, due to His saying after it, ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾.

The construction of His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ has been problematic, and the commentators took various approaches to it. The correct view is that His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is﴾ is an adverbial phrase whose predicate has been fronted for emphasis, and the subject is His saying *wa-yakūnu al-ḥaqq*, and the word *al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of the subject. The original structure is: "His word is the truth, the day He says, 'Be,' and it is." The point of fronting the adverbial phrase is to refute the polytheists who deny that this formation occurs after non-existence.

The description of the word as being the truth is also to refute the polytheists. This word is the very thing said by the verb *yaqūlu* (He says) "Be," and the omission of what is said to *kun* (Be) is because it is evident from the context, meaning: He says to the non-existent thing that is to be: "Be." And His saying *fa-yakūnu* (and it is) is a parenthetical clause, meaning: He says to what He intends to form: "Be," and so the thing addressed by "Be" exists immediately after the command of formation.

The meaning is that He originated the creation of the heavens and the earth with truth, and that He will restore the creation that He began with a true word, so that nothing is free from His first formation or His second formation of the truth. It implies that this is a future word, which is the second creation, in contrast to the first creation, and for this reason the word "day" (*yawm*) is used to indicate that it is a specific formation with a determined appointed day.

In His saying ﴿His word is the truth﴾ there is a form of restriction for emphasis, meaning: He is the complete Truth, because the speech of others, although much of it is true, is exposed to error; and whatever in it is not exposed to error is from the revelation of God or from His favor through reason and correctness. This is a recognition that it returns to the grace of God. A parallel to this is the Prophet's saying in his supplication: "Your word is the truth, and Your promise is the truth."

By *al-qawl* (the word) is meant everything that indicates the will and decree of God Most High on the Day of Gathering, which is the day of "Be," whether it is a command of formation, or a command of reward or punishment, or a report of what people have earned of righteous deeds and their opposites. All of that is from the word of God on that day, and it is truth. He singled out from among the words the command of formation because of what the fronting necessitated by singling it out for mention, as you have come to know.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of this verse and the establishment of its meaning from it, the commentators have other paths that do not follow the clear ways.

His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ is an independent sentence, and its arrangement is like the arrangement of the sentence ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾, except that in fronting the predicate over the subject there is a restriction of the predicate to the subject, meaning: the dominion is restricted to belonging to Him and to no other, to refute what the polytheists might hope for regarding their idols sharing in disposal and judgment on that day. The purpose of this adverbial phrase is to magnify the terror of that day.

The blowing of the Trumpet is an example struck for the formative command with the life of the dead, which encompasses all the dead, so they come to life through it and attend the gathering, just as an army attends at the blowing of horns and the beating of drums. *Al-ṣūr* means the horn. It is reported in a hadith that "the angel charged with blowing the Trumpet is Isrāfīl," and none knows the true nature of this blowing except God Most High. The day of the blowing of the Trumpet is the day of "He says, Be, and it is," but it is expressed here as ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ to convey this awe-inspiring state, and because the day, when it was made an adverbial for the word, was defined by its attachment to the sentence ﴿He says, Be, and it is﴾. And when the day was made an adverbial for the dominion, it was appropriate to define the day by what is among the emblems of dominion and armies.

[Page 309]

The phrase *yawma yunfakhu* (the day it is blown) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and its governing element is the stability (*istiqrār*) in His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾. It is also permissible to make it a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿the day He says "Be," and it is﴾. And ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾ may be made a coordination upon ﴿His word is the truth﴾, on the basis that the whole is one sentence.

From Ibn ʿAbbās: *al-ṣūr* here is the plural of *ṣūra* (form), meaning that it is blown into the forms of existing things.

When the intended purpose of reporting about matters pertaining to God Most High was complete, it was followed by attributes that point to accountability for every great and subtle matter, outward and inward, through His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The style of the speech came in the manner of omitting the subject of the predicate in a context where its attributes precede. So the omission of the subject in such a case follows the customary usage of following reports with a greater report in which the subject of the report is made the predicated element and its omission is required. This has been explained earlier at His saying ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān. Therefore here He said "Knower of the unseen," omitting the subject, and then did not omit the subject in His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾.

*Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is that which is absent. Its explanation has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3] in Sūrat al-Baqara, and at His saying ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-Anʿām: 59] in this sūra.

*Al-shahāda* (the witnessed) is the opposite of the unseen, and it is the matters that people witness and reach by means of their doing. It is said *shahida*, meaning "attended," and its opposite is *ghāba* (was absent). Existing things do not go outside of being described by these two attributes, so it is as if it were said: "The Knower of the states of all existing things." The definite article in *al-ghayb* and *al-shahāda* is for comprehensiveness, meaning: Knower of every unseen and every witnessed.

His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾ is coordinated upon His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾.

The attribute *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise) combines perfection of workmanship, and so it indicates the greatness of power together with the connection of knowledge to what is made. The attribute *al-Khabīr* (the Acquainted) combines knowledge of the known things, both the apparent and the hidden. Thus the two attributes are like a summation (*fadhlaka*) of His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ and of His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

[Page 310]

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verses 71–73 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?﴾

This is a resumptive (*istinaf*) sentence beginning a new clause, intended to make the polytheists despair of some Muslims apostatizing from the religion. The polytheists would try to turn back some of their relatives or those with whom they had some connection, as is related in the report about Sa'id ibn Zayd and what he suffered from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is also narrated that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq invited his father to worship idols, and that the verse was revealed concerning that. The meaning of this is that the verse was revealed [pointing] to that and to other things, since Surah al-An'am was revealed all at once. The polytheists also tried to divert the Prophet (ﷺ) from calling to Islam, while they offered to please him with whatever he loved, as is related in the report about Abu Talib.

The interrogative is a denial and an expression of despair. The first-person plural pronoun "we" (*nun al-mutakallim*) is used along with others because the speech is from the Messenger (ﷺ) about himself and all the Muslims. The phrase ﴿besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 70] is connected to "call upon." What is meant by "that which neither benefits nor harms" is the idols, for they are stones, and their lack of benefit and their inability to inflict harm are evident. Had they been able to inflict harm, they would have harmed the Muslims, because the Muslims had renounced their worship, scorned their adherents, and declared their worthlessness. So when they made the lack of benefit and harm the reason for negating the worship of idols, they thereby alluded, by means of this, to the worship of the One who benefits and harms, which is Allah, glorified is He.

His saying ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ is conjoined to "call upon," so it falls within the scope of the denial. *Radd* (returning) means sending back to the place from which one came, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ [Sad: 33].

*A'qab* is the plural of *'aqib*, which is the back part of the foot. The *'aqib* of anything is its end and its last part. One says: "He returned on his heel" (*raja'a 'ala 'aqibihi*) and "he turned back on his two heels" (*nakasa 'ala 'aqibayhi*), meaning he returned to the place from which he came, because he had been placing it behind him, and so he went back.

The preposition *'ala* here indicates elevation, meaning he returned along the path of his heel, just as one says "he returned behind him." Then it became a common figurative expression for being engaged in a blameworthy state that its possessor had left and then returned to and became engaged in again. The one who sets out on a journey or for a need goes walking toward a goal he intends; if he turns back before reaching his goal, he has wasted his walking. So his condition is represented by the condition of one who turned back on his heels. In the hadith: "O Allah, make the emigration of my companions complete, and do not turn them back on their heels." So in the verse it is likewise a representation of the state of one who apostatizes to polytheism after having embraced Islam, by the condition of one who set out on an important matter and turned back on his heels without accomplishing what he had set out for. This is more eloquent in depicting the evil state than to say: "and we return to disbelief after faith."

The word *ba'da* (after) is annexed to ﴿idh hadana﴾ (when He guided us), and both are nouns of time. *Ba'da* indicates a time subsequent to something, as in His saying ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [Al-Nur: 58]. When *idh* indicates a time defined by something, then *idh* is a noun of time that is inflected and is intended to denote time, and it is not an adverbial object. The meaning is: after the time at which Allah guided us. Its parallel is ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], in Surah Al 'Imran.

* * *

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered; he has companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us."﴾

He advanced, in depicting their state supposing their return on their heels, to another, more precise representation, by His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth﴾. This is a representation by an imagined image founded on the belief of the addressees concerning the conditions of those possessed. The *kaf* (like) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾, meaning: in a state of our being like the one whom the devils have enticed. So this circumstance emphasizes what is contained in ﴿and be turned back on our heels﴾ of the meaning of representing the apostate by one who turns back on his heels.

*Istihwa'* is of the form *istif'al*, meaning seeking the desire and love of a person, that is, drawing a person's desire toward something that the one drawing him is attempting. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi brought it close to the meaning of the transitivizing hamza, saying: *istahwahu* means *ahwahu*, like *istazalla* means *azalla*. In the *Kashshaf* it occurs that it is of the form *istif'al* from *hawa fi al-ard* when one goes in the earth; but this meaning is not known from the speech of the leading lexicographers, and he himself did not mention it in the *Asas*, although he mentioned ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed﴾, and no one who came after him pointed this out.

The Arabs say "the devils have enticed him" when the jinn snatch away his intellect and direct him as they wish. This is close to their saying "he has been bewitched" (*saharathu*), and they believe that the *ghilan* are the sorcerers of the jinn, also called *sa'ala*, whose singular is *si'lah*. They also say: "the jinn have made him wander" (*istahamathu al-jinnu*) when they seek his wandering in obedience to them.

His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ is connected to *istahwathu*, because it implies the meaning of "they carried him away and he went astray in the earth." This is because the condition that the Arabs imagine as the jinn's enticement is accompanied by savagery and the madman's going off on his face in the earth, riding his head, not accepting advice from anyone, as happened with many of their madmen, and those whom they claim the jinn had snatched. Among the most famous of them is 'Amr ibn 'Udayy al-Iyadi al-Lakhmi, son of the sister of Judhayma ibn Malik, king of al-Hira. Some have allowed that "in the earth" be connected to *hayran* (bewildered), but this is far-fetched, since there is no requirement for fronting the complement.

*Hayran* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the one whom the devils have enticed," and it is a description derived from *hayra*, which is the failure to find the way. One says *har yahar* when one wanders in the earth and does not know the road. It is used figuratively for hesitation in a matter such that its way out is not known. *Hayran* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of "the one."

The clause ﴿he has companions﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, meaning he has a company with him at the time the enticement of the jinn befell him. The clause ﴿who call him﴾ is a qualifier of "companions."

*Du'a'* (calling) is speech that indicates a request for an action from the addressee. *Huda* (guidance) is the opposite of misguidance. That is, they call him to what contains his guidance. The choice of the word *huda* here is because of its suitability to the condition being compared. In this word there is an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the representation (*tamthiliyyah*), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 17], in Surah al-Baqarah. Therefore, its being followed by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ has a wonderful effect. In the *Kashshaf* it is permitted that *huda* be a metaphor for the straight path.

The clause ﴿Come to us﴾ is an explanation of ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, because calling has in it the sense of speech. So it is correct that it be explained by what they say when they call him. Because it is an explanation, it is separated from what precedes it. The explanation of the calling to guidance was needed only to fix the representation in the mind of the hearer, since a madman is not addressed with a plain purpose, and so he is not called to guidance in words that would show him to be astray, because stubbornness and obstinacy are part of the nature of madmen. Therefore they call him with what conveys their desire for his company and their love for him, so they say "Come to us," until, once they have gained control of him, they bind him and return with him to his house.

This wondrous representation has been used to illustrate the condition of one who is supposed to have apostatized to the error of polytheism after the guidance of Islam, under the calls of the polytheists to him and his abandonment of his Muslim companions who try to keep him from them. He is like one whose intellect has been corrupted by the enticement of the devils and the jinn, so that he wanders in the earth after having been sane and knowing its paths, and he has left his sane company calling him to agree with them. This wondrous composition is suitable for analysis, so that each part of the image being compared is likened to a part of the image used as the comparison: the apostasy after faith is likened to the loss of the madman's reason, disbelief is likened to wandering in the earth, the polytheists who invite him to apostasy are likened to the devils, and God's calling of people to faith and the descent of the angels with His revelation are likened to the companions who call to guidance. According to this interpretation, the one referred to ("the one whom") applies to an unspecified individual, so it is like a definite noun with the generic article (*al-jins*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq when he was a disbeliever, and his father and mother were calling him to Islam, but he refused. He later embraced Islam at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his Islam was good.

* * *

﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And (we have been commanded): establish prayer and fear Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth; and the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth, and His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾

The clause ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ is a resumptive clause, restating what he was commanded to say to the polytheists when they were called to return to what they had been upon in the time of ignorance. It is narrated that they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Worship our gods for a time, and we will worship your God for a time." During that time they claimed that their religion was guidance, so they were addressed with a restrictive form (*qasr*). That form is ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾, in which both constituents are defined, the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) and the particle of emphasis are used, so four emphases gathered in the clause, because restriction is equivalent to two emphases, since restriction is nothing but emphasis upon emphasis. The separating pronoun is an emphasis, and *inna* is an emphasis. So this was in keeping with the condition of the denying polytheists, who denied that Islam is guidance.

The definition of the predicate (*musnad ilayhi*) by annexation indicates the guidance coming from Allah, exalted is He, which is the religion prescribed, and here it is Islam, by the indication of His saying ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾. He described Islam as the guidance of Allah in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Jews will not be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 120], in Surah al-Baqarah, meaning the Qur'an is the guidance, not their books.

The definition of the predicate by the generic article (*lam al-jins*) indicates the restriction of the genus of guidance to the religion of Islam, as is the usual case with the definition of the predicate by the generic article. This is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), because the context is to refute the polytheists' call to them to return to their religion, which implies their belief that it is guidance. So the restriction is for correction of belief (*qasr li al-qalb*), since they are not upon any guidance. Therefore the restriction of guidance to the guidance of the Qur'an does not mean "complete guidance," unlike what occurs in Surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿and we have been commanded to submit﴾ is conjoined to what is said. This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 56], and His saying ﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah...﴾, the verse.

The *lam* in *li-nuslima* was originally for causation, but the sense of causation has been effaced from it, so it became merely for emphasis. This is the *lam* that frequently occurs after the verb of command and the verb of will. Some called it *lam anna*, with the hamza vowelled with a fatha and the nun sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs say: "I commanded you to do" (*amartuka bi-an taf'ala*), "I commanded you that you do" (*amartuka an taf'ala*), and "I commanded you in order that you do" (*amartuka li-taf'ala*). So the *ba'* is for attachment, and if they omit it, it is implied together with *an*. As for "I commanded you in order that you do," the *lam* is for causation, since he has informed of the cause for which the command occurred. This means that the cause has sufficed in place of mentioning what is caused.

It was also said: the *lam* means *ba'*, and it was said: it is superfluous. In every case, *an* is implied after it, meaning "for the sake of our submitting." The meaning is: "and we have been commanded to Islam," that is, we have been commanded that we submit. The discussion of this *lam* was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [Al-Nisa': 26], in Surah al-Nisa'.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ is connected to *nuslima*, because it carries the sense of devotion to Him, as He said ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]. The discussion of the meaning of Islam was previously given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 131], in Surah al-Baqarah.

In the mention of the name of Allah, exalted is He, with the attribute of lordship over all creation, rather than His proper name, there is an indication of the reason for the command and its rightfulness.

[Page 306]

As for His saying ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾: if you take (*an*) in it to be a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle according to the view of Sībawayh, since the verbal *an* may come before an imperative verb and then conveys both the imperative sense and the verbal sense together, because the imperative form is not used in vain. The statement of the grammarians that it is stripped of the imperative sense means that it has been stripped of the meaning of the imperative verb and given the meaning of the verbal particle, so it falls under the coordination of single words. It is either coordinated with *li-nuslima* (﴿that we may submit﴾) by supposing a deleted preposition before *an*, which is the *bāʾ*, and the deleted particle is indicated by the meaning of the sentence. Or it is coordinated on the meaning of *li-nuslima*, because it occupies the position of *bi-an nuslima* (﴿that we should submit﴾), as has been mentioned earlier from al-Zajjāj. So the sense is: "We were commanded to submit, and then coordinated upon it, *wa-an aqīmū*," meaning, "and we were commanded that we should establish [the prayer]." Coordination upon the meaning and position of the wording is a well-known Arabic usage, as in His saying, ﴿Why did You not defer me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous?﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 10], since the meaning is: "If You defer me, I will give charity and be among the righteous."

If you take *an* in it to be an explanatory particle (*tafsīriyya*), then it is coordination of sentences. The statement "we were commanded, li-nuslima" is then supposed to be "we were commanded, *an aslimū* (be submissive), li-nuslima," and ﴿and that we should establish the prayer﴾ means "li-nuqīma" (so that we may establish). Thus there is *iḥtibāk* (an ellipsis in which one part of a parallel pair is omitted while the other remains, so that each is understood from its counterpart) in the sentence.

More evident than this is that *an* is explanatory. It explains what the coordinating *wāw* indicates of a supposed governing verb coordinated with, namely *"wa-umirnā"* (and we were commanded), since *umirnā* carries the sense of saying without its letters, so the position of the explanatory *an* fits.

The meaning of establishing the prayer has been mentioned at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara.

﴿And fear Him﴾ is coordinated upon *aqīmū* (establish), and what was established concerning His saying ﴿and that you establish﴾ applies to it.

The object pronoun refers to the Lord of the worlds, and it is part of the speech that they were commanded to act upon, by God saying to the believers: "Submit to the Lord of the worlds, establish the prayer, and fear Him." It is also permissible that it be reported in meaning, so that God said, "Fear Me," and it was reported in a form that agrees with the words of the Prophet, who was commanded to say it, through His saying, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, as in the report of the statement of Jesus: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 117].

[Page 306]

His saying ﴿and fear Him﴾ encompasses all the affairs of the religion, and singling out the establishment of the prayer for mention is for emphasis.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ is either coordinated upon the sentence *ittaqūhu* (fear Him), as coordination of a report upon a directive, so it is part of the speech commanded by His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, meaning: "Say to them, 'And it is He to whom you will be gathered.'" Or it is coordinated upon *qul* (say), so it is not part of the speech. In this is an affirmation of the gathering for those who deny it, and a reminder of it for the believers in it, as an encouragement to establish the prayer and to piety.

The sentence ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ contains several emphasizers: the form of restriction (*ḥaṣr*) by definiteness of both parts; and the fronting of the object of *tuḥsharūn* (you will be gathered), which conveys emphasis, because the purpose is to confirm the occurrence of the gathering for those among the polytheists who denied it, and to confirm the promise and threat for the believers. The restriction here is real, since they did not deny that the gathering is to God, but they denied that the gathering would occur. So [the Qur'an] took, in affirming it, the path of metonymy (*kināya*), restricting it to God Most High, which implies its occurrence and that it cannot be except toward God, as an allusion that their gods will not avail them anything.

The sentence ﴿And it is He who created the heavens﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾, and the restriction is real, since there is no rejection of a belief here, because the polytheists acknowledge that God is the Creator of the things in the heavens and the earth, as we mentioned at the beginning of the sūra. So the purpose is to argue, through the restriction, that He is the one deserving of worship, because the creatures are His servants, as in His saying, ﴿Then is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17].

The *bāʾ* in His saying *bi-l-ḥaqq* (with truth) is for accompaniment (*mulābasa*), and the phrase it governs is connected to *khalaqa* (created), or it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun.

*Al-ḥaqq* (truth) originally is a verbal noun of *ḥaqqa* when it is established, then it became a noun for the established matter that is not denied, by the usage of the verbal noun meaning the agent noun, like "Fulān is just" (*ʿadl*). *Al-ḥaqq* is the opposite of *al-bāṭil* (falsehood). So *al-bāṭil* is a name for the opposite of what *al-ḥaqq* is called. *Al-ḥaqq* is commonly applied to an action or speech that is just and the giving of what is deserved to its deserver, and in that sense it is synonymous with justice, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with injustice and oppression. *Al-ḥaqq* is also applied to an action or speech that is sound, right, and reaching the limit of perfection and correctness, and it is synonymous with wisdom and reality, and its opposite is *al-bāṭil*, which is synonymous with frivolity and play. *Al-ḥaqq* in this verse is in the second sense, as in His saying, ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhān: 39], after His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhān: 38], and as in His saying, ﴿They reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 191].

So God Most High brought the heavens and the earth and what is in them from nonexistence into existence for great wisdoms, and He deposited in all created things powers and properties by which the effects proceed that belong to them, and He arranged them in wondrous orders that preserve their kinds and bring forth that for which they were created. The greatest of these is the creation of man, and the creation of reason in him, and knowledge. In this there is a preparation for affirming the recompense, since if the actions of the accountable were neglected, that would be a deficiency in the truth with which the heavens and the earth were created, so He followed it with His saying, ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾.

The sentence ﴿And the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ is coordinated upon the one preceding it, because of the connection of truth to His actions, Exalted is He, so it explains the connection of truth to His command, Exalted is He, indicated by *yaqūlu* (He says). By ﴿the day He says "Be"﴾ is meant the Day of Resurrection, due to His saying after it, ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾.

The construction of His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ has been problematic, and the commentators took various approaches to it. The correct view is that His saying ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is﴾ is an adverbial phrase whose predicate has been fronted for emphasis, and the subject is His saying *wa-yakūnu al-ḥaqq*, and the word *al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of the subject. The original structure is: "His word is the truth, the day He says, 'Be,' and it is." The point of fronting the adverbial phrase is to refute the polytheists who deny that this formation occurs after non-existence.

The description of the word as being the truth is also to refute the polytheists. This word is the very thing said by the verb *yaqūlu* (He says) "Be," and the omission of what is said to *kun* (Be) is because it is evident from the context, meaning: He says to the non-existent thing that is to be: "Be." And His saying *fa-yakūnu* (and it is) is a parenthetical clause, meaning: He says to what He intends to form: "Be," and so the thing addressed by "Be" exists immediately after the command of formation.

The meaning is that He originated the creation of the heavens and the earth with truth, and that He will restore the creation that He began with a true word, so that nothing is free from His first formation or His second formation of the truth. It implies that this is a future word, which is the second creation, in contrast to the first creation, and for this reason the word "day" (*yawm*) is used to indicate that it is a specific formation with a determined appointed day.

In His saying ﴿His word is the truth﴾ there is a form of restriction for emphasis, meaning: He is the complete Truth, because the speech of others, although much of it is true, is exposed to error; and whatever in it is not exposed to error is from the revelation of God or from His favor through reason and correctness. This is a recognition that it returns to the grace of God. A parallel to this is the Prophet's saying in his supplication: "Your word is the truth, and Your promise is the truth."

By *al-qawl* (the word) is meant everything that indicates the will and decree of God Most High on the Day of Gathering, which is the day of "Be," whether it is a command of formation, or a command of reward or punishment, or a report of what people have earned of righteous deeds and their opposites. All of that is from the word of God on that day, and it is truth. He singled out from among the words the command of formation because of what the fronting necessitated by singling it out for mention, as you have come to know.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of this verse and the establishment of its meaning from it, the commentators have other paths that do not follow the clear ways.

His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ is an independent sentence, and its arrangement is like the arrangement of the sentence ﴿and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾, except that in fronting the predicate over the subject there is a restriction of the predicate to the subject, meaning: the dominion is restricted to belonging to Him and to no other, to refute what the polytheists might hope for regarding their idols sharing in disposal and judgment on that day. The purpose of this adverbial phrase is to magnify the terror of that day.

The blowing of the Trumpet is an example struck for the formative command with the life of the dead, which encompasses all the dead, so they come to life through it and attend the gathering, just as an army attends at the blowing of horns and the beating of drums. *Al-ṣūr* means the horn. It is reported in a hadith that "the angel charged with blowing the Trumpet is Isrāfīl," and none knows the true nature of this blowing except God Most High. The day of the blowing of the Trumpet is the day of "He says, Be, and it is," but it is expressed here as ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ to convey this awe-inspiring state, and because the day, when it was made an adverbial for the word, was defined by its attachment to the sentence ﴿He says, Be, and it is﴾. And when the day was made an adverbial for the dominion, it was appropriate to define the day by what is among the emblems of dominion and armies.

[Page 309]

The phrase *yawma yunfakhu* (the day it is blown) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and its governing element is the stability (*istiqrār*) in His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾. It is also permissible to make it a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿the day He says "Be," and it is﴾. And ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion﴾ may be made a coordination upon ﴿His word is the truth﴾, on the basis that the whole is one sentence.

From Ibn ʿAbbās: *al-ṣūr* here is the plural of *ṣūra* (form), meaning that it is blown into the forms of existing things.

When the intended purpose of reporting about matters pertaining to God Most High was complete, it was followed by attributes that point to accountability for every great and subtle matter, outward and inward, through His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The style of the speech came in the manner of omitting the subject of the predicate in a context where its attributes precede. So the omission of the subject in such a case follows the customary usage of following reports with a greater report in which the subject of the report is made the predicated element and its omission is required. This has been explained earlier at His saying ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān. Therefore here He said "Knower of the unseen," omitting the subject, and then did not omit the subject in His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾.

*Al-ghayb* (the unseen) is that which is absent. Its explanation has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3] in Sūrat al-Baqara, and at His saying ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-Anʿām: 59] in this sūra.

*Al-shahāda* (the witnessed) is the opposite of the unseen, and it is the matters that people witness and reach by means of their doing. It is said *shahida*, meaning "attended," and its opposite is *ghāba* (was absent). Existing things do not go outside of being described by these two attributes, so it is as if it were said: "The Knower of the states of all existing things." The definite article in *al-ghayb* and *al-shahāda* is for comprehensiveness, meaning: Knower of every unseen and every witnessed.

His saying ﴿and He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾ is coordinated upon His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾.

The attribute *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise) combines perfection of workmanship, and so it indicates the greatness of power together with the connection of knowledge to what is made. The attribute *al-Khabīr* (the Acquainted) combines knowledge of the known things, both the apparent and the hidden. Thus the two attributes are like a summation (*fadhlaka*) of His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ and of His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

[Page 310]

[Page 311]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the preceding sentences, the first of which is ﴿And your people denied it, though it is the truth﴾ [Al-An'am: 66]. Those sentences contain arguments and disputation concerning the affirmation of divine unity (tawhid) and the refutation of association (shirk). These arguments are followed by a witness from the lives of the prophets, namely the disputation of the first messenger who proclaimed tawhid and debated the refutation of shirk with a decisive proof and a clear argument. It is also the most just argument in the history of religion, since it was a messenger's disputation with his father and his people. It was also the greatest proof against the polytheists among the Arabs, since their forefather had not been a polytheist nor had he approved of shirk among his people. And it is the greatest proof for the Messenger (ﷺ) when he came to them calling them to abandon shirk.

The discussion of opening the narrative with "idh" (when), with the implied meaning "remember," has already been covered at the words of God, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Azar was the father of Ibrahim. There is no doubt that it was known among the Arabs that the name of Ibrahim's father was Azar, since the Arabs were careful to mention Ibrahim (peace be upon him), his lineage and his descendants. It is not the custom of the Qur'an to mention the names of non-prophets, so his name is mentioned in this verse only for a purpose that we will mention. The name does not appear in any other verse. What is found in the books of the Israelites is that the name of Ibrahim's father was (Tarah), with a tā' with two dots above, then an alif, then a rā' with a fatḥa, then an unpointed ḥā'. Al-Zajjaj said: "There is no disagreement among the genealogists that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarah." Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Juwayni al-Shafi'i followed him in his tafsir Al-Nukat. In their statements there is a point to examine, because the disagreement that is denied concerns only whether Azar is a name of Ibrahim's father; this does not imply that he had no other name among his people or others, or in a language other than the language of his people. Many similar cases exist. It has also been said that "Azar" is a descriptive epithet.

[Page 312]

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: It has been said that its meaning is "the aged one" in the language of Khwarazm, which is original Persian. Ibn 'Atiyya said, on the authority of al-Dahhak: "Azar" means "the elder." It is also reported from al-Dahhak that the name of Ibrahim's father in the Persian language was "Azar." Ibn Ishaq, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarah, and Azar was a title for him, like Ya'qub, who was titled Isra'il. Mujahid said: "Azar" is the name of the idol that Ibrahim's father worshipped, so he was given this title. More apparent than this is to say that it was the idol of which Ibrahim's father was the custodian (sadin) of its house.

And on the authority of Sulayman al-Taymi and al-Farra': "Azar" is a word of abuse in their language, meaning "the crooked one," that is, one turned away from the path of goodness. This is an error, because it implies the occurrence in the Qur'an of a non-Arabic term that is neither a proper name nor an arabicized word (mu'arrab). For an arabicized word (mu'arrab, a foreign term adopted into Arabic) must be a non-proper word that the Arabs adopted into their language. In al-Fakhr's tafsir it is stated that among the possibilities is that "Azar" was the paternal uncle of Ibrahim, and the name of father was applied to him, because the paternal uncle may also be called "father." This was attributed to Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. But this is far-fetched and should not be adopted, since the disputation with his father is repeated many times in the Qur'an, so it is unlikely that the meaning is that he was his uncle in all those verses.

Al-Fakhr said: The Shi'a said: none of the fathers and forefathers of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was an unbeliever. They denied that Azar was Ibrahim's father and said he was only his uncle. As for our companions (the Sunni scholars), they did not commit to this. I say: it is as al-Fakhr said, that they did not commit to this. I have explained in a treatise of mine on the purity of the lineage of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that unbelief does not contradict the purity of the prophetic lineage with an innate purity, because the purity under discussion is purity from what is shameful in custom. What appears to me is this: that (Tarah) was given the epithet "Azar" in a foreign land, after the name of the region he came from. In Yaqut's Mu'jam (Geographical Dictionary), "Azar" with a fatḥa on the zay and on the rā' is a district between the market of al-Ahwaz and Ramhurmuz. In the eleventh chapter of the Book of Genesis in the Torah, the land of Tarah, father of Ibrahim, is Ur of the Chaldeans. In Yaqut's Mu'jam, "Ur" with a ḍamma on the hamza and a sukun on the waw is among the regions of Ramhurmuz in Khuzistan. Perhaps it is the Ur of the Chaldeans, or a part of it that was attributed to its inhabitants.
