In the Book of Genesis, Tarah went out, he and his son Ibrahim, from his land, Ur of the Chaldeans, heading to the land of Canaan, and they passed on their way through the town of Haran and stayed there, and Tarah died in

[Page 313 is actually 312 continued]

Haran. Perhaps the people of Haran called him Azar because he came from the district of Azar. In the twelfth chapter of the Book of Genesis there is what indicates that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was made a prophet in Haran while his father was alive.

The Torah does not mention the dialogue between Ibrahim and his father, nor between him and his people. Therefore it is most apparent that "Azar" in the verse is a vocative (munada), and that it is built on the fatḥa. This is supported by the reading of Ya'qub, "Azaru," with a ḍamma. It is also supported by what is narrated: that Ibn 'Abbas read it as "A-izru" with two hamzas, the first with a fatḥa and the second with a kasra; and it is narrated from him that he read it with fatḥa on both hamzas. By this, the mention of his name would be a report of Ibrahim's address to him in a harsh manner, which is what the mention of his proper name requires.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "Azara" with a fatḥa on the rā', and Ya'qub read it with a ḍamma. The exegetes limited themselves, in the reading with fatḥa on the rā', to making it an explanatory apposition (bayan) of "his father," and you have known that there is no requirement for this.

The interrogative in ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ is an interrogative of denial and reproach.

The apparent meaning is that what is related in this verse is one of Ibrahim's stances with his father, a stance of harshness, so it is necessarily the one when his father displayed obstinacy in shirk. This was after his father had said to him, ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾ [Maryam: 46]. It is other than the stance in which he addressed him with the words ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾ [Maryam: 42] and the verses in Surat Maryam.

"Tattakhidh" is the present tense of "ittakhadha," which is an (ifti'al) form derived from "akhadha" (to take). The form ifti'al in it indicates effort and exertion for the sake of intensifying the attainment of the action. The lexicographers said: the original hamza was changed into a tā' for the purpose of assimilation (idgham), for lightness, and they softened the hamza; then they treated the tā' as if it were original, so they sometimes say "takhidha" with the meaning of "ittakhadha." It has been read in both ways the words of God, ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾ [Al-Kahf: 77], and (la-takhidhta 'alayhi ajran). The original usage of "ittakhadha" is to be transitive to one object, and the original of the second object was a state (hal). We promised, at the words of God (﴿They said, "Do you take us as a mockery?"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 67]) in Surat al-Baqarah, that we would explain the usage of "ittakhadha" and its transitivity in this surah. The meaning of "tattakhidh" here is "choose" and "select"; so the intended meaning is: do you worship idols?

[Page 314 is actually 313 continued]

In the verb "tattakhidh" there is an indication that this is something fabricated and contrived, and that idols are not fit to be divinity. In this there is an implicit rebuke of the foolishness of his intellect, that he would make his god something he himself has made.

"Asnam" is the plural of "sanam," and a sanam is a figure representing the shape of a human or an animal. The apparent view is that the consideration of its being worshipped is included in the concept of the word sanam, as the statements of the lexicographers agree, so it is not applied to every image. In Shifa' al-Alil (by al-Khafaji), it is stated that "sanam" is arabicized from "shaman," meaning idol, with a transposition of some of its letters; but it did not mention the language from which it was arabicized. If the worship is considered included in the concept of the noun, then "asnaman" is the object of "tattakhidh," on the basis that "tattakhidh" is transitive to one object according to its ordinary usage; and the point of denial is the object, namely "idols." "Alihatan" (gods) would then be a state of "asnaman," emphasizing the sense of the qualified noun, or an apposition to "asnaman." This is what suits the indefiniteness of "asnaman," since if it were the first object of "tattakhidh" it would have been definite, because its origin is the subject. And on the possibility that sanam is a name for the image, whether or not it is worshipped, "alihatan" would be the second object of "tattakhidh," on the basis that "tattakhidh" is taken to mean "make" and "become," that is: do you make images gods for yourself? Like the words of God, ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 95].

What was related of Ibrahim's speech to his father includes his denial of two things: one of them is his making the images gods, although they are manifestly far below the attribute of divinity; the second is the plurality of gods, and for this reason two plural objects were made of "tattakhidh," and he did not say, "Do you take the idol as a god?"

The clause ﴿Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error﴾ explains the denial in the clause ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾. He emphasized the report with the particle of emphasis because of what this report contains: that their error is evident, which is something the addressee denies. Also, since the addressee had not heard denial of his belief before that, he considers himself rightly guided and does not think that anyone denies what he is upon, and he supposes that his son's denial does not reach the degree of seeing him and his people in manifest error. So perhaps he would interpret it as meaning that he intended something better.

[Page 315 is actually 314 continued]

The seeing may be visual, meaning by it in Ibrahim's speech that the error of his father and his people had become like a thing witnessed, because of its clarity in their acts of drawing near to the stone idols; so it is a state in which the error is visibly seen. In this case, the words ﴿in manifest error﴾ are in the position of a state (hal). It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive (ʿilmiyya), and the words ﴿in manifest error﴾ are in the position of the second object.

The purpose of coordinating "and your people" with the pronoun of the addressee, despite the knowledge that his seeing his father in error requires that he see his peers also in error, is that the situation is one of explicitness, in which one does not suffice with implication (dalalat al-iltizam). And it is to inform him at the first instant of the reason that the agreement of a great multitude with him in his error does not strengthen his religion nor cast doubt on one who denies to him what he is upon.

"Mubin" is an active participle from "abana," meaning "bana," that is, manifest.

Describing the error with "mubin" is an indication of the strength of the corruption of their minds, in that they did not notice their error, although it is like what is visibly seen.

His addressing him with this harsh speech occurred in some of his disputations with his father, after he had first approached him with a call in gentleness, as God related about him in another place: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor avails you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]; ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam: 43], up to his words ﴿Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord. Indeed He is ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. When he saw his determination upon disbelief, he adopted harshness with him, exhausting the methods of admonition, perhaps some of them would be more effective in his father's soul than others, since souls have pathways and the fields of their perspectives are varied. For this reason God said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [Al-Nahl: 125]; and He said to him in another place: ﴿and be harsh upon them﴾ [Al-Tawbah: 73].

So God related about Ibrahim in this verse some of his stances with his father. There is nothing in this that contradicts dutifulness to him (birr), since the open proclamation of the truth without abuse or transgression does not contradict dutifulness. The scholars have never ceased to correct their teachers, imams and fathers in scholarly matters without disparagement. Aristotle said in an objection to Plato: "Plato is a friend, and the truth is a friend, but the truth is more friendly."

[Page 316 is actually 315 continued]

Moreover, the degrees of dutifulness to parents vary across the laws. The sons of Ya'qub said: ﴿By God, indeed you are in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95].

[Page 316]

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿When Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am: 74]. The meaning is: "And when We showed Abraham the malakut (dominion, sovereignty) of the heavens and the earth," with a showing that is not surpassed in clarity within its kind. The demonstrative in His words ﴿Thus﴾ refers to the showing derived from His words ﴿We showed Abraham﴾, meaning: "Like that wondrous showing, We showed Abraham the malakut of the heavens and the earth." This is in the manner of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Its explanation has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. Thus the demonstrative in this usage is always singular and masculine, because it has become like a proverb.

His words ﴿Thus We showed Abraham the malakut of the heavens and the earth﴾ indicate an argument deduced from the evidence of the states of existent things for the existence of their Creator.

Seeing (ru'yah) here is used to mean disclosure and knowledge, so showing (al-ira'ah) means unveiling and making known. It encompasses both perceptible things and intelligible things, all of which are used as proof of the truth. This is a showing of inspiration and divine guidance, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not looked into the malakut of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185]. Abraham, peace be upon him, was initially given inspiration toward the truth at the beginning of his affair, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was initiated with true dreams. It is also permissible that the intended showing is knowledge through revelation. This showing took place in the past, but the Qur'an related it using the present tense to bring that wondrous showing to mind, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿God is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9].

As for malakut, the linguists agreed that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of the pattern of ar-raghabut, ar-rahamut, ar-rahabut and al-jabarut. They said that the waw and the ta' in it are for intensification (al-mubalaghah). Its apparent meaning is that its sense is mulk (with a kasra on the mim, "possession"), since the verbal noun of malaka is al-mulk with a kasra on the mim. Because it contains an added element that indicates intensification, its meaning became strong and powerful dominion. For this reason al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) explained it as lordship (rububiyyah) and divinity (ilahiyyah).

Page 316
In Lisan al-'Arab: "The mulk of God and His malakut is His authority. For so-and-so is the malakut of Iraq," meaning his authority and possession. This implies that it is synonymous with al-mulk with a damma on the mim. In the Bulaq edition of Lisan, a damma was marked over the mim of mulkihi.

In al-Itqan (by al-Suyuti), from 'Ikrimah and Ibn 'Abbas: that malakut is a Nabatean word. It appears, therefore, that the pattern fa'alut in all the occurrences in which it appears is among the borrowed patterns in the Arabic language, and that in Nabatean it indicates intensification. The Arabs adopted it into their language because of the special strength it carries. From this it is deduced that malakut is used as a verbal noun for intensification of dominion, and that al-mulk (with a damma) when it is a great possession (mulk with a kasra) is also called malakut.

In this verse, it is a metaphor under both usages, because it is a case of using the verbal noun while intending the noun of the object (ism al-maf'ul), namely "that which is possessed," like khalq (creation) meaning "the created." This is either from al-milk (with a kasra) or from al-mulk (with a damma).

The idafah (genitive construction) of malakut to "the heavens and the earth" is in the sense of "in" (fi). The meaning is what dominion or possession encompasses, and the intended sense is the dominion of God. The meaning is: We unveil to Abraham the signs of Our creations, or the greatness of Our authority, with an unveiling that makes him aware of their realities and of the knowledge that there is no creator and no one who disposes of what We have unveiled to him except Us.

The conjunction of His words ﴿and that he may be among the certain﴾ with His words "thus" is because "thus" indicated that the comparison serves as an exceptional teaching. From this it is understood that the object of comparison is a cause for an important matter which is of the same kind as the object of comparison. The implied sense is: "Thus We showed Abraham the malakut of the heavens and the earth, with a showing of insight and understanding, so that he would know with knowledge conforming to that understanding, which is complete knowledge, and that he may be among the certain." The explanation of this has already preceded at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Thus We detail the signs, so that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in this surah.

Al-Muqin is one who has knowledge that does not admit doubt, and that is iqan (certainty). What is intended is certainty regarding the knowledge of God, exalted is He, and His attributes. His words ﴿and that he may be among the certain﴾ are more eloquent than saying "and that he may be certain," as has preceded at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 76–79 (part 1 of 2):

Page 317

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not like those that set."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate."﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾

﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a consequence (tafri'*) of His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75], as indicated by His saying ﴿he saw a star﴾, for the star is part of the realm of the heavens, and by His saying in the preceding clause ﴿We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. This particular sight, through which he was guided to a wondrous method of silencing his people and compelling them to acknowledge the corruption of their belief, is a branch of that general showing which encompassed the realm of the heavens and the earth, because the conjunction with fa' (then) demands greater connection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, given the meaning of tafri' (consequence) and causation (tasabbub) inherent in fa'. For this reason, we regard al-Zamakhshari's view that ﴿when the night covered him﴾ is conjoined to "Ibrahim said to his father" and that what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) as lacking elegance.

His saying ﴿the night covered him﴾ means: the night grew dark over Ibrahim, i.e., Ibrahim was enveloped by the darkness of the night. This implies that he was under the sky and not in a house.

From His saying afterwards ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾ it is understood that he was walking with a group of his people who were observing the stars. The people of Ibrahim were Sabians who worshipped the stars and made idols representing them. That was the religion of the Chaldeans, the people of Ibrahim.

Page 318

It is said: "janna-hu al-layl," meaning it concealed him; and "janan al-layl" with a fatha on the jim, and "janna-hu" means it covered visible things with its intense darkness. It is said: "jinna-hu al-layl," and this is the original form. It is also said: "janna 'alayhi al-layl," and this is intended to emphasize the extent of covering by darkness, until it became like a veil. Yet it is not heard in their speech "janna al-layl" used intransitively with the meaning of "aẓlama" (grew dark).

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿he saw a star﴾ is that the sight of the stars came to him incidentally, without deliberately aiming to contemplate them; otherwise the horizon at night is full of stars. The star, when he saw it, was clearly visible in the sky, shining with its light, and that is when it is brightest, in the middle of the sky. The apparent meaning is that he saw a star among them that was exceedingly bright. It is reported from Zayd ibn 'Ali that the star was Venus (al-Zuhara), and from al-Suddi that it was Jupiter (al-Mushtari). It is possible that he looked at the stars and saw a star, so that there is an elliptical omission in the speech, like ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], i.e., he struck, and it parted. The clause ﴿he saw a star﴾ is the response (jawab) of ﹙lamma﹚. Al-kawkab means al-najm (the star).

The clause ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering a question arising from the content of the clause ﴿he saw a star﴾, namely: what did he say when he saw it? So His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is the answer to that.

The demonstrative here is for the purpose of distinguishing the star from among the stars. However, its application to its two counterparts in His saying "when he saw the moon" and "when he saw the sun," "this is my lord, this is my lord," determines that the primary purpose of it is the indication by allusion (kinaya) that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter; when it is found, it is pointed to. This is like the demonstrative in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You have indeed remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection, and this is the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum: 56], and His saying ﴿She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾ [Yusuf: 32], where it was not said "he is the one." Perhaps from it also is His saying ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65], since they did not restrict themselves to "our merchandise has been returned to us." In Sahih al-Bukhari, al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I went to help this man," meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, though he had not been previously mentioned, because 'Ali and his affair were what occupied people's minds during the days of Siffin. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾ [al-An'am: 89] will come, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh. In the hadith of the questioning in the grave: "It will be said to him, 'What is your knowledge about this man?'"

Page 319

(meaning the Messenger ﷺ). This is among the purposes that prompt definition by the demonstrative, which the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) have neglected. Thus it is valid here to take it as used in both its meanings, the explicit and the allusive.

The definiteness of the two predicates (al-juz'ayn) conveys restriction (qasr), because he did not say "this is a lord (rabb)." This indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to draw his people along (istidraj); he began by showing that he did not see a plurality of deities, so that he might lead them to monotheism, and he retained one of their objects of worship, and so he supposed its deserving divinity so that they would not flee from listening to his argument.

The apparent sense of His saying "he said" is that he addressed others with it, because speech (qawl) in its literal sense is utterance, and speech is directed only to an addressee. For this reason the literal sense of "qawl" is the apparent meaning of the verse, both from its wording and from the arrangement of its composition: He ordered His saying ﴿when the night covered him﴾ upon His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75] and His saying ﴿that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75], and He ordered all of that upon His saying ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am: 74], and upon His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾, which he would say only to an addressee; and upon His saying after that ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾; and because he confined himself to refuting that the stars are gods, and used this to demonstrate his innocence from what they associate, even though the invalidity of the divinity of the stars does not necessarily entail the invalidity of the divinity of other bodies, were it not that this was the claim of his people. All of this indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, said that by way of disputation with his people and of giving them slack, so that they might come to receive the proof and not flee at the first instant; thus he had gathered a group of his people and intended to argue against them.

His saying ﴿This is my lord﴾ means: my creator and sustainer, so He is worthy of my worship. He said it by way of supposition, following the belief of his people, so that he might lead them to overturn their conviction. He thus showed that he agreed with them, so that they would be drawn to it, and then he would turn upon them with refutation, showing fairness and the pursuit of truth. There is no doubt about this, that the utterance of what outwardly is disbelief from his tongue, peace be upon him, is permissible, because when he saw that this was a path to guiding his people and rescuing them from disbelief, and he considered it more likely to be accepted by them, it was permissible for him to state it explicitly, aiming to reach the truth, while he did not believe it. His saying this does not increase his people in disbelief, like one who is compelled to utter a word of disbelief while his heart is at peace with faith. For if that is permissible to preserve a single soul and rescue it from destruction, its permissibility for rescuing a group of people from destruction in this world and the next is more fitting. It may also be that this was done by permission from Allah, exalted is He, through revelation.

Page 320

On this basis, the verse implies that his people worshipped the stars and that they were upon the religion of the Sabians, and that religion was widespread in the lands of the Chaldeans in which Abraham, peace be upon him, grew up. And the idols they worshipped, they intended them as images of the stars and representations of them, according to their imaginings and myths, just as the ancient Greeks had. It is also possible that they worshipped the stars and worshipped other images, considering them below the stars, just as the Greeks divided worshipped beings into gods and demi-gods. Moreover, the Sabians believe that the stars are spiritual beings that serve them.

The star set (afala al-najm ufulan): it went down. Uful is specific to the setting of celestial luminaries. It is said: "afala al-najm" and "aflat al-shams," and it is the setting that occurs when the star goes down behind the horizon due to the daily rotation of the earthly sphere. So one does not say "aflat al-shams" or "afala al-najm" when it is hidden by a cloud.

His saying "I do not like" (la uhibb): love here carries the meaning of approval and will, i.e., "I do not approve of the setting one as a god," or "I do not want the setting one as a god." It is known that the object of the love is his willing it as a god for himself, by his saying "this is my lord." The use of "love" for "will" is common in speech, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 108]. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it with an omitted modifier, i.e., "I do not like the worship of the setting ones."

He said "al-afilin" in the form of the masculine plural of rational beings, which is specific to rational beings, based on his people's belief that the stars are rational and exercise control over the cosmos, and that what exists is not worshipped unless it is knowing.

The basis of the argument from setting against the deserving of divinity is that setting is a disappearance and withdrawal from people, and it is the nature of a god to be ever-watchful over the management of his servants. So when the star set, in its state of setting it was concealed from observation by people. He built this argument upon what is common among the people, that the setting of a star is its hiddenness from this world; that is, what disappears does not deserve to be taken as a god,

Page 321

because it does not benefit its servants in what they need at the time of its disappearance. The argument does not concern change, because his people did not know the necessary connection between change and the absence of the attribute of divinity; and because setting is not a change in the star's essence, but is an accident (arad) to the sight of those who observe it. As for the star, it remains in its orbit and its order, setting and returning to appearance, and the people of Abraham know this, so that would not be persuasive to them.

For this reason he argued from the state of setting rather than the state of rising, for although rising occurs after setting, the earlier setting was not observed by them, so setting was briefer in the argument than saying that this rising one had previously been setting.

His saying ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ etc. is a coordination (atf) upon an omitted clause indicated by the speech. The estimate is: "then the moon rose, and when he saw it rising," the clause being omitted for brevity. This implies that the moon rose after the star had set. Perhaps he chose, for disputing with his people, the time when the star sets and the moon rises near that, and that it was the last part of the night, so that sunrise would follow both. He manifested the noun "al-qamar" because he omitted the pronoun's antecedent.

Al-bazigh: the one rising at the beginning of its rising; al-buzugh: the beginning of rising.

His saying "this is my lord," by the definiteness of the two predicates, conveys that it is brighter than the star; so if divinity is deserved by reason of light, then that which is more luminous is more deserving of it than the weaker. The demonstrative is used in its allusive meaning only, namely that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter, as already mentioned.

His saying ﴿Then when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people"﴾ was intended to alert his people to look into knowing the true Lord, and that He is one, and that neither the star nor the moon deserves that. Along with this, he alluded in his speech that he has a lord who guides him, and they did not object to him in this, because they were believers in a plurality of lords. In this there is a preparation of their souls for what he had resolved upon: an explicit statement that he has a lord other than the stars. Then he alluded to his people that they were misguided, and prepared them, before plain speech, for knowledge that they were misguided, because his saying ﴿I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ places in

Page 322

their souls doubt about their belief, whether it might be error; and because of this allusion he did not say "I will surely be misguided," but said ﴿among the misguided people﴾, to indicate that among mankind there is a people who are misguided, meaning his own people.

[p. 323]

He turned to the setting of the moon and reasoned from it to the absence of the (divine) attribute, but he did not negate that attribute merely by seeing the moon rising, even though its setting is certain according to what is customary. This is because he wanted to base the argument on what is observed, which is what is known to the intellects, since observation is stronger.

His saying ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾ means in the morning, after the moon had set. This occurred on one of the nights when the moon sets shortly before sunrise, because the apparent meaning is that this entire argument took place in one sitting.

His saying "This is my lord" uses the demonstrative of the masculine gender, although the sun is treated as feminine. This is because he regarded it as a lord, so the demonstrative took into account the sense of the predicate. It is as if he said: "This body that you call the sun has been shown to be my lord."

The clause "This is greater" serves as the reason for the clause "This is my lord," which entails refuting the lordship of the star and the moon, confining lordship to the sun, and denying it of the star and the moon. For this reason the object of comparison is omitted because it is evident, that is, "it is greater than both of them." The meaning is that the greater, the one that gives more light, is more deserving of divinity.

His saying ﴿He said: "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ is a persuasion to them not to attempt to make him agree with their error. Since divinity was denied to the greatest of the stars they worshipped, it is all the more denied to what is less than them.

*Al-bari'* (free from, innocent of) is an intensive form (*fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*) from *bari'a* with a kasra on the *ra'* only, not *yabra'u* with a fatha on the *ra'* only, meaning "to be released, to be clear of, and to be free from," and it denies association between the one who is free and the one from whom he is free, which is expressed by *min*. From this come ﴿That Allah is free from the polytheists﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:3), ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:69), and ﴿I do not declare myself innocent﴾ (Yusuf 12:53). So the meaning of his saying "free" here is that there is no connection between him and what they associate. The connection in this context is worship, if "what you associate" refers to the idols, or it is adherence and following, if "what you associate" means the act of association.

[p. 323 continues]

The more apparent view is that *ma* in His saying *ma tushrikun* is a relative pronoun, and that the returning pronoun has been omitted for the sake of the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme). That is, *ma tushrikun bihi* ("what you associate with Him"), as will come in His saying ﴿And I do not fear what you associate﴾ (Al-An'am 6:80), because in the act of disavowal it is most common for it to relate to the entities themselves. It also avoids repetition with His saying after it: ﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾ It is also permissible for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning "from your associating," that is, "I do not bear it."

Calling their worship of idols "association" is because his people acknowledged Allah but associated others with Him in divinity, as was the case with the Arabs' association. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses, where argument against them is made by reference to the Creator of the heavens and the earth. It also fits the setting of using the case of Abraham and his people as an example for the polytheists of the Arabs, and it fits His later saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ (Al-An'am 6:82).

The clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Indeed I am free from what you associate,﴾ because freedom from association includes turning the face toward Allah, which is singling Him out in worship. The word *wajh* in His saying "my face" is literal. *Wajjahtu* is derived from *jihah* and *wijhah*, meaning "I turned it toward a direction," that is, "I made such-and-such a direction for it, which it aims at." It is said: "He directed him, and he turned toward such-and-such," if he went toward it. The place intended is called *wijhah* with a kasra on the *waw*, and it seems they formed it on the pattern of *hay'ah* (form, state) from *wajh*, because the one who heads to a place heads with his face toward it. They also formed it on the pattern of *fi'lah* with a kasra on the *fa'*, because the one who heads to a place with his face acquires a state in his face, which is the state of resolve and of fixing the gaze. So the meaning of ﴿I have turned my face﴾ is "I turned it and directed it." This is a figure of speech: his state of turning away from the idols and intending to single out Allah, exalted is He, in worship is likened to one who faces something with his face, intends it, and turns away from anything else.

The relative pronoun is used in His saying ﴿to Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ to indicate the reason for turning to Him in worship, because the stars are among the existing things of the heavens, and idols are among the existing things of the earth, so they are all originated by Allah, exalted is He.

The verb *wajjaha* takes its goal with *ila* (to). It may also take *li* (for) when it is intended that the one who turned did so for the sake of that thing, and this is appropriate when the thing aimed at is one whose pleasure and obedience are to be sought, as you say: "I turned to the beloved." For this reason the transitive use with *li* was chosen here, because in this turning there is pleasing and obedience.

*Fatara* means "created," and its original meaning is "to split." It is said *futira futuran* if it was split, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then look again; do you see any rifts?﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:3), that is, "any defect." He likened creation to the craft of leatherwork and the like, because the craftsman splits the thing before he makes it. This is like what is said: *al-fatq* and *al-falq* (both meaning splitting). So *al-fatr* was applied to bringing a thing into existence and originating it in a form that qualifies it for action.

*Hanifan* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun of the speaker in *wajjahtu*. Its explanation was given earlier at His saying ﴿Say: rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ is coordinated with the circumstantial clause. He denied of himself that he is connected to the polytheists or counted among them.

Since he disavowed their idols, he also disavowed the people, and He combined the two also in Surat al-Mumtahanah when He said: ﴿Indeed we are free from you and from what you worship besides Allah﴾ (Al-Mumtahanah 60:4).

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ provides emphasis for the clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth, a hanif﴾. It was coordinated because its purpose is disavowal of being among the polytheists.

We have followed the view that Abraham's saying, when he saw the luminous bodies, "This is my lord," was a disputation with his people and an attempt to draw them out. He was certain of the denial of their divinity, which is also appropriate to the attribute of prophethood, that it be revealed to him that association is false and the proofs he used against his people. Some exegetes said that this speech was a reflection and an inferential reasoning on his own part, in accordance with His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾, since it indicates that he was in error, because he sought guidance using the future form by means of the conditional particle. This is not necessarily so, because he may have said it to alert his people that they have a lord in whose hand is guidance, as we explained in its place. So his speech would be used in the sense of allusion (*ta'ridh*). Moreover, it may also mean the continuation of guidance and its increase. It may also mean that he sought guidance toward establishing proof, so that his people would not overcome him.

[p. 325]

If we proceed on the basis that this was reasoning within himself before he was certain of monotheism, then this was by inspiration (*ilham*) from Allah, exalted is He. Then His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-An'am 6:75) means: We showed him what is in them of evidence for the existence of the Creator and His oneness before We revealed to him. His saying ﴿He saw a star﴾ would mean he looked at the sky, saw this star, and had not looked at that before. His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ would be a statement within himself in the manner of what a reflective person says within himself, which is inner speech (*hadith al-nafs*), like the words of al-Nabigha about a hunting dog:

*She said to him, "I see no hope,*
*and your master has not been safe, nor has he hunted."*

And like the words of al-'Ajjaj about a wild bull:

*Then he turned and said in reflection:*
*"Life today is in its returning."*

His saying "This is my lord," His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, and His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾ are all used in their literal senses of genuine belief. His saying ﴿He said: "O my people"﴾ is the beginning of his address to his people after the truth had become manifest to him, and then he openly declared his opposition to his people at that time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 76–79 (part 1 of 2):

Page 317

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not like those that set."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate."﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾

﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a consequence (tafri'*) of His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75], as indicated by His saying ﴿he saw a star﴾, for the star is part of the realm of the heavens, and by His saying in the preceding clause ﴿We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. This particular sight, through which he was guided to a wondrous method of silencing his people and compelling them to acknowledge the corruption of their belief, is a branch of that general showing which encompassed the realm of the heavens and the earth, because the conjunction with fa' (then) demands greater connection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, given the meaning of tafri' (consequence) and causation (tasabbub) inherent in fa'. For this reason, we regard al-Zamakhshari's view that ﴿when the night covered him﴾ is conjoined to "Ibrahim said to his father" and that what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) as lacking elegance.

His saying ﴿the night covered him﴾ means: the night grew dark over Ibrahim, i.e., Ibrahim was enveloped by the darkness of the night. This implies that he was under the sky and not in a house.

From His saying afterwards ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾ it is understood that he was walking with a group of his people who were observing the stars. The people of Ibrahim were Sabians who worshipped the stars and made idols representing them. That was the religion of the Chaldeans, the people of Ibrahim.

Page 318

It is said: "janna-hu al-layl," meaning it concealed him; and "janan al-layl" with a fatha on the jim, and "janna-hu" means it covered visible things with its intense darkness. It is said: "jinna-hu al-layl," and this is the original form. It is also said: "janna 'alayhi al-layl," and this is intended to emphasize the extent of covering by darkness, until it became like a veil. Yet it is not heard in their speech "janna al-layl" used intransitively with the meaning of "aẓlama" (grew dark).

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿he saw a star﴾ is that the sight of the stars came to him incidentally, without deliberately aiming to contemplate them; otherwise the horizon at night is full of stars. The star, when he saw it, was clearly visible in the sky, shining with its light, and that is when it is brightest, in the middle of the sky. The apparent meaning is that he saw a star among them that was exceedingly bright. It is reported from Zayd ibn 'Ali that the star was Venus (al-Zuhara), and from al-Suddi that it was Jupiter (al-Mushtari). It is possible that he looked at the stars and saw a star, so that there is an elliptical omission in the speech, like ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], i.e., he struck, and it parted. The clause ﴿he saw a star﴾ is the response (jawab) of ﹙lamma﹚. Al-kawkab means al-najm (the star).

The clause ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering a question arising from the content of the clause ﴿he saw a star﴾, namely: what did he say when he saw it? So His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is the answer to that.

The demonstrative here is for the purpose of distinguishing the star from among the stars. However, its application to its two counterparts in His saying "when he saw the moon" and "when he saw the sun," "this is my lord, this is my lord," determines that the primary purpose of it is the indication by allusion (kinaya) that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter; when it is found, it is pointed to. This is like the demonstrative in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You have indeed remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection, and this is the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum: 56], and His saying ﴿She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾ [Yusuf: 32], where it was not said "he is the one." Perhaps from it also is His saying ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65], since they did not restrict themselves to "our merchandise has been returned to us." In Sahih al-Bukhari, al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I went to help this man," meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, though he had not been previously mentioned, because 'Ali and his affair were what occupied people's minds during the days of Siffin. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾ [al-An'am: 89] will come, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh. In the hadith of the questioning in the grave: "It will be said to him, 'What is your knowledge about this man?'"

Page 319

(meaning the Messenger ﷺ). This is among the purposes that prompt definition by the demonstrative, which the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) have neglected. Thus it is valid here to take it as used in both its meanings, the explicit and the allusive.

The definiteness of the two predicates (al-juz'ayn) conveys restriction (qasr), because he did not say "this is a lord (rabb)." This indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to draw his people along (istidraj); he began by showing that he did not see a plurality of deities, so that he might lead them to monotheism, and he retained one of their objects of worship, and so he supposed its deserving divinity so that they would not flee from listening to his argument.

The apparent sense of His saying "he said" is that he addressed others with it, because speech (qawl) in its literal sense is utterance, and speech is directed only to an addressee. For this reason the literal sense of "qawl" is the apparent meaning of the verse, both from its wording and from the arrangement of its composition: He ordered His saying ﴿when the night covered him﴾ upon His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75] and His saying ﴿that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75], and He ordered all of that upon His saying ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am: 74], and upon His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾, which he would say only to an addressee; and upon His saying after that ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾; and because he confined himself to refuting that the stars are gods, and used this to demonstrate his innocence from what they associate, even though the invalidity of the divinity of the stars does not necessarily entail the invalidity of the divinity of other bodies, were it not that this was the claim of his people. All of this indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, said that by way of disputation with his people and of giving them slack, so that they might come to receive the proof and not flee at the first instant; thus he had gathered a group of his people and intended to argue against them.

His saying ﴿This is my lord﴾ means: my creator and sustainer, so He is worthy of my worship. He said it by way of supposition, following the belief of his people, so that he might lead them to overturn their conviction. He thus showed that he agreed with them, so that they would be drawn to it, and then he would turn upon them with refutation, showing fairness and the pursuit of truth. There is no doubt about this, that the utterance of what outwardly is disbelief from his tongue, peace be upon him, is permissible, because when he saw that this was a path to guiding his people and rescuing them from disbelief, and he considered it more likely to be accepted by them, it was permissible for him to state it explicitly, aiming to reach the truth, while he did not believe it. His saying this does not increase his people in disbelief, like one who is compelled to utter a word of disbelief while his heart is at peace with faith. For if that is permissible to preserve a single soul and rescue it from destruction, its permissibility for rescuing a group of people from destruction in this world and the next is more fitting. It may also be that this was done by permission from Allah, exalted is He, through revelation.

Page 320

On this basis, the verse implies that his people worshipped the stars and that they were upon the religion of the Sabians, and that religion was widespread in the lands of the Chaldeans in which Abraham, peace be upon him, grew up. And the idols they worshipped, they intended them as images of the stars and representations of them, according to their imaginings and myths, just as the ancient Greeks had. It is also possible that they worshipped the stars and worshipped other images, considering them below the stars, just as the Greeks divided worshipped beings into gods and demi-gods. Moreover, the Sabians believe that the stars are spiritual beings that serve them.

The star set (afala al-najm ufulan): it went down. Uful is specific to the setting of celestial luminaries. It is said: "afala al-najm" and "aflat al-shams," and it is the setting that occurs when the star goes down behind the horizon due to the daily rotation of the earthly sphere. So one does not say "aflat al-shams" or "afala al-najm" when it is hidden by a cloud.

His saying "I do not like" (la uhibb): love here carries the meaning of approval and will, i.e., "I do not approve of the setting one as a god," or "I do not want the setting one as a god." It is known that the object of the love is his willing it as a god for himself, by his saying "this is my lord." The use of "love" for "will" is common in speech, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 108]. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it with an omitted modifier, i.e., "I do not like the worship of the setting ones."

He said "al-afilin" in the form of the masculine plural of rational beings, which is specific to rational beings, based on his people's belief that the stars are rational and exercise control over the cosmos, and that what exists is not worshipped unless it is knowing.

The basis of the argument from setting against the deserving of divinity is that setting is a disappearance and withdrawal from people, and it is the nature of a god to be ever-watchful over the management of his servants. So when the star set, in its state of setting it was concealed from observation by people. He built this argument upon what is common among the people, that the setting of a star is its hiddenness from this world; that is, what disappears does not deserve to be taken as a god,

Page 321

because it does not benefit its servants in what they need at the time of its disappearance. The argument does not concern change, because his people did not know the necessary connection between change and the absence of the attribute of divinity; and because setting is not a change in the star's essence, but is an accident (arad) to the sight of those who observe it. As for the star, it remains in its orbit and its order, setting and returning to appearance, and the people of Abraham know this, so that would not be persuasive to them.

For this reason he argued from the state of setting rather than the state of rising, for although rising occurs after setting, the earlier setting was not observed by them, so setting was briefer in the argument than saying that this rising one had previously been setting.

His saying ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ etc. is a coordination (atf) upon an omitted clause indicated by the speech. The estimate is: "then the moon rose, and when he saw it rising," the clause being omitted for brevity. This implies that the moon rose after the star had set. Perhaps he chose, for disputing with his people, the time when the star sets and the moon rises near that, and that it was the last part of the night, so that sunrise would follow both. He manifested the noun "al-qamar" because he omitted the pronoun's antecedent.

Al-bazigh: the one rising at the beginning of its rising; al-buzugh: the beginning of rising.

His saying "this is my lord," by the definiteness of the two predicates, conveys that it is brighter than the star; so if divinity is deserved by reason of light, then that which is more luminous is more deserving of it than the weaker. The demonstrative is used in its allusive meaning only, namely that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter, as already mentioned.

His saying ﴿Then when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people"﴾ was intended to alert his people to look into knowing the true Lord, and that He is one, and that neither the star nor the moon deserves that. Along with this, he alluded in his speech that he has a lord who guides him, and they did not object to him in this, because they were believers in a plurality of lords. In this there is a preparation of their souls for what he had resolved upon: an explicit statement that he has a lord other than the stars. Then he alluded to his people that they were misguided, and prepared them, before plain speech, for knowledge that they were misguided, because his saying ﴿I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ places in

Page 322

their souls doubt about their belief, whether it might be error; and because of this allusion he did not say "I will surely be misguided," but said ﴿among the misguided people﴾, to indicate that among mankind there is a people who are misguided, meaning his own people.

[p. 323]

He turned to the setting of the moon and reasoned from it to the absence of the (divine) attribute, but he did not negate that attribute merely by seeing the moon rising, even though its setting is certain according to what is customary. This is because he wanted to base the argument on what is observed, which is what is known to the intellects, since observation is stronger.

His saying ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾ means in the morning, after the moon had set. This occurred on one of the nights when the moon sets shortly before sunrise, because the apparent meaning is that this entire argument took place in one sitting.

His saying "This is my lord" uses the demonstrative of the masculine gender, although the sun is treated as feminine. This is because he regarded it as a lord, so the demonstrative took into account the sense of the predicate. It is as if he said: "This body that you call the sun has been shown to be my lord."

The clause "This is greater" serves as the reason for the clause "This is my lord," which entails refuting the lordship of the star and the moon, confining lordship to the sun, and denying it of the star and the moon. For this reason the object of comparison is omitted because it is evident, that is, "it is greater than both of them." The meaning is that the greater, the one that gives more light, is more deserving of divinity.

His saying ﴿He said: "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ is a persuasion to them not to attempt to make him agree with their error. Since divinity was denied to the greatest of the stars they worshipped, it is all the more denied to what is less than them.

*Al-bari'* (free from, innocent of) is an intensive form (*fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*) from *bari'a* with a kasra on the *ra'* only, not *yabra'u* with a fatha on the *ra'* only, meaning "to be released, to be clear of, and to be free from," and it denies association between the one who is free and the one from whom he is free, which is expressed by *min*. From this come ﴿That Allah is free from the polytheists﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:3), ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:69), and ﴿I do not declare myself innocent﴾ (Yusuf 12:53). So the meaning of his saying "free" here is that there is no connection between him and what they associate. The connection in this context is worship, if "what you associate" refers to the idols, or it is adherence and following, if "what you associate" means the act of association.

The more apparent view is that *ma* in His saying *ma tushrikun* is a relative pronoun, and that the returning pronoun has been omitted for the sake of the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme). That is, *ma tushrikun bihi* ("what you associate with Him"), as will come in His saying ﴿And I do not fear what you associate﴾ (Al-An'am 6:80), because in the act of disavowal it is most common for it to relate to the entities themselves. It also avoids repetition with His saying after it: ﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾ It is also permissible for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning "from your associating," that is, "I do not bear it."

Calling their worship of idols "association" is because his people acknowledged Allah but associated others with Him in divinity, as was the case with the Arabs' association. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses, where argument against them is made by reference to the Creator of the heavens and the earth. It also fits the setting of using the case of Abraham and his people as an example for the polytheists of the Arabs, and it fits His later saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ (Al-An'am 6:82).

The clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Indeed I am free from what you associate,﴾ because freedom from association includes turning the face toward Allah, which is singling Him out in worship. The word *wajh* in His saying "my face" is literal. *Wajjahtu* is derived from *jihah* and *wijhah*, meaning "I turned it toward a direction," that is, "I made such-and-such a direction for it, which it aims at." It is said: "He directed him, and he turned toward such-and-such," if he went toward it. The place intended is called *wijhah* with a kasra on the *waw*, and it seems they formed it on the pattern of *hay'ah* (form, state) from *wajh*, because the one who heads to a place heads with his face toward it. They also formed it on the pattern of *fi'lah* with a kasra on the *fa'*, because the one who heads to a place with his face acquires a state in his face, which is the state of resolve and of fixing the gaze. So the meaning of ﴿I have turned my face﴾ is "I turned it and directed it." This is a figure of speech: his state of turning away from the idols and intending to single out Allah, exalted is He, in worship is likened to one who faces something with his face, intends it, and turns away from anything else.

The star, when he saw it, was clearly visible in the sky, shining with its light, and that is when it is brightest, in the middle of the sky. The apparent meaning is that he saw a star among them that was exceedingly bright. It is reported from Zayd ibn 'Ali that the star was Venus (al-Zuhara), and from al-Suddi that it was Jupiter (al-Mushtari). It is possible that he looked at the stars and saw a star, so that there is an elliptical omission in the speech, like ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], i.e., he struck, and it parted. The clause ﴿he saw a star﴾ is the response (jawab) of ﹙lamma﹚. Al-kawkab means al-najm (the star).

The clause ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering a question arising from the content of the clause ﴿he saw a star﴾, namely: what did he say when he saw it? So His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is the answer to that.

The demonstrative here is for the purpose of distinguishing the star from among the stars. However, its application to its two counterparts in His saying "when he saw the moon" and "when he saw the sun," "this is my lord, this is my lord," determines that the primary purpose of it is the indication by allusion (kinaya) that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter; when it is found, it is pointed to. This is like the demonstrative in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You have indeed remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection, and this is the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum: 56], and His saying ﴿She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾ [Yusuf: 32], where it was not said "he is the one." Perhaps from it also is His saying ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65], since they did not restrict themselves to "our merchandise has been returned to us." In Sahih al-Bukhari, al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I went to help this man," meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, though he had not been previously mentioned, because 'Ali and his affair were what occupied people's minds during the days of Siffin. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾ [al-An'am: 89] will come, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh. In the hadith of the questioning in the grave: "It will be said to him, 'What is your knowledge about this man?'"

Page 319

(meaning the Messenger ﷺ). This is among the purposes that prompt definition by the demonstrative, which the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) have neglected. Thus it is valid here to take it as used in both its meanings, the explicit and the allusive.

The definiteness of the two predicates (al-juz'ayn) conveys restriction (qasr), because he did not say "this is a lord (rabb)." This indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to draw his people along (istidraj); he began by showing that he did not see a plurality of deities, so that he might lead them to monotheism, and he retained one of their objects of worship, and so he supposed its deserving divinity so that they would not flee from listening to his argument.

The apparent sense of His saying "he said" is that he addressed others with it, because speech (qawl) in its literal sense is utterance, and speech is directed only to an addressee. For this reason the literal sense of "qawl" is the apparent meaning of the verse, both from its wording and from the arrangement of its composition: He ordered His saying ﴿when the night covered him﴾ upon His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the realm of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75] and His saying ﴿that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75], and He ordered all of that upon His saying ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am: 74], and upon His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾, which he would say only to an addressee; and upon His saying after that ﴿O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾; and because he confined himself to refuting that the stars are gods, and used this to demonstrate his innocence from what they associate, even though the invalidity of the divinity of the stars does not necessarily entail the invalidity of the divinity of other bodies, were it not that this was the claim of his people. All of this indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, said that by way of disputation with his people and of giving them slack, so that they might come to receive the proof and not flee at the first instant; thus he had gathered a group of his people and intended to argue against them.

His saying ﴿This is my lord﴾ means: my creator and sustainer, so He is worthy of my worship. He said it by way of supposition, following the belief of his people, so that he might lead them to overturn their conviction. He thus showed that he agreed with them, so that they would be drawn to it, and then he would turn upon them with refutation, showing fairness and the pursuit of truth. There is no doubt about this, that the utterance of what outwardly is disbelief from his tongue, peace be upon him, is permissible, because when he saw that this was a path to guiding his people and rescuing them from disbelief, and he considered it more likely to be accepted by them, it was permissible for him to state it explicitly, aiming to reach the truth, while he did not believe it. His saying this does not increase his people in disbelief, like one who is compelled to utter a word of disbelief while his heart is at peace with faith. For if that is permissible to preserve a single soul and rescue it from destruction, its permissibility for rescuing a group of people from destruction in this world and the next is more fitting. It may also be that this was done by permission from Allah, exalted is He, through revelation.

Page 320

On this basis, the verse implies that his people worshipped the stars and that they were upon the religion of the Sabians, and that religion was widespread in the lands of the Chaldeans in which Abraham, peace be upon him, grew up. And the idols they worshipped, they intended them as images of the stars and representations of them, according to their imaginings and myths, just as the ancient Greeks had. It is also possible that they worshipped the stars and worshipped other images, considering them below the stars, just as the Greeks divided worshipped beings into gods and demi-gods. Moreover, the Sabians believe that the stars are spiritual beings that serve them.

The star set (afala al-najm ufulan): it went down. Uful is specific to the setting of celestial luminaries. It is said: "afala al-najm" and "aflat al-shams," and it is the setting that occurs when the star goes down behind the horizon due to the daily rotation of the earthly sphere. So one does not say "aflat al-shams" or "afala al-najm" when it is hidden by a cloud.

His saying "I do not like" (la uhibb): love here carries the meaning of approval and will, i.e., "I do not approve of the setting one as a god," or "I do not want the setting one as a god." It is known that the object of the love is his willing it as a god for himself, by his saying "this is my lord." The use of "love" for "will" is common in speech, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 108]. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it with an omitted modifier, i.e., "I do not like the worship of the setting ones."

He said "al-afilin" in the form of the masculine plural of rational beings, which is specific to rational beings, based on his people's belief that the stars are rational and exercise control over the cosmos, and that what exists is not worshipped unless it is knowing.

The basis of the argument from setting against the deserving of divinity is that setting is a disappearance and withdrawal from people, and it is the nature of a god to be ever-watchful over the management of his servants. So when the star set, in its state of setting it was concealed from observation by people. He built this argument upon what is common among the people, that the setting of a star is its hiddenness from this world; that is, what disappears does not deserve to be taken as a god,

Page 321

because it does not benefit its servants in what they need at the time of its disappearance. The argument does not concern change, because his people did not know the necessary connection between change and the absence of the attribute of divinity; and because setting is not a change in the star's essence, but is an accident (arad) to the sight of those who observe it. As for the star, it remains in its orbit and its order, setting and returning to appearance, and the people of Abraham know this, so that would not be persuasive to them.

For this reason he argued from the state of setting rather than the state of rising, for although rising occurs after setting, the earlier setting was not observed by them, so setting was briefer in the argument than saying that this rising one had previously been setting.

His saying ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ etc. is a coordination (atf) upon an omitted clause indicated by the speech. The estimate is: "then the moon rose, and when he saw it rising," the clause being omitted for brevity. This implies that the moon rose after the star had set. Perhaps he chose, for disputing with his people, the time when the star sets and the moon rises near that, and that it was the last part of the night, so that sunrise would follow both. He manifested the noun "al-qamar" because he omitted the pronoun's antecedent.

Al-bazigh: the one rising at the beginning of its rising; al-buzugh: the beginning of rising.

His saying "this is my lord," by the definiteness of the two predicates, conveys that it is brighter than the star; so if divinity is deserved by reason of light, then that which is more luminous is more deserving of it than the weaker. The demonstrative is used in its allusive meaning only, namely that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter, as already mentioned.

His saying ﴿Then when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people"﴾ was intended to alert his people to look into knowing the true Lord, and that He is one, and that neither the star nor the moon deserves that. Along with this, he alluded in his speech that he has a lord who guides him, and they did not object to him in this, because they were believers in a plurality of lords. In this there is a preparation of their souls for what he had resolved upon: an explicit statement that he has a lord other than the stars. Then he alluded to his people that they were misguided, and prepared them, before plain speech, for knowledge that they were misguided, because his saying ﴿I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ places in

Page 322

their souls doubt about their belief, whether it might be error; and because of this allusion he did not say "I will surely be misguided," but said ﴿among the misguided people﴾, to indicate that among mankind there is a people who are misguided, meaning his own people.

[p. 323]

He turned to the setting of the moon and reasoned from it to the absence of the (divine) attribute, but he did not negate that attribute merely by seeing the moon rising, even though its setting is certain according to what is customary. This is because he wanted to base the argument on what is observed, which is what is known to the intellects, since observation is stronger.

His saying ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾ means in the morning, after the moon had set. This occurred on one of the nights when the moon sets shortly before sunrise, because the apparent meaning is that this entire argument took place in one sitting.

His saying "This is my lord" uses the demonstrative of the masculine gender, although the sun is treated as feminine. This is because he regarded it as a lord, so the demonstrative took into account the sense of the predicate. It is as if he said: "This body that you call the sun has been shown to be my lord."

The clause "This is greater" serves as the reason for the clause "This is my lord," which entails refuting the lordship of the star and the moon, confining lordship to the sun, and denying it of the star and the moon. For this reason the object of comparison is omitted because it is evident, that is, "it is greater than both of them." The meaning is that the greater, the one that gives more light, is more deserving of divinity.

His saying ﴿He said: "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ is a persuasion to them not to attempt to make him agree with their error. Since divinity was denied to the greatest of the stars they worshipped, it is all the more denied to what is less than them.

*Al-bari'* (free from, innocent of) is an intensive form (*fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*) from *bari'a* with a kasra on the *ra'* only, not *yabra'u* with a fatha on the *ra'* only, meaning "to be released, to be clear of, and to be free from," and it denies association between the one who is free and the one from whom he is free, which is expressed by *min*. From this come ﴿That Allah is free from the polytheists﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:3), ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:69), and ﴿I do not declare myself innocent﴾ (Yusuf 12:53). So the meaning of his saying "free" here is that there is no connection between him and what they associate. The connection in this context is worship, if "what you associate" refers to the idols, or it is adherence and following, if "what you associate" means the act of association.

[p. 323 continues]

The more apparent view is that *ma* in His saying *ma tushrikun* is a relative pronoun, and that the returning pronoun has been omitted for the sake of the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme). That is, *ma tushrikun bihi* ("what you associate with Him"), as will come in His saying ﴿And I do not fear what you associate﴾ (Al-An'am 6:80), because in the act of disavowal it is most common for it to relate to the entities themselves. It also avoids repetition with His saying after it: ﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾ It is also permissible for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning "from your associating," that is, "I do not bear it."

Calling their worship of idols "association" is because his people acknowledged Allah but associated others with Him in divinity, as was the case with the Arabs' association. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses, where argument against them is made by reference to the Creator of the heavens and the earth. It also fits the setting of using the case of Abraham and his people as an example for the polytheists of the Arabs, and it fits His later saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ (Al-An'am 6:82).

The clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Indeed I am free from what you associate,﴾ because freedom from association includes turning the face toward Allah, which is singling Him out in worship. The word *wajh* in His saying "my face" is literal. *Wajjahtu* is derived from *jihah* and *wijhah*, meaning "I turned it toward a direction," that is, "I made such-and-such a direction for it, which it aims at." It is said: "He directed him, and he turned toward such-and-such," if he went toward it. The place intended is called *wijhah* with a kasra on the *waw*, and it seems they formed it on the pattern of *hay'ah* (form, state) from *wajh*, because the one who heads to a place heads with his face toward it. They also formed it on the pattern of *fi'lah* with a kasra on the *fa'*, because the one who heads to a place with his face acquires a state in his face, which is the state of resolve and of fixing the gaze. So the meaning of ﴿I have turned my face﴾ is "I turned it and directed it." This is a figure of speech: his state of turning away from the idols and intending to single out Allah, exalted is He, in worship is likened to one who faces something with his face, intends it, and turns away from anything else.

The relative pronoun is used in His saying ﴿to Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ to indicate the reason for turning to Him in worship, because the stars are among the existing things of the heavens, and idols are among the existing things of the earth, so they are all originated by Allah, exalted is He.

The verb *wajjaha* takes its goal with *ila* (to). It may also take *li* (for) when it is intended that the one who turned did so for the sake of that thing, and this is appropriate when the thing aimed at is one whose pleasure and obedience are to be sought, as you say: "I turned to the beloved." For this reason the transitive use with *li* was chosen here, because in this turning there is pleasing and obedience.

*Fatara* means "created," and its original meaning is "to split." It is said *futira futuran* if it was split, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then look again; do you see any rifts?﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:3), that is, "any defect." He likened creation to the craft of leatherwork and the like, because the craftsman splits the thing before he makes it. This is like what is said: *al-fatq* and *al-falq* (both meaning splitting). So *al-fatr* was applied to bringing a thing into existence and originating it in a form that qualifies it for action.

*Hanifan* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun of the speaker in *wajjahtu*. Its explanation was given earlier at His saying ﴿Say: rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ is coordinated with the circumstantial clause. He denied of himself that he is connected to the polytheists or counted among them.

Since he disavowed their idols, he also disavowed the people, and He combined the two also in Surat al-Mumtahanah when He said: ﴿Indeed we are free from you and from what you worship besides Allah﴾ (Al-Mumtahanah 60:4).

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ provides emphasis for the clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth, a hanif﴾. It was coordinated because its purpose is disavowal of being among the polytheists.

We have followed the view that Abraham's saying, when he saw the luminous bodies, "This is my lord," was a disputation with his people and an attempt to draw them out. He was certain of the denial of their divinity, which is also appropriate to the attribute of prophethood, that it be revealed to him that association is false and the proofs he used against his people. Some exegetes said that this speech was a reflection and an inferential reasoning on his own part, in accordance with His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾, since it indicates that he was in error, because he sought guidance using the future form by means of the conditional particle. This is not necessarily so, because he may have said it to alert his people that they have a lord in whose hand is guidance, as we explained in its place. So his speech would be used in the sense of allusion (*ta'ridh*). Moreover, it may also mean the continuation of guidance and its increase. It may also mean that he sought guidance toward establishing proof, so that his people would not overcome him.

[p. 325]

If we proceed on the basis that this was reasoning within himself before he was certain of monotheism, then this was by inspiration (*ilham*) from Allah, exalted is He. Then His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-An'am 6:75) means: We showed him what is in them of evidence for the existence of the Creator and His oneness before We revealed to him. His saying ﴿He saw a star﴾ would mean he looked at the sky, saw this star, and had not looked at that before. His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ would be a statement within himself in the manner of what a reflective person says within himself, which is inner speech (*hadith al-nafs*), like the words of al-Nabigha about a hunting dog:

*She said to him, "I see no hope,*
*and your master has not been safe, nor has he hunted."*

And like the words of al-'Ajjaj about a wild bull:

*Then he turned and said in reflection:*
*"Life today is in its returning."*

His saying "This is my lord," His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, and His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾ are all used in their literal senses of genuine belief. His saying ﴿He said: "O my people"﴾ is the beginning of his address to his people after the truth had become manifest to him, and then he openly declared his opposition to his people at that time.

It is said: "afala al-najm" and "aflat al-shams," and it is the setting that occurs when the star goes down behind the horizon due to the daily rotation of the earthly sphere. So one does not say "aflat al-shams" or "afala al-najm" when it is hidden by a cloud.

His saying "I do not like" (la uhibb): love here carries the meaning of approval and will, i.e., "I do not approve of the setting one as a god," or "I do not want the setting one as a god." It is known that the object of the love is his willing it as a god for himself, by his saying "this is my lord." The use of "love" for "will" is common in speech, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawba: 108]. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it with an omitted modifier, i.e., "I do not like the worship of the setting ones."

He said "al-afilin" in the form of the masculine plural of rational beings, which is specific to rational beings, based on his people's belief that the stars are rational and exercise control over the cosmos, and that what exists is not worshipped unless it is knowing.

The basis of the argument from setting against the deserving of divinity is that setting is a disappearance and withdrawal from people, and it is the nature of a god to be ever-watchful over the management of his servants. So when the star set, in its state of setting it was concealed from observation by people. He built this argument upon what is common among the people, that the setting of a star is its hiddenness from this world; that is, what disappears does not deserve to be taken as a god,

Page 321

because it does not benefit its servants in what they need at the time of its disappearance. The argument does not concern change, because his people did not know the necessary connection between change and the absence of the attribute of divinity; and because setting is not a change in the star's essence, but is an accident (arad) to the sight of those who observe it. As for the star, it remains in its orbit and its order, setting and returning to appearance, and the people of Abraham know this, so that would not be persuasive to them.
