For this reason he argued from the state of setting rather than the state of rising, for although rising occurs after setting, the earlier setting was not observed by them, so setting was briefer in the argument than saying that this rising one had previously been setting.

His saying ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising﴾ etc. is a coordination (atf) upon an omitted clause indicated by the speech. The estimate is: "then the moon rose, and when he saw it rising," the clause being omitted for brevity. This implies that the moon rose after the star had set. Perhaps he chose, for disputing with his people, the time when the star sets and the moon rises near that, and that it was the last part of the night, so that sunrise would follow both. He manifested the noun "al-qamar" because he omitted the pronoun's antecedent.

Al-bazigh: the one rising at the beginning of its rising; al-buzugh: the beginning of rising.

His saying "this is my lord," by the definiteness of the two predicates, conveys that it is brighter than the star; so if divinity is deserved by reason of light, then that which is more luminous is more deserving of it than the weaker. The demonstrative is used in its allusive meaning only, namely that the thing pointed to is a sought-after, investigated matter, as already mentioned.

His saying ﴿Then when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people"﴾ was intended to alert his people to look into knowing the true Lord, and that He is one, and that neither the star nor the moon deserves that. Along with this, he alluded in his speech that he has a lord who guides him, and they did not object to him in this, because they were believers in a plurality of lords. In this there is a preparation of their souls for what he had resolved upon: an explicit statement that he has a lord other than the stars. Then he alluded to his people that they were misguided, and prepared them, before plain speech, for knowledge that they were misguided, because his saying ﴿I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ places in

Page 322

their souls doubt about their belief, whether it might be error; and because of this allusion he did not say "I will surely be misguided," but said ﴿among the misguided people﴾, to indicate that among mankind there is a people who are misguided, meaning his own people.

[p. 323]

He turned to the setting of the moon and reasoned from it to the absence of the (divine) attribute, but he did not negate that attribute merely by seeing the moon rising, even though its setting is certain according to what is customary. This is because he wanted to base the argument on what is observed, which is what is known to the intellects, since observation is stronger.

His saying ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾ means in the morning, after the moon had set. This occurred on one of the nights when the moon sets shortly before sunrise, because the apparent meaning is that this entire argument took place in one sitting.

His saying "This is my lord" uses the demonstrative of the masculine gender, although the sun is treated as feminine. This is because he regarded it as a lord, so the demonstrative took into account the sense of the predicate. It is as if he said: "This body that you call the sun has been shown to be my lord."

The clause "This is greater" serves as the reason for the clause "This is my lord," which entails refuting the lordship of the star and the moon, confining lordship to the sun, and denying it of the star and the moon. For this reason the object of comparison is omitted because it is evident, that is, "it is greater than both of them." The meaning is that the greater, the one that gives more light, is more deserving of divinity.

His saying ﴿He said: "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ is a persuasion to them not to attempt to make him agree with their error. Since divinity was denied to the greatest of the stars they worshipped, it is all the more denied to what is less than them.

*Al-bari'* (free from, innocent of) is an intensive form (*fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*) from *bari'a* with a kasra on the *ra'* only, not *yabra'u* with a fatha on the *ra'* only, meaning "to be released, to be clear of, and to be free from," and it denies association between the one who is free and the one from whom he is free, which is expressed by *min*. From this come ﴿That Allah is free from the polytheists﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:3), ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:69), and ﴿I do not declare myself innocent﴾ (Yusuf 12:53). So the meaning of his saying "free" here is that there is no connection between him and what they associate. The connection in this context is worship, if "what you associate" refers to the idols, or it is adherence and following, if "what you associate" means the act of association.

[p. 323 continues]

The more apparent view is that *ma* in His saying *ma tushrikun* is a relative pronoun, and that the returning pronoun has been omitted for the sake of the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme). That is, *ma tushrikun bihi* ("what you associate with Him"), as will come in His saying ﴿And I do not fear what you associate﴾ (Al-An'am 6:80), because in the act of disavowal it is most common for it to relate to the entities themselves. It also avoids repetition with His saying after it: ﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾ It is also permissible for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning "from your associating," that is, "I do not bear it."

Calling their worship of idols "association" is because his people acknowledged Allah but associated others with Him in divinity, as was the case with the Arabs' association. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses, where argument against them is made by reference to the Creator of the heavens and the earth. It also fits the setting of using the case of Abraham and his people as an example for the polytheists of the Arabs, and it fits His later saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ (Al-An'am 6:82).

The clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Indeed I am free from what you associate,﴾ because freedom from association includes turning the face toward Allah, which is singling Him out in worship. The word *wajh* in His saying "my face" is literal. *Wajjahtu* is derived from *jihah* and *wijhah*, meaning "I turned it toward a direction," that is, "I made such-and-such a direction for it, which it aims at." It is said: "He directed him, and he turned toward such-and-such," if he went toward it. The place intended is called *wijhah* with a kasra on the *waw*, and it seems they formed it on the pattern of *hay'ah* (form, state) from *wajh*, because the one who heads to a place heads with his face toward it. They also formed it on the pattern of *fi'lah* with a kasra on the *fa'*, because the one who heads to a place with his face acquires a state in his face, which is the state of resolve and of fixing the gaze. So the meaning of ﴿I have turned my face﴾ is "I turned it and directed it." This is a figure of speech: his state of turning away from the idols and intending to single out Allah, exalted is He, in worship is likened to one who faces something with his face, intends it, and turns away from anything else.

The relative pronoun is used in His saying ﴿to Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ to indicate the reason for turning to Him in worship, because the stars are among the existing things of the heavens, and idols are among the existing things of the earth, so they are all originated by Allah, exalted is He.

The verb *wajjaha* takes its goal with *ila* (to). It may also take *li* (for) when it is intended that the one who turned did so for the sake of that thing, and this is appropriate when the thing aimed at is one whose pleasure and obedience are to be sought, as you say: "I turned to the beloved." For this reason the transitive use with *li* was chosen here, because in this turning there is pleasing and obedience.

*Fatara* means "created," and its original meaning is "to split." It is said *futira futuran* if it was split, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then look again; do you see any rifts?﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:3), that is, "any defect." He likened creation to the craft of leatherwork and the like, because the craftsman splits the thing before he makes it. This is like what is said: *al-fatq* and *al-falq* (both meaning splitting). So *al-fatr* was applied to bringing a thing into existence and originating it in a form that qualifies it for action.

*Hanifan* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun of the speaker in *wajjahtu*. Its explanation was given earlier at His saying ﴿Say: rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ is coordinated with the circumstantial clause. He denied of himself that he is connected to the polytheists or counted among them.

Since he disavowed their idols, he also disavowed the people, and He combined the two also in Surat al-Mumtahanah when He said: ﴿Indeed we are free from you and from what you worship besides Allah﴾ (Al-Mumtahanah 60:4).

The clause ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ provides emphasis for the clause ﴿Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth, a hanif﴾. It was coordinated because its purpose is disavowal of being among the polytheists.

We have followed the view that Abraham's saying, when he saw the luminous bodies, "This is my lord," was a disputation with his people and an attempt to draw them out. He was certain of the denial of their divinity, which is also appropriate to the attribute of prophethood, that it be revealed to him that association is false and the proofs he used against his people. Some exegetes said that this speech was a reflection and an inferential reasoning on his own part, in accordance with His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾, since it indicates that he was in error, because he sought guidance using the future form by means of the conditional particle. This is not necessarily so, because he may have said it to alert his people that they have a lord in whose hand is guidance, as we explained in its place. So his speech would be used in the sense of allusion (*ta'ridh*). Moreover, it may also mean the continuation of guidance and its increase. It may also mean that he sought guidance toward establishing proof, so that his people would not overcome him.

[p. 325]

If we proceed on the basis that this was reasoning within himself before he was certain of monotheism, then this was by inspiration (*ilham*) from Allah, exalted is He. Then His saying ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-An'am 6:75) means: We showed him what is in them of evidence for the existence of the Creator and His oneness before We revealed to him. His saying ﴿He saw a star﴾ would mean he looked at the sky, saw this star, and had not looked at that before. His saying ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ would be a statement within himself in the manner of what a reflective person says within himself, which is inner speech (*hadith al-nafs*), like the words of al-Nabigha about a hunting dog:

*She said to him, "I see no hope,*
*and your master has not been safe, nor has he hunted."*

And like the words of al-'Ajjaj about a wild bull:

*Then he turned and said in reflection:*
*"Life today is in its returning."*

His saying "This is my lord," His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, and His saying ﴿Unless my lord guides me﴾ are all used in their literal senses of genuine belief. His saying ﴿He said: "O my people"﴾ is the beginning of his address to his people after the truth had become manifest to him, and then he openly declared his opposition to his people at that time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 80:

﴿And his people argued with him. He said: "Do you argue with me concerning God, when He has already guided me? I do not fear those you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then take heed?"﴾

When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) declared his creed to his people, they began to dispute with him. The sentence "wa-hajjahu" (and his people argued with him) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence "Indi wajjahtu wajhiya lilladhi faṭara al-samawati wa al-ard" (Surely I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth) [al-An'am: 79].

The sentence is joined with the conjunction "wa" rather than "fa" so that it stands independently in reporting its content, although the derivation of its content from what precedes it is evident from the context of the speech.

Page 326
The word "muhajjah" is a reciprocal form (mufa'ala) derived from "hujjah" (proof), which is the evidence supporting a claim. No bare verb is known for this form with the meaning "argued with proof." What is known is the verb "hajja," when it prevailed in argument. If the argument is from both sides, it is literal and this is the basic sense. If it is from one side only, considering that one who seeks to prevail in argument must necessarily receive from his opponent what refutes his argument, so the attempt occurs from both sides; on this basis "muhajjah" was applied to argumentation, or the reciprocal form in it is for emphasis. It is preferable to take it here in its literal sense, so that the meaning is the occurrence of an argument between them and Ibrahim.

Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa mentioned in his lesson on his tafsir that the reciprocal form requires that the one made the doer is the one who initiates the argument, and that some scholars raised an objection regarding the words of the Exalted in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], where He said: ﴿when Ibrahim said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. Thus it began with the speech of Ibrahim, who is the object of the verb, and he answered that Ibrahim initiated the discussion and Nimrod initiated the argument. The linguists did not mention this condition in the usage of the reciprocal form. It is possible that what is intended here is that they took with him the path of proof for the soundness of their religion or for the refutation of his creed while he was listening, so his hearing their speech was treated as a response from him, and the word "muhajjah" was applied to that. Their argument is left unspecified here, since no purpose depends on it, because the purpose is the lesson of Ibrahim's steadfastness upon the truth. The complement of "hajjahu" is omitted, being indicated by the context and by what follows it in the words ﴿Do you argue with me concerning God﴾ and so on.

Their arguments have been mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, among them His words in Surah al-Anbiya': ﴿When he said to his father and his people: "What are these images to which you are devoted?" They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 52] up to His words ﴿And I am among the witnesses to that﴾ [al-Anbiya': 56]; and His words in Surah al-Shu'ara': ﴿He said: "Do they hear you when you call, or do they benefit you or harm you?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 72] and the verses following; and in Surah al-Saffat: ﴿When he said to his father and his people: "What is it you worship? Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 85] up to His words ﴿So We made them the lowest﴾ [al-Saffat: 98]. All of these are real argumentation. Included in the argumentation is what is not a proof but which they regarded as proofs, by threatening him with the wrath of their gods, as His words ﴿and I do not fear those you associate with Him﴾ indicate. The estimated sense is: "And his people argued with him, so they said: such-and-such."

The sentence ﴿He said: "Do you argue with me concerning God"﴾ is the answer to their argument, and for this reason it is separated, in the manner of dialogues, as we previously mentioned in His words ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels: "Indeed I will make on the earth a khalifah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surah al-Baqarah. If the argument is in the true sense of the reciprocal form, then his words "Do you argue with me" close the door of disputation and put an end to it. If "muhajjah" is used in the sense of argument, then his words "Do you argue with me" are a reply to their argument, as in the words of the Exalted ﴿And if they argue with you, say: "I have submitted my face to God"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20].

The interrogation is a rebuke against them and a declaration of despair of his returning to their creed.

The "fi" is for figurative location and is connected to "tuhajjunni"; its entry upon the name of God requires an estimated noun, since argument does not occur over essences, so it is necessary to estimate what the context fits, namely the attributes of God that indicate His oneness, i.e., "concerning the oneness of God." This is like His words ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lut﴾ [Hud: 74], i.e., concerning their destruction.

The sentence "wa-qad hadani" is a circumstantial clause (hal) emphasizing the denial: there is no use in your arguing with me after God has guided me to the truth. It is the nature of an emphasizing circumstantial clause of denial that the possessor's being characterized by it be known to the addressee. Thus the apparent meaning is that Ibrahim addressed them as one who knows that God has guided him, as a metonymy for the manifest signs of guidance.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "atuhajjunni" with a single light nun, and its original form is "atuhajjunnani" with two nuns, one of which was deleted for lightness. The deleted one is the second, which is the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah), according to the preference of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. He said: because the first is the nun of i'rab, while the second prepares for the first person ya' and so it is permissible to delete it for lightness, as they said "layti" for "laytani." Sibawayh held that the deleted one is the first, because the second was brought in to carry the vowel suited to the ya', and the nun of the raf' (nominative) is not vowelled with kasra. Whichever it is, this deletion is used for the purpose of lightness.

From Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': that this reading is a solecism (lahn). If that is correctly ascribed to him, then he was mistaken in his view, or the one who attributed it to him erred. The rest of the readers read it with a doubled nun, by assimilating the nun of the raf' into the nun of protection, also for the purpose of lightness. Therefore the waw is lengthened so that the lengthening serves as a separator between the meeting of the two sukun, because the lengthening is a lightness, and this meeting is what they call the meeting of two sakin in its own category.

The ya' of the first person is deleted in His words "wa-qad hadani" for lightness, both in pausal and continuous recitation, in the reading of Nafi' according to the transmission of Qalun, and in pause only in the reading of some of the ten. This was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿I respond to the call of the caller when he calls Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186].

His words "wa-la akhafu ma tushrikuna bihi" are conjoined upon "atuhajjunni," so that it is a report; or upon the clause "wa-qad hadani," so that it is an emphasis of the denial. Its emphasizing of the denial is more apparent than in "wa-qad hadani," because his not fearing their gods has manifest evidences. So his people either know this or are treated as those who know, as previously mentioned in His words "wa-qad hadani." It indicates that they argued with him concerning oneness and threatened him with the assault of their gods and their touching him with harm, since there is no connection between denying their argument with him and negating his fear of their gods, nor between God's guidance of him and negating his fear of their gods; so it is determined that they threatened him with the cunning of their gods. A parallel to this is what God related about the people of Hud: ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54].

In His words "ma tushrikuna bihi," "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), referring to what their gods were which they made partners with God in divinity.

The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to the name of God, so that the "ba'" is for transitivity of the verb "tushrikun," or it may refer to "ma" as the relative pronoun, so that the "ba'" is causal, i.e., the idols by means of which you associated partners.

His words "illa an yashaa rabbi shay'an" are an exception from what precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyya made it a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati') in the sense of "but." This is the apparent meaning of al-Tabari's speech, and it is the more apparent, for when he negated that he feared harm from their gods, and this could lead the hearers to suppose that he feared nothing, the statement was corrected by what the disconnected exception indicates: "but I fear the will of my Lord regarding some thing of what I fear; so that is what I fear." In this correction there is an added sting for his people, since he did not fear their gods while he feared his Lord, who deserves to be feared, if his people do not acknowledge a lord other than their gods, according to one of the two possibilities mentioned earlier.

Al-Zamakhshari and his followers made the exception connected and emptied (mufrigh), from an omitted antecedent indicated by the context. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "of times," meaning: "I do not fear what you associate with Him ever, because the negated present verb refers to the future in the sense of all tenses, since it is like the negated indefinite noun; that is, except at the time of my Lord's will for some thing I fear from your partners," meaning that my Lord empowers some of them over me, and that is from my Lord's power through them, not from their power over me. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the antecedent be general states, i.e., "except in the state of my Lord's will for some thing I fear among them."

The clause "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge" is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because it may occur to their minds: how does your Lord will something you fear, when you claim that you stand by His good pleasure and support His religion? So this is nothing but doubt about your affair. Therefore it is separated: that is, I am not secure from God's will to inflict harm upon me, even though I am His servant and the supporter of His religion, because He knows best the wisdom of inflicting harm or benefit upon whomever He wills of His servants. This is a station of courtesy with God, the Exalted: ﴿None feels safe from the plan of God except the losing people﴾ [al-A'raf: 99].

The clause "Will you not then take heed?" is conjoined upon the clause "Do you argue with me concerning God, when He has guided me."

The interrogative hamza is placed before the conjunctive fa'.

The interrogation is a denial of their failure to take heed, despite the clear evidences for taking heed. What is meant by taking heed is regarding the attributes of their gods that contradict the station of divinity, and regarding the attributes of the true God which His creation indicates.

[p. 330]

﴿How should I fear what you associate [with Allah], when you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾

The clause "How should I fear" is conjoined (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction) to the clause "and I do not fear what you associate with Him" [6:80], in order to show them that his not fearing their gods is less surprising than their not fearing Allah, the Exalted. This indicates that his people knew Allah, and that they had associated others with Him in divinity. For this reason he argued against them by [pointing to] their association of others with their Lord, whom they acknowledged, without Allah having sent down to them any authority for that.

"Kayfa" (how) is an interrogative of denial (istifhām inkārī, a question expressing rejection), because they had urged him to fear the might of the gods. He rejected this from them and turned the argument against them. So he denied that they did not fear Allah when they associated others with Him without any proof that He had established for them. Thus "kayfa" conveys denial regarding both matters.

They said: In the words "and you do not fear that you have associated," the waw may be conjunctive, so that it is conjoined to the clause "How should I fear what you associate." Then both clauses fall under the denial: his fearing their gods is denounced, and their not fearing Allah is denounced.

The waw may also be circumstantial (li-l-ḥāl, indicating a state), in which case the locus of denial is their urging him to fear their gods while they were turning away from fearing the One whose authority is greater and whose seizure is more severe. Then "kayfa" together with denial conveys the sense of wonder (taʿjīb), in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people while you forget yourselves?﴾ [2:44]. This does not imply that their frightening him with their idols is denounced only in the state of their turning away from fearing Allah, because the intention in this reading is the denial of foolishness and the comparison of one state with another, not the explanation of what is denounced and what is not, as indicated by His saying at its end: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security﴾. This reading is more eloquent.

"Mā ashraktum" is a relative clause (mawṣūl), and its returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "what you associated with [Him]." It is omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿and I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾ [6:80]. The relative clause is in the position of the object of "[with] Him" for "mā ashraktum."

[p. 331]

In His saying "that you have associated," the particle "min" (from), which is connected to "takhāfūna" (you fear), is omitted, because of the regular omission of the preposition before "an" (that). The sense is "from your association [of others with Him]." He did not say "you do not fear Allah," because the people knew Allah and feared Him, but they did not fear associating [others] with Him. The phrase ﴿that for which He has not sent down to you any authority﴾ is a relative clause together with its complement, functioning as the object of "that you have associated."

The meaning of ﴿He has not sent down to you [any authority for it]﴾ is: He did not inform you of the divinity of the idols which you worship, nor command you to worship them, with an information which you know to be from Him. Therefore he used the metaphor of "sending down" (tanzīl) for that information, likening the greatness of its status to elevation, and its reaching those who are below the one informed, to the descent of a high thing to what is lower than it.

"Sulṭān" (authority) means proof (ḥujjah), because it exerts control (tatasallaṭu) over the very person who disputes, i.e., no information from Him came to you that you could make a proof for the validity of your worship of idols.

The fāʾ (so) in His saying ﴿So which of the two parties﴾ is a consequence (tafrīʿ) of the denial, and the wonder is a consequence of both of them, in the form of an interrogation that compels the acknowledgment that they are more deserving of fear of Allah than Ibrahim is of their gods. The interrogation with "ayyu" (which) is for affirmation (taqrīr, establishing a point by question), that his party alone is more deserving of security.

"Farīq" (party) means a large group of people distinguished from others by something that unites them, such as lineage, place, or something else. It is derived from "farraqa," meaning he distinguished. "Firqah" is smaller than "farīq." By "the two parties" here he meant his people and himself, and he applied the term "farīq" to himself by way of predominance (taghlīb). Or he meant himself and those who followed him, if he had followers at that time, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾ [29:26]. Or he meant those who would later exist among the followers of his religion, as is suited by His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [6:82].

The definite article in "al-amn" (security) is for the genus, and it is the opposite of fear. The clause "if you know" is a new independent sentence (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī), and the answer of its condition is omitted, indicated by the interrogation, its estimated form being: "then answer me." In this there is urging towards an answer.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 82:

﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing—those are the ones who will have security, and they are the ones guided.﴾

This sentence is part of the report of Ibrahim's speech, according to the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). It is then an answer from him to his own question: "So which of the two groups is more deserving of security?" He took on answering his own question himself and did not wait for their answer, because the answer is one that the one being questioned can only give in the same way, and this is a rebuke to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is like the scholar who asks and answers himself, i.e., by saying (fa-in qulta qultu, "if you say, I say"). Its parallels have already occurred in this surah.

It was also said: this is not part of the report of Ibrahim's speech, and Ibrahim's speech ended at his words "if you know." Rather, it is a new statement from God Most High to begin a ruling, so the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i), confirming the words of Ibrahim.

It was also said: it is a report of a speech that came from the people of Ibrahim in answer to Ibrahim's question "So which of the two groups is more deserving of security?" This is not valid, because the proper form in that case would be "Those who believe said..." etc., and because if it were the words of his people, their misguidance and obstinacy would not have continued to the point that they threw Ibrahim into the fire.

The object of the verb "they believed" (amanu) is omitted because it is evident from the preceding speech. The estimated phrase is: "those who believed in God."

The literal meaning of "yalbisu" (do not mix) is "to mix," and here it is a metaphor for doing two similar things at the same time. It is likened to the mixing of physical bodies, as in His words: "and do not mix the truth with falsehood."

Dhulm (wrongdoing) is transgression against the right of one who has a right, and what is meant by it here is associating others with God in belief in divinity and in worship. God Most High said: "Indeed, association (shirk) is a tremendous wrong," because it is the greatest transgression, since it is a transgression against the absolute, supreme One who deserves it, for it is His right to be singled out for worship in belief, action and speech, since that is His right over His creatures. Thus in the hadith: "The right of the servants over God is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him." It has been reported that the interpretation of wrongdoing in this verse is association. In the authentic hadith, on the authority of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: when the verse "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing—those are the ones who will have security, and they are the ones guided" was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Muslims and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "It is not as you think; rather it is as Luqman said to his son: 'Indeed, association is a tremendous wrong.'" End of quotation. This is because association combines acknowledging God's divinity with acknowledging the lordship of another as well. Since acknowledging another is a wrong, their belief in God was mixed with a wrong, which is their belief in other than Him. Interpreting it in this sense is the one that suits the metaphor of mixing for this meaning, because belief in God and associating another with Him in that are both of one kind, which is belief in lordship, so they are similar. This is the more evident aspect of the resemblance, since it is the nature of similar bodies that their mixing is more intense, for similarity is the strongest state of comparison according to the people of rhetoric (ahl al-bayan). The meaning: those who believed in God and did not associate anything else with Him in worship.

Al-Zamakhshari took wrongdoing to include acts of disobedience, because disobedience is a wrong to oneself, as in God Most High's words: "So do not wrong yourselves therein" [al-Tawba: 36]. He interpreted the verse according to the principles of the Mu'tazila, because the disobedient person is not secure from eternal abiding in the Fire, so he is equal to the disbeliever in that according to them. Moreover, he made His words "Those who believe and do not mix" to the end part of Ibrahim's speech. If it is reported as Ibrahim's speech, it is not valid to interpret wrongdoing in it as disobedience, since Ibrahim at that time was calling only to monotheism and had not yet received a law (shari'a). And if it is not reported from his speech, it is not appropriate to interpret it there as disobedience, because the placement of this after Ibrahim's speech is intended to confirm and clarify his words. Therefore the truth is that the verse does not need interpretation according to their principles, in view of what we have mentioned.

The demonstrative in His words "those" (ulaika, "﴿أُولَئِكَ لَهُمُ الأمْنُ﴾") serves to draw attention to the fact that the subject is worthy of the predicate because of the qualities of the subject mentioned before. This is like His words: "Those are upon guidance from their Lord."

As for His words "they will have security" (lahumu al-amn), the lam indicates that security is specific to them and established for them, and this is more emphatic than saying "they are secure." What is meant by security is security from the punishment of this world by annihilation and the like, and from what the disbelieving nations were punished with, and from the punishment of the Hereafter, since at that time nothing was required of them except monotheism.

The definite article in "al-amn" is the definition of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), meaning the security mentioned earlier, because it is one single genus. It is not the definition of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), so that the saying of the grammarians would apply: that when a definite noun is repeated as a definite noun, the second is the same as the first; since nothing other than that is admissible here.

His words "and they are the ones guided" (wa hum muhtadun) are conjoined to "they will have security" (lahum al-amn) by coordination of a part of a sentence to a sentence that has the status of a single noun. So "muhtadun" is a second predicate of the demonstrative noun, coordinated to it with "wa" according to one of the two methods of successive predicates.

The pronoun here is a separator (damir al-fasl) to convey the restriction (qasr) of the predicate to the subject, i.e., guidance is restricted to those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing, not to others; that is, others are not guided. This follows the pattern of His words: "And those are the successful" and His words: "Do they not know that God is He who accepts repentance from His servants?" [al-Tawba: 104]. In this there is an indication that those spoken of, having rejected association, have indeed been guided.

It is also permissible that His words "and they are guided" be a nominal clause, with the plural pronoun as the subject and "muhtadun" as its predicate, the clause being conjoined to the clause "those will have security," so that it is a second predicate of the relative noun. The mention of the plural pronoun is for the sake of a good conjunction, since the conjoined-to clause is a nominal sentence, so it was not good to join to it a singular word in the sense of a verb, for one should not say "those have security and are guided" in that form; so the conjoined element takes the form of a clause. In that case the pronoun does not convey restriction, since it was not brought for separation. This construction is like His words: "To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable" [al-Taghabun: 1], and His words: "To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things capable" [al-Hadid: 2], on the view that "wa Huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir" is conjoined to "lahu mulku as-samawati wa al-ard," with what lies between them being a circumstantial clause. This is among the embellishments of connection (muhassinat al-wasl), as is known in rhetoric, and it is among the marvels of Arabic composition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 83:

﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise, Knowing.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause "and his people argued with him." "That" (tilka) is a demonstrative referring to everything Abraham said in disputing with his people. The feminine demonstrative was used because the thing pointed to is an argument (ḥujja), so it is described with ḥujja. Since the thing pointed to is not a perceptible object, it is necessary to consider the demonstrative as referring only to the wording of the statement, as in His saying, ﴿That were the Messengers; some of them We preferred over others﴾ [al-Baqara: 253].

The attribution of "argument" to the Divine Name (Allah) serves to draw attention to its importance and soundness. "We gave it" (ātaynāhā) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the demonstrative, or relative to the predicate.

The essential meaning of ītāʾ (giving) is bestowal; its proper usage is to take a direct object and to occur by handing one thing to another hand. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And gave wealth, despite love for it, to relatives﴾ [al-Baqara: 177]. For this reason it is said: "the upper hand is the giving hand and the lower hand is the receiving hand." It is commonly used figuratively for teaching sciences, conveying good manners, and empowering or appointing someone without a handing of the hand, whether the things granted are substances or meanings. One says: God gave him wealth (ātāhu Allāh mālan); the caliph gave him a command (ātāhu al-khalīfa imāra); God gave him kingship (ātāhu Allāh al-mulk); and "We gave him wisdom" (ātaynāhu al-ḥikma). Thus the giving of the argument is its inspiration to him and the placing in his soul of what expresses it, and this is a favour from God to Abraham, in that He granted him victory over his opponents.

"ʿAlā" (upon) is for figurative elevation, which is the comparison of the victor to one who is above and empowered over the vanquished. It is connected to "our argument," contrary to those who prohibited this. One says: "This is an argument against you (ḥujja ʿalayka) and a witness against you (shāhid ʿalayka)," meaning: that was Our argument against his people, by which We overwhelmed them through Abraham. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "We gave it," because the giving includes the meaning of granting victory.

The clause ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of raising in "We gave it," or a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa) explaining that this kind of giving is a preference for the one given and an honouring of him.

The raising of degrees is a figurative depiction of the elevation of rank. The state of one who is preferred over others is likened to the state of one who climbs a ladder: whenever he rises from one rung to another, there is elevation in every rung. Every part of this figure is suitable for considering the distribution of the comparison: preference resembles raising, and the varying excellences resemble the rungs. The aspect of resemblance is the rarity of attaining this for most people.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar read "darajāt" as a genitive construction with "man" (i.e., "darajāti man"). The attribution of the rungs to the relative pronoun is considered in terms of the connection of the one who ascends to them, since they are attributed to him only when he is ascending upon them.

The use of the plural form "darajāt" is in view of the suitability of "man nashāʾ" for many individuals varying in elevation. The verb of willing indicates that the distinction among them is by the abundance of causes of preference; or the plural is considered in view of the fact that a single preferred person's state varies as the causes of his excellence increase. The rest read "darajātin" with tanwīn, so it is a specifying accusative (tamyīz) for the relation of raising, since raising is figurative for preference, and "darajāt" is figurative for varying excellences.

His saying "man nashāʾ" indicates that this honouring does not belong to everyone, for if it were attained by all people, there would be neither raising nor preference.

The clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), because His saying "We raise by degrees whom We will" raises a question: why are some people raised above others? It is answered that God knows who deserves that and the measure of his deserving, and He creates that according to the scope of His knowledge. Thus "ḥakīm" means "muḥkim," that is, perfecting in creation and in decree.

"Ḥakīm" is placed before "ʿalīm" because this preference manifests wisdom; then "ʿalīm" follows it to indicate that this perfection proceeds in accordance with knowledge.

[p. 337]

The clause ﴿وَوَهَبْنا لَهُ إسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ﴾ ("And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob") is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the preceding clause "ātaynāhā" (We gave it), because its content is honour and distinction. The position of this clause, although it is conjoined, is that of a concluding statement (tadhyīl, a closing summation) for the preceding clauses. Its purpose is to refute polytheism and establish proofs against its corruption, and to show that all the righteous were opposed to it.

Al-wahb and al-hibah mean giving something without compensation. Here it is used metaphorically for bounty and facilitation.

The meaning of "the gift of Jacob to Abraham" is that a son was born to Abraham's son Isaac during Abraham's lifetime, and he grew up and married during his lifetime, and so he was a source of comfort to Abraham (qurrat ʿayn).

The biography of Abraham, peace be upon him, has already been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَإِذِ ابْتَلى إبْراهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِماتٍ﴾ ("And when his Lord tested Abraham with words"). The biographies of Isaac and Jacob have been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَوَصّى بِها إبْراهِيمُ بَنِيهِ ويَعْقُوبُ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob") [al-Baqarah: 132], and His words ﴿وإلَهَ آبائِكَ إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ﴾ ("the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac") [al-Baqarah: 133]. All of this is in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words "﴿كُلًّا هَدَيْنا﴾" ("We guided each one") are an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical insertion). The meaning is: We guided all of these, that is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The genitive complement was omitted because it is evident, and tanwīn (nunation) was substituted for it in kullan, a tanwīn of compensation for the omitted genitive complement, as is the preferred view.

The benefit of mentioning their guidance is to honour Isaac and Jacob, and to show that they were prophets who attained God's guidance just as Abraham did. It also includes a refutation of polytheism, a rebuke to Quraysh and the polytheist Arabs, and a condemnation of them by establishing that the famous righteous people held views opposed to their beliefs, as will be stated explicitly in His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ هُدى اللَّهِ يَهْدِي بِهِ مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ ولَوْ أشْرَكُوا لَحَبِطَ عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("That is the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been worthless") [al-Anʿām: 88].

The clause ﴿ونُوحًا هَدَيْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ("And Noah, We guided before") is conjoined to the interjected clause, meaning: and We guided Noah before them. This is a digression (istiṭrād) by mentioning some of those upon whom God bestowed guidance, and an indication that guidance is the origin, and among the greatest guidance is monotheism, as you know.

[p. 338]

Noah is in the accusative as a direct object placed before "hadaynā" (We guided) for emphasis. "Min qablu" (before) is a circumstantial adjunct (ḥāl) of "Nūḥan." The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is to draw attention to the fact that guidance is rooted in the origins of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Qablu is built on a ḍamma, according to what is well known regarding qablu and its sisters, when the genitive complement that qablu is attached to is omitted, its meaning is intended but not its wording.

The biography of Noah has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى آدَمَ ونُوحًا﴾ ("Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah") [Āl ʿImrān: 33], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

His words "min dhurriyyatihi" (from his descendants) are a circumstantial adjunct of "Dāwūd." Dāwūd is the omitted direct object of "hadaynā." The benefit of this circumstance is to honour these enumerated persons with the nobility of their origin and the origin of their merit, and to honour Abraham or Noah with the virtues of his descendants.

The pronoun attached to it refers to Noah, not to Abraham, because Noah is the nearest mentioned, and because Lot is among the descendants of Noah and not among the descendants of Abraham, as is stated in the Torah. It is possible that Lot was treated as a descendant of Abraham because of his close connection to him. It is also possible that the mention of his name after the list of those who are descendants of Abraham ends is in the accusative for praise, by implying a verb, not as a conjunction.

Some of the biography of Dāwūd has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وقَتَلَ داوُدُ جالُوتَ﴾ ("And David killed Goliath") in Surat al-Baqarah. We complete it here: he is Dāwūd son of Jesse (Yissi), from the tribe of Judah among the Children of Israel. He was born in the village of Bethlehem around 1085 BCE, and died in Jerusalem around 1015 BCE. In his youth he was a shepherd of his father's sheep, and he had knowledge of melody, playing instruments, and slinging with a sling. God revealed to Samuel (Shamwīl), the prophet of the Children of Israel, to bless Dāwūd son of Jesse and anoint him with holy oil so that he would be king over the Children of Israel, according to the traditions of the Children of Israel, announcing that he would become king over Israel after the death of Saul (Shāʾūl), whom God was angry with. When Samuel anointed him in the village of Bethlehem without anyone knowing, [p. 339] it occurred to Saul, who was ill, to take someone who would play the lute for him when the illness overcame him. It happened that they chose Dāwūd for him, so he admitted him among his courtiers to hear his melodies. When Saul's army fought the Canaanites, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, victory went to the Israelites because of Dāwūd, when he struck the Philistine champion Goliath (Jālūt) with his sling between his eyes, felled him, and cut off his head. For this reason Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage. Then Saul turned against Dāwūd, and Dāwūd went out to the land of the Philistines and gathered a group under his leadership. When Saul was killed in the year 1055, a group of the Israelite army in Palestine pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He made Hebron his seat of government. After seven years, the king of Israel who succeeded Saul was killed, and all the Israelites pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He returned to Jerusalem, God gave him prophethood, and commanded him to write the Psalms (al-Zabūr), called by the Jews "al-Mazāmīr."

Sulaymān's biography has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿واتَّبَعُوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطِينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ ("And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon") [al-Baqarah: 102], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ayyūb (Job) is a prophet whose prophethood the Qur'an affirmed. He has a detailed story in the book known as the Book of Job, among the books of the Jews. Some historians think that Job was a descendant of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. Others thought he was a grandson of Esau son of Isaac son of Abraham. In his book, it is stated that Job lived in the land of Uz, which is the land of Hauran in Syria, and it is the dwelling place of the sons of Uz son of Aram son of Shem son of Noah, and they are the origin of ʿĀd, and it was adjacent to the borders of the land of the Chaldeans. The names of places are mentioned in the Book of Job. Some scholars think he was of Arab origin and was from Uz, as indicated by the absence of any mention of his lineage in his book, and by restricting it to saying he was in the land of Uz, who are of the original Arabs (al-ʿArab al-ʿĀribah). They claimed that his speech recorded in his book was in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, translated it into Hebrew. Some think that the speech attributed to him was poetry which Moses translated in his book, and that it was the first poetry known in the original Arabic language. Others say it was the first poetry known to history, because his speech and the speech of his three companions who consoled him for his calamities was necessarily in a poetic style.

Yūsuf (Joseph) is the son of Jacob, and the detailed biography will come in Surat Yūsuf.

Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron) and Zakariyyā (Zechariah) have had their biographies covered in Surat al-Baqarah. The biography of ʿĪsā (Jesus) has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Āl ʿImrān. Yaḥyā (John) has had his biography covered in Āl ʿImrān.

His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ ("And thus We reward the good-doers") are an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses, and the "wa" is for a circumstantial sense, meaning: and thus the gift which We gave to Abraham and the guidance which We gave to his descendants, We reward the good-doers like it. Or: and thus the guidance which We gave the descendants of Noah, We reward the good-doers like Noah. It is therefore known that Noah or Abraham were among the good-doers by way of metonymy (kināyah). The good-doing of Noah is derived from this interjected clause, and the good-doing of Abraham is derived from what God related about him: his calling his people and his exerting every effort to turn them away from their error.

It is also possible that the reference here is to the guidance derived from the first and second "hadaynā," meaning: and thus with this great guidance We reward the good-doers, meaning with its like. The "good-doers" then refers to those guided ones among the descendants of Noah or the descendants of Abraham. The meaning is that they did good, and the reward for their good was that We made them prophets.

As for Ilyās (Elijah), he is known in the books of the Israelites as Elijah (Eliya), and in the lands of the Arabs he is called Ilyās or Mār Ilyās, and he is Elijah the Tishbite. The commentators mention that he was Ilyās son of Phinehas son of Eleazar, or son of Aaron, brother of Moses, so he would be from the tribe of Levi. He existed in the time of King Ahab (Ākhāb), king of Israel, around the year 918 BCE. He was an Israelite from the inhabitants of Gilead (Jilʿād), with a kasra on the jīm and sukūn on the lām, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, and Baalbek is from it. Ilyās was from the tribe of Reuben or from the tribe of Gad, and these two tribes were the inhabitants of the region of Gilead. Elijah is called "al-Tishbī" in the books of the Jews. God sent him to the Children of Israel when they worshipped idols in the time of King Ahab, and they worshipped Baal, the idol of the Canaanites. Elijah admonished them, and there are accounts of his dealings with them. God commanded him to appoint Elisha (al-Yasaʿ) as his successor in prophethood. Then God raised Elijah to heaven in a whirlwind, and no trace of him was seen afterwards. Elisha succeeded him in prophethood during the reign of King Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel.

His words ﴿كُلٌّ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ("each of them among the righteous") are an interjected clause. The tanwīn in "kullun" is a compensation for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all of these enumerated persons. It includes all those mentioned, Isaac and whoever came after him.

As for Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), his biography has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Yasaʿ (Elisha): his name in Hebrew is Elisha (ʾElīshaʿ), with a broken hamza with a kasra, followed by a lām with a yāʾ after it, then a shīn with a dot, then an ʿayn. Its Arabicised form is al-Yasaʿ, with a hamzat al-waṣl and a lām with a sukūn at its beginning, followed by a yāʾ with a fatḥa, in the reading of the majority.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read "al-Laysaʿ" with a hamzat al-waṣl, a fatḥa on the lām, shaddah, followed by a yāʾ with sukūn, on the pattern of ḍaygham. So these are two dialectal forms of it. He was son of Shafāṭ from the people of Abel-Meholah (Ābul Maḥūlah). He was a farmer whom God chose for prophethood through the messenger Elijah during the time of Ahab, and he accompanied Elijah. When Elijah was raised, he kept to the way of Elijah, and miracles appeared to him for the Children of Israel in Jericho (Arīḥā) and elsewhere. He died during the reign of King Joash (Yūʾāsh), king of Israel, and his death was in the year 840 BCE, and he was buried in Samaria (al-Sāmirah). The alif and lām in "al-Yasaʿ" are part of the original word, but the hamza was treated like a hamzat al-waṣl for lightness, so it came to resemble a name into which the lām is added to indicate its origin, like al-ʿAbbās, while it is not one of them.

[p. 343]

As for Yunus, he is the son of Matta, and his name in Hebrew is (Yunan ibn Amittai). He was from the tribe of (Zabulon). In Arabic, his nun may be vocalized with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. He was born in the town of (Gath-hepher) in Palestine. God sent him to the people of (Nineveh) in the lands of Assyria. Its people at that time were a mixture of Assyrians and Jews who were captives of the Assyrians. When he called them to faith and they refused, he threatened them with punishment. The punishment was delayed, so he left in anger and went to (Jaffa). There he boarded a ship of the Phoenicians to go to (Tarshish), a city west of Palestine, west of Tyre, on the sea. It may be that it is one of the harbors of the sea-facing side of Egypt, or one of the harbors of Barqa, because the Jewish books describe that gold, silver, apes, and peacocks were brought to Solomon from Tarshish. Thus it is determined that Tarshish had trade with Abyssinia or the Sudan, and that these products were exported from it. It has been said that it is Tartusha, one of the harbors of al-Andalus. It has also been said that it is Carthage, the port of Ifriqiya near Tunis. It has been said in our histories that the name of Tunis before the Islamic conquest was Tarshish. This is plausible, because its trade with the Sudan may be closer. The sea then rose against the ship, it became heavy, and its sinking was feared. So they cast lots, and Yunus was among those who lost in the drawing. He was thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him. He called out from its belly: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]. God answered him, and the fish cast him onto the shore. God sent him a second time to the people of Nineveh, and they believed; they numbered more than one hundred thousand. His period was at the beginning of the eighth century BC. We have not established the date of his death. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in al-Ahkam, in the commentary on Surat al-Saffat, that his grave is in the village of Jaljun between Jerusalem and the town of al-Khalil, and that he visited it during his journey. The accounts of Yunus will come in Surat Yunus, Surat al-Anbiya, and Surat al-Saffat.

As for Lut, he is the son of Haran ibn Terah, so he is the nephew of Ibrahim. He was born in (Ur of the Chaldeans). His father died before Terah, so Terah took Lut into his care. When Terah died, Lut was living with Ibrahim in the land of Haran (Hauran), after Terah, the father of Ibrahim, had left Ur of the Chaldeans, both heading for the land of Canaan. Ibrahim migrated with Lut to Egypt because of a famine that struck the lands of Canaan. Then they returned to the lands of Canaan. Ibrahim and Lut separated because of a dispute that arose between their herdsmen. Lut moved to (Sodom), which is east of the Jordan, until he was inspired to leave it when God decreed its destruction as a punishment for its people. He went out to (Zoar) with his daughter and his offspring there, who are (the Moabites) and (the children of Ammon).

His saying ﴿And We preferred each over the worlds﴾ is a parenthetical sentence, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis. The tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement that was omitted, meaning: each of those mentioned, from Isaac up to here. (Kull) requires that what it is attached to be encompassing. The rule of encompassment is that the judgment applies to each individual one by one, not to the group as a whole. The intended meaning is that each one of them is preferred over the worlds of people of his own age, except for one who was more excellent than him or equal to him. So the lam in (al-'alamin) is the lam of conventional comprehensiveness. Lut lived in the time of Ibrahim, and Ibrahim was more excellent than him. Among others there were people who lived in one era, and the preference of one of them over another is not known. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: it is possible to say that the intended meaning is that each of the prophets is preferred over every other of the worlds. Then the discussion after this concerns which of the prophets is more excellent than the other; that is a discussion on another topic with no connection to the first. End of quotation. This is not correct, because the requirement of the rule of encompassment is judgment on each individual one by one.

A significant issue of the principles of religion (usul al-din) is connected to this verse: the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, and what follows from establishing that regarding faith and the rights of prophethood. The exegetes have neglected to mention it, though it should have been addressed, because it branches into issues that students of the Islamic sciences need to know, and the most fitting place to mention it is this verse and what has the same meaning as some of it. As for the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, that is because God, the Exalted, said, after counting their names, that these are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and prophethood. So the prophethood of them is an established matter, because the demonstrative (ulaika, "those") is close to explicit text in referring to all the named persons before it, together with what supports and completes it of explicit text on the prophethood of some of them in verses similar to this verse, such as the verse of Surat al-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾ [al-Nisa: 163] and the verses following it, and such as the verses of Surat Maryam: ﴿And mention in the Book Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 41] and the verses following it.

Prophethood carries many rulings related to the one who possesses it and to how Muslims treat the one who is characterized by it. Among them: the meaning of (nabi, prophet) and (rasul, messenger); the meaning of the miracle (mu'jiza), which is the proof of the realization of prophethood or messengership for the one who brings it; and what follows from that of the obligation to believe in what he conveys from God, the Exalted, of law and ethics. Many issues of this are expounded in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam), so refer to it. What concerns us of this in this commentary is what His saying, the Exalted, at its end hints at: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Whoever knows these verses in this surah and knows their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to believe in the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in them.

Our scholars have mentioned that believing that God sent messengers and appointed prophets to guide people is obligatory in general, meaning belief in the sending of unspecified individuals, or in the prophethood of unspecified individuals, without specifying any particular person by name or by anything else that distinguishes him from others, except Muhammad (ﷺ). Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risala: The one who sends (a attribute of God, the Exalted) the messengers to them to establish the proof against them. So the sending of messengers is permissible with regard to God and not obligatory, and it occurs in general, without specifying a particular person. The author of al-Maqasid mentioned that the sending of messengers is needed, and it is a kindness from God to His creation, and it is not obligatory upon Him. The Mu'tazilites and a group of theologians (i.e., from the People of the Sunna) from beyond the river (Transoxiana) said that the sending of messengers is obligatory upon God, the Exalted.

None of our imams mentioned the obligation of believing in a particular prophet other than Muhammad (ﷺ) as a messenger to all creation. Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said: Then He sealed - meaning God - the messengership, the warning, and the prophethood with Muhammad, His prophet (ﷺ), etc., because the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab about Jibril's asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith, that he said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers," etc. He did not specify particular messengers. And in answer to his question about Islam, he said: "Islam is that you testify that there is no deity but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

Whoever knows these verses and understands their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to hold the belief in the prophethood of those mentioned in them. Perhaps many do not recite them, and many of those who recite them do not understand their implications correctly. They are not required to seek out understanding of them and belief in what they indicate, since that is not among the principles of faith and Islam, but it belongs to the deeper understanding of religion (tafaqquh fi al-din).

Al-Qadi Iyad said in the seventh section of the chapters of the third chapter of the fourth part of his book al-Shifa: All of this (i.e., what he mentioned of the imposition of disbelief or of a crime that requires punishment on whoever speaks about them in a way that contradicts what is due to them) concerning those about whom something is said, i.e., the prophets or the angels, by what we have stated regarding the totality of the angels and prophets, i.e., regarding their collectivity and not regarding each one of them, as al-Khafaji said. By "all" he means every single individual of those whose being among them we have verified, either by explicit mention in His Book, or by verifying their knowledge through mass-transmitted report (mutawatir), definite consensus (ijma'), and a famous report agreed upon. The "waw" in this division means "or." As for the one whose announcement of his identity has not been established and on whom there is no consensus that he is among the prophets, such as al-Khidr, Luqman, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, and Khalid ibn Sinan, who is mentioned as the prophet of the people of al-Rass, then the ruling regarding the one who reviles them or disbelieves in them is not the same as the ruling regarding what we have mentioned before. End of quotation.

When you know this, you know that what occurred in three verses composed by someone, which Shaykh Ibrahim al-Bayjuri mentioned in the section on faith in his commentary on Jawhara al-Tawhid:

It is a binding duty on everyone who is under obligation to know the prophets in detail, who are known.
Among them, for our proof, are eight, after ten; and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and with the Chosen One they are sealed.

This does not hold except with forced interpretation, because the knowledge of that being "binding" (hatm) according to its technical sense implies that it is obligatory, and no one holds this. If he meant by "binding" a matter that should not be neglected, then it is emphatic in relation to his saying "on everyone who is under obligation." So if he had replaced it with "everyone who is under instruction," it would be better.

Perhaps he meant by "binding" that it is necessarily incumbent upon whoever knows this not to deny that these are prophets by specific identification. But he intended a distinction between the obligation to know something and the prohibition of denying it after it has become known.

As for the messengership of Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb, their mention has been repeated in many verses.

As for knowing the prophethood of Dhu al-Kifl, there is room for consideration, since in Surat al-Anbiya he is described only as one of the patient and the righteous. The exegetes differed concerning several of the prophets, and it is attributed to the majority that he was a prophet. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid reported that Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. The mention of this will come in Surat al-Anbiya.

As for Adam, he was a prophet from the time he was in the Garden, for God spoke to him more than once. He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, relented toward him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. So he was sent down to the earth honored with the attribute of prophethood. The story of the two sons of Adam in Surat al-Ma'ida indicates that Adam conveyed a law to his sons, according to His saying, the Exalted, in it: ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous. If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I will not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin and be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 27].

So what we rely upon is that whoever denies the prophethood of a particular person named in the Qur'an among the prophets, in Surat al-Nisa, Surat Hud, Surat al-An'am, and Surat Maryam, and the one denying knows for certain the verse in which he is described as a prophet, and he has been informed of the evidence for the validity of what he denies and has been brought back to it, but he insists on denying it, then that denial is disbelief, because he denied something known by necessity after having been alerted to it, so that he cannot excuse himself by ignorance or by an acceptable interpretation.

[p. 347]

Know that I sought to uncover the veil over the reason for limiting the mention of these prophets to the prophets from among the offspring of Abraham or the offspring of Noah, on the two readings concerning the referent of the pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyatihi). It did not become clear to me. I also sought the reason for this particular order of their names and for the linking of some of these names to others by conjunction, but it did not appear to me. My strongest assumption is that among these aspects is that these men were known to the People of the Book and to the polytheists who borrowed their knowledge of the prophets from the People of the Book. Also, the reason for their order may arise from beginning with the mention that Isaac and Jacob were a gift to Abraham, and they were a father and his son. So the transition from one to another arose through a connection that made the transition appropriate. Also, the distribution of their names over three verse-endings (fawasil, sing. fasilah, the rhyming unit at the end of a verse) does not lack a connection that gathers the owners of those names in the single verse-ending that includes all of them. It is possible that the lightness of these names when Arabicized, in letters and in meter, had an effect in their being singled out for mention over other names, such as Shm'un (Simeon), Shmwyl (Samuel), Hizqyal (Ezekiel) and Nahmiya (Nehemiah). Also, those counted in these three verses were distributed among virtues. Among them are messengers, prophets, kings, and people of noble and honorable character: patience, struggle against the self, struggle in the way of God, and perseverance
[p. 348]
in conveying monotheism (tawhid), the law (shari'ah), and noble character. This is what His saying at the end of the verses indicates: "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood. And among them are the two roots of the Arab and Israelite nations."

When He mentioned Isaac and Jacob, He followed their mention with the mention of two prophets from the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, who are a father and his son among the prophets: David and Solomon. He began with them before the rest of the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, because they attained two great glories: the glory of the Hereafter through prophethood, and the glory of this world through kingship. Then He followed with the mention of "two prophets" who were alike in that harm befell both of them and that relief from their distress came through their patience: they are Job and Joseph. Then, with the mention of two brothers, messengers, Moses and Aaron. Moses suffered the like of what befell Joseph: plotting against him to kill him, his deliverance from that, and his being raised in the house of kingship. So these six were included in the first verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And thus do We reward the good-doers."

Then with the mention of two prophets, a father and his son: Zechariah and John (Yahya). It was appropriate that after them there be mentioned two messengers who had no offspring: Jesus ('Isa) and Elias (Ilyas). They are alike in that both were raised up to heaven. As for Jesus, his ascension is mentioned in the Qur'an. As for Elias, his ascension is mentioned in the books of the Israelites, and the commentators among the early generations did not mention it. It has been said that Elias is Idris, and on this basis his elevation is mentioned in His saying: "And mention in the Book Idris; indeed he was a truthful one and a prophet" [Maryam: 56], and "We raised him to a high station" in Surah Maryam. Jesus was mentioned first as a conjunction following John, because they were close, being cousins on the mother's side, and because Jesus was a messenger while Elias was a prophet who was not a messenger. These four were included in the second verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "All of them were of the righteous." He linked Elisha (al-Yasa') because he was the successor and disciple of Elias. He placed between Elias and Elisha the mention of Ishmael, a conclusion by mentioning the prophet to whom the lineage of the Arabs from the offspring of Abraham traces back. They were concluded with Jonah (Yunus) and Lot, because each of them was sent to a small nation. These four were included in the third verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And We preferred each over the worlds."
[p. 349]
His saying "and of their fathers" is conjoined to His saying "each." So the sense is: "And We guided some of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took "min" (of) as a noun meaning "some," that is: "And We guided some of their fathers," according to his method in His saying: "Of those who are Jews, they distort [words]" (al-Nisa': 46). Ibn 'Atiyyah and those who followed him supposed that the conjoined object is omitted, its estimate being: "And of their fathers, a great multitude, or many who were guided." Then "min" is partitive and linked to "We guided."

The dhurriyyat (offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, and it refers to those who descend from a human being: sons, the nearer ones, and their sons. So it includes the children of sons and the children of daughters. Its being in the plural is intended to show that guidance attached to the offspring of each of those mentioned who had offspring, to indicate that in the guidance of some of the offspring there is honor for the forefather. So each one of these is meant to have guidance occur in his offspring, even though their offspring trace back to a single forefather, Noah, peace be upon him. Then, if the guidance meant is the guidance similar to the guidance explicitly stated, which is the guidance of prophethood, then "fathers" includes figures like Adam and Idris, peace be upon them, for they are the fathers of Noah. "Offspring" includes the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Joshua (Yusha') and Daniel (Danyal). They are from the offspring of Noah and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The prophets from the sons of Ishmael, peace be upon him, include figures such as Hanzalah ibn Safwan and Khalid ibn Sinan, and Hud and Salih from the offspring of Noah, and Shu'ayb from the offspring of Abraham. "Brothers" includes the rest of the tribes, the brothers of Joseph.

If what is meant by guidance is what is more general than prophethood, it includes the righteous among the fathers, such as Abel (Habil) son of Adam. And "offspring" includes all the righteous of the nations, such as the People of the Cave, of whom He said: "And We increased them in guidance" (al-Kahf: 13). It also includes Saul (Talut), king of Israel, and Mudar and Rabi'ah, for it has been transmitted that they were both Muslims, narrated by al-Daylami from Ibn 'Abbas. It also includes the believer of the family of Pharaoh and the wife of Pharaoh. "Brothers" includes Haran son of Terah, brother of Abraham, who was the father of Lot, and Esau (Eisu), brother of Jacob, and others besides these whom God the Exalted knows.
[p. 350]
Al-ijtiba' (selection, ijtiba': choosing and preferring) is the act of choosing and selecting. They said it is derived from al-jabi, which means gathering, and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (collection of land tax). Also jaby al-ma' in the basin, from which the basin (al-jabiyah) is named. So the infixed form (ifti'al) in it is for emphasis, like al-idtirar (compulsion). The basis of the derivation is that gathering only happens for something desired, to obtain it because one needs it. The meaning is: God chose them and made them the place of His guidance, because He knows best where to place His message, His prophethood, and His guidance.

He conjoined His saying "and We guided them" to "We chose them" with a conjunction that emphasizes the affirmation of their guidance, out of concern for this guidance. So He explained that He guided them to a straight path (sirat mustaqim), that is, to that by which one attains what the people of perfection strive to attain. So He made the straight path an example for this, comparing the state of one who acts to attain the perfection he seeks to the state of one who walks upon a straight road that brings him to what he wants, proceeding without hesitation, confusion, or going astray. He mentioned from the words of the compound expression that indicates the state being compared only a part of it, which is "the straight path," because it indicates all the omitted words for brevity.

The straight path is monotheism (tawhid) and faith in what must be believed of the fundamental virtues in which the revealed laws (shara'i') agree. The purpose, along with praising them, is an allusion to the polytheists who opposed their creed, as indicated by His saying after that: "Those are the guided by God," up to His saying: "And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been void from them" (al-An'am: 88).

[p. 337]

The clause ﴿وَوَهَبْنا لَهُ إسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ﴾ ("And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob") is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the preceding clause "ātaynāhā" (We gave it), because its content is honour and distinction. The position of this clause, although it is conjoined, is that of a concluding statement (tadhyīl, a closing summation) for the preceding clauses. Its purpose is to refute polytheism and establish proofs against its corruption, and to show that all the righteous were opposed to it.

Al-wahb and al-hibah mean giving something without compensation. Here it is used metaphorically for bounty and facilitation.

The meaning of "the gift of Jacob to Abraham" is that a son was born to Abraham's son Isaac during Abraham's lifetime, and he grew up and married during his lifetime, and so he was a source of comfort to Abraham (qurrat ʿayn).

The biography of Abraham, peace be upon him, has already been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَإِذِ ابْتَلى إبْراهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِماتٍ﴾ ("And when his Lord tested Abraham with words"). The biographies of Isaac and Jacob have been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَوَصّى بِها إبْراهِيمُ بَنِيهِ ويَعْقُوبُ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob") [al-Baqarah: 132], and His words ﴿وإلَهَ آبائِكَ إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ﴾ ("the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac") [al-Baqarah: 133]. All of this is in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words "﴿كُلًّا هَدَيْنا﴾" ("We guided each one") are an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical insertion). The meaning is: We guided all of these, that is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The genitive complement was omitted because it is evident, and tanwīn (nunation) was substituted for it in kullan, a tanwīn of compensation for the omitted genitive complement, as is the preferred view.

The benefit of mentioning their guidance is to honour Isaac and Jacob, and to show that they were prophets who attained God's guidance just as Abraham did. It also includes a refutation of polytheism, a rebuke to Quraysh and the polytheist Arabs, and a condemnation of them by establishing that the famous righteous people held views opposed to their beliefs, as will be stated explicitly in His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ هُدى اللَّهِ يَهْدِي بِهِ مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ ولَوْ أشْرَكُوا لَحَبِطَ عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("That is the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been worthless") [al-Anʿām: 88].

The clause ﴿ونُوحًا هَدَيْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ("And Noah, We guided before") is conjoined to the interjected clause, meaning: and We guided Noah before them.
