This is a digression (istiṭrād) by mentioning some of those upon whom God bestowed guidance, and an indication that guidance is the origin, and among the greatest guidance is monotheism, as you know.

[p. 338]

Noah is in the accusative as a direct object placed before "hadaynā" (We guided) for emphasis. "Min qablu" (before) is a circumstantial adjunct (ḥāl) of "Nūḥan." The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is to draw attention to the fact that guidance is rooted in the origins of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Qablu is built on a ḍamma, according to what is well known regarding qablu and its sisters, when the genitive complement that qablu is attached to is omitted, its meaning is intended but not its wording.

The biography of Noah has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى آدَمَ ونُوحًا﴾ ("Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah") [Āl ʿImrān: 33], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

His words "min dhurriyyatihi" (from his descendants) are a circumstantial adjunct of "Dāwūd." Dāwūd is the omitted direct object of "hadaynā." The benefit of this circumstance is to honour these enumerated persons with the nobility of their origin and the origin of their merit, and to honour Abraham or Noah with the virtues of his descendants.

The pronoun attached to it refers to Noah, not to Abraham, because Noah is the nearest mentioned, and because Lot is among the descendants of Noah and not among the descendants of Abraham, as is stated in the Torah. It is possible that Lot was treated as a descendant of Abraham because of his close connection to him. It is also possible that the mention of his name after the list of those who are descendants of Abraham ends is in the accusative for praise, by implying a verb, not as a conjunction.

Some of the biography of Dāwūd has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وقَتَلَ داوُدُ جالُوتَ﴾ ("And David killed Goliath") in Surat al-Baqarah. We complete it here: he is Dāwūd son of Jesse (Yissi), from the tribe of Judah among the Children of Israel. He was born in the village of Bethlehem around 1085 BCE, and died in Jerusalem around 1015 BCE. In his youth he was a shepherd of his father's sheep, and he had knowledge of melody, playing instruments, and slinging with a sling. God revealed to Samuel (Shamwīl), the prophet of the Children of Israel, to bless Dāwūd son of Jesse and anoint him with holy oil so that he would be king over the Children of Israel, according to the traditions of the Children of Israel, announcing that he would become king over Israel after the death of Saul (Shāʾūl), whom God was angry with. When Samuel anointed him in the village of Bethlehem without anyone knowing, [p. 339] it occurred to Saul, who was ill, to take someone who would play the lute for him when the illness overcame him. It happened that they chose Dāwūd for him, so he admitted him among his courtiers to hear his melodies. When Saul's army fought the Canaanites, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, victory went to the Israelites because of Dāwūd, when he struck the Philistine champion Goliath (Jālūt) with his sling between his eyes, felled him, and cut off his head. For this reason Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage. Then Saul turned against Dāwūd, and Dāwūd went out to the land of the Philistines and gathered a group under his leadership. When Saul was killed in the year 1055, a group of the Israelite army in Palestine pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He made Hebron his seat of government. After seven years, the king of Israel who succeeded Saul was killed, and all the Israelites pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He returned to Jerusalem, God gave him prophethood, and commanded him to write the Psalms (al-Zabūr), called by the Jews "al-Mazāmīr."

Sulaymān's biography has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿واتَّبَعُوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطِينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ ("And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon") [al-Baqarah: 102], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ayyūb (Job) is a prophet whose prophethood the Qur'an affirmed. He has a detailed story in the book known as the Book of Job, among the books of the Jews. Some historians think that Job was a descendant of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. Others thought he was a grandson of Esau son of Isaac son of Abraham. In his book, it is stated that Job lived in the land of Uz, which is the land of Hauran in Syria, and it is the dwelling place of the sons of Uz son of Aram son of Shem son of Noah, and they are the origin of ʿĀd, and it was adjacent to the borders of the land of the Chaldeans. The names of places are mentioned in the Book of Job. Some scholars think he was of Arab origin and was from Uz, as indicated by the absence of any mention of his lineage in his book, and by restricting it to saying he was in the land of Uz, who are of the original Arabs (al-ʿArab al-ʿĀribah). They claimed that his speech recorded in his book was in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, translated it into Hebrew. Some think that the speech attributed to him was poetry which Moses translated in his book, and that it was the first poetry known in the original Arabic language. Others say it was the first poetry known to history, because his speech and the speech of his three companions who consoled him for his calamities was necessarily in a poetic style.

Yūsuf (Joseph) is the son of Jacob, and the detailed biography will come in Surat Yūsuf.

Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron) and Zakariyyā (Zechariah) have had their biographies covered in Surat al-Baqarah. The biography of ʿĪsā (Jesus) has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Āl ʿImrān. Yaḥyā (John) has had his biography covered in Āl ʿImrān.

His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ ("And thus We reward the good-doers") are an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses, and the "wa" is for a circumstantial sense, meaning: and thus the gift which We gave to Abraham and the guidance which We gave to his descendants, We reward the good-doers like it. Or: and thus the guidance which We gave the descendants of Noah, We reward the good-doers like Noah. It is therefore known that Noah or Abraham were among the good-doers by way of metonymy (kināyah). The good-doing of Noah is derived from this interjected clause, and the good-doing of Abraham is derived from what God related about him: his calling his people and his exerting every effort to turn them away from their error.

It is also possible that the reference here is to the guidance derived from the first and second "hadaynā," meaning: and thus with this great guidance We reward the good-doers, meaning with its like. The "good-doers" then refers to those guided ones among the descendants of Noah or the descendants of Abraham. The meaning is that they did good, and the reward for their good was that We made them prophets.

As for Ilyās (Elijah), he is known in the books of the Israelites as Elijah (Eliya), and in the lands of the Arabs he is called Ilyās or Mār Ilyās, and he is Elijah the Tishbite. The commentators mention that he was Ilyās son of Phinehas son of Eleazar, or son of Aaron, brother of Moses, so he would be from the tribe of Levi. He existed in the time of King Ahab (Ākhāb), king of Israel, around the year 918 BCE. He was an Israelite from the inhabitants of Gilead (Jilʿād), with a kasra on the jīm and sukūn on the lām, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, and Baalbek is from it. Ilyās was from the tribe of Reuben or from the tribe of Gad, and these two tribes were the inhabitants of the region of Gilead. Elijah is called "al-Tishbī" in the books of the Jews. God sent him to the Children of Israel when they worshipped idols in the time of King Ahab, and they worshipped Baal, the idol of the Canaanites. Elijah admonished them, and there are accounts of his dealings with them. God commanded him to appoint Elisha (al-Yasaʿ) as his successor in prophethood. Then God raised Elijah to heaven in a whirlwind, and no trace of him was seen afterwards. Elisha succeeded him in prophethood during the reign of King Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel.

His words ﴿كُلٌّ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ("each of them among the righteous") are an interjected clause. The tanwīn in "kullun" is a compensation for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all of these enumerated persons. It includes all those mentioned, Isaac and whoever came after him.

As for Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), his biography has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Yasaʿ (Elisha): his name in Hebrew is Elisha (ʾElīshaʿ), with a broken hamza with a kasra, followed by a lām with a yāʾ after it, then a shīn with a dot, then an ʿayn. Its Arabicised form is al-Yasaʿ, with a hamzat al-waṣl and a lām with a sukūn at its beginning, followed by a yāʾ with a fatḥa, in the reading of the majority.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read "al-Laysaʿ" with a hamzat al-waṣl, a fatḥa on the lām, shaddah, followed by a yāʾ with sukūn, on the pattern of ḍaygham. So these are two dialectal forms of it. He was son of Shafāṭ from the people of Abel-Meholah (Ābul Maḥūlah). He was a farmer whom God chose for prophethood through the messenger Elijah during the time of Ahab, and he accompanied Elijah. When Elijah was raised, he kept to the way of Elijah, and miracles appeared to him for the Children of Israel in Jericho (Arīḥā) and elsewhere. He died during the reign of King Joash (Yūʾāsh), king of Israel, and his death was in the year 840 BCE, and he was buried in Samaria (al-Sāmirah). The alif and lām in "al-Yasaʿ" are part of the original word, but the hamza was treated like a hamzat al-waṣl for lightness, so it came to resemble a name into which the lām is added to indicate its origin, like al-ʿAbbās, while it is not one of them.

[p. 343]

As for Yunus, he is the son of Matta, and his name in Hebrew is (Yunan ibn Amittai). He was from the tribe of (Zabulon). In Arabic, his nun may be vocalized with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. He was born in the town of (Gath-hepher) in Palestine. God sent him to the people of (Nineveh) in the lands of Assyria. Its people at that time were a mixture of Assyrians and Jews who were captives of the Assyrians. When he called them to faith and they refused, he threatened them with punishment. The punishment was delayed, so he left in anger and went to (Jaffa). There he boarded a ship of the Phoenicians to go to (Tarshish), a city west of Palestine, west of Tyre, on the sea. It may be that it is one of the harbors of the sea-facing side of Egypt, or one of the harbors of Barqa, because the Jewish books describe that gold, silver, apes, and peacocks were brought to Solomon from Tarshish. Thus it is determined that Tarshish had trade with Abyssinia or the Sudan, and that these products were exported from it. It has been said that it is Tartusha, one of the harbors of al-Andalus. It has also been said that it is Carthage, the port of Ifriqiya near Tunis. It has been said in our histories that the name of Tunis before the Islamic conquest was Tarshish. This is plausible, because its trade with the Sudan may be closer. The sea then rose against the ship, it became heavy, and its sinking was feared. So they cast lots, and Yunus was among those who lost in the drawing. He was thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him. He called out from its belly: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]. God answered him, and the fish cast him onto the shore. God sent him a second time to the people of Nineveh, and they believed; they numbered more than one hundred thousand. His period was at the beginning of the eighth century BC. We have not established the date of his death. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in al-Ahkam, in the commentary on Surat al-Saffat, that his grave is in the village of Jaljun between Jerusalem and the town of al-Khalil, and that he visited it during his journey. The accounts of Yunus will come in Surat Yunus, Surat al-Anbiya, and Surat al-Saffat.

As for Lut, he is the son of Haran ibn Terah, so he is the nephew of Ibrahim. He was born in (Ur of the Chaldeans). His father died before Terah, so Terah took Lut into his care. When Terah died, Lut was living with Ibrahim in the land of Haran (Hauran), after Terah, the father of Ibrahim, had left Ur of the Chaldeans, both heading for the land of Canaan. Ibrahim migrated with Lut to Egypt because of a famine that struck the lands of Canaan. Then they returned to the lands of Canaan. Ibrahim and Lut separated because of a dispute that arose between their herdsmen. Lut moved to (Sodom), which is east of the Jordan, until he was inspired to leave it when God decreed its destruction as a punishment for its people. He went out to (Zoar) with his daughter and his offspring there, who are (the Moabites) and (the children of Ammon).

His saying ﴿And We preferred each over the worlds﴾ is a parenthetical sentence, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis. The tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement that was omitted, meaning: each of those mentioned, from Isaac up to here. (Kull) requires that what it is attached to be encompassing. The rule of encompassment is that the judgment applies to each individual one by one, not to the group as a whole. The intended meaning is that each one of them is preferred over the worlds of people of his own age, except for one who was more excellent than him or equal to him. So the lam in (al-'alamin) is the lam of conventional comprehensiveness. Lut lived in the time of Ibrahim, and Ibrahim was more excellent than him. Among others there were people who lived in one era, and the preference of one of them over another is not known. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: it is possible to say that the intended meaning is that each of the prophets is preferred over every other of the worlds. Then the discussion after this concerns which of the prophets is more excellent than the other; that is a discussion on another topic with no connection to the first. End of quotation. This is not correct, because the requirement of the rule of encompassment is judgment on each individual one by one.

A significant issue of the principles of religion (usul al-din) is connected to this verse: the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, and what follows from establishing that regarding faith and the rights of prophethood. The exegetes have neglected to mention it, though it should have been addressed, because it branches into issues that students of the Islamic sciences need to know, and the most fitting place to mention it is this verse and what has the same meaning as some of it. As for the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, that is because God, the Exalted, said, after counting their names, that these are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and prophethood. So the prophethood of them is an established matter, because the demonstrative (ulaika, "those") is close to explicit text in referring to all the named persons before it, together with what supports and completes it of explicit text on the prophethood of some of them in verses similar to this verse, such as the verse of Surat al-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾ [al-Nisa: 163] and the verses following it, and such as the verses of Surat Maryam: ﴿And mention in the Book Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 41] and the verses following it.

Prophethood carries many rulings related to the one who possesses it and to how Muslims treat the one who is characterized by it. Among them: the meaning of (nabi, prophet) and (rasul, messenger); the meaning of the miracle (mu'jiza), which is the proof of the realization of prophethood or messengership for the one who brings it; and what follows from that of the obligation to believe in what he conveys from God, the Exalted, of law and ethics. Many issues of this are expounded in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam), so refer to it. What concerns us of this in this commentary is what His saying, the Exalted, at its end hints at: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Whoever knows these verses in this surah and knows their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to believe in the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in them.

Our scholars have mentioned that believing that God sent messengers and appointed prophets to guide people is obligatory in general, meaning belief in the sending of unspecified individuals, or in the prophethood of unspecified individuals, without specifying any particular person by name or by anything else that distinguishes him from others, except Muhammad (ﷺ). Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risala: The one who sends (a attribute of God, the Exalted) the messengers to them to establish the proof against them. So the sending of messengers is permissible with regard to God and not obligatory, and it occurs in general, without specifying a particular person. The author of al-Maqasid mentioned that the sending of messengers is needed, and it is a kindness from God to His creation, and it is not obligatory upon Him. The Mu'tazilites and a group of theologians (i.e., from the People of the Sunna) from beyond the river (Transoxiana) said that the sending of messengers is obligatory upon God, the Exalted.

None of our imams mentioned the obligation of believing in a particular prophet other than Muhammad (ﷺ) as a messenger to all creation. Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said: Then He sealed - meaning God - the messengership, the warning, and the prophethood with Muhammad, His prophet (ﷺ), etc., because the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab about Jibril's asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith, that he said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers," etc. He did not specify particular messengers. And in answer to his question about Islam, he said: "Islam is that you testify that there is no deity but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

Whoever knows these verses and understands their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to hold the belief in the prophethood of those mentioned in them. Perhaps many do not recite them, and many of those who recite them do not understand their implications correctly. They are not required to seek out understanding of them and belief in what they indicate, since that is not among the principles of faith and Islam, but it belongs to the deeper understanding of religion (tafaqquh fi al-din).

Al-Qadi Iyad said in the seventh section of the chapters of the third chapter of the fourth part of his book al-Shifa: All of this (i.e., what he mentioned of the imposition of disbelief or of a crime that requires punishment on whoever speaks about them in a way that contradicts what is due to them) concerning those about whom something is said, i.e., the prophets or the angels, by what we have stated regarding the totality of the angels and prophets, i.e., regarding their collectivity and not regarding each one of them, as al-Khafaji said. By "all" he means every single individual of those whose being among them we have verified, either by explicit mention in His Book, or by verifying their knowledge through mass-transmitted report (mutawatir), definite consensus (ijma'), and a famous report agreed upon. The "waw" in this division means "or." As for the one whose announcement of his identity has not been established and on whom there is no consensus that he is among the prophets, such as al-Khidr, Luqman, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, and Khalid ibn Sinan, who is mentioned as the prophet of the people of al-Rass, then the ruling regarding the one who reviles them or disbelieves in them is not the same as the ruling regarding what we have mentioned before. End of quotation.

When you know this, you know that what occurred in three verses composed by someone, which Shaykh Ibrahim al-Bayjuri mentioned in the section on faith in his commentary on Jawhara al-Tawhid:

It is a binding duty on everyone who is under obligation to know the prophets in detail, who are known.
Among them, for our proof, are eight, after ten; and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and with the Chosen One they are sealed.

This does not hold except with forced interpretation, because the knowledge of that being "binding" (hatm) according to its technical sense implies that it is obligatory, and no one holds this. If he meant by "binding" a matter that should not be neglected, then it is emphatic in relation to his saying "on everyone who is under obligation." So if he had replaced it with "everyone who is under instruction," it would be better.

Perhaps he meant by "binding" that it is necessarily incumbent upon whoever knows this not to deny that these are prophets by specific identification. But he intended a distinction between the obligation to know something and the prohibition of denying it after it has become known.

As for the messengership of Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb, their mention has been repeated in many verses.

As for knowing the prophethood of Dhu al-Kifl, there is room for consideration, since in Surat al-Anbiya he is described only as one of the patient and the righteous. The exegetes differed concerning several of the prophets, and it is attributed to the majority that he was a prophet. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid reported that Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. The mention of this will come in Surat al-Anbiya.

As for Adam, he was a prophet from the time he was in the Garden, for God spoke to him more than once. He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, relented toward him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. So he was sent down to the earth honored with the attribute of prophethood. The story of the two sons of Adam in Surat al-Ma'ida indicates that Adam conveyed a law to his sons, according to His saying, the Exalted, in it: ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous. If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I will not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin and be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 27].

So what we rely upon is that whoever denies the prophethood of a particular person named in the Qur'an among the prophets, in Surat al-Nisa, Surat Hud, Surat al-An'am, and Surat Maryam, and the one denying knows for certain the verse in which he is described as a prophet, and he has been informed of the evidence for the validity of what he denies and has been brought back to it, but he insists on denying it, then that denial is disbelief, because he denied something known by necessity after having been alerted to it, so that he cannot excuse himself by ignorance or by an acceptable interpretation.

[p. 347]

Know that I sought to uncover the veil over the reason for limiting the mention of these prophets to the prophets from among the offspring of Abraham or the offspring of Noah, on the two readings concerning the referent of the pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyatihi). It did not become clear to me. I also sought the reason for this particular order of their names and for the linking of some of these names to others by conjunction, but it did not appear to me. My strongest assumption is that among these aspects is that these men were known to the People of the Book and to the polytheists who borrowed their knowledge of the prophets from the People of the Book. Also, the reason for their order may arise from beginning with the mention that Isaac and Jacob were a gift to Abraham, and they were a father and his son. So the transition from one to another arose through a connection that made the transition appropriate. Also, the distribution of their names over three verse-endings (fawasil, sing. fasilah, the rhyming unit at the end of a verse) does not lack a connection that gathers the owners of those names in the single verse-ending that includes all of them. It is possible that the lightness of these names when Arabicized, in letters and in meter, had an effect in their being singled out for mention over other names, such as Shm'un (Simeon), Shmwyl (Samuel), Hizqyal (Ezekiel) and Nahmiya (Nehemiah). Also, those counted in these three verses were distributed among virtues. Among them are messengers, prophets, kings, and people of noble and honorable character: patience, struggle against the self, struggle in the way of God, and perseverance
[p. 348]
in conveying monotheism (tawhid), the law (shari'ah), and noble character. This is what His saying at the end of the verses indicates: "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood. And among them are the two roots of the Arab and Israelite nations."

When He mentioned Isaac and Jacob, He followed their mention with the mention of two prophets from the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, who are a father and his son among the prophets: David and Solomon. He began with them before the rest of the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, because they attained two great glories: the glory of the Hereafter through prophethood, and the glory of this world through kingship. Then He followed with the mention of "two prophets" who were alike in that harm befell both of them and that relief from their distress came through their patience: they are Job and Joseph. Then, with the mention of two brothers, messengers, Moses and Aaron. Moses suffered the like of what befell Joseph: plotting against him to kill him, his deliverance from that, and his being raised in the house of kingship. So these six were included in the first verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And thus do We reward the good-doers."

Then with the mention of two prophets, a father and his son: Zechariah and John (Yahya). It was appropriate that after them there be mentioned two messengers who had no offspring: Jesus ('Isa) and Elias (Ilyas). They are alike in that both were raised up to heaven. As for Jesus, his ascension is mentioned in the Qur'an. As for Elias, his ascension is mentioned in the books of the Israelites, and the commentators among the early generations did not mention it. It has been said that Elias is Idris, and on this basis his elevation is mentioned in His saying: "And mention in the Book Idris; indeed he was a truthful one and a prophet" [Maryam: 56], and "We raised him to a high station" in Surah Maryam. Jesus was mentioned first as a conjunction following John, because they were close, being cousins on the mother's side, and because Jesus was a messenger while Elias was a prophet who was not a messenger. These four were included in the second verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "All of them were of the righteous." He linked Elisha (al-Yasa') because he was the successor and disciple of Elias. He placed between Elias and Elisha the mention of Ishmael, a conclusion by mentioning the prophet to whom the lineage of the Arabs from the offspring of Abraham traces back. They were concluded with Jonah (Yunus) and Lot, because each of them was sent to a small nation. These four were included in the third verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And We preferred each over the worlds."
[p. 349]
His saying "and of their fathers" is conjoined to His saying "each." So the sense is: "And We guided some of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took "min" (of) as a noun meaning "some," that is: "And We guided some of their fathers," according to his method in His saying: "Of those who are Jews, they distort [words]" (al-Nisa': 46). Ibn 'Atiyyah and those who followed him supposed that the conjoined object is omitted, its estimate being: "And of their fathers, a great multitude, or many who were guided." Then "min" is partitive and linked to "We guided."

The dhurriyyat (offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, and it refers to those who descend from a human being: sons, the nearer ones, and their sons. So it includes the children of sons and the children of daughters. Its being in the plural is intended to show that guidance attached to the offspring of each of those mentioned who had offspring, to indicate that in the guidance of some of the offspring there is honor for the forefather. So each one of these is meant to have guidance occur in his offspring, even though their offspring trace back to a single forefather, Noah, peace be upon him. Then, if the guidance meant is the guidance similar to the guidance explicitly stated, which is the guidance of prophethood, then "fathers" includes figures like Adam and Idris, peace be upon them, for they are the fathers of Noah. "Offspring" includes the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Joshua (Yusha') and Daniel (Danyal). They are from the offspring of Noah and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The prophets from the sons of Ishmael, peace be upon him, include figures such as Hanzalah ibn Safwan and Khalid ibn Sinan, and Hud and Salih from the offspring of Noah, and Shu'ayb from the offspring of Abraham. "Brothers" includes the rest of the tribes, the brothers of Joseph.

If what is meant by guidance is what is more general than prophethood, it includes the righteous among the fathers, such as Abel (Habil) son of Adam. And "offspring" includes all the righteous of the nations, such as the People of the Cave, of whom He said: "And We increased them in guidance" (al-Kahf: 13). It also includes Saul (Talut), king of Israel, and Mudar and Rabi'ah, for it has been transmitted that they were both Muslims, narrated by al-Daylami from Ibn 'Abbas. It also includes the believer of the family of Pharaoh and the wife of Pharaoh. "Brothers" includes Haran son of Terah, brother of Abraham, who was the father of Lot, and Esau (Eisu), brother of Jacob, and others besides these whom God the Exalted knows.
[p. 350]
Al-ijtiba' (selection, ijtiba': choosing and preferring) is the act of choosing and selecting. They said it is derived from al-jabi, which means gathering, and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (collection of land tax). Also jaby al-ma' in the basin, from which the basin (al-jabiyah) is named. So the infixed form (ifti'al) in it is for emphasis, like al-idtirar (compulsion). The basis of the derivation is that gathering only happens for something desired, to obtain it because one needs it. The meaning is: God chose them and made them the place of His guidance, because He knows best where to place His message, His prophethood, and His guidance.

He conjoined His saying "and We guided them" to "We chose them" with a conjunction that emphasizes the affirmation of their guidance, out of concern for this guidance. So He explained that He guided them to a straight path (sirat mustaqim), that is, to that by which one attains what the people of perfection strive to attain. So He made the straight path an example for this, comparing the state of one who acts to attain the perfection he seeks to the state of one who walks upon a straight road that brings him to what he wants, proceeding without hesitation, confusion, or going astray. He mentioned from the words of the compound expression that indicates the state being compared only a part of it, which is "the straight path," because it indicates all the omitted words for brevity.

The straight path is monotheism (tawhid) and faith in what must be believed of the fundamental virtues in which the revealed laws (shara'i') agree. The purpose, along with praising them, is an allusion to the polytheists who opposed their creed, as indicated by His saying after that: "Those are the guided by God," up to His saying: "And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been void from them" (al-An'am: 88).

[p. 337]

The clause ﴿وَوَهَبْنا لَهُ إسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ﴾ ("And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob") is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the preceding clause "ātaynāhā" (We gave it), because its content is honour and distinction. The position of this clause, although it is conjoined, is that of a concluding statement (tadhyīl, a closing summation) for the preceding clauses. Its purpose is to refute polytheism and establish proofs against its corruption, and to show that all the righteous were opposed to it.

Al-wahb and al-hibah mean giving something without compensation. Here it is used metaphorically for bounty and facilitation.

The meaning of "the gift of Jacob to Abraham" is that a son was born to Abraham's son Isaac during Abraham's lifetime, and he grew up and married during his lifetime, and so he was a source of comfort to Abraham (qurrat ʿayn).

The biography of Abraham, peace be upon him, has already been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَإِذِ ابْتَلى إبْراهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِماتٍ﴾ ("And when his Lord tested Abraham with words"). The biographies of Isaac and Jacob have been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَوَصّى بِها إبْراهِيمُ بَنِيهِ ويَعْقُوبُ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob") [al-Baqarah: 132], and His words ﴿وإلَهَ آبائِكَ إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ﴾ ("the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac") [al-Baqarah: 133]. All of this is in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words "﴿كُلًّا هَدَيْنا﴾" ("We guided each one") are an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical insertion). The meaning is: We guided all of these, that is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The genitive complement was omitted because it is evident, and tanwīn (nunation) was substituted for it in kullan, a tanwīn of compensation for the omitted genitive complement, as is the preferred view.

The benefit of mentioning their guidance is to honour Isaac and Jacob, and to show that they were prophets who attained God's guidance just as Abraham did. It also includes a refutation of polytheism, a rebuke to Quraysh and the polytheist Arabs, and a condemnation of them by establishing that the famous righteous people held views opposed to their beliefs, as will be stated explicitly in His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ هُدى اللَّهِ يَهْدِي بِهِ مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ ولَوْ أشْرَكُوا لَحَبِطَ عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("That is the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been worthless") [al-Anʿām: 88].

The clause ﴿ونُوحًا هَدَيْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ("And Noah, We guided before") is conjoined to the interjected clause, meaning: and We guided Noah before them. This is a digression (istiṭrād) by mentioning some of those upon whom God bestowed guidance, and an indication that guidance is the origin, and among the greatest guidance is monotheism, as you know.

[p. 338]

Noah is in the accusative as a direct object placed before "hadaynā" (We guided) for emphasis. "Min qablu" (before) is a circumstantial adjunct (ḥāl) of "Nūḥan." The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is to draw attention to the fact that guidance is rooted in the origins of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Qablu is built on a ḍamma, according to what is well known regarding qablu and its sisters, when the genitive complement that qablu is attached to is omitted, its meaning is intended but not its wording.

The biography of Noah has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى آدَمَ ونُوحًا﴾ ("Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah") [Āl ʿImrān: 33], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

His words "min dhurriyyatihi" (from his descendants) are a circumstantial adjunct of "Dāwūd." Dāwūd is the omitted direct object of "hadaynā." The benefit of this circumstance is to honour these enumerated persons with the nobility of their origin and the origin of their merit, and to honour Abraham or Noah with the virtues of his descendants.

The pronoun attached to it refers to Noah, not to Abraham, because Noah is the nearest mentioned, and because Lot is among the descendants of Noah and not among the descendants of Abraham, as is stated in the Torah. It is possible that Lot was treated as a descendant of Abraham because of his close connection to him. It is also possible that the mention of his name after the list of those who are descendants of Abraham ends is in the accusative for praise, by implying a verb, not as a conjunction.

Some of the biography of Dāwūd has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وقَتَلَ داوُدُ جالُوتَ﴾ ("And David killed Goliath") in Surat al-Baqarah. We complete it here: he is Dāwūd son of Jesse (Yissi), from the tribe of Judah among the Children of Israel. He was born in the village of Bethlehem around 1085 BCE, and died in Jerusalem around 1015 BCE. In his youth he was a shepherd of his father's sheep, and he had knowledge of melody, playing instruments, and slinging with a sling. God revealed to Samuel (Shamwīl), the prophet of the Children of Israel, to bless Dāwūd son of Jesse and anoint him with holy oil so that he would be king over the Children of Israel, according to the traditions of the Children of Israel, announcing that he would become king over Israel after the death of Saul (Shāʾūl), whom God was angry with. When Samuel anointed him in the village of Bethlehem without anyone knowing, [p. 339] it occurred to Saul, who was ill, to take someone who would play the lute for him when the illness overcame him. It happened that they chose Dāwūd for him, so he admitted him among his courtiers to hear his melodies. When Saul's army fought the Canaanites, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, victory went to the Israelites because of Dāwūd, when he struck the Philistine champion Goliath (Jālūt) with his sling between his eyes, felled him, and cut off his head. For this reason Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage. Then Saul turned against Dāwūd, and Dāwūd went out to the land of the Philistines and gathered a group under his leadership. When Saul was killed in the year 1055, a group of the Israelite army in Palestine pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He made Hebron his seat of government. After seven years, the king of Israel who succeeded Saul was killed, and all the Israelites pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He returned to Jerusalem, God gave him prophethood, and commanded him to write the Psalms (al-Zabūr), called by the Jews "al-Mazāmīr."

Sulaymān's biography has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿واتَّبَعُوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطِينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ ("And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon") [al-Baqarah: 102], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ayyūb (Job) is a prophet whose prophethood the Qur'an affirmed. He has a detailed story in the book known as the Book of Job, among the books of the Jews. Some historians think that Job was a descendant of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. Others thought he was a grandson of Esau son of Isaac son of Abraham. In his book, it is stated that Job lived in the land of Uz, which is the land of Hauran in Syria, and it is the dwelling place of the sons of Uz son of Aram son of Shem son of Noah, and they are the origin of ʿĀd, and it was adjacent to the borders of the land of the Chaldeans. The names of places are mentioned in the Book of Job. Some scholars think he was of Arab origin and was from Uz, as indicated by the absence of any mention of his lineage in his book, and by restricting it to saying he was in the land of Uz, who are of the original Arabs (al-ʿArab al-ʿĀribah). They claimed that his speech recorded in his book was in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, translated it into Hebrew. Some think that the speech attributed to him was poetry which Moses translated in his book, and that it was the first poetry known in the original Arabic language. Others say it was the first poetry known to history, because his speech and the speech of his three companions who consoled him for his calamities was necessarily in a poetic style.

Yūsuf (Joseph) is the son of Jacob, and the detailed biography will come in Surat Yūsuf.

Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron) and Zakariyyā (Zechariah) have had their biographies covered in Surat al-Baqarah. The biography of ʿĪsā (Jesus) has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Āl ʿImrān. Yaḥyā (John) has had his biography covered in Āl ʿImrān.

His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ ("And thus We reward the good-doers") are an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses, and the "wa" is for a circumstantial sense, meaning: and thus the gift which We gave to Abraham and the guidance which We gave to his descendants, We reward the good-doers like it. Or: and thus the guidance which We gave the descendants of Noah, We reward the good-doers like Noah. It is therefore known that Noah or Abraham were among the good-doers by way of metonymy (kināyah). The good-doing of Noah is derived from this interjected clause, and the good-doing of Abraham is derived from what God related about him: his calling his people and his exerting every effort to turn them away from their error.

It is also possible that the reference here is to the guidance derived from the first and second "hadaynā," meaning: and thus with this great guidance We reward the good-doers, meaning with its like. The "good-doers" then refers to those guided ones among the descendants of Noah or the descendants of Abraham. The meaning is that they did good, and the reward for their good was that We made them prophets.

As for Ilyās (Elijah), he is known in the books of the Israelites as Elijah (Eliya), and in the lands of the Arabs he is called Ilyās or Mār Ilyās, and he is Elijah the Tishbite. The commentators mention that he was Ilyās son of Phinehas son of Eleazar, or son of Aaron, brother of Moses, so he would be from the tribe of Levi. He existed in the time of King Ahab (Ākhāb), king of Israel, around the year 918 BCE. He was an Israelite from the inhabitants of Gilead (Jilʿād), with a kasra on the jīm and sukūn on the lām, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, and Baalbek is from it. Ilyās was from the tribe of Reuben or from the tribe of Gad, and these two tribes were the inhabitants of the region of Gilead. Elijah is called "al-Tishbī" in the books of the Jews. God sent him to the Children of Israel when they worshipped idols in the time of King Ahab, and they worshipped Baal, the idol of the Canaanites. Elijah admonished them, and there are accounts of his dealings with them. God commanded him to appoint Elisha (al-Yasaʿ) as his successor in prophethood. Then God raised Elijah to heaven in a whirlwind, and no trace of him was seen afterwards. Elisha succeeded him in prophethood during the reign of King Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel.

His words ﴿كُلٌّ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ("each of them among the righteous") are an interjected clause. The tanwīn in "kullun" is a compensation for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all of these enumerated persons. It includes all those mentioned, Isaac and whoever came after him.

As for Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), his biography has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Yasaʿ (Elisha): his name in Hebrew is Elisha (ʾElīshaʿ), with a broken hamza with a kasra, followed by a lām with a yāʾ after it, then a shīn with a dot, then an ʿayn. Its Arabicised form is al-Yasaʿ, with a hamzat al-waṣl and a lām with a sukūn at its beginning, followed by a yāʾ with a fatḥa, in the reading of the majority.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read "al-Laysaʿ" with a hamzat al-waṣl, a fatḥa on the lām, shaddah, followed by a yāʾ with sukūn, on the pattern of ḍaygham. So these are two dialectal forms of it. He was son of Shafāṭ from the people of Abel-Meholah (Ābul Maḥūlah). He was a farmer whom God chose for prophethood through the messenger Elijah during the time of Ahab, and he accompanied Elijah. When Elijah was raised, he kept to the way of Elijah, and miracles appeared to him for the Children of Israel in Jericho (Arīḥā) and elsewhere. He died during the reign of King Joash (Yūʾāsh), king of Israel, and his death was in the year 840 BCE, and he was buried in Samaria (al-Sāmirah). The alif and lām in "al-Yasaʿ" are part of the original word, but the hamza was treated like a hamzat al-waṣl for lightness, so it came to resemble a name into which the lām is added to indicate its origin, like al-ʿAbbās, while it is not one of them.

[p. 343]

As for Yunus, he is the son of Matta, and his name in Hebrew is (Yunan ibn Amittai). He was from the tribe of (Zabulon). In Arabic, his nun may be vocalized with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. He was born in the town of (Gath-hepher) in Palestine. God sent him to the people of (Nineveh) in the lands of Assyria. Its people at that time were a mixture of Assyrians and Jews who were captives of the Assyrians. When he called them to faith and they refused, he threatened them with punishment. The punishment was delayed, so he left in anger and went to (Jaffa). There he boarded a ship of the Phoenicians to go to (Tarshish), a city west of Palestine, west of Tyre, on the sea. It may be that it is one of the harbors of the sea-facing side of Egypt, or one of the harbors of Barqa, because the Jewish books describe that gold, silver, apes, and peacocks were brought to Solomon from Tarshish. Thus it is determined that Tarshish had trade with Abyssinia or the Sudan, and that these products were exported from it. It has been said that it is Tartusha, one of the harbors of al-Andalus. It has also been said that it is Carthage, the port of Ifriqiya near Tunis. It has been said in our histories that the name of Tunis before the Islamic conquest was Tarshish. This is plausible, because its trade with the Sudan may be closer. The sea then rose against the ship, it became heavy, and its sinking was feared. So they cast lots, and Yunus was among those who lost in the drawing. He was thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him. He called out from its belly: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]. God answered him, and the fish cast him onto the shore. God sent him a second time to the people of Nineveh, and they believed; they numbered more than one hundred thousand. His period was at the beginning of the eighth century BC. We have not established the date of his death. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in al-Ahkam, in the commentary on Surat al-Saffat, that his grave is in the village of Jaljun between Jerusalem and the town of al-Khalil, and that he visited it during his journey. The accounts of Yunus will come in Surat Yunus, Surat al-Anbiya, and Surat al-Saffat.

As for Lut, he is the son of Haran ibn Terah, so he is the nephew of Ibrahim. He was born in (Ur of the Chaldeans). His father died before Terah, so Terah took Lut into his care. When Terah died, Lut was living with Ibrahim in the land of Haran (Hauran), after Terah, the father of Ibrahim, had left Ur of the Chaldeans, both heading for the land of Canaan. Ibrahim migrated with Lut to Egypt because of a famine that struck the lands of Canaan. Then they returned to the lands of Canaan. Ibrahim and Lut separated because of a dispute that arose between their herdsmen. Lut moved to (Sodom), which is east of the Jordan, until he was inspired to leave it when God decreed its destruction as a punishment for its people. He went out to (Zoar) with his daughter and his offspring there, who are (the Moabites) and (the children of Ammon).

His saying ﴿And We preferred each over the worlds﴾ is a parenthetical sentence, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis. The tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement that was omitted, meaning: each of those mentioned, from Isaac up to here. (Kull) requires that what it is attached to be encompassing. The rule of encompassment is that the judgment applies to each individual one by one, not to the group as a whole. The intended meaning is that each one of them is preferred over the worlds of people of his own age, except for one who was more excellent than him or equal to him. So the lam in (al-'alamin) is the lam of conventional comprehensiveness. Lut lived in the time of Ibrahim, and Ibrahim was more excellent than him. Among others there were people who lived in one era, and the preference of one of them over another is not known. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: it is possible to say that the intended meaning is that each of the prophets is preferred over every other of the worlds. Then the discussion after this concerns which of the prophets is more excellent than the other; that is a discussion on another topic with no connection to the first. End of quotation. This is not correct, because the requirement of the rule of encompassment is judgment on each individual one by one.

A significant issue of the principles of religion (usul al-din) is connected to this verse: the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, and what follows from establishing that regarding faith and the rights of prophethood. The exegetes have neglected to mention it, though it should have been addressed, because it branches into issues that students of the Islamic sciences need to know, and the most fitting place to mention it is this verse and what has the same meaning as some of it. As for the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, that is because God, the Exalted, said, after counting their names, that these are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and prophethood. So the prophethood of them is an established matter, because the demonstrative (ulaika, "those") is close to explicit text in referring to all the named persons before it, together with what supports and completes it of explicit text on the prophethood of some of them in verses similar to this verse, such as the verse of Surat al-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾ [al-Nisa: 163] and the verses following it, and such as the verses of Surat Maryam: ﴿And mention in the Book Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 41] and the verses following it.

Prophethood carries many rulings related to the one who possesses it and to how Muslims treat the one who is characterized by it. Among them: the meaning of (nabi, prophet) and (rasul, messenger); the meaning of the miracle (mu'jiza), which is the proof of the realization of prophethood or messengership for the one who brings it; and what follows from that of the obligation to believe in what he conveys from God, the Exalted, of law and ethics. Many issues of this are expounded in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam), so refer to it. What concerns us of this in this commentary is what His saying, the Exalted, at its end hints at: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Whoever knows these verses in this surah and knows their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to believe in the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in them.

Our scholars have mentioned that believing that God sent messengers and appointed prophets to guide people is obligatory in general, meaning belief in the sending of unspecified individuals, or in the prophethood of unspecified individuals, without specifying any particular person by name or by anything else that distinguishes him from others, except Muhammad (ﷺ). Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risala: The one who sends (a attribute of God, the Exalted) the messengers to them to establish the proof against them. So the sending of messengers is permissible with regard to God and not obligatory, and it occurs in general, without specifying a particular person. The author of al-Maqasid mentioned that the sending of messengers is needed, and it is a kindness from God to His creation, and it is not obligatory upon Him. The Mu'tazilites and a group of theologians (i.e., from the People of the Sunna) from beyond the river (Transoxiana) said that the sending of messengers is obligatory upon God, the Exalted.

None of our imams mentioned the obligation of believing in a particular prophet other than Muhammad (ﷺ) as a messenger to all creation. Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said: Then He sealed - meaning God - the messengership, the warning, and the prophethood with Muhammad, His prophet (ﷺ), etc., because the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab about Jibril's asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith, that he said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers," etc. He did not specify particular messengers. And in answer to his question about Islam, he said: "Islam is that you testify that there is no deity but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

Whoever knows these verses and understands their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to hold the belief in the prophethood of those mentioned in them. Perhaps many do not recite them, and many of those who recite them do not understand their implications correctly. They are not required to seek out understanding of them and belief in what they indicate, since that is not among the principles of faith and Islam, but it belongs to the deeper understanding of religion (tafaqquh fi al-din).

Al-Qadi Iyad said in the seventh section of the chapters of the third chapter of the fourth part of his book al-Shifa: All of this (i.e., what he mentioned of the imposition of disbelief or of a crime that requires punishment on whoever speaks about them in a way that contradicts what is due to them) concerning those about whom something is said, i.e., the prophets or the angels, by what we have stated regarding the totality of the angels and prophets, i.e., regarding their collectivity and not regarding each one of them, as al-Khafaji said. By "all" he means every single individual of those whose being among them we have verified, either by explicit mention in His Book, or by verifying their knowledge through mass-transmitted report (mutawatir), definite consensus (ijma'), and a famous report agreed upon. The "waw" in this division means "or." As for the one whose announcement of his identity has not been established and on whom there is no consensus that he is among the prophets, such as al-Khidr, Luqman, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, and Khalid ibn Sinan, who is mentioned as the prophet of the people of al-Rass, then the ruling regarding the one who reviles them or disbelieves in them is not the same as the ruling regarding what we have mentioned before. End of quotation.

When you know this, you know that what occurred in three verses composed by someone, which Shaykh Ibrahim al-Bayjuri mentioned in the section on faith in his commentary on Jawhara al-Tawhid:

It is a binding duty on everyone who is under obligation to know the prophets in detail, who are known.
Among them, for our proof, are eight, after ten; and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and with the Chosen One they are sealed.

This does not hold except with forced interpretation, because the knowledge of that being "binding" (hatm) according to its technical sense implies that it is obligatory, and no one holds this. If he meant by "binding" a matter that should not be neglected, then it is emphatic in relation to his saying "on everyone who is under obligation." So if he had replaced it with "everyone who is under instruction," it would be better.

Perhaps he meant by "binding" that it is necessarily incumbent upon whoever knows this not to deny that these are prophets by specific identification. But he intended a distinction between the obligation to know something and the prohibition of denying it after it has become known.

As for the messengership of Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb, their mention has been repeated in many verses.

As for knowing the prophethood of Dhu al-Kifl, there is room for consideration, since in Surat al-Anbiya he is described only as one of the patient and the righteous. The exegetes differed concerning several of the prophets, and it is attributed to the majority that he was a prophet. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid reported that Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. The mention of this will come in Surat al-Anbiya.

As for Adam, he was a prophet from the time he was in the Garden, for God spoke to him more than once. He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, relented toward him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. So he was sent down to the earth honored with the attribute of prophethood. The story of the two sons of Adam in Surat al-Ma'ida indicates that Adam conveyed a law to his sons, according to His saying, the Exalted, in it: ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous. If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I will not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin and be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 27].

So what we rely upon is that whoever denies the prophethood of a particular person named in the Qur'an among the prophets, in Surat al-Nisa, Surat Hud, Surat al-An'am, and Surat Maryam, and the one denying knows for certain the verse in which he is described as a prophet, and he has been informed of the evidence for the validity of what he denies and has been brought back to it, but he insists on denying it, then that denial is disbelief, because he denied something known by necessity after having been alerted to it, so that he cannot excuse himself by ignorance or by an acceptable interpretation.

[p. 347]

Know that I sought to uncover the veil over the reason for limiting the mention of these prophets to the prophets from among the offspring of Abraham or the offspring of Noah, on the two readings concerning the referent of the pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyatihi). It did not become clear to me. I also sought the reason for this particular order of their names and for the linking of some of these names to others by conjunction, but it did not appear to me. My strongest assumption is that among these aspects is that these men were known to the People of the Book and to the polytheists who borrowed their knowledge of the prophets from the People of the Book. Also, the reason for their order may arise from beginning with the mention that Isaac and Jacob were a gift to Abraham, and they were a father and his son. So the transition from one to another arose through a connection that made the transition appropriate. Also, the distribution of their names over three verse-endings (fawasil, sing. fasilah, the rhyming unit at the end of a verse) does not lack a connection that gathers the owners of those names in the single verse-ending that includes all of them. It is possible that the lightness of these names when Arabicized, in letters and in meter, had an effect in their being singled out for mention over other names, such as Shm'un (Simeon), Shmwyl (Samuel), Hizqyal (Ezekiel) and Nahmiya (Nehemiah). Also, those counted in these three verses were distributed among virtues. Among them are messengers, prophets, kings, and people of noble and honorable character: patience, struggle against the self, struggle in the way of God, and perseverance
[p. 348]
in conveying monotheism (tawhid), the law (shari'ah), and noble character. This is what His saying at the end of the verses indicates: "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood. And among them are the two roots of the Arab and Israelite nations."

When He mentioned Isaac and Jacob, He followed their mention with the mention of two prophets from the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, who are a father and his son among the prophets: David and Solomon. He began with them before the rest of the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, because they attained two great glories: the glory of the Hereafter through prophethood, and the glory of this world through kingship. Then He followed with the mention of "two prophets" who were alike in that harm befell both of them and that relief from their distress came through their patience: they are Job and Joseph. Then, with the mention of two brothers, messengers, Moses and Aaron. Moses suffered the like of what befell Joseph: plotting against him to kill him, his deliverance from that, and his being raised in the house of kingship. So these six were included in the first verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And thus do We reward the good-doers."

Then with the mention of two prophets, a father and his son: Zechariah and John (Yahya). It was appropriate that after them there be mentioned two messengers who had no offspring: Jesus ('Isa) and Elias (Ilyas). They are alike in that both were raised up to heaven. As for Jesus, his ascension is mentioned in the Qur'an. As for Elias, his ascension is mentioned in the books of the Israelites, and the commentators among the early generations did not mention it. It has been said that Elias is Idris, and on this basis his elevation is mentioned in His saying: "And mention in the Book Idris; indeed he was a truthful one and a prophet" [Maryam: 56], and "We raised him to a high station" in Surah Maryam. Jesus was mentioned first as a conjunction following John, because they were close, being cousins on the mother's side, and because Jesus was a messenger while Elias was a prophet who was not a messenger. These four were included in the second verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "All of them were of the righteous." He linked Elisha (al-Yasa') because he was the successor and disciple of Elias. He placed between Elias and Elisha the mention of Ishmael, a conclusion by mentioning the prophet to whom the lineage of the Arabs from the offspring of Abraham traces back. They were concluded with Jonah (Yunus) and Lot, because each of them was sent to a small nation. These four were included in the third verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And We preferred each over the worlds."
[p. 349]
His saying "and of their fathers" is conjoined to His saying "each." So the sense is: "And We guided some of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took "min" (of) as a noun meaning "some," that is: "And We guided some of their fathers," according to his method in His saying: "Of those who are Jews, they distort [words]" (al-Nisa': 46). Ibn 'Atiyyah and those who followed him supposed that the conjoined object is omitted, its estimate being: "And of their fathers, a great multitude, or many who were guided." Then "min" is partitive and linked to "We guided."

The dhurriyyat (offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, and it refers to those who descend from a human being: sons, the nearer ones, and their sons. So it includes the children of sons and the children of daughters. Its being in the plural is intended to show that guidance attached to the offspring of each of those mentioned who had offspring, to indicate that in the guidance of some of the offspring there is honor for the forefather. So each one of these is meant to have guidance occur in his offspring, even though their offspring trace back to a single forefather, Noah, peace be upon him. Then, if the guidance meant is the guidance similar to the guidance explicitly stated, which is the guidance of prophethood, then "fathers" includes figures like Adam and Idris, peace be upon them, for they are the fathers of Noah. "Offspring" includes the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Joshua (Yusha') and Daniel (Danyal). They are from the offspring of Noah and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The prophets from the sons of Ishmael, peace be upon him, include figures such as Hanzalah ibn Safwan and Khalid ibn Sinan, and Hud and Salih from the offspring of Noah, and Shu'ayb from the offspring of Abraham. "Brothers" includes the rest of the tribes, the brothers of Joseph.

If what is meant by guidance is what is more general than prophethood, it includes the righteous among the fathers, such as Abel (Habil) son of Adam. And "offspring" includes all the righteous of the nations, such as the People of the Cave, of whom He said: "And We increased them in guidance" (al-Kahf: 13). It also includes Saul (Talut), king of Israel, and Mudar and Rabi'ah, for it has been transmitted that they were both Muslims, narrated by al-Daylami from Ibn 'Abbas. It also includes the believer of the family of Pharaoh and the wife of Pharaoh. "Brothers" includes Haran son of Terah, brother of Abraham, who was the father of Lot, and Esau (Eisu), brother of Jacob, and others besides these whom God the Exalted knows.
[p. 350]
Al-ijtiba' (selection, ijtiba': choosing and preferring) is the act of choosing and selecting. They said it is derived from al-jabi, which means gathering, and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (collection of land tax). Also jaby al-ma' in the basin, from which the basin (al-jabiyah) is named. So the infixed form (ifti'al) in it is for emphasis, like al-idtirar (compulsion). The basis of the derivation is that gathering only happens for something desired, to obtain it because one needs it. The meaning is: God chose them and made them the place of His guidance, because He knows best where to place His message, His prophethood, and His guidance.

He conjoined His saying "and We guided them" to "We chose them" with a conjunction that emphasizes the affirmation of their guidance, out of concern for this guidance. So He explained that He guided them to a straight path (sirat mustaqim), that is, to that by which one attains what the people of perfection strive to attain. So He made the straight path an example for this, comparing the state of one who acts to attain the perfection he seeks to the state of one who walks upon a straight road that brings him to what he wants, proceeding without hesitation, confusion, or going astray. He mentioned from the words of the compound expression that indicates the state being compared only a part of it, which is "the straight path," because it indicates all the omitted words for brevity.

The straight path is monotheism (tawhid) and faith in what must be believed of the fundamental virtues in which the revealed laws (shara'i') agree. The purpose, along with praising them, is an allusion to the polytheists who opposed their creed, as indicated by His saying after that: "Those are the guided by God," up to His saying: "And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been void from them" (al-An'am: 88).

[p. 337]

The clause ﴿وَوَهَبْنا لَهُ إسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ﴾ ("And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob") is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the preceding clause "ātaynāhā" (We gave it), because its content is honour and distinction. The position of this clause, although it is conjoined, is that of a concluding statement (tadhyīl, a closing summation) for the preceding clauses. Its purpose is to refute polytheism and establish proofs against its corruption, and to show that all the righteous were opposed to it.

Al-wahb and al-hibah mean giving something without compensation. Here it is used metaphorically for bounty and facilitation.

The meaning of "the gift of Jacob to Abraham" is that a son was born to Abraham's son Isaac during Abraham's lifetime, and he grew up and married during his lifetime, and so he was a source of comfort to Abraham (qurrat ʿayn).

The biography of Abraham, peace be upon him, has already been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَإِذِ ابْتَلى إبْراهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِماتٍ﴾ ("And when his Lord tested Abraham with words"). The biographies of Isaac and Jacob have been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَوَصّى بِها إبْراهِيمُ بَنِيهِ ويَعْقُوبُ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob") [al-Baqarah: 132], and His words ﴿وإلَهَ آبائِكَ إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ﴾ ("the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac") [al-Baqarah: 133]. All of this is in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words "﴿كُلًّا هَدَيْنا﴾" ("We guided each one") are an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ, a parenthetical insertion). The meaning is: We guided all of these, that is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The genitive complement was omitted because it is evident, and tanwīn (nunation) was substituted for it in kullan, a tanwīn of compensation for the omitted genitive complement, as is the preferred view.

The benefit of mentioning their guidance is to honour Isaac and Jacob, and to show that they were prophets who attained God's guidance just as Abraham did. It also includes a refutation of polytheism, a rebuke to Quraysh and the polytheist Arabs, and a condemnation of them by establishing that the famous righteous people held views opposed to their beliefs, as will be stated explicitly in His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ هُدى اللَّهِ يَهْدِي بِهِ مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ ولَوْ أشْرَكُوا لَحَبِطَ عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("That is the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been worthless") [al-Anʿām: 88].

The clause ﴿ونُوحًا هَدَيْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ("And Noah, We guided before") is conjoined to the interjected clause, meaning: and We guided Noah before them. This is a digression (istiṭrād) by mentioning some of those upon whom God bestowed guidance, and an indication that guidance is the origin, and among the greatest guidance is monotheism, as you know.

[p. 338]

Noah is in the accusative as a direct object placed before "hadaynā" (We guided) for emphasis. "Min qablu" (before) is a circumstantial adjunct (ḥāl) of "Nūḥan." The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is to draw attention to the fact that guidance is rooted in the origins of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Qablu is built on a ḍamma, according to what is well known regarding qablu and its sisters, when the genitive complement that qablu is attached to is omitted, its meaning is intended but not its wording.

The biography of Noah has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى آدَمَ ونُوحًا﴾ ("Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah") [Āl ʿImrān: 33], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

His words "min dhurriyyatihi" (from his descendants) are a circumstantial adjunct of "Dāwūd." Dāwūd is the omitted direct object of "hadaynā." The benefit of this circumstance is to honour these enumerated persons with the nobility of their origin and the origin of their merit, and to honour Abraham or Noah with the virtues of his descendants.

The pronoun attached to it refers to Noah, not to Abraham, because Noah is the nearest mentioned, and because Lot is among the descendants of Noah and not among the descendants of Abraham, as is stated in the Torah. It is possible that Lot was treated as a descendant of Abraham because of his close connection to him. It is also possible that the mention of his name after the list of those who are descendants of Abraham ends is in the accusative for praise, by implying a verb, not as a conjunction.

Some of the biography of Dāwūd has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿وقَتَلَ داوُدُ جالُوتَ﴾ ("And David killed Goliath") in Surat al-Baqarah. We complete it here: he is Dāwūd son of Jesse (Yissi), from the tribe of Judah among the Children of Israel. He was born in the village of Bethlehem around 1085 BCE, and died in Jerusalem around 1015 BCE. In his youth he was a shepherd of his father's sheep, and he had knowledge of melody, playing instruments, and slinging with a sling. God revealed to Samuel (Shamwīl), the prophet of the Children of Israel, to bless Dāwūd son of Jesse and anoint him with holy oil so that he would be king over the Children of Israel, according to the traditions of the Children of Israel, announcing that he would become king over Israel after the death of Saul (Shāʾūl), whom God was angry with. When Samuel anointed him in the village of Bethlehem without anyone knowing, [p. 339] it occurred to Saul, who was ill, to take someone who would play the lute for him when the illness overcame him. It happened that they chose Dāwūd for him, so he admitted him among his courtiers to hear his melodies. When Saul's army fought the Canaanites, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, victory went to the Israelites because of Dāwūd, when he struck the Philistine champion Goliath (Jālūt) with his sling between his eyes, felled him, and cut off his head. For this reason Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage. Then Saul turned against Dāwūd, and Dāwūd went out to the land of the Philistines and gathered a group under his leadership. When Saul was killed in the year 1055, a group of the Israelite army in Palestine pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He made Hebron his seat of government. After seven years, the king of Israel who succeeded Saul was killed, and all the Israelites pledged allegiance to Dāwūd as king over them. He returned to Jerusalem, God gave him prophethood, and commanded him to write the Psalms (al-Zabūr), called by the Jews "al-Mazāmīr."

Sulaymān's biography has been given at the words of the Exalted: ﴿واتَّبَعُوا ما تَتْلُو الشَّياطِينُ عَلى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمانَ﴾ ("And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon") [al-Baqarah: 102], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ayyūb (Job) is a prophet whose prophethood the Qur'an affirmed. He has a detailed story in the book known as the Book of Job, among the books of the Jews. Some historians think that Job was a descendant of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. Others thought he was a grandson of Esau son of Isaac son of Abraham. In his book, it is stated that Job lived in the land of Uz, which is the land of Hauran in Syria, and it is the dwelling place of the sons of Uz son of Aram son of Shem son of Noah, and they are the origin of ʿĀd, and it was adjacent to the borders of the land of the Chaldeans. The names of places are mentioned in the Book of Job. Some scholars think he was of Arab origin and was from Uz, as indicated by the absence of any mention of his lineage in his book, and by restricting it to saying he was in the land of Uz, who are of the original Arabs (al-ʿArab al-ʿĀribah). They claimed that his speech recorded in his book was in the Arabic language, and that Moses, peace be upon him, translated it into Hebrew. Some think that the speech attributed to him was poetry which Moses translated in his book, and that it was the first poetry known in the original Arabic language. Others say it was the first poetry known to history, because his speech and the speech of his three companions who consoled him for his calamities was necessarily in a poetic style.

Yūsuf (Joseph) is the son of Jacob, and the detailed biography will come in Surat Yūsuf.

Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron) and Zakariyyā (Zechariah) have had their biographies covered in Surat al-Baqarah. The biography of ʿĪsā (Jesus) has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Āl ʿImrān. Yaḥyā (John) has had his biography covered in Āl ʿImrān.

His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ ("And thus We reward the good-doers") are an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses, and the "wa" is for a circumstantial sense, meaning: and thus the gift which We gave to Abraham and the guidance which We gave to his descendants, We reward the good-doers like it. Or: and thus the guidance which We gave the descendants of Noah, We reward the good-doers like Noah. It is therefore known that Noah or Abraham were among the good-doers by way of metonymy (kināyah). The good-doing of Noah is derived from this interjected clause, and the good-doing of Abraham is derived from what God related about him: his calling his people and his exerting every effort to turn them away from their error.

It is also possible that the reference here is to the guidance derived from the first and second "hadaynā," meaning: and thus with this great guidance We reward the good-doers, meaning with its like. The "good-doers" then refers to those guided ones among the descendants of Noah or the descendants of Abraham. The meaning is that they did good, and the reward for their good was that We made them prophets.

As for Ilyās (Elijah), he is known in the books of the Israelites as Elijah (Eliya), and in the lands of the Arabs he is called Ilyās or Mār Ilyās, and he is Elijah the Tishbite. The commentators mention that he was Ilyās son of Phinehas son of Eleazar, or son of Aaron, brother of Moses, so he would be from the tribe of Levi. He existed in the time of King Ahab (Ākhāb), king of Israel, around the year 918 BCE. He was an Israelite from the inhabitants of Gilead (Jilʿād), with a kasra on the jīm and sukūn on the lām, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, and Baalbek is from it. Ilyās was from the tribe of Reuben or from the tribe of Gad, and these two tribes were the inhabitants of the region of Gilead. Elijah is called "al-Tishbī" in the books of the Jews. God sent him to the Children of Israel when they worshipped idols in the time of King Ahab, and they worshipped Baal, the idol of the Canaanites. Elijah admonished them, and there are accounts of his dealings with them. God commanded him to appoint Elisha (al-Yasaʿ) as his successor in prophethood. Then God raised Elijah to heaven in a whirlwind, and no trace of him was seen afterwards. Elisha succeeded him in prophethood during the reign of King Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel.

His words ﴿كُلٌّ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ("each of them among the righteous") are an interjected clause. The tanwīn in "kullun" is a compensation for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all of these enumerated persons. It includes all those mentioned, Isaac and whoever came after him.

As for Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), his biography has been covered in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Yasaʿ (Elisha): his name in Hebrew is Elisha (ʾElīshaʿ), with a broken hamza with a kasra, followed by a lām with a yāʾ after it, then a shīn with a dot, then an ʿayn. Its Arabicised form is al-Yasaʿ, with a hamzat al-waṣl and a lām with a sukūn at its beginning, followed by a yāʾ with a fatḥa, in the reading of the majority.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read "al-Laysaʿ" with a hamzat al-waṣl, a fatḥa on the lām, shaddah, followed by a yāʾ with sukūn, on the pattern of ḍaygham. So these are two dialectal forms of it. He was son of Shafāṭ from the people of Abel-Meholah (Ābul Maḥūlah). He was a farmer whom God chose for prophethood through the messenger Elijah during the time of Ahab, and he accompanied Elijah. When Elijah was raised, he kept to the way of Elijah, and miracles appeared to him for the Children of Israel in Jericho (Arīḥā) and elsewhere. He died during the reign of King Joash (Yūʾāsh), king of Israel, and his death was in the year 840 BCE, and he was buried in Samaria (al-Sāmirah). The alif and lām in "al-Yasaʿ" are part of the original word, but the hamza was treated like a hamzat al-waṣl for lightness, so it came to resemble a name into which the lām is added to indicate its origin, like al-ʿAbbās, while it is not one of them.

[p. 343]

As for Yunus, he is the son of Matta, and his name in Hebrew is (Yunan ibn Amittai). He was from the tribe of (Zabulon). In Arabic, his nun may be vocalized with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. He was born in the town of (Gath-hepher) in Palestine. God sent him to the people of (Nineveh) in the lands of Assyria. Its people at that time were a mixture of Assyrians and Jews who were captives of the Assyrians. When he called them to faith and they refused, he threatened them with punishment.
