The punishment was delayed, so he left in anger and went to (Jaffa). There he boarded a ship of the Phoenicians to go to (Tarshish), a city west of Palestine, west of Tyre, on the sea. It may be that it is one of the harbors of the sea-facing side of Egypt, or one of the harbors of Barqa, because the Jewish books describe that gold, silver, apes, and peacocks were brought to Solomon from Tarshish. Thus it is determined that Tarshish had trade with Abyssinia or the Sudan, and that these products were exported from it. It has been said that it is Tartusha, one of the harbors of al-Andalus. It has also been said that it is Carthage, the port of Ifriqiya near Tunis. It has been said in our histories that the name of Tunis before the Islamic conquest was Tarshish. This is plausible, because its trade with the Sudan may be closer. The sea then rose against the ship, it became heavy, and its sinking was feared. So they cast lots, and Yunus was among those who lost in the drawing. He was thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him. He called out from its belly: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]. God answered him, and the fish cast him onto the shore. God sent him a second time to the people of Nineveh, and they believed; they numbered more than one hundred thousand. His period was at the beginning of the eighth century BC. We have not established the date of his death. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in al-Ahkam, in the commentary on Surat al-Saffat, that his grave is in the village of Jaljun between Jerusalem and the town of al-Khalil, and that he visited it during his journey. The accounts of Yunus will come in Surat Yunus, Surat al-Anbiya, and Surat al-Saffat.

As for Lut, he is the son of Haran ibn Terah, so he is the nephew of Ibrahim. He was born in (Ur of the Chaldeans). His father died before Terah, so Terah took Lut into his care. When Terah died, Lut was living with Ibrahim in the land of Haran (Hauran), after Terah, the father of Ibrahim, had left Ur of the Chaldeans, both heading for the land of Canaan. Ibrahim migrated with Lut to Egypt because of a famine that struck the lands of Canaan. Then they returned to the lands of Canaan. Ibrahim and Lut separated because of a dispute that arose between their herdsmen. Lut moved to (Sodom), which is east of the Jordan, until he was inspired to leave it when God decreed its destruction as a punishment for its people. He went out to (Zoar) with his daughter and his offspring there, who are (the Moabites) and (the children of Ammon).

His saying ﴿And We preferred each over the worlds﴾ is a parenthetical sentence, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis. The tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement that was omitted, meaning: each of those mentioned, from Isaac up to here. (Kull) requires that what it is attached to be encompassing. The rule of encompassment is that the judgment applies to each individual one by one, not to the group as a whole. The intended meaning is that each one of them is preferred over the worlds of people of his own age, except for one who was more excellent than him or equal to him. So the lam in (al-'alamin) is the lam of conventional comprehensiveness. Lut lived in the time of Ibrahim, and Ibrahim was more excellent than him. Among others there were people who lived in one era, and the preference of one of them over another is not known. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: it is possible to say that the intended meaning is that each of the prophets is preferred over every other of the worlds. Then the discussion after this concerns which of the prophets is more excellent than the other; that is a discussion on another topic with no connection to the first. End of quotation. This is not correct, because the requirement of the rule of encompassment is judgment on each individual one by one.

A significant issue of the principles of religion (usul al-din) is connected to this verse: the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, and what follows from establishing that regarding faith and the rights of prophethood. The exegetes have neglected to mention it, though it should have been addressed, because it branches into issues that students of the Islamic sciences need to know, and the most fitting place to mention it is this verse and what has the same meaning as some of it. As for the validity of the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in it, that is because God, the Exalted, said, after counting their names, that these are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and prophethood. So the prophethood of them is an established matter, because the demonstrative (ulaika, "those") is close to explicit text in referring to all the named persons before it, together with what supports and completes it of explicit text on the prophethood of some of them in verses similar to this verse, such as the verse of Surat al-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾ [al-Nisa: 163] and the verses following it, and such as the verses of Surat Maryam: ﴿And mention in the Book Ibrahim﴾ [Maryam: 41] and the verses following it.

Prophethood carries many rulings related to the one who possesses it and to how Muslims treat the one who is characterized by it. Among them: the meaning of (nabi, prophet) and (rasul, messenger); the meaning of the miracle (mu'jiza), which is the proof of the realization of prophethood or messengership for the one who brings it; and what follows from that of the obligation to believe in what he conveys from God, the Exalted, of law and ethics. Many issues of this are expounded in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam), so refer to it. What concerns us of this in this commentary is what His saying, the Exalted, at its end hints at: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Whoever knows these verses in this surah and knows their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to believe in the prophethood of those whose names are mentioned in them.

Our scholars have mentioned that believing that God sent messengers and appointed prophets to guide people is obligatory in general, meaning belief in the sending of unspecified individuals, or in the prophethood of unspecified individuals, without specifying any particular person by name or by anything else that distinguishes him from others, except Muhammad (ﷺ). Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risala: The one who sends (a attribute of God, the Exalted) the messengers to them to establish the proof against them. So the sending of messengers is permissible with regard to God and not obligatory, and it occurs in general, without specifying a particular person. The author of al-Maqasid mentioned that the sending of messengers is needed, and it is a kindness from God to His creation, and it is not obligatory upon Him. The Mu'tazilites and a group of theologians (i.e., from the People of the Sunna) from beyond the river (Transoxiana) said that the sending of messengers is obligatory upon God, the Exalted.

None of our imams mentioned the obligation of believing in a particular prophet other than Muhammad (ﷺ) as a messenger to all creation. Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said: Then He sealed - meaning God - the messengership, the warning, and the prophethood with Muhammad, His prophet (ﷺ), etc., because the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab about Jibril's asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith, that he said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers," etc. He did not specify particular messengers. And in answer to his question about Islam, he said: "Islam is that you testify that there is no deity but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

Whoever knows these verses and understands their meaning, it becomes obligatory for him to hold the belief in the prophethood of those mentioned in them. Perhaps many do not recite them, and many of those who recite them do not understand their implications correctly. They are not required to seek out understanding of them and belief in what they indicate, since that is not among the principles of faith and Islam, but it belongs to the deeper understanding of religion (tafaqquh fi al-din).

Al-Qadi Iyad said in the seventh section of the chapters of the third chapter of the fourth part of his book al-Shifa: All of this (i.e., what he mentioned of the imposition of disbelief or of a crime that requires punishment on whoever speaks about them in a way that contradicts what is due to them) concerning those about whom something is said, i.e., the prophets or the angels, by what we have stated regarding the totality of the angels and prophets, i.e., regarding their collectivity and not regarding each one of them, as al-Khafaji said. By "all" he means every single individual of those whose being among them we have verified, either by explicit mention in His Book, or by verifying their knowledge through mass-transmitted report (mutawatir), definite consensus (ijma'), and a famous report agreed upon. The "waw" in this division means "or." As for the one whose announcement of his identity has not been established and on whom there is no consensus that he is among the prophets, such as al-Khidr, Luqman, Dhu al-Qarnayn, Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, and Khalid ibn Sinan, who is mentioned as the prophet of the people of al-Rass, then the ruling regarding the one who reviles them or disbelieves in them is not the same as the ruling regarding what we have mentioned before. End of quotation.

When you know this, you know that what occurred in three verses composed by someone, which Shaykh Ibrahim al-Bayjuri mentioned in the section on faith in his commentary on Jawhara al-Tawhid:

It is a binding duty on everyone who is under obligation to know the prophets in detail, who are known.
Among them, for our proof, are eight, after ten; and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and with the Chosen One they are sealed.

This does not hold except with forced interpretation, because the knowledge of that being "binding" (hatm) according to its technical sense implies that it is obligatory, and no one holds this. If he meant by "binding" a matter that should not be neglected, then it is emphatic in relation to his saying "on everyone who is under obligation." So if he had replaced it with "everyone who is under instruction," it would be better.

Perhaps he meant by "binding" that it is necessarily incumbent upon whoever knows this not to deny that these are prophets by specific identification. But he intended a distinction between the obligation to know something and the prohibition of denying it after it has become known.

As for the messengership of Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb, their mention has been repeated in many verses.

As for knowing the prophethood of Dhu al-Kifl, there is room for consideration, since in Surat al-Anbiya he is described only as one of the patient and the righteous. The exegetes differed concerning several of the prophets, and it is attributed to the majority that he was a prophet. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid reported that Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet. The mention of this will come in Surat al-Anbiya.

As for Adam, he was a prophet from the time he was in the Garden, for God spoke to him more than once. He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, relented toward him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. So he was sent down to the earth honored with the attribute of prophethood. The story of the two sons of Adam in Surat al-Ma'ida indicates that Adam conveyed a law to his sons, according to His saying, the Exalted, in it: ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous. If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I will not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin and be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 27].

So what we rely upon is that whoever denies the prophethood of a particular person named in the Qur'an among the prophets, in Surat al-Nisa, Surat Hud, Surat al-An'am, and Surat Maryam, and the one denying knows for certain the verse in which he is described as a prophet, and he has been informed of the evidence for the validity of what he denies and has been brought back to it, but he insists on denying it, then that denial is disbelief, because he denied something known by necessity after having been alerted to it, so that he cannot excuse himself by ignorance or by an acceptable interpretation.

[p. 347]

Know that I sought to uncover the veil over the reason for limiting the mention of these prophets to the prophets from among the offspring of Abraham or the offspring of Noah, on the two readings concerning the referent of the pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyatihi). It did not become clear to me. I also sought the reason for this particular order of their names and for the linking of some of these names to others by conjunction, but it did not appear to me. My strongest assumption is that among these aspects is that these men were known to the People of the Book and to the polytheists who borrowed their knowledge of the prophets from the People of the Book. Also, the reason for their order may arise from beginning with the mention that Isaac and Jacob were a gift to Abraham, and they were a father and his son. So the transition from one to another arose through a connection that made the transition appropriate. Also, the distribution of their names over three verse-endings (fawasil, sing. fasilah, the rhyming unit at the end of a verse) does not lack a connection that gathers the owners of those names in the single verse-ending that includes all of them. It is possible that the lightness of these names when Arabicized, in letters and in meter, had an effect in their being singled out for mention over other names, such as Shm'un (Simeon), Shmwyl (Samuel), Hizqyal (Ezekiel) and Nahmiya (Nehemiah). Also, those counted in these three verses were distributed among virtues. Among them are messengers, prophets, kings, and people of noble and honorable character: patience, struggle against the self, struggle in the way of God, and perseverance
[p. 348]
in conveying monotheism (tawhid), the law (shari'ah), and noble character. This is what His saying at the end of the verses indicates: "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood. And among them are the two roots of the Arab and Israelite nations."

When He mentioned Isaac and Jacob, He followed their mention with the mention of two prophets from the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, who are a father and his son among the prophets: David and Solomon. He began with them before the rest of the offspring of Isaac and Jacob, because they attained two great glories: the glory of the Hereafter through prophethood, and the glory of this world through kingship. Then He followed with the mention of "two prophets" who were alike in that harm befell both of them and that relief from their distress came through their patience: they are Job and Joseph. Then, with the mention of two brothers, messengers, Moses and Aaron. Moses suffered the like of what befell Joseph: plotting against him to kill him, his deliverance from that, and his being raised in the house of kingship. So these six were included in the first verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And thus do We reward the good-doers."

Then with the mention of two prophets, a father and his son: Zechariah and John (Yahya). It was appropriate that after them there be mentioned two messengers who had no offspring: Jesus ('Isa) and Elias (Ilyas). They are alike in that both were raised up to heaven. As for Jesus, his ascension is mentioned in the Qur'an. As for Elias, his ascension is mentioned in the books of the Israelites, and the commentators among the early generations did not mention it. It has been said that Elias is Idris, and on this basis his elevation is mentioned in His saying: "And mention in the Book Idris; indeed he was a truthful one and a prophet" [Maryam: 56], and "We raised him to a high station" in Surah Maryam. Jesus was mentioned first as a conjunction following John, because they were close, being cousins on the mother's side, and because Jesus was a messenger while Elias was a prophet who was not a messenger. These four were included in the second verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "All of them were of the righteous." He linked Elisha (al-Yasa') because he was the successor and disciple of Elias. He placed between Elias and Elisha the mention of Ishmael, a conclusion by mentioning the prophet to whom the lineage of the Arabs from the offspring of Abraham traces back. They were concluded with Jonah (Yunus) and Lot, because each of them was sent to a small nation. These four were included in the third verse-ending, which ends with His saying: "And We preferred each over the worlds."
[p. 349]
His saying "and of their fathers" is conjoined to His saying "each." So the sense is: "And We guided some of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took "min" (of) as a noun meaning "some," that is: "And We guided some of their fathers," according to his method in His saying: "Of those who are Jews, they distort [words]" (al-Nisa': 46). Ibn 'Atiyyah and those who followed him supposed that the conjoined object is omitted, its estimate being: "And of their fathers, a great multitude, or many who were guided." Then "min" is partitive and linked to "We guided."

The dhurriyyat (offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, and it refers to those who descend from a human being: sons, the nearer ones, and their sons. So it includes the children of sons and the children of daughters. Its being in the plural is intended to show that guidance attached to the offspring of each of those mentioned who had offspring, to indicate that in the guidance of some of the offspring there is honor for the forefather. So each one of these is meant to have guidance occur in his offspring, even though their offspring trace back to a single forefather, Noah, peace be upon him. Then, if the guidance meant is the guidance similar to the guidance explicitly stated, which is the guidance of prophethood, then "fathers" includes figures like Adam and Idris, peace be upon them, for they are the fathers of Noah. "Offspring" includes the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Joshua (Yusha') and Daniel (Danyal). They are from the offspring of Noah and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The prophets from the sons of Ishmael, peace be upon him, include figures such as Hanzalah ibn Safwan and Khalid ibn Sinan, and Hud and Salih from the offspring of Noah, and Shu'ayb from the offspring of Abraham. "Brothers" includes the rest of the tribes, the brothers of Joseph.

If what is meant by guidance is what is more general than prophethood, it includes the righteous among the fathers, such as Abel (Habil) son of Adam. And "offspring" includes all the righteous of the nations, such as the People of the Cave, of whom He said: "And We increased them in guidance" (al-Kahf: 13). It also includes Saul (Talut), king of Israel, and Mudar and Rabi'ah, for it has been transmitted that they were both Muslims, narrated by al-Daylami from Ibn 'Abbas. It also includes the believer of the family of Pharaoh and the wife of Pharaoh. "Brothers" includes Haran son of Terah, brother of Abraham, who was the father of Lot, and Esau (Eisu), brother of Jacob, and others besides these whom God the Exalted knows.
[p. 350]
Al-ijtiba' (selection, ijtiba': choosing and preferring) is the act of choosing and selecting. They said it is derived from al-jabi, which means gathering, and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (collection of land tax). Also jaby al-ma' in the basin, from which the basin (al-jabiyah) is named. So the infixed form (ifti'al) in it is for emphasis, like al-idtirar (compulsion). The basis of the derivation is that gathering only happens for something desired, to obtain it because one needs it. The meaning is: God chose them and made them the place of His guidance, because He knows best where to place His message, His prophethood, and His guidance.

He conjoined His saying "and We guided them" to "We chose them" with a conjunction that emphasizes the affirmation of their guidance, out of concern for this guidance. So He explained that He guided them to a straight path (sirat mustaqim), that is, to that by which one attains what the people of perfection strive to attain. So He made the straight path an example for this, comparing the state of one who acts to attain the perfection he seeks to the state of one who walks upon a straight road that brings him to what he wants, proceeding without hesitation, confusion, or going astray. He mentioned from the words of the compound expression that indicates the state being compared only a part of it, which is "the straight path," because it indicates all the omitted words for brevity.

The straight path is monotheism (tawhid) and faith in what must be believed of the fundamental virtues in which the revealed laws (shara'i') agree. The purpose, along with praising them, is an allusion to the polytheists who opposed their creed, as indicated by His saying after that: "Those are the guided by God," up to His saying: "And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been void from them" (al-An'am: 88).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 88:

﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides thereby whom He wills of His servants. And had they associated others with Him, all that they used to do would have been rendered worthless for them.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), meaning: do not be amazed at their guidance and the misguidance of others.

The reference to "guidance" (al-huda), which is a verbal noun derived from the three verbs of guidance mentioned in the preceding verse, and especially the one mentioned last in His words, ﴿And We guided them to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 87]. The demonstrative has increased the emphasis on the matter of guidance, as it is treated as though it were something present before the eye, so the demonstrative adds complete distinction. He described the guidance as "the guidance of Allah" to ennoble its matter and to show that it is protected from error and misguidance. In this there is an allusion to what the polytheists hold of what they claim to be guidance and receive from their elders, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who established the worship of idols for them, and like the soothsayers (kuhhan) and their kind. This statement has come in the manner of a summary (fadhlaka) of the states of guidance that have been repeatedly mentioned, like the verses of Hatim al-Ta'i:

"For Allah there is a poor man (su'luk) whose resolve engages him, and who proceeds against misfortunes and time, advancing."

Then, after seven more verses in praise of that poor man, he said:

"So if he perishes, his praise is good, and if he lives, he will not sit down weak and blamed."

His words, the Exalted, ﴿He guides thereby whom He wills of His servants﴾, is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relative to "the guidance of Allah." What is meant by "whom He wills" are those whom Allah has chosen and selected. He knows best about them and their readiness to receive His guidance, their abandoning of obstinacy, their turning toward seeking good, their aspiring toward it, and their progressing in it until they reach the rank of Allah bestowing upon them revelation, or success and true inspiration.

So in His words "whom He wills" there is a vagueness that moves souls to seek the guidance of Allah the Exalted and to expose themselves to His breezes. In it there is also an allusion to the polytheists who denied the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ out of envy, and for this reason He followed it with His words, ﴿And had they associated others with Him, all that they used to do would have been rendered worthless for them﴾, to magnify the matter of polytheism and that it is not forgiven for anyone, even if he reached a great level of virtuous deeds, like those mentioned and praised. "The waw" is for the circumstantial. "Habita" means "perished," i.e., its reward became void. It has already been mentioned in His words, the Exalted, ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 89:

﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, judgment, and prophethood. But if these (disbelievers) reject them, We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.﴾

Page 352

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) serving to honour them. It is a second summary (fadhlaka, a concluding recapitulation), because the first summary refers back to the guidance mentioned in the preceding verses, whereas this one refers back to the fact that they are among those guided.

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is used to add emphasis on distinguishing them and to fix their conduct firmly in the minds of the hearers. Those referred to are the ones named individually and the ones mentioned in summary in His words "and from their fathers, their offspring and their brothers."

"﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾" is the predicate (khabar) of the demonstrative.

By "the Book" is meant the category: that is, the books (kutub). The giving of a Book may be by sending down that which is written, as was sent down to the messengers and some of the prophets; and what was sent down to them is considered a book, because its nature is that it be written, whether or not it was actually written. The Qur'an explicitly states that Abraham had scrolls, in His words "the scrolls of Abraham and Moses." Jesus had his speech which was written in the Gospel. David had the speech that issued from him as a proclamation from God, and he was a prophet (nabi') but not a messenger (rasul). Solomon had the Proverbs, the Ecclesiastes (al-Jami'ah), and the Song (al-Nashid) attributed to him, all three being rulings that God commanded. It is said that Idris wrote wisdom in scrolls; he is the one whom the Israelites call (Akhnukh), the Copts call (Tuta), and the sages call (Hermes). The giving of the Book may also be by giving the prophet the understanding and clarification of the books revealed before him, as was given to the prophets of the Children of Israel after Moses, such as Yahya, to whom He said, "O Yahya, take the Book with strength."

"Judgment" (hukm) is wisdom (hikmah), that is, knowledge of the paths of good and of averting evil. He said concerning Yahya, "And We gave him judgment while he was a child" [Maryam: 12], and Yahya was not a judge (hakim), that is, a qadi; judgment may also be interpreted as judging with truth, as in His words concerning David and Solomon, "And to each We gave judgment and knowledge."

The giving of these three is distributed: some were given all of them, namely the messengers among them and the prophets who judged between people, such as David and Solomon; and some were given some of them, namely the prophets who were not messengers, and the righteous among them who were not prophets. This is according to the inclusion of the demonstrative of their fathers, offspring and brothers.

Page 353

The "fa" in His words "﴿But if they reject﴾" is a conjunction linking the conditional clause to the clause "those to whom We gave the Book," and it is made to follow and branch from it, because the purpose of the preceding clauses, from His words "and when Abraham said to his father Azar," is to disparage the matter of polytheism by arguing for its corruption through the rejection of it by people of merit and goodness. Thus the conjunctive fa carries a wonderful placement within the rules of the composition of speech.

The pronoun in "bihā" refers to the things mentioned: the Book, the judgment and the prophethood.

The demonstrative in His words "hā'ulā'" refers to the polytheists of Mecca, and it is a demonstrative for someone present in the minds of the hearers, as it occurs in the hadith on the questioning in the grave, where it is said to him, "What is your knowledge of this man?" meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). And in al-Bukhari, al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I went to help this man," meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

I have surveyed the places of the verses of the Qur'an and found that it frequently expresses the polytheists of Quraysh by the word "hā'ulā'," as in His words, "Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers," and I have not seen anyone draw attention to this before.

The disbelief of the polytheists in the prophethood of those prophets follows from their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and for this reason God later relates of them that they said, "God did not send down anything upon any human being" [al-An'am: 91].

The meaning of "wakkalnā bihā" is: We granted them success in believing in them, observing them, and upholding their rights. Here the entrusting (tawkil) is a metaphor, because the true meaning of entrusting is the owner's assignment of the management of his property to one who takes charge of managing it, relieving him of the burden of guarding it and of caring for what sustains its survival, its goodness and its growth. One says, "I entrusted him with the thing" (wakkaltuhu 'ala al-shay') and "I entrusted him with the thing" (wakkaltuhu bi al-shay'), so it takes "ʿalā" and "bi". In this verse it is used metaphorically for granting success in belief in prophethood, the Book, the judgment, and in considering what they call to and caring for it, likening that care to the care of the agent, and likening the granting of success to it by ascribing consideration to the agent, because agency requires the existence of the entrusted thing in the hand of the agent together with its guarding and care. Thus the metaphor "wakkalnā" with this meaning is a wonderful brevity that corresponds to what the disbelief in them implies of rejecting them, which entails neglecting their limits.

Page 354

"The people" (al-qawm) are the believers who believed in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), the Qur'an, and those before him among the messengers, and what came to them of books, judgment and prophethood. The primary intended referents are the believers who were in Mecca and those among the Ansar in Medina who believed, since this surah was revealed shortly before the Hijrah. The author of al-Kashshaf interpreted "the people" as the prophets previously mentioned, claiming that the structure of the verse compelled him to this, but that is a forced interpretation with no real basis.

Describing the people as "not disbelievers in them" indicates that they hastened to belief in them as soon as they were called to it; therefore the description is made with a nominal clause consisting of (laysa) and its predicate, because laysa functions like a negative particle, being a non-inflecting verb, so its clause indicates the continuing negation of disbelief from them. The preposition bi- was introduced into the predicate of (laysa) to emphasize that negation, so it becomes a continuous, emphatic negation.

The meaning is: if the polytheists reject your prophethood and the prophethood of those before you, their disbelief will not harm you, because We have granted success to a people of believers in believing in you and in them. This is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) for the aversion of some of his people from his call.

The placement of the prepositional phrase "bihā" before its governing element in "﴿laysū bihā bikāfirīn﴾" is for the sake of preserving the verse-ending (fasilah), together with attention to the antecedent of the pronoun: the Book, the judgment and the prophethood.

[p. 355]

﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance.﴾

This is an independent sentence, begun afresh for the purpose of drawing attention to its content. It also serves as a restatement of the two sentences preceding it: "And We guided them to a straight path," and "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and prophethood." Restatement is properly set apart, and the consequent clause "so follow their guidance" is built upon it.

The people indicated by the demonstrative are the same people indicated by the phrase "those to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and prophethood," for they are the ones whom Our Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow in their guidance.

The repetition of the demonstrative serves to confirm the distinction of the one pointed to, and to give the statement the emphasis that repetition implies.

The definiteness of the predicate and the subject conveys a restriction (qaṣr) of the class of "those whom God guided" to those mentioned, both in detail and in summary. This is because the refined among mankind cannot be other than those named, together with their fathers, their offspring and their brothers. Among their fathers is Adam, the father who encompasses all of mankind. Thus "guidance" here means the guidance of mankind, that is, being turned away from error, and the restriction is real. The righteousness of the angels is not considered, for theirs is an innate righteousness.

He turned from the first person pronoun to the explicit divine name to join this statement with awe and majesty.

His saying "so follow their guidance" is a consequence drawn from the perfection of that guidance, and a transition to mentioning the share of Muhammad (ﷺ) in God's guidance, after the prophets and their way had been extensively mentioned before him. This indicates the lofty rank of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that it is a rank worthy of being singled out for mention, since he was not mentioned together with the earlier prophets. It also indicates that he combined the guidance of the earlier ones, that the virtues were completed in him, and that he was granted all the scattered distinctions and great excellences. In singling him out for mention and not counting him among the earlier ones, there is a subtle indication of his unique eminence and singular station, and a subtle regard for the circumstance that his message came after the passing of those distant or adjacent ages. For this reason, he placed the prepositional phrase "by their guidance" before its governing verb, to give importance to that guidance, because it is your comprehensive rank, combining virtues and excellences. It is therefore not fitting for him to follow a guidance that is less than their guidance.

For this reason, no one among those who turned to monotheism (taḥannuf) in the pre-Islamic era, or who became Christian or Jewish, was ever followed by the Prophet (ﷺ). He met Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl before prophethood in Baladaḥ, and offered him to eat with him from his food-cloth. Zayd said, "I do not eat what you slaughter on your idols," supposing that the Prophet (ﷺ) followed the religion of the pre-Islamic era. God inspired Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, to remain silent about answering him, as an inspiration to keep a stored secret, so he did not say to him, "I do not slaughter on an idol." He also met Waraqah ibn Nawfal more than once in Mecca. He met Buhayrā the monk, and did not follow any of those. He remained upon the natural disposition (fiṭrah) until revelation came to him.

The verb iqtadā is a derived form (iftiʿāl) from "qudwah," which may be vocalized with a damma or a kasra on the qāf. Analogy with "iswah" (model) indicates that the kasra is more common in it. Al-Miṣbāḥ says the damma is more common. In the Maqāmāt of al-Ḥarīrī occurs "wa-qudwatu al-shaḥḥādhīn" (and the exemplar of beggars), which is vocalized with a damma. Al-Wāsiṭī mentioned it in his explanation of the words of the Maqāmāt under the qāf with damma, and also related the fatḥa on the qāf, which is rare. The qudwah is the one whose conduct another imitates. No simple verb (fiʿl mujarrad) is known for it in the language, so only "iqtadā" is heard. It seems they regarded qudwah as a fixed noun and derived from it the form iftaʿala to indicate effort, just as they derived from the noun "kharīf" (autumn) "ikhtarafa," from "uswah" "ā'tasā," and from the noun "nimr" (tiger) "tanammara," and from "ḥajar" (stone) "taḥajjara." Qudwah may also be used as a verbal noun for iqtadā. One says, "I have in so-and-so a qudwah," as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed there has been for you in them an excellent example﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah: 6].

In His saying "so follow their guidance" there is an allusion to the polytheists that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not come except upon the way of all the messengers, and that he was not an innovation among the messengers.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) being commanded to follow their guidance indicates that God gathered to him a virtue from their virtues, which each one was singled out for, whether what they shared and agreed upon, or what they differed and diverged on. For one follows only what God has made him aware of from the virtues and biographies of the messengers, and that is the moral character described as great in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4].

[p. 357]

His guidance includes what relates to the foundations of the sharīʿahs (religious laws), and what relates to the purification of the soul and good character. As for what consists of branches from that and detailed rulings, from all that God conveyed to him through revelation, and which He did not command him to follow in Islam, nor clarified its abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of a ruling by a later one), our scholars have differed on whether the divine laws prior to Islam are considered among the rulings of the sharīʿah of Islam when God conveyed them to the Messenger (ﷺ) and did not place in his sharīʿah anything that abrogates them.

I hold that the basis for the argument in this is that when God, the Exalted, mentions in His Book, or reveals to His Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, the narration of a ruling from the earlier sharīʿahs in a context of commendation and favor, and nothing accompanies it indicating that it was legislated as a hardship upon its adherents as a punishment for them, nor anything indicating that it is not to be acted upon, then that indicates that God, the Exalted, wants from the Muslims that they act upon its like, provided that there is nothing among the rulings of Islam contradicting it, nor among its foundations anything rejecting it, such as the foundation of ease. And analogy (qiyās) upon an Islamic ruling should not require anything that contradicts a ruling from the sharīʿahs of those before us. There is no proof in the verses in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow those before him, such as this verse, and such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Naḥl: 123], and such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He has legislated for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13]. This is because what is intended by these is the foundations of religious belief and the bases of legislation about which the sharīʿahs do not differ. Therefore whoever argues from the saying of the Exalted, "so follow their guidance," his argument is weak.

Al-Ghazālī said in al-Mustaṣfā: He intended by "guidance" monotheism and the indication of rational proofs for the oneness of God and His attributes, because He, the Exalted, commanded him to follow their guidance, and if what was meant by guidance were their sharīʿahs, it would be a command to follow differing and abrogating and abrogated laws. So this indicates that He meant the guidance common to all of them. End of quotation. The meaning of this is that the verse does not stand as a proof against the one who disagrees, so there is no barrier to its providing a basis for one who holds the authority of the law of those before us on the attributes I mentioned earlier.

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in the tafsīr of Sūrat Ṣād, it is related from al-ʿAwwām who said: I asked Mujāhid about the prostration of Ṣād, and he said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās, "From where did you prostrate?" (that is, from what evidence did you take to prostrate in this verse, intending that it is a narration about the prostration of David, and there is no command to prostrate in it). He said: Do you not recite, ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾? David was among those whom your Prophet was commanded to follow, so David prostrated for it, and the Messenger of God prostrated for it.

The positions on this question are four.

The first position is the position of Mālik as transmitted by Ibn Bukayr, ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and al-Qarāfī, and they attributed it to most of Mālik's companions: that the laws of those before us are rulings for us, because God conveyed them to us. The evidence for this is what is established in the authentic collections concerning the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the case of al-Rubayyiʿ bint al-Naḍr, when she broke the front tooth of a slave-girl deliberately. He commanded that her tooth be broken. Her mother went back to him and said, "By God, her tooth shall not be broken." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her, "The Book of God is retaliation." And there is no ruling of retaliation for teeth in the Book of God except what He related from the law of the Torah in His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45], up to His saying: ﴿and the tooth for the tooth﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45]. And what is in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God, the Exalted, says in His Book: Establish prayer for My remembrance." He said this only because God said it as a narration of His address to Moses, peace be upon him. And the apparent meaning of this verse, since "guidance" is a verbal noun in construct, its apparent meaning is generality, and it is not granted that context specifies it, as al-Ghazālī held. The scholars of the Mālikīs related something similar from the companions of Abū Ḥanīfah. Likewise Ibn Ḥazm related it from them in his book "al-Iʿrāb fī al-Ḥayrah wa al-Iltibās al-Wāqiʿayn fī Madhāhib Ahl al-Ra'y wa al-Qiyās." In the commentary Tawḍīḥ of Ṣadr al-Sharīʿah it is related from a group of their companions, without specifying them. Al-Qurṭubī related it from many companions of al-Shāfiʿī. It is transmitted in the books of the Ḥanafīs from the general body of al-Shāfiʿī's companions.

The second position: most of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ẓāhirīs held that the law of those before us is not law for us. They argued by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 48]. Al-Qurṭubī attributed this view to many companions of Mālik and companions of al-Shāfiʿī. In Tawḍīḥ of Ṣadr al-Sharīʿah, this view is attributed to a group of their companions.

The third: one is bound to follow the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾. I have not found the identity of the one to whom this view is attributed.

The fourth: one is only bound to follow the law of Jesus, because it is the last of the laws, and it abrogated what came before it. I have not found the identity of the proponent of this view. Ibn Rushd said in al-Muqaddimāt: This is the weakest of the opinions.

The ha' in His saying "iqtadih" (follow him/it) is quiescent (sākinah) according to the majority of reciters. It is the ha' al-sakt (the pausal ha') that is added when pausing on a verb with a weak final radical whose final letter is dropped for the jussive. It is retained in pausal reading and dropped in continuous reading. It was written in the Muṣḥaf, because they used to write word endings in consideration of the state of pause. The majority of reciters retained it in continuous reading, and this is from treating continuous reading as pausal, which occurs in eloquent speech. The better course for the reader is to pause on it, following the more eloquent reading. The majority of reciters kept it quiescent, except the transmission of Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir, for he vocalized it with a kasra. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī explained this reading by saying that it makes the ha' a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of "iqtad" (follow), that is, "follow the following," and not the pausal ha'. It is like the ha' in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a punishment with which I shall not punish anyone of the worlds﴾, meaning, I shall not punish anyone with that punishment. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf omitted the ha' in continuous reading, according to the prevalent analogy.

[p. 360 — continues]

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it. It is only a reminder to the worlds.﴾

This is a new sentence, following that great exposition which comprises the circumstances of many nations. It contains an allusion to the prophethood of a group of prophets and righteous persons, and an explanation of the method of argument in supporting the religion, and that he (ﷺ) came only as the paths of those messengers came. Therefore God concluded it with a command to His Messenger that he should remind his people that he is reminding them, as the messengers reminded their peoples, and that he

I did not come with anything except sincere advice to them, just as the messengers came. He opened the speech with the verb "Say" (qul) to draw attention to its importance, as has been mentioned several times in this surah. He introduced this with His saying: "I ask of you no wage for it," meaning: I am not seeking any benefit for myself in conveying the Qur'an. This is so that it serves as a pointer to the evidence of his truthfulness, for if he wanted some benefit for himself, he would have flattered them and conformed to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, in Surah Hud, at His saying, relating about Hud: ﴿O my people, I ask you for no wage for it. My wage is only from the One who created me. Will you not reason?﴾ [Hud: 51]: No messenger came but that he confronted his people with this statement, because their concern was sincere advice, and sincere advice is not purified or made pure except by cutting off greed. As long as there is any suspicion of it, it neither benefits nor takes effect. End of quote.

I say: Allah also related something similar about Noah in His saying in Surah Hud: ﴿And O my people, I ask you for no wealth for it. My wage is only from Allah﴾ [Hud: 29]. He also said to His Messenger in Surah al-Shura: ﴿Say: I ask you for no wage for it, except affection among relatives﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. So the purpose of His saying "I ask you for no wage for it" is not to refute a belief held by someone or to deny an accusation that had been made, but rather its purpose is admonition and drawing attention to the purely sincere advice of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his mission, and that it is for the benefit of people, from which he draws no benefit for himself.

The pronoun in His saying "for it" ('alayhi) and in His saying "it is not" (in huwa) refers to something known in people's minds; for knowing the intended referent of the pronoun makes mention of its antecedent unnecessary, like His saying, Exalted is He: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [Sad: 32], and as in the hadith of 'Umar in the account of the Prophet's (ﷺ) oath of abstention: "My Ansari companion came down on his turn and struck my door a severe blow and said: Is he there? etc." The implied meaning is: I ask you for no wage in return for the conveying or the calling, and my calling and my conveying are nothing but a reminder through the Qur'an and other statements.

The word "reminder" (dhikra) is a verbal noun of "remembrance" (dhikr, with a kasra), which is the opposite of forgetfulness, and it was mentioned earlier. What is meant here is the reminder of monotheism, resurrection, reward and punishment.

He made the calling a reminder to the worlds because his calling, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is general to all people.

This indicates that the absence of asking a wage from them is for two reasons: first, that it is a reminder and sincere advice for their benefit, so he has no need of any recompense from them; and second, that it is a reminder for others among mankind as well, and is not specific to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being." Say, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people, which you make into scraps (qaratis) that you display while concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say, "God." Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾

The presence of the conjunctive waw at the beginning of this sentence indicates that it was revealed in harmony with the sentences before it, and that both it and what precedes it address one purpose, which is to refute the claims of the polytheists. It is thus a conjunction to the sentence "﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾ [al-An'am: 89]", and it is not an independent sentence addressing a different purpose. The waw of the pronoun in His words "qadaru" (they measured) refers back to what the demonstrative "hā'ulā'" (these) in His words refers to, as you have learned just now. This is because the polytheists, when they sensed that the proof was established against them by the revelation of the Qur'an, that it is not an innovation among what was sent down to the Messengers, and that it refuted their saying, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?", they went to extremes in obstinacy and denial. So they said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being," and they ignored what they used to say about Abraham, peace be upon him, and what they knew of the mission of Moses, peace be upon him, and his Book. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that the ones who said this were the polytheists of Quraysh.

This verse came in this position as a consequence of what preceded it, namely the mention of the prophets and what they brought of guidance, laws and books. Therefore, those who said "God has not sent down anything to any human being" have come with falsehood and lies, and have denied what is known through mass transmission (tawatur) across generations of humankind. This sentence is like what God related about them in His words, "And those who disbelieve say, 'We will never believe in this Qur'an or in what came before it.'" Some of the imams of tafsir (exegesis) made this a report of the saying of some of the Jews, and they differed over whether the speaker was specific or unspecified. From Ibn 'Abbas as well, and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and al-Suddi, it is reported that the one who said "God has not sent down anything to any human being" was some of the Jews. It is also reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah that the speaker was Malik ibn al-Sayf al-Qurazi, who was one of the rabbis of the Jews in Medina, and that he was fat. He came to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet said to him, "I adjure you by Him who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you not find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He became angry and said, "By God, God has not sent down anything to any human being." It is also reported from al-Suddi that its speaker was Finhas the Jew. The meaning of all of this is that the one among them who said it either said it out of ignorance of what is in their books, and so he is among their common people, or he said it out of contentiousness and obstinacy. I suppose that these reports are what led their transmitters to claim that these verses were revealed in Medina, as was mentioned earlier in the discussion of the beginning of this surah.

Accordingly, the placement of these verses in this position is due to the connection with His words, "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book," and the sentence is like an interjection in the course of refuting the arguments of the polytheists. The literal meaning of "qadaru" is that they determined the measure (qadr) and fixed it, i.e., they knew it with certainty.

"Al-qadr" (measure), with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the dal, is the standard or limit of a thing. It is used metaphorically for knowing a matter in its essence and for managing a matter. It is said, "The people measured their affair" (qadaru amrahum, with a damma on the dal in the present tense, yaqduruhu), meaning they fixed it and arranged it. In a hadith, 'A'isha said: "So measure the measure of the young girl who is new in age" (faqdaru qadra al-jariya al-hadītha al-sinn). Here it is used metaphorically for correct knowledge, i.e., they did not recognize God with true recognition, and they did not know His affairs and His dispositions with true knowledge. Thus "haqqa" (true) is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object, because it is attached to the verbal noun "qadrihi" (His measure), and the attribution here is of a quality to what it qualifies. The original form is: "They did not measure God with His true measure."

"Idh qalu" (when they said) is a temporal adverbial clause, meaning: they did not measure Him at the time they said, "God has not sent down...". This is because when they denied a great matter among the affairs of God, namely the matter of His guiding people and conveying His will to them through the Messengers, [page 363] they had already shown ignorance of what leads to ignorance of an attribute of God, the Exalted, which is the attribute of speech, and they ignored His mercy toward people and His kindness to them.

Their saying this includes all of humankind, because the indefinite noun occurs in a context of negation, indicating the negation of the category, and it includes everything that was sent down, by its being connected with "min" (any) in the scope of negation, to indicate that the category is comprehensive as well. It also includes God's sending down revelation to humans, through negating what relates to these two generalities.

By "shay'" (anything) here is meant something of revelation. For this reason God commanded His Prophet to silence them with an interrogative of affirmation and compulsion, in His words, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?" He reminded them of a matter they cannot deny, because it is widely known (mutawatir) in the lands of the Arabs, namely the mission of Moses and his coming with the Torah, which is studied among the Jews in the neighboring town of Mecca. The Jews traveled to Mecca for trade and other purposes, and the people of Mecca traveled to Yathrib and its surroundings, where the Jews and their rabbis were. For this reason God did not remind them of the mission of Abraham, peace be upon him, because they were ignorant that God had sent down scrolls to him, so there could be a dispute about the manner of his mission and prophethood. Since this cannot be denied, as the answer at the end of the verse requires with His words, "Say, 'God,'" it is established that God sent down a Book to one of the human beings. Thus their saying "God has not sent down anything to any human being" is refuted, according to the rule for refuting a universal negative with a particular affirmative. The command to say was placed first to emphasize this silencing, and otherwise the whole Qur'an is something the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to say.

"Nur" (light) is a metaphor for clarity and truth, since truth is likened to light, just as falsehood is likened to darkness. Abu al-Qasim 'Ali al-Tanukhi said:

"It is as if the stars amid its darkness are customs, among which a novelty has appeared."

For this reason "huda" (guidance) is conjoined to it. A parallel is His words in surah al-Ma'idah: "Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light" [al-Ma'idah: 44]. If "light" were applied to the cause of guidance, it would be correct, were it not for this conjunction, as God said about the Qur'an: "But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants" [al-Shura: 52]. "Nuran" (as light) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

By "al-nas" (the people) is meant the Jews, i.e., so that it might guide them. The definite article in it is for comprehensiveness, but it is a customary comprehensiveness, i.e., the people who are his own people, the Children of Israel.

His words "taj'aluna-hu qarati-sa" (you make it into scraps) may be a causal attribute of the Book, and it may be an interjection between the conjoined items.

The readers differed. Those among the ten readers other than Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "tajʿalūnahu" (you make it), "tubdūnahā" (you display them) and "tukhfūna" (you conceal) with the second-person marker (ta' of address). Given this, either the address is to people other than the polytheists, since it is apparent that they had no role in the Book that was sent down to Moses, nor did they engage in displaying some of it and concealing some of it. Thus it is necessary that it be an address to the Jews, by way of "idmaj" (interweaving, i.e., moving from one address to another), as an allusion to the Jews and as a way of making them hear it, even though they were not present, in the manner of "I address you, but mean you, and listen, O neighbor." Or it is an "iltifat" (shift) from the third-person form, which is what the context requires, to the second-person form of address. The proper form would be "yajʿalūnahu" with the imperfect third-person ya', as the other readers besides these three read.

Or it is an address to the polytheists. The meaning of them making the Book of Moses into scraps, displaying some of it and concealing some of it, is that they asked the Jews about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and the Jews read to them what is in the Torah about adherence to the Sabbath, i.e., the religion of the Jews, and concealed the mention of the Messenger ﷺ who would come after. So the concealing and displaying are ascribed to the polytheists metaphorically, because they were a manifestation of that concealing and displaying. Perhaps this happened from the Jews after Islam entered Medina and some of the Aws and Khazraj embraced Islam, when the Jews realized the harmful consequences of that for them, so they incited the polytheists with what would increase their determination to oppose. I have already presented [page 364] evidence that supports the view that Surat al-An'am was revealed at the end of the period the Messenger of God ﷺ spent in Mecca, and that leads us to think that this period was the beginning of the Jews' interference with Quraysh in opposing the Islamic call in Mecca, when it reached Medina.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "yajʿalūnahu, yubdūnahā, yukhfūna" with the third-person ya'. Thus the third-person pronouns refer to something known to the speaker, namely the Jews of that time who were known for this.

"Qaraṭīs" is the plural of "qirṭās" (sheet, paper). It was discussed earlier in His words, "And even if We had sent down to you a Book on paper" [al-An'am: 7] in this surah. It is a page, of whatever material it was, whether of parchment, paper or cloth. That is, you make the Book that was sent down to Moses into scattered pages, intending to display some of it and conceal another part of it.

His words "tubdūnahā wa tukhfūna kathīran" (you display them and conceal much) are a qualifier of "qaraṭīs": you display some of them and conceal much of them. So it is understood that the meaning is: you make it into pages for the purpose of displaying some and concealing some.

This qualifying clause is in a position of blame, because God sent down His Books for guidance, and guidance by them depends on displaying them and making them known. Whoever divides them to display some and conceal some has opposed God's purpose in them. But if they had made it into pages for some other purpose, their act would not be blameworthy, just as the Muslims wrote the Qur'an in separate parts for the purpose of aiding recitation, and as the writing of tablets in the kuttab (Qur'anic schools) is for a benefit.

In the Jami' al-'Utbiyya, in the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim from Malik: Malik, may God have mercy on him, was asked about the Qur'an being written in sixths (asdas) and sevenths (asbā') in the mushafs (copies). He strongly disliked this and criticized it, and said, "The Qur'an should not be divided, and God has gathered it, while these people divide it, and I do not approve of that." End of quotation.

Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: The Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ piece by piece until it was complete and gathered together as a whole. Therefore it is necessary to preserve its being gathered. This is the reason for Malik's dislike of dividing it. End of quotation.

I say: Perhaps he disliked it out of fear that it would become a means to the scattering of the parts of a single mushaf, so that one part of it would fall into the hands of some Muslims, who would then assume that this part is the whole Qur'an. The meaning of Malik's words, "God has gathered it," is that God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to gather it after it had been sent down in installments. This indicates that God intended its gathering, so it should not be divided into parts. The jurists of the school have permitted dividing the Qur'an for learning, and touching a part of it without wudu', and among this is writing it on tablets.

His words "wa 'ullimtum mā lam ta'lamū" (and you were taught what you did not know) are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from a speech that is implied, indicated by the force of the interrogative, because it has the force of "inform me," since the interrogative includes the meaning of a verb.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 91 (part 2 of 2):

The use of the interrogative with the noun that signifies seeking to specify the agent of the sending down (inzal) strengthens the sense of the verb within the interrogation, since the interrogative noun includes both a verb and an agent, both of which are the subject of the question. That is, "Tell me about that, when Allah has taught you through the Qur'an, which you denied was from Allah, [things] you did not know." You argued for denying it by negating that Allah would send down anything to a human being. Had you been fair, you would have found that the sign of its descent from Allah is firmly present in it, so there is no need, with it, to seek proof for it. This address applies more precisely to the polytheists, because they had no knowledge of the reports of the prophets or of the conditions and organization of revelation. When Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, came to them, those who believed came to know that with firm knowledge, and those who remained in their disbelief came to know it through what reached them from hearing the Qur'an at the call and from their mingling with the Muslims. Allah described them with the like of this in other verses, such as His saying, ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you; neither you nor your people knew it before this﴾.

It is also possible that the clause "and you were taught" (wa 'ullimtum) is coordinated with the clause "who sent down the Book" (anzal al-kitab), according to the meaning, as if it were said: "and He taught you what you did not know."

The reason the verb 'ullimtum is in the passive form is the prominence of the agent, and because he will say, "Say: Allah" (qul Allah).

If we interpret the verse according to the narration about Malik ibn al-Sayf mentioned earlier, then the interrogative with the words "who sent down the Book" is affirmative (taqriri), either to refute the apparent content of their statement, [namely] the one who denied the sending down of a Book to a human being, following the method of silencing the debater by exposing what his speech entails of corrupt consequences, like the corruption of the definition's being either consistently applied or reversed; or to refute their intended aim in denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ by the method of obligation, because they had shown that the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was like something impossible. So it was said to them, by way of affirmation: "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?" and they can only say: "Allah." When they acknowledge that, then the One who sent down a Book to Moses, why would He not send down the like of it to Muhammad?! As Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54], and so on.

Then, according to this view, the reading "you make it into scrolls" (taj'alunahu qara-tis) with the second-person ta' is in its apparent sense, and its reading with the third-person ya' is a shift (iltifat). Its point is that when He had informed about them with this shameful act, they were made as if absent from the station of address.

The addressee of "and you were taught" in this aspect is the Jews, so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "you make it," meaning: you make it into scrolls, hiding some of it, while Allah has taught you through the tongue of Muhammad what you did not know; and this is part of the parenthetical speech in which it is inserted.

On the reading "(yaj'aluna-hu qara-tis)" with the third-person ya', the return to address after the third person would also be an iltifat. Its goodness is that when He had informed about them with something good, He returned to the station of address; or because the station of address is more suitable to favour (imtinan).

Know that the composition of the verse is suitable for responding to both groups, in accordance with what the two narrations require. According to the first narration, the plural waw in "qadarū" and "qālū" refers to what the pronoun of these (people) refers to. According to the second narration, the plural waw is used for a single specific person, by way of allusion (ta'rid) to an individual, in the manner of "What is the matter with people who impose conditions that are not in the Book of Allah," and this is of the type of the return of a pronoun to an unmentioned referent, relying on its being present in the mind of the listener.

His saying "Say: Allah" is the answer to the affirmative interrogative. The questioner has himself taken on the answer, because the one questioned cannot do otherwise than answer thus, since he cannot be obstinate, as I established in the explanation of His saying, ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 12] in this surah.

The meaning is: "Say: Allah sent down the Book to Moses." And if "and you were taught what you did not know" is coordinated with the clause "sent down," then the answer includes it, that is, "Allah taught you what you did not know," so it is an answer about the passive verb with an active verb, in the manner of the saying of Dirar ibn Nahshal or al-Harith al-Nahshali lamenting his brother Yazid:

Let the humble one weep for Yazid over a dispute, and the one shaken by what the calamities cast down.

As if he were asked who weeps for him, and he said: "the humble one."

The conjunction "then" in His saying "then leave them in their discourse, playing" is for the sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi): that is, arguments and proofs do not benefit them, so leaving them and their immersion after the delivery is the better course; yet arguing against them is for their rebuke and the cutting off of their excuses.

His saying "in their discourse" is connected to "leave them." The clause "playing" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the plural pronoun.

The discussion of "dhar" was given earlier at His saying, ﴿And leave those who took their religion as play and amusement﴾.

The discussion of "khawd" (immersion) was given earlier at His saying, ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾.

And "play" (la'ib) was discussed earlier in this surah at ﴿And leave those who took their religion as play and amusement﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 92:

Page 369
﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which is before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Towns and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers ever watchful.﴾
"And this is a Book" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "Say: Allah" (qul Allāh), meaning: "And say to them: Allah sent down the Book to Moses, and this is a Book which We have sent down."

The reference (ishāra) is to the Qur'an, because the dispute concerning it, from their claim denying that it was sent down from Allah, and from their rebuke with the sending down of the Torah, makes the Qur'an like something present and witnessed. So the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishāra) was used to increase its distinction, strengthening its presence in minds.

Opening the speech with the demonstrative noun, which conveys the most complete distinction of the Book, and constructing the verb "We sent down" upon the predicate of the demonstrative (kitāb, which is in meaning identical to it), serves to add emphasis, as if it were said: "And this, We have sent it down."

The word "Book", whose proper position would be the object of "We sent down", was made the subject (musnad ilayhi), and the verb "We sent down" was attached to its pronoun, to convey the affirmation of its sending down by expressing it twice. All of this is for the honouring of this Book.

The clause "We have sent it down" may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the demonstrative noun, or a parenthetical clause (muʿtaridha) between it and its predicate. "Blessed" (mubārak) is a second predicate. The mubārak is a passive participle of bārakahu, and bāraka ʿalayhi, bāraka fīhi, bāraka lahu, when one makes blessing (barakah) for him. Barakah is the abundance and growth of good, and it is said: bārakahu. The Exalted said: ﴿That blessed is whoever is in the Fire and whoever is around it﴾ [al-Naml: 8], and it is said: bāraka fīhi, the Exalted said: ﴿and blessed therein﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 10].

Perhaps their saying (bāraka fīhi) relates to that whose blessing is attained by others in its time or place, whereas (bārakahu) relates to that whose blessing is a quality of it; (bāraka ʿalayhi) makes blessing firmly established upon him, and (bāraka lahu) makes things blessed for his sake, i.e., blessed in what belongs to him.

The Qur'an is blessed because it indicates the great good, so blessing is present in it, as if blessing were placed in its words; and because Allah the Exalted has deposited in it a blessing for its reader who occupies himself with it, a blessing in this world and in the Hereafter; and because it includes, in acting upon it, the perfection of the soul and its purification through theoretical knowledge and then practical knowledge. Thus blessing is inseparable from its recitation and its understanding. Fakhr al-Din said: The sunnah of Allah the Exalted has been that the one who seeks it (i.e., this Book) and holds fast to it attains the honour of this world and the happiness of the Hereafter. I have transmitted kinds of transmitted and rational sciences, yet through none of those sciences did there accrue to me kinds of worldly happiness like what accrued to me through serving this science (meaning tafsir).

"Confirming" (muṣaddiq) is a predicate about "Book" without a conjunction.

Muṣaddiq was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿confirming that which is before it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿and confirming that which is before me﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 50] in Surat Āl ʿImrān. The "alladhī" in His saying ﴿alladhī bayna yadayhi﴾ is a relative pronoun used with the meaning of a plural. Since the plural of alladhī, which is alladhīna, is not used in Arabic speech except when rational beings or their like are meant, such as ﴿Indeed those whom you invoke besides Allah are servants like you﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 194], due to treating idols as rational beings in customary usage, the singular alladhī is used for the plural of non-rational things, such as His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And he who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the righteous﴾ [al-Zumar: 33].

What is meant by ﴿alladhī bayna yadayhi﴾ is what preceded it of the books of the prophets, especially the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, because they are the last of the revealed books that people have handled, and it confirms the books revealed before these three, which are the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa.

The meaning of the Qur'an confirming them is in two respects. One of them: in these books is the promise of the coming of the Messenger who follows the prophethood of the people of those books, so the coming of the Qur'an has manifested the truth of what those books promised and indicated that they are from Allah.

Second: the Qur'an confirms their prophets, affirms them, mentions their light and their guidance, and brings what they brought of the roots of religion and sharia. Then, what it brought of rulings that were not established in them does not contradict them. As for what it brought of rulings that differ from the rulings mentioned in them, of the branches of sharia, that is sometimes explained as being due to the difference of interests, or because Allah intended ease for this community.

The meaning of "bayna yadayhi" is what preceded it. Its explanation was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what is before it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying ﴿and confirming what is before me of the Torah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 50] in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

As for the clause ﴿and that you may warn the Mother of Towns﴾, the presence of the conjunctive wāw at its beginning prevents linking "li-tundhira" to the verb "We sent it down", and prevents making the prepositional phrase a predicate of "kitāb", contrary to al-Taftazani, since a predicate that is a prepositional phrase does not take the conjunctive wāw, and there is no parallel to that in usage. So the presence of the causal lām together with wāw prevents making it another predicate of "kitāb". Therefore there is no escape, when directing its coordination with what precedes it, from positing an ellipsis or interpreting some of its wording. In my view, it is coordinated upon an implied element indicated by the context. The estimate: "that the People of the Book may believe in its confirmation, and that you may warn the polytheists." A similar estimate applies generally in the like of this verse according to what suits being estimated. This is among the varieties of eloquent usage. Its parallel is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is but one God, and that people of understanding may take heed﴾ [Ibrahim: 52] in Surat Ibrahim.

It occurs in al-Kashshaf that "wa-li-tundhira" is coordinated upon what the description of the Book indicates, as if it were said: "We sent it down for blessings, and confirming what came before it, and warning." That, though it holds in this verse, is not good in the verse of Surat Ibrahim, because the word "balaghun" is a noun that contains nothing indicating causation; "li-l-nās" is connected to it, and the lām in it is for conveying, not for causation, so it is necessary to estimate something after it, such as: "so that they may be alert, or lest they be seized heedlessly, and that they may be warned by it."

Warning (indhār) is informing about what carries an expectation of harm, and its opposite is good tidings (bishārah). It was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119] in Surat al-Baqarah. He restricted it to this because the aim is to frighten the polytheists, when they said ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human﴾ [al-Anʿam: 91].

Page 370
"Umm al-Qura" is Mecca. "Umm" of a thing is a widespread metaphor for the matter to which things return and around which they gather. The literal sense of umm is the female who gives birth to a child, to whom the child returns and with whom it remains. The metaphorical use of "umm" for origin and return became so common that it became literal, and from it the banner was called "umm", the top of the head was called "umm al-ra's", and al-Fatiha was called "Umm al-Qur'an". This has been discussed in naming al-Fatiha. Mecca was called Umm al-Qura only because it is the oldest and most famous of the towns, and the towns of the land of the Arabs did not become settled except after it; so the Arabs named it Umm al-Qura, and the Arabs of the Hijaz before it were dwellers of tents.

Warning the Mother of Towns is by warning its people, and this is metonymic ellipsis (majāz al-ḥadhf), like His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. His saying ﴿and those around it﴾ indicates it, i.e., the tribes dwelling around Mecca, such as Khuzaʿa, Saʿd ibn Bakr, Hawazin, Thaqif, and Kinanah.

The reason for restricting the verse to the people of Mecca and those around it is that they are the ones with whom the speech and the dispute were conducted, from His saying ﴿And your people denied it, though it is the truth﴾ [al-Anʿam: 66], since the surah is Meccan. There is nothing in the causal clause requiring that the warning by the Qur'an be restricted to them, so that we would need to claim that "those around it" means all the people of the earth.

Abu Bakr alone, from ʿAsim, read "wa-li-tundhira" with the second person, which is the reading of the majority, while he read "(wa-li-yundhira)" with the third-person ya', so that the pronoun refers back to "kitāb".

His saying ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it﴾ is a precaution against the warning encompassing the believers who at that time were in Mecca and around it, known by this relation apart from the other people of Mecca. For this reason He expressed them by this relative pronoun, since it is like a title for them, and it distinguishes them from the people of polytheism, because the people of polytheism denied the Hereafter.

There is no indication in this relative pronoun of causation, for the Jews and Christians believe in the Hereafter and did not believe in the Qur'an, but they were not among the people of Mecca at that time.

He informed about the believers that they believe in the Qur'an, by way of implication that they are not the intended recipients of the warning, so it is known that they are deserving of its opposite, which is good tidings.
