He increased their praise by His saying ﴿and they are over their prayers ever watchful﴾, as a notice of the completeness of their faith and its sincerity, since prayer is the act specific to Muslims, for the pilgrimage was performed by both Muslims and polytheists. This is like His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], ﴿who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. The pilgrimage had not been prescribed for Muslims during the period of the revelation of this surah.

[Page 374]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will reveal the like of what God has revealed"?﴾

When the refutation of their claim had been completed, namely their denial of sending messengers, of sending down revelation, and of inspiration, which arose from their false statement when they said, ﴿God has not sent down anything to any human﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and when this was followed by affirming what had led them to deny the sending of messengers and the sending down of revelation to a human, which is the affirmation that this Book is sent down from God, he next followed it with the refutation of what the polytheists had fabricated of the misguided laws concerning their practices, which 'Amr ibn Luhayy had prescribed for them, namely the worship of idols, and their claim that they are intercessors for them with God, and what follows from that: the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released), the sa'iba (a camel released to roam freely), and the animals slaughtered without the name of God being mentioned over them, and other such things. They deny the message at one time, while at another they claim that God commanded them to do certain things. How, then, did the commands that God gave them, according to their claim, reach them, when they themselves said, ﴿God has not sent down anything to any human﴾ [al-An'am: 91]? Thus it follows that they have lied against God regarding what they claimed God had commanded them, because they had cut off the path by which God's will reaches His creation, which is the path of messengership. Thus they came out with the most astonishing of statements.

[Page 374 continues]

He mentioned those who made light of the Qur'an. Some of them said, "It has been revealed to me," and some of them said, "I say the like of what the Qur'an says." Therefore the meaning of His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾ is to ridicule the doctrines of the people of polytheism and misguidance among them, despite their diversity and confusion. It is also possible that the intended meaning, in addition to this, is to absolve the Prophet (ﷺ) of what they accused him of, namely lying against God, when they said, ﴿God has not sent down anything to any human﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. This is because whoever knows that there is no greater injustice than fabricating against God and claiming revelation falsely would not do such a thing. This is in the sense of the statement of Heraclius to Abu Sufyan: "I asked you whether you had accused him of lying before he said what he said, and you replied no. I know that he would not abandon lying to people and then lie against God."

The interrogative is one of denial, so it has the meaning of negation, i.e., no one is more unjust than these people who have these attributes. Its context here is that of an indirect allusion that they are the liars, a refutation of their denial of the sending down of the Book. This denial is indicated by the implication of His words ﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it﴾ [al-An'am: 92], since it implies that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, who are the polytheists, deny it. Among them is the one who said, "It has been revealed to me," and among them is the one who said, "I will reveal the like of what God has revealed," and among them are those who fabricated lies against God by claiming that God commanded them to the practices of their pre-Islamic ignorance. A similar indirect allusion is His saying in Surat al-Ma'ida: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from God? Those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 60], and so on, following His saying ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game, from among those given the Book before you, nor the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 57], and so on.

The discussion of "and who is more unjust" has already been presented at His saying ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God from having His name mentioned in them﴾ [al-Baqara: 114] in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-iftira' (fabrication) means invention, and it was already discussed at His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 103] in Surat al-Ma'ida.

"Man" (who) is a relative pronoun, and it is intended in a generic sense, i.e., everyone who fabricated or said, and the intended meaning is not one specific individual. Those who fabricated lies against God are the polytheists, because they declared things lawful and unlawful according to their own desires and claimed that God had commanded them to do so, and they attributed to God falsely that He had partners who intercede with Him.

And ﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause of "man", i.e., everyone who claimed prophethood falsely. The messengers had always warned people against those who falsely claim prophethood, as I have previously mentioned. It has been reported that the intended reference of this is Musaylima, the pretender of the people of al-Yamama, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and 'Ikrima. This implies that Musaylima claimed prophethood before the Hijra of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Madina, since the surah is Meccan. The correct view is that Musaylima did not claim prophethood except after he came as a delegation to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Madina, with his people, Bani Hanifa, in the ninth year (AH), hoping that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would make the affair his after him. When he returned disappointed, he claimed prophethood among his people.

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya, it is stated that the intended reference of this verse, along with Musaylima, is al-Aswad al-'Ansi, the pretender in Sana'a. No one other than Ibn 'Atiyya has said this. al-Tabari only mentioned al-Aswad as a parallel to Musaylima, since al-Aswad al-'Ansi did not claim prophethood except at the end of the life of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The correct view is that the intended meaning is general, and it does not harm this that it is restricted to one or two individuals at a certain time, nor that the verse applies to them.

As for ﴿whoever says, "I will reveal the like of what God has revealed"﴾, al-Wahidi said in Asbab al-Nuzul (occasions of revelation), citing Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima, that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh al-'Amiri, who had embraced Islam in Mecca and used to write down the revelation for the Prophet (ﷺ). Then he apostatized and said, "I say the like of what God has revealed," mockingly. This too does not satisfy the heart, because 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh apostatized after the Hijra and joined Mecca, whereas this surah is Meccan. al-Qurtubi mentioned from 'Ikrima, and Ibn 'Atiyya from al-Zahrawi and al-Mahdawi, that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to say, "I can produce something to rival the Qur'an." They memorized some of his statements, and that was by way of mockery. They also narrated that one of the polytheists said, "It is only the words of a poet, and I will produce the like of it." This had been repeated among the polytheists, as the Qur'an indicated. Therefore the correct view is that the intended meaning of the relative clause is general, to include everyone from whom this statement proceeded and whoever follows them in this in the future.

[Page 375]

Their saying ﴿the like of what God has revealed﴾ either means that they said this expression in mockery, as they said ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely mad﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], or it is a report by God, Exalted, in meaning, i.e., he said, "I will reveal the like of this speech," and God expressed it by His saying ﴿what God has revealed﴾, as in His saying ﴿and their saying, "We killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of God"﴾ [al-Nisa': 157].

* * *

﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are stretching out their hands: "Yield up your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the torment of humiliation for what you used to say against God other than the truth, and for being arrogant towards His signs."﴾

The sentence ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾, because this is a threat of punishment for those wrongdoers who fabricated against God, who said "It has been revealed to us," and who said ﴿I will reveal the like of what God has revealed﴾.

The word "the wrongdoers" in His saying ﴿when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ includes those people and includes all the polytheist wrongdoers. For this reason, the definiteness in "al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers) is the definiteness of the genus, which conveys comprehensiveness.

The address in "tara" (you see) is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to whoever is capable of seeing, so it is not restricted to one particular addressee.

Then the supposed seeing may be intended as sight (ru'yat al-basar) if the situation described is one of the events of the Day of Resurrection, and it may be knowledge ('ilmiyya) if the situation described is one of the states of the death throes and the seizing of their souls at death.

The object of "tara" is omitted, and it is indicated by the adverbial phrase that follows it. The estimated meaning is: "If only you could see the wrongdoers when they are in the agonies of death," i.e., their time in the agonies of death. It is permissible to make "idh" (when) a noun without the sense of a time adverb, so that it becomes the object, as in His saying ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]. Then the estimated meaning is: "If only you could see the time when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death." On this interpretation, seeing must be understood as knowledge, because a time cannot be seen.

The purpose of this conditional is to magnify the situation, and for this reason the answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, as is the custom in contexts of magnification. Its parallels in the Qur'an are numerous. The estimated meaning is: "You would see a tremendous matter."

Al-ghamra, with a fatha on the ghayn, is that which overwhelms, i.e., covers and so engulfs from water such that it leaves the one overwhelmed with no escape. Its use as a metaphor for severe hardship became widespread, comparing it to the hardship suffered by a drowning person when a valley or flood overwhelms him, until the word ghamra became literal in convention for extreme hardship.

The plural "al-ghamarat" (the agonies) may be because there are multiple agonies according to the number of wrongdoers, so the plural form is used in its literal sense. It may also be for the purpose of intensifying the magnification of what befalls them, indicating that these are kinds of hardships with multiple forms and states that cannot be expressed by a single name. Accordingly, this may be a threat of a punishment they will meet in this world at the time of the death throes. Since death has its agonies, the agony of death is made into agonies.

The particle "fi" (in) is for metaphorical containment, to indicate how closely the agonies encompass them, as though they were a container enclosing them and surrounding them.

Thus death in this sense is used in its real meaning, and its agonies are the pains of the death throes.

[Page 378]

The clause ﴿Yield up your souls!﴾ may be a report of the words of the angels to them at the seizing of their souls. Then the expression "agonies" is a single metaphor, and death is literal. The meaning of extending the hand is a figurative representation of the severity in taking their souls, and there is no extending and no hands. "Anfus" (souls) means spirits, i.e., "Bring out your spirits from your bodies," i.e., "Hand over your spirits." The command is for humiliation and distress, meaning harshness in seizing their souls, and they will not leave them any rest nor treat them gently. This implies that they will resist, so they will not let their spirits go. On this interpretation, it is a threat of pains at the death throes, as a recompense in this world for their polytheism. The polytheists were in doubt about resurrection, so they were threatened with something about which there is no doubt, namely the situation of the seizing of the spirits, in that God will send angels upon them who will seize their spirits with severity and violence and make them taste torment during that. This threat has a great effect on their souls, because they used to fear the severity of the death throes. It is like His saying ﴿If only you could see when those who disbelieved are taken by the angels, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50], and so on. His saying ﴿Yield up your souls!﴾ on this interpretation is issued by the angels.

It is also possible that this is a threat of what the polytheists will encounter of the severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection, in connection with His subsequent saying ﴿And you have come to Us alone﴾ [al-An'am: 94]. Then the agonies of death are a representation of their state on the Day of Gathering, in struggling with severe hardships and the terrors of the Resurrection, with a state of theirs in the agonies of death and the severe pains of the death throes. So death is a representation and not a reality. The purpose of the representation is to bring the situation closer, since otherwise their terrors on that Day are more severe than the agonies of death, but there is nothing in common usage more extreme than this representation as an indication of the severity of pain. This is like the saying "I found the pain of death," the words of Abu Qatada about the battle of Hunayn, "He embraced me with an embrace from which I found the scent of death," and the words of al-Harith ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi:

"I smelled the scent of death from their side
in a narrow passage, while the horses had not scattered."

The clause ﴿while the angels are stretching out their hands﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., "while the angels are extending their hands"

[Page 379]

toward the polytheists, to seize them and push them to reckoning in the second interpretation, or to seize their spirits in the first interpretation. Then the extension of the hands is literal, in that the angels take forms in the shapes of human beings. It is also possible that the extension of the hands is a metonymy for touching and inflicting pain, as in His saying ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 28].

The clause ﴿Expel your souls﴾ is a continuation of an implied saying (maqul li-qawl mahdhuf). Omitting the verb of saying in such a context is common, and the saying here comes from the side of God, may He be exalted. The implied meaning is: We say to them, "Expel your souls," and "souls" (anfus) means the essences (dhawat). The imperative is for incapacitation (lil-ta'jiz), meaning: expel your souls from this punishment if you are able. The expulsion (ikhraj) is a metaphor for rescue and deliverance, since this situation occurs before they enter the Fire. It is also permissible to keep the expulsion in its literal sense if this situation occurs at the time they enter the Fire.

The definite article in "al-yawm" (the day) is for a known reference (li'l-'ahd), and it is the Day of Resurrection in which this saying takes place. Applying "the day" to it is well known. If one takes "al-ghamarat" (the agonies) to mean the agony at death (al-naz' 'inda al-mawt), then "al-yawm" is used in the sense of a time, namely the time when their souls are seized.

The clause ﴿Today you will be recompensed﴾ etc. is a resumptive statement of warning (isti'naf wa'id), set apart for independence and emphasis, and it is from the speech of the angels.

"Tujzawn" means you will be given recompense (jaza'). Recompense (jaza') is the return for an action and what is paid in exchange for it, whether a reward or a punishment. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿a recompense in full measure﴾ [al-Naba' 26], and there is the proverb: "A person is repaid for what he has done: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil." One says: jazahu yajzihi, so he is jazin. It takes a direct object for the thing given as recompense, and takes the preposition bi for the thing being repaid for, as in this verse. For this reason, the bi in God's saying in Surat Yunus ﴿And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like﴾ [Yunus 27] has been interpreted as an explanatory genitive (idafa bayaniyya), meaning: its recompense is an evil deed, and the object of bi is the evil deed being repaid for, as Ibn Jinni preferred. Al-Akhfash said the bi there is superfluous, based on God's saying ﴿and the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]. It is also said: jazah with the form of mufa'ala (jazah/jazza). Al-Raghib said: "Jazza" did not come in the Qur'an.

Page 380

Al-Hun means humiliation (al-hawan), which is abasement (al-dhull). Al-Zajjaj explained it as severe humiliation, and the author of al-Kashshaf followed him, but no other lexicographers said this. The statements of the lexicographers imply that al-hun is synonymous with al-hawan. Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾.

The idafa of "punishment" (al-'adhab) to "al-hun" serves to convey what the idafa implies of the meaning of specification and possession: the punishment that is firmly established in the humiliation and inseparable from it.

The bi in His saying ﴿for what you used to say﴾ is the bi of exchange (ba' al-'iwad), to transitivize the verb tujzawn to the thing for which one is repaid. It is also permissible to make the bi causal (lil-sababiyya), meaning: you are recompensed with the punishment of humiliation because of your saying, and it is known that the recompense is according to that, with ma being a verbal-masdar (masdariyya). Then, if this saying came from God, the mention of the name of Majesty (ism al-jalala) is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, for the purpose of awe. The original would have been: "for what you used to say against Me."

"Taqulun" was given the meaning of "takdhibun" (you lie), so the phrase "against God" was linked to it, and it becomes known that this saying is a lie against God, like His saying ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqa 44], etc. With this, it becomes valid to treat the verb taqulun as intransitive, so no object is assumed for it, because what is meant is that they lie. It is also valid to make "other than the truth" the object of taqulun; "other than the truth" is falsehood, and attributing it to God is nothing but a lie.

"For what you used to say" includes the three sayings mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾ up to His saying ﴿like what God has sent down﴾, and others.

"Ghayr al-haqq" (other than the truth) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the relative ma, or an adjective of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), or it is the direct object of taqulun.

His saying ﴿and you were arrogant toward His signs﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you used to say﴾, meaning: and by your arrogance toward His signs. Arrogance (al-istikbar) is turning away with little concern, and in this sense it takes the signs as its object. Or the signs are meant as contemplating them, so the arrogance is in its literal sense, meaning: you are arrogant against reflecting on the signs and you see yourselves as greater than the one who owns those signs.

Page 381

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted for the purpose of awe. The meaning: you would see a dreadful matter. Omitting the answer of "law" in such a context is common in the Qur'an. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And if those who did wrong could see when they see the punishment﴾ [al-Baqara 165] in Surat al-Baqara.

If the assumed speech in the phrase ﴿Get out your souls﴾ [al-An'am: 93] is a saying from Allah the Exalted, then His saying ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the phrase ﴿Get out your souls﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. That is, when the angels drive them toward the punishment, it is said to them: "Get out your souls," and it is said to them: "You have certainly come to Us alone." The clause is therefore in the place of the accusative, governed by the omitted saying. On the possibility that ﴿the agonies of death﴾ [al-An'am: 93] is literal, that is, at the moment of extraction, the verb *ji'tumūnā* (you have come to Us) is the past tense used for the near future, like *qad qāmati al-ṣalāh* (the prayer has been established). At that moment they are close to returning to the sheer disposal of Allah over them.

If the assumed speech is the speech of the angels, then the clause ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. The discourse then shifts from addressing those who take heed of the condition of the wrongdoers to addressing the wrongdoers themselves, with a warning of what will be said to them on that Day. On the first interpretation, *ji'tumūnā* is literally in the past, since at the time this saying is addressed to them, their coming before Allah has already taken place. *Qad* here is for affirmation (*tahqīq*).

On the second interpretation, the past tense is used for the future, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, and *qad* serves as a supporting element (*tarshīḥ*) for the metaphor (*isti'āra*).

[Page 382]

Their being told that they have come does not mean the literal sense of the report, since their coming is known to them. Rather, it is used to rebuke them and to make them confront the truth of what they were warned of through the Messenger, which they denied: the return to life after death for reckoning before Allah.

This meaning may also be combined with the sense of being within reach and arriving at what they supposed they would never arrive at, as in the saying of the Exalted ﴿and found Allah with him﴾ [al-Nur: 39], and in the verse of the rajaz poet:

*"Allah may well make the night-traveller's guide wake up [in the morning]"*

The pronoun in *ji'tumūnā* is the pronoun of Majesty (Allah), not the pronoun of the angels, as is shown by His saying ﴿as We created you﴾.

*Furādā* (alone) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the nominative pronoun in *ji'tumūnā*, meaning: isolated from everything you used to take pride in during the first life, of wealth, children and helpers. The more evident view is that *furādā* is the plural of *fardān*, like *sukārā* is the plural of *sakrān*. The unmodified *furādā* is not synonymous with the modified *firād* (*furād*), because *firād* means "one by one," as with *thalāth* and *rubā'* among the modified numerals. *Furādā* with the short vowel is the plural of *fardān* in the sense of "one who is alone." Its plural form here is because each one of them came alone, apart from his wealth.

His saying ﴿as We created you the first time﴾ is a comparison of the coming, in which is intended the meaning of revival after death, which they used to deny, although they saw it with their own eyes. The *kāf* (as) is for comparing the new creation to the first creation, and it is therefore in the position of an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*).

The *mā* following the *kāf* is verbal-source (*maṣdariyya*). The sense is: "like Our creating you," that is, you came to Us as created beings, just as We created you the first time. This is like His saying the Exalted ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Nay, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15].

[Page 383]

*Al-takhwīl* means bestowing bounty. It is said that its origin is giving *khawal* (with two fatḥas), which means servants, that is, giving slaves, and then it was used figuratively for giving anything at all that benefits. The sense is: you left behind what We bestowed upon you of wealth and other things.

*Mā* is a relative pronoun. The meaning of their leaving it behind them is their distance from it. This is an image for the state of one who is far from something by one who departs from it while walking, for he leaves behind him whoever departs from him at the moment of departure, since if he walked while it was before him, he would reach it. For this reason, one who intends something is represented as having it before him, and what a person prepares for himself is said to be "he has sent it forward" (*qaddamahu*).

*Wa taraktum* (you left) is coordinated with *ji'tumūnā*, and it explains the meaning of *furādā*. However, the second clause adds further explanation of the meaning of isolation by mentioning the manner of this isolation, because both reports are used for rebuke and reproach. They came to the Resurrection while they used to deny that coming, and they left what they had in this world, while their state was that of one who intends to live forever. For this reason the clause is coordinated and not separated. Abu al-Baqa' made the clause a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the *wāw* in *ji'tumūnā*, so that leaving what they were given becomes the place of the chastisement.

The same applies to the clause ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾, which is coordinated with *ji'tumūnā* and *taraktum*, because this report is also meant for rebuke and affliction. The polytheists, when their hearts were disturbed about the matter of Islam, would comfort themselves that their gods would intercede for them with Allah. Some have narrated that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said this, and perhaps he said it in mockery or ignorance, and that the verse was revealed as a refutation of him. That is, the verse contains a response to him, not that it was revealed specifically to nullify his saying, because these verses are connected to one another. In His saying ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾ there is also an explanation and confirmation of His saying ﴿alone﴾.

His saying ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾ is a mockery of them, because they have no intercessors. The address is directed to them in the manner of one who awaits something, that is, one who looks for something and does not see it, [Page 384] like His saying in another verse ﴿and He will say: "Where are My partners whom you used to contest about?"﴾ [al-Nahl: 27]. This is based on the principle that negating an attribute from something generally implies the existence of that thing. So in this statement there is an implication that their intercessors exist but have not come. For this reason the negated verb is in the present form, which indicates the present state, rather than the past, to show that the absence of seeing the intercessors continues up to now. Thus there is an implication that seeing them is possible in the future, and this is an added intensification of the mockery.

The intercessors are added to the pronoun of the addressees because the intended intercessors are well known, namely the deities they worshipped, and who they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to Allah in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], ﴿and they say: "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18]. The meaning has been further established by describing them in His saying ﴿whom you claimed to be partners in you﴾.

*Al-za'm* means false speech, whether it is said deliberately knowing it to be false, as in His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you?﴾ [al-Nisa': 60], or from bad belief, as here, and in His saying ﴿and on the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated partners: "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ [al-An'am: 22]. This has already been discussed in these two verses in Surat al-Nisa' and in this surah.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿in you are partners﴾ is for emphasis, which is directed by astonishment at this claim, since they made the idols partners of Allah in their own selves, while they knew that the Creator is Allah the Exalted, who alone deserves worship. So from where would the idols' partnership with Allah in deserving worship come? That is, if they had claimed for the idols something hidden whose origin of creation is unknown, the wonder would be less. But the full wonder is at their claim of partnership in their own selves, because when they worshipped the idols, and worship is due only on account of being the Creator, it followed for them from their worship that they must claim the idols are partners of Allah in the very selves of His creation, that is, in their creation. For this reason the "selves" are linked to the attribute that indicates partnership.

[Page 385]

The meaning of intercession was discussed earlier at His saying the Exalted ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Certainly, the bond between you has been cut﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'nāf bayānī*) following ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾, because when the polytheists hear His saying ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾, the hope of meeting their intercessors is stirred in them, and they look eagerly to learn their way out. So it is said to them: ﴿Certainly, the bond between you has been cut﴾, to make them despair after the mocking encouragement. The pronoun attached to *bayn* refers to the addressees and their intercessors.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read the *nūn* of *baynakum* with a fatḥa. On this reading, *bayn* is a locative adverb (*ẓarf makān*) indicating the place of gathering and connection in what is added to it. The rest read the *nūn* of *baynukum* with a ḍamma, which removes *bayn* from the adverbial function, so it becomes a declinable noun, and "cutting" is attributed to it by way of figurative attribution (*majāz 'aqlī*).

The omission of the subject of *taqaṭṭa'a* on the reading with fatḥa is because the intended meaning is the occurrence of the cutting. Its subject is therefore an undefined noun, of what is suitable for cutting, namely connection. The sense is: "the rope has been cut," or something similar. The Exalted said ﴿and their means were cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166]. This structure has become like a proverb due to this conciseness. The mention of cutting used figuratively for distance and the nullification of connection has become common in the speech of the Arabs, following the metaphor of the rope for connection, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*"The ties of my love and longing were cut, the evening we passed by Ḥamāh and Shayzar."*

For this reason it is good to omit the subject in the verse on this reading, since the context indicates it, and it became like a proverb. Al-Zamakhshari took the verbal noun derived from *taqaṭṭa'a* as the subject, that is, by attributing the verb to its own verbal noun under this interpretation, meaning: the cutting occurred between you. Al-Taftazani said: "It is better that it is attributed to the pronoun of the matter, because it is fixed in souls," that is, "the matter has been cut off between you."

Close to this is what is said: *baynakum* is an attribute placed in the position of the qualified noun that is the subject, meaning "the matter of your connection." On this view the usage is of the type of the pronoun whose referent is not mentioned because it is known from the verb, like His saying ﴿until she was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. But this does not apply to the hidden pronoun, since the hidden pronoun is not present in the speech; what calls for positing it is the existence of its referent indicating it. As for the statement here, which has neither a referent nor a pronoun, it is necessary to make it an omitted subject, as I have explained to you from the beginning. It should not be objected that ﴿she was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32] contains no pronoun, since the *tā'* is a sign of attributing the verb to a feminine subject. We respond that the verified view is that the *tā'* in a verb attributed to a pronoun is itself the subject.

On the reading with ḍamma, *baynukum* is the subject, that is, it is removed from the adverbial function and made a noun for the place in which the referent of the attached pronoun gathers, and the locative noun is therefore a metonymy (*kināya*) for the separation of the people of the place that was the site of gathering. The locative sense here is figurative, like His saying ﴿Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1].

His saying ﴿and they have strayed from you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿the bond between you has been cut﴾, and it is part of the mockery and despair. The meaning of *ḍalla* is the opposite of guidance, that is, your intercessors did not know your place after the bond between you was cut, so they did not find their way to you in order to intercede for you. *Mā* here is a relative pronoun whose referent is the intercessors, due to the unity of its relative clause with the clause ﴿those whom you claimed to be partners in you﴾. That is, "those whom you used to claim as partners." The two objects of the verb of claiming are omitted, since the similar construction in ﴿whom you claimed to be partners in you﴾ indicates them. The deities are referred to by *mā*, which is commonly used for non-rational beings, to make clear the uselessness of these deities. Ibn 'Atiyya and others explained *ḍalla* as meaning "vanished," "lost," or "went away," and they took *mā* as verbal-source, meaning: your claim that they would intercede for you has gone away. What we have mentioned in explaining the verse is more eloquent and more forceful.

[p. 387]

﴿Indeed, God is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living. That is God; so how are you deluded?﴾ ﴿He is the Splitter of the dawn, and He made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i), moving from the establishment of tawhid (divine oneness), resurrection (ba'th), and prophethood (risalah), along with the various exhortations and proofs that run through these matters, to reasoning from and reflection upon the creation of God and the wonders of His visible creatures. It establishes that He alone is God, which entails the negation of divinity from whatever cannot do the like of this wondrous making. Therefore it is not right for anything else to be worshipped or to be associated with God in worship, since it has no claim to divinity. This is a refutation of the polytheism of the Arab idolaters, and, by a stronger implication, a refutation of the belief of the atheistic naturalists (al-dahriyyun) among them. The verse also contains a favour bestowed upon those addressed, namely the idolaters, as indicated by His saying ﴿so how are you deluded?﴾, i.e., "so how do you disbelieve the blessing?" It also contains knowledge and certainty for the believing affirmers, and an increase in their knowledge of their Lord and in their gratitude.

The opening of the sentence with inna (indeed) is used even though no one denies that God is the doer of the actions mentioned here. However, the reflection and reasoning upon the sign of the seed in the power of the Creator to bring the dead back to life, just as He has power to cause the living to die, is a subtle consideration. The idolaters turned away from it and boldly denied resurrection. Their condition was thus like that of one who denied or doubted that God is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone, so the statement is emphasised with the particle inna.

The nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is used to indicate the permanence and continuity of this attribute, because it is an essential attribute of God, the Exalted. It is the attribute of the act, or the attribute of power and its objects, in the terminology of those who do not affirm attributes of action (sifat al-af'al). Since the intention is to be content with the indication of the splitting of the grain and the date-stone as a proof of God's power to bring the living out of the dead, and to move from that to its indication of bringing the living out of the dead in the resurrection, no particle of restriction (qasr) is used in this statement, since the context is not one of restriction.

[p. 388]

Al-falq (splitting) is the cleaving and separating of one part of a thing from another. The intended splitting is that from which the fibres of the plant and the tree and their roots emerge, and it is therefore the locus of the lesson concerning God's knowledge, power and wisdom.

Al-habb (grain) is a collective noun for what the plant bears, its singular being habba. Al-nawa (date-stone) is a collective noun of nawāt, and the nawāt is the kernel of the date. It is also applied to the kernels found in fruits from which their trees grow, such as grapes and olives, and this is al-ajam (stones), with a vowel on the first letter, a collective noun of ujma. The clause ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ is in the position of a second predicate (khabar thani) of the subject of inna. It serves as an explanation of the intended meaning of the clause before it, namely the splitting from which He brings forth a plant or a growing tree possessing vegetative life, after the grain and the stone were a hard body with no life or growth in it. For this reason it is preferable to separate this clause from the one before it, although it is more general than it, since it indicates the bringing forth of animals from the fluid of the sperm-drop or from eggs. It is thus another predicate, but by its generality it explains the first predicate, and therefore the separation of the clause is fitting, or the omission of the conjunction between the predicates.

The clause ﴿and brings the dead out of the living﴾ is conjoined to ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, because it is a statement of the opposite of the content of ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, and another wondrous making that indicates the perfection of power and negates the operation of nature in creation. This is because the act issuing from a knowing and choosing agent occurs in contrary states, unlike an act that proceeds from a natural cause. In this statement there is also a completion of the explanation of what the phrase ﴿the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ left in general terms, because the splitting of the grain from the plant and of the date-stone from the tree includes various general states, among them the state of the plant and tree bearing fruit: grain that dries out while still on its stalk and so has no life in it, and kernels within fruits that are dry and lifeless, like the kernels of olives and dates. It also goes beyond this explanation by bringing forth eggs, milk, musk, pearls and the bezoar stone (al-bazhar) from the inner parts of living animals. Thus the emergence of the two opposites from the divine power becomes fully manifest.

[p. 389]

The conjunction of this statement has been preferred, because it is like a completion of His saying ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, meaning that He does both things together, like His saying after it, ﴿He is the Splitter of the dawn, and He made the night for rest﴾. Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) made it a conjunction to ﴿the Splitter of the grain﴾, on the basis that the content of His saying ﴿brings the dead out of the living﴾ contains no explanation of the content of ﴿the Splitter of the grain﴾, because the bringing forth of the living from the dead results from the splitting of the grain, and not the reverse. This is contrary to the apparent sense, because the relation of the description ﴿brings the dead out of the living﴾ to the predicate ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ is stronger than its relation to the predicate ﴿the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾.

The clause ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ has been phrased as a verbal sentence (fi'liyya) to indicate that this act is renewed and repeated at every moment; it is therefore a known intended meaning and not a matter of chance or coincidence.

In His saying ﴿and brings the dead out of the living﴾, the participle form (ism) is used to indicate continuity and permanence. Thus the total result is that both acts are renewed and also constant, i.e., abundant and essential. This is because neither of the two acts takes precedence over its counterpart in the ruling, so the style contains something like what the rhetoricians call ihtibak (interlocking the two halves of a parallel statement).

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ (dhalikum) is used for additional distinction, and also as a reproach for the foolishness of the idolaters addressed, for their heedlessness of this indication that He alone is God. That is: that Doer of great acts, the splitting and the bringing forth of the living from the dead and of the dead from the living, is the One whom creation knows by His great name as the one God, to whom alone the attribute of divinity belongs. So do not equate anything else with Him in divinity. For this reason He follows with the particle of consequence fa (so) and says ﴿so how are you deluded?﴾

Al-ifk (deluding) with a fatha on the hamza is the verbal noun of afakahu, yaˈfikuhu, from the pattern of daraba, meaning to turn someone away from a place or from an action. That is: how are you turned away from His oneness?

Anna (how) means "from where". It is an interrogative of wonder and denial, i.e., there is no cause that turns you away from His oneness. The verb tu'fakun (you are deluded) is in the passive, because the one who turns them away from the oneness of God is not specified. It is a combination of things: the whispering of Satan, the misleading of their leaders and great men, and the desires of their own souls.

[p. 390]

The clause ﴿That is God; so how are you deluded?﴾ is a resumed statement, whose purpose is admonition, so the clause ﴿That is God; so how are you deluded?﴾ is a parenthetic interjection (i'tiraḍ).

﴿He is the Splitter of the dawn﴾ may be a fourth predicate of the subject of inna, or it may be an adjective of the Name of Majesty (Allah) which is the predicate of the demonstrative. In that case His saying ﴿so how are you deluded?﴾ is a parenthetic interjection.

Al-isbah (dawn), with a kasra on the hamza, is in origin the verbal noun of asbaha al-ufuq, when the horizon became one of dawn. It was applied to al-sabah (morning), which is the light of daybreak, and it stands in opposition to the night, which is what is meant here.

The splitting of the dawn is a metaphor for the appearance of light in the darkness of the night. The darkness is likened to a splitting, as the light emerges from it, and the word salkh (stripping) is likewise used metaphorically for this, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip the day from it﴾ (Yasin 37). Thus the annexation of "Splitter" (fāliq) to "dawn" (al-isbah) is genuine (haqiqiyya), while the relation is metaphorical by the slightest connection. We shall explain this in the next verse, because the active participle has a semblance of the noun, so it takes a genuine annexation, and it has a semblance of the verb, so it takes a verbal (lafziyya) annexation. Here, since it indicates a quality in the past, its resemblance to the verb is weakened, because it resembles the imperfect only in form and in the time of the present or future. Some also consider the sense of the object to be intended, by way of extension, with the preposition omitted, meaning "splitting from the dawn", so that it is in the accusative by removal of the governing particle. For this reason they called the morning falaq with two fathas, in the pattern of what has the meaning of the passive participle, as they said maskan, meaning maskun ilayhi (a place in which one dwells). On this view the annexation is verbal by interpretation, and it is not an annexation of an adjective to its complement, since dawn is not the object of the splitting. The meaning is "splitting from the dawn", and so it is understood that what is split is the night. For this reason they explained it as "the splitter of the darkness of the dawn", that is, the darkness which is followed by morning, namely the dim darkness before dawn. The splitting of the night from the morning is more wondrous in its display of power, and more effective in conferring the favour of blessing, because darkness is non-existence and light is existence. Creation is the manifestation of power,

[p. 391]

and non-existence is not a manifestation of power unless it is imposed upon something existent, which is annihilation. The splitting of the dawn is also a blessing upon people, so that they may benefit from their life and their earning.

(﴿and He made the night for rest﴾) is a conjunction upon ﴿the Splitter of the dawn﴾.

The majority read it in the form of the active participle with the genitive "al-layl" (the night), for the sake of matching the two descriptions in nominal form and annexation. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it as jaʿala in the past tense, with "al-layl" in the accusative.

He expressed with respect to the night the root "making" (ja'l), because darkness is non-existence, so the exercise of power in it is its exercise in removing what prevents that darkness from the lights that appear on the horizon. The meaning is that God split the dawn by His power as a blessing from Him upon the existent beings, and He did not make the light continuous on the horizon, but made it a passing light divided into periods, so that the darkness would return to the horizon as a mercy from Him toward existent beings, so that they might rest after weariness and labour, and gain repose for themselves.

Al-sakan (rest), with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the kaf in the pattern of the synonym of the passive participle, like al-falq when it is taken as an object by extension with the governing particle omitted, is that to which one rests, that is, that to which the soul is at peace and the heart is tranquil. Resting in it is figurative. The wife is called sakan, and the house is called sakan, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And God has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling (sakan)﴾ (al-Nahl 80). So the meaning of "He made the night a sakan" is that it was made so that the soul might find rest from the fatigue of labour.

He conjoined al-shams (the sun) and al-qamar (the moon) to al-layl (the night) in the accusative, observing the position of al-layl, because it stands in the position of the object of jā'il (the one who makes), on the basis of the verbal (lafziyya) annexation. Conjunction upon the position is common in many places in Arabic speech, such as the nominative of a conjoined noun after inna, and the accusative of a conjoined noun after the predicate of laysa when it is governed by a bi-preposition.

Al-husban (reckoning) is in origin the verbal noun of ḥasaba, with a fatha on the sin, like al-ghufran (forgiveness), al-shukran (gratitude), and al-kufran (ingratitude),

[p. 392]

that is, He made them a reckoning, that is, a sign of reckoning for people, by which they calculate the times of the night and the day, the months, the seasons, and the years through their movements. This is a blessing upon people and a reminder of the manifestation of knowledge and power. For this reason, the sun was given a reckoning just as the moon was, because many nations reckon their months and years by the course of the sun, through its entry into the zodiacal signs and its completion of its cycle through them. The Arabs reckon by the course of the moon through its stations. This is what Islam brought, while in the Jahiliyya the Arabs used to make intercalation (kabs) to convert the year into equal seasons. Thus the point of the blessing is more general than the legal consideration in reckoning months and years by the lunar calendar. That this was possible for people is due to God's making the movements of the sun and the moon follow a single order that does not vary, and that is among the greatest proofs of God's knowledge and power. This is according to what appears to people of it; if they were to become acquainted with the secrets of that wondrous order, the lesson in it would be greater still.

The predication of the two by a verbal noun (masdar) is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), because it has the meaning of the active participle, i.e., reckoning (hasibayn). The ones who reckon are the people, by means of the sun and the moon.

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ (dhalika) refers to the making (al-ja'l) derived from jā'il (the one who makes).

The measure (al-taqdir) means: He set things according to a known measure, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He created everything and measured it precisely﴾ (al-Furqan 2).

Al-'Aziz: the Victorious, the Irresistible. God is truly al-'Aziz, because all created beings cannot escape His power. Al-'Alim is an intensive form (mubalaghah) denoting great knowledge, because the placing of things in such a wondrous order can only proceed from a Knower of immense knowledge.

[p. 387]

The splitting of the dawn is a metaphor for the appearance of light in the darkness of the night. The darkness is likened to a splitting, as the light emerges from it, and the word salkh (stripping) is likewise used metaphorically for this, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip the day from it﴾ (Yasin 37). Thus the annexation of "Splitter" (fāliq) to "dawn" (al-isbah) is genuine (haqiqiyya), while the relation is metaphorical by the slightest connection. We shall explain this in the next verse, because the active participle has a semblance of the noun, so it takes a genuine annexation, and it has a semblance of the verb, so it takes a verbal (lafziyya) annexation. Here, since it indicates a quality in the past, its resemblance to the verb is weakened, because it resembles the imperfect only in form and in the time of the present or future. Some also consider the sense of the object to be intended, by way of extension, with the preposition omitted, meaning "splitting from the dawn", so that it is in the accusative by removal of the governing particle. For this reason they called the morning falaq with two fathas, in the pattern of what has the meaning of the passive participle, as they said maskan, meaning maskun ilayhi (a place in which one dwells). On this view the annexation is verbal by interpretation, and it is not an annexation of an adjective to its complement, since dawn is not the object of the splitting. The meaning is "splitting from the dawn", and so it is understood that what is split is the night. For this reason they explained it as "the splitter of the darkness of the dawn", that is, the darkness which is followed by morning, namely the dim darkness before dawn. The splitting of the night from the morning is more wondrous in its display of power, and more effective in conferring the favour of blessing, because darkness is non-existence and light is existence. Creation is the manifestation of power,

[p. 391]

and non-existence is not a manifestation of power unless it is imposed upon something existent, which is annihilation. The splitting of the dawn is also a blessing upon people, so that they may benefit from their life and their earning.

(﴿and He made the night for rest﴾) is a conjunction upon ﴿the Splitter of the dawn﴾.

The majority read it in the form of the active participle with the genitive "al-layl" (the night), for the sake of matching the two descriptions in nominal form and annexation. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it as jaʿala in the past tense, with "al-layl" in the accusative.

He expressed with respect to the night the root "making" (ja'l), because darkness is non-existence, so the exercise of power in it is its exercise in removing what prevents that darkness from the lights that appear on the horizon. The meaning is that God split the dawn by His power as a blessing from Him upon the existent beings, and He did not make the light continuous on the horizon, but made it a passing light divided into periods, so that the darkness would return to the horizon as a mercy from Him toward existent beings, so that they might rest after weariness and labour, and gain repose for themselves.

Al-sakan (rest), with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the kaf in the pattern of the synonym of the passive participle, like al-falq when it is taken as an object by extension with the governing particle omitted, is that to which one rests, that is, that to which the soul is at peace and the heart is tranquil. Resting in it is figurative. The wife is called sakan, and the house is called sakan, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And God has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling (sakan)﴾ (al-Nahl 80). So the meaning of "He made the night a sakan" is that it was made so that the soul might find rest from the fatigue of labour.

He conjoined al-shams (the sun) and al-qamar (the moon) to al-layl (the night) in the accusative, observing the position of al-layl, because it stands in the position of the object of jā'il (the one who makes), on the basis of the verbal (lafziyya) annexation. Conjunction upon the position is common in many places in Arabic speech, such as the nominative of a conjoined noun after inna, and the accusative of a conjoined noun after the predicate of laysa when it is governed by a bi-preposition.

Al-husban (reckoning) is in origin the verbal noun of ḥasaba, with a fatha on the sin, like al-ghufran (forgiveness), al-shukran (gratitude), and al-kufran (ingratitude),

[p. 392]

that is, He made them a reckoning, that is, a sign of reckoning for people, by which they calculate the times of the night and the day, the months, the seasons, and the years through their movements. This is a blessing upon people and a reminder of the manifestation of knowledge and power. For this reason, the sun was given a reckoning just as the moon was, because many nations reckon their months and years by the course of the sun, through its entry into the zodiacal signs and its completion of its cycle through them. The Arabs reckon by the course of the moon through its stations. This is what Islam brought, while in the Jahiliyya the Arabs used to make intercalation (kabs) to convert the year into equal seasons. Thus the point of the blessing is more general than the legal consideration in reckoning months and years by the lunar calendar. That this was possible for people is due to God's making the movements of the sun and the moon follow a single order that does not vary, and that is among the greatest proofs of God's knowledge and power. This is according to what appears to people of it; if they were to become acquainted with the secrets of that wondrous order, the lesson in it would be greater still.

The predication of the two by a verbal noun (masdar) is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), because it has the meaning of the active participle, i.e., reckoning (hasibayn). The ones who reckon are the people, by means of the sun and the moon.

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ (dhalika) refers to the making (al-ja'l) derived from jā'il (the one who makes).

The measure (al-taqdir) means: He set things according to a known measure, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He created everything and measured it precisely﴾ (al-Furqan 2).

Al-'Aziz: the Victorious, the Irresistible. God is truly al-'Aziz, because all created beings cannot escape His power. Al-'Alim is an intensive form (mubalaghah) denoting great knowledge, because the placing of things in such a wondrous order can only proceed from a Knower of immense knowledge.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 97:**

﴿It is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾

It is a conjunction ('atf) upon the clause ﴿And He who splits the night for rest﴾ [al-An'am: 96]. This is a reminder of God's oneness, of the great creation of the stars, and of the blessing that comes from the order of their movement, since they are a guidance for people, who are guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea.

[Page 393]

The regulation of the stars' motions, their risings and their settings, was among the earliest human sciences, appearing among the ancient Chaldeans and Egyptians. That order is what guided scholars to codify the science of astronomy (al-hay'ah).

The primary purpose of this report is to establish, by proof, the oneness of God in divinity. For this reason it is phrased with an exclusive construction (qasr) by means of the definiteness of the predicate and the subject, because the fact that the creation of the stars is from God, and that they are something by which one is guided, is not denied by the addressees. Yet they did not act in accordance with what this requires, namely singling Him out in worship.

Al-nujum (the stars) is the plural of najm, which is the kawkab, that is, the luminous spherical body that appears on the horizon at night and appears small to the eye. Therefore the moon is not a najm.

Ja'ala here means khalaqa (created), so it takes one object. The phrase lakum is attached to ja'ala, and the pronoun refers to all of mankind, so the lam in lakum indicates purpose (ta'lil).

His saying ﴿that you may be guided by them﴾ is a second cause of ja'ala, and the lam is also for causation. The first lam indicates the intent of granting favour, which is why it is followed by a pronoun referring to persons, as in His saying ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]. The second lam indicates the wisdom of the creating and the reason for the favour, which is that great benefit. Since being guided is among the states of the addressees, the position of ﴿that you may be guided﴾ is close to the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) by repeating the governing verb. This has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿It will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114] in surah al-Ma'idah.

By "the darknesses" is meant intense darkness, so the plural form is used to express intensity. It has been mentioned earlier, at His saying ﴿And He left them in darknesses, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in surah al-Baqarah, that the common usage is to say zulumat (darknesses), not zulmah (darkness).

The idafah (construct phrase) of "darknesses" to "land and sea" is in the sense of "in" (fi), because the darknesses occur in these two places, that is, that you may be guided by them in travelling through the darknesses. Whoever denies that the idafah is in the sense of "in" takes it as an idafah in the sense of lam, for the least connection, as in kawkab al-kharqa'.

The idafah for the least connection is either a linguistic metaphor (majaz lughawi) based on resemblance, so it is a metaphor (isti'arah) according to the apparent words of al-Miftah in the discussion of eloquence and fluency, where he made the idafah of "water" to "earth" in His saying ﴿O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44] a metaphor, comparing the connection of water to earth with the connection of ownership to owner. (End of quotation.) So he used in it the idafah which is in the sense of the lam of ownership, and this is a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). Or it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli) according to al-Taftazani's view in another place, when he said regarding kawkab al-kharqa': the real meaning of the lam-idafah is complete exclusivity, so the idafah for least connection is a judgemental metaphor (majaz hukmi). Perhaps al-Taftazani sees the difference in the metaphor as differing according to how near the idafah for least connection is to the meaning of exclusivity and how far it is from it, as the difference between the two examples appears. Moreover, the phrase "for the least connection" indicates a rational metaphor, because it is the attribution of the judgement, or its meaning, to something that is connected to what it belongs to.

The clause ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾ is a resumptive (mustanafah) clause for recording, conveying, and cutting off the excuse of those who do not believe. The lam is for causation (ta'lil) and is attached to fassalna (We have detailed), as in his saying:

*And the day I slaughtered my mount for the maidens*

That is, We have detailed them for the sake of a people who know.

The detailing of the signs has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Thus We detail the signs﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in this surah. Making the detailing for a people who know is an implicit rebuke to those who did not benefit from this detailing, that they are a people who do not know.

[Page 394]

[Page 395]

The definiteness in "the signs" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), so it includes the sign of the creation of the stars and others.

Knowledge ('ilm) in the speech of the Arabs is the perception of things as they really are. Al-Samaw'al or 'Abd al-Malik al-Harithi said:

*So the knowing and the ignorant are not equal*

And al-Nabighah said:

*And the ignorant of a thing is not like one who knows it*

Those who know are those who have benefited from the proofs of the signs, and they are those who believe in God alone, as He said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [al-An'am: 99].

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 6, verse 98:**

﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul, and [for you there is] a place of lodging and a place of storage. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾

This is a reminder of the creation of man and how this great multitude came into being from a single soul, as is known to them. The One who brought people into being and created them is the one truly deserving of their worship, not anything else they associated with Him. Reflecting on the creation of man is among the greatest proofs (of God's oneness). God says: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat: 21).

The restriction (qasr) produced by defining both the subject and the predicate is an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists, since they associated with their Creator others who did not create them, in the manner I explained in the verse before this one.

Al-insha' means bringing into existence and originating. The pronoun in "you" (aktum) refers to all of mankind. The "single soul" is Adam, peace be upon him.

As for His words ﴿a place of lodging (fa-mustaqarr)﴾: the fa' indicates a consequence of "He produced you." It is the consequence of something that includes (mushtamil) the thing it is connected to (muqarin) being placed upon what includes it (mushtamil). The majority read *mustaqarr* with a fatha on the qaf, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the qaf. According to the reading with a fatha on the qaf, it is a mim-prefixed verbal noun (masdar mimi), and *mustawda'* is likewise. Both are in the nominative because they are the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' whose khabar is omitted), the implied sense being "for you" or "among you." Or they are the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied sense being "so you are a place of lodging and a place of storage." Describing (someone) with a verbal noun is for emphasis regarding what is produced by it, meaning: from your creation there resulted lodging and storage, i.e., for you.

According to the reading with a kasra on the qaf, *al-mustaqirr* is an active participle (ism fa'il), and *al-mustawda'* is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from *istawda'ahu*, meaning *awda'ahu* (he deposited it with him). The sense is: "Among you is one who is settled, whom We have settled, so he is settled; and among you is one deposited, whom We have deposited, so he is deposited."

*Al-istiqrar* is *al-qarar* (settling), and the *sin* and *ta'* in it are for emphasis, like in *istajaba*. It is said: *istaqarra fi al-makan* with the meaning of *qarra* (he settled in the place). This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿For every news is a fixed time (mustaqarr)﴾ in this surah.

*Al-istida'*: is requesting leaving, and its root derives from *al-wad'*, which is leaving something on the condition that the deposited thing is retrieved. It is said: *istawda'ahu malan* when he placed property with him as a trust (wadi'ah). Thus *al-istida'* indicates a temporary placement, while *al-istiqrar* indicates a permanent or long placement.

The commentators differed about what is meant by *al-istiqrar* and *al-istida'* in this verse, though they agreed that they are opposites. From Ibn Mas'ud: *al-mustaqarr* is existence on the surface of the earth, and *al-mustawda'* is existence in the grave. According to this view, the statement is a warning to them that the life of people in this world is followed by being placed in graves, and that this placement is a temporary deposit until the resurrection, which is the first life, in refutation of those who denied the resurrection.

From Ibn 'Abbas: *al-mustaqarr* is in the womb, and *al-mustawda'* is in the loins of the man. This was also related from Ibn Mas'ud, and it was said by Mujahid, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and al-Zajjaj explained it this way. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "Among the things that indicate the strength of this view is that a single drop of semen does not remain in the loins of the father for a long time, while the fetus remains in the mother's womb for a long time." There are other explanations besides these that do not satisfy the heart, and we have turned away from prolonging them.

Al-Tabari said: "God did not specify one meaning to the exclusion of others. There is no doubt that among the children of Adam there is one who is settled in the womb and deposited in the loins; and among them is one who is settled on the surface or in the belly of the earth and deposited in the loins of men; and among them is one settled in the grave and deposited on the surface of the earth. So every settled or deposited (person) in any of these senses is included in the generality of His words ﴿a place of lodging and a place of storage﴾." End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What the reasoning requires is that the son of Adam is deposited in his father's loins and is not settled therein, because he inevitably moves on; then he moves to the womb, then he moves to this world, then he moves to the grave, then he moves to the gathering, then he moves to Paradise or Hell. In each stage between these two states he is settled in relation to the one before it and deposited in relation to the one after it." End of quote.

The more evident view is that *al-istida'* is not restricted to graves; rather, it is a deposit from the time of creation, because the intended purpose is to remind them of the second life. Also, the more evident view is that the *waw* is not for division (taqsim), but rather the better view is that it is for combination (jam'), meaning: He produced you, so your condition is settling and depositing, and you, while settled on the earth, are deposits in it, and your return is to your Creator, just as a deposit returns to its depositor. The choice of expressing this with these two verbal nouns was only to intend the abundance of this sentence (tawfir hadhihi al-jumlah).

According to the reading with a kasra on the qaf, *mustaqirr* is an active participle, *mustawda'* is a passive participle, and the meaning is the same.

His words ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾ are a confirmation of their similar statement mentioned earlier, intended as a reminder and a clearing of excuse (i'dhar).

He changed from "who know" (ya'lamun) to "who understand" (yafqahun) because the indication of their creation through these stages of settling and depositing, and the wisdom in them, is a subtle indication that requires reflection. The addressees were turning away from it, so He expressed knowledge of it as understanding (fiqh). This contrasts with the indication of the stars for the wisdom of guidance by them, which is a repeated indication. It is also an indirect allusion (ta'rid) that the polytheists do not know and do not understand. Knowledge is the cognition that agrees with reality, and understanding (fiqh) is the perception of subtle things. Thus the detailing of the signs was realized for the believers, and benefit from it was negated for the polytheists. For this reason He said after this, ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ (Al-An'am: 99).

*Page 396 and 397 markers are as they appear in the source.*

[Page 399]

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the growth of every thing, then We brought forth from it green vegetation, from which We bring forth grain piled up; and from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low; and gardens of grapevines, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at their fruit when it bears fruit and at its ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

The discussion of the restrictive form (qasr) in His saying ﴿And it is He who sent down﴾ and so on is like the discussion of its earlier counterpart.

The *min* in His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), because rainwater forms in the upper atmospheric layers, which are frigid, when earthly vapour rises to them. The vapour then becomes dense, which is the cloud, and then it turns into water.

Thus *al-sama'* (the sky) is the name of the highest layers of the atmosphere, where rain forms. It has already been discussed in His saying, ﴿or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], in Surat al-Baqarah.

He shifted from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in His saying ﴿then We brought forth﴾, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person).

The *ba'* is causal (sababiyyah): God made the water the cause of the emergence of vegetation. The pronoun governed by the *ba'* refers back to the water.

*Al-nabat* (vegetation) is the name of what grows. It is a verbal noun from *nabata* (to grow), and it was applied to the growing thing by way of metaphor (majaz), which became a widespread conventional usage, so that *al-nabat* became a term shared between the noun and the verbal noun.

[Page 399 continues]

*Shay'* (thing) here means a kind of vegetation, by the indication of the fact that *nabat* is in construct with it. The meaning is: We brought forth by the water what grows of the kinds of plants. Vegetation is a genus that has many species. Among it is *zar'* (crops), which has soft stems like reeds; among it is *shajar* (trees), which has thick stems like the palm tree and the grapevine; and among it is *najm* and *abb*, which grow flat against the ground. This generalization indicates that these things differ in attributes, fruits, natures, specific properties and tastes, yet all of them grow from the rainwater, which is one. That is a sign of the greatness of power. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. It is a reminder to people, so that they may reflect on the subtleties that God has placed in them of the various powers that cause their states to differ.

The *fa'* in His saying ﴿So We brought forth by it the growth of every thing﴾ is the *fa'* of consequence (tafri').

His saying ﴿So We brought forth from it green vegetation﴾ is a detailed explanation of the content of the clause ﴿So We brought forth by it the growth of every thing﴾. So the *fa'* is for detail, and *min* is either for the starting point or partitive (tab'idiyyah). The pronoun it governs refers back to the vegetation. That is, from the vegetation there was green growth, palm trees, gardens and trees. This is the division of the genus into its species.

*Al-khadir* is that whose colour is green. It is said *akhdar* and *khadir*, just as it is said *a'war* and *'uwir*. The word *khadir* is also used as a name for moist vegetation that is not a tree, such as fodder and fresh shoots. In the hadith: "What the spring produces includes what kills by bloating or what only comes close to killing; except the eater of green growth, who eats until her flanks are distended..." (the hadith continues). This is what is meant here, given His description of it: ﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, since grain emerges from moist vegetation.

The clause ﴿We bring forth from it﴾ is a description of the word ﴿green﴾, because it has become a noun. The *min* is either connective (ittisaliyyah) or for the starting point, and the pronoun it governs refers back to ﴿green﴾.

*Al-habb* (grain) is the fruit of vegetation, such as wheat and barley, and all cereal crops.

[Page 400]

*Al-mutarakib* (piled up) is that which is packed together on the ear of grain, like wheat and others. The form *tafā'ul* here is for intensification, in the sense of one part mounting another.

The clause ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿So We brought forth from it green vegetation﴾. It may also be parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), in which case the *wa* is parenthetical. The phrase ﴿from the palm trees﴾ is then the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿clusters﴾ is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar).

The purpose of the statement here is to express wonder at the emergence of clusters from the spathe and at the beauty it contains. This makes clear the reason why the style of this clause differs from the styles before and after it: its parts are not coordinated in the manner of single words. Moreover, the position of this clause among its sisters conveys what its sisters convey of lesson and divine favour.

The definition in *al-nakhl* (the palm trees) is the generic definition of familiar reference (ta'rif al-'ahd al-jinsi). The definite article was used here to indicate that it is the familiar kind known to the Arabs, for the palm tree was their tree, its fruit their staple, and its orchards a source of contentment for their souls. You may also make it a circumstantial clause (hal) from *al-nakhl*, relying on the verbal definiteness, as in His saying ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate, similar﴾. And it is permissible for ﴿from its spathes﴾ to be an apposition for a part (badl ba'd) of ﴿the palm trees﴾, with the repetition of the preposition governing the item being replaced.

*Qinwan* (clusters), with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, is the plural of *qinw*, also with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, according to the well-known form among the Arabs, other than the dialect of Qays and the people of the Hijaz, who put a *damma* on the *qaf*. So *qinwan* with a *kasra* is a broken plural (jam' taksir). This pattern is rare, except for the plural of *fu'al*, *fu'l* and *fa'l* when they are hollow with a *waw* in the middle, and of *fu'al*.

*Al-qinw* is the stalk of dates, like a cluster for grapes. It is also called *al-'idhq* (with a *kasra* on the 'ayn), and it is also called *al-kibasah* (with a *kasra* on the *kaf*).

*Al-tal'* is the sheath of the date stalk, which appears when it first emerges. It is shaped like a large citron, closed over the stalk; then it opens like the form of two sandals, and the cluster emerges from it gathered together. At that stage it is called *al-ighriḍ*, and then it becomes a *qinw*.

*Daniyah* means near. The meaning is near to hand, as in His saying ﴿its fruits hanging low﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]. The clusters that hang low are a part of the clusters of the palm trees, singled out for mention here by way of incorporating divine favour within the reminder of the perfection of craftsmanship. The favour is more complete with the clusters that hang low. The low-hanging ones are those whose palm is short and does not exceed the height of a person reaching for them. There is no need to mention those far out of reach, because the reminder has been achieved by the low-hanging ones, and the favour has been augmented by its completeness.

*Wa jannat* (and gardens) in the accusative is coordinated with ﴿green﴾. What was attributed to Abu Bakr from 'Asim, reading *jannatun* in the nominative, is not authentic.

His saying ﴿of grapevines﴾ is a specification (tamyiz) in the genitive, governed by the explanatory *min* (min bayaniyyah), because the gardens relate to the grapevines in the way that measures do, as one says *jaribun tamran* (a plot of dates). On this basis the verb of bringing forth is transferred to the gardens and not to the grapevines, so one does not say *wa a'nabanw fi jannat* (and grapevines in gardens).

*Al-a'nab* is the plural of *'inab*, which is the plural of *'inabah*. Originally it is the fruit of the vine tree. The word *'inab* is also applied to the vine tree itself, by way of an implied construction (taqdir mudaf), meaning *shajarat 'inab* (a grapevine tree), and this usage became common, so the implied word was forgotten. Al-Raghib said: "*'Inab* is said of the fruit of the vine and of the vine itself." (End of quotation.)

It is not known that the singular is applied to the vine tree. I have not found in their speech the singular *'inabah* applied to the vine tree. But it is applied in the plural, as one says *'inab*, meaning the vine. Such is His saying ﴿and We made grain grow in it﴾ [*'Abasa*: 27] ﴿and grapes﴾ [*'Abasa*: 28]. One also says *a'nab* in this way, as here. The apparent sense of al-Raghib's words is that *'inabah* is said of the vine tree, for he said: "*'Inab* is said of the fruit of the vine and of the vine itself, its singular being *'inabah*." (End of quotation.)

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾ is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿gardens﴾. The definiteness in both of them is generic, like the definiteness in His saying ﴿and from the palm trees﴾. The meaning of "the olive and the pomegranate" is their trees. Originally they are names of the two fruits, and then they were applied to their two trees, as has been mentioned regarding the grapes. Although these two trees were not as important to the Arabs as the palm tree, nevertheless, because of their scarcity in the lands of the Arabs and the Arabs' eagerness to enjoy their fruit and their admiration for owning them, they were mentioned in the context of reminding people of God's wondrous creation and His favour. The olive tree existed in al-Sham and in Sinai, and the pomegranate tree existed in al-Ta'if.

His saying ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) and a clause coordinated with it. The *wa* is for division (taqsim), by the indication that one single thing cannot be both similar and dissimilar. That is, some of it is similar and some of it is dissimilar.
