These two are circumstantial clauses for the olive and the pomegranate together. The form is singular and not plural, in consideration of the singular form of the word.

*Al-tashabuh* and *al-ishtibah* are synonyms, like *al-tasawi* and *al-istiwa'*, and both are derived from *al-shabah* (resemblance). Their combination in the verse is for variety, out of dislike of repeating a word, and because the active participle from *tashabuh* is more suited to pausing, since it has the lengthening of the voice, unlike *mushtabihan*. This is one of the marvels of eloquence.

*Al-tashabuh* is the sameness of a thing in one state while differing in its other states. That is, some of its trees resemble one another and some of them do not resemble one another; or some of its fruit resembles other fruit and some does not. Thus *tashabuh* covers things that are close in colour, taste or shape, which people seek in their various conditions according to their differing tastes. *Ikhtilaf* (difference) is counted as that in which some of it differs from others in attributes that people seek, according to the variety of their desires. Among the branches of the tree some are thick and some thin; among the colours of its leaves some are dark and some deep; among the colours of its fruit there are differences, and likewise in its taste. This is like His saying, ﴿and We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. The purpose of restricting it with this condition is to draw attention to the fact that they were created by intention and choice, not by chance.

It is also possible to make this circumstantial clause apply to everything mentioned before in His saying ﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾,

[Page 403]

since all of that is both similar and dissimilar. Al-Zamakhshari made it a circumstantial clause for the olive, because it is the thing coordinated with, and he supposed a second circumstantial clause for the pomegranate indicated by the first, with the implied meaning: "and the pomegranate is likewise." What led him to this is that he does not hold that one circumstantial clause may have multiple referents, nor that there is a conflict over a circumstantial clause, and he took as a parallel the singular predicate after a subject and a coordinated item in the verse of al-Azraq ibn Tarafah al-Bahili, in reply to a man from Banu Qushayr when they disputed over a well. The Qushayri said: "You are a thief, the son of a thief," and he replied:

*He accused me of a thing from which I and my father were innocent, and because of the well he accused me.*

There is no harm in this parsing from the standpoint of meaning, because the attention drawn to what is in some vegetation of signs of deliberate choice directs minds to what is in its like among similar things.

The clause ﴿Look at its fruit﴾ is an explanation of the clauses before it, whose aim is to reach knowledge of God's creation and power. The pronoun added to *thamarihi* (its fruit) refers back to what the pronoun in ﴿similar﴾ referred to, whether by specification or generalization.

The thing commanded is the gaze of insight and reflection on its stages.

*Al-thamar* (fruit) is the harvest that the tree yields. It is with a *fatha* on the *tha'* and *mim* in the reading of most, as the plural of *thamarah* with a *fatha* on the *tha'* and *mim*. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a *damma* on the *tha'* and *mim*, which is a broken plural, as *khashabah* becomes *khushub* and *naqah* becomes *nuq*.

*Al-yan'* is ripeness and maturity. One says *yana'a* (with a *fatha* on the *nun*), *yay'a'u* (with a *fatha* or *kasra* on the *nun*). It is also said *ayna'a*, *yuni'u*, *yan'an*, with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a silent *nun* after it.

*Idha* (when) is an adverb of time for the occurrence of the verb. So it means the time at which the content of the clause it is attached to begins, that is, at the moment of the beginning of its fruiting. His saying ﴿and its ripening﴾ was not restricted by "when it ripens," because when it has ripened its development is complete and its harvest is due, so there is no lesson left in looking at it, since its stages have ended.

[Page 404]

The clause ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ is the reason for the command to look. The position of *inna* here is that of the *lam* of causation, as in the verse of Bashshar:

*Indeed that success lies in early morning.*

The reference of *dhalikum* (that) is to the whole of what was mentioned, from His saying ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the growth of every thing﴾ up to His saying ﴿its ripening﴾. So the singular demonstrative is used with the sense of "what was mentioned," as was discussed in His saying ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Here "for a people who believe" (liqawmin yu'minun) is a description of the signs. The lam is for causation (ta'lil), and what is caused is the implicit sense of guidance and benefit contained in the signified content of the signs. He has explicitly stated in this that the signs only benefit the believers, by his saying in the two other verses "for a people who know" and his saying "for a people who understand" (Al-An'am: 98). This also completes the allusion that those who do not know and do not understand are those who do not believe, meaning the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 100:

﴿They ascribed to God partners, the jinn, though He created them, and they falsely attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe.﴾

It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the sentences before it in the manner of one story joined to another (ʿaṭf al-qiṣṣa ʿalā al-qiṣṣa). The subject pronoun in *jaʿalū* ("they made") refers back to *qawmuka* ("your people") in His words ﴿and your people denied it﴾ [Al-An'am: 66].

This is a transition to mention another form of shirk among the Arabs: their making the jinn partners to God in worship, just as they made the idols partners to Him in that. The religion of the Arabs in the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance) was a mixture of idol worship, Sabianism (ʿibadat al-kawākib, the worship of the stars), the worship of the devils (shayāṭīn), the Magianism of the Persians, and elements of Judaism and Christianity. Because of their ignorance at that time, the Arabs would receive from the neighbouring nations, to which they travelled, various beliefs, some close to one another and some far apart, and they took them without reflection or scrutiny, since knowledge was absent among them. Sound knowledge is what protects the intellects from having false notions and false beliefs nest in them. So the origin of the Arabs' religion in the Jahiliyya was the worship of idols, and beliefs such as the belief in the authority of the jinn and the devils, and the like, crept into them along with it.

The Arabs affirmed the jinn and attributed to them actions. For this reason they feared the jinn, sought their protection, made amulets (maʿādhāt) and incantations (ruqā) for them, and sought their favour through offerings and by omitting the invocation of God over some slaughtered animals. They believed that the soothsayer (kāhin) is brought news from the heaven by the jinn, and that the poet has a devil (shayṭān) who inspires him with poetry. Then, when they tried to explain these practices and combined them with their belief in the divinity of God, Exalted is He, they justified this by saying that the jinn have a relation with God, Exalted is He. Therefore they said: "The angels are the daughters of God, from the mothers of the chiefs of the jinn," as His words indicate: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [As-Saffat: 158], and He said: ﴿Ask them: "Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?"﴾ [As-Saffat: 149] ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [As-Saffat: 150] ﴿Surely it is from their own lie that they say﴾ [As-Saffat: 151] ﴿"God has begotten," and they are indeed liars﴾ [As-Saffat: 152]. For this reason many of the Arab tribes made a part of their worship directed to the angels and the jinn. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And on the day He gathers them all, He will say to the angels: "Were these the ones who used to worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40] ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them"﴾ [Saba': 41].

Those who claimed that the angels are the daughters of God were Quraysh, Juhayna, Banu Salama, Khuzaʿa, and Banu Mulayh. Some of the Arabs were Magians who worshipped the devil, and claimed that he is the god of evil and that God is the god of good, and they made the angels the soldiers of God and the jinn the soldiers of the devil. They claimed that God created the devil from His own essence, then entrusted to him the management of evil, so he became the god of evil. They had taken this from the Mazdakite religion (al-Dīyāna al-Mazdakiyya), which holds to two gods: a god of good, who is Yazdān, and a god of evil, who is Ahriman, and he is the devil.

So His words ﴿the jinn﴾ [Saba': 41] are the first object of *jaʿalū* ("they made"), and *shurakāʾa* ("partners") is its second object, because the intended meaning of the context is the jinn, not partners in general, since the making of partners for God has already been established before. *Lillāh* ("for God") is connected to *shurakāʾa*. The second object is placed before the first because it is the locus of wonder and denial, so it became more important, and its mention came first.

The placement of the prepositional phrase *lillāh* before the object *shurakāʾa* in the phrase *lillāh shurakāʾa* serves to emphasise and to express wonder at the error of their minds, in that they make partners for God from among His creatures, since the polytheists acknowledge that God is the creator of the jinn. This fronting therefore runs contrary to what the apparent structure would require, for the sake of what required its opposite. The words of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, by al-Zamakhshari) make the fronting of the prepositional phrase in the verse serve emphasis on their belief in a partner for God, an emphasis appropriate to its context, namely censure and denunciation. The author of al-Miftah (Miftah al-ʿUlum, by al-Sakkaki) followed him, saying, in regard to the fronting of some complements before others for the sake of attention: by fronting it, it is placed before your eyes, as you find when someone says to you, "You know partners for God," your hair stands on end and you say: "Partners for God?!" And upon this is His word, Exalted is He, ﴿They made for God partners﴾. End of quote. So the fronting of the prepositional phrase runs in accordance with what the apparent structure requires.

*Al-jinn* (with a kasra on the jim) is a name for existent beings among the immaterial entities that have no bodies, possessing a fiery nature, and which have particular effects in certain actions that affect some existing things in ways that great powers do not affect. They are of the kind of the devils (shayāṭīn). The duration of the existence of their individuals is not known, nor is the manner of the survival of their species. The Qur'an has affirmed them in general terms, and the Arabs had tales about their imagining. They imagined them able to take the forms of all existing things, and claimed that if they touch a person they harm and kill him; that they snatch some people in the deserts; that they have a crashing sound and voices in the deserts; they claimed that the echo is from the jinn; this has been mentioned under His words ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth﴾ [Al-An'am: 71]; and that they may recite poetry, and that they appear to the soothsayers and the poets.

The clause ﴿and He created them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the *waw* is the *waw* of the circumstance.

The object pronoun in *khalaqahum* may refer to what the pronoun in *jaʿalū* refers to, that is, "and He created the polytheists." The point of this circumstantial clause is wonder at their making partners for God while He is their creator, in the manner of His words ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [Al-Waqiʿa: 82]. On this reading the plural pronouns are consistent, and the wonder in this case is at their making this, although God is in fact their creator. How, then, do they not consider that the requirement of creation is that He be singled out for divinity, since there is no basis for claiming it for one who does not create, as in His words ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ [An-Nahl: 17]. So the wonder on this reading is at their ignorance and poor judgement.

It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿and He created them﴾ refers to the jinn, because that pronoun is correctly applied to them in view of their having intellect. The point of the circumstantial clause is wonder at the error of the polytheists in associating with God in worship some of His creatures, while they know that they are created by God, Exalted is He. For the polytheists said that God is the creator of the jinn, as has preceded, and that there is no creator but Him. So the wonder is at their contradiction of what their knowledge requires. The estimate then is: "and He created them as is in their knowledge," that is, "and He created them without dispute." This reading is more evident.

The clause ﴿and they falsely attributed﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause "and they made," and the pronoun refers to the polytheists.

The majority of readers recite *wa-kharaqū* with a light *rāʾ* (*kharaqū*), but Nafiʿ and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a doubled *rāʾ* (*kharraqū*).

*Al-kharq* originally means cutting and splitting. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: it is cutting and splitting in the manner of corruption, without reflection, and from it is His word ﴿Did you sink it to drown its people?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 71]. It is the opposite of *khalq* (creation), for *khalq* is doing a thing with measure and gentleness, while *kharq* is without measure. No other of the masters of linguistics restricted it in this way. Whatever the case, *al-kharq* has been used figuratively for lying, just as *iftarā* and *ikhtalaqa* (to fabricate) were used for it, from *al-farī* and *al-khalq*. In al-Kashshaf: al-Hasan was asked about His word ﴿and they falsely attributed﴾ and he said: it is an Arabic word which the Arabs used to say; when a man told a lie in the assembly of a people, some of them would say: "He has indeed *kharaqahā*, by God." The reading of Nafiʿ conveys intensification in the action, because the *tafʿīl* form indicates the strength of the occurrence of the action. So the meaning of *kharraqū* is that they lied against God in the manner of fabrication, that is, they attributed to Him sons and daughters falsely.

[Page 408]

As for their attribution of sons to God, the Qur'an has related it from them here. The intended meaning is that the polytheists attributed to Him sons and daughters. It is not meant that the Jews (by their saying ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾ [At-Tawba: 30]) or the Christians (by their saying "Jesus is the son of God") are intended, as all the exegetes have interpreted it, because that does not fit the context, confuses the return of the pronouns, and breaks the structure of the speech. The correct view is that the intended meaning is that some of the polytheists attributed sons to God, and they are those who acquired some of Magianism, because when they made the devil to be begotten by God, Exalted is He, in that they said that when God created the world He contemplated His dominion and magnified it, so there arose in Him self-admiration from which the devil was generated. They may also have said that God doubted His own power, so the devil was generated from His doubt. Thus it became necessary for them that the devil is begotten of God, Exalted is He above what they say, and so it became necessary for them to attribute a son to God, Exalted is He.

Perhaps some of them used to say that the jinn are the sons of God and the angels are the daughters of God, or that among the angels there are males and females. This belief may have been drawn from the Jews, for they made the angels the sons of God. It is found in the beginning of the sixth chapter of the Book of Genesis: "And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them, that the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose. And when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown."

As for their attribution of daughters to God, it is well known among the Arabs, as they made the angels females and said: they are the daughters of God.

His words ﴿without knowledge﴾ are connected to *kharraqū*, that is, they fabricated with fabrication out of ignorance and error, because it is a fabrication that does not cohere with reason and knowledge, so they uttered their saying out of blindness and ignorance. The meaning of "knowledge" here is knowledge in its correct sense, which is a judgement of the mind that corresponds to reality, arising from necessity or from proof.

[Page 409]

The *bāʾ* is the *bāʾ* of accompaniment, that is, they were accompanied by the ignorance of their fabrication from beginning to end. They fabricated without a motive or proof, and found no currency for what they fabricated. Its necessary consequence is the absurdity of their speech, its corruption, and its lack of coherence. This is the place of the *bāʾ* of accompaniment in the verse, whose meaning no other particle conveys.

The clause ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, declaring Him free of all that was reported about them. *Subḥān* is a verbal noun in the accusative, in apposition to its verb. The original sentence is "I glorify God with glorification." When it was substituted for its verb it became *subḥāna Allāh*, by its being added to its original object. It has been discussed before in His words ﴿They said: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us"﴾ [Al-Baqara: 32] in Surat al-Baqara.

The meaning of *taʿālā* is "He exalted Himself," and it is a *tafāʿul* form from height (*ʿulūw*). The *tafāʿul* here is for intensification in the attribution. The height here is figurative: that is, He is not diminished by what they describe Him with, meaning He is not described by that, because being characterised by such a thing is a deficiency, and He is not reached by deficiency. So the avoidance of defects was likened to elevation, because an elevated thing is not stuck with the filth which by nature lies on the ground. Just as deficiency was likened to lowliness, perfection was likened to height. So the meaning of "exalted above that" is that such a thing does not reach Him.

His words ﴿what they describe﴾ are connected to *taʿālā*, so *ʿan* ("above") is for transcendence, and it has entered upon the relative pronoun, that is, above that which they describe.

*Al-wasf* (description) is the report about the states and attributes of a thing and what distinguishes it. It is therefore a clarifying and detailed report of its states, to the point that it is as if the reporter describes the thing and characterises it.

The verb ﴿they describe﴾ was chosen in the verse because what they attributed to God comes back to describing Him with partners and sons, that is, He is far removed from being characterised by it. As for their having described Him with it, that is a fact that has occurred.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 101:

Page 410
﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a child when He has no consort, and He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things?﴾
This is a resumed (mustaʼnafah) sentence, and it begins the statement of the great power of God, the Exalted. It also serves to strengthen the declaration of His transcendence in His saying ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100], so it takes the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the content of that declaration, with its own content as well. By this consideration, its separation (fasl) from what precedes it by conjunction ('atf) was preferred, for what they describe is their saying that He has sons and daughters. That declaration (tanzih) includes the negation of the thing from which He is declared free and the refutation of it. So the refutation was given a reason: that He is the Creator of the greatest of created things in indicating power. Thus, if you claim the sonship of the jinn and the angels because of their greatness among created things, while you do not see the jinn or the angels, why do you not claim sonship for the heavens and the earth, which are visible to you and whose greatness you see? This refutation is like the "naqd" (demolition of the opponent's premise) in the science of disputation and debate.

His saying ﴿Originator﴾ is the predicate of a subject that is obligatorily omitted in such a construction, and it is an instance of omitting the subject (al-musnad ilayh) in accordance with customary usage when speech about something is followed by a single-word predicate about it, as has preceded in several places.

The discussion of ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ has already occurred at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116] and ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The argument for the negation of sonship from God, may He be exalted, by the origination of the heavens and the earth is that the creation of the locus (mahall) requires the creation of what inheres in it (hall). The polytheists say that the angels are in the sky and the jinn are in the earth and the wastelands. Therefore, it follows that the angels and jinn are originated (huduth); otherwise the inhering entity would exist before the existence of its locus. When their origination is established, the negation of sonship from God, may He be exalted, is established, because the son of a god is only a god, and so he would be eternal (qidam), whereas his origination has been established.

Page 411
For this reason He followed their saying "God has taken a son" with His saying, "﴿Glorified is He! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾" [al-Baqarah: 116], in Surat al-Baqarah. We have already pointed to this at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1] at the beginning of this surah.

The sentence ﴿How could He have a child﴾ takes the position of a reason for the content of the declaration of transcendence through refutation. It was not conjoined to the preceding sentence because the method of refutation differs: the first sentence refuted their claim from the side of the corruption of the doubt, so it was like the naqd in debate. This sentence refuted the claim from the side of refuting the reality, so it is as if it were from the side of the error of the proof, because their saying that the angels are God's daughters and the jinn are God's sons includes an implicit proof for sonship, namely that they are noble created beings. So this refutation is by arguing with what contradicts the claim, namely the absence of a consort, who is the origin of birth. Thus this second refutation is like the mu'arada (counter-argument) in debate.

Anna (أنّى) means "from where" and also "how."

The waw in ﴿and He has no consort﴾ is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal), because this is known to the addressees, and therefore it was expressed in the form of a circumstantial clause.

The ṣāḥibah (صاحبة) is the wife, because she accompanies the husband in most of his conditions. The absence of a wife was taken as a given, because they did not claim it, so the absence of a child was made binding on them because the condition of procreation is absent. This is based on conventional argumentation, according to what is known in the reality of birth.

His saying "and He created all things" is conjoined (ʻatf) to the sentence "Originator of the heavens and the earth" in terms of its apparent meaning, which is the description with attributes of greatness and power. So after He informed that He, may He be exalted, is the originator of the heavens and the earth, He informed that He is the creator of every thing, meaning every existent, which includes the essences of the heavens and the earth and includes what is in them. The angels are among what the heavens contain, and the jinn are among what the earth contains according to them. So He is the creator of these two kinds, and the creator cannot be a father, as you know. In this sentence there is also a refutation of the child,

Page 412
and this is a third refutation, by way of universality, after a partial refutation had been made. The meaning is that all existents are equal in the attribute of being created, and if He had children, they would not be created.

The sentence ﴿and He is Knowing of all things﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding summation) to complete the instruction of the addressees in some of the attributes of perfection established for God, the Exalted. It is a sentence conjoined to ﴿and He created all things﴾ in terms of the description it contains, not in terms of rejoinder. Because this last sentence takes the position of a tadhyil, He shifted in it from the pronoun to the noun in His saying "with every thing" rather than saying "with it," because tadhyil statements are intended to be independently self-sufficient in meaning, for they resemble proverbs in being speech that gathers many meanings.

[Page 413]

The demonstrative noun (*ism al-isharah*, "the pointing word") comes after the preceding attributes and predicates in order to alert the listener that the one being pointed to deserves the predicates and attributes that follow the demonstrative. This is as was explained earlier at His words ﴿That is Allah; how then are you deluded?﴾ [al-An'am: 95], before this, and at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The one pointed to is the one described by the attributes contained in the predicates mentioned earlier. For this reason, the demonstrative is not followed by an explicative (*bayan*) or an apposition (*badal*). The meaning is: "That is the One who originated the heavens and the earth, who created everything, and who knows everything: it is Allah, that is, the One you know." His words "your Lord" (*rabbukum*) are an attribute (*sifah*) of the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*). The clause ﴿there is no god but He﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of "your Lord" or an attribute. His words ﴿Creator of all things﴾ are an attribute of "your Lord" or of the Name of Majesty. We did not make it a predicate because the predication has already been made earlier by similar expressions in His words ﴿and He created all things﴾ [al-An'am: 101].

[Page 413]

The clause "so worship Him" is derived from (*mufarra'ah*) His words "your Lord; there is no god but He." He has made the command to worship Him a consequence of His being described with lordship (*rububiyyah*) and oneness (*wahdaniyyah*), because lordship necessitates the right to be worshipped, and sole lordship necessitates restricting worship to Him. This restriction has been understood from the consequential linkage.

The reason for commanding them to worship Him is that the polytheists had turned away from worshipping Allah, the Exalted, to the extent that, in their belief, they directed no acts of piety except to the idols. They would visit them, offer sacrifices to them, make vows to them, seek their help, and call upon them for support. They only mentioned Allah during the season of the Hajj. Even then, they mixed this with drawing near to the idols: they placed (*Hubal*) above the Ka'bah, and placed (*Isaf* and *Na'ilah*) above al-Safa and al-Marwah. Many of them would chant the talbiyah for (*Manat*) at the end of the Hajj. Thus they turned away from worshipping Allah, the Exalted. Therefore they were commanded to worship Him explicitly, and they were commanded to confine worship to Him by way of indication (*ima'*) through the consequential linkage.

The clause ﴿and He is Guardian over all things﴾ may be coordinated (*ma'tufah*) with the preceding attributes, in which case the clause "so worship Him" is a parenthetical insertion (*mu'taridah*). It may also be coordinated with the clause "so worship Him," based on the permissibility of coordinating a declarative statement (*khabar*) with an imperative (*insha'*) and vice versa (and this is the correct view). This serves to complete the justification for the command to worship Him alone to the exclusion of others: He is the one who takes charge of all things, of creation, provision, and bounty, and of everything a person seeks to have preserved for him. Therefore the proper course is to worship Him, and there is no proper basis for worshipping anyone else. The Name *al-Wakil* ("the Guardian") comprises the meanings of protection and watchful oversight, as was explained earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Surat Al 'Imran.

[p. 414]

﴿No vision comprehends Him, but He comprehends [all] vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾

This is an independent sentence (*jumla ibtida'iyya*) that serves to affirm His exaltedness, may He be exalted, and the breadth of His knowledge. Because of His greatness, He is far too exalted for any of the sights of created beings to encompass Him. This also implies an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to the negation of divinity from the idols,

[p. 415]

which are bodies (*ajsam*), limited, confined, and occupying space (*mutahayyiza*). That they can be perceived by sight is one of the characteristics of created things, and it is not fitting for divinity. Had they been gods, they would have been veiled from sight. The same applies to the stars that some of the Arabs worshipped. As for the jinn and the angels, whom some people worshipped, although they are not perceived by sight in ordinary experience for all people and not at all times, the polytheists claim that the jinn appear to them at times in the deserts and elsewhere. Shamir ibn al-Harith al-Dabbi said:

*They came to my fire, and I said: "Who are you?"
They said: "The jinn." I said: "Ghimu zalaman."*

They also imagine that the angels appear to some people, taking this from the Jews.

The basic meaning of *al-idrak* (comprehension, attainment) is reaching the sought object. It is used figuratively for the perception of the sensible by a sense, or of the intelligible by the intellect. One says: *adraka basari* ("my sight perceived") and *adraka 'aqli* ("my intellect comprehended"), likening the instrument of knowledge to a person or a horse that reaches its goal, comparing the intelligible to the sensible. One says: *adraka fulanun bi-basarihi* ("so-and-so perceived with his sight") and *adraka bi-'aqlihi* ("with his intellect"), but one does not say *adraka fulanun* without qualification. Later scholars of kalam (*al-mutakallimun*) and the philosophers (*al-hukama'*) adopted the convention of calling intellectual awareness *idrak*, and they made *idrak* a genus (*jins*) in the definition of conception (*tasawwur*) and assent (*tasdiq*). They also described the one who has sound understanding as *darraka* (perceptive, discerning).

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿and He comprehends [all] vision﴾, it is possible that attributing *idrak* to the Name of God is by *mushakala* (harmonization of wording) with what precedes it, namely His statement ﴿No vision comprehends Him﴾. It is also possible that *idrak* here is used metaphorically for *tasarruf* (control, disposal), since the meaning of *idrak* is *nawal* (attainment, reaching).

[p. 415, continued]

*Al-absar* is the plural of *basar*, which is the name of the faculty by which seeing takes place, spread throughout the pupil of the eye, which is in the center of the iris, and by which visible objects are perceived. The meaning is: the sights of those who see do not encompass Him, because the one who truly perceives is the seer, not the organ. The organ is only a means of perception, since it conveys the image to the common sense (*al-hiss al-mushtarak*) in the brain. The purpose of this is to show the difference between the specific nature of the true God and the specific nature of their gods in this world. God is not seen, whereas their idols are seen. That distinction is appropriate to His greatness, may He be exalted, for the non-encompassing of a thing by sights is a result of its greatness, so that sights cannot bear it. Thus the generality of the indefinite noun (*'umum al-nakira*) in a context of negation (*siyaq al-nafy*) indicates the negation that any of the sights of those who see in this world can comprehend Him, as the context indicates.

There is no indication in this verse that God will not be seen in the Hereafter, as the deniers of the vision (*nufat al-ru'ya*), who are the Mu'tazila, have held. This is because the affairs of the Hereafter have states that do not follow our ordinary experience. It is even more fitting that there is no indication in it that God may be seen in the Hereafter. Whoever tries to derive that has burdened himself with what cannot be established, as al-Fakhr (al-Razi) did in his commentary.

The disagreement about seeing God in the Hereafter is widespread among the groups of the mutakallimun. The majority of Ahl al-Sunna affirmed it, because of the abundance of apparent evidences from the Book and the Sunna, while agreeing that it is a kind of seeing that differs from ordinary seeing. It is reported from Malik, may God have mercy on him: "If the believers did not see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection, the unbelievers would not have been reproached with veiling in His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿No indeed! Surely they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15]." It is also reported from him: "God was not seen in this world because He is everlasting (*baqi*), and the everlasting is not seen by the perishable. When they are in the Hereafter and are given everlasting sights, they will see the everlasting by the everlasting." As for the Mu'tazila, they deemed the vision of God in the Hereafter impossible, because it entails being confined to a direction (*al-infiyaz fi al-jiha*). We have all agreed on the transcendence of God above confrontation (*al-muqabala*) and direction (*al-jiha*). We have also agreed on the possibility of complete intellectual unveiling (*al-inkishaf al-'ilmi*) for the believers in the Hereafter regarding the reality of the Truth, may He be exalted, and on the impossibility of an image of the seen object being imprinted in the eye, or of a ray emerging from the eye connecting with the seen object, may He be exalted, because the conditions of sight in the Hereafter are different from the conditions familiar in this world. Our scholars have discussed both the evidences for possibility (*al-jawaz*) and the evidences for actual occurrence (*al-wuqu'*). This is among the matters that must be believed in summarily, with verification. The evidences of the Mu'tazila and our answers to them are mentioned in the books of kalam, and they are not the purpose of tafsir. All of them ultimately return to acting upon the apparent meaning (*i'mal al-zahir*) or interpreting it (*ta'wilih*).

Then our imams differed as to whether God was seen by the Prophet ﷺ. A group of the Companions denied that, among them 'A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hurayra,

[p. 416]

may God be pleased with them, and they held to the generality of this verse, as is recorded in the hadith of al-Bukhari from 'Ikrima from 'A'isha. The majority affirmed it. It is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Accordingly, the generality would be restricted (*makhsus*). 'Iyad addressed this in *al-Shifa'*. The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about it and answered with a reply whose wording the narrators differed on, so God, through that difference, veiled the real matter, completing His purpose and showing kindness to His servants.

His statement ﴿and He comprehends [all] vision﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the sentence ﴿No vision comprehends Him﴾. The attribution of *idrak* to the pronoun of His Name, may He be exalted, is either because the verb *yudriku* is borrowed for the meaning of *yanalu* (reaching, attaining), meaning that nothing goes outside His disposal, as one says: "He overtook him and caught him" (*lahiqahu fa-adrakahu*). Thus the meaning is: He has power over sight, that is, over those who see. Or because the verb *yudriku* is borrowed for the meaning of *ya'lamu* (knows), to harmonize with His statement ﴿No vision comprehends Him﴾, meaning: no sights know Him. That is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for knowledge of hidden things, because the sights are the fine lenses which are the intermediary of the sense of vision, or they are the sense itself, which is more hidden. Its plural form is due to the consideration of those who perceive.

In His statement ﴿No vision comprehends Him, but He comprehends [all] vision﴾ there is an embellishment of *tibaq* (antithesis).

The clause ﴿and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿No vision comprehends Him﴾, so it is a second attribute. Or it is a *tadhyil* (appended concluding statement) serving as *ihtiras* (precautionary qualification, a safeguard), to repel the assumption that one whom sights do not comprehend does not know the states of those whom they do not comprehend.

*Al-Latif* is a descriptive adjective derived from *al-lutf* or from *al-latafa*. One says *latafa* with a fatha on the *ta'*, meaning "he was gentle," "he honored," and "he showed kindness." It is transitive with *bi* and with *li*, according to whether one considers the meaning of "being gentle" or "doing good." For this reason the gift and the token by which a person is honored are called *latafan* (with a vowel on the *ta'*), and their plural is *alatafun*. The adjective from this is *lati* and *latif*. So *al-Latif* is an active participle in the sense of intensification (*mubalagha*), which indicates the omission of a verb from its doer, and from it is His statement, may He be exalted, quoting Joseph: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. One also says *lutufa*, with a damma on the *ta'*, meaning "he became fine and light," the opposite of "he became heavy and dense."

[p. 417]

*Al-Latif* is either a *sifa mushabbaha* (attribute-like adjective) or an *ism fa'il* (active participle). If it is considered a descriptive adjective derived from *lutufa* (with a damma), then it is a *sifa mushabbaha* indicating an attribute of the essence of God, may He be exalted, namely the attribute of His transcendence above the encompassing of His reality by minds or the encompassing of His essence and attributes by the senses. Thus choosing it to express this attribute regarding God, may He be exalted, is the utmost clarity and elegance of expression, because it is the nearest root in the Arabic language to bringing close the meaning of His attribute, may He be exalted, according to what the language has established for it in the common usage of people. It is thus close to being among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous/analogical terms). Accordingly, it is more general than the content of the clause ﴿No vision comprehends Him﴾. It thus functions after the preceding clause as a *tadhyil* or as an inference of the particular from the universal, so the attribute before it becomes firmer. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it in this sense in *al-Kashshaf*, because it is more suitable to this context, and it is one of the well-known meanings of the word in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Fakhr found it good, and al-Raghib and al-Baydawi permitted it. This is the interpretation that should be adopted in every place where the attribute *al-Latif* is combined with the attribute *al-Khabir*, as here and in Surat al-Mulk.

If *al-Latif* is considered an active participle from *latafa* (with a fatha), then it is one of the forms of intensification, indicating His attribution of gentleness, kindness to His creatures, perfection of His craftsmanship in that, and abundance of His acting in that way. Thus it indicates an attribute of His actions. In this sense the rest of the exegetes and those who explained the meaning of His Name *al-Latif* among the Most Beautiful Names took it. This meaning is appropriate in every place where His attribute is mentioned alone, transitive with *li* or *bi*, such as ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾ [Yusuf: 100], and His statement ﴿God is Subtle to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19]. Al-Zamakhshari explained His statement ﴿God is Subtle to His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19] with this meaning, so how excellent is his insight. If it is understood in this sense here, it is an attribute independent of what precedes it, for an increased affirmation that He deserves to be singled out for worship to the exclusion of others.

*Khabir* is a *sifa mushabbaha* from *khabura*, with a damma on the *ba'* in the past tense, *khubran* with a damma on the *kha'* and sukun on the *ba'*, meaning "knew" and "recognized." Thus *al-Khabir* is the one described as having knowledge of the matters about which one reports, knowledge that agrees with reality.

[p. 418]

The occurrence of *al-Khabir* after *al-Latif* in the first interpretation is the occurrence of another attribute which is more general than the content of ﴿and He comprehends [all] vision﴾. Thus the *tadhyil* is completed by it, and the *tadhyil* then contains the embellishment of *nashr ba'da al-laff* (ordering after enumeration). In the second interpretation, its position is that of *ihtiras* regarding the meaning of *al-Latif*, meaning: He is the Gentle, the Kind, who is All-Aware of the places of gentleness and kindness and of those who deserve them.

This is a transition from the argument against the polytheists, and from establishing God's Oneness through His lordship, which runs from His saying (Al-An'am: 95) "Indeed, God splits the grain and the date-stone" to His saying (Al-An'am: 103) "And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware." The speech is therefore resumed by addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) with a command to say, "say," at the beginning of the sentence. The verb of saying is omitted, as is customary, because of the indication in His saying "and I am not a guardian over you." The occasion for this resumed speech after the discourse conveyed to them from God Most High is that it serves as a reminder, an explanation, and a summing-up (fadhlaka) of what preceded. Thus it is understood as: "Say, O Muhammad: There have come to you insights (basa'ir) from your Lord."

Basa'ir is the plural of basirah (insight). The basirah is the intellect through which meanings and realities become manifest, just as the basar (sight) is the perception of the eye through which bodies are made visible. The term "insights" is applied to that which is the cause of them.

Attributing "coming" to the insights is a metaphor (isti'arah) for their reaching their intellects. It is likened to the arrival of something that was absent, in order to give prominence to what has reached them by treating it as an absent thing whose arrival is awaited, like His saying (Al-Isra': 81) "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished." The verb "jaa'a" (came) is without the feminine marker, although its subject is a feminine plural, because a verb whose subject is a broken plural, or a feminine plural, may be used either with or without the feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith).

The "min" (from) is initial (ibtida'iyyah), and it is linked to "jaa'a" or it describes "basa'ir." God's address has been made with it in the position of the beginning of the journey from His side, and He is exalted above place and time. Therefore the "beginning" is a linguistic metaphor (majaz lughawi), or it is a metaphor by omission, with the implied meaning: "from the will of your Lord." The intended purpose is to give prominence to these teachings and reminders through which the insights come, and to urge acting upon them, because they are conveyed to them from One whose guidance contains no defect or error, together with what the mention of the Lord and its attribution to Him produces in terms of awe and of strengthening the call to act upon these insights.

For this reason he follows it with His saying "So whoever sees, it is for his own self," meaning: there is no excuse for you to persist in misguidance after these insights, and they benefit no one but you. "Whoever sees, it is for his own self": "sees" means whoever knows the truth has known with a knowledge that benefits his own self, and whoever is blind, meaning who strays from the truth, has strayed, and his burden is upon his own self.

The verb "sight" in His saying "sees" is used metaphorically (isti'arah) for knowledge of the truth and acting upon it, because the one guided by this guidance that comes from God is like one for whom the path has been illuminated by the full moon or something else, so he sees it and walks in it. On this understanding it is possible that "sees" is a concise analogy (tamthil), in which is implied the comparison of the state of one who guides to the truth, when he acts upon what he has been guided to, with the state of one who sees when he benefits from his sight.

The "blindness" in His saying "is blind" is used metaphorically for obstinacy and persistence in misguidance after what ought to have turned him away has come to him, because the obstinate person after that is like a blind person who does not benefit from the illumination of a path nor from the guidance of an experienced guide (khirrit). It is also permissible to regard it as an analogy, as it is regarded in its opposite above.

He used the "li" (for) in the first clause as a metaphor for benefit, because it indicates possession, and a thing is only possessed if it is beneficial and stored for calamities. "Ala" (upon) is used in the second for harm and for responsibility, because a harmful thing is heavy on its owner, imposing hardship upon him, and is like a load placed on his back. This is well known in eloquent speech. God Most High said (Fussilat: 46) "Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self," and He said (Al-Isra': 15) "Whoever is guided, he is guided only for his own self, and whoever goes astray, he goes astray only to his own detriment," and He said (Al-'Ankabut: 13) "And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens." For this reason sin is called a "wizr" (burden), as was previously mentioned in His saying (Al-An'am: 31) "They carry their burdens upon their backs." The "li" has come in the place of "ala" in some verses, such as His saying (Al-Isra': 7) "If you do good, you do good for your own selves, and if you do evil, it is against them."

In the verse there is the embellishment of paronomasia (jinas al-ishtiqaq) between "basa'ir" and "absara" (sees), and the observance of correspondence in sight and insights. In it there is also the embellishment of antithesis (mutabaqah) between His saying "sees" and "is blind," and between the "li" and the "ala."

His saying "for his own self" is linked to an omitted element indicated by the conditional verb. Its implied form is: "So whoever sees, it is for his own self he sees." The response is joined by the "fa" (then) because its first element is a prepositional phrase in the genitive, which is not suitable to follow the conditional particle.

The structure of the verse was composed in this way to signal that "for his own self" is, in the implied construction, placed before its omitted complement. The implied form is: "So for his own self he sees." Had it not been intended to signal this fronting, he would have said: "So whoever sees, sees for his own self," as He said (Al-Isra': 7) "If you do good, you do good for your own selves." The context requires fronting the complement here in order to convey restriction (qasr), that is: "So for his own self alone he sees, not for the benefit of anyone else," because they used to think that by turning away from his call to guidance they were enraging the Prophet (ﷺ). The indication of this is that this statement is spoken by the Prophet (ﷺ), and the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) has alluded to this. This differs from the verse "If you do good, you do good for your own selves" (Al-Isra': 7), which relates words addressed to the Children of Israel from God Most High, and they did not imagine that their good deeds benefit God or that their evil deeds harm Him.

The discussion of His saying "and whoever is blind, it is against them" is parallel to the discussion of His saying "So whoever sees, it is for his own self." The verb "blind" (amiya) is made transitive by the particle "ala" because blindness, since it is metaphorical, is a harm that falls upon its possessor.

The nominal clause "And I am not a guardian over you" completes what is included in His saying "So whoever sees, it is for his own self, and whoever is blind, it is against them," meaning: no part of that will reach me. Your benefit does not return to me, and your harm does not come back upon me, and I am not a trustee over your benefit or over your avoidance of harm. So do not think that you can scheme against me by turning away from guidance and persisting in misguidance.

The "hafiz" (guardian) is the one who protects and to whom the watching over and safeguarding of another is entrusted. He is in the position of the "wakil" (trustee), except that the trustee is one to whom protection is delegated by the side of the thing protected, whereas the guardian is more general, because he may act on behalf of the protected thing and on behalf of its allies. This is close in meaning to His saying (Al-An'am: 66) "And your people denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a trustee over you."

The use of the nominal clause here is precise, because "hafiz" is a descriptive word that does not convey the same meaning as another, so the verb "hafiza" (he guarded) cannot take its place. Hence "hafiz" is an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) for which an implied verb is postulated, transferred to the pattern "fa'ula" with a "u" vowel on the middle radical, which is not pronounced, like "rahim" (merciful).

The fronting of the predicate-subject in the nominal clause does not convey exclusivity (ikhtisas), contrary to what the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's commentary might suggest, although the scholar al-Taftazani inclined toward it, and the scholar al-Jurjani remained silent about it. That is a holding to the apparent sense. The fronting of "over you" before "a guardian" is for emphasis and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasilah).

Page 422

It is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*) serving as a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) on what precedes it. The *waw* is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyya*), so it is connected to the clause ﴿There has come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104], which is God Most High addressing His Messenger ﷺ, with an implied *qul* ("say"), as explained earlier. The demonstrative in *wa-kadhalika* ("and thus") refers to the "turning" (*taṣrīf*) derived from His words *nuṣarrifu al-āyāt* ("We turn the signs"). That is: "Just as that turning, We turn the signs." A parallel to this occurred more than once before, the first being His words ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143] in Surat al-Baqara.

The discussion of *taṣrīf al-āyāt* was given earlier, in His words ﴿Look how We turn the signs﴾ [al-An'am: 46] in this surah.

His words ﴿and that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ are conjoined (*ma'ṭūf*) to *wa-kadhalika nuṣarrifu al-āyāt*. The explanation of this type of conjunction was given earlier, in its counterpart: ﴿And thus We detail the signs, and that the way of the criminals may become evident﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in this surah. However, the present case differs from that one in a certain respect: the statement of the polytheists to the Messenger ﷺ, "You have studied," is not suitable to be the *cause* (*'illa*) of the turning of the signs. Therefore the *lam* must be taken as used metaphorically (*musta'āra*) to mean *consequence* and *outcome*, like the *lam* in His words ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 8]. The meaning is: "so he became for them an enemy." Likewise here: We turn the signs in this clear manner, so that they suppose you acquired it by study and instruction, and therefore they say, "You have studied." The meaning is: We turn the signs and make them clear in a way that is characteristic of a scholar who has studied knowledge, so the polytheists say, "You have studied this and received it from scholars and books," because of their turning away from sound reflection, which would lead them to recognize that such clarification issuing from a man they know to be unlettered (*ummiyy*) can only come from a revelation from God to him. This is like His words, ﴿We know that they say, "He is only taught by a human being"﴾ [al-Naḥl: 103]. They had indeed said this before, and they keep saying it and increase it in proportion to the increase in the turning of the signs. So the sequence of their saying upon the turning is likened to the sequence of a final cause (*'illa ghā'iyya*), and the particle that is set for causation is borrowed for this meaning by way of subsequent metaphor (*isti'āra tab'iyya*). For this reason some grammarians named such a *lam* "the *lam* of becoming" (*lam al-ṣayrūra*). They did not mean that becoming is one of the meanings of *lam*; rather it is an expression of the resulting sense of the meaning.

*Al-dirāsa* (studying) is reading with deliberation for memorization or for understanding. It was discussed earlier, at His words ﴿and because you used to study﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 79] in Surat Āl ʿImrān. Its verb is of the pattern of *naṣara* (*faʿala*, form I). One says *darasa al-kitāb*, meaning "he learned the book." It was mentioned in His words ﴿because you used to teach the Book and because you used to study﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 79], and in His words ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾ [al-A'rāf: 169]. The house in which the Jews learned was called *al-midrās*, and the house in which students live and learn was called *al-madrasa*. The meaning is: they say, "You have learned," as a slander against the Messenger's ﷺ unlettered status, lest it follow for them that what he brought of knowledge is a revelation from God Most High.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *darasta* without an *alif* and with a *fatḥa* on the *tāʾ*. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read *dāraswta* (*dārasta*), in the form of *mufāʿala* (form III), with a *fatḥa* on the *tāʾ*, meaning: they say, "You have read (to them), and it was read to you," that is, "You have studied with the People of the Book and discussed with them their practices." Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read *darasta* in the past tense with the feminine *tāʾ*, referring to *al-āyāt* (the signs), meaning: they have been repeated (*takarrarta*).

As for the *lam* in His words ﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾, it is the true *lam* of causation (*lam al-taʿlīl al-ḥaqīqiyya*).

The pronoun in *nubayyinuhu* refers to the Qur'an, because it is the referent of "the signs," and because it is known from the context.

*Al-qawm* (the people) are those who were guided and believed, as explained earlier in His words ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. The statement is an allusion (*taʿrīḍ*), as explained earlier.

The meaning is that this turning produced guidance for those who are granted success, and obstinacy (*mukābara*) for those who are forsaken, like His words, ﴿By it He leads many astray and by it He guides many; and He leads astray none but the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqara: 26].

This is a resumptive statement addressed to the Prophet (peace be upon him), commanding him to turn away from the slander of the polytheists and not to be concerned with their words. Beginning with the command to follow what has been revealed to him serves as an introduction to the command to turn away from the polytheists. It is not the primary purpose of the discourse, because the Messenger's (ﷺ) following of what was revealed to him is an established matter in all its meanings. The intended aim of the command is therefore constancy in following it. The meaning is: turn away from the polytheists by following what has been sent down to you from your Lord.

By "what was revealed to him" is meant the Qur'an.

Ittiba' (following) originally means tracing the footsteps of one who walks. It was then used for acting in the manner of another, as in the verse ﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهم بِإحْسانٍ﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100] ("and those who followed them in goodness"). It was then used for carrying out a command and acting on what the one followed orders, and this is called i'timar (compliance). Its verb may take the person followed as its direct object, so one says: "I followed so-and-so" in these three senses, and in all of them there is an elided noun (muḍāf), because following does not relate to the essence of a person.

The use of ittiba' in the sense of compliance is common in the Qur'an, since the Qur'an came with commands and prohibitions and ordered people to follow it. It is also used in the sense of constant companionship, by way of majāz mursal (metonymy in which a related meaning is intended). For whoever follows someone accompanies him. From this usage, the jinn-spirit (ra'iy) in the superstitions of the Arabs was called tābi'a (follower), and from it whoever accompanied a Companion (ṣaḥābī) and narrated from him was called a tābi'ī (Successor).

It is therefore possible that ittiba' in the verse means constant compliance with what the Qur'an commanded regarding turning away from the harm and obstinacy of the polytheists. The ittiba' commanded here is then following in a specific matter, and this has been commanded more than once, so the command to the act is continuous within the command to persist in it.

It is also possible that it is a command to persist in calling to God, to proclaim it openly, and to summon the polytheists to monotheism and faith, without any softness or leniency entering into this, so that their insolence and their denial of him do not have an effect on his own self, weakening his call and his eagerness for their faith, and so that he does not believe that attempting to bring them to faith is of no benefit. Thus what is meant by "what was revealed to him" is what was revealed of the Qur'an as an address to the polytheists, or as a command to call them to Islam and not to cease doing so. The discourse then becomes a strengthening of the Prophet's (ﷺ) resolve in the stations of his call to God. This is the fitting reading of the verse ﴿ولا تَسُبُّوا الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-An'ām: 108] ("And do not revile those they call upon besides God"), as we will explain. This has already been discussed.

God therefore reminds him that God is able to transform their hearts so that they accept Islam by another creation. But God willed that faith be attained by those who believe through the customary means of guidance and being guided, in order that God distinguish the wicked from the good and that the ranks of souls be manifest in the fields of receiving the message. God willed that souls differ in good and evil, a difference arising from the differences in the modes of creation, the making, the upbringing and the receptivity, and from the degrees of the servants' connection with their Creator and their hope from Him. The polytheists reached the nadir of shirk through causes and means that are successive and ordered, natural, moral and social, which came into being over times and conditions. When God sent to them the guide, their listening to his guidance varied according to the variation in the firmness of their intellects in error and their antiquity in it, and according to the variation in the preparation of their souls for good and their resistance to it. God did not make people's faith come about through violations of customary patterns, nor through altering the nature of intellects. This is the principle governing the meaning of verses like this one. This, then, is the meaning of the negation of God's will in this context, the intent of which is to reassure the heart of the Messenger (peace be upon him) and to remind him of the realities of the situation. This is because this is a truth that reveals the reality and cannot serve as an excuse for one who demands of them that they not be among those whom God did not will to guide. The estimated meaning is: "Had God willed their not associating partners, they would not have associated partners." God therefore reminds him that he has discharged the trust and conveyed the message, and that He did not send him compelling them to come to Him as Muslims, but sent him only as one conveying His message. **Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 6, verse 108 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God, lest they revile God in hostility without knowledge. Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds. Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

This is coordinated with His saying ﴿and turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Anʿam: 106]. It clarifies further the meaning of the turning away that is commanded. What we have said is confirmed by the fact that the intended turning away is not abandoning the call (daʿwa), but overlooking their abuse and vile speech while continuing to pursue the call through the Qur'an. The prohibition against reviling their idols indicates persistence in calling them and refuting their beliefs, while Muslims avoid reviling what they invoke besides God.

Sabb (reviling) is speech that indicates belittling someone or attributing to him a deficiency or disgrace, whether by falsehood or truth; it is synonymous with shatm (insult). Attributing to someone an error in opinion or action is not sabb, nor is attributing to him error in religion when it comes from one who differs in religion.

The addressees of this prohibition are the Muslims, not the Messenger ﷺ, because the Messenger was not foul-mouthed or a reviler; his great character prevents him from that. Moreover, he calls them with what is revealed to him of the Qur'an, and if God wills, He withholds from him what He reveals. The Muslims, out of zeal for Islam, sometimes exceeded the limit, so that lapses occurred in which they reviled the idols of the polytheists.

Al-Tabari narrated from Qatada, who said: "The Muslims used to revile the idols of the unbelievers, and they would retaliate by reviling [God]. So God forbade them to revile their Lord out of hostility." This is the most sound of what has been related concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, and the most fitting with the wording of the verse.

As for what al-Tabari narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when the saying of God, ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 98] was revealed, the polytheists said: "If you do not desist from reviling our gods and insulting them, we will certainly revile your God," and so this verse was revealed concerning that, it is weak. This is because ʿAli ibn Abi Talha is weak and has objectionable reports, and he did not meet Ibn ʿAbbas. Furthermore, it is far-fetched that this is the intended meaning of the prohibition in this verse, because that (the reviling of God by the polytheists) is an occurrence in the Qur'an, so it is not fitting that it be forbidden by the phrase "do not revile"; rather it would have been said: "Do not loudly revile those who invoke other than God," for example, just as He said in the other verse: ﴿Do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent in it, but seek a middle way between that﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 110].

Likewise is what he narrated from al-Suddi, that when the death of Abu Talib drew near, the Quraysh said: "We will go in to him and ask him to forbid his nephew from us, for we are ashamed to kill him after his death." So a group of their leaders went to Abu Talib and said: "You are our chief," and they addressed him with what they intended. Abu Talib then summoned the Messenger of God ﷺ and said to him: "These are your people and the sons of your paternal uncle. They want you to leave them and their gods, and they will leave you and your God." They said: "Either you cease insulting our gods, or we will certainly insult you and insult the one who commands you." Al-Suddi did not say that this was the occasion of revelation of this verse, but rather he made it an explanation of the verse. What we have raised against what was related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha also refutes it.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "Here there are two difficulties. The first is that the people agreed that Surat al-Anʿam was revealed all at once, so how can it be said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was such-and-such, and that the unbelievers acknowledged God and used to say: 'We worship the idols so that they may be intercessors for us with God'? How then is it conceivable that the unbelievers would dare to revile God?" End of quotation.

I say: The first difficulty is resolved by the fact that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) does not necessarily have to be concurrent with the revelation, for the occasion may precede its time, and then it is referred to in the revealed verse, so the verse becomes a response to their statements. Al-Razi himself gave a similar answer when commenting on His saying ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-Anʿam: 111] and what follows.

The second difficulty is resolved by the fact that the polytheists said: "If you do not desist from reviling our gods, we will certainly revile your God." Its meaning is that they deny that God is his God, and for this reason they denied the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say: "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?" And it increased them in aversion﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. Thus they deny that God commanded him to disparage their gods, because they claim that their gods are close to God. They only claim that a devil commands the Prophet ﷺ to revile the idols. Do you not see the saying of a woman from among them when the revelation paused at the beginning of the mission: "I see that his devil has forsaken him"? And that was the occasion of revelation of Surat al-Duha.

Al-Razi's answer to this: some of them did not affirm the existence of God, and they were the materialists (al-dahriyyun); or the intended meaning is that they reviled the Messenger, peace be upon him, and God treated the reviling of the Messenger as the reviling of God, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. End of quotation. However, in this interpretation there is a remoteness for which there is no need.

The correct way of interpreting the verse is that the reviling prohibited in it does not mean what has come in the Qur'an of establishing deficiencies in their gods, by which the non-divinity of these gods is indicated, such as His saying ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 179] in Surat al-Aʿraf. As for what is other than this, such as His saying ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 195], it is neither insult nor reviling, because that is by way of argument and is not a deliberate attack (tasaddi) for insult. Rather, what is meant in the verse is what issues from some Muslims of words of blame and disparagement directed at the gods of the polytheists. This is like what is related in the biography (al-Sira) that ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi came as an envoy from the people of Mecca to the Messenger of God ﷺ at al-Hudaybiyya, and among what he said was: "By God, it is as if I see these people (meaning the Muslims) have fled from you," and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was present, so Abu Bakr said to him: "Suck the clitoris of al-Lat!" through the end of the report.

The reason for the prohibition against reviling their idols is that reviling does not bring about any religious benefit (maslaha diniyya), for the purpose of the call is to argue for the refutation of polytheism and to demonstrate the impossibility that the idols be partners with God the Exalted. This is what distinguishes truth from falsehood, what the one who is right establishes, and what the one who is wrong cannot achieve. As for reviling, it is within the power of both the one who is right and the one who is wrong, so it appears as if the two are equal. The one who is wrong may, through his shamelessness and obscenity, achieve what the one who is right cannot, so it appears to people that he has overcome the one who is right. Moreover, since reviling their gods would fuel their anger and increase their obstinacy, it has come to contradict God's purpose from the call. For He said to His Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125], and He said to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech﴾ [Taha: 44]. Thus reviling became an obstacle to the purpose of the mission, so this reviling became purely a mischief and was not mixed with any benefit. This is not like changing the wrong (taghyir al-munkar) when it is feared that it will lead to a mischief, because changing the wrong is a benefit in itself, while its leading to mischief is incidental. This is a field in which the views of the qualified scholars (al-ʿulama al-mujtahidin) differ according to the weighing of benefits and harms in terms of strength and weakness, certainty and probability. The same applies to the conflict of all benefits and harms.

The ruling of this verse is muhkam (firm, not abrogated). Al-Qurtubi said: "The scholars said: its ruling remains in this community in every circumstance. Whenever the unbeliever is in a position of strength, and it is feared that if the Muslims revile his idols or the matters of his law, he will revile Islam or the Prophet, peace be upon him, then God, Mighty and Majestic, has not permitted the Muslim to revile their crosses or their churches, because that is equivalent to inciting disobedience." End of quotation; that is, to increasing disbelief. It is not reviling to refute what contradicts Islam among their beliefs in the context of argument; rather, reviling is to confront them with it outside the setting of debate. A parallel to this is what our scholars said regarding what issues from the dhimmis of reviling God the Exalted or the Prophet ﷺ: if what issues from them is part of the roots of their disbelief, it is not counted as reviling; but if they exceed that, it is counted as reviling. The jurists express this by their saying: "that which contains disbelief (ma bihi kufr)" and "that which does not contain disbelief (ghayr ma bihi kufr)."

Our scholars have argued from this verse for establishing a principle of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) according to the Malikis, which is termed the question of blocking the means (masʾalat sadd al-dharaʾiʿ). Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "God forbade in His Book that anyone do a permissible act which leads to a forbidden one, and for this reason our scholars relied on this verse regarding blocking the means (sadd al-dharaʾiʿ), which is every contract that is permissible outwardly but may lead to, or be used as a path to, something forbidden." He said, in commenting on Surat al-Aʿraf at His saying ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 163]: "Malik, may God be pleased with him, and Ahmad in some of his narrations followed him in this, and it was hidden from al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with them both, despite their mastery of the Shariʿa. It is every act that is outwardly permissible by which one reaches something forbidden." End of quotation. Al-Mazari, in the chapter on deferred sales (buyuʿ al-ajal) in his commentary on al-Talqin, defined sadd al-dhariʿa as "prohibiting what is permissible lest it become a path to what is impermissible." End of quotation. What is meant is blocking the means of corruption (dharaʾiʿ al-fasad), as al-Qarafi made clear in Tanqih al-Fusul and in the Eighty-Fifth (sic: Fifty-Eighth) Difference, where he said: "The dhariʿa is the means to a thing. The meaning of blocking the means is cutting off the source of the means of corruption. The community has agreed that the means are of three kinds. The first is recognized by consensus, such as digging wells on the roads of the Muslims, putting poison in their food, and reviling idols when it is known of the person that he would then revile God the Exalted. The second is disregarded by consensus, such as cultivating grapes, which is not prohibited for fear of wine, and like sharing residences out of fear of fornication. The third is disputed, such as deferred sales, where Malik, may God be pleased with him, took the means into account, and others disagreed." End of quotation. By "the one who disagreed" he meant al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with them both.

This principle falls under the principle of means and ends, for this principle is a branch of the principle of giving the means the ruling of the end, specifically regarding the means of bringing about a mischief. Jurists do not differ on taking into account the meaning of blocking the means in the category in which al-Qarafi related the consensus on taking the means into account. The principle has no heading in the usul of the Hanafis and the Shafiʿis; they did not address it by affirmation or denial. al-Ghazali did not mention it in al-Mustasfa among the spurious principles (al-usul al-mawhuma) at the end of the second pillar on the evidences of the rulings (adillat al-ahkam).

"ʿAdwan" with a fatha on the ʿayn, sukun on the dal, and a light waw is the reading of the majority. It is a verbal noun meaning transgression and injustice, and it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maful mutlaq) of "yasubbu" (they revile), because ʿadw here is an attribute of the reviling, so it is valid for it to take its place in the absolute object to specify its type. Yaʿqub read ʿuduwwan with a damma on the ʿayn and the dal and a shadda on the waw; it is a verbal noun like al-ʿadw.

Describing their reviling as ʿadw is an implicit indication that the Muslims' reviling of the idols of the polytheists is not aggression. This reviling is made to be ʿadw whether what is meant by it is God, or what is meant by it is the one who commands the Prophet ﷺ with what he brought; for the one who commanded the Prophet ﷺ with what he brought is in reality God the Exalted, so they encountered aggression against His majesty.

Part 2 of the commentary: translation begins.

"Bi-ghayri 'ilm" (without knowledge) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in yasubbū, meaning out of ignorance. Because of their ignorance of God, nothing restrains them from reviling Him, and they revile Him without knowing that they are reviling God, since they are reviling the One who commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) with what he brought, so their reviling coincides with reviling God Most High, because it is He who commanded him with what he brought.

It is also permissible that "bi-ghayri 'ilm" be a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah kāshifah, a clarifying qualifier) of "'adwan" (transgression), because that transgression occurs only from not knowing the magnitude of the crime they committed, or it occurs with knowledge of it, but their state in embarking upon it resembles the state of not knowing the gravity of its outcome.

And His saying ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ means: as We made attractive to these people the evil of their deeds. ﴿We made attractive to every community their deeds﴾. So the thing pointed to is what God related of them in His saying ﴿And they attributed to God partners, the jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 100] up to His saying ﴿so that they revile God in transgression without knowledge﴾. Their boldness in these crimes and their blindness to considering their evil consequences arose from the beautification of them in their souls and their reckoning that they were paths of benefit for them, and of salvation and success in this world through the care of their idols. Upon this same custom, and by a similar beautification, God made attractive the deeds of the earlier nations with the messengers who were sent among them, so they would oppose them, disobey their counsel, and act boldly against their Lord who had sent them. When the pointed-to thing was likened to beautification, the listener knew that what the demonstrative referred to belongs to the category of beautification. The demonstrative is used here in a manner different from His saying ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] and its parallels, because what follows it relates to the conditions of others than those spoken of, rather to conditions more general than theirs. In this statement there is an allusion (ta'rīḍ) to a threat that the punishment will befall the polytheists of the Arabs just as it befell those in this world.

The reality of God's making these things attractive to them is that He created them with intellects in which such an act seems good, in the manner previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated partners﴾ [al-An'am: 107]. This is the rule in its parallels.

Tazyīn (beautification) is a form (taf'īl) derived from zayn, which is goodness, or from zīnah (adornment), which is that by which a thing is made good-looking. So tazyīn is making a thing possess adornment, or displaying it as adornment, or attributing it to adornment. Here it means displaying it in the form of adornment even though it is not so, so the taf'īl in it indicates attribution, like tafsīq (declaring someone a transgressor). In His saying ﴿But God has endeared to you faith and made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 7], it means making it an adornment, so the taf'īl indicates making, because it is good in itself.
