And because His saying ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ contains an allusion to a threat of punishment for the nations, He followed the statement with "thumma" (then), which indicates graded sequence (tartīb rutbī), in His saying ﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, because what the sentence joined by "thumma" contains is greater than what the sentence it is joined to contains, since the threat introduced by "thumma" is more severe and more grievous, for the punishment of this world is temporary and not everlasting. The meaning is: and greater than that, they will return to God, and He will hold them to account. The shift from the name of Majesty (Allah) to "their Lord" serves to magnify the threat and to give the reason for deserving it, namely that they return to their Owner who created them, yet they denied His blessings and associated partners with Him, so they are like runaway slaves who wander about and then fall into the hand of their master.

Al-inbā' is informing, which is making them aware of the evil of their deeds. It is used here in its implied meaning, which is rebuke and punishment, because punishment is the intended outcome of informing a criminal of his crime. The fa' here indicates sequence following the return, signifying the swiftness of punishment immediately upon returning to Him.

[Page 435]

The clause "They swore by God their most emphatic oaths" (﴿وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ﴾) is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the clause "Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord" (﴿اتَّبِعْ ما أُوحِيَ إلَيْكَ مِن رَبِّكَ﴾) [al-An'am: 106] and what follows it. The pronoun refers to the people in His saying "Your people denied it, though it is the truth" (﴿وكَذَّبَ بِهِ قَوْمُكَ وهو الحَقُّ﴾) [al-An'am: 66], like the pronouns that came after that verse. The meaning of "If a sign came to them" (﴿لَئِنْ جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ﴾) is a sign other than the Qur'an. This refers to some of their pretexts for persisting in disbelief after the decisive proofs had become manifest to them; they had made excuses with it during some of their objections to Islam. Al-Tabari and others related from Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and al-Kalbi, with some of them adding to what others said: "that the Quraysh asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a sign like the sign of Moses (peace be upon him) when he struck the rock with his staff and water gushed from it, or like the sign of Salih, or like the sign of Jesus (peace be upon them all). And that they said, when they heard His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿If We will, We could send down upon them a sign from the sky, and their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4], that they swore that if a sign came to them as they asked, or as they were threatened, they would all surely believe." And that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) asked God to bring them a sign as they had asked, out of eagerness that they would believe. This verse was therefore revealed concerning that meaning, because this surah gathered much of their circumstances and their disputations.

The discussion of "They swore by God their most emphatic oaths" (﴿وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ﴾) is similar to the discussion of His saying in the Surah of al-Ma'idah: "Are these the ones who swore by God their most emphatic oaths?" (﴿أهَؤُلاءِ الَّذِينَ أقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ﴾) [al-Ma'idah: 53].

Oaths (al-Aymān) have already been discussed at His saying "God will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned" (﴿لا يُؤاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ في أيْمانِكم ولَكِنْ يُؤاخِذُكم بِما كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 225] in the Surah of al-Baqarah.

The clause "If a sign came to them" (﴿لَئِنْ جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ﴾) and so on explains the clause "They swore by God" (﴿وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ﴾).

The lam in "If a sign came to them" (﴿لَئِنْ جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ﴾) is the lam that prepares for the oath (al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam), because it indicates that the condition has been made a condition within the oath, and so it indicates an elided oath in most cases. Here it has come together with the verb of swearing, because it has become inseparable from the conditional clause that serves as the answer to the oath, so it does not part from it even with the verb of swearing present. The lam in "they would surely believe in it" (﴿لَيُؤْمِنُنَّ بِها﴾) is the lam of the oath, that is, the lam of its answer.

By "sign" (al-āyah) is meant what they proposed to the Messenger (ﷺ), by which they meant an extraordinary event contrary to habit, indicating that God had granted their proposal so that He would confirm His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Therefore "a sign" (āyah) is indefinite, meaning: whatever sign it might be, of the kind within which, in their supposition, signs are confined.

The "coming" (majī') of the sign is a metaphor for its becoming manifest, because a manifest thing resembles the presence of an absent one, and therefore "coming" is borrowed for it.

The explanation of the meaning of the sign (āyah) and its derivation has already been given at His saying "Those who disbelieved and denied Our signs are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever" (﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ النّارِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 39] in the Surah of al-Baqarah.

[Page 436]

The meaning of "the signs are with God" (﴿إنَّما الآياتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾) is that the signs are among the effects of God's power and will. The means by which signs come into existence are among His attributes, so He is capable of them. For this reason they are likened to things stored with Him, and when He wills to make them manifest to people, He does so. Thus the word "with" (ʿinda) here is a metaphor. The name of a place of very close proximity is used to express the sense of exclusive possession and sole control, as a metaphorical relation (majāz mursal), because exclusive control is among the necessary consequences of a thing being in the very close proximity of a place by custom, like His saying "With Him are the keys of the unseen" (﴿وعِنْدَهُ مَفاتِحُ الغَيْبِ﴾) [al-An'am: 59].

The restriction by "only" (innamā) refutes the polytheists' supposition that signs are within the power of the Prophet (ﷺ), if he is a prophet. They took the Prophet's (ﷺ) failure to grant their proposed sign as a sign of the absence of his prophethood. So God commanded him to answer that signs are with God, not with the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and God knows best what signs He will manifest.

As for His saying "And what would make you aware that when they come they will not believe?" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكم أنَّها إذا جاءَتْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾), the majority read "annahā" with the hamza of "an" opened. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Khalaf, and Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim in one of the two transmissions from Abu Bakr read "innahā" with the hamza of "inna" kissed (i.e., with a kasra).

The majority read "lā yu'minūn" (they will not believe) with the third-person masculine plural ya' (yā' al-ghaybah). Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and Khalaf read it with the second-person ta' (tā' al-khiṭāb), and in that case the address is to the polytheists.

This clause has been a stumbling block for the exegetes in explaining its meaning and structure. Let us present what has appeared to us regarding its position, its structure, and the explanation of its meaning, then follow it with the statements of the exegetes. What appears to me is that the wāw in it may be the wāw of conjunction (wāw al-ʿaṭf) and may be the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl).

As for the case of its being the wāw of conjunction, it is that it is conjoined to the clause "The signs are only with God" (﴿إنَّما الآياتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾) as an independent statement. It is an independent statement directed by God to the believers, and it is not part of the speech that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was commanded to say by His saying "Say: The signs are only with God" (﴿قُلْ إنَّما الآياتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾).

[Page 437]

The addressee of "it makes you aware" (﴿يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) is most apparently the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and the believers, and this is according to the reading of the majority, "they will not believe" (﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) with the third-person ya'. The addressee of "it makes you aware" (﴿يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) is the polytheists according to the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and Khalaf "lā tu'minūn" (you will not believe) with the second-person tā', and in that case the clause "And what would make you aware" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) is part of what the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say in His saying "Say: The signs are only with God" (﴿قُلْ إنَّما الآياتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾).

The "mā" is interrogative, used for doubt and awakening, so that the oath of the polytheists would not deceive them and their nonsense would not be passed off on them. If the address is to the Muslims, then there is in the interrogation nothing of denial, reproach, or harshness, since neither the context of the speech nor the state of the Muslims in what is transmitted from reports indicates an intention to reproach or harden them. It is not established that the Muslims hoped for the faith of the polytheists, or that they would be granted the manifestation of a sign according to their proposal. And how could that be, when the Muslims recite His saying "Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe" (﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ حَقَّتْ عَلَيْهِمْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) [Yunus: 96] and "Even if every sign came to them" (﴿ولَوْ جاءَتْهم كُلُّ آيَةٍ﴾) [Yunus: 97]; these are in the Surah of Yunus, which was revealed before the Surah of al-An'am. The Muslims knew the polytheists' lying in religion and their shifting in fabricating excuses. The purpose of the speech is to establish this for the Muslims, and the report is conveyed in the form of a question, because interrogation by its nature prepares the hearer's soul to seek an answer to that question, so that he readies himself to grasp what follows it.

"Al-ishʿār" (making aware) is informing about a known matter that by its nature is hidden and subtle. It is said: "So-and-so felt (shaʿara) of such-and-such," meaning he knew it and perceived it. The verb requires a complement after its object, and it is necessary that His saying "that when they come they will not believe" (﴿أنَّها إذا جاءَتْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) is that complement, so it is in the sense of the preposition bāʾ of genitive (bāʾ al-jarr). The estimate is: "by the fact that when they come they will not believe," so the elision of the preposition before the opened "anna" is a regular elision.

The hamza of "anna" is opened in the reading of the majority. The meaning is: "Is there one who makes you aware that when it comes they will not believe?" That is, by their non-belief.

[Page 438]

This is the explanation of the meaning and the structure. The difficulty lies only in the presence of the negative particle in His saying "they will not believe" (﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾), because "And what would make you aware" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) has the sense of their saying "what would make you know" (mā yudrīkum), and the common usage in a parallel construction of this kind is that the object of the verb of knowing in it is the matter that the addressee would ordinarily expect to occur. The matter that is expected to occur in such a context is that they will believe, because that is what their oath requires: "If a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it" (﴿لَئِنْ جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ لَيُؤْمِنُنَّ﴾). So when the object of awareness was made the negation of their faith, it became an unusual complement by the custom of using this kind of construction.

What the examination of the features of eloquent speech and its distinctions requires is that "And what would make you aware" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) not be measured against what has become common in Arabic speech, "mā yudrīka" (what would make you know), because the construction "mā yudrīka" has spread in speech until it has become like a proverb, with a specific usage that they scarcely deviate from, as is the way of proverbs not to be changed from what they were used for. That usage is that the noun "mā" in it is an interrogative of denial, and the object of "yudrīka" is the matter that the speaker denies to the addressee. So if we measured the use of "And what would make you aware that when they come they will not believe" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكم أنَّها إذا جاءَتْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) upon the use of "what would make you know" (mā yudrīkum), the presence of the negative particle would contradict the intended meaning. This is the source of the hesitation of the scholars of exegesis and of Arabic grammar concerning the purpose of "lā" (not) in this verse. But when we seek the reason for the departure in this verse from the usage of the construction "mā yudrīkum" to the choice of the construction "mā yush'iruкum," we know that this departure was to observe a particularity in the construction departed to: it is a construction for which there is no fixed established usage, and therefore it runs according to what the form and arrangement allow in the use of particles, verbs, their objects, and their complements.

[Page 439]

So let us take the interrogative noun here to mean alerting and casting doubt on the supposition, and let us take the verb "yush'iruкum" to its basic sense according to its like among verbs of knowledge. If this is so, then the negation of the polytheists' faith upon the coming of a sign and its affirmation are equal in the hypothesis that the interrogative demands. The speaker would then have the choice between saying "that when it comes they will not believe" and saying "that when it comes they will believe." The side of negation was preferred only to indicate that it is the weightier side which ought to be relied upon in this supposition.

This is the difference between the two constructions. There are countless distinctions in the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿānī, the branch of rhetoric dealing with the meanings of structures), and the expert in this science should not overlook them; ʿAbd al-Qāhir (al-Jurjānī) has indicated many kinds of them, so let this distinction be added to its like.

If, however, you insist on analogizing "wa-mā yush'irukum" to "mā yudrīkum" in every respect, as the exegetes have followed, then take the predominant usage of "mā yudrīka" to be the apparent sense of the usage of "mā yush'irukum," and take the attachment of the negated element to the verb as going against the apparent requirement, for the sake of that same alerting nuance; the matter is then made easy.

As for the case of the wāw in His saying "and what would make you aware" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) being the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), then "mā" is an indefinite noun described by the clause "it makes you aware" (﴿يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾). Its meaning is "a thing described as making you aware that when they come they will not believe." This thing is what the Qur'an has already revealed, such as His saying "Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe" (﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ حَقَّتْ عَلَيْهِمْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) [Yunus: 96] and "Even if every sign came to them" (﴿ولَوْ جاءَتْهم كُلُّ آيَةٍ﴾) [Yunus: 97], and likewise what they tested of the polytheists' shifting in escaping the abandonment of their fathers' religion. The clause is then a circumstantial clause, meaning: while the Qur'an and inductive observation have made you aware of their lying, so do not hope for their faith if a sign came to them, nor for the truthfulness of their oaths. He (Exalted) said: "Indeed, they have no oaths" (﴿إنَّهم لا أيْمانَ لَهُمْ﴾) [al-Tawbah: 12]. I am truly astonished how this reading of "mā" as an indefinite described noun escaped the exegetes, when they resorted to things far stranger than that.

[Page 440]

If the address in "and what would make you aware" (﴿وما يُشْعِرُكُمْ﴾) is taken as addressed to the polytheists, then the interrogation is for denial and reproach, and the object of the verb "yush'iruкum" is elided, indicated by His saying "if a sign came to them" (﴿لَئِنْ جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ﴾). The estimate is: "And what would make you aware that We would bring you a sign as you wish?"

We have no need for the artificial constructions the exegetes contrived. In al-Kashshaf: the believers hoped for the faith of the polytheists if a sign came to them, and they wished for its coming; so God (Exalted) said: "And what would make you know that they will not believe?" That is, you do not know that I know they will not believe. This is based on treating "mā yush'iruкum" as equivalent in usage to their saying "mā yudrīka" (what would make you know).

Sibawayh related from al-Khalil that God's words "annaha" (أنّها) mean "la'allaha" (لعلها), i.e., "perhaps when a sign comes they will not believe in it." He said: "(anna) may come in the sense of (la'alla)," meaning that in "la'alla" there is a dialect that says "la'anna," with the ʿayn changed to a hamza and the last lam changed to a nun, and that they sometimes delete the first lam for lightness, as they delete it in their saying "ʿallaka an taf'ala," so that "anna" becomes (la'alla). Al-Zamakhshari followed him, as did some lexicographers, and they recited verses of poetry.

From al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi: "la" (لا) is extra (zaʾida), just as they claimed its extra use in God's words ﴿And it is forbidden to a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya': 95].

Ibn ʿAtiyya mentioned that Abu ʿAli al-Farisi made "annaha" a causal clause (taʿlil) for His words ﴿with God﴾, meaning: He does not bring it to them, because when it comes they will not believe; this is on the basis that "ʿind" is a metaphor (kinaya) for their being prevented from answering what they asked for.

On the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Khalaf, and Abu Bakr, in one of the two narrations from him, reading "innaha" with a kasra on the hamza, the clause is a new sentence (istiʾnaf). The object of "yush'irukum" is omitted because it is evident from His words ﴿they will surely believe in it﴾. The estimate is: "And what makes you aware that they will not believe when a sign comes?"

On the reading of Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and Khalaf with the second person ta' (taʾ al-mukhatab): the justification of Khalaf's reading, who read "innaha" with a kasra on the hamza, is that the clause "annaha idha ja'at" [i.e., "innaha idha ja'at"] be an address directed to the polytheists. As for the reading of Ibn ʿAmir and Hamza, who read "annaha" with a fatha on the hamza, the pronoun of address in His words ﴿and what makes you aware﴾ may be taken as directed to the polytheists by way of iltifat (shift of address), on the basis of pausing at ﴿yush'irukum﴾.

**[p. 442]**

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿that when it comes they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109], so that it serves as an elucidation (bayan) of his words ﴿they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109]. That is, by disabling their sight from that sign and their intellects from being guided by it, so that they do not perceive the proofs the sign contains, and their hearts do not grasp the manner of its indication, and thus their affirmation of it is nullified. This happens when God deprives them of setting right their perception, because their intellects were created averse to sound knowledge, by what prepared them for that: their detachment from the roots of the polytheists, their upbringing among the people of misguidance, and their receiving of their misguidance, as I explained just before. So He described that state, which contradicts the sound natural disposition (fitrah), as a "turning" of their intellects and sights, and because they had been turned away from what is known to people of sound intellects. The call to polytheism within them is not a turning from a state that had been good, since they had not been in that state for any period; rather it is a turning because they came contrary to what they ought to have been.

The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ ("by it") refers to the Qur'an, which is understood from ﴿if a sign comes to them﴾ [al-An'am: 109], for they meant a sign other than the Qur'an.

The kaf in ﴿kamā lam yu'minū bihi awwala marrah﴾ ("just as they did not believe in it the first time") is for comparison (tashbih), likening the state of their not believing, after a sign they had demanded comes to them, to their earlier state. The meaning is: We turn their hands and sights, so they do not believe in the sign that comes to them, just as they did not believe in the Qur'an before. The turning of their hearts and sights in this sense takes place in this world, and it is abandonment (khidhlan).

It is also permissible that the clause ﴿wa-nuqallibu af'idatahum wa-abṣārahum﴾ ("And We turn their hearts and their sights") be a resumptive (istiʾnāf) clause, with the wāw being for resumption;

[p. 443 follows]

or that it be conjoined (maʿtūfah) to the clause ﴿they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109]. The meaning would then be: "We are turning their hearts and their sights," that is, in the Fire of Hell, as a metonymy (kināyah) for the turning of their entire bodies. He singled out their hearts and sights because they are the cause of their turning away from taking warning from the signs, as in His saying ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116], meaning they bewitched people by what their eyes imagined to them.

On this reading, the kaf in ﴿kamā lam yu'minū bihi﴾ is for causation (taʿlil), as in His saying ﴿remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198].

I say: this reading is confirmed by His saying ﴿awwala marrah﴾ ("the first time"), since on this second reading there are no "two times," so the phrase ﴿awwala marrah﴾ must be interpreted as the first life, in this world.

The word al-taqlīb is the verbal noun of qallaba, which indicates the intensity of turning a thing away from its original state. Qalb may mean making what faces the sight of a thing no longer face it, as in His saying ﴿so he began turning his hands over﴾ [al-Kahf: 42], and the saying "he turned the back of the shield," and close to this is His saying ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. It may also mean changing the state of a thing into its opposite, since this resembles turning the essence of the thing itself.

The kaf in ﴿kamā lam yu'minū bihi﴾ is apparently for comparison, in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109], and the ﴿mā﴾ is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyyah). The meaning: they will not believe in the manner of the non-belief they showed the first time. The pronoun governed by the bāʾ refers to the Qur'an, since it is known from the context, as in His saying ﴿and your people denied it﴾ [al-An'am: 66]. The point is that obstinacy is their disposition: just as they did not believe in the past in the sign of the Qur'an, which contains the greatest proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger (peace be upon him), so in the future they will not believe in another sign if it comes to them. On this reading, His saying ﴿wa-nuqallibu af'idatahum wa-abṣārahum﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) by conjunction between the circumstantial clause and its subject.

It is also permissible to make the comparison pertain to the turning, so that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿nuqallibu﴾: We turn their hearts and sights away from the natural disposition of hearts and sights, just as We turned them, so they did not believe in it the first time, when they recoiled from

[p. 444 follows]

faith the first time the Messenger (peace be upon him) called them. This comparison then stands in the force of an explanation (bayān) of the turning, which is made a circumstantial clause of the non-existence of their faith, in that the cause of their turning away from faith still persists, because God has deprived them of rectifying their hearts.

Some exegetes permitted that the kaf be for causation, on the view that this is one of its meanings, and ﴿remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] was explained on this basis. The meaning then: We turn their hearts because they disobeyed and were obstinate, and did not believe in the Qur'an the first time it challenged them. So We make their hearts and sights continually turned away from the proper function of intellects and sights. This is a recompense for them for their not caring to reflect on the matter of God and the sending of His Messenger, and for their levity in rushing to denial before a sincere reflection.

The hearts are mentioned before the sights because ﴿af'idah﴾ means intellects, and they are the seat of motives and deterrents; when a flash of inference shines upon the heart, it directs the senses toward things and reflects on them. It is apparent that the reason for combining hearts and sights, and not being content with hearts alone, is that the hearts specialize in grasping purely rational signs, such as the sign of the Prophet's being unlettered and the sign of inimitability. Since rational signs did not restrain them, and they did not benefit by their hearts, because these had been turned away from the natural disposition, they asked for visible, manifest signs, such as ascending into the sky and sending down to them a book on paper. God informed His Messenger (peace be upon him) and the Muslims that even if a visible sign came to them they would not believe, because their sights too are turned, just as their intellects are turned.

"Awwal" is masculine in form though it is in construct with "marrah" (feminine), by the idafa of an adjective to its noun, because the original form of awwal is an elative noun (ism al-tafḍīl). When an elative noun is joined to an indefinite noun, it is fixed in the singular and masculine, as you say: "Khadījah is the first of women in faith," and you do not say "the first (feminine) of women."

The word "marrah" means one of the two occasions on which signs came: the first occasion is the coming of the Qur'an, and the second occasion is the coming of the requested sign, which is a hypothetical occasion.

[p. 445 follows]

"Wa-nadharuhum" is conjoined to "nuqallibu." It is thus established that the meaning of ﴿We turn their hearts﴾ is that We leave them in the turning upon which they were created, so they were filled with transgression and obstinacy against the truth, and it turned their sights away from observation and inference. For this reason He attributed the transgression to their inner selves, to indicate that it is rooted in them and that they grew up upon it, and that they were deprived of the softness of heart from which fear and remembrance arise.

"Ṭughyān" (transgression) and "ʿamah" (blind bewilderment) were discussed earlier at His saying ﴿and He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The locative sense in ﴿fī ṭughyānihim﴾ ("in their transgression") is figurative, to indicate that transgression encompasses them, that is, their hearts. The clause ﴿wa-nadharuhum﴾ is conjoined to "nuqallibu." The clause ﴿yaʿmahūn﴾ ("wandering blindly") is a circumstantial clause from the object pronoun in ﴿wa-nadharuhum﴾. In this there is an indication that the blind bewilderment arises from the transgression.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 111:

Page 5
﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered together against them every thing face to face, they would not have believed, unless Allah willed. But most of them are ignorant.﴾

The clause ﴿And even if We had sent down﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the clause ﴿And what will make you realize﴾ [al-An'am: 109], given that the clause ﴿And what will make you realize﴾ [al-An'am: 109] is itself conjoined to the clause ﴿Say: The signs are only with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 109]. Thus all three form a response to the content of the clause (﴿And they swore by Allah with their strongest oaths that if a sign came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 109]) etc., and an explanation of the clause (﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109]).

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the mockers, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and al-Harith ibn Handhala, from among the people of Makkah, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a group of the people of Makkah and said: "Show us the angels testifying for you, or raise for us some of our dead so that we may ask them whether what you say is true." It was also said: the polytheists said: "We will not believe you until Qusayy is raised and informs us of your truthfulness, or you bring us Allah and the angels as a guarantor (qabilan)," meaning a surety. So the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, as a rebuttal to them. And Allah related of them (﴿And they said: We will not believe you﴾ [al-Isra': 90]) up to His words (﴿or you bring Allah and the angels as a guarantor﴾ [al-Isra': 92]) in Surah al-Isra'.

He mentioned three of the extraordinary matters (khawariq al-'adat) in accordance with their suggestions, since they had proposed these, and His words ﴿and We gather against them every thing﴾ point to the totality of what they asked for and other than it.

Page 6
Al-hashr means gathering, and from it is ﴿and his armies were gathered for Solomon﴾ [al-Naml: 17]. It has been made to include the sense of sending forth and dispatching, hence it is construed with (ʿalā), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿We sent against you Our servants﴾ [al-Isra': 5].

"Every thing" (kull shay') encompasses all existing things, but the context restricts it to every thing of what they asked for, or of the kind of extraordinary matters and signs. This is from the general term intended in a specific sense, like His words concerning the wind of 'Ad: ﴿It destroys every thing by the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25]. The indicator (qarina) is what precedes it, His words: (﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them﴾).

His words (qibalan) were read by Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far with a kasra on the qaf and fatha on the ba', and it means facing and confronting, i.e., We gathered every such thing before them directly (ʿiyanan). The rest read it with a damma on the qaf and ba', which is a dialect of (qibal) meaning facing and direct observation. Some exegetes interpreted it with other interpretations, far from the usage and unsuitable to the meaning.

﴿They would not have believed﴾ (ma kanu li-yu'minu) is stronger than (la yu'minun) in negating their faith, despite all of this, because they are obstinate, arrogant, and not seeking the truth. For if they had sought the truth with fairness, the miracle of the Qur'an would have sufficed them, if the clarity of the truth to which the Messenger, upon him blessings and peace, calls had not sufficed them. So the meaning is the report of the negation of their faith in the most fitting circumstances for one who believes to believe, so how much more so when that is not the case. The intended meaning is the eternal negation of their faith.

This "law" (lau) is what is called the Suhaybi "law" (lau al-Suhaybiyya), and we will explain the discussion of it at His words, the Exalted: ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse﴾ [al-Anfal: 23] in Surah al-Anfal.

His words ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ are an exception from the general circumstances included in the generality of the negation of their faith. The estimate is: except by the will of Allah; that is, in the state in which Allah wills to change their hearts so that they believe willingly, or that He compels them to faith by empowering His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, over them, as Allah willed that by the conquest of Makkah and what followed it.

Page 7
So in His words ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ there is an allusion (ta'rid) to promising the Muslims with that, and the letter ba' was omitted with (an).

The name of Allah (ism al-jalala) is mentioned explicitly in place of the pronoun, because the name of Allah suggests the station of absoluteness, which is the station of ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], and it suggests that this occurs in accordance with wisdom, since the name of Allah comprises all attributes of perfection.

The contrastive conjunction (istidrak) in His words ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾ refers back to His words ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, which implies that they would believe if Allah willed their faith. That is because they only asked for signs in order to justify remaining upon their religion; they were determined to reject the call to faith, and they only pretexted with excuses by asking for signs in mockery. Thus their faith seemed to them to be among the impossibilities. So Allah made clear to them that if He willed their faith, they would believe. Ignorance (al-jahl) in this sense is the opposite of knowledge. In this there is additional alert to what His words ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ point to, namely that this will happen, and indeed many of them believed after this verse. Ascribing ignorance to most of them indicates that among them are intelligent people who reckon that.

It is also possible that the contrastive conjunction refers to what the conditional clause and its response contain, namely the negation of their faith despite the signs being shown to them; that is, they will not believe, and that will increase their ignorance upon their ignorance. Thus the intended ignorance is the opposite of forbearance, since they are mockers. Ascribing ignorance to most of them serves to exclude a few of them, who are people of judgment and forbearance, for their faith is hoped for if the signs were to appear to them. By this explanation the position of the contrastive conjunction becomes clear.

Thus the pronoun in "they are ignorant" refers to the polytheists without doubt, like the rest of the pronouns preceding it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 112:

[p. 8]
﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy—devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with ornate speech as deception. And had your Lord willed, they would not have done so, so leave them and what they fabricate.﴾

This is an interjected statement (i'tiraD), intended to console the Messenger ﷺ, and the waw is the waw of interjection (waw al-i'tiraD), because the sentence serves as a summation (fadhlakah). It comes as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ after the mention of what grieves him from the circumstances of his people's disbelievers and their obstinacy in rejecting his call. God informs him that these are his enemies, and that the enmity of such people toward someone like him is a sunnah (established practice) among the sunan of God Most High in testing all His prophets; there is none of them who did not have enemies. Thus the enmity of these people toward the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, was not something novel in the affairs of the messengers. The meaning of the speech is: Are you not a prophet, when We have appointed for every prophet an enemy, and so on to the end.

The demonstrative in His words "and thus" refers to the appointing derived from the verb "We have appointed," as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. So the kaf is in the accusative position as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb "We have appointed."

His words "an enemy" are the first object of "We have appointed," and His words "for every prophet," the prepositional phrase, are the second object of "We have appointed." Its being placed before the first object is for emphasis, because it is the intended purpose from the context, since the aim is to inform that this is God's sunnah concerning all His prophets, whereby exemplarity, emulation and consolation are achieved. Moreover, placing it first alerts the hearer from the outset that it is a predicate, and that it is not connected to "an enemy," lest the listener imagine that "devils of mankind" is an object, which would turn the speech toward informing about the states of the devils, or about specifying who the enemy of the prophets is; and that would contradict the eloquence of the speech.

[p. 9]
"Devils" (shayatin) is an apposition (badal) to "an enemy." The structure was formed in this way because the primary intent is to inform that the polytheists are enemies of the Messenger ﷺ. Whoever parses "devils" as an object of "appointed," with "for every prophet" as an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) connected to "an enemy," has corrupted the meaning.

"Enemy" (`aduww) is a noun that applies to the singular and the plural. God says: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4], and this has been discussed earlier at His words: ﴿If he is from a people hostile to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 92] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The shaytan (devil), in origin, is a type of existent beings that are immaterial and hidden; it is a type within the genus of jinn. This was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. The term "shaytan" is also applied, metaphorically, to the misleader who commits evil acts among people, and from this comes "the devils of the Arabs" for a group of their wicked men, among them Nashib al-A'war, and his son Sa'd ibn Nashib the poet. This is by way of comparison, and this usage became widespread in their speech.

"Ins" (mankind): the human being (al-insan), and it is derived from ta'annus (companionship) and ilf (familiarity), because humankind becomes familiar with humankind and feels at ease with him; so he is named ins and insan.

﴿Devils of mankind﴾ is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the people who act in the manner of devils through cunning and deception. The idafa of "devils" to "mankind" is a metaphorical idafa, on the presumption of partitive "min" by way of metaphor, based on the metaphor which requires that these humans be devils; so they are devils, and they are part of mankind. That is: mankind has recognized individuals, and individuals who are not recognized, to whom the name of devils is applied. Thus, in this respect, it is an idafa of the more specific to the more general in one respect. The "devils of the jinn" are literal, and the idafa is genuine, because some of the jinn are devils, some are not devils, and some are righteous. The enmity of the devils of the jinn toward the prophets is manifest, and the prophets came only to warn against the actions of the devils. God Most High said to Adam: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117].

[p. 10]
The clause "inspiring" (yuhi) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the appointing derived from "We have appointed" is qualified by it; so this inspiration is part of what was appointed.

"Inspiration" (wahy) is hidden speech, like whispering, and what is intended by it includes the casting of whispering into the soul of a discourse that is embellished in the form of speech.

The inspiring part is the devils of the jinn, who cast into the minds of the devils of mankind the ideas of the capacity to teach evil, so they become leaders of the people of evil and corruption.

"Zukhruf" means adornment, and gold was called zukhruf because it is adorned with it as jewelry. The idafa of "zukhruf" to "speech" is an idafa of attribute to the qualified: i.e., ornate speech (al-qawl al-zukhruf), i.e., embellished (al-muzakhraf). This is a description by a static noun that has the meaning of a derived noun, since it has the meaning of "adornment." The description of speech as zukhruf conveys that it needs embellishment and ornamentation. Speech needs this only if it does not contain in itself what gives it acceptance; and this is because it leads to harm which the speaker needs to adorn and beautify in order to conceal what is harmful in it, for fear that whoever is enticed by it will recoil from it. That adornment is thus a pretense by which they captivate souls, just as one decorates a toy for children with colors and gilding.

"Zukhruf al-qawl" is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object of the verb "yuhi," because the idafa of "zukhruf" to "speech," which is of the kind of inspiration, makes zukhruf a substitute for the verbal noun that specifies the kind of inspiration.

"Ghurur" means deception and enticement with benefit for the purpose of harm. This was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 196] in Surat Ali 'Imran.

"Ghurur" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) of the verb "yuhi"; i.e., they inspire ornate speech in order to deceive them.

[p. 11]
The discussion of the meaning of the will in His words: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿They would not have believed unless God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and His words: ﴿And had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107]. The clause is parenthetical between the object of purpose and the thing it is conjoined to.

The pronoun in the accusative in His words "they did it" refers either to the inspiration derived from "yuhi," or to the polytheism mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107], or to the enmity derived from His words "for every prophet an enemy."

The pronoun in the nominative refers to the devils of mankind and jinn, or to the polytheists, or to the enemy. Upon it is based the command to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, to leave them and their fabrication. This is leaving in the sense of disregarding concern for their deception and the vexation it causes, not turning away from admonishing and calling them, as was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 106]. The "waw" here means "together with."

﴿And what they fabricate﴾ is a relative clause in the accusative as an object with (maf'ul ma'ahu). What they fabricate is their false lies, from their claim of divinity for the idols, and what follows from that of false beliefs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 113:

﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may commit what they are committing.﴾

The phrase "wa-litasgha ilayhi" (﴿And that ... may incline to it﴾) is conjoined to "ghurura" (deception), because "ghurura" carries the sense of "li-yaghurrahum" (in order that they may deceive them). The lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and what follows it is in the position of a verbal noun; that is, "wa-li-sagh" (and for the inclination), meaning the inclining of their hearts toward their inspirations, so that the proof is established against them.

The meaning of tasgha is "tamil" (to incline). It is said: sagha yasgha sagwan and yasgu sagwan, with ya and with waw. The verse follows the form with ya because it was written in the Mushaf in the form of ya. Its literal meaning is physical inclination; it is said: sagha, that is, mala (he inclined), and asgha, that is, amala (he caused to incline). In the hadith of the cat, that he (ﷺ) tilted the vessel toward her (asgha ilayha al-ina'). From this comes the usage asgha in the sense of "istama'a" (to listen), because its original sense was that he inclined his hearing or his ear; then they omitted the object due to frequent usage. Here it is metaphorical for following and accepting speech.

﴿Those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-An'am: 150] are the polytheists. He specified among the attributes of the polytheists their not believing in the Hereafter, and described them by this relative clause to hint at some effects of the whisperings of the devils upon them. This attribute is the greatest of what harmed them, since because of it they do not take care in what they do, out of fear of consequences and seeking good, but rather they follow their desires and what is made attractive to them of their appetites, turning away from the corruptions and disbelief contained therein, since they do not expect any recompense for good or evil. Therefore their minds incline to the deception of the devils, and do not incline to the call of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the righteous.

The conjunction of "wa-liyarḍawhu" (and that they may be pleased with it) to "wa-litasgha" is such that, although inclining entails and causes approval, the apparent form would have required that it be conjoined with the fa' (so) and that the lam of purpose not be repeated. This apparent form was departed from to indicate that it is independent as a cause of purpose; so it was conjoined with waw and the lam was repeated to emphasize this independence. Thus it indicates that the inclining of their hearts toward it would not have sufficed for them to act upon it, except that they were pleased with it.

The conjunction of ﴿and that they may commit what they are committing﴾ to "wa-liyarḍawhu" is like the conjunction of "wa-liyarḍawhu" to "wa-litasgha."

Al-iqtiraf is the ifti'al form from qarafa, when one earns an evil deed. Allah the Exalted said after this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾ [al-An'am: 120]. There He mentioned an object for "yaksibun" (they earn), because kasb encompasses good and evil; but He did not mention an object for "yaqtarifun" here, because it does not occur except as the earning of evil. And He did not say "yajzawna bima kanu yaksibun" (they will be recompensed for what they used to earn), in order to intend the emphasis of the meaning of sin.

It is said: qarifa, iqtarafa and qarafa; the form ifti'al and the form mufa'ala in it are for intensification, and this root signals something blameworthy. They have related that it is said: "qarifa fulanun li-'iyalihi" (so-and-so earned for his dependents), but I do not consider this sound.

The use of the nominal sentence in the relative clause in His saying ﴿what they are committing﴾ indicates their firm establishment in that committing and their persistence in it.

[Page 14]

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) addressed by God to His Messenger ﷺ, with an implied verb of saying (taqdir al-amr bi'l-qawl), as shown by the context. Compare God's words ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], meaning "they say." His earlier words ﴿There has come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104] come after He told him about the various forms of the disbelievers' obstinacy, their denial, and their insistence on demanding miraculous signs. They made those signs a judge between themselves and the Messenger ﷺ regarding the truth of his call. After God exposed their enmity toward His Messenger ﷺ and their slander against him, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to turn away from them and leave them and what they fabricate. He informed him that he was not charged with being a guardian over their faith, and that they would return to their Lord, who would inform them of what they used to do. After all this, God taught His Messenger ﷺ to address them with words that serve as an answer to their statements and their evasions. On this basis it follows that he does not seek any judge between himself and them other than God Most High, to whom their return is.

[Page 15]

And if they hope for anything else from Him, they hope for something outrageous. Thus the implied saying is required, because the discourse fits only as the words of the Prophet ﷺ.

The particle fa (then) marks the answer as a consequence of the whole of their statements and proposals. It is therefore a coordination of instruction (ʿatf al-talqin) with fa, just as it came with waw in His words ﴿He said: "I am making you an imam for the people." He said: "And of my offspring?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. An example with fa is His words in Surat al-Zumar: ﴿Say: "Is it other than God that you order me to worship, you ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64]. It is as if the polytheists invited the Prophet ﷺ to submit the matter of his prophethood to a judgment based on the signs they had proposed to him. So he answered them that he does not set up God's religion as a matter for adjudication. For this reason, the denial that He should take as judge anyone other than God Most High is stated, even though God's judgment is evident in the revelation of the Book, explained in detail and in truth, and by the testimony of the People of the Book within themselves. Among the reasons for placing the object first is that the fronted element contains an answer to a demand the addressee had made, as indicated by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) in His words ﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 164] in this surah.

The hamza is for interrogation expressing denial (istifham inkari). That is: "You thought that, and so you thought something outrageous."

The fronting of ﴿Is it other than God﴾ before "abtaghi" (I seek) is because the object is the locus of the denial, and so it is the proper element to be attached to the interrogative hamza of denial, as occurred earlier in His words ﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in this surah.

"Hakam" (judge) is the one specialized in judging whose ruling cannot be overturned. It is more specific than "hakim" (ruler or judge), which is why "al-Hakam" is among God's names, while "al-Hakim" ... is not listed among them. "Hakaman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

The meaning is: I do not seek a judge between myself and you other than God, who has issued His judgment against you that you are enemies who commit wrongdoing.

[Page 16]

The discussion of seeking (ibtigha') has already been treated under His words (Is it other than the religion of God that you seek?) in Surat Al 'Imran.

His words ﴿And He it is who sent down to you the Book, explained in detail﴾ are part of the statement commanded, and the waw is for the circumstantial state: that is, I do not turn away from appealing to Him. He has explained His judgment by sending down the Qur'an to you, so that you may reflect on it and know from it my truthfulness and that the Qur'an is from God. The circumstantial clause is formed as a nominal sentence with two definite parts, in order to convey restriction (qasr) while also conveying the basic content of the statement. The meaning is: and the case is that He sent down the Book to you, and no one else sent it down. The reason for this is that the Qur'an contains evidence that it is from God through its inimitability (i'jaz), through the unlettered (ummi) condition of the one to whom it was sent down, and because in it there is evidence of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, following from the established fact that it was sent down from God. He has informed that He sent Muhammad ﷺ to mankind in its entirety, and within the arguments and reports of the Qur'an there is evidence of the truthfulness of the one who brought it. Thus the form of the restrictive circumstantial clause conveys both matters: that it is from God, and that the judgment rests with the Messenger ﷺ as to truthfulness.

By "the Book" is meant the Qur'an, and the definite article is for a known referent present to the audience (al-'ahd al-huduri). The pronoun in "ilaykum" (to you) is addressed to the polytheists, since the Qur'an was sent down to all people for guidance through it. Thus, as God said ﴿With what He has sent down to you, He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ [al-Nisa': 166], He also said ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174]. Here, His words "to you" record against them that it has reached them, so they cannot feign ignorance.

"Mufassal" means explained and made clear. Mention of detailed explanation (tafsil) has already occurred in His words ﴿And thus We detail the verses that the way of the criminals may become evident﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in this surah.

The clause ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down﴾ is coordinated with the implied saying, so it is a resumptive sentence like it. Or it is coordinated with the clause ﴿Is it other than God that I seek﴾, or with the clause ﴿And He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾. It is then a coordination of instruction, by which speech attributed to God is conjoined with speech attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, in support of what the speech attributed to the Prophet ﷺ contains about the Qur'an being the truth and being from God.

[Page 17]

By "those to whom God gave the Book" is meant the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews, because "the Book" here is the Torah, which was known among the Arabs in general, and especially among the people of Mecca, because Jews frequented it for trade, and the people of Mecca frequented the dwellings of the Jews in Yathrib and its villages. Since the intended addressees of this ruling are the rabbis of the Jews specifically, He said ﴿We gave them the Book﴾ and did not say "the People of the Book."

The meaning of the knowledge of those given the Book that the Qur'an is sent down from God is that they find it confirming what is in their own Book. They know that Muhammad ﷺ did not study their Book with any of them, for had he studied it, the matter would have spread among them, and they would have announced it among the people at the appearance of his call, and they were most eager for that. Yet they did not claim it. Their knowledge of this does not require their acceptance of Islam, since obstinacy and envy keep them from it. It has also been said that by "those to whom God gave the Book" is meant those rabbis of the Jews who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq. In that case the relative pronoun in His words ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book﴾ is definite by reference to a known group. It is also reported from 'Ata' that ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ are the chief companions of Muhammad ﷺ: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, and 'Ali, and in that case "the Book" is the Qur'an.

The pronoun in "annahu" (that it) refers to the Book mentioned in His words ﴿And He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾, which is the Qur'an.

The "bi" in His words "bil-haqq" (in truth) is for accompaniment (mulabasa), that is, accompanied by the truth. This is the accompaniment of the signifier with the signified, since its meanings, its reports, its promise, its threat, and everything it contains are true.

[Page 18]

The majority read "munazzal" with a light z, while Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read it with the doubled z. The meaning is close or identical, as already discussed in His words ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3] at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

The address in His words ﴿So never be among the doubters﴾ may be taken as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. In that case the consequence is drawn from His words ﴿They know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾, meaning: do not be among those who doubt that they know this. The intended purpose is to affirm the report, like one who says after stating a report: "This is beyond doubt." Thus the negated doubt is doubt that the People of the Book know this, since it is strange that they both know it and disbelieve in it. It may also be an address to an unspecified person, so as to include everyone who needs such an address. That is: do not be, O listener, among the doubters, meaning those who are uncertain that the Qur'an is from God. In that case the consequence is drawn from His words ﴿It is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾, meaning: this matter has become clear, so do not be among those who doubt it.

It is also possible that the addressee is the Messenger ﷺ, and that the intended referent of the speech is the polytheists who doubt, by way of allusion (ta'ridh), as one says: "It is you I mean, yet listen, O neighbor." Of this kind is His words ﴿It has been revealed to you and to those before you: if you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. This last view is the best of the views, and the consequence in it is as in the second view.

In all of these views, the omission of the object of doubt (al-imtira') is because it is evident from the context, relying on the indication. Since these three views are not contradictory, it is valid that all of them are intended by the verse, so that the minds of the hearers may reach whatever they arrive at from them. This, in my view, is among the purposes of the Qur'an's conciseness (ijaz) and is the meaning of comprehensive speech (al-kalam al-jami'), and similar instances occur in many verses, and it is one of the distinctive features of the Qur'an.

[p. 18]

This sentence is coordinated with the sentence ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ (al-An'am 6:114), because that sentence is a quotation of a supposed speech, the implied meaning being "Say: Shall I seek a judge other than God?" This takes into account what that sentence contains of His words: (﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, detailed﴾ [6:114]). When the Book was described as sent down from God, and described as clear in its indication by His words (﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, detailed﴾ [6:114]), and then by the testimony of the scholars of the People of the Book that it is from God, through His words ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord﴾ [6:114], He informed His Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, and the believers, that this Book is complete in its indication and conclusive in its proof for every group, believer and disbeliever alike, that its promise and its threat are true, and that its command and its prohibition are just. It is also permissible that this sentence be coordinated with the sentence (﴿We have made for every prophet an enemy﴾ [6:112]), with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), as we will explain.

The word "completion" (tamām) is used in a figurative sense. It may mean the thing reaching the best that it can reach of what is intended from it. The literal meaning of completion is that a thing has all its parts, while deficiency is that it lacks some of its parts. Thus the term is borrowed for the abundance of the qualities that are sought in its kind. Or it may mean realization (taḥaqquq): the word tamām is used for the occurrence and realization of what is awaited. One says: "What so-and-so reported has come to pass (tamma)," and "He fulfilled his promise (atamma waʿdahu)," i.e., he realized it. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [2:124], i.e., he acted upon them without negligence or leniency. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience﴾ [7:137], i.e., His promise to them became manifest through His words ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [28:5], and so on. From this meaning is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God perfects His light﴾ [61:8], i.e., He realizes His religion and establishes it, because He made perfection (itmām) in opposition to extinguishing (iṭfāʾ), which is used for removal, also figuratively.

As for His saying "the words of your Lord" (kalimāt rabbika), it was read by the majority with the plural form, while ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf read it in the singular (kalimat). It is said that what is meant by "the words" or "the word" is the Qur'an, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes, and it is transmitted from Qatāda. This is the most apparent and suitable view, given the linking of this sentence with the sentence ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book﴾ [6:114]. As for the reading in the singular, the use of "word" (kalima) for the Qur'an is in view of its being a Book from God, so it is from His speech and His saying. "Word" and "speech" (kalām) are synonymous, and the Arabs say "the word of Zuhayr" meaning his poem. The term "words" (al-kalimāt) has been applied in the Qur'an to the heavenly scriptures, in His saying: (﴿So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in God and His words﴾ [7:158]), i.e., His scriptures. As for the reading of "words" in the plural, its application to the Qur'an is in view of what it contains of sentences and verses, or in view of the kinds of its purposes, of command and prohibition, good tidings and warning, admonitions and information, argumentation and guidance, and other things. The meaning of its completeness is that every purpose that came in the Qur'an has come perfectly fulfilling what the seeker seeks from it.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya considered it unlikely that what is meant by "the words of your Lord," whether in plural or singular, is the Qur'an. He inclined to the view that what is meant is the speech of God, i.e., His word was carried out and His decree executed. Close to this is what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: "The words of God are His promise." It has also been said: "The words of God are His command, His prohibition, His promise and His threat," and this is explained so in al-Kashshāf (of al-Zamakhsharī), and it is close to the words of Ibn ʿAṭiyya. But the context testifies that explaining "the words" as the Qur'an is more apparent.

The words "true and just" (ṣidqan wa ʿadlan) are in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) according to Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, by interpreting the verbal noun as an active participle, i.e., "truthful and just." Thus it is a circumstantial clause of "words," and this is suitable for the meaning of completion being realization. al-Ṭabarī made both of them accusatives of specification (tamyīz) of the relation, i.e., "it was complete in respect of truthfulness and justice," as if he said: "Its truthfulness and its justice were completed," and this is suitable for the meaning of completion being the reaching of a thing to the best that is sought from its kind. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is not correct." I say: There is no basis for his not deeming it correct.

Truthfulness (ṣidq) is conformity to reality in information, and the realization of the report in promise and threat, and the enforcement of command and prohibition. Thus truthfulness includes everything in the words of God of the kind of information about the affairs of God and the affairs of creatures.

Truthfulness is also used figuratively for a thing being complete in the properties of its kind.

[p. 19]

Justice (ʿadl) is giving each one who deserves what he deserves, repelling aggression and injustice from the oppressed, and managing the affairs of people in what is good for them. Its explanation was previously given at His saying: ﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾ [4:58] in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

Thus justice includes everything in the words of God of managing the affairs of creatures in this world and the Hereafter.

So, according to the first explanation of "the words" or "the word," the meaning is that the Qur'an has reached the furthest that books can reach in clarity of indication and eloquence of expression, that it is truthful in its reports and just in its rulings, so that one does not find in its reports anything that contradicts reality, nor in its rulings anything that contradicts truth. This is a kind of challenge and argument for the rightness of the Qur'an.

And according to the second and third explanations, the meaning is: what God said and what He promised and threatened and what He commanded and forbade has been carried out, all of it truthful, i.e., not failing, and just, i.e., not unjust. This is a threat to the polytheists that the threat with which He threatened them will surely come upon them. It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾ [7:137], i.e., what He promised them of possessing the easts and wests of the earth in which He had blessed was fulfilled. And His saying: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been justified against those who disbelieved, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ [40:6], i.e., the words of His threat have been justified.

The meaning of ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾ is the negation of the category of those who change the words of God, i.e., those who nullify what He intended in His words.

Substitution (tabdīl) was explained previously at His saying: ﴿He said: Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [2:61] in Sūrat al-Baqara. It was explained there that it has no bare verb form, and that the original root of its material is tabdīl, and that substitution in its real sense is putting one thing in place of another. It may be in essences, as He said: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to another earth﴾ [14:48], and al-Nābigha said:

[Poem, p. 21]
I knew them living there, noble; then they were changed into the wild cattle's ... of the heavy-bellied she-oxen [i.e., the ruins became the abodes of wild beasts].

It may be in attributes, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He will surely change their fear into security﴾ [24:55].

It is used figuratively for the nullification and annulment of a thing, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿They want to change the words of God﴾ [48:15], i.e., oppose them and annul what they entail. This is His saying: ﴿Say: You will not follow us; thus God has said before﴾ [48:15]. That is because annulment entails bringing something opposite to the thing annulled, so this implication is the relation of the figurative usage. It was previously explained at His saying: ﴿So whoever alters it after having heard it﴾ [2:181] in Sūrat al-Baqara. In His saying ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾ it is used figuratively in the sense of opposition or annulment, according to the two possibilities in the meaning of completion in His saying "the words of your Lord were completed." The negation of the changer is a metonymy (kināya) for the negation of change.

If what is meant by "the words" is the Qur'an, as previously explained, then the meaning of the negation of a changer of His words is the negation of bringing anything that would annul or nullify it or oppose it, by showing that there is in it something not complete. If anyone brings something that annuls it by lying and falsehood, that is not an annulment, but only obstinacy in the form of annulment, with respect to the wording of the Qur'an and its arrangement. And the negation of what would nullify its meanings and the realities of its wisdom, and the negation of altering what it legislated and ruled, and this last negation is a metonymy for the prohibition against Muslims opposing it. Thereby substitution is used in its literal, figurative and metonymic senses.

It is also permissible that the sentence "the words of your Lord were completed" be coordinated with the sentence "We have made for every prophet an enemy" (6:112), with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion. Then "the words" means what God established and decreed of making enemies for every prophet who embellish speech in misleading, so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to them, and they follow them and commit evil deeds. The meaning of completion here is realization. Then His saying ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾ is the negation that anyone can change the sunna of God and what He has decreed and ordained, as in His saying: ﴿So you will not find any change in the sunna of God, nor will you find any alteration in the sunna of God﴾ [35:43].

[p. 22]

This verse then has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed, until Our help came to them. And there is no changer of the words of God﴾ [6:34]. In it there is consolation for the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, and reassurance for him and the believers that the promised victory will arrive in its due time.

His saying ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) to the sentence ﴿The word of your Lord has been completed in truthfulness and justice; there is no changer of His words﴾. That is, He is the One who is aware of the sayings and knows what is in hearts. This is an allusion to a threat to whoever strives to change His words. The All-Hearing is the One who knows the voices of creatures, among which are those things inspired by the devils of mankind and jinn, one to another, so nothing of them escapes Him. And He is also the All-Knowing of those who want to change the words of God, in the meanings previously mentioned, so nothing of what they plunge into is hidden from Him, of plotting by night and nullifying it.

And "the All-Knowing" is more general: the All-Knowing of the conditions of creation, the All-Knowing of the places where His words occur and the locations of their completion, and the One who arranges their completion by His wisdom, and the One who determines the times of their occurrence.

So He mentioned these two attributes here: a threat to those included in the previous verses of blame, and a promise to the one commanded to turn away from them and their fabrications, and to judge between them by God, and to those who know that God has sent down His Book with truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 116 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God. They follow nothing but conjecture, and they do nothing but guess.﴾

[p. 23] It follows the mention of the obstinacy of the polytheists, their enmity toward the Messenger (ﷺ), their alliance with the devils, their acceptance of what the devils of the jinn and humankind whisper to them, and their committing of evil deeds in obedience to their allies. It also reassures the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) that he encounters what the prophets before him encountered, namely the effects of the enmity of the devils of humankind and the jinn. It does so by mentioning what makes light for the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims the numerical superiority and power of the polytheists that they see, and the smallness and weakness of the Muslims. It also warns them against trusting the polytheists' words, and guides them to oppose the polytheists in all their conditions and not to listen to their opinions, because they lead people astray from the way of God. It further commands them to hold fast to what God guides them to. Thus the clause ﴿And if you obey﴾ is connected to the clause ﴿Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of humankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112], and to the clause ﴿Shall I seek other than God as a judge?﴾ [al-An'am: 114] and what follows it, up to ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-An'am: 115].

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended audience is the Muslims, like His saying: ﴿If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

With the conditional verb, the particle (إن, in) is used. Its original use is for a condition that is rarely realized, or for an impossible condition when it is mentioned as a hypothetical, as the impossible is supposed. It appears that the polytheists, when they despaired of the apostasy of the Muslims, as His saying indicates: ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than God that which neither benefits us nor harms us?﴾ [al-An'am: 71] and the verse that follows, began to cast doubts and suspicions upon the Muslims regarding the rulings of their religion. This is indicated by His saying after this: ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah that: "The polytheists said: 'O Muhammad, tell us about a sheep when it dies, who killed it?' – they meant eating a sheep that died of natural causes without slaughter – He said: 'God killed it.' You claim that what you and your companions kill is lawful, and what a dog or a falcon kills is lawful, but what God kills is unlawful!' So something of that entered the hearts of some Muslims."

In the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, shall we eat what we kill, and not eat what God kills?' So God revealed: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118], the verse." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan (good) gharib (strange) hadith." Thus, from this and similar matters, God warned the Muslims against these people, and confirmed them in the belief that they are upon the truth, even if they are few, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Say: The evil and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of evil impresses you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100].

Al-ta'ah (obedience) is a noun derived from al-taw' (willing compliance), which is the verbal noun of ta'a yatu'u, meaning to submit, and doing what one is commanded willingly without resistance. Obedience is thus the opposite of compulsion. It is said: ta'a and atha'a. It is used figuratively for accepting a statement. From this is what came in the hadith: "If they obey you in that, then inform them that God has enjoined upon them the zakah of their wealth." From this is His saying: ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18], meaning that his word is accepted. Otherwise, the one interceded with is higher than the intercessor, so the meaning is not that he is submitted to. The obedience here is used in this figurative sense, namely accepting a statement.

﴿Most of those on earth﴾ means most of the inhabitants of the earth.

"Earth" (al-ard) is used for the whole terrestrial globe upon which humans, animals and plants live, and it is the whole world. It is also used for a part of the terrestrial globe known among the addressees, and this is a common usage, as in His saying: ﴿And after him We said to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land﴾ [al-Isra': 104], meaning the Holy Land; and His saying: ﴿or they be banished from the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], meaning the land in which they waged war against God. The more apparent view is that what is meant in the verse is the well-known meaning, namely the whole terrestrial globe, as is the usual use of the word in the Qur'an. It has also been said that it means Mecca, because it is the land known to the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Whichever is the case, most of those on earth are astray and lead others astray. As for the terrestrial globe, the majority of its inhabitants hold misguided beliefs and unjust laws.

Among those with corrupt beliefs regarding divinity are the Magians, the polytheists, the worshippers of idols, the worshippers of the stars, and those who affirm multiple gods. Regarding prophethood, there are the Jews and Christians. [p. 25] And among those with unjust laws are people of all groups. Each of them, if he is obeyed, calls only to his own religion and sect, and so he leads one astray from the way of God. They vary in this error in number and degree. Following their laws does not free one from error, even if some of them contain some correctness. Those few among people who are guided are, in that era, the Muslims, and those who have not been reached by the call of Islam from the monotheists who are righteous and seeking the truth, in the east and west of the earth.

The reason for this majority is that truth and guidance require sound intellects, virtuous souls, reflection on what is beneficial and harmful, giving precedence to truth over desire, rectitude over appetite, and love of good for people. These are qualities that, when any one of them is lacking, error enters the soul in proportion to what has been diminished of these qualities. Their gathering in souls only occurs through complete moderation of intellect and soul. This is achieved either by divine creation and teaching, which is the state of the Messengers and prophets, or by divine inspiration, as the sages of Greece and others who were upon truth had, such as the people of unveiling (al-mukashafat) and the people of illuminative wisdom (al-hikmah al-ishraqiyyah), whom they sometimes call taste (al-dhawq). Or it is achieved by following a sinless guide, as was the case with the companions of the Messengers and prophets and the best of their communities. Therefore, it is inevitable that most of those on earth are misguided, and the guided are few. Whoever follows them, they lead astray.

The verse does not require that most people on earth lead others astray, because most of the inhabitants of the earth are not devoted to misguiding people. Rather, they are content with their own error and are preoccupied with their own affairs. What the verse requires is that most of them, if the Muslim accepts their word, will say to him only what is misleading, because they do not present to him anything except their own error. So the verse implies, by way of necessary implication (iltizam), that most people on earth are astray, because the guided person's follower is not led astray. Every vessel drips with what is in it. A similar meaning to this verse is His saying in the surah of al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: The evil and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of evil impresses you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100].

Know that this does not include those who err in ijtihad (independent reasoning) among the Muslims, because the mujtahid in matters of disagreement (ikhtilaf) seeks to hit upon the truth through his ijtihad, by searching the legal evidences, and he continues to seek out what opposes his ijtihad. When the error becomes clear to him, he returns from his opinion. So there is no error in obeying him regarding the way of God, because among the way of God are the methods of reasoning and debate in the understanding of religion.

His saying: ﴿they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾ is an analogy for the state of one who calls to disbelief and corruption, and whom one accepts, with the state of one who misleads a person seeking guidance to the road: he describes for him a road other than the road that leads to the destination. This is a figurative representation (tamthil) that admits distribution of the comparison, such that each part of the figure being compared is likened to a corresponding part of the figure to which it is compared. The attribution of "the way" to the name of God is a clue that it is a metaphor (isti'arah). The way of God is either the evidences of truth, or the truth itself.

Then God explained the cause of their being led astray and their leading others astray: they hold to and adhere only to misguided beliefs and foolish religions, which they consider to be truth, because they did not exhaust the capacity of their intellects in tracing the evidences of truth. So He said: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾.
