Following (al-ittiba') is used figuratively for the mind's acceptance of what is said and of the opinions and evidences that occur to the mind, and adopting them. This is the most complete sense of following. Moreover, following is also used for a person acting by his own opinion, as if he follows it.

In the terminology of the Qur'an, conjecture (zann) is an erroneous belief without evidence, which its holder considers to be true and sound. God said: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾ [Yunus: 36]. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of conjecture, for conjecture is the most false of speech." It is not the conjecture that our jurists have established in legislative matters, for they meant by it a prevailing knowledge in reflection, with a low probability of error, because certainty is difficult to attain in the legal evidences (al-adillah al-taklifiyyah). For certainty in them, if it is the certainty intended by the philosophers, depends on evidence that ends in self-evident truth (darurah) or demonstrative proof (burhan), and these two apply only to the foundations of the questions of monotheism. [p. 27] And if it means certainty that God has commanded or forbidden, this is rare in most matters of legislation, except what is known of religion by necessity, or what the person has attained through sense perception, and this is specific to what some of the Companions received directly from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or what was attained through mass transmission (tawatur). Mass transmission is rare after the era of the Companions and Successors, as is known from the principles of jurisprudence.

The clause ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), arising from His saying: ﴿they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾. It explains the cause of their going astray: that they followed doubts without reflecting on their corrupt consequences. Therefore, by conjecture is meant the conjecture of their forefathers, as the apparent meaning of the verb "they follow" indicates.

The clause ﴿and they do nothing but guess﴾ is coordinated (atf) with the clause ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾. The presence of the coordinating particle prevents this clause from being an emphasis or an explanation of the preceding clause, so it is determined that what is meant by this clause is other than what is meant by the clause ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾.

The opinions of the exegetes have varied regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿and they do nothing but guess﴾. It has been said: "they guess" means they lie in claiming that what they follow is certain. It has also been said: it is conjecture, namely their conjecture that their forefathers were upon the truth. Guessing (al-kharṣ) is their estimating themselves to be upon the truth.

The more correct view is that the meaning of the first clause is what they received from their forefathers, as the verb "they follow" indicates, and the meaning of the second clause is what they deduce from additions to what their forefathers left them, and from their doubts which they consider to be compelling proofs, such as their saying: "How do we eat what we have killed, and what a dog or a falcon has killed, but not what God has killed?" as was mentioned just above. This is indicated by the verb "they guess," with its meaning of estimation and reflection.

Guessing (al-kharṣ) is a conjecture arising from an inner feeling based on approximation, not resting on any evidence shared by rational people. It is synonymous with estimation (al-hazr) and conjecture (al-takhmin). From it comes estimating the palm and vine (kharṣ al-nakhl wa al-karm), that is, estimating the amount of fruit in them according to what the observer perceives based on his experience. The use of kharṣ for their false conjectures is very elegant, because these are conjectures for which there is no evidence beyond what appeals to those who hold them. Some exegetes and lexicographers explained kharṣ as lying. This explanation is deficient, as its proponents looked to the general sense that the context gives in verses like this one and like His saying: ﴿Killed were the guessers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 10]. The context is not describing most of those on earth as liars, but branding them as those who take their beliefs from illusory indications. So kharṣ is whatever is not knowledge. God said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that; they only guess﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20]. If the intent were to describe them as lying, the word "they lie" (yakdhibun) would have been more explicit than "they guess" (yakhrusun).

Know that the context calls for condemning reasoning based on estimation (khars), since it is guesswork and conjecture that cannot be precisely determined. Yet what is related from 'Attab ibn Asid counters this, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that grapes be estimated (yukhras) just as dates are estimated." Malik and al-Shafi'i acted upon it, and its interpretation is that it is a concession (rukhsa), facilitating matters for the owners of palm trees and vines so that they may benefit by eating their fruit fresh, and the zakat is taken from them according to what the estimate determines. Likewise in dividing the fruit among partners, and likewise in the case of the 'ariyya, where the one who granted the 'ariyya buys it back from the one to whom he granted it. Abu Hanifa disagreed on this and considered the hadith of 'Attab abrogated (mansukh).

**Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 6, verse 117:**

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾

This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of His saying: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you﴾ [al-An'am: 116], because its implication is a warning against their misguiding influence and an expectation that they will lead him astray. This implies that the Muslims want guidance, so let them avoid the misguided, and let them seek guidance through God, who guides them. This is also the function of (inna) when it comes in a statement that does not need to remove doubt or denial. (Anna) serves to emphasize the statement and connect it to what precedes it, such that it takes the place of the conjunctive (fa') of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), and it indicates causation. Since the preceding verses included an explanation of the straying of those who stray and the guidance of those who are guided, the saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ serves as a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to all those purposes.

[Page 29]

The definiteness of the subject through the construct in His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾ serves to honor the one referred to by the possessive, and to show that the guidance of the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, is the guidance, and that those about whom He informed that they are misleaders have no share in guidance, because they did not take God as their Lord. Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Answer him. Say: God is our Protector, and you have no protector."

"A'lam" (most knowing) is a superlative form, indicating that no one among the misguided or among the guided is beyond God's knowledge, and that other than God may know some of the guided and some of the misguided, but much knowledge of both groups escapes him, and the hidden secrets of some of both groups are concealed from him.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿He is most knowing﴾ is the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), serving to restrict the predicate to the subject. Thus, the superior knowledge regarding the misguided and the guided is restricted to God Most High, and no one shares it with Him. The reason for this restriction is that people do not doubt that their knowledge of the misguided and the guided is limited, because whenever anyone knows some of the conditions of people, the conditions of many people remain hidden from him, and everyone knows the deficiency of his knowledge and is certain that there is someone more knowing than the knowledgeable among them. But the polytheists reckoned that superior knowledge is an attribute of God Most High and of their gods, so by this restriction it was negated that anyone shares with God the attribute of absolute superior knowledge.

"Man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, and its grammatical position is accusative by the removal of the preposition, which is the (ba'), as is indicated by the presence of the (ba') in His saying ﴿and He is most knowing of the guided﴾. This is because the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil) does not govern a direct object by itself, due to the weakness of its resemblance to the verb. Rather, it only reaches its object through (bi) or (li) or (ila). Its governing of the object directly is rare, and its proper construction here is with (bi), so the (ba') was omitted as a brief elision, relying on the context.

[Page 30]

The particle was omitted from the first clause and mentioned in the second, not the reverse, although the usual pattern is that the context precedes. This is because the superlative form is attached to a plural in which the one preferred is one of them, as in: "He is the most knowing of scholars and the most generous of the generous." Since the objects in those cases do not show their grammatical case on their endings, the object could be confused with the genitive complement. This does not create ambiguity in the first clause, because the relative clause there indicates that what is meant is that God knows them best. So it is not to be imagined that the meaning is: "God is the most knowing of those who stray from His way," i.e., the most knowing of all who know among them, since it does not occur to any listener to say: "So-and-so is the most knowing of the ignorant," because that is a contradictory statement, as misguidance is ignorance. Thus the corruption of the meaning serves as an indicator of the intended sound meaning, and this is one of the types of contextual indication (qarina haliyya). This differs from if he had said: "and He is the most knowing of the guided," where the listener might suppose that what is meant is that God is the most knowing of the guided, i.e., the most knowledgeable of the guided, since guidance stems from knowledge.

This is what occurred to me regarding the subtle point of omitting the particle from His saying ﴿He is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾, the preposition (harf al-jarr) by which (a'lam) is transitive.

This verse is a transition from the argument with the polytheists and the exposure of their misguidance, which was concluded with His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 117]. The discourse then moved from that to explaining the laws of guidance for the guided, and to nullifying the laws that the misguiders had legislated. This explanation removes ambiguity and confusion. For this reason, the rulings prescribed for the Muslims were set alongside their opposites, which the polytheists and their forebears had legislated.

What the particle *fa'* (so) implies of sequence requires that this sentence be connected to the one before it. The connection is this: His saying, ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of God﴾ [al-An'am: 116], included the nullification of the doubt the polytheists had cast upon the Muslims concerning the prohibition of carrion (*maytah*). They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You claim that what you and your companions kill is lawful to eat, and what God kills is unlawful, and that this is included in His saying: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾." When God forbade following them and called their legislation "conjecture," He based on this the command here: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾. That is, at the time of its killing, that is, what has been slaughtered or sacrificed with the name of God mentioned over it. The prohibition is against eating what the name of God has not been mentioned over, which includes carrion, since the name of God is not mentioned over carrion. For this reason this verse was followed by the verse ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Thus it is clear that the *fa'* indicates a consequence drawn from what is already understood from the preceding verse.

The imperative in His saying, ﴿So eat﴾, is for permission. Since it would not occur to anyone that what has had the name of God mentioned over it is unlawful to eat, because this was not known among the Muslims or the polytheists, it is understood that the purpose of the permission is not to lift a hardship, but to specify what is permitted and to distinguish it from its opposite, namely carrion and what is slaughtered on the *nusub* (stone altars). The address is to the Muslims.

His saying, ﴿of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾, indicates that the relative clause refers to the slaughtered animal, because the Arabs used to mention, at the time of slaughtering or sacrificing, the name of whatever was intended by that act of ritual slaughter (*dhakāh*), announcing it aloud. For this reason it was said concerning it: ﴿that which has been dedicated to other than God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173], meaning, that which is proclaimed. The meaning is: eat what has been ritually slaughtered and do not eat carrion. Therefore "that over which the name of God has been mentioned" is a metonymy for the slaughtered animal, since the invocation of the name occurs at the time of slaughter.

Tying the permission to what has had the name of God mentioned over it implies that what has not had the name of God mentioned over it is not eaten by Muslims. This "other" is equivalent in meaning to what has had the name of other than God mentioned over it, because their custom was that whenever they slaughtered an animal they mentioned God's name over it if it was an offering (*hady*) in the Hajj or a sacrifice for the Ka'bah. If it was a sacrifice to idols or to the jinn, they mentioned over it the name of the one they sought nearness to. Thus His saying, ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾, implies the prohibition of eating what has had the name of other than God mentioned over it, and the prohibition of what has had neither the name of God nor the name of other than God mentioned over it, because the abandonment of mentioning God's name among them could only occur with the intention of avoiding mentioning it.

From this it is also understood that carrion and the like are prohibited, that is, what was not intended to be ritually slaughtered, because the mention of God's name or the name of another occurs only when the intention is to slaughter the animal, as is well known among them. Thus this sentence specifies the permissibility of eating what has been ritually slaughtered, to the exclusion of carrion, in accordance with the custom of the Muslims, since the prohibition is directed at them. Among the things that support this is what is in *al-Kashshāf* (Zamakhsharī's commentary), that the jurists interpreted His later saying, ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121], as referring to carrion. This is based on the understanding that the name of God is mentioned at the time of slaughter, and not on what has had the name of other than God mentioned over it, by deriving it from the context of permission and restricting it to this, and not to anything else. There is in the verse no form of restriction (*qasr*) and no argument from contrary implication (*mafhūm mukhālafah*). Rather, some of its meaning comes from the explicit wording and some from its context. This latter kind of indication is among the implications of constructions understood by reason, which are described neither as literal nor as figurative.

By this it is known that the verse has no bearing on the ruling concerning forgetting to mention God's name at the time of slaughter, for that is a separate question with its own evidences. It is not the business of Qur'anic legislation to address rare circumstances.

The preposition *'alā* (over) here expresses figurative elevation, indicating the strong connection of the act of mentioning to the slaughtered animal itself, in the sense that the name of God is to be mentioned over it at the moment of performing the slaughter, not before it or after it.

His saying, ﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾, is a restriction on the implied limitation drawn from the verb of permission and from the attachment of the prepositional phrase to it. It is an exhortation to adhere to this and not to be lax about it, to the extent that it was made one of the signs that its performer is a believer. This is because mentioning the name of other than God over most slaughtered animals was the emblem of the people of polytheism.

As for omitting the mention of the name: if it is intentional, in order to avoid mentioning God's name, then it is equivalent to mentioning the name of other than God. If it is by oversight, its ruling is known from evidences other than this verse, among them His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and other evidences from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ).

[Page 33]

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah 6, verse 119:

﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to?﴾

This is coordinated (*'atf*) with His saying: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118]. The address is to the Muslims.

The *ma* is interrogative (*istifhamiyya*), but it is used in the sense of negation. That is, it is not established for you that you should abstain from eating what the name of God has been mentioned over; i.e., eat of what the name of God has been mentioned over. The *lam* indicates possession (*ikhtisas*), and the phrase is a stative complement (*zarf mustaqirr*) functioning as the predicate of *ma*, meaning: what is established for you.

*An la ta'kulu* is in the genitive case, governed by an elided *fi* ("in") together with *anna*. It is connected to what is in the predicate of the sense of "being established." The explanation of this type of construction has already been given under His saying: ﴿They said, "And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246] in Surah al-Baqarah.

None of the exegetes has clarified the reason for coordinating this with what precedes it, nor the motive for this address, except what al-Khafaji related in his gloss on the *tafsir* from one whom he titled "'Alam al-Huda" (the Standard of Guidance), who probably meant al-Sharif al-Murtada: that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that the Muslims used to scruple about eating good things, out of asceticism and renunciation. End of quotation.

It seems he means abstention from eating meat, so that God's saying ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ is a digression (*istitrad*) occasioned by His saying before it: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118]. This implies that the interrogation is used for reproach. But I do not think what this one titled "the Standard of Guidance" said is correct, nor does it have any basis at all. Al-Tabari said: "We do not know of any one of the predecessors of this community who refrained from eating what God had made lawful of the slaughtered animals." 

[Page 34]

In my view, the occasion of revelation of this verse is what was mentioned just above: that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ and to the Muslims, when God had forbidden the eating of carrion: "Shall we eat what we kill, and not eat what God kills?" meaning carrion. Something then occurred in the hearts of some of the Muslims, so God revealed ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾. That is, God informed them of the invalidity of the polytheists' deceptive analogy, that carrion is more fitting to be eaten than what the slaughterer has killed with his own hand. God thus showed people the difference between carrion and what has been properly slaughtered: the latter has the name of God mentioned over it, while over carrion the name of God is not mentioned. This is a decisive and effective distinction.

I turn away from disputing with the polytheists, because the address is directed to the Muslims to nullify the polytheists' argument. It thus ends up as a refutation of the polytheists by way of allusion (*ta'ridh*). This is of the same kind as His saying in refuting the polytheists' statement: ﴿They say, "Trade is only like usury"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], when He said: ﴿But God has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], as was explained there. Accordingly, the meaning of the interrogation in His saying "And what is [the matter] with you that you should not..." turns into the sense: "Let the polytheists not tempt you to eat carrion, because you eat what the name of God has been mentioned over." This is what they said, but it is a far-fetched interpretation that does not fit the context of the verse.

His saying: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*), explaining what precedes it. That is: nothing should keep you from anything of all that God has made lawful for you, because God has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, so do not transgress it to something else. The apparent meaning of this is that God had previously explained to them what He had forbidden them of foods; perhaps this was by a revelation other than the Qur'an. It is not correct that the intended reference is His saying at the end of this surah: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], etc., because this surah was revealed all at once according to the sound view, as was mentioned in the introduction to its *tafsir*. Hence it is incompatible for what comes later in recitation to have been revealed earlier. Nor can the intended reference be His saying in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], because Surah al-Ma'idah is Medinan by consensus, while this Surah al-An'am is Meccan by consensus.

His saying: ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ is an exception (*istithna'*) from the relative pronoun's returning pronoun, which is the object pronoun governed by *harrama* ("forbade"), elided because of its frequent use. The *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: except that which you are compelled to. The forbidden things are of various kinds, and from them is excepted what one is compelled to of their individual instances, so it becomes lawful. This is therefore a continuous exception (*istithna' muttasil*) without any need to make the *ma* in ﴿what you are compelled to﴾ a verbal-noun (*masdariyya*) particle.

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf read ﴿wa qad fassala﴾ with the verb in the active voice. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read it in the passive voice. Nafi', Hafs (on the authority of 'Asim), and Abu Ja'far read ﴿ma harrama﴾ with the verb in the active voice; the rest read it in the passive voice. The meaning in both pairs of readings is one and the same.

The *idtirar* (compulsion) has already been explained in Surah al-Ma'idah.

* * *

﴿And indeed many lead [others] astray by their desires without knowledge. Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

This is a warning against imitating the polytheists in forbidding some livestock to some categories of people.

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾. It is also permissible for the *wa* to be circumstantial (*hal*), in which case the statement is an allusive warning against being among those whom the people of desires lead astray without knowledge.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub read *la-yadillun* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, meaning that they themselves are astray. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with a *damma* on the *ya'*, meaning that they lead people astray. The meaning is one and the same, because the one who is astray is by nature one who leads others astray, and because the one who leads astray is generally not anything but astray, unless he intends to deceive others. The intended purpose is the warning against them, and that is achieved in both readings.

The *ba'* in *bi-ahwa'ihim* indicates cause (*sababiyya*) in both readings. The *ba'* in *bi-ghayri 'ilm* indicates accompaniment (*mula'aba*), meaning: they lead astray, following their desires, accompanied by the lack of knowledge.

By *'ilm* (knowledge) is meant a certainty that corresponds to reality, based on evidence. This is like His saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116]. Among these were the leaders of the polytheists in the past, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, the first to establish for them the worship of idols, who split the ears of the *bahirah* (she-camel), released the *sa'ibah* (free-roaming animal), and protected the protected. And those after him were like those who said: "What God has killed is more deserving that we eat it than what we have killed with our own hands."

His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*). It contains an announcement to the Messenger ﷺ of God's threat against these misguided misleaders. The report of God's knowledge of them is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for His seizing them with punishment and that He will not let them escape, because His being knowing of them does not require informing about it. It is also a warning to them, because they hear the Qur'an and it is recited to them at the time of the call.

The mention of "the transgressors" after the mention of "the misguided" is an indication that they are the ones intended; otherwise the statement would have no coherent connection. It is as if He said: "Indeed your Lord is most knowing of them while they are transgressors." God named them transgressors, and *i'tida'* means wrongdoing, because they took up error without any proof or reflection, so they were transgressors against themselves and transgressors against everyone they invited to agree with them.

[Page 35]

This indicates that everyone who speaks about religion without knowledge, or who calls people to something he does not know to be true or false, is a transgressor and wrongdoer against himself and against people. Likewise, everyone who issues legal rulings while not being qualified to do so.

**Surah 6, verse 120:**

﴿وذَرُوا ظاهِرَ الإثْمِ وباطِنَهُ﴾ ("And leave the outward and the inward of sin.")

This is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*), and the *waw* is a parenthetical *waw*. The meaning is: if you wish for asceticism and nearness to God, then draw near to Him by abandoning sin, not by abandoning what is permissible (*mubah*). This is similar in meaning to His saying, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and so on.

The verb (*dhara*) was discussed earlier, at His saying, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ [al-An'am: 70], in this surah. Sin (*ithm*) was discussed at His saying, ﴿In them is great sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The definite article in *al-ithm* is the definite article of comprehensiveness (*ta'rif al-istighraq*), since in meaning it defines both its outward and its inward aspects. The purpose of these two descriptions is to generalise all the instances of sin, because they are confined to these two aspects, as one says, "the east and the west," "the land and the sea," intending to encompass all directions.

The outward of sin is what people see, and its inward is what people do not perceive and what occurs in secret. This matter is comprehensively covered by abandoning all acts of disobedience. Many Arabs would show off good deeds before people and then, when alone, commit sins. Concerning some of them came His saying, ﴿And among the people is one whose speech in the life of this world pleases you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents. And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals. And God does not like corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], and ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes him to sin. So sufficient for him is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206].

* * *

[Page 38]

﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾ is a justification for the command to abandon sin, and a warning and a notice of excuse for those addressed. Therefore the statement is emphasised with *inna* ("indeed"), which in such a context, that is, a context following a command or a report, conveys the meaning of causation and replaces the *fa'* (particle of consequence). Its well-known example is the verse of Bashshar:

"Indeed, that success lies in early rising."

The verb is expressed with the noun "sin" in a place where a pronoun would be expected. He did not say "those who earn it," in order to intensify the condemnation of sin and so that it would be firmly fixed in the mind of the listener, and so that the sentence would stand independently and proceed like proverbs and maxims.

The letter *sin*, which is designated for the future report, is used here to express the certainty of occurrence and its continuity.

Since the verb "earn" (*yaksibun*), which takes sin as its object, was used for the sinners, in the phrase describing their recompense the verb "commit" (*yaqtarifun*) was used. This is because *iqtiraf*, when used without qualification, means acquiring sin, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿that they may commit what they are committing﴾ [al-An'am: 113].

And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for it is indeed a transgression (fisq). Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you, and if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists.

The clause "And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned" is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause "So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned" [al-An'am: 118].

[p. 39]

The "ma" in His words "of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). Its referent here is the slaughtered animal (dhaki), by indication of the preceding verse, whose referent is that, by indication of the context. Since the preceding verse had already established the permissibility of eating what has had the name of God mentioned over it, and had implied a prohibition against what has not had the name of God mentioned over it, which is carrion (maytah), and since the ruling regarding eating carrion and the distinction between it and what was slaughtered (dhukkiya) with the name of God mentioned over it was complete, this verse conveys a prohibition and a warning against eating what has had the name of other than God mentioned over it. The meaning of "over which the name of God has not been mentioned" is that the mention of God's name over it was deliberately abandoned and avoided. This can only happen with the intention that the slaughter not be for God, and this is equivalent to its being for other than God, since in their view there is no intermediate state in ritual slaughter (dhakah) between mentioning the name of God and mentioning the name of other than God. This was explained earlier at His words: "So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned" [al-An'am: 118].

What confirms that this is the intended meaning is His words here, "for it is indeed a transgression," and His words in the following verse: "or a transgression (fisqan) over which other than God has been invoked" [al-An'am: 145]. Thus it is known that what is described as a transgression here is what is described as such there, and it is specified there as being that over which other than God has been invoked. Also, by indication of its being followed by His words: "And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists," because polytheism occurs only by mentioning the names of idols over what is slaughtered, not by omitting the invocation.

Perhaps the polytheists, in their scheming against the Muslims regarding the matter of ritual slaughter, were content to ask them to omit the invocation, so that they would mention neither God nor the idols. Thus the intended purpose of the verse would be to warn the Muslims against this deliberate omission, which is aimed at deception, and against invoking over the slaughtered animals the names of other than their gods.

If we take into account the purpose and the context, then the relative pronoun is intended to refer to a specific thing over which the name of God was not mentioned, and its ruling is restricted to that specific thing. The question of the obligation of invoking God's name in ritual slaughter, whether it is a condition or not, and even the ruling on forgetting it, would not be related to it. But if we regard this purpose as being in the position of a cause of revelation (sabab li-l-nuzul), and we take the relative pronoun as applying to everything over which the name of God has not been mentioned, then the verse is among the general (al-'amm) statements revealed on a specific occasion, and it is not restricted to the case of the occasion. It is to this consideration that the majority of jurists, who differ regarding the ruling on invoking God's name over the slaughtered animal, have inclined.

[p. 40]

This is a matter on which the jurists disagree, with several opinions. One of them: if a Muslim forgets to invoke God's name at the slaughter, his slaughtered animal is eaten; but if he deliberately omits the invocation, out of contempt or avoidance of it, it is not eaten. This is like what some of the Black Muslims in Tunisia and some lands of Islam do, who claim that jinn possess them, so they ward off their harm by sacrificing offerings to the jinn and do not mention God's name over them, because they claim that the jinn flee from the name of God Most High out of fear of it. This is widespread among them in Tunisia and Egypt. So this slaughtered animal is not eaten.

The basis of these jurists is the apparent meaning of the verse, with its specification or restriction to other than forgetting, in application of the principle that the ruling is lifted from people in cases of forgetting. As for one who deliberately omits the invocation, not out of contempt or avoidance, but who is lax about it, Malik, according to the well-known opinion, Abu Hanifa, and a group, and it is a narration from Ahmad, said: it is not eaten. There is no doubt that ignorance is like forgetting, and perhaps they relied on taking the more cautious course in view of the verse's possible meanings, limiting themselves to the apparent sense of the wording without the aid of the context.

The second: al-Shafi'i and a group, and Malik in a narration from him, said: it is eaten. In my view, the evidence for this opinion is that the invocation is a completion of the act of worship (qurbah), and slaughter is partly an act of worship and partly not an act of worship. The ruling on invoking God's name does not reach the level of invalidating the permissibility.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that they interpreted "what has not had the name of God mentioned over it" as referring specifically to carrion, and to what has had the name of other than God mentioned over it. In Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi, from Imam al-Haramayn: the mention of God's name is only legislated in acts of worship (qurab), and slaughter is not an act of worship. It is evident that one who does it deliberately is sinful, and that one who does it out of contempt is more sinful. As for deliberately omitting the invocation in order to please other than God, its ruling is the ruling of one who invoked other than God Most High. It was also said: if one deliberately omits the invocation, eating it is disliked (makruh). This was said by Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Qassar and Abu Bakr al-Abhari of the Malikis. This is not considered a disagreement, but rather a clarification of Malik's opinion in one of his two narrations. Ashhab and al-Tabari said: the slaughter of one who deliberately omits the invocation is eaten, if he did not omit it out of contempt.

[p. 41]

Abdullah ibn Umar, Ibn Sirin, Nafi', Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Dawud said: it is not eaten if the name was not invoked over it, whether deliberately or through forgetting, taking the apparent meaning of the verse without reflecting on its purpose and context. The most preponderant of the opinions is the opinion of al-Shafi'i and the other narration from Malik: if one deliberately omits the invocation, it is eaten. The verse only intended by it the prohibition of what has had other than God invoked over it, by the many indications we mentioned above. The one who deliberately omits the invocation may be sinful, but his sin does not invalidate his slaughter, like prayer in a usurped land according to other than Ahmad.

The clause "And indeed it is a transgression" is conjoined to the clause "And do not eat," as a predicative statement (khabar) conjoined to an imperative (insha') according to the opinion of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) who permit it, and this is the correct view, especially when the conjunction is with the particle wa. Some who prohibit conjoining a predicative statement to an imperative without wa have permitted it with wa, and this is the opinion of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, who cited this verse as evidence, as in Mughni al-Labib. Al-Razi and a group made it a circumstantial clause (hal), "over which the name of God has not been mentioned," on the basis of prohibiting the conjunction of a predicative statement to an imperative.

The pronoun in His words "And indeed it is a transgression" refers to "what has not had the name of God mentioned over it." Describing it by the verbal noun fisq (transgression) is an intensification in describing the act, which is mentioning the name of other than God, to the point that the transgression has exceeded being an attribute of the act and has become an attribute of the object acted upon. So it is among the verbal noun used with the meaning of the passive participle, like khalq meaning makhluq (created). This is parallel to making it fisq in His later words: "or a transgression over which other than God has been invoked" [al-An'am: 145].

The emphasis with inna is for the increase of affirmation. Al-Kashshaf made the pronoun refer to the eating derived from "do not eat," meaning: indeed, eating it is a transgression.

His words: "And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you" are conjoined to "And indeed it is a transgression," meaning: beware of the disputing of the allies of the devils in this matter. The intended "allies of the devils" are the polytheists, who are referred to in His earlier words: "some of them inspire to others" [al-An'am: 112], which has already been explained.

Disputation (mujadalah) is verbal contention for the purpose of persuading by opinion, and its explanation was given earlier at His words: "And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves" [al-Nisa': 107] in Surat al-Nisa'. What is intended here is disputing in order to nullify the rulings of Islam and to make disbelief and its rites attractive, like their saying: "How can we eat what we kill with our own hands, and not eat what God has killed?"

His words: "And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists" omit the object of "obey them," being indicated by the context. That is: if you obey them in what they dispute with you about, which is the reviling of Islam and doubt about the soundness of its rulings. The clause "indeed you are polytheists" is the answer (jawab) of the condition. The emphasis of the predicate with inna is to affirm that they will indeed join the polytheists if they obey the devils, even though they do not call upon partners with God, because discrediting the rulings of Islam is equivalent to polytheism, and therefore emphasis was needed. Or it means: indeed you are going to arrive at polytheism, for the devils will lead you step by step through disputation until they bring you to polytheism, so the active participle is intended to refer to the future.

The meaning is not: if you obey them in associating partners with God, and you do associate partners with God, then indeed you are polytheists. For if that were the case, there would be no cause for emphasizing the predicate, nor any benefit in informing that they are polytheists.

The clause "indeed you are polytheists" is the answer of the condition, and it is not joined with the particle fa, because when the condition is in the form of a past verb, the answer may be bare of fa. This was stated by Abu al-Baqa' al-'Ukbari, and al-Baydawi followed him, because the influence of a past condition on its consequence is weak. Just as the consequence may be in the present tense when its condition is in the past, so also it may be a nominal clause not joined with fa. Moreover, many of the verifying grammarians permit the omission of the answer's fa outside cases of necessity. Al-Mubarrad and Ibn Malik permitted it, [p. 43] in his commentary on Mushkil al-Jami' al-Sahih, and counted among it the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, if you leave your heirs wealthy, it is better than leaving them in need (ʿalah)," according to the narration with the kasra of the hamza in "in," not the narration with the fatha of the hamza.

[Page 44]

The waw in His saying, ﴿Is he who was dead, then We gave him life...﴾, is a conjunctive particle joining the interrogative clause to the clause ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. This is because His saying ﴿And if you obey them﴾ [al-An'am: 121] implies that the dispute mentioned before it was a dispute over religion, in which the conditions of the polytheists were presented favorably and the rulings of Islam, including the prohibition of carrion and of what has been slaughtered in the name of other than God, were presented unfavorably. When God warned the Muslims against the stratagems of the allies of the devils and their disputation, by saying ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121], He followed this with a denunciation of the state of the polytheists and a description of the good state of the Muslims when they abandoned polytheism. He therefore brought two allegories for the two states and denied the equivalence of one to the other, as a warning about the bad condition of the people of polytheism and the good condition of the people of Islam.

The hamza is an interrogative particle used in the sense of denying the equivalence of the two states. The first state is that of those who embraced Islam after having been polytheists. It is the one likened to the condition of a man who was dead, placed in darkness, and then became living in a clear light, and walked on the path leading to the goal among the people. The second state is that of the polytheist, which is likened to the condition of one who is in darkness and does not come out of it, because he is in darkness. In the speech there is concision by ellipsis (ijaz hadhf) in three places, relying on what is mentioned in place of what is omitted. Thus His saying ﴿Is he who was dead﴾ means: "Is the equal of him who was dead," or: "Is the description of him who was dead."

[Page 44 continues]

His saying ﴿And We made for him a light by which he walks among the people﴾ indicates that the thing likened to is the condition of one who was dead in darkness.

His saying ﴿like one whose likeness is in the darknesses﴾ is to be understood as: "like one whose likeness is the likeness of a dead person." The antecedent of (man, "one who") is therefore "dead," as indicated by its being set against "dead" in the likened state. It is thus known that the part of the likened image that is the dead person, because the likened and the likened-to are equal in the original state, namely the state of both groups being polytheists. The word "likeness" (mathal) here means "state" (halah). The negation of resemblance here means the negation of equality, and the negation of equality is a metonymy (kinaya) for preferring one of the two states over the other with a preference that is not ambiguous. That is the meaning of the negation of resemblance, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], and His saying: ﴿Is he who was a believer like him who was a wicked person? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah: 18].

The kaf in His saying ﴿like one whose likeness is in the darknesses﴾ is the kaf of comparison, and it is a comparison negated by an interrogation of denial.

The speech proceeds along the method of presenting the condition of one who embraced Islam and was freed from polytheism by the condition of one who was dead and then made alive, and presenting the condition of one who remains in polytheism by the condition of a dead person remaining in his grave.

Thus the clause ﴿Is he who was dead﴾ through to its end includes the allegory of the first state, and the clause ﴿like one whose likeness is in the darknesses﴾ and what follows it includes the allegory of the second state. These are two likened states and two states that are likened-to. By mentioning the kaf of comparison and the interrogative hamza of denial, it results that the meaning of the speech is the negation of resemblance between one who embraced Islam and one who remained in polytheism. Also, from the combination of the two clauses, there are two compound comparisons in the structure of the speech.

However, the presence of the kaf of comparison in His saying "like one whose likeness," together with the absence of an explicit mention of the two things compared in the two structures, has raised a doubt about whether these two comparisons are of the type of the allegorical comparison (al-tashbih al-tamthili) or of the type of the allegorical metaphor (al-isti'ara al-tamthiliyya). Al-Qutb al-Razi, in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, adopted the first type, while al-Taftazani adopted the second. The more evident view is that of al-Taftazani, that they are two allegorical metaphors. As for the kaf of comparison, it is directed to the resemblance that is negated in the two clauses taken together, not to the resemblance of the two states to the two states. The object of the kaf of comparison is therefore different from the object of the allegory of the two states. Between these two considerations there is a subtle difference.

What is meant by "the darknesses" is the darkness of the grave, because of its suitability to the dead person, and by the evident sense of (fi, "in") as a true sense of place and the evident true sense of the verb "to come out."

The comparison has come wondrously, for it has made the condition of the Muslim, after he has come to Islam, like the condition of one who had no good and no benefit, like a dead person. Polytheism prevents the distinction between truth and falsehood, and turns its possessor away from striving toward what contains his good and salvation. He is in a darkness in which, even if he were to regain consciousness, he would not know where to turn. When God guides him to Islam, his condition changes: he begins to distinguish between truth and falsehood, and knows the good from the corrupt. He becomes like the living, and begins to strive toward what contains righteousness and to shun the path of corruption. Thus he is in a light by which he walks among the people.

By this allegory it has been made clear that people of sound intellects are preferred over their opposites.

The ba' in His saying ﴿by which he walks﴾ is the ba' of causation (al-ba' al-sababiyya). The people explicitly mentioned in the likened image are the living who are never absent from human society.

The people implicit in the likened image are the Muslim's companions from among the Muslims. The allegorical structure has come complete, suitable both for considering the likeness of state to state and for considering the likeness of each part of the likened state to a part of the likened-to state, as you have come to know. That is the highest form of allegory.

The clause ﴿not coming out of it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun attached to the genitive by the annexation of (mathal, "likeness"). That is: darknesses in which there is no hope for the one who falls into them of any opening with some light, as long as he remains in the state of associating partners with God.

[Page 46]

The clause ﴿Thus it has been made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the allegory mentioned before it raises in the mind of the hearer a question: how did they accept for themselves remaining in these misguidances, and how did they not perceive the gap between their condition and the condition of those who embraced Islam? If they, before the coming of Islam, were heedless of the degradation of their condition in their beliefs and actions, how is it that when Islam called them to the truth and set up for them the proofs and evidences, they remained in their error and did not desist from it, though they were people of intellect and acuteness? It was therefore fitting that the speech explain to him the cause of their persistence in error. That cause is that what they did was made attractive to them by the devils, this wondrous adornment, such that if anyone wished to bring it near, he would not find any adorned error clearer or more wondrous than it. Thus their error is compared only to itself, in the manner of their saying: "Foolishness is like its name."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿Thus it has been made attractive to the disbelievers﴾ refers to the adornment derived from the verb "made attractive" (zayyana). That is: like that adornment, wondrous in its cunning and subtlety, He made attractive to these disbelievers their deeds, in the manner previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The agent of the adornment is omitted, so the verb is put in the passive, because the intended thing is the occurrence of the adornment, not knowing who caused it. The one who adorns is their devils and their allies, as in His saying: ﴿And thus their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137]. Also, because the devils among mankind are the ones who directly carry out the adornment, while the devils among the jinn are the ones asked to adorn. The disbelievers meant here are the polytheists about whom the discussion has been in the preceding verses, up to His saying: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 123:

﴿And thus We placed in every town the greatest of its criminals, that they might plot therein. But they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾

Page 47
It is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Thus were their deeds made attractive to the disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. It therefore has the status of the explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani, a resumptive clause that explains a cause), to explain another of the causes of the polytheists' persistence in their misguidance. That is the plotting of the greatest men of their town against the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and their turning of stratagems to block the common folk from following the call of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The one indicated by the words "thus" (wa-kadhalika) is the allies of the devils, by way of interpreting "thus" as referring to what was mentioned.
The meaning: Like this arrangement which We made for the polytheists of Makkah, We placed in every town that has passed away greatest men who obstruct people from good. Thus He compares the greatest criminals among the people of Makkah in polytheism with the greatest criminals among the people of the towns in the other nations. That is to say: the matter of these people is neither novel nor peculiar to the enemies of this religion, for it is the way of the criminals with the earlier Messengers.

So "ja'l" (placing) here means creation and the establishing of the cosmic laws (al-sunan al-kawniyya), which are the laws of creating the causes of good and the causes of evil in every society, and especially towns.

In this there is an indication that the people of the desert (al-badawa) are closer to accepting good than the people of towns, because by the simplicity of their natures they possess the sound primordial nature (al-fitra al-salima). So when they hear good, they accept it. Unlike the people of towns, who, because of their clinging to their customs and what they are accustomed to, recoil from everything that would change it for them. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who persisted in hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101], so He made hypocrisy among the Bedouins simple hypocrisy, and hypocrisy among the people of Madinah rebellious (marid) hypocrisy.

"Ja'l" may also mean "tasyir" (making into), namely making a creature into a specific attribute, or making a created thing move to an attribute after it was in another attribute. Then the struggle between good and evil is in proportion to the dominance of the people of one over the people of the other. When the people of good prevail, the callers to evil and corruption are constrained; and when the matter is reversed, the callers to evil expand and multiply.

Page 48
For this reason the ancient sages never ceased to exert effort in bringing about the virtuous city which Plato described in his book, and which almost realized its attributes in the city of Athens in the time of its republic. But it was not truly realized except in the city of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his time and the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs in it.
The saying of God Most High has drawn attention to this meaning: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit abomination therein, and the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 16], according to the reading with the shadda on the mim in "amarna" (We commanded, emphatic form).

The more evident reading of the structure of the verse is that "ja'ala" means "created and brought into existence," and it is transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. Its object is ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾.

His saying ﴿in every town﴾ is an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) attached to "ja'ala." It was placed before the object, although it is less connected to the verb than the object, because the fact that this is the condition of all towns is the most important point in this report, so that the people of Makkah may know that their state has followed the pattern of the people of the towns to whom messengers were sent.

In the words ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ there is brevity, for it dispenses with saying: "We made criminals and made for them greatest men," and that the allies of the devils are the greatest criminals of the people of Makkah. As for His saying "that they might plot" (li-yamkuru), it is attached to "ja'ala," meaning that the plotting should take place. In this reading there is an indication that their plotting is not of great importance.

It is possible that "ja'ala" means "sayyara" (made/rendered), in which case it is transitive to two objects: ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾, where "mujrimiha" is the first object and "akabira" is the second object; meaning: We made its criminals greatest men. The second object is placed first for emphasis on it because its matter is strange, since the criminals becoming great leaders and masters is a wondrous matter, as they are not fit for lordship, as Tufayl al-Ghanawi said:

People cannot be set right in disorder, with no chiefs among them, and no chiefs when their ignorant ones rule.

Affairs are guided by people of judgment so long as they are sound, but if they turn away, they are led by the wicked.

The placement of ﴿in every town﴾ is for the purpose mentioned in its placement under the first possibility. In this possibility there is a notice of the dominance of corruption over them and the aggravation of its harm, and an indication of the necessity of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) leaving that town, and a notice of the approaching end of the polytheists' lordship, since the criminals have taken it over; for their remaining in polytheism made them criminals among those who had embraced Islam among them. Perhaps both possibilities are intended by the speech, so that the hearers may consider both of them. This is one of the aspects of the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, as was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know it as they know their own sons. Those who have lost themselves do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 114].

The lam in "li-yamkuru" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), for among the purposes of God Most High in establishing the order of the existence of the righteous and the corrupt is that the righteous should work for righteousness and the corrupt should work for corruption. Plotting is among the corruptions. The lam of causation does not imply exclusivity, for God Most High has many wisdoms in creating their likes, among which is this wisdom. Thereby the nobility of truth and righteousness becomes manifest and its light shines, and the collapse of falsehood before it becomes evident after a long struggle. It is also possible that this is the lam called the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqiba), which in reality is a metaphorical use of the lam in the sense of the fa' of sequence, as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

Makkah entered into the generality of ﴿every town﴾, and it is the primary intended object, because it is the present town in which plotting took place; so the intended meaning is particular. The meaning: "Thus We placed in Makkah the greatest of its criminals, that they might plot therein, just as We placed the like of them in every town." He generalized the report only for the purpose of reminding the polytheists in Makkah of what befell the towns before them, such as the town of al-Hijr, Saba' and al-Rass, as in His saying: ﴿Those towns—We relate to you some of their news. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not to believe﴾ [al-A'raf: 101],

Page 50
and for the purpose of consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), that he is not novel among the Messengers in the denial of his people, their plotting against him, and his promise of victory.

His saying ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾: "akabir" is the plural of "akbar," and "akbar" is a term for the great one and chief of a people; one says: "They inherited glory, the greatest, the greatest." So the form af'al in it does not indicate increase in size, neither in age nor in body. It thus became like a non-derived noun, and for this reason it is pluralized when it is predicated of a plural or when a plural is described by it; had it been regarded as a derived noun, its rule would have been to remain singular and masculine. It is pluralized as "akabir," as one says "muluk akabir" (great kings). So the pattern of "akabir" in the plural is fa'a'il, like "afadil," the plural of "afdal," and "ayamin" and "a'sha'im," the plurals of "ayman" and "ash'am," for birds passing on the right and left in the terminology of augury and divination.

Know that the grammarians' convention regarding the patterns of plurals, in the chapter of broken plurals and in the chapter of diptotes, is to look at the form of the word without regard to its original and augmented letters, unlike the convention of the scholars of morphology (sarf) in the chapter of the unaugmented and augmented verbs. So the hamza of "akbar" is treated in the plural as if it were original, although it is augmented.

In His saying ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ there is brevity, for the meaning is: "We placed in every town criminals, and We placed for them greatest men." Since the existence of the greatest men requires the existence of those below them, he dispensed with mentioning them by mentioning the greatest criminals.

Plotting (al-makr) is inflicting harm on another secretly and by trickery. It is among deception and blameworthy conduct, and it is not excused except in war, and it is excused in politics if harm cannot be averted except by it. As for its attribution to God in His saying: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], it is by way of mushakala (attribution by parallelism), because before it is "wa-makaru" (they plotted), meaning they plotted against the people of God and His messengers. The plotting meant here is the scheming of the leaders of the polytheists against the people, to turn them away from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from following Islam. Mujahid said: "They sat at every pass, deterring people from following the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Page 51
The object of "li-yamkuru" has been omitted for its clarity; that is: "that they might plot against the Prophet (peace be upon him), thinking that turning people away from following him would harm him and grieve him, and that he would not know of it." Perhaps this action of theirs occurred when the Muslims increased in the final period of their stay in Makkah, shortly before the migration to Madinah. Therefore God Most High said: ﴿But they plot only against themselves﴾. The waw is for the circumstantial state (hal); that is: in their plotting they only harm themselves. Plotting is here used for its outcome, which is harm, by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), for the ultimate aim and outcome of plotting is the harming of the one plotted against. Since the harm was realized for the plotters and not for the one plotted against, plotting was applied to harm.

The form of restriction (qasr) was used, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is not reached by any hurt or harm from their turning people away from following him, while harm reaches the plotters in this world through the punishment of killing and capture, and in the Hereafter through the punishment of the Fire, if they do not believe. Thus harm is restricted to them by way of specific restriction (al-qasr al-idafi), which is qasr qalb (restriction by reversal).

His saying ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ is a second circumstantial clause. They, while in the state of plotting against the Prophet, are characterized by the fact that they plot only against themselves, and by the fact that they do not perceive the reaching of the consequence of their plotting upon them. Perception (al-shu'ur) means knowledge.

[Page 52]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And thus did We place in every town great men of its criminals﴾ [al-An'am: 123], because this is a discussion of some of the circumstances of the great criminals of Makkah, and they are the intended referent of the comparison in His words: ﴿And thus did We place in every town great men of its criminals﴾ [al-An'am: 123]. Makkah is the intended referent of the generality of "every town," as has already been explained. So the object pronoun in His words "جاءَتْهم" (came to them) refers to ﴿great men of its criminals﴾ [al-An'am: 123], taking into account the particular that is intended by the generality, since the saying ﴿We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾ is not attributed to all the great criminals of all the towns.

The meaning is: "When a sign from the signs of the Qur'an comes to them", that is, when a sign is recited to them in which they are called to faith. He expressed the arrival (مجيء) as the conveying of the sign or its recitation, likening the conveying to the arrival of the caller or messenger. What is meant is that they are not convinced by the miracle of the Qur'an, and that they seek tangible miracles like the miracle of Musa and the miracle of ʿIsa. This is in the sense of their saying: ﴿Let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], due to their ignorance of the divine wisdom in the variation of miracles in a manner suited to the condition of the one to whom the messenger is sent. As Allah the Exalted related: ﴿And they say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 50] ﴿Say: "Signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 50] Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed, in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 51]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed in the like of them, but what I was given is revelation which Allah revealed to me," and so on in the hadith.

The word "إيتاء" (giving) was used for the manifestation of the miracle before them in the report of their speech, when it was said: ﴿until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾, because the miracle, since it was for convincing them of the truthfulness of the Messenger (peace be upon him), resembled a thing given to them.

The meaning of ﴿what the messengers of Allah were given﴾ is "like what Allah gave the messengers of the miracles which they showed to their peoples." So what they intend by "the messengers of Allah" is the messengers whose reports had reached them.

It has been said: the one who said this was a group of the leaders of the polytheists in Makkah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, each one of them desires that he be given scrolls unrolled﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52]. It is narrated that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If prophethood were to be given, I would be more deserving of it than you, for I am older than you in years and greater in wealth and children." And Abu Jahl

[Page 53]

said: "The Banu ʿAbd Manaf competed with us in nobility, until when we became like two racehorses, they said: 'From us is a prophet to whom revelation comes.' By Allah, we will never accept him nor follow him, unless revelation comes to us as it comes to him."

So this verse was an allusion to what proceeded from these two. On this view, the meaning is: "until revelation comes to us as it comes to the messengers." Or the meaning of "messengers of Allah" is all the messengers. They turned away from saying "like what Muhammad (ﷺ) was given," because they do not believe that revelation comes to him.

The meaning of "نُؤْتى" (we are given) on this aspect is "we are given like what the messengers were given, which is revelation." Or they intended by "messengers of Allah" Muhammad (ﷺ), and expressed him with the plural form as an indirect reference, as one says: "Some people say such-and-such," and what is meant is a specific individual. From it is His saying: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 105] and similar. And their application to him of "messengers of Allah" would be a mockery of him (ﷺ), as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿And they say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], and His saying: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is mad!﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 27].

* * *

﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (iʿtirad) responding to their saying: ﴿until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾, on both possibilities in the interpretation of their saying.

On the first aspect of the meaning of their saying ﴿until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾, His saying ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ is a refutation: that Allah is most knowing of the miracles suitable for the people to whom the messenger is sent. So "حَيْثُ" (where) is a metaphor for the figurative place of the miracle, which is the people in whom one of them manifests it; they are treated as if they were a place for the manifestation of the miracle. "Messages" (الرسالات) is used absolutely for miracles, because they resemble a message that Allah sends to people. Close to this is the statement of the scholars of kalam (theology): the way in which a miracle indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) is that the miracle stands in place of Allah's statement, "This Messenger has spoken truthfully about what he reports from Me," by the sign that I break the custom as proof of his being believed.

On the second aspect of the meaning of their saying ﴿until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾, His saying ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ is a refutation of them: that a message is not given at the request of the one who asks for it, with an indirect implication that people like them are not fit for it. So the referent of "حَيْثُ" (where) is the person whom Allah chose for His message.

Here "حَيْثُ" is a noun denoting place, used metaphorically for the one sent with the message, based on likening the message to a deposit placed in a place of trust, in the manner of the implicit metaphor (الاستعارة المكنية). The attribution of a place is imaginative (تخييل), and it is another explicit metaphor likening the messengers to the place where the message is established.

"حَيْثُ" here is not an adverb of place (ظرف), but a noun of place stripped of adverbial function, because "حَيْثُ" is a flexible adverb (ظرف متصرف) according to the view of the careful grammarians. So it is here in the position of an accusative by removal of the preposition, which is "بِ" (in), because "أَعْلَمُ" (most knowing), being an elative noun (اسم تفضيل), does not govern an object. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾ [al-Anʿam: 117], as has preceded above.

The clause ﴿He places His message﴾ is a qualifier of "حَيْثُ" when "حَيْثُ" is stripped of the adverbial sense, and the connecting pronoun of the qualifying clause to the qualified noun must be omitted; the estimate is: "where He places in it His messages."

The verse conveys that prophethood is not something attained by wishes or by desires, but Allah knows who is fit for it and who is not. Had He known who is fit for it and willed to send him, He would send him. Souls vary in receiving the divine overflow, in readiness for it, and in capacity to bear its burden. So none is fit for prophethood except a soul created near to the angelic souls, far from the vices of animality, free from the diseases of the heart.

[Page 55]

So the verse indicates that the Messenger is created with a nature suited to the purpose of Allah in sending him, and Allah when creating him knows that He will send him. Allah may create souls fit for prophethood while there is no wisdom in sending their owners. Thus readiness prepares for Allah's choosing, but does not necessitate it. This is the meaning of the saying of some of the theologians: innate readiness does not necessitate prophethood, contrary to the philosophers. It may be that the intention of the philosophers is not far from the intention of the theologians. Ibn Sina in al-Isharat (The Pointers) alluded to something of this in the ninth namat (section).

In His saying ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ there is a statement of the great rank of the Prophet (ﷺ), and an admonition of the lowness of the souls of the leaders of the polytheists in attaining the station of prophethood and the absence of their readiness, as it is said in the proverb: "Your nest is not here, so go away" (لَيْسَ بِعُشِّكِ فادْرُجِي).

The majority read "رِسالاتِهِ" (His messages) in the plural. Ibn Kathir and Hafs from ʿAsim read it in the singular. Since the intended meaning is the genus, the plural and singular are equal.

* * *

﴿Those who committed crime will be struck with humiliation before Allah and severe punishment for what they used to plot﴾

This is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf) arising from His saying: ﴿that they may plot therein﴾ [al-Anʿam: 123], and it is a threat to them for their plotting and their saying: ﴿We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of Allah were given﴾.

So what is meant by "الذين أجرموا" (those who committed crime) is the great criminals among the polytheists in Makkah, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿for what they used to plot﴾, since the attribute of plotting was affirmed for the great criminals in the preceding verse. Their mention with ﴿those who committed crime﴾ is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, since the expected form would be "سيصيبهم صغار" (humiliation will strike them). The expected form was departed from in order to use the relative clause, so that it indicates the reason for basing the predicate on the relative clause; that is: humiliation and punishment only struck them because of their crime.

"الصغار" (humiliation), with the ṣād vowelled with fatḥa, means abasement. It is derived from "الصِّغَر" (smallness), which is lowliness and deficiency of a thing below the measure of its like.

Allah made their punishment abasement and torment, to suit their arrogance, their tyranny, and their disobedience to Allah the Exalted. Humiliation and punishment occur to them in this world through defeat, the loss of leadership, the punishment of killing and capture, and fear. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes, while we await for you that Allah will afflict you with punishment from Him or by our hands?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]. Both matters occurred on the day of Badr and the day of Uhud: the leaders of the polytheists were destroyed. And in the Hereafter through their being disgraced among the people of the gathering and their punishment in Hell.

The meaning of "عِنْدَ اللَّهِ" (before Allah) is that it is a humiliation decreed before Allah, so it is a fixed and certain humiliation, because the thing which Allah the Exalted makes has its effect appear among all people, since it is a creation that does not leave its owner. As it occurs in the hadith: "When Allah loves a servant, He commands Jibril, so he loves him; then He commands the angels, so they love him; then acceptance is placed for him among the people of the earth." So there is no need to estimate "مِن" (from) in His saying ﴿before Allah﴾, nor to take "عندية" (being before) as meaning attainment in the Hereafter, as many exegetes have followed.

The "ب" (for) in ﴿for what they used to plot﴾ is causal, and "ما" (what) is verbal-masdar: meaning "because of their plotting," that is, their act of plotting; or it is a relative pronoun: meaning "because of that which they used to plot," with plotting taken as a noun, so a governed returning pronoun is estimated as an omitted direct object.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 125:

[p. 57]
﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight, as though he were climbing up into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe.﴾

The fa' (فاء, "so") here connects the sentence that follows it to the content of what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life…﴾ [al-An'am: 122], and what follows from it of branches and interjections. This consequence is a refutation of their pretexts, based on their reason: ﴿Until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and that Allah has prevented them from what they made their faith conditional upon obtaining. Thereupon there follows an explanation of the cause that truly determines the faith of the believer and the disbelief of the disbeliever, which is Allah's guidance of the believer and His leading astray of the disbeliever. That is the real influence, not the apparent causes. From this it is known that the greatest of the criminals, even if they were given what they asked for, would not believe, unless Allah wills their guidance to Islam, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been fulfilled will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 96], and as He said: (﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We had gathered before them all things, they would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]).

Guidance (al-huda) relates only to beneficial matters, because its reality is reaching the path that leads to the intended place, and its metaphorical sense is the soundness of reason. For this reason it was not necessary to mention its object here, since it is evident that it is guidance to Islam, together with the indication in His saying: ﴿He expands his breast to Islam﴾. As for His saying: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23], it is sarcasm. Misguidance (al-dalal) occurs only in harmful states, because its reality is going astray from the desired path; therefore it implies harm even when its object is not mentioned. Here it is the state of being characterized by disbelief, because in it is the squandering of the good of Islam; thus it is like straying from what is sought, even though the one who strays is not seeking Islam, but he is such that if he were to face his affair in the future as he has turned his back on it, he would seek it.

[p. 58]
The reality of sharh (شرح, "expansion") is cutting flesh; a sharihah (شريحة) is a piece of flesh cut thin so that it may be cooked. It is used in their speech figuratively for explanation and disclosure, and it is also used figuratively for the clarity of a matter, the certainty of the soul regarding it, and the tranquility of mind toward it, such that one does not waver about it nor feel distress over it. This is the more apparent of the two interpretations in His saying: ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

The breast (al-sadr) is meant here as the inner self, figuratively for understanding and reason, by the relation of location. Thus the meaning of ﴿He expands his breast﴾ is: He makes for his self and his reason a readiness and acceptance for attaining Islam, and prepares him for it until he settles into it and is content with it. For this reason it is likened to expansion (sharh), and what results for the soul is called inshirah (انشراح, "being expanded").
