It is said: "My soul was not expanded toward such-and-such," and "it was expanded toward such-and-such." When the light of divine success descends upon the heart, the heart becomes as if widened, because lights widen the perception of things. Al-Tabari and others narrated, from Ibn Mas'ud, that: "People said: O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah expand the breast for Islam? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: He causes light to enter it and it expands. They said: Is there a sign by which it is known? He said: Turning penitently to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

As for the meaning of ﴿And whomever He wills to leave astray﴾: it means whomever He wills to continue in his misguidance through disbelief, or whomever He wills to leave astray from being guided to Islam. The intended sense is a future misguidance, either in the sense of the continuation of past misguidance, or in the sense of being led astray from accepting Islam. It is not intended that He leads him astray through his former disbelief, because that has already passed and been settled.

The word ḍayyiq (ضيّق), with shaddah on the yā' in the form fayʿil, is an intensive description of a thing as narrow. It is said ḍāqa ḍīqan (with kasrah on the ḍād) and ḍaykan (with fatḥah). The more well-known is the kasrah of the ḍād in the verbal noun, and the more analogical is the fatḥah. It is also said with the yā' lightened in the form faʿl, as with mayyit and mayt. Although their patterns differ, and the pattern fayʿil originally conveys more intensity in the occurrence of the act than the pattern faʿl does, usage has equalized them according to the more correct view. The more apparent view is that the original of ḍayq, with lightening, is a description by way of the verbal noun, so both are equal in conveying intensity through description. Both readings are attested for this verse: the majority read it with the shaddah on the yā', and Ibn Kathir with the lightening of it.

The word ḍayyiq has been borrowed for the opposite of what sharh was borrowed for, so it is meant to describe one who is not prepared to accept faith and whose soul does not settle toward it, such that his mind is agitated when Islam is presented to him. This is like His saying: ﴿their breasts are restricted﴾ [al-Nisa': 90], which has been discussed in Surat al-Nisa'.

The word ḥaraj (حرج) with kasrah on the rā' is an adjectival form (ṣifah mushabbahah) from their saying ḥaraja al-shay'u ḥarajan, on the pattern of fariḥa, meaning it became extremely constricted. It is like their saying danifa, qamina, fariqa, and ḥadhira. Nafi' and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, and Abu Ja'far, read it thus. As for the rest, they read it with fatḥah on the rā' in the form of the verbal noun, so it is a description by the verbal noun for intensity, like their saying rajulun danafun (with fatḥah on the nūn) and farad (with fatḥah on the rā').

Following ḍayyiq with ḥaraj is to reinforce the meaning of constriction, because ḥaraj contains an element of extreme intensity of constriction that ḍayyiq does not have.

The meaning is: He makes his breast not expanded to accept Islam, by the indication of its being contrasted with His saying: ﴿He expands his breast to Islam﴾.

He adds to the state of the one led astray from Islam a further clarification through a simile, saying: ﴿as though he were climbing up into the sky﴾.

The majority read it: (yaṣṣaʿʿadu), with shaddah on the ṣād and shaddah on the ʿayn, as a form yataffaʿal from al-ṣuʿūd (climbing), meaning: with the effort of climbing. The tā' of the tafaʿʿul was changed to ṣād, because the tā' resembles the emphatic letters, and therefore in the ifti'al pattern it is regularly changed to ṭā' after emphatic letters. Then it is assimilated sometimes into its like or its near-equivalent, and it may also be changed in what resembles the ifti'al when lightening by assimilation is intended, so it is assimilated into one of the emphatic letters, as here. For the lightening of one of the three consecutive moving letters of "yatasaʿʿadu" was intended, so the tā' was made quiescent and then assimilated into the ṣād as assimilation into a близкий sound for lightening.

Ibn Kathir read it: (yaṣʿadu), with a quiescent ṣād and a fatḥah on the ʿayn, lightened. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read: (yaṣṣāʿadu), with shaddah on the ṣād and an alif after it, its original being yatasāʿadu.

The clause ﴿as though he were climbing up﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (ṣadrahu) or from ṣadrihi. The state of the polytheist is depicted when he is called to Islam, or when he is alone with himself and reflects on the call to Islam, by the state of one ascending, for the one ascending has difficulty breathing during the ascent. This is the depiction of an intelligible state by an imagined state, since ascending into the sky does not actually occur.

As for "sky" (al-sama'), it may be taken in its familiar meaning, and it may be that "sky" was applied to the atmosphere that rises above the earth. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "sama'" does not mean the canopy over the earth; rather, as Sibawayh said: "al-qaydud al-ṭawīl fī ghayr samā'" — that is, in a state of ascent without height in the sense of climbing." Abu 'Ali intended to support, by Sibawayh's statement, that the name sama' is applied to the open space extending upward; but Sibawayh's expression is not an interpretation of the verse.

The particle fī (في) may mean "to" (ilā), and it may mean the sense of location: either in the sense that he has reached the sky and begun to climb through its levels, so the state is imaginative, or by interpreting "sky" as the atmosphere.

The clause ﴿Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) to the preceding one, and therefore it is separated from it.

[p. 61]
Rijs (الرجس) is filth and corruption, and it is applied to moral and spiritual filth. What is meant here is the filth of the soul, which is the filth of polytheism, as He said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], meaning: a disease in their hearts additional to the disease of their hearts previously; that is, it entrenched the disease in their hearts. It has been discussed in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are filth from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]. So rijs encompasses all spiritual corruptions, including the constriction and tightness of the breast, and by this generality the clause is a concluding clause; it is not specific to the constriction of the breast, so as to be an instance of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun.

His saying "thus" (kadhalika) stands in for an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) intended as comparison, and the meaning is: Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe in a manner like this tightness and severe constriction which He placed in the breasts of those who do not believe.

The "upon" (ʿalā) in His saying ﴿upon those who do not believe﴾ conveys the firm establishment of defilement upon the disbelievers, so the "upon" is a figurative use of firm establishment, like: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The intended meaning is its firm establishment in their hearts and the manifestation of its effects upon them.

The present tense is used in (yaj'al) to convey continual renewal in the future; that is, this is the custom of Allah toward everyone who turns away from faith and turns aside from it.

﴿Those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 150] is a relative clause (mawsul) that indicates the cause of the predicate; that is, Allah places defilement firmly upon them because they turn away from receiving it with fairness, so Allah makes their hearts increase in hardness. The relative clause encompasses every one who turns away from faith, so it includes the polytheists referred to, and it includes others from everyone who is called to Islam and turns away from it, such as the Jews of Medina, the hypocrites, and others.

By this generality the clause becomes a concluding clause, and the use of the relative pronoun conforms to the apparent requirement; it is not an instance of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun.

This is a commentary passage on Q. 6:126, and I'll translate it as it stands.

﴿This is the path of your Lord, straight.  We have detailed the signs for a people who remember.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿Whoever Allah wills to leave astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾ [al-Anʿam: 125] up to its end, because this is an illustration (tamthīl) of the state of the guidance of the Qur'an as a straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm), which does not exhaust its follower. Thus this is the opposite of the state of the illustration in His saying: ﴿as if he were climbing up into the sky﴾ [al-Anʿam: 125]. The illustration of Islam as the straight path includes the illustration of the Muslim as one who travels a straight path, and so it provides clarification of His saying: ﴿He expands his breast for Islam﴾ [al-Anʿam: 125]. This sentence was coordinated, although it has the status of an explanation of the preceding sentence, so that it would be intended for informing through coordination; and it is an address turned toward the Prophet ﷺ in direct speech.

The demonstrative "this" (hādhā) refers to something present in the mind, namely the religion of Islam, and the connection is His saying: ﴿He expands his breast for Islam﴾ [al-Anʿam: 125]. The ṣirāṭ literally means the road, and here it is used figuratively for the action that leads to the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. Its being attributed to the Lord (rabb) serves to magnify the status of what is attributed, so it is known that it is the best of paths; and the attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of the Messenger is an honouring of the one attributed to, and a consolation for the Messenger ﷺ regarding what is in this sunnah of some people remaining not following his religion.

The mustaqīm literally means that which is free from crookedness, and it is used figuratively for correctness, because of its freedom from error; i.e., the sunnah of Allah which accords with wisdom, and which is not contravened, nor is it hindered by anything.

It is permissible that the demonstrative refers to something present to the senses, namely the Qur'an, because it is heard, like His saying: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anʿam: 155]. Then the straight path is figurative for what reaches the intended beneficial goal, like His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-Anʿam: 153]. And "straight" (mustaqīman) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from "path" (ṣirāṭ), emphasizing the meaning of its attribution to Allah.

﴿We have detailed the signs﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) and a summation (fadhlaka) of what preceded. What is meant by "the signs" (al-āyāt) are the signs of the Qur'an. From the elegance of the word "signs" here is that it contains a double meaning (tawriya) with the signs of the road by which the traveler is guided.

The lām in ﴿for a people who remember﴾ denotes cause; i.e., We detailed the signs for their sake, because they are the ones who benefit from its details.

By "the people" are meant the Muslims, because they are the ones whom the signs benefited and who were reminded by them.

[Page 63 continues here]

The pronoun in ﴿for them is the abode of peace﴾ refers to "a people who remember."

The sentence may be a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question), because praising them for having the verses made clear to them, and for remembering by them, prompts the question of what results from the clarification of the verses for them and their remembrance of them. So it is said: ﴿for them is the abode of peace﴾.

Or it may be a qualifier of ﴿for a people who remember﴾ [al-An'am: 126].

Fronting the prepositional phrase (*taqdim al-majrur*) serves to restrict (*ikhtisas*) the reward to the people who remember, and not to others.

*Al-dar* is the place of settling and dwelling. It is synonymous with, or close to, *al-mahall* (place of alighting). It is feminine in implied gender, so its diminutive is *duwayra*. *Al-dar* is derived from the verb *dara*, "to turn," because of the frequent circulation of its inhabitants. It is also said *al-darah*, but what is well known of *al-darah* is that it is a wide land between mountains.

*Al-salam* means security. Here it means complete security, which none of the existing things that one fears, whether substances or accidents, can disturb for its possessor.

Thus it is permissible that by *dar al-salam* is meant Paradise. It was called "abode of peace" because true safety is in it, since it is a place of security from every thing hateful to the soul. Therefore it is purely for pleasant bliss. It is also said that *al-Salam* is one of the names of God, Exalted; i.e., the abode of God, in glorification of it, as the Ka'bah is called "the House of God."

It is also permissible that what is meant is the station of security with God, i.e., the state of safety from His anger and punishment, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

*How many a time has Amr brought poverty upon a dwelling after wealth,*
*and how many a time has Amr enriched [one] after destitution.*

The word *'inda* ("with") is used in a figurative sense for relative nearness (*al-qurb al-i'tibari*), intended to show the elevated rank, as is indicated by his saying after it: ﴿and He is their guardian﴾. It is also permissible that it is used figuratively for protection, because a precious thing is placed in a place near its owner so as to keep it. Then the meaning is the affirmation of that for them, and that it is a promise like a protected, stored thing, just as one says: "If you do such-and-such, then you have with me such-and-such," as a confirmation of the promise.

The shift from annexing *'inda* to a pronoun of the speaker to annexing it to a noun (*ism zahir*) is for the purpose of honoring them, by indicating that this is a gift from the One who is their Master. This is fitting to His bounty and kindness toward them and His pleasure with them, as opposed to the earlier contrast in His saying: ﴿Those who committed crimes will be struck with humiliation before God﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

The sentence ﴿and He is their guardian﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿for them is the abode of peace﴾, to generalize God's guardianship over them in all their affairs, because it is part of the completeness of the favor. *Al-waliyy* is used in the sense of helper and in the sense of one who befriends.

His saying ﴿because of what they used to do﴾ may be connected to the sense of the predicate in ﴿for them is the abode of peace﴾, by way of the meaning of the verb; i.e., that was established for them because of what they used to do. Then the *ba'* is causal (*sababiyyah*): because of their deeds that resulted from Islam. Or the *ba'* is for exchange (*'iwad*): that is for them as a recompense for their deeds. In this case the sentence ﴿and He is their guardian﴾ is parenthetical (*mu'taridah*) between the predicate and its complement.

It is also permissible that ﴿because of what they used to do﴾ is connected to "their guardian" (*waliyyuhum*), i.e., He is their helper, and the *ba'* is causal: because of their deeds He befriended them. Or the *ba'* is for accompaniment (*mula'abah*), and ﴿because of what they used to do﴾ is meant to refer to the recompense of their deeds, with the omission of a modifier (*hadhf mudaf*) indicated by the context.

[Page 64 continues here]

The definiteness of the predicate by annexation in his saying "their guardian" (*waliyyuhum*) conveys the information that God is the guardian of the people who remember, so that they know the greatness of this favor and give thanks for it, and so that the polytheists know this and are enraged by it. This is because defining the predicate by annexation differs from its definition by other means of definiteness, since definiteness by annexation is the weakest degree of definiteness, to the point that it may approach indefiniteness, according to what the scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) have stated, that the original function of annexation is based on definiteness of reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*). Thus one does not say *ghulam Zayd* ("Zayd's servant") except for a servant known between the speaker and the addressee by that relation. But annexation may depart from that in usage, so that it comes to function like an indefinite noun specified by a description. So you say: "Zayd's servant came to me with a letter from him," while you mean a servant of his who is not specified for the addressee. Then the definite-by-annexation becomes like the definite with the article of genus, i.e., it conveys a definiteness that distinguishes the genus from among all other genera. Thus definiteness by annexation serves the same purpose for which definiteness by *al-* serves.

For this reason there is in his saying ﴿and He is their guardian﴾ no restriction (*qasr*), nor the conveying of a known judgment about a known thing.

Among what increases you in certainty about this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿That is because God is the protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11]. The conjunction of ﴿and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11] with His saying ﴿because God is the protector of those who believe﴾ [Muhammad: 11] shows that what is meant by the first is the conveying of God's guardianship over those who believe, and not the informing that whoever is known to be the protector of those who believe is God.

[Page 66]

When he mentioned the reward of the people who take heed of the signs, which is the abode of peace, it was fitting that he follow it with mention of the recompense of those who do not take heed, which is also the recompense of the Hereafter. So the clause ﴿And on the Day when He gathers them﴾, etc., is coordinated with the clause ﴿For them is the abode of peace with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. The meaning is: "And for the others, the Fire is their abode, wherein they will abide forever." He has depicted this report in the form of what happens in their reckoning on the Day of Gathering, and then it leads to the final outcome of that reckoning, which is their abiding in the Fire.

The word ﴿Day﴾ (yawm) is in the accusative either as a direct object of a verb omitted in the sense of "Remember" (udhkur), following the manner of its parallels in the Qur'an, or as an adverb of time governed by the implied verb of saying (al-fi'l al-qawl al-muqaddar).

The pronoun object of ﴿We gather them﴾ refers either to ﴿those who committed crime﴾ [al-An'am: 124], mentioned in His words ﴿Humiliation from Allah will befall those who committed crime﴾ [al-An'am: 124], or to ﴿those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125] in His words ﴿Thus Allah places filth upon those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. These are the counterpart of those who take heed, for the community of Muslims is regarded as the addressees, being one group together with the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, whereas the polytheists are regarded as a separate group distant from them, by the third-person pronoun. Thus the intended ones are the polytheists who died in polytheism. The word ﴿all﴾ (jami'an) is emphasized to include all the polytheists, their leaders, their devils, and the rest of their associates. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the devils and their allies in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies﴾ [al-An'am: 121], etc.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ with the nun of majesty, as an iltifat (a shift from one grammatical person to another). Hafs from 'Asim and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with the yā' of the third person.

Since the gathering is attributed to the divine name (Allah), it is determined that the call in His words ﴿O assembly of jinn﴾ comes from Allah, exalted is He. Therefore it is necessary to supply a statement issued by the speaker, i.e., "We say: O assembly of jinn," because a call is only a statement.

[Page 67]

The clause ﴿O assembly of jinn﴾, etc., is the quoted speech of an omitted saying, indicated by the style of the discourse. The estimate is: "We say," or "saying."

Al-ma'shar (the assembly) is a group whose matter and condition are one, such that a quality or an action brings them together. It is a collective noun with no singular form from its own root. It is also pluralized as ma'ashir, and it has the same meaning. It is derived from mu'ashara (companionship) and mukhalata (association).

Most often the word ma'shar is annexed to a noun that specifies the quality by which its referents are gathered, and here that quality is that they are jinn. For this reason, when something is coordinated with what is annexed to it, it is in the form of the dual or plural of ma'shar. The dual is like His words: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], etc. That is: "O assembly of jinn, and O assembly of mankind." The plural is like your saying: "O assemblies of the Arabs, the non-Arabs, and the Berbers."

The jinn were mentioned in His words ﴿And they made for Allah partners, the jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 100] in this surah. The intended meaning of "jinn" here is the devils and their helpers from among the kind of jinn. Mankind (al-ins) was mentioned in His words ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112] in this surah.

Al-istikthar (to consider or make something abundant) means extreme abundance. The sīn and tā' in it are for intensification, like al-istilam (touching), al-istikhda' (deceiving), and al-istikbar (arrogance). It is construed with min of explanation (min al-bayaniyya) to the thing of which an abundance is taken, as one says: "He multiplied (istakthara) from the blessings," or "from the wealth," meaning he increased its gathering. And "the commander multiplied (istakthara) the soldiers." It is not construed directly, in order to distinguish this meaning from istakthara in the sense of regarding a thing as much, as in His words: ﴿And do not bestow favor, seeking to gain more﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 6].

His words ﴿you have multiplied from mankind﴾ are by omission of a noun governed by the annexation. The estimate is: "from the misguidance of mankind," or "from their misleading." So the meaning of ﴿you have multiplied from mankind﴾ is "you have increased in taking them" (i.e., in making them followers of you). That is, you exceeded the limit in seducing them and enticing them, so you subjugated a great many of them.

[Page 68]

The speech is a rebuke and a reproach to the jinn, meaning: most of mankind were compliant with you. The jinn include the devils, who mislead people and subjugate them through whispering, imagination, terror, touching, and the like, until people imagined their power and that they were in need of them. So they sought their favor through appeasement and by leaving the name of Allah off their sacrifices and in their affairs. To the point that the traveler, when he descended into a valley, would say: "I seek refuge in the lord of this valley," or "in the master of this valley," meaning by it the chief of the jinn, or he would say: "O lord of the valley, I seek your protection," meaning the master of the jinn. The Arabs believed that the deserts and the wide valleys between the mountains were inhabited by jinn, and they imagined the sounds of the winds to be the chirping of jinn. Al-A'sha said:

"And a land like the back of a shield, desolate,
Where the jinn at night, at its edges, make their chirping sound."

In the speech there is an allusion to the rebuke of mankind who followed them, obeyed them, and went to excess in seeking their pleasure, and who did not hear anyone calling them to abandon following them, as His words that come later indicate: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. This is a gradual progression in rebuke and the cutting off of excuses.

The intended meaning of ﴿their allies﴾ (awliya'uhum) is the allies of the jinn, that is, those who are loyal to them and who devote themselves to attachment to their conditions. The allies of the devils are the polytheists who arrived at the place of gathering in polytheism. It was said that it refers to disbelievers and to disobedient Muslims. This is false, because the disobedient person, although he has obeyed the devils, is not their ally: ﴿Allah is the ally of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. Also, because Allah, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], and said: ﴿And they will testify against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 130].

The phrase ﴿from mankind﴾ is an explanation of the allies.

He has limited the narration to the answer of mankind, because the polytheist people are the intended audience of admonition by this verse.

[Page 69]

The meaning of ﴿Some of us benefited from others﴾ is that one party gained and obtained its desire and its pleasure; that is, the jinn enjoyed mankind and mankind benefited from the jinn. So each "some" (ba'd) is intended to mean one of the two groups, because it is a part of the combined whole of the two groups. They said "Some of us benefited from others" and did not make mankind the addressees of the rebuke, because they wished to make an excuse on behalf of their allies from the jinn, and to deflect the rebuke from them: that the jinn were not the ones who alone benefited from subjugating mankind; rather each of the two groups gained benefit from its companion. These speakers of the excuse may have intended to share the guilt, as an acknowledgment of the truth and as sincerity toward their allies, or they may have intended to make an excuse for themselves, since they knew that the rebuke of the deceiving jinn implicitly rebukes the deceived. So they acknowledged and made an excuse, saying that what they did was not rebellion against Allah nor contempt for His command, but it was for the fulfillment of desires from both sides, and that is what is meant by "enjoyment."

Because they were not addressed initially, and because their speech was an insertion into the address, the sentence of their saying was not separated as the sentences of dialogue are separated in question and answer. Rather, it was coordinated with the clause of the presumed saying, because it is another saying that arose on that day.

The verb ﴿their allies said﴾ is expressed in the past tense, although it refers to the future, because of the statement "We gather them." This is to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. Thus from this there is an indication of the certainty of the whole report, and that it is inevitably going to happen, since part of it cannot be certain while part of it is not.

The enjoyment of mankind by the jinn is their benefit in the immediate life through the facilitation of their desires, the opening of the doors of pleasures and passions for them, and their safety from the jinn's assault. The enjoyment of the jinn by mankind is the jinn's benefit through the multiplication of their followers from among the people of error, their help in misleading people, their standing against the callers to good, and their cutting off of the path of righteousness. So each of the two groups helped the other to achieve what was in its soul, of what suits its nature and what pleases it in fulfilling its desire.

[Page 70]

His words ﴿And we have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾ are a submission to Allah. That is: the period of respite has ended, and we have reached the term which You appointed for us to fall into Your grasp. So now the ways are closed and we find no escape. In the speech there is grief and remorse upon the manifestation of the fact that their allies did not avail them anything, and the ending of the time of their rebellion and their arrogance, and the moment when they would receive the recompense of their deeds, like His words: ﴿And he found Allah with him, so He paid him his account in full﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

The verse indicates that the addressed jinn were silenced, so they found no answer, and they left their allies to defend them. This is one of the manifestations of the fact that the followed cannot avail their followers on that day: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166].

The clause ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾ is separated from the one before it in the manner of speech in dialogue, as was previously mentioned at His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The pronoun of address in His words ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾ is directed to mankind, since they are the intended audience of the verse, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them﴾ [Saba': 41]; ﴿So today no one among you has power to benefit or harm another. And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny"﴾ [Saba': 42], and His words: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together"﴾ [Hud: 119].

The statement's coming in the past form is to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, although it is future, by the indication of His words "We gather them," as was previously mentioned. Its attribution to the absent third person is in view of what occurred in the speech of the allies: ﴿Our Lord, they enjoyed...﴾, etc.

Al-mathwa (the abode) is a noun of place from thawa bi-l-makan, when one resides in a place for lasting residence or a long stay. He has explained the staying (thawa') by abiding forever in His words: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

His words ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ are certainly part of what is said to them at the gathering, because it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun of "your abode," so it must be connected to what precedes it.

[Page 71]

As for His words ﴿except what Allah wills﴾, the apparent structure indicates that it is part of what is said to them, because the original sense of an exception is that it removes something from what precedes it in the speech.

It is also permissible that it be an address from Allah to His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, coming as an interjection between what He related to him about the state of the polytheists and their allies on the Day of Gathering, and His words to him: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, All-Knowing﴾. In that case the pause would be at His words "abiding therein forever."

The exception in His words ﴿except what Allah wills﴾, according to both interpretations, is either an exception from the generality of the times indicated by His words "abiding therein forever," since abiding (khulud) is the stay of eternity, and eternity encompasses all times; so "ma" is a temporal verbal particle (masdariyya), and therefore the verb after it is in the sense of a verbal noun. That is: "except for the time of Allah's will to end your abiding." Or it is an exception from the generality of "abiding ones" implied in the pronoun of "abiding therein"; that is: "except a group whom Allah willed not to abide in the Fire."

With this, the meaning of the verse became a point of difficulty for all the exegetes, because it is established in the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslim community that the polytheists will not be forgiven and that they will abide forever in the Fire, without exception for any group or any period.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 128 (part 2 of 2):

I have counted ten interpretations of it for them. Some of them are not complete, and some are far-fetched if the phrase "except as God wills" is taken to be part of what is said to the polytheists and their allies on the Day of Gathering. Only one of them holds up, when the exception is treated as an interjection placed between the report of what is said to the polytheists on the Day of Gathering and what was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. In that case this interjection is an address to the living polytheists who hear the threat, giving them a warning that they may still embrace Islam. Then (ma) is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, not a temporal one. That is, "except the will of God regarding their not abiding," meaning the state of His will, which is the state of His granting some of the polytheists success in accepting Islam during their lives. This would be an explanation and confirmation of what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "God made an exception for a people whom He knew in advance would become Muslims." And also from him: "This verse requires a pause (waqf) regarding all the disbelievers." If what is reported from him is sound, it must be interpreted as having been said before he knew that the scholars agreed that the polytheists will not be forgiven.

You may also treat (ma) in this sense as a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), since it is frequently used for a rational being. If the phrase "abiding (khālidīn)" is taken to be part of what is said on the Day of Gathering, the interpretation of the verse becomes that the exception is not intended to exclude any time or state. Rather it is a kinaya (a figure of speech in which the intended meaning is implied indirectly), meaning that this abiding was decreed by God, freely chosen, with no one compelling Him to it, to show the completeness of His power and the purity of His will. It is as if He were saying: "If I willed, I would annul that."

This may be supported by the fact that God mentioned a parallel to it regarding the people of Paradise, in His saying: ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein will be groaning and wailing﴾ [Hud: 106] ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is an effective doer of what He intends﴾ [Hud: 107] ﴿And as for those who are made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills — a gift never cut off﴾ [Hud: 108]. Observe how He followed His saying ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107] in the punishment of the wretched with His saying ﴿indeed your Lord is an effective doer of what He intends﴾ [Hud: 107], and how He followed His saying ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107] in the bliss of the people of happiness with His saying ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hud: 108]. Thus He nullified the apparent meaning of the exception by His saying ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hud: 108]. This is the meaning of the kinaya through the exception. Then one turns, after this, to the proofs indicating that the abiding of the polytheists is not restricted to a time or a state.

This exception may also be of the type of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite.

His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl), and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. If His saying ﴿abiding therein, except as God wills﴾ is part of what is said to the allies of the jinn on the Day of Gathering, then His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾ is a clause interjected between the sayings, to show that what He ordained as abiding in punishment for polytheism He ordained by His wisdom and knowledge. If His saying "abiding (khālidīn)" etc. is an independent interjected statement, then His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾ is a concluding phrase for the interjection and a confirmation of the intended meaning of the will: making the deserving of eternal abiding in punishment dependent on dying in polytheism, and making deliverance from that dependent on faith.

The Wise (al-Ḥakīm) is the One who places things in their appropriate positions and causes in their proper effects. The Knowing (al-ʿAlīm) is the One who knows what is contained within all His creation of states that merit reward and punishment.

[Page 73]

It is part of the parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) or part of the concluding generalization (tadhyil), according to the two possibilities mentioned earlier. The wāw is either a wāw of circumstance (ḥāl) and parenthetical, as mentioned earlier, or it is a wāw of conjunction (ʿaṭf) on His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise and Knowing﴾ [al-Anʿām: 128].

The demonstrative refers to the turning over (tawliya) derived from نُوَلِّي. The demonstrative is masculine because the feminine form of "tawliya" is only grammatical, not real, so what is permissible for its verb that governs an explicit noun is permissible for its demonstrative. The meaning is: Just as We placed between these polytheists and their allies, We place among all the wrongdoers some of them alongside others.

Tawliya comes from both walā' and wilāya, because both are said of its transitive verb, walla, meaning "made someone a walī (ally/guardian)." It is of the pattern of aʿṭā and takes two objects. This is how they explained it. The apparent sense of their statement is that one says: "Ḍabba walla Tamīman," when they form an alliance among them. This is because one says: "Tawallat Ḍabba Tamīman," meaning "Ḍabba allied with Tamīm." When the verb is made transitive by doubling (taḍʿīf), one says: "Walleit Ḍabba Tamīman." This is of the same type as His saying: ﴿We will turn him over to what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 115], meaning: We will hold him to what he bound himself to. So the meaning of ﴿We place some of the wrongdoers over others﴾ is: We make some of them allies of others. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And their allies among mankind said﴾ [al-Anʿām: 128], and it treats both groups as wrongdoers, because whoever takes a people as allies becomes one of them.

[Page 74]

When Allah makes a group allies of the wrongdoers, He has made them wrongdoers by the consequence. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who did wrong, lest the Fire touch you﴾ [Hūd: 113], and He said: ﴿Some of them are allies of others. Whoever among you allies with them is one of them. Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Māʾida: 51].

It is also said that walla means "made someone a wālī (governor)," so it takes two objects of the aʿṭā pattern as well. One says: "Walla ʿUmar Abā ʿUbayda al-Shām (ʿUmar appointed Abū ʿUbayda over Syria)," just as one says: "Awlāhu" (he appointed him), because one says: "Wallā Abū ʿUbayda al-Shām (Abū ʿUbayda governed Syria)." For this reason the exegetes said: It is possible that the meaning of ﴿We place some of the wrongdoers over others﴾ is: We make some of them governors over others, that is, We empower some of them over others. The meaning is that He made the jinn, who are wrongdoers, empowered over the polytheists, who are also wrongdoers, so each wrongs in proportion to his power. The intended "wrongdoers" (al-ẓālimīn) in the verse are the polytheists, as the comparison in His saying "Just as (kadhālika)" requires.

The verse may, by indication (ishāra), include every wrongdoer, indicating that Allah empowers over the wrongdoer someone who wrongs him. ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr interpreted it this way during his call (da'wa) in Mecca. When news reached him that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān had killed ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Ashdaq after ʿAmr had rebelled against him, he mounted the pulpit and said: "Indeed the son of al-Zarqāʾ" (meaning ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, because Marwān was nicknamed al-Azraq and al-Zarqāʾ, since he had blue eyes) "has killed the lateem of Satan. ﴿Just as We place some of the wrongdoers over others, because of what they earned﴾."

For this reason it was said: If the wrongdoer does not desist from his wrongdoing, another wrongdoer will be empowered over him. Al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) said: If the subjects wish to be rid of a wrongdoing ruler, let them abandon wrongdoing. It has also been said:

No wrongdoer is ever left but that he will be tried by another wrongdoer.

His saying ﴿because of what they earned﴾: the bāʾ in بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ is causal (sababiyya), meaning: it is a recompense for their persistence in polytheism.

[Page 75]

The purpose of the verse is admonition and warning: to warn against being deceived by the guardianship of wrongdoers, to seek out the followers' welfare for those they follow, and to explain one of the sunan (laws) of Allah among the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 130 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say, "We bear witness against ourselves." And the worldly life deceived them, and they will bear witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers.﴾

This is part of the dialogue that takes place on the Day of Gathering, and the sentence is separated (from what precedes) because it stands in the context of enumerating their crimes, by which they deserved eternal abiding (in the Fire), in order to nullify their excuse and to declare that they are deserving of what they are requited with. So He repeats their address, as one who is rebuked and censured is addressed, so that his terror increases.

The hamzah in ﴿أَلَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ﴾ is the interrogative of confirmation (al-istifham al-taqriri). The question was framed as a negation of the coming of the messengers to them, because when the one being confronted (al-muqarrar) is in a state of being involved in what is affirmed against him, such that he is one who might be expected to answer in the negative, his confirmation is brought in as a negation of the matter whose affirmation is intended. Then, once he affirms it, his confession is more decisive against his excuse in being held to account for it, just as one says to the offender: "Are you not the doer of such and such?" and "Are you not the one who said such and such?"

This method may also be followed in a context of testing the extent to which the one questioned (al-mas'ul al-muqarrar) is firm in certainty regarding what is affirmed against him, so the interrogative is brought in as a negation of the thing affirmed against him, until, if he has any doubt about it, he becomes confused and falters. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He took from the children of Adam... Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. And since the state of these jinn and humankind was one of rebellion against God, casting off righteous deeds behind their backs, and turning away from faith, as the state of one whose ear has not been touched by any command to good or prohibition of evil, (the verse) came, in their confirmation regarding the sending of messengers,
Page 76
in the form of an interrogative negating the coming of the messengers to them, so that when they found no room to deny the coming of the messengers, and acknowledged their coming, that was more fitting for seizing them with punishment.

As for "the messengers" (al-rusul): its apparent meaning is that it is the plural of rasul in the well-known sense in the terminology of the Law, i.e., one sent by God to the servants with what guides them to what is obligatory for them of belief and action. It may also be the plural of rasul in the linguistic sense, which is one sent by another, as in His saying: ﴿When the messengers came to her﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13], and they are the messengers of the disciples (al-hawariyyun) after Jesus.

The description of the messengers by His saying "from among you" serves to increase the establishment of the proof; i.e., messengers whom you know and hear. So "min" may be connective (ittisaliyyah), like the one in their saying: "I am not from you and you are not from me." It is not partitive, unlike the one in His saying: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2]. That is because the messengers of God are only from humankind, since the station of conveying a message from God does not befit being given except to the most noble of kinds among angels and humans, and the kind of jinn is lower than humans, for they were created from fire.

"Min" may also be partitive, and the intended meaning of the pronoun in "minkum" would be specifically humankind by way of synecdoche (taghlib), or the pronoun returns to part of what was mentioned before it, as in His saying: ﴿From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas pearl and coral only emerge from the salt sea. As for holding the jinn accountable for opposing the messengers, God may create in the jinn an inspiration of the obligation to listen to the call of the messengers and to act upon it, as His saying in Surat al-Jinn indicates: ﴿Say, "It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened and said, 'Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an.'"﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], and He said in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿They said, "O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] ﴿"O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. That is because the apparent indications require that the jinn have a connection with this world and knowledge of the conditions of its people: ﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them﴾ [al-A'raf: 27].
Page 77

Thus the view of those who held that there were messengers from among the jinn sent to their own kind is weak, and it is attributed to al-Dahhak. Accordingly, His saying "did there not come to you" is turned away from its apparent sense of including both the humankind and the jinn. No report from the Prophet ﷺ has been established that God sent messengers from among the jinn to their kind. It is possible that the messengers of the jinn were groups among them who listened to the prophets, understood what they called to, and conveyed that to their peoples, as the verse in Surat al-Ahqaf requires. So the holding of the jinn accountable for associating partners with God requires that the knowledge of God's oneness has reached them, for the proofs of divine unity are rational and need nothing but something that stirs reflection. When God created for the jinn knowledge of what the messengers of God bring of the call to reflection on tawhid, then the accountability for not believing in God's oneness became incumbent upon them, and they deserved punishment for associating partners, without depending on the messengers having directed their call to them.

Among the fine expressions of our Imams is that they say: "Faith is obligatory upon the one who has been reached by the call," without saying: "upon the one to whom the call has been directed." The ways in which the call reaches people are many. It is not established in the Qur'an or in sound reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, or any other of the messengers, was sent to the jinn, for lack of wisdom in that, and for lack of suitability between the two kinds, and the impossibility of their mixing. But from al-Kalbi it is reported that Muhammad ﷺ was sent to humankind and jinn; this was said by Ibn Hazm, and Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr preferred it and reported a consensus upon it. Thus it would be among the special features of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, honoring his rank.

Engaging in this matter is something from which the scholar should keep himself aloof, because it is an engagement in the conditions of a world that does not fall under our perceptions. God has informed us that all worlds are subject to His authority, and obedience to Him is incumbent upon them, when they are perceptive and fit for responsibility. The purpose of the verse we are discussing is to inform the polytheists that they are commanded to affirm God's oneness and submit to Islam, and that their allies among the devils of humankind and jinn will not escape accountability for rejecting Islam, let alone their followers and common folk. So the mention of the jinn with humankind in His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾ on the Day of Resurrection is for the rebuke and humiliation of the polytheists regarding what they neglected in the world of worshipping the jinn or seeking refuge in them,
Page 78

in the manner of His saying: ﴿And the Day He gathers them together with what they worshipped besides God, and He says, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], and His saying: ﴿And when God says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?'"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

"Al-qass" like "al-qasas" means reporting. From it comes "al-qissah" for a report. The meaning is: they will relate to you the reports that indicate God's oneness, His command and prohibition, His promise and threat. This was called qass because most of it consists of reports about the attributes of God, the messengers and their nations and what befell them, and about the recompense of bliss or punishment. So what is meant by "the signs" (al-ayat) is the signs of the Qur'an and the statements that are recited, which the jinn understand by inspiration, as previously mentioned, and which humankind understood directly if they know Arabic, and through translation if they do not.

"Al-indhar" is informing about what frightens and is disliked; it is the opposite of glad tidings (al-bisharah). It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119] in Surat al-Baqarah. It transitively takes an object directly, which is the one to whom the news is conveyed, and it takes the thing reported about with "bi" and also directly. It is said: "anzartuhu bi-kadha" and "anzartuhu kadha." God said: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire blazing﴾ [al-Layl: 14], ﴿Say, "I have warned you of a thunderbolt"﴾ [Fussilat: 13], ﴿and that you may warn of the Day of Assembly﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. Since the meeting on the Day of Gathering includes good for the people of good and evil for the people of evil, and since these addressees had become purely inclined to evil, the report of the messengers to them about meeting that Day was made a warning, because it is the aspect that was realized in them from the totality of the messengers' reports to them about what that Day holds and its evil. The description of the Day by the demonstrative in His saying "this your Day" serves to magnify the matter of that Day by what is witnessed in it, such that expression cannot encompass its description, so one turns away from description to indication, as in His saying: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [al-Tur: 14].

The meaning of their saying "We bear witness against ourselves" is the acknowledgment of what the interrogative contained of the coming of the messengers to them. This is evidence that the entry of the negative particle into the interrogative sentence is intended only to cut off excuse, and that it is a matter the one questioned cannot deny. Therefore they answered in summary: so "They said, 'We bear witness against ourselves'," meaning: we acknowledge the coming of the messengers to us.
Page 79

"Shahadah" was used in the sense of acknowledgment, because the origin of testimony is informing about a matter that the informant has verified and clarified. From it: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], and "shahida 'alayhi" means he informed about him with the report of one who is certain and verified. Therefore they said: "We bear witness against ourselves," meaning: we acknowledge the coming of the messengers to us. There is no contradiction between this acknowledgment and their denial of association in His saying: ﴿Then their only argument will be that they say, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23], because the thing reported about differs in the two verses.

The sentence "they said" (qalu) is separated because it runs in the manner of dialogue.

The sentence ﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿They said, "We bear witness"﴾, in consideration of the first being a report about the manifestation of the truth to them, and their knowledge at that time that they had disobeyed the messengers and the One who sent them, and turned away from meeting that Day. So they knew, and the listener to their report knew, that they had fallen into this noose only because the worldly life deceived them; and were it not for that deception, their deeds would not be what a sensible person would choose for himself.

What is meant by "the life" is its conditions as they obtained for them: of frivolity, boasting, arrogance, obstinacy, treating the realities lightly, and being deluded by what benefits neither in the immediate nor in the hereafter.

The purpose of this report about them is to disclose their condition and to warn the listeners against persisting in becoming entangled in the like of it, for their situation is the same.

The sentence ﴿And they bore witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾, and it is a report used for expressing wonder at their condition, and for condemning their opinion in the world, the badness of their outlook on the signs, and their turning away from reflecting on the consequences. This report is ordered after the preceding report, which is their being deceived by the worldly life, because that deception was the cause of their falling into this state, until they surrendered and bore witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers in God in the world. As for humankind, it is because they associated partners with Him and worshipped the jinn; and as for the jinn, it is because they incited
Page 80

humankind to worship them and set themselves up as partners to God, so both groups of these are disbelievers. This is like what God reported about them, or about the like of them, with a similar wondering report in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze"﴾ [al-Mulk: 10] ﴿So they will acknowledge their sin﴾ [al-Mulk: 11]. Observe how He made their acknowledgment of their sin a consequence of their saying, though their saying is itself the acknowledgment; a thing is not made a consequence of itself. But the report was intended to express wonder at their condition and to give a lesson through them, when they were compelled to acknowledgment in the end.

Their testimony against themselves regarding disbelief came after the purification (al-tamhis, the sifting of deeds) and compulsion, so it does not contradict the fact that they denied disbelief at the outset of the reckoning, when they said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "I find things that contradict one another for me. Allah says: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], and He says: ﴿except that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23], so they have concealed." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed Allah forgives the sins of the people of sincerity (ahl al-ikhlas). So the polytheists said: 'Come, let us say: we were not polytheists.' Then Allah sets a seal upon their mouths, and their hands speak."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 131:

﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities wrongfully while their people were unaware.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), conveying a threat, admonition and lesson concerning the negligence of the people of misguidance regarding the benefit of the call of the messengers, and an alert to the value of sending messengers to the nations. The purpose is that the polytheists may reconsider their situation while they are still in this world before the Day of Gathering, and know that the outcome of turning away from the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) is loss, so that they may make amends for their affairs out of fear of missing the opportunity. It is also a warning of the imminent descent of punishment upon them, and an awakening for the polytheists that their condition is like that of those spoken of when they die in their polytheism.

The demonstrative in His words (dhalika) refers to something mentioned in the preceding discourse, namely the nearest thing mentioned, as is the case with demonstratives referring to something not perceived by the senses. So the referent is what was mentioned before, or it is the coming of the messengers, which the discourse has been about in the narration of the admission of the polytheists on the Day of Gathering concerning the coming of their messengers to them. This is the verbal noun derived from His words: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. For when He related that statement to the listening people, that related statement became as if present, so it was correct to point to something derived from it.

The demonstrative noun is either a subject (mubtada'), or a predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: "That matter" or "The matter is that," as indicated by the implied pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) after (an).

(An) is a lightened form of the heavy (an), and its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter, as is its usage when lightened. This is because this report has a matter which deserves to be known, and the clause is the predicate of (an). The preposition of cause (lam al-ta'lil) that enters upon (an) is omitted, since the omission of the preposition of (anna) is common and widespread. The estimate is: "That matter," or "The matter is that," because it, i.e., the matter, is that your Lord would never destroy the cities.

The clause ﴿your Lord would never destroy the cities wrongfully while their people were unaware﴾ is a great matter among the affairs of God Most High, namely the matter of His justice and mercy, His pleasure for His servants in good and righteousness, His dislike of their evil deeds, and His manifestation of the effect of His lordship over them by guiding them to the paths of good, and by not seizing them with destruction before advancing warning and alert to them.

There is concision in the discourse, for it is known from it that God destroys the cities whose people persist in polytheism when they turn away from the call of the messengers; that He does not destroy them except after sending to them messengers as warners; and that He intends to place upon them the burden of their destruction, so that no thought remains in their souls that they might say: "Had our Lord had mercy on us, He would have informed us and given us an excuse," as God Most High said: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so we could follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134], i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ), or before the Qur'an.

So he confined this meaning to the meaning that the reason for sending is that the cities are not destroyed while in heedlessness, and this indicates the omitted meaning.

Destruction (ihlak) is the annihilation of the existence of a thing and the causing of the living to die. God Most High said: ﴿That whoever perishes might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives might live upon clear proof﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. So the destruction of cities is the annihilation of their people and the ruin of them, and their revival is the restoration of their populating with inhabitants and building. God Most High said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], i.e., the town. Here the destruction of cities includes the annihilation of their inhabitants, because the destruction has attached itself to the very cities, so there is no need for a metonymic figure in applying "cities" to their people as in: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], since the literal sense is correct here; and because His words ﴿while their people were unaware﴾ prevent it. Do you not see His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they commit wickedness therein, and the word is justified against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 16], where He made its destruction its ruin; and His words: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town which was rained upon with a rain of evil. Did they not see it?﴾ [al-Furqan: 40].

The ba' in (bi-zulm) is causal, and injustice (zulm) is polytheism; i.e., He destroys them because of polytheism occurring in them, so He destroys the city and destroys its people who committed it. For this reason He did not say "by the injustice of its people," because what is intended is that the existence of injustice in it is the cause of its destruction, and the destruction of its people is all the more so, since they are the primary target of destruction.

The clause ﴿while their people were unaware﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the cities." Here He explicitly mentioned "its people" to draw attention to the fact that the destruction of the cities comes as a result of the deeds of their inhabitants: ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 132:

﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they did, and your Lord is not unaware of what they do.﴾

Page 83
A safeguard against His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reforming﴾ [al-An'am: 131], serving as an alert that the righteous among the people of the towns, where polytheism and wrongdoing predominated, are not deprived of the reward of their righteousness.

The tanwin in (wa-li-kullin) is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted; that is, "and for all of them," i.e., for all the people of the destroyed towns there are degrees. This means that their conditions differ in the Hereafter: the believers among them will not have their faith wasted, while the disbelievers will be gathered to punishment in the Hereafter after having been punished in this world. God may save the believers among the people of the towns before the punishment descends, and this is a degree they attained in this world, namely the degree of manifesting God's care for them; their degree will also be raised in the Hereafter. As for the disbelievers, the punishment of destruction befalls them, and then they proceed to the punishment of the Hereafter.

A town may be destroyed along with its believers and then they proceed to bliss, so the difference in their degrees becomes apparent in the Hereafter. This is another condition, and it is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not afflict those who have wronged among you exclusively﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God sends a punishment upon a people, the punishment strikes everyone among them, and then they are resurrected according to their deeds." In the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, in al-Bayhaqi's Shu'ab, traced to the Prophet: "When God sends His wrath upon the people of His vengeance while among them are the righteous, they are taken along with them, and then they are resurrected according to their intentions and deeds." Ibn Hibban authenticated it. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh, Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with her, she said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today a breach has been opened in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this," and he made the sign of ninety (i.e., he formed ninety with two fingers, by the sign of ninety in reckoning, expressed by the 'uqad, with the 'ayn vowelled with a damma and the qaf with a fatha). It was said: "Shall we be destroyed while among us are the righteous?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases."

Darajat (degrees) are that by which one ascends from the bottom to the top, on a ladder or in a building. If the intent is descent into a low place such as a well or the like, they are called darakat (depths).

Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God will raise those among you who believe and those who were given knowledge by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11], and He said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa: 145]. Since the word (kull) is intended to refer to all the people of the town, and the word (darajat) is used, this is an indication of giving precedence to the condition of the believers, so that the hearts of the Muslims of Makkah may be reassured that there is no harm upon them from the punishment of its polytheists. Thus there is in it an indication that God will save them from punishment in this world through the emigration (hijra), and in the Hereafter by resurrecting them according to their deeds and intentions, because they did not fall short in denouncing the polytheists. In this verse there is therefore an announcement that they will leave the town upon which the punishment has been decreed, for God afflicted the people of Makkah with hunger and fear, then with the raid, after He had saved His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. It is known from the word "degrees" that their lowest levels are depths, so (darajat) was preferred for the purpose of conveying the good news to the believers after the warning to the polytheists.

The (min) in His saying ﴿according to what they did﴾ is causative; that is, from their deeds, i.e., because of the difference in their deeds.

His saying ﴿and your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ).

The majority read (ya'malun) with the third-person masculine prefix, so the pronoun refers to the people of the towns, and the intended meaning is the polytheists of Makkah. It is then a consolation and reassurance, lest he (ﷺ) become impatient for God's promise of victory, and it is an allusion to a threat to the polytheists, in the manner of "Hear, O neighbor" (wa-isma'i ya jarah). Ibn 'Amir read it with the second-person feminine prefix (ta'), so the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and those Muslims with him. It is then a promise of reward for their righteous deeds, following up on the expression "degrees" as stated earlier, so that it may be a comfort to them against the threat of the people of the towns, the possessors of wrongdoing. Both readings, as far as I reckon, are intended by God, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 133:

﴿And your Lord is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy﴾

Page 85
The clause ﴿And your Lord is the Free of need﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ [al-An'am: 132], as a statement about His knowledge and His mercy, in contrast to the report about their deeds. Both clauses contain a warning (wa'id) and a promise (wa'd). In the second clause there is a metonymy (kinaya) for His exaltedness above the need for the faith of the polytheists and their allegiance, as in His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7], and a metonymy for His mercy, since He granted the polytheists respite and did not hasten punishment for them, as He said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. Had He taken them to account for what they earned, He would have hastened for them the punishment﴾ [al-Kahf: 58], in Surat al-Kahf.

His saying "your Lord" (rabbuka) is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun. The expected form would have been "and He is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy," but the usual form was departed from because the name "Lord" indicates care for the welfare of the one being nurtured, and so that the clause would stand independently, passing into the status of proverbs and maxims, and to honour the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Ghaniyy (the Free of need) is the one who does not need anything other than himself. The true Free of need is Allah the Exalted, since He never needs anything else in any state. The scholars of kalam have said that the attribute of Free-of-need established for Allah the Exalted includes in its meaning the necessity of existence (wujub al-wujud), because the dependence of the contingent (mumkin) upon the willing Originator who tips one side of its existence over the side of its non-existence is the most intense dependence. I reckon that the meaning of al-Ghaniyy in common linguistic usage is the attribute of existence, unless that is a technical usage of the theologians specific to the meaning of absolute Free-of-need. What indicates what I have said is that among His names, the Exalted, is al-Mughni (the Enricher), and the meaning of it does not take into account that He is the Originator of existing things. The discussion of the meaning of al-Ghaniyy has already preceded at His saying: ﴿If he is rich or poor﴾ [al-Nisa': 135] in Surat al-Nisa'.

Defining the predicate with the definite article (al-) requires restricting it to the subject; that is, restricting free-of-need to Allah. This is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i), in view of the fact that the free-of-need of other than Allah the Exalted, being an imperfect free-of-need, is treated as if it were non-existent. That is: "Your Lord is the Free of need, not other than Him." His free-of-need, the Exalted, is real. The mention of the attribute "Free of need" here is a preparation (tamhid) for the ruling that follows it, which is ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾. It is thus the presenting of evidence before the claim, a reminder of the nearness of the certainty of the claim.

Page 86
﴿Possessor of mercy﴾ is a second predicate.
He turned away from describing Him with the attribute "the Merciful" (al-Rahim) to describing Him as "Possessor of mercy" because "Free of need" is an essential attribute of Allah, and creatures benefit only from the necessary consequences of that attribute, which is His generosity towards them, since He does not diminish anything of His free-of-need. This differs from the attribute of mercy, for its connection benefits creatures. So it was given preference with the word (dhu), because (dhu) is a word through which one reaches description by kinds, and its meaning is "possessor of." It indicates the strength or abundance of what it is attached to. So one does not say "dhu insaf" (possessor of justice) except of one who is strong in justice, and one does not say "dhu mal" (possessor of wealth) of one who has little wealth. The intended purpose of describing Him as "Possessor of mercy" here is a preparation for the meaning of respite contained in His saying: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾; that is, let no one say: "Why has He not destroyed these deniers?" That is, it is because of His mercy that He granted them respite, as an excuse for them.

* * *
﴿If He wills, He will take you away and will make succeed after you whom He wills, as He produced you from the descendants of another people﴾
This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to threaten the polytheists who used to deny the warning of punishment by destruction, saying: ﴿When is this victory, if you should be truthful?﴾ [al-Sajda: 28]. This is what His saying after it indicates: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape﴾ [al-An'am: 134].

The address may be to the Prophet ﷺ, and its intended purpose is an allusion to those among the polytheists who are heedless of this, so that it becomes an explicit threat.

The meaning: If Allah wills, He will hasten your annihilation and will make succeed after you whom He wills of those who believe in Him, as He said: ﴿And if you turn away, He will exchange you for another people, then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. That is: His granting you respite is only because He is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy.

Page 87
The conditional clause and its answer are a third predicate of the subject. The object of (yasha'u) is omitted according to its customary manner of omitting the object of the verb of willing.

Al-idhhab (taking away) is a metaphor for annihilation, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18].

Al-istikhlaf (making succeed) is making a successor (khalaf) to a thing. Khalaf is the replacement for a thing that has passed away. The sin and ta' in it are for emphasis. The word (ma) is a general relative pronoun; that is: whomever He wills of believers or disbelievers, according to what His wisdom requires. This is an allusion to eradication, because the apparent sense of the pronoun indicates generality.

The comparison in His saying: ﴿as He produced you from the descendants of another people﴾ is a comparison in the bringing into existence of beings after other beings, not in the sense that the created things are extracted from the remnants of the non-existent, just as He produced mankind in a second creation from the descendants of those whom Allah saved in the ark with Noah, peace be upon him. So the speech is an allusion to the destruction of the polytheists and the salvation of the believers from punishment.

The particle of comparison (ka) in the phrase is in the place of accusative, a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), because it describes an omitted noun whose assumed form is "successorship as He produced you," since the production describes the manner of the succession. (Min) is for beginning (ibtida'iyya). The meaning of dhurriyya and its derivation has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿He said: And of my descendants﴾ [al-Baqara: 124] in Surat al-Baqara.

The description of a people as (ākharīn, "others") is to indicate difference; that is, people who are not from the tribes of the Arabs. This is an alert to the great power of Allah the Exalted to produce peoples from peoples who differ from them in language, customs and dwelling places. This is a metonymy for the distance of eras and the succession of created generations, because difference between roots and branches does not arise except over distant times. So far apart are the conditions of the people of Noah and the conditions of the Arabs addressed, and between them lie different and distant centuries.

[Page 88]

﴿Surely what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape it.﴾

This clause is a *badal ishtimal* (inclusive substitute, an apposition) for the clause ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. Divine will (mashi'ah) encompasses two states: the state of not destroying them and the state of bringing that destruction about. This clause therefore informs us that God's will has been directed toward carrying out the threat He made to them, namely the removal.

It is also possible to take the clause as an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as a reply to a question that an idolater might raise while mocking the threat: "If we have been given respite and the uprooting has been delayed for us, then we have escaped the threat, and perhaps people after us will meet it." So the statement ﴿Surely what you are promised is coming﴾ comes as the answer to this question that arises from the preceding speech, affirming that what the idolaters were threatened with is certainly going to happen, even if it is delayed.

The emphasis with (*inna*) suits the situation of one who is hesitant and seeking assurance, and the emphasis is increased with the *lam* of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*), because they were deeply immersed in denying that what they were threatened with would come to pass, and in mocking it. They said: ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], seeking to confound the Messenger (ﷺ) and to show that his threat had failed.

The verb ﴿tu'adun﴾ in the passive form allows it to be either the imperfect of *wa'ada yaʿidu* (to promise) or the imperfect of *u'ida yuʿadu* (to threaten). The more obvious reading is the first. It is an elegant feature of eloquence that the verb is in the passive, so that its wording fits the condition of both the believers and the idolaters. Had it been in the active, one of two forms would have been fixed: "what We promise you" or "what We threaten you with". This is a fine way of addressing the audience, so that each group among the listeners takes from it what suits its condition. It is well known that the threat against the idolaters implies a promise to the believers, but the principal intended matter is the threat against the idolaters. For this reason the speech is followed by ﴿and you cannot escape﴾, which serves as a *tarshih* (a supporting element that reinforces one of the two possible meanings of the speech).

[Page 89]

The verb *al-ityan* (coming) is used metaphorically for occurrence, likening the promised thing, awaited to occur, to an awaited person who is expected to arrive, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly or openly﴾ [al-An'am: 47], in this surah.

The true meaning of *al-mu'jiz* (one who causes inability) is that which makes one who seeks something unable to obtain it, i.e., unable to reach it. It is used figuratively to mean escaping the grasp of one who pursues. As Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i said:

*Did you not see that the earth is wide and spacious?*
*Will any patch of its patches escape me?*

That is, no patch of it escapes me, nor can an enemy who pursues me reach it.

So the meaning of ﴿and you cannot escape Me﴾ is: you will not escape My threat, or you will not be beyond My power. The phrase suits both possibilities.

The use of the nominal sentence in ﴿and you are not ones who can escape﴾ serves to express stability and permanence in the attribution of the predicate to the subject, and it is the attribution of its negation to the subject. This is because the particularities that are considered in the affirmative case are also considered in the negative case, since negation is only a mode of the attribution, and the particularities are requirements of the structural conditions of the sentence. Negation differs from affirmation only in considering the additional restrictions beyond the basic structure. Negation is considered to be directed at these restrictions in particular, and these are the restrictions of the concepts of opposition (*mafahim al-mukhalafah*). Otherwise, many particularities assumed with affirmation would be nullified when the sentence containing them is negated. An example is the indication of renewal in the verbal predicate in the verse of Ju'ayyah ibn al-Nadr:

*The minted dirham does not visit our purse,*
*but passes by it while it is departing.*

For there is no difference in indicating renewal between this half-line and saying: "The dirham visited our purse."
