Likewise His saying, ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]: the first indicates that the negation of their lawfulness is a renewed ruling that is not abrogated. These are thus two considerations. I have already pointed to some of this when explaining His saying, ﴿God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 135:

[Page 90]
﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your standing; indeed I am acting. So you will come to know to whom the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not be successful."﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) following His saying: ﴿What you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it﴾ [al-An'am: 134]. Its primary purpose is the threat against the polytheists, as has passed. He followed it with what is purely directed to their threat, namely the command used for warning and intimidation, so that they may be given respite in their misguidance, a respite which conveys, in ordinary discourse, that what is commanded increases the one commanded in deserving punishment and in drawing near to it. God commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to call them and threaten them, and He commanded that he begin his address to them with the call (nida') for the sake of attending to what would be said to them, since the call draws the attention of those addressed. The speaker was the representative of the people, because of what he feels: that he has been moved by their condition when he warned them with His saying: ﴿What you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it﴾ [al-An'am: 134], for it is the way of one who loves for his people what he loves for himself.

The call is addressed to the obstinate people, as indicated by the context which shows that the command is for threat, and that their action is contrary to his action, as shown by His saying "act" (i'malu) together with "indeed I am acting" (inni 'amilun).

Thus the command in His saying "act" (i'malu) is for equalization and leaving-be (al-taswiyah wal-takhliyah), to show despair of their compliance with the advice, to the extent that the advisor changes his advice into permission for them to do what they wish to do, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Act as you wish﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. This usage is a metaphor (isti'arah), since the one who is angered against, and despaired of his turning back, is likened to one commanded to do what he was forbidden from, so that it is as if that forbidden thing has become obligatory. This is mockery (tahakkum).

Al-Makanah means al-makan (place). It came in the feminine form just as al-Muqamah came for al-muqam, and al-Darah as a noun for al-dar, and al-Ma'ah for the water around which one camps. It is said: "ahl al-ma'" and "ahl al-ma'ah."

Here al-makanah is a metaphor for the state in which a person is clothed, the state being likened, in its encompassing and in its possessor being clothed by it, to the place that contains a thing, as has been passed. [Page 91]
The use of "the abode" (al-dar) just earlier, in His saying: ﴿For them is the abode of peace﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. Or al-makanah may be a metonymy (kinayah) for the state, because a person's states appear in his place and dwelling; therefore it is said: "O so-and-so, according to your makanah," meaning: remain upon what you are upon and do not deviate from it.

The object of (i'malu) is omitted, because the verb has been placed in the position of the intransitive; meaning: act your customary deed, which is your habit, namely turning away and denying the truth.

And (ʿala) is used for firmness of position by way of subsequent metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), and it is suitable to the metaphor of makanah for state, since elevation (ʿilawah) suits a place. So it is a tarshih (nurturing) of the metaphor, borrowed from what suits the likened-to to what suits the likened. The meaning: keep to your state; there is no hope for me in following you.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿ʿala makanatikum﴾ in the singular, while Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "makanatikum" in the plural, as the plural of makanah, the plural being according to the plural of the genitive.

The clause (inni ʿamilun) is a justification (ta'lil) for the implication of equalization in the command in His saying (i'malu); meaning: your insistence on what you are upon does not harm me, but I persist in my action; that is, I do not abandon what I am upon of faith and calling to God.

The omission of the complement of (inni ʿamilun) is for generality together with brevity, and its detail will come in its counterpart in surah al-Zumar.

The warning of threat is consequent upon their action and his action: ﴿so you will come to know﴾ with the fa' of sequence, to indicate that this threat is a branch of that intimidation.

The particle of futurity (sawfa) is intended to emphasize occurrence, since the two particles of futurity confirm the future just as qad confirms the past. Therefore Sibawayh said, regarding (lan), that it is for negating "will do," and from him al-Zamakhshari took its meaning as emphasizing negation.

[Page 92]
This is explicit in threat, because their being informed that they will know indicates that he knows that this will occur without doubt. His resolve that he is acting upon his makanah and opposed to their action indicates that he is certain of his good end and their bad end; for had it not been so, he would have done as they did, since the sensible person does not accept harm for himself. So His saying ﴿so you will come to know﴾ indicates that their knowledge occurs in the future, while as for him, he knows from now, and this contains a kinayah for his confidence that he is rightly guided and that they are falsifiers. A parallel of this verse will come in the story of Shu'ayb in surah Hud.

His saying ﴿to whom the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs﴾ is an interrogative, and it suspends the verb of knowledge from operating, so it is not given two objects, being sufficient with the meaning of the interrogative; for the estimate is: "you will know which of us the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs to." The position of (man) is nominative as a subject, and the clause ﴿the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs to him﴾ is its predicate.

Al-ʿAqibah in the language means the last of the matter and the effect of the doer's action; so the outcome of everything is what emerges from the thing and appears at its end of trace and result. Its feminine form is according to the interpretation of state; one does not say "ʿaqib al-amr," but "ʿaqibah" and "ʿuqba."

The usage has specified the word al-ʿaqibah for the good last end. Al-Raghib said: al-ʿaqibah and al-ʿuqba are specific to reward, like ﴿and the ultimate outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-A'raf: 128], and with an idafah it may be used for punishment, like ﴿then the end of those who did evil was the worst﴾ [al-Rum: 10]. Few have noted this, and it is from his precision; its evidences in the Qur'an are many.

Al-Dar is the place where people settle, whether land or building, and it has passed earlier at His saying: ﴿For them is the abode of peace﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. The definition of al-dar here is the definition of genus.

So it is possible that the word al-dar is absolute, in its literal meaning, and the idafah of (ʿaqibah) to (al-dar) is a true idafah; that is, the good outcome attained in the abode, which is winning the abode and prevailing in the dispute over it, by analogy with what the Arabs used to contend over dwellings and pastures. On this basis His saying ﴿to whom the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs﴾ is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah makniyyah), in which the condition of the believers who succeed in their action, together with the condition of the polytheists, is likened to the condition of one who prevails in possessing the abode of his enemy; the compound expression indicating the image likened is omitted, and it is hinted at by mentioning what is among its attendants, namely "the ultimate outcome of the abode." For allegory may be explicit and may be implicit, even if they did not divide it into these two, yet this division is unavoidable.

It is also possible that al-dar is a metaphor for the state in which a person has settled, likening the state to the place in containing, so the idafah of (ʿaqibah) to (al-dar) is an explanatory idafah; that is, the good ultimate outcome which is his state, and the statement is then an explicit metaphor.

Among its excellences here is that it is built upon the metaphor of makanah for state in His saying ﴿act according to your makanah﴾, so the meaning becomes: act in your abode what you are doing, you will come to know to whom the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs.

Along with that, the speech contains an allusion that the ultimate outcome of that abode, that is the land of Makkah, will belong to the Muslims, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. However, His saying ﴿to whom the ultimate outcome of the abode belongs﴾ has been interpreted with a meaning other than this.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿man takunu﴾ with a feminine (ta') prefix, while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a masculine (ya') prefix, because the feminine of ʿaqibah is not real; so when it occurs as a subject, it is permissible to join it to the feminine sign or to leave it without.

The clause ﴿indeed, the wrongdoers will not be successful﴾ is an appendix (tadhyil) to the threat, functioning as a justification; that is: because the wrongdoers will not be successful, the outcome of the abode will belong to the Muslims, not to you, because you are wrongdoers.

The definition in "al-zalimun" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), so it includes these wrongdoers from the outset. The pronoun made the subject of (inna) is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), to draw attention to the importance of this report and that it is a matter of great magnitude.

[Page 94]

﴿They assign to Allah a share of what He has created of crops and livestock, and they say, "This is for Allah," by their claim, and "This is for our partners." But what is for their partners does not reach Allah, while what is for Allah reaches their partners. Evil is what they judge.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) with its counterparts, the passages in which their sayings and actions are reported, from His words: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said, "Allah has not sent down anything to a human being."﴾ [Al-An'am: 91]; His words: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 100]; His words: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it﴾ [Al-An'am: 109]; and His words: ﴿And when a sign comes to them, they say, "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah."﴾ [Al-An'am: 124]. Whatever lies between these is a refutation of their sayings, a rejection of their doctrines, and illustrations and parallels. The pronoun of the plural refers to the polytheists, who are the subject of the discourse from the beginning of the surah, from His words: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [Al-An'am: 1]. This is the beginning of the explanation of their false legislations, and the first of them is what they made obligatory upon themselves, in their wealth, for the idols, resembling the obligatory charities. They used to make these obligatory upon themselves by commitment, like vows, or by a determination from those who legislated for them, as will come.

The word *ja'l* (making, assigning) here means "disposing" and "dividing," as in the saying of 'Umar concerning the matter of *mā afā' Allāh 'alā rasūlihi* (what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger), over which al-'Abbas and 'Ali disputed, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would place it in the position of the wealth of Allah; that is, he would place it and dispose of it. The true meaning of *ja'l* is "to make into" (*taṣyīr*), and just as it has come to express figurative meanings, so *ja'ala* has come (with those meanings). Thus the meaning of (*ja'alū lillāh*, "they assigned to Allah") is they disposed of and placed for Allah; that is, they designated for Him a share, because designation includes a notional making and transfer. Likewise is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Talha: "I think you should make it (*taj'alahā*) for the nearest relatives," that is, that you dispose of it to them. This *ja'ala* is transitive to one object, and this transitivity is the most common of its uses, to the extent that its transitivity to two objects is in reality one object and a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of it.

[Page 95]

The meaning of *dhara'a* is "to bring something into being and multiply it," so it is applied to growth, because bringing something into being is a multiplying and a growing.

﴿*mimmā dhara'a*﴾ ("of what He created") is connected to (*ja'alū*, "they assigned"), and *min* here is partitive (*tab'īḍiyya*), so it functions as the object. The *mā* is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*), and the use of the relative pronoun is to indicate by its clause the foolishness of their opinions, since they made Allah possess part of His own possession, for what He created is His possession, and it is rightfully His without any assignment from them.

The choice of the verb *dhara'a* here is because it is the one that indicates the intended meaning, since the purpose is to explain their corrupt legislations regarding the yields of their wealth. Later He will explain their legislation regarding the principles of their wealth in His words: ﴿And they say, "These are livestock and crops, forbidden [ḥijr]"﴾ [Al-An'am: 138], and so on.

﴿*mina al-ḥarth wa al-an'ām*﴾ ("of the crops and livestock") is an explanation of the relative *mā*.

*Al-ḥarth* means here crops and trees. It is originally an application of the verbal noun to the sense of the passive participle, and then this application became common until *al-ḥarth* became a conventional literal term for gardens and farms. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Go early to your tilth, if you are going to harvest﴾ [Al-Qalam: 22].

*Al-naṣīb* means portion and share. It has been mentioned in His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 202] in Surah al-Baqarah. The implied meaning is: they assigned to Allah a share, and to other than Him another share. From the context it is understood that the other share is for their gods, and this was made explicit in the consequence (*tafrī'*) of His words: ﴿They say, "This is for Allah, by their claim, and this is for our partners."﴾

The two demonstratives refer to the share determined for Allah and the share determined for the partners, and each of the two demonstratives points generally to one of the two shares, since in this context there is no purpose in specifying which was assigned to Allah and which was assigned to their partners.

*Al-za'm* means false belief, or what is close to error, as has preceded at His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you?﴾ [Al-Nisa': 60] in Surah al-Nisa'. It is pronounced with three vowels on the *zāy*, the best known being with a *fatḥa* on the *zāy*, and similarly *al-za'm* with the *rā'* having three vowels.

[Page 96]

al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read it with a *fatḥa* on the *zāy*, and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ḍamma* on the *zāy*. The phrase (*bi-za'mihim*, "by their claim") is attached to (*qālū*, "they said"), and the phrase (*bi-za'mihim*) was placed directly after part of the object of the saying so that it would be connected to what they assigned to Allah. Thus the astonishment at their judgment is arranged, that what was for Allah reaches their partners; that is, they were not content with their false claim until they backed away from it and associated their partners in what they had assigned to Allah by their claim.

The *bā'* that enters on *za'mihim* is either in the sense of *min* (from), meaning they said that with their tongues and announced it as a statement arising from the claim, that is, from false belief; or it is causal, meaning they said that because they claimed it.

The locus of the claim is what the division between Allah and the gods necessitated. Otherwise, saying that it belongs to Allah is a true statement, but since they said it with the meaning of specifying Allah's right in that share to the exclusion of another share, their statement became a false claim.

*Al-shurakā'* here is the plural of *sharīk*, that is, Allah's partner, exalted is He, in divinity. Since this became well known among them, it became like a proper name by dominance, so it dispensed with being annexed to what contains the derived meaning from which it comes, namely partnership. Then, because of its dominance in this meaning, it became like a title (*laqab*), so they annexed it to their pronoun and said: *li-shurakā'inā* ("for our partners"), a notional annexation (*iḍāfa ma'nawiyya*) and not a verbal one (*iḍāfa lafẓiyya*); that is, for the partners who are known through us. Ibn 'Abbas and his companions said: The polytheists used to assign to Allah from their crops, that is, their produce, their trees and their livestock, a share, and to the idols a share. What was for the idols they spent upon them, and what was for Allah they fed to the guests and the needy, and they never ate from it at all.

They also used to assign the *baḥīra*, the *sā'iba*, the *waṣīla* and the *ḥām* to the idols. Ibn Ishaq mentioned that Khawlan had an idol named "Amm Anas," and they would divide from their livestock and crops shares between it and Allah. So whatever entered the portion of "Amm Anas" from the portion of Allah that they had designated for Him, they left for the idol; and whatever entered the portion of Allah from the portion of "Amm Anas," they returned to him. Among them was a clan called the Adīm. He said: concerning them was revealed His words: ﴿They assigned to Allah from what He created﴾, to the end of the verse.

And His words: ﴿So what is for their partners does not reach Allah, while what is for Allah reaches their partners﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: When they gathered the crop, and the wind blew and carried some of what was for Allah to what was for their partners, they left it there and said, "Allah is free of it." And when it carried some of what was for their partners to what was for Allah, they returned it. When the property of their idols was destroyed by drought, they took a replacement from what was for Allah, and they did not do that with what was for Allah. When water from what they had assigned to Allah burst out and flowed onto what was for the one for the idols, they left it; and when water from what was for the idols burst out and entered the crop of the one for Allah, they blocked it.

When a year of famine struck them, they used what they had assigned to Allah and spent it on themselves, and they left what they had assigned to their partners for the partners. When what they had assigned to Allah was destroyed, they said, "Our gods must have some expenditure," and they took what they had assigned to Allah and spent it on them. When what was for Allah became barren and what was for their gods increased, they said, "If Allah had willed, He would have made what is for Him grow," and they would not return anything from what was for their gods to what they had assigned to Allah.

So His words ﴿does not reach Allah﴾ are an intensification in protecting Allah's share from being given to what is for Allah's partners, since if it does not reach Him, then it is all the more certain that it will not be taken when it has reached Him.

*Yaṣilu* is transitive to the name of Allah (*ism al-jalāla*) and to the name of their partners. The intended meaning is: it does not reach the share assigned to Allah, or to their partners; because when they assigned a share to Allah and a share to their partners, they had perceived that share as guarded for the one to whom it was assigned and in his custody, so it is as if it had reached his very self.

The sentence ﴿*sā'a mā yaḥkumūn*﴾ ("Evil is what they judge") is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nāf*) to establish the condemnation of their legislations. *Sā'a* here has the meaning of *bi'sa* ("how wretched"), and *mā* is the subject of *sā'a*; it is a relative pronoun whose clause is *yaḥkumūn*, and the returning pronoun in the accusative has been omitted. The specified object of the blame has also been omitted, indicated by *ja'alū* ("they assigned"); that is: evil is what they judge, their assigning. He called it a judgment (*ḥukm*) in mockery (*tahakkum*), because they appointed themselves to determine rights, so by their judgment they separated Allah's right from the right of the idols, then they permitted the idols to take Allah's right while Allah could not take the right of the idols. So it was a false judgment, like His words: ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 50].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 137 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And thus did their partner-deities make the killing of their children seem attractive to many of the polytheists, in order to ruin them and to confuse them about their religion. Had God willed, they would not have done it. So leave them alone with what they fabricate.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the preceding sentence, ﴿And they assigned to God a share of what He created of crops and livestock﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. The implied sense is: (They assigned) and their partner-deities made the killing of their children seem attractive to them, so they killed their children. This is the report of one kind of their false legislations, and it relates to their handling of their offspring after he had mentioned their handling of the produce of their wealth. God has magnified this amazing beautification of corruption, which made the most abhorrent things appear good: their killing of those most dear to them, who are their own sons and daughters. It is therefore described with the very same word "beautification," to indicate that if anyone wished to illustrate it with something equally monstrous and shameful, he could only illustrate it by itself, because nothing reaches the level of being more manifest in its kind than it. So he resorts to likening it to itself, in the manner of their saying: "Foolishness is like its name." The implied sense is: the partner-deities of the polytheists made attractive to many among them a beautification like that beautification which they had made attractive to them, and it is that very same thing. The detailed explanation of this has already passed in his words, ﴿And thus We made you a midmost nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of "tazyin" (beautification) is embellishment (tahsin), and it has already passed in his words, ﴿Thus We made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ [al-An'am: 108], in this surah.

[p. 99]

The meaning of this beautification here is that they imagined to them benefits and advantages in this killing, by presenting to them the harm of begging and the shame concerning women, that women cannot be expected to bring any benefit to the tribe, that they make the fathers cowardly at the meeting with the enemy, and that they prefer their husbands over their fathers. Thus they bring them meanings that sell well among them, for the Arabs were excessive in jealousy and in being driven by defeat and shame, as al-Nabighah said:

"Lest my leadership be taken, and my women too, until they die free."

He said, ﴿among many of the polytheists﴾, because the killing of children was not practised by all tribes. It was practised among Rabi'ah and Mudar, and these two are the bulk of the Arabs, and not every father from these two tribes did it.

He attributed the beautification to the partners either: (a) by intending the partner-satans, so that the beautification is the satans' beautification through whispering, and the attribution is then a true rational attribution (al-isnad al-haqiqi al-'aqli); or (b) because the beautification arose for them from the spreading of their elders among them, or from a law established for them by someone who instituted the worship of idols and imposed rights for them over their wealth, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy. In that case the attribution of the beautification to the partners is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the idols are the cause of that through one or two intermediaries. This is like His saying: ﴿So their gods, which they called upon besides God, did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came, and they added nothing but ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

What is meant by "killing of children" in this verse and similar ones is wa'd (infanticide by burying), which is burying young daughters alive so that they die suffocated by the dust. They used to do this out of fear of poverty, as God said: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31], and out of fear that the female would be exposed to need when her father died, or out of fear of captivity (al-sibaʾ). In Al-Rawd al-Unuf, citing al-Naqqash in his tafsir, it is mentioned that they used to bury those daughters who were blue-eyed, or spotted, or with a white blemish, or with a split lip, out of pessimism about them, and this was from the weakness of their illusions. He said that this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿When the buried girl is asked, for what sin was she killed?﴾ [al-Takwir: 8-9]. It was also said that they did this out of extreme jealousy, fearing that the women might commit something that would bring shame upon their families.

Al-Mubarrad mentioned in al-Kamil, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah, that Tamim withheld the tribute from al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir. So he sent against them his brother al-Rayyan ibn al-Mundhir, who drove off the camels and took the children captive. The Banu Tamim then sent a delegation to him, they repented and asked him for the women. Al-Nu'man said: "Every woman who chose her father shall be returned to him, and whoever chose her companion" (that is, the one to whom she had gone by capture) "shall be left with him." All of them chose their fathers except one daughter of Qays ibn 'Asim, who chose her companion 'Amr ibn al-Mushmarij. Qays then vowed that no daughter should be born to him except that he would kill her. This is a pretext used by those who buried their daughters; they say: "We did it out of pride (anafah)." God has refuted that in the Qur'an, by His saying: ﴿Those who killed their children have certainly lost, in foolishness﴾ [al-An'am: 140].

Al-Bukhari mentioned that Asma' bint Abi Bakr said: Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl used to revive buried girls. He would say to a man who intended to kill his daughter: "Do not kill her; I will take on her burden for you." He would take her, and when she grew up he would say to her father: "If you wish, I will give her to you; and if you wish, I will take on her burden for you."

It is well known that they used to bury the girl at the moment of her birth, before her mother saw her. God said: ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ [al-Nahl: 58]. ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given good news of. Shall he keep it despite contempt, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Nahl: 59].

Sa'sa'ah ibn Mu'awiyah, from Mujashi', who was the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, used to redeem buried girls, doing the same as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl did. Al-Farazdaq took pride in this in his poetry, in his saying:

"And among us is the one who prevented the burying mothers (from burying), and revived the buried girl, so she was not buried."

His grandfather lived to see Islam and became a Muslim. Nothing is known in the history of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period of killing their children other than this burying, except what came from the vow of 'Abd al-Muttalib, which we will mention. We do not know whether something like that occurred in the Jahiliyyah before 'Abd al-Muttalib, or whether he was the one who originated it and was not followed in it. There is no doubt that burying was a custom established by the leaders of polytheism for their people, since they did not act except on their opinion. It was therefore a misguidance they introduced to their people, with the pretext of freeing themselves from the obstacles to their raids against their enemies, and from the burden of poverty and captivity. Perhaps the servants of the idols (sadanah) used to urge them to carry out the matter of burying when they saw some of them being sluggish, as al-Kashshaf indicated when he said: "The meaning is that their partners, from the satans or from the servants of the idols, made attractive to them the killing of their children by burying or by sacrifice." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The partners according to this reading are those who take up the burying of other people's daughters, so they are the killers."

The story of 'Abd al-Muttalib supports this. He vowed that if God granted him ten male children who reached the age of protecting him from his enemy, he would sacrifice one of them at the Ka'bah. When his sons reached ten in number, he called them to fulfil his vow, and they obeyed him. He sought the decision by the arrows (istaqsama bil-azlam) at Hubal, the idol, and Hubal was inside the Ka'bah. The arrow fell upon his son 'Abd Allah, and he took him to slaughter him between Isaf and Na'ilah. Quraysh said to him: "Do not slaughter him until you have made an excuse concerning him. If there is a ransom for him, we will ransom him." They advised him to consult a soothsayer (arrafah) in Khaybar. They rode to her, asked her, and related the story to her. She said: "Bring near your companion, and bring near ten camels, then cast the arrows upon them and upon him. If it falls upon your companion, add more camels until your Lord is pleased." They did so, and the arrow fell upon 'Abd Allah. 'Abd al-Muttalib kept adding ten camels, casting the arrows upon them, and the arrow kept falling upon 'Abd Allah, until the camels reached one hundred. He then cast the arrows upon the camels, and the arrow fell upon the camels, so he slaughtered them.

Perhaps the servants of the idols used to mix the matter of burying with the intention of drawing near to the idols of some tribes, as was an inherited custom among the Canaanites of the Syrian Nabateans, who used to bring their children near to the idol Malik. So the attribution of the killing to the partners is used in its literal and figurative senses.

[p. 102]

Al-Jumhur read (zayyana) with a fatha on the zay and nasb of (qatla) as the object of (zayyana), and raf' of (shurakaʾuhum) as the subject of (zayyana), and jarr of (awladihim) by the idafah of (qatla) to it, as the idafah of a verbal noun to its object.

Ibn 'Amir read: "zuyyina li-kathirin mina al-mushrikina qatlu awladahum shurakaʾihim," with the verb "zuyyina" in the passive, raf' of "qatlu" as the deputy subject, nasb of "awladahum" as the object of "qatlu," and jarr of "shurakaʾihim" by the idafah of "qatlu" to it, as the idafah of a verbal noun to its agent. The word "shurakaʾihim" is likewise written in this way in the 'Uthmanic Mushaf which was in the lands of Syria. This is evidence that those who wrote that word observed the reading "shurakaʾihim" with a kasrah. They were people of eloquence and of thoroughness in the chain of transmission of the Qur'anic readings, since the word (shurakaʾihim) was written with a yaʾ after the alif, and this indicates that the hamzah is kasrah. The meaning, according to this reading, is that a beautifier made attractive to many of the polytheists that their partners should kill their children. The attribution of the killing to the partners is by way of rational metaphor, either because the partners are the cause of the killing if the killing was an offering to the idols, or because those who legislated the killing for them were the ones who upheld the religion of polytheism, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and those after him. If the intended killing is burying, then the partners are the cause, and if burying was an offering to the idols, even if it was not an offering to them (which is the known case), the partners are the cause of the cause, since it is from the laws of polytheism.

There is nothing in this reading that conflicts with the eloquence of the speech, because the i'rab (grammatical inflection) shows the meanings of the words and their positions. Their inflections differ between raf', nasb, and jarr so that there is no ambiguity, and the inflection of their words is clearly evident in them. Therefore the arrangement of its words in this form is not considered a complexity that undermines eloquence, unlike the complexity in the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And there is none like him among people, except one made king, whose maternal grandfather is alive, whose father approaches him (in rank)."

This is because it combined with the defect in the arrangement of the speech a defect in the pillars of the sentence and the multiplicity of similar pronouns surrounding it. There is nothing in the verse that contradicts established usage except the separation between the mudaf (the first term of the construct) and the mudaf ilayhi (the second term) by the object, and the matter in this is

[p. 103]

easy, because the object is not foreign to the mudaf and mudaf ilayhi. Al-Zamakhshari, however, came with terror, outcry, and lamentation regarding this: "How is the mudaf separated from the mudaf ilayhi by the object?" The drum of denial added a further note, and he said: "What led him to that is that he saw in some of the Mushafs 'shurakaʾihim' written with a yaʾ." This is a practice of al-Zamakhshari in belittling the mutawatir readings whenever they contradict what the science of grammar has codified, because he imagines that the readings are the choices and analogies of the readers, whereas they are in fact sound, mass-transmitted narrations. The i'rab provides an indication of the intended meaning and does not undermine eloquence.

The compilations of grammar were intended only to fix the prevalent rules of the Arabic language so that those learning Arabic might follow them. They are not restricted to the usage of the eloquent Arabs. The readers are a proof against the grammarians, not the reverse. The rules of grammar only forbid the analogical extension by later generations of what occurred rarely in eloquent speech, and rarity does not contradict eloquence. Would one suppose of someone like Ibn 'Amir that he reads the Qur'an in following the written form of the letters of orthography? Such a thing would not deceive beginners in the science of Arabic. Would not the form of the Mushaf in that shape have been a guide to al-Zamakhshari, to notice the reason for that writing? As for Ibn 'Atiyyah, he said: "It is a weak reading in the usage of the Arabs." He means that this separation is rare, but this does not prove the weakness of the reading, because rarity does not contradict eloquence.

Ibn 'Atiyya (Ibn Atiyya) weakened this reading on the grounds that it does not suit the causal particle in His saying: ﴿that they may ruin them﴾. Ibn Atiyya's weakening of it is a misconception, since there is no contradiction between their adorning for them the killing of their children and the causal sense, for the causal particle (lam al-ta'lil, the particle of purpose) is used for the outcome figuratively, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. And it is strange what al-Tabari said: "The reading I do not permit other than is with the zay vowelled with a fatha, the ''qatl'' (killing) in the accusative, the ''awladihim'' (their children) in the genitive, and ''shurakauhum'' (their associates) in the nominative." This was in keeping with his habit of setting himself up as the judge in weighing between the readings.

The lam in ﴿li-yurduhum﴾ is the lam of outcome if by "the associates" are meant the idols; that is, they adorned for them that act for the sake of benefiting them, and it turned out to harm them in ways they did not know. If by "the associates" are meant the jinn, that is, the devils, then the lam is the lam of causation, because leading into evil is part of the nature of whispering, for it finds evil pleasing and is drawn toward it as the scorpion is drawn to sting, without intending that what it calls them to should be ruinous and confusing. Their allies do not intend to harm them, but when they called them to things which are in reality harms, their adornment was causally connected with ruin and confusion, even if they did not perceive it. This is unlike one who calls for a reason which is then shown to be otherwise. The pronoun refers to the associates, and the causal clause concerns the adornment.

"Al-irda'" (ruin) is causing someone to fall into ruin (al-radaa), and "al-radaa" is death, and it is used figuratively or metaphorically for severe harm, and that is what is meant here.

"Labbasa 'alayhi" means he caused him to fall into confusion (al-labs), which is mixing and confusion. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying: ﴿And We would surely have confused for them what they confuse﴾ [al-An'am: 9] in this surah. That is: they mix up their religion for them, making them think that misguidance is right guidance and that it is what God desires from them. So they draw near to God and to the idols, so that the idols bring them near to God, and they do not distinguish between what God is pleased with and what He is not pleased with. They imagine to them that burying daughters alive is a benefit. Among their sayings is: "Burying the daughters is from honour" (the "buna" and "makrumah" with the ha' pronounced as a sukun at the end of both). Their original form is the taa' of the feminine plural, but it was altered to lighten the proverb. Such is the nature of misleading doubts and assumed proofs that are not based on any evidence. So the meaning of ﴿and that they may confuse them in their religion﴾ is that they produce for them a religion mixed from kinds of falsehood, as one says: "Widen the robe," that is, make it wide. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that they bring confusion into them regarding the religion they were upon, which is the religion of Isma'il, peace be upon him, that is, the ḥanīfiyya; so they put into it things of falsehood which mix with the truth.

As for the discussion of the meaning of ﴿And had God willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they fabricate﴾, it is like the discussion of His earlier saying: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. The pronoun of the subject in "fa'aluhu" (they did it) refers to the polytheists; that is, had God willed, He would have preserved them from the adornment of their associates. Or it refers to the associates; that is, had God willed, He would have prevented them from misleading their followers. The pronoun of the object refers to the killing or to the adornment, distributed according to the two possibilities for the pronoun of the subject.

What is meant by "what they fabricate" is what they fabricate against God by attributing to Him that He commanded them to what they committed. Their fabrication was following the fabrication of their associates, so it was called fabrication, because they adopted it without reflection or reasoning. It is as though they shared with those who invented it among the devils, or the custodians of the idols, or the leaders of the religion of polytheism. They used to disguise to the people that this was among what God had commanded, as is indicated by His saying in the verse after this: "a fabrication against Him," and His saying at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who testify that God has forbidden this﴾ [al-An'am: 150].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 138:

﴿They say: "These are livestock and tilled land, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we will" — by their own claim — "and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden, and livestock over which they do not mention the name of God, fabricating against Him. He will repay them for what they used to fabricate."﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And thus did their partners make attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [6:137]. This is another kind of their false religion, and it returns to placing restrictions on their own disposal of some of their wealth and specifying its uses. In this coordination there is also an indication that what they said came from the prompting of their partners and the custodians (sadana) of their idols, as we said regarding the meaning of "their partners made attractive to them."

The demonstratives "this" (hadhihi) and "these" (hadhihi) refer to something present in the minds of the speakers at the time that statement was uttered. That is, one of them would say: "This idol, its disposal is such-and-such, and this one, its disposal is such-and-such." So the demonstrative is part of the quoted speech, as they speak while explaining the rulings of their religion, just as the distributor of shares says: "This is for so-and-so, and this is for the other." He summarized this here, since there is no purpose in detailing it, because the purpose is to express wonder at the corruption of their law, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿They say: "This is for God" — by their claim — "and this is for our partners."﴾ [6:136]. They divided this into three categories.

The first category: livestock whose owner is restricted from benefiting from it, and only the one designated by the owner may benefit from it. What is taken from what is narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd and others is that they would designate some of their livestock, crops and fruits, restricting themselves from benefiting from them, and would assign them to whomever they wished among the custodians of the idol-houses and their servants. Such livestock would be slaughtered when the one assigned to it sees fit, so that it would serve the needs of the people and the visitors and guests at the idol-houses. Likewise, crops and fruits would be given to the one assigned to them, who spends them wherever he is designated. Among this category are things specified by name, with a fixed established ruling, such as the baḥīra (a she-camel whose ear was slit), which is neither slaughtered nor eaten unless it dies a natural death; then its meat is lawful for men but not for women. If it has milk, only the custodians of the idols and their guests may drink it. Likewise the sāʾiba (a freed animal) whose milk is enjoyed by travellers and the custodians; if it dies, its meat is treated like that of the baḥīra. Likewise the ḥāmī (a stallion set free), as was mentioned in surah al-Ma'ida.

So the meaning of "none may eat of them" (lā yaṭamuhā) is: none may eat its flesh; that is, eating its flesh is forbidden. The plural "nu" in "nashāʾu" (we will) refers to the speakers; that is, they say: none may eat of them except whom we will, i.e., whom we designate to eat of them. In al-Kashshaf he said: they mean the servants of the idols and men, but not women.

The word ḥarth (tilled land) originally means cutting the earth with an iron tool in order to sow or plant in it. This verbal noun is used to refer to the place that is tilled, and to land that is sown or planted even if there is currently no crop on it. From this is His saying: ﴿Go early to your tilled land, if you are going to harvest﴾ [68:22], where He called it a ḥarth at the time of harvesting the fruit.

al-Ḥijr is a name for what is forbidden (al-maḥjūr), like dhibḥ for what is slaughtered (al-madhbūḥ). So the prohibition on livestock is a prohibition on eating their meat, and the prohibition on tilled land is a prohibition on eating the grain, dates and fruits. For this reason He said: ﴿none may eat of them except whom we will﴾.

His saying "by their claim" (bi-zaʿmihim) is a parenthetical insertion between "none may eat of them except whom we will" and "and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden."

The bāʾ in "bi-zaʿmihim" means "concerning" (ʿan), or it indicates accompaniment (lil-mulābasa); that is, they say this with their false belief. Because when they said "none may eat of them," they did not mean that they prevented people from eating them except those they wished, since that is their own action and not their claim. Rather, by the negation they meant the negation of permissibility; that is, it is not lawful for anyone to eat of them except whom we will. So the meaning is: they believed these to be forbidden to anyone other than those they designated, even themselves, and they are not forbidden. This is the position of the phrase "by their claim." The preceding of "by their claim" was mentioned just before, at His saying: ﴿They say: "This is for God" — by their claim﴾ [6:136].

The second category: livestock whose backs are forbidden, i.e., riding them is forbidden. Among them is the ḥāmī: no one rides it. It has a followed rule, as was mentioned in surah al-Ma'ida. Among them are livestock whose backs they forbid by vow. One of them would say: "If the she-camel does such-and-such regarding offspring, or the continuous pairing among a number of females, and if the stallion does such-and-such, then its back is forbidden." Abu Nuwas alluded to this in his verse praising al-Amin:

"When the mounts bring us to Muhammad, their backs are forbidden to men."

So His saying "and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden" is coordinated with "there are livestock and tilled land, forbidden." It is therefore like a predicate of the demonstrative. It is understood to be coordination of a category because it comes after the completion of the descriptions that were applied to the predicate of the demonstrative and to the item coordinated with it. The estimated sense is: "They said: 'These are livestock and tilled land, forbidden, and these are livestock whose backs are forbidden.'"

The verb "were forbidden" (ḥurrimat) is in the passive because the agent is evident; that is, God forbade their backs, by the indication of His saying: ﴿fabricating against Him﴾.

The third category: livestock over which they do not mention the name of God; that is, they do not mention the name of God at its slaughter or sacrifice. They claim that what is offered to the jinn or to the idols is mentioned by the name of that to which it is offered, and they claim that God commanded this so that it would be purely an offering for what it was designated for. Because of this claim, He said: ﴿fabricating against Him﴾, since it is not conceivable that God would be attributed with forbidding the mention of His name over what is offered to others, unless they claimed that this is part of the offering which God is pleased with, since it is for His partners, as they used to say: "Here I am, O God, You have no partner except a partner who belongs to You, whom You possess and whom he does not possess."

It is narrated from a group of exegetes, among them Abu Wa'il, that the livestock over which they do not mention the name of God was, for them, a custom with regard to some livestock that no pilgrimage was to be performed upon. Such animals were ridden in every way except for the pilgrimage. It is these that are meant by His saying: ﴿and livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾, because the pilgrimage does not go without mention of God at the time of riding the mount, such as the talbiya and the takbir. Therefore "they do not mention the name of God over them" is a metonymy for prohibiting the pilgrimage upon them. The apparent view is that these are the ḥāmī, the baḥīra and the sāʾiba, since when they assigned their benefit to the idols, they did not allow them to be used for anything other than serving the idols.

His saying "and livestock over which they do not mention the name of God" is coordinated with His saying: [p. 109] ﴿and livestock whose backs are forbidden﴾. It is coordination of a category upon a category, by the indication of the completion of the descriptions of the item coordinated upon, as was mentioned in its parallel.

The phrase ﴿fabricating against Him﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of "they said" (qālū); that is, they said that statement as a statement of fabrication, since fabrication is one kind of speech. So it is valid for it to be in the accusative as an absolute object specifying the type of speech. Fabrication (iftirāʾ) is lying for which the speaker has no basis. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Then whoever fabricates a lie against God after that, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [3:94] in surah Al 'Imran, and at His saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ [5:103] in surah al-'Uqud. Their saying was fabrication because they relied in it on something that did not come to them from God at all, but rather from the misguidance of their elders.

The clause ﴿He will repay them for what they used to fabricate﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (istiʾnāf bayānī), because fabricating against the Creator is a grave matter in the view of all creation. So the report of it raises the question of one who asks what punishment they will receive for their fabrication. He was answered that God will repay them for what they used to fabricate. The recompense has been left unspecified for the sake of awe, so that minds may go in every possible direction regarding the kinds of recompense for sin. The bāʾ in "bi-mā" means "for" (ʿan), or it indicates exchange and compensation (lil-badaliyya wal-ʿiwaḍ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 139:

﴿They say: "What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives; but if it is stillborn, then they are partners in it. He will repay them for their description. Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing."﴾

It is a conjunction with His saying: ﴿And they say, "These livestock and crops are forbidden, sealed off"﴾ [al-An'am: 138], and the verb (wa-qalu, "they said") is repeated because the subject of what is said differs.

The reference is to livestock known among them by their attributes, as has been mentioned previously, or to the livestock mentioned before. In this verse, no purpose is served beyond a general summary of the things they forbade, because the aim is to express wonder at the corruption of their law, as has been mentioned just above. This is a report about their religion concerning the fetuses of the livestock which they sealed off or whose backs they forbade. They used to say of the fetuses of the baheera and the sa'iba: if they come out alive, their eating is lawful to the males only, not the females; and if they come out dead, their eating is lawful to both males and females. Therefore, what is "in the wombs" means fetuses without any doubt, given His saying: ﴿but if it is stillborn﴾. They also used to say concerning the milk of the baheera and the sa'iba: men drink it, not women. Some exegetes thought that what is "in the wombs of the livestock" means their milk, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. This is not what the verse should mean, but the import of Ibn 'Abbas's words is that what is in the wombs includes the milk, because it follows the fetuses and arises from their birth.

Al-khalisa: the lawful, i.e., the permitted; that is, there is no trace of prohibition in it, i.e., in eating it. Its opposite is His saying: (and forbidden).

The feminine form of khalisa is because the intended referent of the relative (ma) is the fetuses; the meaning of (ma) was observed in khalisa, and the wording of (ma) was observed in the masculine of muharram.

Al-muharram: the prohibited; that is, its eating is prohibited. So the attribution of exclusivity and prohibition to the entities is by way of interpreting it as the prohibition of what it is intended for, namely eating, or eating and drinking, by the indication of implication (dalalat al-iqtida').

Al-azwaj is the plural of zawj, which is a description of the second of two things in relation to the other; each one of two things is a zawj, and for this reason the husband of a woman is called zawj and the woman is called the zawj of a man. It is a description that persists in one state, so it is not made feminine, dualized, or pluralized. It has been discussed previously at His saying: ﴿O Adam, dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqara: 35] in Surat al-Baqara.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is prohibited to married women, because they called them azwaj and attributed them to their own pronoun, so it is determined that they are the women married to them, as one says: "the wife of so-and-so." If we take it according to its apparent meaning, which in my view is preferable, this indicates that they considered it ill-omened for their wives to eat something having a certain attribute, which they disliked befalling their women, such as barrenness, or bad companionship with husbands, rebelliousness, or separation, or other illusions and fabrications of the people of ignorance; or because it is the offspring of sacred livestock, it is not lawful for women. For women were regarded among the ancients before Islam as impure and defiled, on account of menstruation and the like. The Children of Israel used to prevent women from entering the mosques, and the Arabs would not eat with a menstruating woman. Kabsha bint Ma'd Yakrib said, rebuking her people:

"And do not drink except the leftovers of your women, when their hind parts are stained with blood."

The majority of exegetes said: the word azwaj was applied to women in general; that is, it is a metonymic figure (majaz mursal) by the relation of generality and specificity, so it includes the widow but does not include daughters. Some said: it means daughters; that is, by the first metaphor. Perhaps they considered it ill-omened to eat from it by daughters, lest they suffer difficulty in marriage, or something they would be ashamed of, or the like, and the common customs among them indicated this meaning.

As for His saying: ﴿but if it is stillborn, then they are partners in it﴾, that is: if what is in the wombs of the livestock is born dead, its eating is lawful for the men and the wives, or for the men and the women, or for the men, the women, and the daughters, because its coming out dead nullifies the ill-omen it carries for the woman, or removes its sanctity, or the like.

Al-Jumhur recited: wa-in yakun with the yā' (third person) and the accusative (mayyita). Ibn Kathir recited (mayyitatun) with the nominative, taking kana as complete (tammah). The pronoun of (yakun) has been made masculine, because it is permissible for the predicate concerning a singular relative noun to observe the masculine, since its wording is free of a feminine marker; and its intended sense may be observed, so the predicate follows that consideration, and both have been combined in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave from your presence﴾ [Muhammad: 16].

Ibn 'Amir recited with the tā' (feminine) following the feminine of khalisa; that is: if the fetuses are (in takun al-ajinna); and he recited (mayyita) with the accusative. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited with the feminine and the accusative.

The clause ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), as I said regarding the clause ﴿He will repay them for what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-An'am: 138] just above.

Al-wasf: mentioning the states of the described thing and what distinguishes it, for one who wishes to distinguish it for some purpose. It has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100] in this surah.

The description here is what they attributed to the fetuses of permissibility and prohibition for one group over another; this is a description in explaining the lawful and unlawful of it, like His saying: ﴿And do not say, for what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116].

Their recompense for it is a recompense of evil, by the context, since He named their previous claims a fabrication against Allah.

The recompense was made to govern the description directly, on an implied omission: He will repay them the recompense of their description; the verb (yajziyahum) was made to include the sense of (yu'tihim), that is, a recompense commensurate with it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ is a justification for the recompense being commensurate with the offence of their description. (Inna) indicates connection and causation, and it does the work of the fa' (therefore). The Wise places things in their proper places, and the All-Knowing is aware of the deeds of those who are recompensed, so He does not neglect from them anything that deserves recompense.

[Page 113]

﴿Those have indeed lost who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and forbade what God had provided for them, fabricating against God. They have indeed gone astray, and they were not guided.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that restates the point) placed as a *fadhlaka* (summary) of the preceding discourse, which explained their error in killing their children and in prohibiting some of the lawful things to those for whom they were lawful.

The verb is emphasized with *qad* (indeed) to draw attention to the fact that their loss is established. This emphasis conveys wonder at how they became blind to the loss they are in. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: "If it pleases you to know the ignorance of the Arabs, then recite what comes after the one hundred and thirtieth verse of Surat al-An'am, *'Those have indeed lost who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge'*, up to *'and they were not guided'*." That is, from His saying, *﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has produced of the crops and livestock﴾* [al-An'am: 136]. He counted it as after the one hundred and thirtieth verse approximately, and it is the one hundred and thirty-sixth in the count.

Their action is described as loss because the true meaning of loss is the diminishing of a merchant's capital. The merchant intends profit, which is increase. When he suffers loss, he ends up with the opposite of what he worked for. For this reason, the Qur'an frequently uses the metaphor of loss for the deeds of those who act seeking God's pleasure and reward but end up incurring His wrath and punishment, because they wearied themselves and obtained the opposite of what they toiled for. Those who killed their children sought to benefit themselves by escaping harms in this world, harms that might possibly befall them through their daughters. Instead, they fell into certain harms in this world and in the Hereafter. Offspring is a blessing from God to parents, who find comfort in them and rely on them to fulfill their needs. It is a blessing to the tribe, which grows and gains strength. It is a blessing to the whole world through the multiplication of those who populate it and through the benefits people derive from the gifts and crafts of offspring. And it is a blessing to the offspring themselves through the pleasures and delights of life that they attain.

For these benefits, God's wisdom required the establishment of the system of procreation, to preserve the species, to populate the world, and to reveal the gifts within humans that benefit them and their people. Their action was also a transgression against the right of the daughter, which God granted her, namely the right to life until the appointed term for her ends. This is a natural right that the father does not own. Therefore, it is clear injustice, undertaken in hope of benefit to someone other than the wronged party, and it does not harm anyone to benefit another. When some of the Arabs killed their daughters by burying them alive (*wa'd*), they neglected great and certain interests and committed harms that were actually realized. They did this because they wanted to escape slight harms that were not certain to occur. So, undoubtedly, in their action they were like the merchant who sought profit and ended up losing the very capital he had. For this reason, God called their action *safah* (foolishness), because *safah* is lightness and disturbance of the intellect. Their act was pure foolishness, that is, a foolishness greater than the loss of abundant interests and the commission of great harms and a shameful crime, all to escape slight harms that may or may not occur. The expression of the subject by the relative pronoun indicates that the relative clause is the cause of the predicate, since their loss results from the killing of their children.

His saying *"safahan"* (foolishly) is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) specifying the type of killing: that it was a killing of foolishness with no sound judgment behind it, unlike killing an enemy or killing a murderer. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of *alladhina qatalu* (those who killed), describing them with the verbal noun because they were foolish people reaching the utmost foolishness.

The *ba'* in His saying *"bi-ghayri 'ilm"* (without knowledge) indicates accompaniment. It is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, either from *safahan*, in which case it is an emphatic circumstance, since foolishness can only occur without knowledge, or from the subject of *qatalu*. In the latter case, when they committed the killing they were ignorant of their own foolishness, of the vileness of their deed, and of the outcome of the harm they had assumed would befall them, since what they expected may turn out differently. Had they weighed benefits and harms, they would never have undertaken this atrocious act.

The purpose of stating that it was *"without knowledge"* after having said that it was *safah* is to alert that they committed all the corruptions in the world while arranging their lives in the best order, and that in this they are deluded by themselves and ignorant that they are ignorant. *﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in their work﴾* [al-Kahf: 104].

The discussion of burying alive (*wa'd*) has preceded just now, and it will come in Surat al-Isra' at His saying: *﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾* [al-Isra': 31].

The majority read *"qatalu awladahum"* with a light *ta'* (qatalu). Ibn 'Amir read it with a doubled *ta'* (qattalu), because it is killing with intensity. The majority's reading does not fail to convey this meaning, since attributing the act of killing to the children indicates that it is a hideous killing.

His saying *"wa harramu ma razaqahumu Allah"* (and they forbade what God had provided for them) reproaches them for their loss in forbidding for themselves some of what God had provided, so they were deprived of its benefit and deprived others of benefiting from it. This applies to all polytheists, unlike those who killed their children. When a relative pronoun refers to a group, it is correct for the coordinated clauses following its relative clause to be distributed among the groups of that collective, as in His saying: *﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God, and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who enjoin justice among people, give them the news of a painful punishment﴾* [Al 'Imran: 21].

*"Ifteraan"* (fabricating) is in the accusative as an absolute object of *harramu* (forbade), specifying the type of prohibition: that they attributed it to God falsely.

The clause *"qad dallu"* (they have indeed gone astray) is a fresh, independent resumption, to add emphasis to the establishment of their error.

*Al-dalal* (error) is deviation from the path that leads to the intended goal. They aimed to reach worldly benefits and to draw near to God and to their associates, but they fell into great corruptions. God removed them further away because of their sins, so they were like one who intends to arrive but takes another road.

The coordination of *"wa ma kanu muhtadin"* (and they were not guided) upon *"qad dallu"* serves the purpose of emphasizing the content of the clause *dallu*, because the content of this clause negates the opposite of the first clause, so that it returns to confirming its meaning.

When the Arabs emphasize with something like this, they may use it without coordination, considering the eventual meaning of the two clauses, that they are with this consideration of one meaning, and that is the proper form of emphasis, as in His saying: *﴿They are dead, not alive﴾* [al-Nahl: 21], and His saying: *﴿So that Day will be a difficult day, not easy for the disbelievers﴾* [al-Muddaththir: 9–10], and the verse of al-A'sha:

*"Though you see us barefoot, having no sandals"*

They may also use it with coordination, and this coordination is formal, because it takes into account that the concepts of the two clauses differ, and it does not take into account their eventual meaning, as in His saying: *﴿Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾* [Ta-Ha: 79], His saying: *﴿Then I would indeed have gone astray, and I am not among the guided﴾* [al-An'am: 56], and the verse of al-Mutanabbi:

*"Separation has wronged my weakness and did not act justly"*

Similarly, this verse came with coordination to convey, through the conjunction, that the two clauses are two reports about their evil deeds.

*Kana* (was) here is treated as if it were a superfluous particle, because it is superfluous in meaning, though it is functioning grammatically. The intended meaning is "and they are not guided". So the presence of *kana* here serves to strengthen the negation, in the same position it holds with the *lam* of denial (*lam al-juhud*). The intended meaning is not that they were not guided before they killed their children and forbade what God had provided, because this does not carry an eloquent purpose.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who brings into being gardens, both trellised and untrellised, and the palm trees and crops of varying produce, and the olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar.﴾

The wāw in ﴿وهُوَ الَّذِي أنْشَأ﴾ (wa-huwa alladhī ansha') is for conjunction (ʿaṭf), so this sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿وحَرَّمُوا ما رَزَقَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ (And they have forbidden what God has provided for them) [al-Anʿām: 140], as a reminder of God's favour upon people through what He brought into being for them on earth that benefits them. After clarifying the bad conduct of the polytheists regarding what God had bestowed upon all people, together with the folly of their opinions in forbidding some of it to themselves, He conjoined to it the mention of the favour in this matter, to bring them down toward perceiving the truth and turning back from error. For this reason, most of what was mentioned in its counterpart earlier was repeated in this verse, in His saying: ﴿وهُوَ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأخْرَجْنا بِهِ نَباتَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ فَأخْرَجْنا مِنهُ خَضِرًا نُخْرِجُ مِنهُ حَبًّا مُتَراكِبًا ومِنَ النَّخْلِ مِن طَلْعِها قِنْوانٌ دانِيَةٌ وجَنّاتٍ مِن أعْنابٍ والزَّيْتُونَ والرُّمّانَ مُشْتَبِهًا وغَيْرَ مُتَشابِهٍ انْظُرُوا إلى ثَمَرِهِ إذا أثْمَرَ ويَنْعِهِ﴾ (It is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth by it the growth of every thing; then We bring forth from it green produce, from which We bring forth grain piled up; and from the palm tree, from its spathe, hanging clusters within reach; and gardens of grapevines, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and its ripening.) [al-Anʿām: 99]. This is because the purpose of the first verse was to argue that He is the Maker, and that He alone is the Creator; so how can they associate others with Him? For this reason it was concluded with His saying: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكم لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe) [al-Anʿām: 99], and conjoined to it His saying: ﴿وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ الجِنَّ﴾ (And they have made the jinn partners with God) [al-Anʿām: 100], and so on.

The purpose of this verse is the expression of favour and the nullification of what contradicts favour; for this reason it is concluded with His saying: ﴿كُلُوا مِن ثَمَرِهِ إذا أثْمَرَ﴾ (Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit).

The address is directed to both believers and polytheists, since it is a matter of consideration and favour, and believers have the greatest share of that. For this reason He followed it with the command to render God's right in it, by His saying: ﴿وآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حِصادِهِ﴾ (And give its due on the day of its harvest), since that address is not suitable for the polytheists.

The definiteness of the predicate (al-musnad) indicates restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ); that is, He is the One who brought it into being, not other than Him. The purpose of this restriction is the nullification of any other having a share in them, in refutation of what they had assigned from the tillage and livestock as the portion of their idols, although it is God who brought it into being.

Inshā' (ינشاء) means bringing into existence and creating. God says: ﴿إنّا أنْشَأْناهُنَّ إنْشاءً﴾ (Indeed We have brought them into being with a (special) creation) [al-Wāqiʿah: 35], meaning the women of Paradise.

The jannāt (gardens) are the places of land in which many trees grow such that they conceal (yajinn), i.e., cover, whatever is in them. This was already discussed at His saying: ﴿كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍ بِرَبْوَةٍ﴾ (like a garden on a height) [al-Baqarah: 265] in Surat al-Baqarah. Its inshā' is its growing, and facilitating that by providing it with what helps it to thrive and repelling what corrupts it or cuts off its growth, as in His saying: ﴿أأنْتُمْ تَزْرَعُونَهُ أمْ نَحْنُ الزّارِعُونَ﴾ (Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the Growers?) [al-Wāqiʿah: 64].

Al-maʿrūshāt means the raised ones. It is said: "ʿarasha al-karmah" when he raised the vine on pillars so that its growth would be upward and not on the surface of the ground, because that is better for its grapes, since they are not lying on the ground. ʿArasha is a verb derived from al-ʿarsh, which is the roof. The pillars on which the branches of trees are raised, so that they become like a roof under which the sitter shades himself, are called al-ʿarīsh. From this is what is mentioned in the Sīrah: the ʿarīsh that was made for the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr, and on its site a mosque was built afterwards, which exists today in Badr.

Describing the gardens as maʿrūshāt is a rational metonymy (majāz ʿaqlī); rather, it is the trellising that is in them, and the trellised things are their trees. The untrellised ones are the vines left to spread flat on the surface of the ground, or raised slightly. Among their beauties is that they adorn the face of the earth, so that the beholder sees all of it green.

His saying: ﴿مَعْرُوشاتٍ وغَيْرَ مَعْرُوشاتٍ﴾ is an attribute of (jannāt). It is intended to beautify the described thing and to remind of God's blessing in inspiring people to make them in two forms, for mentioning the beauties of what God has brought into being increases the favour. Like His saying concerning the livestock: ﴿ولَكم فِيها جَمالٌ حِينَ تُرِيحُونَ وحِينَ تَسْرَحُونَ﴾ (And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you drive them out) [al-Naḥl: 6].

﴿مُخْتَلِفًا أُكْلُهُ﴾ (of varying produce) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of al-zarʿ (the crops), being the nearest of the mentioned items to the ḥāl. It is known that the palm trees and the gardens are likewise. The purpose is to remind of the wondrous creation of God, so mentioning the ḥāl with one of the kinds conveys the recollection of its like in the other kind. This is like His saying: ﴿وإذا رَأوْا تِجارَةً أوْ لَهْوًا انْفَضُّوا إلَيْها﴾ (And when they see a trade or amusement, they break away to it) [al-Jumuʿah: 11], meaning: and to it.

It is a ḥāl muqaddarah (a future/anticipated circumstance) according to the apparent view of the grammarians, because it is independent of the inshā'. In my view, if the governing element of the ḥāl is something whose meaning occurs over times, and the ḥāl is contemporaneous with some of the times of its governing element, then it is worthy of being contemporaneous, as here.

Al-ukul, with a ḍammah on the hamzah and sukūn on the kāf, is read by Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr; the rest read it with ḍammah on both. It means that which is eaten; that is, varying in what is eaten from it.

﴿والزَّيْتُونَ والرُّمّانَ﴾ (and the olives and pomegranates) is conjoined to: gardens, palm trees and crops. What is meant is the olive tree and the pomegranate tree. The discussion of its counterpart was already given at His saying: ﴿وهُوَ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً﴾ [al-Anʿām: 99] in this surah.

Except that there He said: (mushtabihan) and here He said: (mutashābihan); both have one meaning, because similarity arises from two sides, so the form of tafāʿul is not for intensification. Do you not see that they are equal in His saying: ﴿وغَيْرَ مُتَشابِهٍ﴾ in both verses?
