﴿كُلُوا مِن ثَمَرِهِ إذا أثْمَرَ وآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حِصادِهِ ولا تُسْرِفُوا إنَّهُ لا يُحِبُّ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾

He changed the style of narration about the states of the polytheists and turned to address the believers with this favour and this ruling. These sentences are parenthetical (muʿtaraḍah), and they are an indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the folly of the polytheists' minds for forbidding to themselves what God had bestowed upon them.

Al-thamar: with fatḥah on the thāʾ and the mīm, and with ḍammah on both, and it has been read with both, as its explanation was given in its counterpart.

The command is for permission (ibāḥah), by the indication that eating is a right of the person which is not obligatory for him to do,

صفحة ١٢٠ *(page 120)*

so the indication is evident, and the purpose is to refute those who restricted themselves from some of the tillage.

﴿إذا﴾ (idhā, "when") indicates a time-frame, since it is an adverb; that is, at the time of its bearing fruit. The purpose of restricting it with this adverb is the permission to eat from it at its appearance and before its harvest, as a preparation for His saying: ﴿وآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حِصادِهِ﴾ (And give its due on the day of its harvest); that is, eat of it before rendering its due. This is a concession and a favour, because the ʿazīmah (strict original ruling) is that they should not eat except after giving its due, lest they monopolize something of it to the exclusion of those entitled to it. However, He permitted people to eat, as a widening upon them, to eat of it green before it dries, because they find it pleasant that way. For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿ولا تُسْرِفُوا﴾ (and do not be excessive), as will come.

The singularity of the two pronouns in His saying: ﴿مِن ثَمَرِهِ إذا أثْمَرَ﴾ is according to considering the referent as interpreted as the mentioned thing.

The command in His saying: ﴿وآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حِصادِهِ﴾ is a specific address to the believers, as already mentioned. This command is apparent as obligatory, by the indication that the commanded thing is called a ḥaqq (right).

The ḥaqq is attributed to the pronoun of the mentioned thing by the closest connection; that is, the right that is in it.

The ḥaqq has been left general, relying on what they know of it, and it is: the right of the poor, the kin, the weak, and the neighbours. The Arabs, when they cut their fruits, would give from them to whoever was present of the needy and relatives. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿فانْطَلَقُوا وهم يَتَخافَتُونَ﴾ (So they set off, whispering to one another) [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿أنْ لا يَدْخُلَنَّها اليَوْمَ عَلَيْكم مِسْكِينٌ﴾ (That no needy person shall enter it today against you) [al-Qalam: 24]. When Islam came, it made this ḥaqq obligatory upon the Muslims and named it a ḥaqq, as in His saying: ﴿والَّذِينَ في أمْوالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَعْلُومٌ﴾ (And those in whose wealth there is a known right) [al-Maʿārij: 24] ﴿لِلسّائِلِ والمَحْرُومِ﴾ (for the beggar and the deprived) [al-Dhāriyāt: 19]. He named it zakāh in many verses, but He left its quantity unspecified and left unspecified the kinds in which the ḥaqq is, entrusting them in that to their eagerness for good. This was before the prescribing of its thresholds (nuṣub) and its amounts. Then zakāh was legislated, and the Sunnah clarified its thresholds and amounts.

صفحة ١٢١

Al-ḥaṣād (harvest), with kasrah or fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, is the cutting of the fruit and the grain from their roots. It is a maṣdar on the pattern fiʿāl or faʿāl. Sībawayh said: "They used the maṣdars when they wanted the end of the time, on the pattern fiʿāl, and these are: al-ṣirām, al-jizāz, al-jidād, al-qiṭāʿ and al-ḥiṣād." Perhaps the language varies in some of this—i.e., the dialects differ: some tribes said ḥaṣād with fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, and some said ḥiṣād with kasrah on the ḥāʾ; so there were fiʿāl and faʿāl in it. When they wanted the verb on the pattern faʿalta, they said: ḥaṣadtuhu ḥaṣdan and qaṭaʿtuhu qaṭʿan, meaning only the action, not the end of the period.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read it with kasrah on the ḥāʾ; Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with fatḥah on the ḥāʾ.

Zakāh was prescribed at the beginning of Islam along with the prescribing of ṣalāh, or shortly after it, because its obligation is necessary for sustaining the needy among the Muslims, who were numerous in the early days of Islam; for those who embraced Islam had been cast off by their families and clients, had denied their rights, and had seized their property. So it was necessary that the wealthy and strong among the Muslims fill their need. Mention of zakāh has come in many verses revealed at Makkah, such as Surat al-Muzzammil and Surat al-Bayyinah, which are among the early surahs of the Qur'an; so zakāh is the companion of ṣalāh.

The saying of some commentators that zakāh was prescribed in Madinah aims at fixing its amounts by the verse: ﴿خُذْ مِن أمْوالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهم وتُزَكِّيهِمْ بِها﴾ (Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow) [al-Tawbah: 103], which is Madani. Then they went on to deny that the ḥaqq here means zakāh, since these surahs are Makkan by consensus; and that verse only confirms the obligation after settling in Madinah, and because what is meant by it is taking it from the hypocrites as well. Zakāh was fixed, by specifying the types of zakātable goods and the thresholds and amounts to be paid, at Madinah; so this does not contradict that the origin of its obligation was in Makkah. Mālik interpreted it as the specific zakāh fixed in the narration of Ibn al-Qāsim and Ibn Wahb from him, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas ibn Mālik, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, and a large group of the Successors. Perhaps they hold that zakāh was prescribed initially with the fixing of thresholds and amounts. Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, ʿAṭāʾ, Ḥammād, Ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid interpreted it as other than zakāh, and made the command one of recommendation (nadb). Al-Suddī, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, al-Nakhaʿī, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr in one narration from him interpreted it as an obligatory charity which was then abrogated by zakāh.

God made the ḥaqq obligatory on fruits and grain on the day of harvest because harvesting is done for storage, and a person stores what he wants for food; so storage is the sign (maẓinnah) of wealth which necessitates giving zakāh, and harvest is the beginning of that sign. Whoever has only one or two trees eats their fruit green before it dries; therefore the Sharīʿah permitted the owner of the fruit to eat of the fruit when it bears fruit, and did not obligate him to give the right of the poor except at harvest. Furthermore, harvesting fruits, which is their plucking, is cutting them for storage; as for harvesting grain, it is cutting the ears from the roots of the crop, and then the grain in the ear is threshed so that it may be stored, so that threshing is considered a remainder of the harvest. It appears from this that the ḥaqq becomes due on what is harvested from the mentioned items, such as raisins, dates, grain, and olives, whether for their oil or their seed, unlike pomegranates and fruits.

According to the preferred view, this verse is not abrogated, but it is specified and clarified by other verses and by what the Prophet ﷺ explained; so its generality is not to be relied upon. It is reported from al-Suddī that it was abrogated by the verse of zakāh, meaning: ﴿خُذْ مِن أمْوالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً﴾ (Take from their wealth a charity) [al-Tawbah: 103]. The earlier scholars used to call specification "abrogation" (naskh).

His saying: ﴿ولا تُسْرِفُوا﴾ (and do not be excessive) is conjoined to "eat"; that is, eat without being excessive. Isrāf and sarf: exceeding what suffices of satisfying the self with the desired thing. Already mentioned

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 2 of 2):

In his words, the Exalted: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly﴾ [An-Nisa: 6] in Surat an-Nisa. This is an incorporation (idmaj) of the prohibition of extravagance, and it is a prohibition of guidance and reform. That is: do not be extravagant in eating. This is like His words: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾ [Al-A'raf: 31].

When a person becomes accustomed to extravagance (israf), it leads him to expand in acquiring desirable things, so he commits many blameworthy acts for its sake, and he moves from one pleasure to another without stopping at any limit.

It has also been said that it is coordinated (atf) with ﴿and give its due﴾, meaning: and do not be extravagant with what remains after its due has been given, so that you spend more than what is obligatory. This applies only to spending and eating and the like. As for spending it in good and in benefiting people, this is not extravagance. For this reason, it is considered an error of interpretation (khata' al-tafsir) to explain it as a prohibition of extravagance in charity, and [it is also an error] to rely on what they mention: that Thabit ibn Qays cut down five hundred palm trees, distributed all their fruit, and did not bring any of it into his house, and that the verse was revealed because of that.

His words: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ are a resumptive statement (isti'naf) intended to generalize the ruling of the prohibition of extravagance. It is emphasized with (inna) to increase the affirmation of the ruling. It thus explains that extravagance is among the actions that He does not love, and so it is among the morals from which one must refrain. The negation of love admits of different degrees, so it is known that the negation of love intensifies in proportion to the strength of the extravagance. This is a general ruling (hukm mujmal), and it is apparent in indicating prohibition. The explanation of this generality lies within other textual proofs, and generality is intended.

Because the interpretation of this prohibition and of His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ is obscure, the opinions of the exegetes (mufassirun) differed regarding the meaning of the extravagance that is forbidden, so that they might specify it as unlawful extravagance. Some of them even said that it is abrogated (mansukh). You have learned the way of safety from all of that.

[Page 124]

The reason God does not love the extravagant is that excess in enjoying pleasures and good things, and frequent spending of wealth to obtain them, generally leads to the depletion of wealth and to greed for increasing them. When the extravagant person's wealth runs short, he seeks to obtain money by corrupt means in order to quench his craving for pleasures, and this becomes his habit. Perhaps his wealth runs short, and it becomes hard for him to give up his habit, so he lives in distress and constriction. Perhaps he seeks money by unlawful means, and so falls into what he will be held accountable for in this world or in the Hereafter. Then this may leave his dependents in want and in a hard livelihood, and blame, reproach, and disputes arise from it, which lead to what is not praiseworthy: the disruption of the order of the family.

As for abundant spending in acts of righteousness, it does not lead to this, because the one who spends in them does not reach the degree of one who spends for the love of his pleasures, since the motive of wisdom is receptive to reflection and limitation, unlike the motive of desire. For this reason it has been said, in a statement that holds both in its positive and negative form: there is no good in extravagance, and no extravagance in good. The meaning of this verse is also found in His words in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant; indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ [Al-A'raf: 31], and in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He dislikes for you gossip, excessive questioning, and squandering of wealth."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 142:

﴿And of the cattle, [some] for carrying and [some] for spreading out. Eat of what God has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you.﴾

حَمُولَةً is coordinated with ﴿gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. The meaning is: "And He produced from the cattle what is for carrying and for spreading out." The restrictive force (qasr) of the preceding clause therefore extends to it, so the meaning is: He is the One who produced from the cattle what is for carrying and spreading out, not the gods of the polytheists. The polytheists were thus wrong in assigning to the idols a right over the cattle.

The مِن in ﴿ومِنَ الأنْعامِ﴾ is ibtida'iyyah (the "min" of origin or starting point), because "beginning" is a meaning that suits both "carrying" and "spreading out," being the broadest of the meanings of "min." The prepositional phrase is either attached to أنْشَأ (produced), or it is a circumstantial modifier (hal) of حَمُولَةً, which was originally an attribute; when it was placed first, it shifted into this form.

Whichever is the case, the fronting of the prepositional phrase before the object, which is the element that deserves fronting in the ordering of complements, or the fronting of the attribute before the noun it qualifies, serves to emphasize the matter of the cattle, since they are the primary concern of the context. That context is the nullification of the prohibition of some of them and the nullification of assigning a portion of them to the idols. As for carrying and spreading out, these are a favour (imtinan) that is inserted into the main topic to multiply its purposes. Moreover, the favour in this respect has a clear effect in nullifying the prohibition of some of them, which is a narrowing of the blessing and a rejection of the grace. The brevity is also completed, since this saves saying: "And He produced for you the cattle, and He produced from them what is for carrying and spreading out," as will come later.

Al-an'am (the cattle) are camels, cows, sheep and goats, which was explained at the start of surah al-Ma'idah. Al-hamula, with a fatha on the ha', is what is loaded with goods or people. One says: "He carried the goods" and "He carried so-and-so." God says: ﴿When they come to you that you may carry them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92]. It takes the feminine and singular form, like ṣarūrah for one who has not performed the Hajj: one says "a woman ṣarūrah" and "a man ṣarūrah."

As for al-farsh, its interpretation in this verse has been disputed. It is said that al-farsh is what cannot bear loads of the camels, meaning that it is ridden in the way that a carpet is spread out. This is the view of al-Raghib. It is also said that al-farsh is the young of the camels, or of the cattle in general, since they are close to the ground and so are like a carpet. It is said that al-farsh is what is slaughtered, because it is spread upon the ground at the time of slaughter or afterwards, meaning it is sheep, goats and cows, since they are slaughtered. In al-Lisan, from Abu Ishaq: the people of the language agreed that al-farsh is the young of the camels.

al-Kashshaf added: "Or al-farsh is what is woven from their wool, fleece and hair, al-farsh." He means that this is as God said: ﴿And from their wool, fur and hair, furnishings and provision for a time﴾ [al-Nahl: 80], and He said: ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], ﴿And they carry your loads﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], the verse. Also, they used to spread out the skins of sheep and goats to sit upon them.

The word farshan is suitable for all these meanings, and all its interpretations are appropriate to the context, so they should all be intended by the verse. It seems that no other word could match the word farsh in gathering these meanings, and this is one aspect of the inimitability of the Qur'an in terms of its eloquence. So al-hamula refers specifically to camels, while al-farsh may refer to camels, cows and sheep, according to the varying meanings of the term farsh, which are suitable for each kind, along with its combination with the word min, which is suitable for the beginning.

The meaning, then, is: "And He produced from the cattle what you carry and ride, namely large camels and small camels; and what you eat, namely cows and sheep; and what is a farsh for you, namely what is shorn from them and their hides." The listener knows that when God produced from the cattle what is for carrying and spreading out, they should remember that they eat from them. Thus the speech achieves brevity, and for this reason He follows with His words: ﴿Eat of what God has provided for you﴾.

The clause ﴿Eat of what God has provided for you﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah), like the verse ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. The connection between the command to eat and the mention of the cattle is that, since His words "and farshan" are something suited to slaughter, as mentioned before, He follows this with permission to eat what is fit to be eaten from them. He limited himself to the command to eat, because that is the purpose of the context, namely the nullification of the prohibition of what they had forbidden to themselves, and as a preparation for His words: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. So the command to eat here is used to mean a prohibition of its opposite, which is not eating from some of them. That is, "Do not forbid what has been made lawful for you from them, following the deception of Satan through whisperings to the leaders of the polytheists who set for them those false customs." The command here does not mean mere permission.

He shifted from the pronoun, such that one would say "eat from them," to the use of the relative clause ﴿of what God has provided for you﴾, because of the implication in the relative clause's content that those who forbade to themselves, or to some of them, eating from some of them were misguided, and so they deprived themselves of some of what God had provided for them.

The meaning of ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ is a prohibition against matters of polytheism, for the first of Satan's footsteps in this respect is his embellishment to them of forbidding some of what God provided for them to themselves.

"The footsteps of Satan" is a figurative expression (tamthil). It was discussed earlier, at His words: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], in surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the prohibition. The position of inna in it does away with the need for the resultative fa' (fa' of consequence), as was mentioned more than once before, and its explanation was given in the verse of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 143–144 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Eight pairs: two of the sheep and two of the goats. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿And two of the camels and two of the cattle. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."﴾

Page 128

The phrase ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ ("eight pairs") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to (min al-an'ām, "of the livestock," mentioned earlier), serving as a preparatory introduction (tawṭi'a) to the division of the livestock into four categories. This in turn serves as a preparation for the refutation of the polytheists, with His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾. That is: He produced from the livestock the beasts of burden, and so on to the end, in the state of being ﴿eight pairs﴾.

Al-azwāj (pairs) is the plural of zawj, and zawj is a name for a thing joined to another in a relation of constant association. So the zawj is the second of a pair, and each of those two is called a zawj, by way of considering that it is joined. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35] in Surat al-Baqarah. The word zawj is commonly applied to the male and female of human beings bound together by a marriage contract, and this usage has been extended by metaphor to the male and female of animals whose males and females pair together, such as the wild ass and its female, and the male pigeon and its female, because of their resemblance to the human couple. The word zawj is also applied to a kind within a species, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of all fruits He made therein two pairs, two﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:3] in Surat al-Ra'd.

Both of the last two usages are suitable here, because the camel, the cattle, the sheep and the goat are kinds of livestock, and because each of these has a male and a female. The meaning is that Allah created from the livestock their males and their females. So the pairs here are pairs of the kinds, and the intended meaning is not one particular pair, since they are not identified by their individual selves. Thus, "eight pairs" means four males from four kinds and four females likewise.

His saying: ﴿two of the sheep and two of the goats﴾ replaces "two" with respect to His saying "eight pairs". The word "two" is a detailing substitute (badal tafṣīl), and the meaning is "two of them," that is, of the pairs: a male and a female, each of which is a pair for the other. The purpose of this detailing is to arrive at mentioning the categories of males and females, as a preparation for the argument that follows in His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾, and so on.

In the detailing, the method of distribution was followed, to distinguish closely related kinds. Camels are slaughtered by cutting the throat, and cattle are slaughtered and also have their throats cut. Among cattle there is a kind that has a hump, which is more similar to camels; it is found in the lands of Persia and entered the lands of the Arabs, and it is the buffalo. The Arab cattle have no hump, and their bull is called al-farīsh.

Since in the Jahiliyyah they had forbidden some sheep, among them what is called the waṣīla, as has been mentioned earlier, and some camels, such as the baḥīra and the waṣila as well, but they had not forbidden some goats nor any of the cattle, it was appropriate that this division should come before the argument, as a preparation for their arbitrariness, since they forbade some individuals of certain kinds and did not forbid some of other kinds, while the alleged causes of prohibition could apply to every kind. So this is a general refutation of what they had legislated, and that it is not part of the religion of Allah; for had it come from other than Allah, they would have found in it much disagreement.

This argument is called in the science of debate and inquiry "taḥakkum" (arbitrariness).

Al-ḍa'n (sheep), with a hamza, is a collective noun for the flock of small livestock, with no singular from its own form; the singular of ḍa'n is shāh and its plural is shā'. It has been said that it is the plural of ḍā'in. Al-ḍa'n is a kind of livestock of the cloven-hoofed type that has wool.

Al-ma'z (goats) is a collective noun whose singular is māʿiz, and it is a kind of livestock resembling sheep, of the cloven-hoofed type, with long hair. It is said: ma'z with a sukūn on the ʿayn and ma'az with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. The first reading (with sukūn) is that of Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Ja'far and Khalaf, and the rest read the second.

After the completion of the mention of the favour and the preparation for the proof, the style of speech changed, and it began with addressing the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, to dispute with the polytheists and to expose their fabrication against Allah in what they claimed of forbidding what they had invented forbidding, of kinds and categories of livestock, upon those whom they designated among people, by His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden"﴾ and the verses that follow. So this speech is a refutation of the polytheists, nullifying what they had legislated, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you﴾ and the verse.

So His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾ up to its end, in both places, is an interjection after His saying: ﴿and of the goats two﴾, and His saying: ﴿and of the cattle two﴾. The pronoun in (﴿ḥarrama﴾) refers to the name of Allah in His saying: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ [al-An'ām 6:142], or in His saying: ﴿and they forbade what Allah has provided them﴾ [al-An'ām 6:140] and the verse. In the repetition of the interrogation twice there is an implicit allusion to error, so the rebuke and reproach, which is followed by an explicit statement in His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ and the verse.

There is no doubt that the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden"﴾ in both places is the nullification of the forbidding of what the polytheists forbade eating, and the negation of attributing that prohibition to Allah, exalted is He. The only question is the way in which this intended meaning is derived from the structure of the speech, and this is among the difficult matters.

Al-Fakhr said: The commentators are unanimous that the interpretation of this verse is that the polytheists used to forbid some of the livestock, so Allah argued against their claim by mentioning the sheep, the goats, the camels and the cattle, and mentioning from each of these four two pairs, male and female. If He had forbidden the females, it would necessarily follow that all their females are forbidden; and if He had forbidden what the wombs of the two females contain, it would necessarily follow that all the offspring are forbidden. The summary of the meaning is the negation that Allah forbade anything of what they claimed He forbade, by way of sabr and taqsīm (systematic enumeration and division), which is one of the methods of debate.

I say: This is what al-Ṭabarī attributed to Qatādah, Mujāhid and al-Suddī, and this does not hold up, because the sabr is not complete; the cause of prohibition is not confined to the category of kind, rather most often its cause is some attribute or state of the forbidden thing.

Al-Baghawī said: They said: ﴿These are livestock and tilth, forbidden﴾ [al-An'ām 6:138], and they said: (﴿What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'ām 6:139]), and they forbade the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla and the ḥām. When Islam came, they argued with the Prophet ﷺ, and their spokesman was Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Jushamī. They said: "O Muhammad, we have heard that you forbid things which our fathers used to do." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "You have forbidden kinds of the cattle without any basis; Allah created these eight pairs only for eating and benefiting from them. So from where has this prohibition come, from the side of the male or from the side of the female?" Mālik ibn ʿAwf was silent and was bewildered. End of quote. That is, this was before Mālik ibn ʿAwf embraced Islam. Al-Baghawī did not attribute it to a specific speaker, and it is close to what Qatādah, al-Suddī and Mujāhid said. Thus it becomes clear that the whole debate concerns forbidding the eating of some of these kinds of livestock, and the lack of distinction between what they had forbidden eating and what they had not forbidden, despite the sameness of the kind or category.

What is derived from the words of the leading scholars of Arabic regarding the structure of the argument against the polytheists is that the interrogative in His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ in both places is a denial-interrogative (istifhām inkārī). In al-Kashshāf it is said: the hamza in (﴿al-dhakarayn﴾) is for denial, and the meaning is: a denial that Allah, exalted is He, should forbid, from the two genera of sheep, any of the kinds of its males and females and what its females carry, and likewise with the two genera of camels and cattle. Ṣāḥib al-Miftāḥ explained this in the chapter on demand, saying: "If you intend by it—that is, by the interrogative—denial, then weave it on the pattern of negation: say, in denying the act itself, 'Did you strike Zayd?' and say, in denying that the addressee has a struck person, 'Was it Zayd you struck or ʿAmr?' For when you deny the one whom the striking is supposed to fall between them—that is, according to his claim—there results from it—that is, from the denial directed at him—the denial of the striking in a demonstrative manner." Among this is His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females﴾. Its commentator al-Quṭb al-Shīrāzī said: because the absence of the locus of prohibition entails the absence of prohibition, since it is an accident that cannot exist without a substrate in which it subsists; so when its locus is absent, it is absent. End of quote.

I say: the direction of the argument is this: if Allah had forbidden the eating of some of the males of one of the two kinds, He would have forbidden the rest, and if He had forbidden some of the females, He would have forbidden the rest; for the nature of Allah's rulings is that they apply uniformly to things united in kind and attribute. And if He had forbidden some of what is in the bellies of the livestock to the women, He would have forbidden it to the men. Since He did not forbid some of them to some while the kinds and conditions are alike, it follows that He did not forbid the part alleged to be forbidden; for Allah's rulings are tied to wisdom. This indicates that what they forbade, they forbade of their own accord, arbitrarily and without reason, and their forbidding of what they forbade was a fabrication against Allah. The proof stood against them and compelled them, as the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Jushamī mentioned just above indicate. For this reason He recorded it against them by His saying: ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful.﴾ So His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ means: if Allah had forbidden the two males, He would have equated their prohibition between men and women; and likewise regarding the two females. The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ in both places is used for affirmation and denial, by the indication of His saying before it: ﴿He will repay them for their description; indeed, He is Wise, Knowing﴾ [al-An'ām 6:139], and His saying: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-An'ām 6:142]. It is known that using the interrogative for other than the sense of seeking understanding is either a metaphor or a metonymy.

For this reason, ʾam must be disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa), meaning "rather" (bal), with the sense of a transitional turning away (iḍrāb intiqālī), enumerating them, and an interrogative is to be understood after it. So the single noun after ʾam is the object of a deleted verb, and the estimated sense is: "Or shall I forbid the two females?" Likewise the estimate in His saying: ﴿or what the wombs of the two females contain﴾ and likewise in its counterpart.

His saying: ﴿two of the sheep and two of the goats﴾ together with His saying: ﴿and of the camels two and of the cattle two﴾ belongs to the method of sabr and taqsīm mentioned among the methods of establishing the ratio (ʿilla) in the science of the principles of jurisprudence.

The clause ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for the clause

Page 133

﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females﴾, because the denial that Allah forbade anything of the males and females of those two categories entails the refutation of their claim that Allah forbade what they mentioned. From this it follows that they must be asked for evidence for their claim. So the position of the clause (﴿the two males﴾) is like a questioning request for clarification in the science of the etiquette of inquiry, and the position of the clause ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾ is like a prohibition. This is a mockery, because knowledge is not sought from them; and this mockery follows the form of the interrogative and is a branch of it.

Here it is purely metaphorical, or it is the implied meaning transferred to in metonymy.

The dual of "the two males" and "the two females" is with respect to the males and females of the two kinds.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 6, verses 143–144 (part 2 of 2):

The verb *ḥarrama* (forbade) is made transitive (*taʿdiya*, making a verb take an object) to *"al-dhakarayn"* (the two males) and *"al-unthayayn"* (the two females), and to what the wombs of the two females contain. This is by way of an understood genitive, a noun omitted but known from the context. The meaning is: *"He forbade the eating of the two males or the two females, and so on."*

The definite article in His saying ﴿the two males﴾ and in His saying ﴿what the wombs of the two females contain﴾ is the definite article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), as in *al-Kashshāf*.

The *bāʾ* in *"bi-ʿilmin"* (﴿with knowledge﴾) may be causative of the verb of informing (*ʾinbāʾ*), so that *ʿilm* means "that which is known." It may also be the *bāʾ* of accompaniment (*mulābasa*), meaning: *"Inform me with an informing that accompanies knowledge."* Here *ʿilm* is the opposite of ignorance (*jahl*), meaning: *"the informing of knowledge."* Since they were unable to give such information, this shows that they forbade what they forbade out of ignorance and foolishness, not out of knowledge. And it is the way of one who presumes to forbid and permit that he should be a person of knowledge.

His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ means: in your claim that Allah forbade what you say He forbade. For if they were truthful in the prohibition of these things, they would be able to explain what Allah had forbidden, would reveal the wisdom in the prohibition of what they had forbidden, and would attribute its prohibition to Allah, exalted is He.

His saying ﴿And of camels, two﴾ up to His saying ﴿the wombs of the two females﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to:
[Page 134]
﴿And of goats, two﴾. This is because it is part of the complete detailing of the eight pairs, and what was said about the earlier one applies to it. The intended purpose is to nullify the prohibition of the *baḥīra*, the *sāʾiba*, the *ḥāmī*, and what is in the bellies of the *baḥāʾir* and the *sawāʾib*.

The *ʾam* in His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿa*), signifying a transitional turning away (*iḍrāb intiqālī*). It therefore indicates an implied interrogative after it wherever it occurs. This interrogative is denunciatory and also confirmatory (*taqrīrī*), as the context shows.

*Al-shuhadāʾ* means those present, the plural of *shahīd*, which means one present. That is: *"witnesses at the time when Allah enjoined you."* So *"idh"* (when) is an adverbial of time governing *"shuhadāʾ"*, and it is annexed to the clause *"waṣṣākumu"* (He enjoined you).

*Al-īṣāʾ* (enjoining) means commanding something to be done in the absence of the one commanding, so that the one commanded is emphatically charged with carrying it out, because the absent one's case calls for emphasis. The term *īṣāʾ* is applied to what Allah commanded because people did not witness Allah at the time they did what He commanded them. Thus Allah's command was a binding one, and it is expressed by *īṣāʾ* as a warning to them to guard against neglecting the commands of Allah. For this reason *īṣāʾ* is applied to the command of Allah in many places in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:11].

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿by this﴾ refers to the prohibition derived from His saying *"ḥarrama"* (He forbade). This is because denying the whole of the prohibition implicitly includes the nullification of a specific prohibition that they had claimed, and which they themselves knew. Therefore it is correct to refer to the prohibition in a general way. The denial was specifically directed at the situation of direct witnessing, as a mockery of them, because they used to deny the Messenger (ﷺ). Their situation is like that of one who places himself in the position of someone present in the presence of Allah, exalted is He, to hear His commands. Or it may be that since this was not part of the law of Ibrāhīm or Ismāʿīl, peace be upon them, and no messenger came with it from Allah, and they did not claim it, there remains only that Allah addressed them with it directly.

His saying ﴿Who, then, is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ follows as a consequence of the denial in His saying ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females…﴾ up to His saying ﴿when Allah enjoined you with this﴾.
[Page 135]
That is: from that nullification and denial there follows a question, made by the speaker with a tone of denial, about the one who is characterized by an excess of wrongdoing among the wrongdoers, namely those who lied against Allah in order to mislead people. That is: there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah. So once it is established that he is the most unjust of the wrongdoers…

The polytheists are either those who originated polytheism, namely the chief polytheists, such as ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy, who originated the worship of idols and was the first to institute the *baḥīra*, the *sāʾiba*, the *waṣīla* and the *ḥāmī*, and those after him among the tyrants of the polytheists who established for them the practice of setting aside a portion of their wealth for the houses of idols and their attendants. These are fabricators. Or they are those who followed those people with determination and obstinacy and took part with them. They followed people who were not qualified to convey anything from Allah, and their duty was to be careful about whom they followed, and to follow someone whom they believed to be a conveyer of Allah's message, namely the messengers. Among their misguidance was that when the true Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, came to them, they denied him, although they had affirmed the liars, supported them and given them victory.

From the verse it is derived that among injustice is that one should venture into giving legal opinions in religion without having reasonable assurance (*ghalaba ʿalā al-ẓann*) that he is giving the correct ruling that pleases Allah. If he is a mujtahid, this is by relying on the evidence which gives him reasonable assurance that it coincides with the intent of Allah, exalted is He. If he is a muqallid (one who follows a school), it is by relying on what gives him reasonable assurance that it is the position of the imam whom he follows.

His saying ﴿without knowledge﴾ has already been discussed in a similar context above.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ may be a causal clause explaining why they are among the most unjust of people. This is because the meaning of increased injustice is only fulfilled when their wrongdoing has no giving-up of it, since misguidance becomes more firmly rooted in the soul through the repetition of its states and manifestations. When they deliberately sought to mislead, or followed those who deliberately did so out of obstinacy, they distanced themselves from seeking guidance and from reconsidering their own state, and this encourages them
[Page 136]
to increase and to delight in those states, until they become a settled habit and disposition in them, so that giving them up becomes difficult. Accordingly, in this sense *"inna"* conveys the meaning of causation (*taʿlīl*).

It is also possible that the clause is a threat and a warning to them, if they do not give up what they are engaged in: that Allah will deprive them of success and leave them in their error and confusion. Allah guided many of the polytheists, namely those who were not in this position in polytheism; that is, they were not leaders or obstinate in their polytheism. Those who were in this position are those whom Allah deprived of guidance, such as the notables of Quraysh, the people of the well (*al-qalīb*) on the day of Badr. As for those who embraced Islam by fighting, such as most of the people of Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and likewise Hawāzin and those after them, these submitted to Islam compliantly, then came to know that their gods had not availed them anything, and so guidance was attained for them after that. They became among the best of the Muslims and helped Allah with true help. Therefore the negation of guidance from them is meant either as its negation from a group of the polytheists, namely those who died in polytheism, or as the negation of pure guidance, which indicates the purity of the soul and the light of the heart, but not the guidance that is attained after entering Islam, which is guidance of a second rank, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those of you who spent before the conquest and fought are not equal [to others]; they are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 143–144 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Eight pairs: two of the sheep and two of the goats. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿And two of the camels and two of the cattle. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."﴾

Page 128

The phrase ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ ("eight pairs") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to (min al-an'ām, "of the livestock," mentioned earlier), serving as a preparatory introduction (tawṭi'a) to the division of the livestock into four categories. This in turn serves as a preparation for the refutation of the polytheists, with His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾. That is: He produced from the livestock the beasts of burden, and so on to the end, in the state of being ﴿eight pairs﴾.

Al-azwāj (pairs) is the plural of zawj, and zawj is a name for a thing joined to another in a relation of constant association. So the zawj is the second of a pair, and each of those two is called a zawj, by way of considering that it is joined. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35] in Surat al-Baqarah. The word zawj is commonly applied to the male and female of human beings bound together by a marriage contract, and this usage has been extended by metaphor to the male and female of animals whose males and females pair together, such as the wild ass and its female, and the male pigeon and its female, because of their resemblance to the human couple. The word zawj is also applied to a kind within a species, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of all fruits He made therein two pairs, two﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:3] in Surat al-Ra'd.

Both of the last two usages are suitable here, because the camel, the cattle, the sheep and the goat are kinds of livestock, and because each of these has a male and a female. The meaning is that Allah created from the livestock their males and their females. So the pairs here are pairs of the kinds, and the intended meaning is not one particular pair, since they are not identified by their individual selves. Thus, "eight pairs" means four males from four kinds and four females likewise.

His saying: ﴿two of the sheep and two of the goats﴾ replaces "two" with respect to His saying "eight pairs". The word "two" is a detailing substitute (badal tafṣīl), and the meaning is "two of them," that is, of the pairs: a male and a female, each of which is a pair for the other. The purpose of this detailing is to arrive at mentioning the categories of males and females, as a preparation for the argument that follows in His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾, and so on.

In the detailing, the method of distribution was followed, to distinguish closely related kinds. Camels are slaughtered by cutting the throat, and cattle are slaughtered and also have their throats cut. Among cattle there is a kind that has a hump, which is more similar to camels; it is found in the lands of Persia and entered the lands of the Arabs, and it is the buffalo. The Arab cattle have no hump, and their bull is called al-farīsh.

Since in the Jahiliyyah they had forbidden some sheep, among them what is called the waṣīla, as has been mentioned earlier, and some camels, such as the baḥīra and the waṣila as well, but they had not forbidden some goats nor any of the cattle, it was appropriate that this division should come before the argument, as a preparation for their arbitrariness, since they forbade some individuals of certain kinds and did not forbid some of other kinds, while the alleged causes of prohibition could apply to every kind. So this is a general refutation of what they had legislated, and that it is not part of the religion of Allah; for had it come from other than Allah, they would have found in it much disagreement.

This argument is called in the science of debate and inquiry "taḥakkum" (arbitrariness).

Al-ḍa'n (sheep), with a hamza, is a collective noun for the flock of small livestock, with no singular from its own form; the singular of ḍa'n is shāh and its plural is shā'. It has been said that it is the plural of ḍā'in. Al-ḍa'n is a kind of livestock of the cloven-hoofed type that has wool.

Al-ma'z (goats) is a collective noun whose singular is māʿiz, and it is a kind of livestock resembling sheep, of the cloven-hoofed type, with long hair. It is said: ma'z with a sukūn on the ʿayn and ma'az with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. The first reading (with sukūn) is that of Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Ja'far and Khalaf, and the rest read the second.

After the completion of the mention of the favour and the preparation for the proof, the style of speech changed, and it began with addressing the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, to dispute with the polytheists and to expose their fabrication against Allah in what they claimed of forbidding what they had invented forbidding, of kinds and categories of livestock, upon those whom they designated among people, by His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden"﴾ and the verses that follow. So this speech is a refutation of the polytheists, nullifying what they had legislated, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you﴾ and the verse.

So His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females"﴾ up to its end, in both places, is an interjection after His saying: ﴿and of the goats two﴾, and His saying: ﴿and of the cattle two﴾. The pronoun in (﴿ḥarrama﴾) refers to the name of Allah in His saying: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ [al-An'ām 6:142], or in His saying: ﴿and they forbade what Allah has provided them﴾ [al-An'ām 6:140] and the verse. In the repetition of the interrogation twice there is an implicit allusion to error, so the rebuke and reproach, which is followed by an explicit statement in His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ and the verse.

There is no doubt that the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿Say: "Has He forbidden"﴾ in both places is the nullification of the forbidding of what the polytheists forbade eating, and the negation of attributing that prohibition to Allah, exalted is He. The only question is the way in which this intended meaning is derived from the structure of the speech, and this is among the difficult matters.

Al-Fakhr said: The commentators are unanimous that the interpretation of this verse is that the polytheists used to forbid some of the livestock, so Allah argued against their claim by mentioning the sheep, the goats, the camels and the cattle, and mentioning from each of these four two pairs, male and female. If He had forbidden the females, it would necessarily follow that all their females are forbidden; and if He had forbidden what the wombs of the two females contain, it would necessarily follow that all the offspring are forbidden. The summary of the meaning is the negation that Allah forbade anything of what they claimed He forbade, by way of sabr and taqsīm (systematic enumeration and division), which is one of the methods of debate.

I say: This is what al-Ṭabarī attributed to Qatādah, Mujāhid and al-Suddī, and this does not hold up, because the sabr is not complete; the cause of prohibition is not confined to the category of kind, rather most often its cause is some attribute or state of the forbidden thing.

Al-Baghawī said: They said: ﴿These are livestock and tilth, forbidden﴾ [al-An'ām 6:138], and they said: (﴿What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'ām 6:139]), and they forbade the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla and the ḥām. When Islam came, they argued with the Prophet ﷺ, and their spokesman was Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Jushamī. They said: "O Muhammad, we have heard that you forbid things which our fathers used to do." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "You have forbidden kinds of the cattle without any basis; Allah created these eight pairs only for eating and benefiting from them. So from where has this prohibition come, from the side of the male or from the side of the female?" Mālik ibn ʿAwf was silent and was bewildered. End of quote. That is, this was before Mālik ibn ʿAwf embraced Islam. Al-Baghawī did not attribute it to a specific speaker, and it is close to what Qatādah, al-Suddī and Mujāhid said. Thus it becomes clear that the whole debate concerns forbidding the eating of some of these kinds of livestock, and the lack of distinction between what they had forbidden eating and what they had not forbidden, despite the sameness of the kind or category.

What is derived from the words of the leading scholars of Arabic regarding the structure of the argument against the polytheists is that the interrogative in His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ in both places is a denial-interrogative (istifhām inkārī). In al-Kashshāf it is said: the hamza in (﴿al-dhakarayn﴾) is for denial, and the meaning is: a denial that Allah, exalted is He, should forbid, from the two genera of sheep, any of the kinds of its males and females and what its females carry, and likewise with the two genera of camels and cattle. Ṣāḥib al-Miftāḥ explained this in the chapter on demand, saying: "If you intend by it—that is, by the interrogative—denial, then weave it on the pattern of negation: say, in denying the act itself, 'Did you strike Zayd?' and say, in denying that the addressee has a struck person, 'Was it Zayd you struck or ʿAmr?' For when you deny the one whom the striking is supposed to fall between them—that is, according to his claim—there results from it—that is, from the denial directed at him—the denial of the striking in a demonstrative manner." Among this is His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females﴾. Its commentator al-Quṭb al-Shīrāzī said: because the absence of the locus of prohibition entails the absence of prohibition, since it is an accident that cannot exist without a substrate in which it subsists; so when its locus is absent, it is absent. End of quote.

I say: the direction of the argument is this: if Allah had forbidden the eating of some of the males of one of the two kinds, He would have forbidden the rest, and if He had forbidden some of the females, He would have forbidden the rest; for the nature of Allah's rulings is that they apply uniformly to things united in kind and attribute. And if He had forbidden some of what is in the bellies of the livestock to the women, He would have forbidden it to the men. Since He did not forbid some of them to some while the kinds and conditions are alike, it follows that He did not forbid the part alleged to be forbidden; for Allah's rulings are tied to wisdom. This indicates that what they forbade, they forbade of their own accord, arbitrarily and without reason, and their forbidding of what they forbade was a fabrication against Allah. The proof stood against them and compelled them, as the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Jushamī mentioned just above indicate. For this reason He recorded it against them by His saying: ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful.﴾ So His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ means: if Allah had forbidden the two males, He would have equated their prohibition between men and women; and likewise regarding the two females. The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males﴾ in both places is used for affirmation and denial, by the indication of His saying before it: ﴿He will repay them for their description; indeed, He is Wise, Knowing﴾ [al-An'ām 6:139], and His saying: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-An'ām 6:142]. It is known that using the interrogative for other than the sense of seeking understanding is either a metaphor or a metonymy.

For this reason, ʾam must be disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa), meaning "rather" (bal), with the sense of a transitional turning away (iḍrāb intiqālī), enumerating them, and an interrogative is to be understood after it. So the single noun after ʾam is the object of a deleted verb, and the estimated sense is: "Or shall I forbid the two females?" Likewise the estimate in His saying: ﴿or what the wombs of the two females contain﴾ and likewise in its counterpart.

His saying: ﴿two of the sheep and two of the goats﴾ together with His saying: ﴿and of the camels two and of the cattle two﴾ belongs to the method of sabr and taqsīm mentioned among the methods of establishing the ratio (ʿilla) in the science of the principles of jurisprudence.

The clause ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for the clause

﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females﴾, because the denial that Allah forbade anything of the males and females of those two categories entails the refutation of their claim that Allah forbade what they mentioned. His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ may be a causal clause explaining why they are among the most unjust of people. This is because the meaning of increased injustice is only fulfilled when their wrongdoing has no giving-up of it, since misguidance becomes more firmly rooted in the soul through the repetition of its states and manifestations. When they deliberately sought to mislead, or followed those who deliberately did so out of obstinacy, they distanced themselves from seeking guidance and from reconsidering their own state, and this encourages them
[Page 136]
to increase and to delight in those states, until they become a settled habit and disposition in them, so that giving them up becomes difficult. Accordingly, in this sense *"inna"* conveys the meaning of causation (*taʿlīl*).

It is also possible that the clause is a threat and a warning to them, if they do not give up what they are engaged in: that Allah will deprive them of success and leave them in their error and confusion. Allah guided many of the polytheists, namely those who were not in this position in polytheism; that is, they were not leaders or obstinate in their polytheism. Those who were in this position are those whom Allah deprived of guidance, such as the notables of Quraysh, the people of the well (*al-qalīb*) on the day of Badr. As for those who embraced Islam by fighting, such as most of the people of Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and likewise Hawāzin and those after them, these submitted to Islam compliantly, then came to know that their gods had not availed them anything, and so guidance was attained for them after that. They became among the best of the Muslims and helped Allah with true help. Therefore the negation of guidance from them is meant either as its negation from a group of the polytheists, namely those who died in polytheism, or as the negation of pure guidance, which indicates the purity of the soul and the light of the heart, but not the guidance that is attained after entering Islam, which is guidance of a second rank, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those of you who spent before the conquest and fought are not equal [to others]; they are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:10].

[p. 137]

This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), arising from the nullification of the prohibitions which the polytheists had invented. The question naturally arises from a Muslim questioner about the prohibitions that are established, since the false prohibitions have been nullified. Therefore the Messenger ﷺ was addressed with the explanation of the prohibitions in the Law of Islam, after he had been addressed with the explanation of what is not forbidden among what the polytheists had forbidden, in His saying: ﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ [al-An'am: 144], and the verses that follow.

The speech that he was commanded to say begins with His saying ﴿I do not find﴾, as an *idmaj* (incorporation), a rebuttal of the polytheists within the explanation of what was forbidden to the Muslims. This rebuttal proceeds by way of *kinayat al-iyma'* (allusive implication), in that the forbidding of what they claimed to be forbidden is not explicitly denied; rather, he says, "I do not find it in what has been revealed to me." From this it is understood that its prohibition is not from God in His Law, because there is no way to forbid anything that people consume except through information from God, the Exalted. For God is the One who makes lawful what He wills and forbids what He wills, according to His knowledge and wisdom. And that information comes only by way of revelation or what is derived from it. So if a ruling is not found in the revelation nor in its derivatives, then it is a ruling that is not true. Thus the nullity of the prohibition they claimed is established by way of allusion, and this is an inferential method, for in it is the negation of a thing by negating what necessarily entails it.

*(Ajidu)* means "I find/attain," whose verbal noun is *al-wajd* and *al-wijdan*. Here it is a metaphor for the obtaining and reaching of a thing. It is said: "I found so-and-so a helper," meaning "I obtained him." Thus obtaining a thing is likened to finding and attaining what is sought. It is transitive to one object.

By *(﴿mā ūḥiya﴾)* ("what has been revealed") is meant what God informed His Messenger ﷺ of by revelation other than the Qur'an. For the Qur'an that was sent down before this verse does not contain the prohibition of carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine. Rather, the Qur'an was sent down with the prohibition of what is mentioned in this verse, and then in Surat al-Ma'idah.

*(Al-ṭā'im)* means "the eater." It is said: *ṭaʿima* (like *ʿalima*) when one eats food. It is not said of one who drinks. As for *ṭaʿima* meaning "to taste," it is used for tasting foodstuffs and drinks, and its use is mostly in negation. Its explanation was given earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, he is of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], in Surat al-Baqarah. Accordingly, the verse is confined to explaining the forbidden foods.

His saying *(﴿yaṭʿamuhu﴾)* ("which he eats") is a qualifier of *(﴿ṭā'im﴾)*, and it is an emphasizing qualifier, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

The exception is from the general scope of the states that are indicated by the indefinite noun occurring in the context of negation. That is: "I do not find any existing thing forbidden except its being carrion, etc.," i.e., except the existing thing being carrion, etc. Thus the exception is *muttasil* (contiguous).

The restriction (*ḥaṣr*) derived from the negated statement and the exception is real according to the time of the revelation of this verse. For at that time there were no forbidden foods other than these mentioned. For the verse is Meccan, and then Surat al-Ma'idah was sent down at Medina, and so more things were added to the prohibitions, as will come shortly.

*(Al-masfūḥ)* is the poured, flowing [blood], which is what comes out of the slaughter-place and the throat, or from bloodletting in some of the veins of the limbs, so that it flows. The Arabs used to eat the blood that flows from the jugular veins of a slaughtered animal, or from the throat of the slaughtered camel. They would collect it in a intestine or a skin, dry it, and then roast it. Sometimes they would bleed a camel from its legs, taking what they needed of the blood without the camel dying. Sometimes they mixed the blood with wool, and they called it *al-ʿilhiz*. This was done in times of famine.

Restricting blood with *al-masfūḥ* serves to draw attention to the pardon of the blood that seeps from the veins of meat when it is cooked, since it is impossible to avoid it.

His saying ﴿for it is an abomination﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the coordinated items. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the flesh of swine. The more apparent view is that it refers to all that precedes it. The singular pronoun is used in accordance with its interpretation as "the mentioned thing," that is, "the mentioned thing is an abomination," just as the demonstrative is used in the singular, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

*(Al-rijs)* means the wicked and the filthy. Its explanation was given earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus God places abomination upon those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125], in this surah. If the pronoun refers only to the flesh of swine, then describing it as *rijs* is an alert to its condemnation, a condemnation beyond the prohibition. Describing it thus is a warning against consuming it, and an assurance to the Muslims regarding its prohibition, since most of the Arabs used to eat the flesh of swine, unlike carrion and blood, which they would not eat except in destitution.

The wickedness of swine is known to God, the Exalted, who created it. It has recently become clear that its flesh contains harmful animal particles for its consumer, as established by zoology and medical science. It has been said that what is meant is that it is impure, because it eats impurities. But this is not sound, because some animals eat impurities, and they are called *al-jallālah* (animals that feed on filth), and they are not forbidden to eat according to the most correct opinions of the scholars.

If the pronoun refers to the three, by way of interpreting it as "the mentioned things," then His saying ﴿for it is an abomination﴾ is an alert to the reason for the prohibition, namely that it is for the averting of a harm that results from eating these things, and that harm is physical. As for carrion, it is because of the decay into which the animal's body turns after death; and also because the disease that caused its death may pass on to its eater. As for blood, it is because it contains harmful substances, and also because drinking it produces a craving for it.

*(Al-fisq)* means departing from something. It is a technical term in the Law for departing from faith or from lawful obedience. Therefore, the forbidden act is described with it, in view of its being a cause of its doer's departure from obedience. The Qur'an has called what was dedicated to other than God *fisq* in the preceding verse and in this verse. Thus it became a well-known description of what is dedicated to other than God. For this reason, He followed it with His saying: ﴿dedicated to other than God﴾. So the clause ﴿dedicated to other than God﴾ is a qualifier of, or an explanation of, *fisqan* ("a transgression"). In this there is an alert that the prohibition of what is dedicated to other than God is not because its flesh is harmful, but because that is disbelief in God.

The verse has indicated that the forbidden animal foods are restricted to these four. This restriction is according to what was forbidden on the day this verse was revealed. For nothing else of the animal meat that they eat had been forbidden in Mecca, and these surahs are all Meccan according to the correct view. Then at Medina other things were forbidden, namely: the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and that which wild beasts have eaten, according to the verse in Surat al-'Uqud. And the flesh of domestic donkeys was forbidden by the command of the Prophet ﷺ, with differences among the scholars as to whether its prohibition is essential, like swine, or because on that day they were the carriers of the army of Khaybar; and as to whether its prohibition, according to those who hold that it is essential, is continuous or *mansukh* (abrogated). The issue is not among the aims of exegesis, so we have no need for what they have burdened themselves with regarding the interpretation of the restriction of the forbidden things in this verse to the four. Likewise the issue of the prohibition of the flesh of every animal with fangs among the predators, and the flesh of birds of prey, which al-Qurtubi has expounded. The meaning of ﴿dedicated to other than God﴾ was given earlier in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *(illā an yakūna)* with a yā' (third person), and *(maytatan)* in the accusative, along with what is coordinated with it. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamzah read it with a tā' (second person) and *(maytatan)* in the accusative, along with what is coordinated with it, according to those other than Ibn 'Amir. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a tā' and *(maytatun)* in the nominative. This reading poses a difficulty: the items coordinated with *(maytatan)* are accusative, namely: ﴿or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for it is an abomination, or a transgression dedicated to other than God﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf did not address this. This reading has been explained as follows: ﴿or flowing blood﴾ is coordinated with *(an)* and its complement, since it is in the position of the accusative by way of exception. So the estimate is: "except the existence of a carrion," and when the existence was expressed by the complete verb *yakūnu*, what had been its complement became nominative.

His saying ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ has been discussed earlier regarding its parallel in Surat al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173].

The predicate in the apodosis, namely *(Rabbuka)* ("your Lord"), came defined by a construct (*idafah*) rather than by proper name, as in the verse in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 192]. This is because the word *al-Rabb* indicates compassion, gentleness, and guardianship toward the one who is nurtured. It is an alert that God made this concession for the Muslims who worshipped Him and did not associate anything with Him, and that He turned away from the polytheists who associated others with Him. For the construct indicates specificity, since it is equivalent to the particle of specificity. So when He expressed the Forgiving, may He be exalted, as the Lord of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, it is known that He is the Lord of those who followed him, and that He is not the Lord of the polytheists in the sense of the guardianship implied by the word "Lord." This is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11]; that is, no protector who deals with them through the effects and marks of guardianship. This is because this verse occurs within the context of argument against the polytheists, unlike the verse in al-Baqarah, which begins with His saying: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172].

The statement that He is Forgiving and Merciful, although this is known from many passages, here is a *kinayah* (allusion) for permission to consume those forbidden things in the state of necessity, and for the lifting of the sin of prohibition from them at that time. It is thus in the sense of His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿then there is no sin upon him; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173].

[Page 142]

The clause "And upon those who became Jews We prohibited every animal with claws" is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause introduced by "Say" (qul). It is a declarative statement conjoined to an imperative. The meaning is: state to them what was prohibited in Islam, and mention to them what We prohibited for those who became Jews before Islam. The connection is this: when God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to explain what God had forbidden to eat of animals, and in the course of that there was an indication that what God had forbidden is foul, some of it unfit to be eaten by bodies, about which He said, ﴿for it is an abomination﴾ [al-Anʿam: 145], and among it is what does not meet the obligation of thanking the Creator, about which He said, ﴿or a profanity over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ [al-Anʿam: 145], He followed that with mention of what He prohibited for the Children of Israel, a specific prohibition for a specific wisdom related to their circumstances, and temporary until the coming of the final law. The purpose of mentioning this last point is to make clear to the polytheists that what they had forbidden is not part of God's legislation either now or in the past, and so it is pure error.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb in "And upon those who became Jews We prohibited" serves to express restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), meaning: upon them and not upon other nations.

The word ẓufr (claw, hoof-nail) is the bone beneath the skin at the tip of the fingers of humans and animals, and of talons. It corresponds to the hoof and the cloven hoof, and it belongs to camels, predatory beasts, dogs, cats, rabbits, hyraxes and the like. These are prohibited to the Jews by the explicit text of the law of Moses, peace be upon him. In chapter fourteen of the Book of Deuteronomy: "The camel, and the hare, and the coney, ... therefore ye shall not eat of them."

The word shuḥūm is the plural of shaḥm (fat), which is the fatty substance that accompanies the flesh in the body of an animal. God permitted the Jews to eat the flesh of cattle and sheep, but prohibited them the fat of these, except what was on the back.

The word ﴿al-ḥawāyā﴾ (the entrails-sacs) is conjoined to "their backs," so the intended meaning is conjunction to what is permitted, not to what is prohibited. That is: "or what the ḥawāyā carried." It is the plural of ḥawiyya, which are the fatty sacs that contain the intestines.

As for ﴿what is mixed with bone﴾, it is the fat that clings around the bone of the animal, from the marrow. It is excused, because it is difficult to separate it from the bone.

The apparent view is that these fats were prohibited to them by the law of Moses, peace be upon him. They are the prohibitions that the verse in Surat al-Nisaʾ summarized with His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We prohibited for them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 160], as we indicated there. This is because the transgressions for which they were censured there were all things they introduced after Moses, peace be upon him. So His saying ﴿That is what We recompensed them for their rebellion﴾ refers to the rebellion they introduced during the time of Moses, peace be upon him, during the period of wandering, of which God informed about them, such as their saying: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and their saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 24], and their worship of the calf. Much of that was enumerated against them in Surat al-Baqarah.

The reason these prohibitions are a recompense for their rebellion is that their rebellion arose from the hardness of their souls and the domination of the animal power within them over the angelic power. Perhaps God prohibited these matters for them as a lightening of their hardness. In this there is also a display of His favour upon the Muslims in permitting for them all animals except what the Qur'an prohibited and the Sunnah prohibited, of matters on which the scholars have not disagreed, and what they disagreed about.

God did not mention the prohibition of pork, although it is among what the text of the Torah included, because He mentioned here only what was specifically prohibited to them that was not prohibited in Islam. That is, what its prohibition was temporary.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb in "And of the cattle and sheep We prohibited for them" is for emphasis on explaining this, because when one hears the prohibition of every animal with claws, the mind turns toward these two, and awaits the ruling concerning them. So fronting the prepositional phrase has the effect of beginning with ﴿as for﴾ (amma).

The clause ﴿That is what We recompensed them for their rebellion﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) that explains the cause of the prohibition of what was forbidden to them.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿That is what We recompensed them﴾ refers to the prohibition derived from His saying "We prohibited." It is in the position of the second object of "recompensed them," fronted before its verb and its first object, for emphasis on it and to affirm that the prohibition is a recompense for their rebellion.

The clause ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ is a concluding clause for the preceding clause, intended to establish that God prohibited that for them, and to nullify their claim that God did not prohibit anything for us, and that we prohibited that for ourselves, following the example of Jacob in what he prohibited for himself. For when the Jews distanced themselves by God's prohibiting for them what He had permitted to others, though they claim to be the ones brought near to God above all nations, they denied that God had prohibited that for them and that it was a punishment for them. So they used to claim that those prohibited things were prohibited by Jacob for himself as a vow to God, and his sons followed him by example. Their claim is not correct, because Jacob only prohibited for himself the flesh and milk of camels, as the commentators mentioned, and as His saying indicates: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had forbidden for himself before the Torah was sent down﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 93] in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

The prohibition of that for himself, by a vow or a bodily benefit, does not extend to anyone other than himself from his descendants. And these things that God mentioned as prohibited for the Children of Israel are stated as prohibited in the Torah, so how can they deny their prohibition?

So the emphasis is a refutation of the Jews. The parallel to His saying here, ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾, is His saying in Surat Āl ʿImrān after His saying ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 93]: ﴿Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 93], up to His saying: ﴿Say: "God has spoken truly"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 95].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 147:

﴿Then if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy, yet His punishment will not be turned back from the guilty people."﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the preceding discourse, which refuted the prohibitions they had invented, beginning from His words: ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143] and onward. That is, if they do not desist after this clarification.

Page 145

And they denied you concerning the negation of God's prohibition of what they claimed He had forbidden. So warn them of God's punishment, that perhaps they may desist from what they claimed, and remind them of His vast mercy, that perhaps they will hasten to seek that which brings His mercy to them by following the guidance of Islam. Thus the pronoun in (kadhdhabuka, "they denied you") refers to the polytheists, which is what is apparent from the context both before and after the verse. On this interpretation, it is possible that in His words (﴿say: Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy﴾) there is an alert to them that the postponement of punishment from them is a respite that falls within God's mercy, a temporary mercy, perhaps that they may submit. Accordingly, the meaning of the verb (kadhdhabuka) is continuity: that is, if they persist in denial after these proofs.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to ﴿those who were Jews﴾ [al-An'am: 146], as a continuation of the digression. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi, who said that the Jews said: "God did not forbid us anything; we only forbade what Israel forbade himself." The meaning of the verse then is the supposition that they deny His statement: ﴿And upon those who were Jews We prohibited﴾ [al-An'am: 146], and so on, since their claims contradict that. They are such that they deny what is in this verse, and respite becomes confused with approval, so it is said to them: ﴿Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy﴾, and among His mercy is His granting respite to the guilty, largely in this world.

His words: ﴿yet His punishment will not be turned back from the guilty people﴾ contain conciseness through omission, the implied meaning being: "and He is possessed of might, and His punishment will not be turned back from the guilty people when He wills it." This is a warning and an expectation, and it is a concluding clause (tadhyil), since His words ﴿from the guilty people﴾ include them and others, and it implies that they are guilty.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 148:

﴿The idolaters will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise did those before them deny until they tasted Our might. Say: "Have you any knowledge that you could bring forth for us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess."﴾

Page 146
