It is a resumption, by which the discourse returns to the disputation with the idolaters after it had been interrupted by His saying: ﴿Say: "I find not in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it"﴾ [al-An'am: 145] up to His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. When God had cut off their argument concerning the prohibition of what they had prohibited and the division of what they had divided, He pursued what remained to them of argument, which is the argument of one who is refuted and defeated, whom disputation has exhausted and who has no argument left; for he clings to feeble excuses to promote his error, saying: "This is a matter that has been decreed and predestined."

If the pronoun of plurality in His saying ﴿But if they deny you﴾ [al-An'am: 147] refers back to the idolaters, then His saying here ﴿The idolaters will say﴾ is a explicit mention in the place of the implicit pronoun, to intensify the reprehensibility of their statements. The report of God about them, that they will say this, if the revelation of this verse was before the revelation of the verse in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And those who associated said: "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped besides Him anything, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him"﴾ [al-Nahl: 35], is the more probable. For Surat al-Nahl is counted as revealed after Surat al-An'am. Then the report that they will say it is an indication of what their souls conceal of falsifying this argument; so it is one of the miracles of the Qur'an, of the kind of reporting the unseen, like His saying: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. If, however, the revelation of this verse was after the revelation of the verse in Surat al-Nahl, then the report that they will say it means that they will repeat their familiar excuse.

The summary of this argument is that they argue against the Prophet ﷺ that what they are upon would not be, had it not been by God's pleasure; for had He not been pleased with it, He would have turned them away from it and not facilitated it for them. They say this in the context of silencing the Messenger ﷺ and nullifying his judgment upon them as being in error. This is the doubt of the foolish intellects who do not distinguish between God's exercise of creation and decree and the preservation of the laws of existence, which we call will and volition, and between His exercise through command and prohibition, which we call pleasure and love. The first is the exercise of bringing into being, and the second is the exercise of obligation. They reckon that their being able to lay down the foundations of idolatry and of prohibition and permission is nothing but that God created in them the capacity for that. Thus they reckon that when He did not restrain the reins of their actions, He was pleased with what they did; and that had He not been pleased with it, He would have been unable to strip them of their capacity. They reckon that God is concerned with the evil of their conduct in what He has created them upon. Were it as they imagine, falsehood and truth would be one and the same thing, and this is what no sound intellect can comprehend.

For the foolish intellects, when they imagine this, are attentive only to the side of their own creed and turn away from the side of their opponent. When they say: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾, they are heedless of being told from the side of the Messenger: "Had He willed, I would not have told you that your action is error." Thus, according to their doubt, God would have willed a thing and its opposite: He willed that they associate, and He willed that the Messenger say to them: "Do not associate."

The cause of this error, which afflicts those of misguided nations and which shows in the minds of some common Muslims in their excuses for disobediences and crimes, when they say: "It is God's command," or "It is written with God," or something similar, is ignorance of the fact that God's wisdom in ordering the system of this world required that He place a veil between His exercise in the conditions of created beings and their exercise in their own conditions in accordance with their will. That veil is the law of the linking of effects to their causes, and of the linking of the conditions of existing things in this world with one another. Part of it is what the majority of the Ash'arites call acquisition (kasb) and capacity (istita'ah), and what the Mu'tazilites and some of the Ash'arites call power (qudrah). That is the locus of obligation, which indicates what God is pleased with and what He is not pleased with. God set the system of this world in wisdom, making its stability depend on things managing their affairs from their own essences, according to powers He deposited in existing things so that they strive toward that for which they were created. He gave man a distinction by placing in him an intellect that enables him to change his conditions according to his needs, and He placed in his intellect the means of guidance to good and evil. Likewise He appointed for him callers to good who alert him to it if heedlessness overtakes him or desire veils him. If he does not restrain himself from his error, then he has betrayed the expanse of his intellect by folding it up.

Page 147

By this it became clear how the people of error confuse the will of the servants with the will of God. Therefore God refuted here their saying: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers﴾, because they made what is a will of their own into a will of God Most High. Moreover, He has affirmed His will in His saying: ﴿And had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107]. So that is the will of bringing into being the intellects and of bringing into being the order of the community.

This will by which they pleaded is a hidden will, whose reality the intellects of mankind cannot reach to comprehend. Therefore God blamed them for leaning on it while ignorant of its reality, and He said: (﴿Likewise did those before them deny﴾). He compared their denial to the denial of those deniers who were before them, and by that He alluded to the fact that the aim of the idolaters in this argument was the denial of the Prophet ﷺ. An explanation of this meaning has already been given in this surah at His saying: ﴿And had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107].

There is nothing in this verse that serves as an argument for us against the Mu'tazilites, nor for the Mu'tazilites against us, even though each of the two groups has tried to make it so; because both groups agree on the invalidity of the idolaters' argument.

In the verse there is an argument against the Jabriyyah.

His saying ﴿Likewise did those before them deny﴾ means: those before them denied their prophets just as these have denied you. This indicates that the idolaters, by their saying ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾, intended the denial of the Prophet ﷺ when he invited them to abandon what they believe, on the argument that God was pleased with it for them and willed it from them with a will of approval. Likewise the nations before them denied their messengers, relying on this same doubt; and God called their argumentation a denial, because they put it in the manner of denial and silencing, not because its content is something the Messenger ﷺ and the Muslims do not say. For we say that as He Most High said: ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107], we mean by it a correct meaning; so their speech belongs to the category of true speech by which falsehood is intended. It occurs in al-Kashshaf that it was read: "kadhalika kadhaba alladhina min qablihim" with the dhal of (kadhdhaba) lightened.

Page 148

Al-Tibi said: This is a fabricated reading or an anomalous one, meaning anomalous to an extreme degree; no one has transmitted it from anyone among the people of the anomalous readings, and perhaps it was made up by some Mu'tazilites in the debate, as is understood from the words of al-Fakhr.

His saying ﴿until they tasted Our might﴾ is a limit to the denial, the purpose of which is their persisting in it until the last moments of their existence; then when they tasted God's might, they perished and were annihilated. The limit here is not for cessation and turning back from the act, because it is evident that return is not conceivable after their extermination.

Dhawq (tasting) is a metaphor for perception and feeling, so it is the use of the restricted in the unrestricted; this has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿That he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Ba's (might) has been discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah, and its being added to the pronoun of God Most High is for its glorification and magnification.

God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to answer their speech, whether actual or expected, with His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you any knowledge that you could bring forth for us?"﴾ The phrase (qul) is separated [without a conjunction], because it functions as a saying and a reply, as has been established more than once. He used the interrogative whose purpose is silencing and mockery, given what is known of their clinging to such argumentation.

The interrogative uses (hal), because it indicates a request for the establishing of the predication being asked about. The basic nature of (hal) is that it is a particle meaning "qad" (indeed), because it is specific to verbs; and it frequently occurs after the interrogative hamzah, so the meaning of interrogation came to predominate over it, and the omission of the hamzah with it became frequent, until the hamzah was forgotten in common usage and appeared with it only rarely. Something of this was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91] in Surat al-'Uqud. Thus by (hal) he indicated that he is asking about a matter he wants to be established, as if he desires its occurrence, so he urges them to produce it; and when they fail, that will be a decisive cutting-off of their claim.

Page 150

The purpose of this interrogative is mockery of them in their saying: (﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾) up to (﴿nor would we have forbidden﴾). So he displayed to them the kind of speech that one who is impressed by their words would display; and the indication of mockery is apparent, because it is not supposed that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and the believers would seek knowledge from the idolaters, especially when he tells them plainly of their ignorance and misguidance morning and evening.

Knowledge ('ilm) is that which is the opposite of ignorance (jahl), and bringing it forth is informing of it. The conveying of a known fact to one who is ignorant of it has been likened to the bringing out of a hidden thing. This is like the comparison in the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: ("and a knowledge he has scattered in the breasts of men"). For this reason the use of (indakum, "with you") has a fine effect; because (ʿinda), in its original sense, indicates a place specific to that to which its word is attached, so it is suitable to concealment. Were it not that its use in the figurative sense has become so widespread that it has become like the literal, I would say that the mention of ("with you") here is a sustaining of the metaphor of bringing out for informing.

The bringing forth of knowledge is made to follow upon the "with you" by the fa' of causation, to indicate that the question is aimed at what results from it.

The lam in ﴿that you could bring forth for us﴾ is for purpose and benefit, indicating that its object is in need of what it is connected to; that is: that you bring it forth for our sake, i.e., for our benefit. The meaning: you have excelled in this knowledge which you have displayed, in your inference that God commanded you to associate and to forbid what you have forbidden, by an indication of will in that; for had He willed, you would not have done that. So increase us from this knowledge.

This answer resembles the "man'" (prohibition) in the terminology of the people of disputation. Since this interrogative was a formal one, and the speaker was certain of the absence of what he asked about, he followed it with the answer in His saying: ﴿You follow nothing but conjecture﴾.

The clause ﴿You follow nothing but conjecture﴾ is resumptive, because it is the beginning of speech with a turning away

Page 151

from the preceding speech. After mocking them, He became serious in His answer, saying: ﴿You follow nothing but conjecture﴾, i.e., you have no knowledge; the most you have is false conjecture and guessing. This resembles the "sanad" (supporting ground) of the prohibition in the usage of the people of disputation. Conjecture here means false conjecture, and this is a common usage of it, as has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture, and they do nothing but guess﴾ [al-An'am: 116] in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 149:

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive proof. So if He had willed, He would have guided you all."﴾

This is a response to their saying: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. It completes the previous response, since it adds to the refutation of their claim. It resembles what the people of disputation call al-mu'arada (a counter-argument that turns the opponent's own premise against him).

The imperative verb "say" is repeated to draw attention to what follows the verb "qul" (say). It is repeated three times in succession without a conjunction, and the reason is what was mentioned earlier, that the speech is conducted in the manner of debate and exchange.

The fa' (so) is fa' fasihah (an eloquent fa' that implies an unstated clause). It signals an omitted conditional clause, and the implied meaning is: "If your saying is merely following conjecture, guesswork and faulty interpretation, then to Allah belongs the conclusive proof."

Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject (li-Allah al-hujjah) gives exclusivity: the proof belongs to Allah, not to you. From this it is understood that their proof is refuted.

Al-hujjah (proof) is that which indicates the truthfulness of someone in his claim, and indicates that the one who reasons has hit upon the truth. Its meaning was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿so that there will not be for people against you any argument﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], in surah al-Baqarah.

Al-balighah (conclusive) means "that which reaches" its goal, i.e., reaching the purpose for which it was intended, which is defeating the opponent and nullifying his argument. An example is His saying: ﴿profound wisdom﴾ [al-Qamar: 5]. Thus "reaching" (al-bulugh) is a well-known metaphor for the attainment of the aim of a thing, so there is no need to construct a concealed metaphor in "proof" by likening it to a traveller reaching a destination, with "reaching" as the indicator of that concealed metaphor. Nor is there need to make the attribution of "reaching" to "proof" a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), meaning that its owner has reached his intention, because the metaphor in the sense of "reaching" cannot be avoided. Therefore interpreting it in this way from the outset is preferable. The meaning is: to Allah belongs the proof that prevails over you; that is, your argument is not a proof.

[Page 152]

The fa' in His saying ﴿so if He had willed﴾ is the fa' of consequence, following from the manifestation of Allah's proof against them. It follows from the refutation of their argument that Allah, had He willed, would have guided them; that is, had He willed their guidance by something more than sending the Messenger, peace be upon him, by changing their intellects so that they came to be contrary to what they were created for, He would have done so, with a special kind of care for them or by a supernatural custom for their sake, since nothing overpowers Him. But His wisdom required that He not extend His care to everyone, but restrict it to some of His chosen ones, and that He not depart from His way of guidance, which is to set minds in order and alert them to the truth through sending messengers, establishing evidences, and calling to His path with wisdom and good admonition. Therefore the will intended in His saying ﴿so if He had willed, He would have guided you﴾ is other than the will intended in what Allah related of their saying: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. Otherwise, what He denied against them would have affirmed a counterpart of it right after the denial, and the argument would be self-contradictory, since guidance amounts to not associating and not prohibiting. So it cannot be correct to make both of them the answer to the counterfactual "law" (law al-imtina'iyyah). Hence the will intended in the rebuttal against them is the hidden, concealed will, which is the will of creation (mashi'at al-takwin), and the will denounced against them is what they intended by reasoning from what actually happened to approval and love.

This is the explanation of this verse, whose brevity has scattered many understandings regarding how it should be explained. Its distance from the usual tafsir works is not hidden, and so is the comparison between those and what is stated here.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 150:

﴿Say: "Bring forth your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." But if they testify, do not testify along with them, and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and they ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

Page 153

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), marking a shift from the method of argument and debate in refuting their claim to the method of clarification (tabyin). The meaning is: bring forth those who testify that Allah has forbidden this, in order to thoroughly refute their claim from all its aspects.

For this reason, the Messenger ﷺ is again commanded to say to them what will expose the falsehood of their claim.

The repetition of the verb (qul, "say") without a conjunction serves to capture attention, and because it falls within the manner of dialogue, as we have mentioned above.

(Halumma) is a verb-form of command meaning "come" or "bring." It may be intransitive, as in Allah's words: ﴿Halumma ilayna﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18], and transitive, as it is here. In the dialect of the people of the Hijaz (lughat ahl al-Hijaz), it remains in one fixed form and does not take endings that agree with the addressee: one says "halumma ya Zayd," "halumma ya Hind," and so on. In the dialect of the people of al-'Aliyah, that is, Banu Tamim, it takes endings that agree with the addressee: they say "halummi ya Hind," "halumma," "halummu," and "halumman." In this verse it has come in the more eloquent form, so He said: ﴿halumma shuhada'akum﴾.

Ash-shuhada' (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid in the sense of shahid (witness). The command is for the purpose of making them helpless (ta'jiz), since they will not find witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden what they attribute to Him of the matters of their religion mentioned earlier.

The word shuhada' is made an idafah to the pronoun of the addressees in order to increase their helplessness, because it is the condition of the one who has the right to have witnesses whom he knows, and brings them forward when called upon to establish his right. Thus it is said to a man: "Mount your horse and catch up with so-and-so," because every household among the Arabs does not lack a horse, so one says this to him even when one does not know a particular horse of his, but the normal state is that he has a horse. And from this is His saying: ﴿They draw their outer garments close around them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 59], though one of them may not have an outer garment, as occurs in the hadith that he was asked: "If one of us does not have an outer garment?" He said: "Let her sister put on her one of her outer garments."

Page 154

He described them with the relative pronoun in order to reinforce the meaning of preparing the likes of them for testimony. The seeker places himself in the position of one who thinks they are not without witnesses for their right, witnesses who by their nature would testify for them. This is a preparation for their manifest helplessness if they do not bring them, as is the reliable assumption about them. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you?﴾ [al-An'am: 144], for He knows that there are no witnesses there.

The demonstrative (hadha, "this") points to something known from the context, namely what the discussion has been about from the beginning of the debate, from His saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143] and the verses following. Its reference was also already indicated by His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you?﴾ [al-An'am: 144].

Then He branched off on the supposition that they might bring witnesses who testify. His saying: ﴿But if they testify, do not testify along with them﴾ means: if the improbable is supposed, and they bring you witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this that they claim, then deny them, and know that they are witnesses of falsehood. So His saying: ﴿do not testify along with them﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for denying them, because one who confirms someone agrees with him in what he says. The prohibition against agreeing with them was therefore used in its necessary implication, which is denial. Otherwise, the prohibition against testifying with them is directed at one who knows that he will not testify with them, since he does not believe it, let alone that his testimony would be a case of obtaining what is already obtained. Thus the indicator of the metonymy is evident.

Joined to the prohibition against confirming them is the prohibition against following their desires, by His saying: ﴿and do not follow the desires of those who denied﴾.

He used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿those who denied Our signs﴾, because in this relative clause there is a reminder that the polytheists deny the signs of Allah, so they are among those whose following is to be avoided. It was said that by "those who denied" the Jews are meant, based on what preceded concerning the possibility that they are the intended referents of His saying: ﴿But if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy"﴾ [al-An'am: 147]. Their religion was called a desire (hawa) because it has no basis in any sound support, but rather satisfies desire. The word hawa has come to be applied mainly to the love of what is agreeable and immediate whose outcome is harm, and it was already discussed under His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Page 155

His saying: ﴿and those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to ﴿those who denied﴾. The intended sense is that it is conjoined to the relative clause, because the two relative clauses share the same referents, namely the polytheists. This is like the conjoining of attributes in the saying of a speaker, which al-Farra' cited:

"To the sovereign, the lord, the son of the Hama'im, and the lion of the battle in the crowd."

The apparent expectation was that the relative pronoun would not be repeated, since the conjunction particle suffices without it. But the speech was framed contrary to what the apparent expectation requires, in order to increase the exposure of them, as is one of the subtleties of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun. It was also said that by "those who denied the signs" is meant those who denied the Messenger ﷺ and the Qur'an, namely the People of the Two Books, and by "those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and they ascribe equals to their Lord" are meant the polytheists. The meaning of ﴿they ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ was already given under His saying: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1] at the beginning of this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 151 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him; be good to your parents; do not kill your children because of poverty, for We provide for you and for them; do not approach indecencies, whether apparent or hidden; and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand."﴾

This is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), marking a shift from refuting their claimed prohibition of eating livestock to calling them to know the things that are truly forbidden. Their knowledge is true, and it is more worthy of being known than what they invented through their slander and embellished with their disputation. The connection of this shift is clear: the setting is one of teaching and guidance. For this reason, the address begins with the command to the Messenger, peace be upon him, to "say," to draw attention, as was mentioned just before.

[Page 156]

It is followed by the verb "ta'alaw" ("come"), to emphasise the purpose they are being shifted to, namely that it is more beneficial to them than those trivialities with which they were preoccupied. This follows the style of the Almighty's words: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and His words: ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the upkeep of the Sacred Mosque equal to [the deeds of] one who believes in God and the Last Day?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], and so on. [This is] so that they may know the gap between what their own people are called to and what Islam calls them to of sublime deeds, and so that they may realise that they have wasted their times and their minds.

Opening it with a request for presence is evidence that the address is to the polytheists who were in aversion.

He has recited to them rulings that they had been acting contrary to, which had corrupted their condition in their jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance). This contains a recording against them of their evil deeds, which is understood from the prohibition against them and the command to their opposites.

The rulings contained in these conjoined clauses in the three verses that open with His words, ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾, are divided into three categories. The first: rulings by which the general social condition among people is reformed, and this is what is opened with His words: (﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾). The second: that by which the order of people's dealings with one another is preserved, and this is what is opened with His words: ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. The third: a comprehensive universal principle encompassing all guidance, which is following the path of Islam and guarding against departing from it towards the ways of misguidance, and this is what is opened with His words: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾.

Each of these categories has been concluded with the charge to it, with His words (﴿This He has enjoined upon you﴾), three times.

[Page 157]

"Ta'ala" is an imperative verb. Its origin is for one who is commanded to ascend to a place higher than his own place. Perhaps this is because, when they called to an important matter, the caller would climb a height so that his voice could be heard. Then the use of "ta'ala" spread to the request for coming, metaphorically, by the relation of generality (ʿalaqat al-iṭlāq). This is a common metaphor that became a conventional literal usage. Its origin is an imperative verb, and there is no escaping the meaning of ascending (al-ta'ālī), which is the effort of rising, and then it was transferred to requesting approach in general. Hence it was said that it is a verb-name (ism fi'l) of the imperative meaning "advance" (iqdam), because they found it did not inflect in speech: one does not say "ta'altu" meaning "I came," nor "ta'ālā ilayya fulān" meaning "so-and-so came to me." Whatever the case, it has received markers suited to the state of the one addressed, so one says "ta'alaw" and "ta'alayna." On this basis, the majority of grammarians preferred that it is an imperative verb and not a verb-name, and because if it were a verb-name, these markers would not attach to it, and it would be like "hallumma" and "hayhāt."

"Atlu" is the answer to "ta'alaw." Recitation (al-tilawa) is reading, relating and reporting the wording. It was mentioned before at His words: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. And "an la tushrikū" ("that you associate nothing") is an explanation of the recitation, since it has the sense of saying.

Among the things forbidden by God to them are items that are not of the kind of meats, as an indication that attention to the forbidden indecencies is more important than devoting oneself to studying the rulings on foods. This is an implicit rebuke to the polytheists, who turned their resolve to explaining foods and neglected purifying their souls and restraining corruption from people. A parallel to this is His words: (﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32]) up to His words: ﴿My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], and so on.

Some of the prohibited things are mentioned in the form of a prohibition, and some in the form of an explicit or implied command, because commanding a thing necessitates prohibiting its opposite. The reason for the difference in the form of the request for these enumerated items we will explain.

"An" here is explicative (tafsiriyya) for the verb "atlu," because recitation has in it the sense of saying. Thus the clause ﴿that you associate nothing﴾ is in the position of an explicative apposition ('atf bayan).

[Page 158]

The beginning with the prohibition of association is because correcting belief is the key to the door of reform in this world and to success in the next.

His words ﴿and be good to your parents﴾ are conjoined to the clause "an la tushrikū." "Ihsanan" is a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, i.e., "and be good to your parents with goodness." It is a command to goodness towards them, which implies the prohibition of its opposite, namely harming one's parents. On this basis, it has come here among what God has forbidden, because what is forbidden is harming the parents. He turned away from prohibiting harm to a command of goodness out of care for the parents, because God wanted their righteousness, and righteousness is goodness, and the command to it implies the prohibition of harming them by way of the implication of the discourse (fahwa al-khitab). Many Arabs in their jahiliyyah were people of coarseness, and many of them did not honour their fathers when old age weakened them. For this reason, the Qur'an's exhortation to goodness towards parents recurred frequently.

His words ﴿and do not kill your children because of poverty﴾ are a clause conjoined to the clause before it, intended as a prohibition against burying daughters alive (al-wa'd). Its explanation has preceded at His words in this surah: ﴿And thus their partners made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137].

The "min" here is causal (ta'lilliyya), and its origin is the initial sense (ibtida'iyya), so the caused thing is treated as if it originates from its cause.

"Imlaq" is poverty. That poverty is the cause of killing children happens in two ways: that it is actual, existing in fact, and this is what is meant here, and this is what the causal "min" requires; or that it is expected to occur, as He said in the verse of surah al-Isra': ﴿and do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31], because they used to bury their daughters either from inability to provide for them, or from anticipating that. Isḥaq ibn Khalaf said, and he is an early Islamic poet:

When I remember my daughter as she laments me,
my tears flow over my daughter, with blood.
I fear poverty will one day befall her,
and the veil will be lifted from flesh upon the earth [ḍam].

[206]

[Page 159]

This has been mentioned before at His words: ﴿And thus their partners made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137] in this surah.

The clause ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾ is an interjected, resumed clause, serving as the cause of the prohibition against killing them, a refutation of their excuse, because they had made poverty an excuse for killing children. And given that poverty is not fit to be a motive for killing a soul, God has made clear that when He created children, He had already decreed their provision. It is foolishness for a father to suppose that his inability to provide for them entitles him to kill them, and it would have been more fitting for him to earn for them.

He turned away from the path of the third person, in which the discourse had run from His words "what your Lord has forbidden," to the path of the first person with the pronoun in "We provide for you," as a reminder of the One who commanded this entire statement, so that it is as if God interjected His own speech in the midst of the speech of His Messenger, whom He had commanded, and so He spoke to people Himself, and as an affirmation of the Messenger's truthfulness, peace be upon him.

He mentioned God's provision for them together with the provision of their fathers, and He placed the provision of the fathers first, to indicate that just as He provided for the fathers so that they did not die of hunger, so He provides for the children. Moreover, poverty befell the fathers, so why should the children be killed on its account?

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate here is for the sake of conveying exclusivity: that is, "We provide for you and for them," not that you provide for yourselves and do not provide for your children. I have already explained that many tribes used to bury daughters alive, and therefore they were warned in this verse.

The clause ﴿and do not approach indecencies, whether apparent or hidden﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is a prohibition against committing sins. It has forbidden approaching them, and this is more emphatic in warning than forbidding involvement in them, because nearness to a thing is the likely cause of falling into it. Since sin has no nearness or distance, the nearness here is intended as a metonymy for the least involvement in sin, because it is customary to say this about settled matters of place: when one says "do not approach it," it is understood that the prohibition is against approaching it, so that the prohibition against involvement is even more so. When the literal meaning is impossible here, the implied meaning (al-ma'na al-iltizami) is determined, in the most eloquent manner.

"Al-fawahish" are the great sins, those that include corruptions. Its explanation has preceded at His words: (﴿He only commands you to evil and indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169]) in surah al-Baqarah.

"Ma zahara minha" is what they display openly and do not conceal, such as anger and slander. "Ma bataṅ" is what they conceal, and most of it is fornication and theft, and both were widespread among the Arabs.

Among the exegetes, some explained "al-fawahish" as fornication, and took "what is apparent of them" to be what their foolish ones did in taverns and houses of prostitutes, and "what is hidden" to be taking secret lovers. This was narrated from al-Suddi. It was narrated from al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas: the people of jahiliyyah considered fornication lawful in secret and found it abhorrent in public, so God forbade fornication both in secret and in public. In my view, the plural form in "al-fawahish" favours the first explanation, as in His words: (﴿Those who avoid major sins and indecencies, except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32]). Perhaps what led these people to explain the indecencies as fornication is His words in surah al-Isra' in verses that enumerated great prohibitions resembling the verses of this surah: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an indecency and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra': 32]. But it does not follow that the intended meaning of the similar verses is one thing. The discussion of "ma zahara wa ma bataṅ" has preceded at His words: (﴿Leave the apparent sin and its hidden [form]﴾ [al-An'am: 120]) in this surah.

He followed this with the prohibition against killing a soul, which is among the indecencies if "indecencies" is explained in its more general sense, singling it out for mention because it is a great corruption, and because it was widespread among the Arabs.

The definite article in "al-nafs" is the definite article of genus (ta'rif al-jins), so it conveys comprehensiveness (istighraq).

[Page 161]

It is described with "allati harrama Allah" ("which God has forbidden") to emphasise the prohibition, that it is an ancient prohibition. God forbade the killing of the soul from the time of Adam. The linking of the prohibition to "the soul" is by way of implication necessitated (dalalat al-iqtida'), meaning that God forbade killing it, according to what is well known in linking prohibition and permission to the very essences of things: it is intended to link it to the sense in which that thing is used, as in His words: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], meaning their eating. It is also possible that the meaning of "harrama Allah" is that God made it a sanctuary (haram), i.e., a thing held sacred that may not be transgressed against, as in His words: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾ [al-Naml: 91]. And in the hadith: "Indeed I make sacred what lies between its two lava plains" (hurrah).

His words ﴿except by right﴾ are an exceptive clause of the emptied type (istithna' mufarragh) from the generality of states of the killing, meaning: do not kill it in any state, or for any cause you claim, except for a cause of right. So the "ba'" is for accompaniment or causation.

The truth (al-Haqq) is the opposite of falsehood (al-batil). It is the matter that is established (haqqa), meaning it is proven not to be false according to the ruling of the Shari'ah, and according to people of sound and unbiased minds, free from caprice or particular desire. Thus, the matter upon which minds agree to accept is what the revealed laws agree upon, or what a particular inclination has agreed upon as being that which may come to pass, which is what a particular law agreed upon for a specific nation or era.

The definite article in "al-haqq" is for the genus, and what is meant by it is that in which the quiddity (mahiyyah) of truth, explained earlier, is realized. Wherever it is used in Islam, what is meant by it is its quiddity in the view of Islam. Islam has specified the right to take a soul by the Qur'an and the Sunnah: these are the killing of one who wages war (al-muharib) and retaliation (al-qisas), and these two are by the explicit text of the Qur'an; the killing of an apostate from Islam after he has been asked to repent; the killing of a married adulterer (al-zani al-muhsan); and the killing of one who refuses to perform the prayer after being given time until its time has passed. These three are reported in hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ). Also included is killing that arises from compulsion and from defence that is permitted by the Shari'ah. That is the killing of those among the rebels (al-bughat) who are killed, which is by the explicit text of the Qur'an, and the killing of those who are killed among those who withhold the zakah, which is by the consensus of the Companions.

Jihad, however, is not included in His saying: "except by right." But the killing of a captive in jihad, when it is for a benefit, is a right. We have elaborated on the discussion of the like of this verse in Surah al-Isra'.

The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿That He has enjoined upon you﴾ refers to the totality of what was mentioned. For this reason the demonstrative was used in the singular with regard to what was mentioned; had he used the plural demonstrative it would have been eloquent. Among its examples is: ﴿Each of those was accountable for it﴾ [al-Isra': 36].

The meaning of enjoining (al-wisayah) has already been explained at His saying: "﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you?﴾ [al-An'am: 144]" a little earlier.

His saying: ﴿so that you may reason﴾ means in hope that they will reason, i.e., that they become people of intellect, because involvement in some of the prohibited matters indicates baseness of intellect, to the extent that those who engage in them are placed in the position of one who does not reason; therefore it is hoped that they will reason.

His saying: ﴿That He has enjoined upon you, so that you may reason﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) made the end of the verse. It thereby points to the completion of a category of prohibitions: those prohibitions whose prohibition returns to reforming the social condition of the Ummah, through reforming belief, preserving the order of the family, abstaining from corruptions, and preserving the human species by abandoning mutual killing.

[Page 163]

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity﴾. He joined the clause "and do not approach" to the clause that explained the verb "recite" (*atlu*), as a conjunction of prohibitions that return to preserving the rules of dealing among people, in order to establish the rules of the Islamic community and its civility, and to secure people's trust in one another.

He began with preserving the right of the weak, who cannot defend their right to their property, namely the orphan. So He said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾. "Approaching" (*al-qurban*) is a metaphor for dealing with the orphan's property, and the disposal of it, as was mentioned just before in His words: ﴿And do not approach the indecencies﴾ [Al-An'am: 151].

Since this requires the prohibition of disposing of the orphan's property, even by storing and safeguarding it (which exposes his property to loss), the exception is stated: ﴿except in the best manner﴾, i.e., except in the condition that is best. The relative pronoun is an adjective of an omitted noun that is supplied to match the feminine relative pronoun, so it is estimated as "the condition" or "the quality."

The preposition *bi* (with) indicates association: "except while associated with the quality or condition that is best," or you may estimate it from the verb "approach" as "except by the approach that is best." The omission of the qualified noun is obligatory in this type of construction, and treating it as feminine functions as a proverb. From this is His saying: ﴿Repel with that which is best the evil﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 96], i.e., repel the evil with the good quality. Of this kind is that they used the relative pronoun in the feminine as a modifier of an obligatorily omitted noun, and they also omitted its complement, as in their proverbial saying: "after *al-latayya* and *al-lati*," i.e., after the base calamity and the great calamity, as Sulami ibn Rabi'a al-Dabbi said:

*And indeed I saw the discord of the clan among them,*
*and I sufficed (to deal with) its base side, the lesser one.*

"*Al-lati*" and "*ahsan*" (best) are a superlative with its comparison removed, i.e., "the good," which is the beneficial one that carries no harm to the orphan or to his property.

He said here, "and do not approach," as a warning against taking his property, even by the least means of taking, because he cannot defend himself. For this reason He did not say here "and do not eat" [Al-An'am: 121], as He said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And do not consume your properties among yourselves by false means﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 188].

*Al-ashudd* (maturity) is a noun denoting a person's strength, derived from *al-shadd*, which is binding and securing.

[Page 164]

What is meant by it in this verse and its like, where the discussion concerns the orphan, is his reaching the strength by which he emerges from the weakness of childhood. This is puberty together with soundness of mind, because what is intended is his reaching the capacity to dispose of his property. A child is prevented from disposing of property only because of weakness in his mind. This differs from what is meant by it in describing men, for it refers to a man reaching the furthest limit of strength among men, which is from forty years to fifty. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 15]. And Suhaym ibn Wathil said:

*A brother of fifty, my maturity has gathered (in me),*
*and the constant handling of affairs has tempered me.*

*Al-bulugh* (reaching) is arrival, and here it is a metaphor for gradual progress through the stages of strength that bring one out of the feebleness of youth.

"*Hatta*" (until) is the limit of the exception, which is the approach by the best means, i.e., the disposal of it until its owner reaches his maturity, that is, then it is handed over to him, as He said in the other verse: ﴿And if you perceive in them sound judgment, then hand over to them their properties﴾ [An-Nisa': 6], to the end of the verse.

The reason for specifying the orphan's right to his property for protection is that this right is a likely target of aggression from the guardian, and the likelihood that there is no one to defend him, because among them there was no weak person except that he had relatives and clients who would defend him if he sought their protection or called them for help. As for the orphan, aggression against him comes only from the person closest to him, who is his guardian, since among them no one would take charge of an orphan except the closest of people to him. The guardians used to be lavish with their orphans' property, aggress against it, and neglect the orphans so that they would not grow up in a way that let them know their rights. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [Ad-Duha: 6]. Because the orphan is a likely target for neglect, God, exalted is He, did not enjoin the property of a non-orphan, since its owner defends himself, or seeks defense through his guardians and helpers.

﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾

[Page 165]

He joined the command to give full measure and weight, which concerns trade, for they used to sell dates and raisins by measure, and they used to weigh gold and silver. They would cheat (*tatfif*) out of greed for profit, so He commanded them to give full measure. He turned away from forbidding cheating, as in the words of Shu'ayb: "﴿And do not diminish the measure and the scale﴾ [Hud: 84]," indicating that they are commanded to the limit at which justice is fully realized, and not diminishing equals full giving. But in choosing the command to give full measure there is concern for it, so that souls turn toward the side of fulfilment and not toward the side of abandoning its opposite. In it is also a reminder to them of the generosity they boast of, as if it were said to them: Where is your generosity that you compete in? Why do you not display it when you measure or weigh, so that you give more than justice by giving the one who receives the measure abundantly, let alone stealing his due from him? This is a warning to them about the corruption of their character and the imbalance of its qualities.

The preposition *bi* in His words "with justice" indicates association, and *al-qist* is justice. It was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18] in Surat Al 'Imran, i.e., give full measure while bound by justice, by not wronging the one who receives the measure of his due.

* * *

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾. The apparent connection of the clause "And give full measure" etc. to the clause "We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity" is that it is related to what came before and completes it, so it is a precaution: We do not burden you with perfect justice in measure and weight down to the grain and the mote, but We burden you with what you think is justice and fulfilment.

The purpose of this precaution is that people should not abandon dealing among themselves out of fear of error or heedlessness, which would lead to the cessation of many benefits. In this precaution He turned away from the third-person mode on which the speech was built from His words: ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [Al-An'am: 151], because of the favour contained in this precaution. So God Himself took up addressing people in it directly, using the first-person mode, adding to the favour, and confirming the one who conveys it. The enjoining of giving full measure and weight returns to preserving the buyer's property from the likelihood of loss, because the situation of measuring and weighing is one of the buyer's heedlessness, since the seller is the one who holds the measure or the scale. And because the buyer, out of his desire to obtain the measured or weighed goods, may tolerate the cheating, the seller is enjoined to give full measure and weight. This command indicates, by the implication of the address (*fahwa al-khitab*, the argument a fortiori), the obligation to preserve property even against what is more serious than cheating. Cheating is nothing but secretly taking a small amount of what is sold, which does not appear at the time of measuring. So taking more than that amount of property is more deserving of preservation and of avoiding aggression against it.

It is also possible that the clause "We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity" is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) to the clauses before it, recording against them that all that they were called to is within their power and ability.

This has been mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿God does not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286] at the end of Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾. This comprehends all dealings among people by means of speech, namely testimony, judgment, praise and blame (*ta'dil* and *tajrih*, the assessment of a witness's integrity or flaws), consultation, reconciliation between people, and reports describing the qualities of things in dealings: the qualities of goods for sale, of hired services, and of defects; and in promises, bequests, and oaths. Likewise praise and vilification such as slander. All of this falls under what proceeds from speech.

Justice in that means that there should be nothing in speech of aggression against rights:

[Page 166]

by nullifying them or concealing them, such as hiding the defects of goods, claiming defects in sound goods, or lying about prices, as when a merchant says: "I was given this commodity for such and such a price," when he was not given it, or: "this commodity cost me such and such."

Included in this is adherence to truthfulness in assessing and criticizing witnesses, and in giving sincere advice in consultation, and speaking the truth in reconciliation. As for testimony and judgment, the command of justice in them is evident. If one who speaks makes a promise, he does not break it. If he makes a bequest, he does not wrong the claimants to inheritance. He does not swear falsely. If he praises someone, he praises him for what is truly in him. As for abuse, refraining from it is obligatory, even if it is true, for refraining from it is justice, because God commanded it.

In the conditional particle in His words "And when you speak" there is an indication that a person has latitude to remain silent if he fears to speak justly. As for saying what is unjust, wrong, or false, there is no way for him to that. All lying is speech without justice, though some silence is obligatory.

In the *Muwatta'* it is reported that a man proposed to a man for his sister, and the brother mentioned that she had committed some misconduct. This reached 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who struck him, or nearly struck him, then said: "What have you to do with reporting?"

The waw in His words "even if" is the waw of circumstance, and "even if" (*law*) is a concessive particle that expresses emphasis on the circumstance in which the listener might suppose the ruling does not include it, because it is singled out among the rest of the circumstances covered by the ruling. Its explanation was given before at His words: ﴿Never will there be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he should ransom himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran. The situation of kinship between the speaker and the person about whom the speech is made may lead the speaker to say what is not just, to benefit his relative or to ingratiate himself with him. So they were alerted to the obligation to adhere to justice in speech in that situation. The hidden pronoun in *kana* (was) refers to something known from the discourse, i.e., "even if the one about whom the speech is made is a near relative."

[Page 167]

"Qurba" is kinship, and it is understood that the person is a relative of the speaker. That is, when you say something for his sake or against him, be just, and do not say other than the truth, nor to repel harm from him by denying the right he has, nor to benefit him by inventing a right for him against another, or by clearing him of what he did against another. God, exalted is He, has said about justice in testimony in judgment: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives﴾ [An-Nisa': 135].

The demand for truth in speech has come in the form of a command to justice, rather than a prohibition of injustice or falsehood, because He restricted it with the conditional particle, which implies the utterance of speech. Once speech is uttered, it cannot be free of being either true or false, and the command that it be true is more fitting to the Lawgiver's purpose for two reasons. The first is that God loves the manifestation of truth through speech, so in the command that it be just there is a command to manifest it, and a prohibition of silence without a valid reason. The second is that the prohibition of speaking falsehood or lies applies to speech whose outward form is not true, and this is blameworthy except under fear or for the sake of gentleness, or in matters that do not involve manifesting a truth. These are the allusions (*ma'arid*) about which the hadith says: "Indeed, in allusions there is an alternative to lying."

* * *

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾

He concluded these recited verses with the command to fulfil the covenant by His words: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. The covenant of God that is commanded to be fulfilled is every covenant that carries the meaning of attribution to God, which

[Page 168]

The construction (*idafah*, annexation) permits this reading. Here the *idafah* may be the annexation of the verbal noun to its agent, meaning the covenant that God made binding upon you through the laws (*shara'i'*). It may also be the annexation of the verbal noun to its object, meaning the pledge you made to God that you would do it, which you bound yourselves to and undertook. It may further be an annexation of the slightest connection, meaning the covenant that God commanded to be preserved and warned against breaching. This refers to the covenants made among people with one another, whether between tribes or between individuals.

Because of the meanings that arise from the capacity of the *idafah* to convey them, the expression was phrased by attributing the noun "covenant" to the Name of Majesty through the *idafah*, rather than through a verb. It was not phrased as "and by what you covenanted with God concerning it" or something similar, which would admit only one meaning. Since the address in "Come" (*ta'alaw*) is directed to the polytheists, the covenant must be something whose nature is already established among them. This is the covenants they concluded through alliance, peace, or the like, and so He calls them to fulfil what they had agreed upon. It is attributed to God because they used to swear oaths by God when contracting, and for this reason they called a covenant a *hilf* (alliance). Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Remember the alliance of Dhu al-Majaz, and what was put forward in it: the covenants and the guarantors."

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"We are found to be the strongest of them in protecting what is theirs, and the most faithful of them when they swear an oath."

Thus the verse commands them to fulfil (their covenants), and the Arabs used to praise one another for this. Among the covenants established among them were the Alliance of the Fudul (*Hilf al-Fudul*) and the Alliance of the Perfumed (*Hilf al-Mutayyabin*). Both existed in the pre-Islamic period to remove injustice and oppression from those dwelling in Makkah. This was a realisation of God's covenant to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that He would make Makkah a secure land, and whoever entered it would be safe. The polytheists nevertheless transgressed against the weak among the believers and wronged them, such as 'Ammar, Bilal, 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, and others. So He says to them, in what He recites to them, that breaking the covenant of God concerning the security of Makkah, and breaking your covenants concerning it, is more deserving that you should forbid it than your false claims regarding what you have forbidden and distinguished. This is the correct interpretation of His words: "And fulfil the covenant of God."

The placing of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb serves to give importance to the matter of the covenant and to turn the listener's mind toward it, so that what follows of the command to fulfil it becomes firmly fixed in his mind. The meaning is: if you consider fulfilling covenants to be praiseworthy, then the covenant of God is more deserving of fulfilment, and you yourselves have chosen it. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting therein is grave﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], then He said: ﴿but hindering from the way of God, disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater in the sight of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

* * *

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you may be mindful.﴾

This is a repetition of His similar statement before it, and you know that this concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) was used to end one category of the rulings.

With this injunction He added "that perhaps you may be mindful" because these four matters were known among the Arabs to be praiseworthy. Therefore the command to them and the exhortation to them is a reminder of what they already knew about them, but they forgot it through the dominance of desire and the veil of polytheism over their hearts.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read "tadhdhakkarun" (تَذَّكَّرُونَ) with a shadda on the dhal, through the assimilation (*idgham*) of the second ta' into the dhal after converting it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, and Khalaf read it with the dhal unstressed, by deleting the second ta' for lightness (*takhfif*).

[Page 170]

[Page 171]

The conjunction *wa* (and) is coordinated with the clause "﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾ [6:151]", because the coordinated items share the same purposes of address and the same order. It also fits the concluding phrases that follow these purposes, each ending with "﴿so that you may understand﴾", "﴿so that you may remember﴾", and "﴿so that you may be mindful of God﴾". This is a comprehensive statement requiring adherence to the revelation that comes to the Messenger ﷺ in the Qur'an.

The readers Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read *anna* with a open hamza and a doubled nun.

From al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, it is coordinated with "﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾", so it is in the accusative position governed by the verb *atlu* (recite). The implied meaning is: "And I recite to you that this is My path, straight."

From Abu 'Ali al-FARISI: according to the analogy of Sibawayh's view, *anna* is to be linked to His statement "﴿follow it﴾". The implied meaning is: "And because ﴿this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾", according to Sibawayh's analogy in His statement, exalted is He, "﴿for the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾" [106:1]. He said regarding His statement, exalted is He, "﴿And that the mosques are for God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾" [72:18], that the meaning is: "And because the mosques are for God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God." End of quotation.

So *anna* is followed by a dropped *lam* of causation, which is well known to be omitted with *anna* and *an*. The construction of the verse is: "Follow My path, because it is a straight path." Thus a transposition occurs in the structure through the implied causation, applied to the verb which should have been coordinated. The causation thus takes the place of a condition because of this fronting, as if it were said: "Since this is My path, straight, follow it."

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *wa-inna* with a kasra on the hamza and a doubled nun, so there is no transposition in the structure of the speech. His statement "follow it" is then a consequence of an established assertion that His path is straight.

Amir and Ya'qub read *wa-an*

[Page 172]

with an open hamza and a sukun on the nun, as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, its noun being an implied pronoun of the matter, and the sentence following it is its predicate. The better interpretation is that *anna* is explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), coordinated with "﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾". The reason for repeating *anna* is the change in the style of speech from what precedes it.

The demonstrative refers to Islam, meaning: "And that Islam is My path." The demonstrative refers to something present in the minds of the addressees through the repeated descent of the Qur'an and hearing the sayings of the Messenger, peace be upon him, such that people knew and clarified it. It is thus treated as if it were witnessed, and the demonstrative noun, which is designed to specify a thing through direct observation along with a pointing gesture, is applied to it. It may also be that the demonstrative refers to all the legislation and admonitions mentioned earlier in this surah, since they have become like a present, witnessed thing, as in His statement, exalted is He, "﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾" [11:49].

*Sirat* (path): the broad, main road. It has already been discussed in His statement "﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾" [1:6]. The intended meaning is Islam, as indicated by His statement at the end of the surah: "﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion﴾" [6:161], because the purpose of the surah is to achieve righteousness in this world and the Hereafter. It is therefore likened to the road that leads the traveler to his aim and destination.

When Islam is likened to the path and treated as something witnessed, it becomes like a clear, evident road, and so it is ascribed as being *straight*, meaning there is no crookedness in it, because a straight road is easier for the traveler to walk and quicker to reach its destination.

The pronoun of the first person attached to *sirat* refers to God, as His statement indicates: "﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾" [42:52] "﴿the path of God﴾" [42:53], according to one of the two methods of reporting speech when the speech contains the pronoun of the speaker or the pronoun of the one who commands the speech, as was previously mentioned at His statement, exalted is He, "﴿I said to them nothing except what You commanded me: that worship God, my Lord and your Lord﴾" [5:117], in the Surah of al-'Uqud. The verse has departed from the third-person manner that the speech had followed from

[Page 173]

His statement "﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾" [6:151], in order to hint at the protection of this path from error, because its being the path of God is sufficient to show that it leads to success. Thus it is valid to make the command to follow it a consequence of merely its being the path of God. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the Prophet who was commanded to speak, but this would require building the consequence of the command to follow it upon the claim that it is clearly straight. Otherwise, its being the path of the Prophet does not necessitate that the command to follow it is a consequence of him, with regard to the addressees who denied him.

His statement "straight" (*mustaqiman*) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the demonstrative noun. What made it valid as a circumstantial clause is that the demonstrative is built on the claim that it is witnessed, which requires that it is present in the mind with all its general features, and what they tested and knew of it, and that this shows them that in the state of straightness it is as if it were something perceptible. For this reason, circumstantial clauses from demonstrative nouns are frequent, as in "﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾" [11:72], and they did not use it as a predicate.

*As-Subul* (the paths): the ways. Their occurrence here opposite the straight path indicates an implied attribute, meaning: the scattered paths that are not straight. These are what they call *bunayyat al-tariq* (side lanes), which are roads branching off from the main road, going off, which some passers-by take individually to their homes or pastures. They do not reach a town or a settlement, and no one can travel along them except one who understands and is accustomed to them. Therefore, His statement "﴿so that you are separated from His path﴾" is a consequence of the prohibition, meaning: these are scattered roads, and they cause the one who walks them to be separated from the main road. This is not because *sabil* is a name for a narrow road that does not lead anywhere, for *sabil* is synonymous with *sirat*. Do you not see His statement: "﴿Say: This is my way﴾" [12:108]? Rather, it is because the contrast and the report of their being scattered indicate that the intended meaning is specific paths described as not straight.

The *ba'* in His statement "*bikum*" (with you) is for accompaniment: that is, the paths are scattered accompanying you, meaning you will be scattered along with their scattering. This figurative accompaniment makes the *ba'* function as the transitive hamza,

[Page 174]

as the grammarians said, in such expressions as *dhahabtu bi-Zaydin* (I went with Zayd), which means *adhhabtuhu* (I caused him to go). The meaning is then: "﴿so that He scatters you away from His path﴾", that is, you do not encounter His path.

The pronoun attached to *sabilihi* (His path) refers to God, exalted is He, by the context. If the first-person pronoun in His statement "*sirati*" (My path) refers to God, then the pronoun in *sabilihi* is a shift from *sabili* (My path).

Al-Nasa'i in his *Sunan*, Ahmad and al-Darimi in their *Musnads*, and al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak*, report from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ drew a line for us one day, then said: This is the path of God. Then he drew lines to his right and to his left, that is, to the right of the first drawn line and to its left, then said: These are paths; upon each path there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited: "﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow the paths, for they will separate you from His path﴾."

Ahmad, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh report from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ when he drew a line, and drew two lines to his right and two lines to his left, then placed his hand on the middle line, that is, the one between the other lines, and said: This is the path of God. Then he recited this verse: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow the paths, for they will separate you from His path. That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may be mindful of God﴾."

What occurred in the first narration, "and drew lines", is in terms of the totality of what is on the right and left. This is its drawing, approximately:

His statement "﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may be mindful of God﴾" is a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) repeating its two preceding counterparts. The demonstrative "*dhalikum*" (that) refers to the path, and the enjoining of it means the enjoining of what it contains.

The hope is attached to God-consciousness because this path includes abstention from prohibited things and adds to that the performance of good deeds. So when the traveler follows it, he becomes one of the *muttaqun* (the God-conscious), meaning those who are characterized by *taqwa* (God-consciousness) in its legal sense, as in His statement, "﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾" [2:2].

Then We gave Moses the Book, complete [in perfection] for the one who did good, and as a detailed explanation of all things, and as guidance and mercy, that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord.

"Thumma" (then) here is a conjunction coordinating with the clause "Qul ta'alaw" (Say: Come), so it does not coordinate individual words, and therefore one should not suppose that it indicates a lapse of time. Rather, it is detached from that meaning when it coordinates clauses, and it indicates a lapse in rank, which is a figurative delay; this is the function of "thumma" when it coordinates clauses. Some exegetes found the way "thumma" is used in this verse difficult, because Moses, peace be upon him, being given the Book is not of a higher rank than reciting what God has forbidden among the prohibitions and what He has obligated of following the path of Islam. The opinions of the exegetes regarding the sense of "thumma" here have multiplied into several views: those of al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Muslim, and others, each seeking to escape this difficulty.

The view I hold is that "thumma" has not departed from its known meaning of indicating a lapse in rank, and that the lapse in rank of Moses, peace be upon him, being given the Book, relative to reciting what God has forbidden in the Qur'an and what he was commanded of adhering to the path of Islam, only becomes apparent after considering the purpose of the arrangement of the discourse. The purpose of mentioning Moses, peace be upon him, being given the Book is not for its own sake, but is a preparation for His saying: ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 155], so that His saying is arranged upon it: ﴿lest you say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾ [al-An'am: 156] up to His saying "and guidance and mercy." The meaning of the discourse is: and beyond that, this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, in which is gathered what was given to Moses, peace be upon him, which is the greatest of what was given to the prophets before him, and what is in the Qur'an, which confirms what is before it and is a guardian over it; if you follow it and fear God, We shall have mercy upon you, and you have no excuse, lest you say, "If a Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than the People of the Two Books." So this is a more important purpose, gathering the following of all that the Qur'an comprises, and it is introduced to persuade the addressees of the merit of taking up this Book.

The occasion of this transition: what was mentioned of the path of God, which is Islam. When the polytheists denied the call of Islam, God reminded them that He gave Moses, peace be upon him, the Book, as was well known among them, as we explained at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They did not appraise God with true appraisal when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon a human being." Say, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?"﴾ [al-An'am: 91], in this surah, so that it moves on to the mention of the Qur'an and the exhortation to follow it. Thus the reminder of the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, serves as a preparation for that purpose.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the well-known one, namely the Torah. "Tamaman" (complete) is a state (hal) of "al-Kitab," and "tamam" means perfection; that is, that Book was a perfection for the goodness among the Children of Israel, which is a remnant of what they had received from their forefathers: the righteousness of Abraham, and what Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, peace be upon them, were upon. So the Torah completed their righteousness and removed the corruption that had afflicted them, and the removal of corruption is a completion of righteousness. Describing the Torah with "tamam" is an intensification in the sense of "the one who completes."

The relative pronoun in His saying "ʿala alladhi ahsan" (for the one who did good) is meant generically, which is why its singular and plural are the same. What is meant here is the group that does good, that is, complete for the goodness of the good-doers among the Children of Israel; the verb is treated as intransitive, meaning "the one who was characterized by goodness."

"Tafsil" means explanation, and it was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in this surah.

"Kull shay'" (all things) is meant to refer to the greatest things, that is, the important matters whose rulings in religious affairs need explanation. So "kull" is used in the sense of abundance, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] in Surat al-Baqarah. Or it is in the sense of "the great among things," as if it gathered all things together.

Or "shay'" is meant as "an important thing," and it would then be an elision of the qualifier, as in His saying: ﴿who takes every ship by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound ship, and similarly His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book of anything﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

As for His saying: ﴿that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾, "la'alla" (perhaps) expresses hope that they would believe in the meeting with their Lord. The pronoun refers to something known from the context, namely the Children of Israel, since it is known from the giving of the Book to Moses, peace be upon him, that those who benefit from it are his people, the Children of Israel. The meaning of this is: perhaps they, if they strive in their deeds in a manner suitable to believing in the meeting with their Lord. For the Children of Israel had believed in meeting God before the Torah was revealed, but there befell them over long periods of time, from the phases of their neighborhood with the Copts, and the humiliation, exile, destitution, and enslavement that reached them, what removed knowledge from them and withered the virtuous characters, so they forgot the watchfulness of God, Exalted is He, and they corrupted, until their state became like that of one who does not believe he will meet God. So God wished to reform them by sending Moses, peace be upon him, so that they would return to what their righteous predecessors had been upon: watchfulness of God, Exalted is He, fear of meeting Him, and desire to meet Him while He is pleased with them. This is an allusion to the people of Makkah and those among the Arabs who were like them, for their predecessors were upon guidance and righteousness, but there entered among them one who misled them, instilled in them polytheism and denial of resurrection, so God sent to them Muhammad (ﷺ) to bring them back to guidance and make them believe in the meeting with their Lord.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing element is for emphasis on the matter of resurrection and recompense.

[Page 178]

﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may be shown mercy.﴾ ﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them? We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment, for what they used to turn away.﴾

The clause ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf, coordination) to the clause ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Anʿam: 154]. The meaning is: We gave Moses the Book [6:154], and We have sent down this Book, as was mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [6:154]... and so on.

The opening of the clause with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), the construction of the verb upon it, and making the Book, whose proper place is to be the object of ﴿We have sent it down﴾, into the subject (mubtada'), all of this is for the sake of emphasising the Book and praising it. A parallel to this has already occurred: ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what is before it﴾ [6:92] in this surah.

The command to follow it, being based on its being sent down from God and on its being blessed, is clear, because whatever is of this kind is not doubted by anyone as something to be followed.

The word "following" (ittiba') has been applied, by way of metaphor, to acting upon what is in it. Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [6:50] and His saying: ﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [6:106] in this surah.

[Page 179]

The address in His saying "follow it" is to the polytheists, by the indicator of His saying: ﴿lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾.

The clause "We have sent it down" is in the place of a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a Book", and "blessed" is a second qualifier. These two are the purpose of the information, because its being a Book about which there is no doubt is not in question; rather, they doubted its being sent down from God and its being blessed. The conjunction of "blessed" to "We have sent it down" is apt, because the passive participle, by virtue of its derivation, has the force of a verb. The meaning of "be mindful" (ittaqū) is: be people characterised by taqwa, which is taking hold of the religion of truth and acting upon it. His saying "that you may be shown mercy" is a promise for following it, and an indirect threat of the punishment of this world and the next if they do not follow it.
