His saying "lest you should say" is in the place of a causal clause for the verb "We have sent it down", with the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil) elided, as is well known regarding its elision with "an". The estimate is: "so that you do not say", that is, because of your saying that in the future, meaning in view of your saying and in anticipation of its occurrence. So the saying is the motive for the sending down of the Book.

The context indicates that this saying was the motive for sending down this Book. The motivating cause of something does not necessarily have to be a final cause (ʿillah ghaʾiyyah). Thus this meaning of the lam is the reverse of the meaning of the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah). The meaning comes down to this: the sending down of the Book has wisdoms in it, among them the wisdom of cutting off their excuse that no Book was sent down to them, or out of aversion to their saying that, or in order to avoid their saying it. This is by the aid of the context, out of preference for brevity; for this reason a noun is understood, such as: "out of aversion to" or "to avoid". On this estimate the grammarians of Basra proceeded. The grammarians of Kufa held that it is on the estimate of the negative particle "lā", so the estimate for them is: "lest you not say", and the outcome is one. Parallels to this in the Qur'an are numerous, such as His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [4:176], and His saying: ﴿Follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾ [39:55], ﴿lest a soul should say: "Alas for me, for what I neglected regarding God's side"﴾ [39:56].

[Page 180]

And His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains, lest it should shake with you﴾ [16:15], meaning to avoid its shaking with you. And the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm:

"We hastened the hospitality lest they insult us"

This saying may have come from them previously, for it came in the verse of Surah al-Qasas: ﴿When the truth came to them from Us they said: "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"﴾ [28:48]. It may also be that it was anticipated, and then they said it afterwards. Whichever it is, it was anticipated that they would repeat and reiterate it, a saying that accords with the reality of the matter. It was therefore anticipated that it would be uttered when blame was directed at them for their falling short of their neighbours among the Jews and Christians in respect of completing the virtues, the goodness of conduct and the perfection of religiosity; and when they would be questioned in the Hereafter about following their misguidance; and when they would witness what the people of the righteous communities attain of bliss and elevation of ranks in God's reward, so they would long for a share of that and make the excuse that they had been deprived of guidance in this world.

The Jews and Christians in the lands of the Arabs were in a condition more complete than the conditions of the people of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). Do you not see the saying of al-Nābighah, praising the family of al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Ḥārith, and they were Christians:

"Their assembly is the sanctity of God, and their religion is upright, so they hope for nothing but good ends.
They do not reckon good as having no evil after it, nor do they reckon evil as an inescapable blow."

The ṭāʾifah (group) is a large multitude of people. Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ [4:102] in Surah al-Nisāʾ. What is meant by the "two groups" here is the Jews and the Christians.

"The Book" is meant as a genus, confined to the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. The meaning of "the sending down of the Book upon them" is that they were addressed with the heavenly Books that were sent down to their prophets. The Arabs were not addressed with what was sent down to others. This is therefore a first excuse from them. There is another excuse, arising from their disinclination to take on the virtues and righteous deeds, and it is their saying: ﴿and we were indeed unaware of their study﴾, that is, "we were indeed unaware of following their guidance, because we were not taught", so "study" here is meant as teaching.

[Page 181]

"Study" (dirāsah) is reading with repetition for memorisation or for reflection, so the mere recitation of a book is not study. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they say: "You have studied"﴾ [6:105] has passed in this surah, and its detailed discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿and by what you used to study﴾ [3:79] in Surah Āl ʿImrān.

"Heedlessness" (ghaflah) is the forgetfulness arising from lack of attentiveness, that is, we did not concern ourselves with what their books contained, so that we might follow their guidance. Thus the coming of the Qur'an was a reminder to them of the perfect guidance, and a sufficiency that dispenses with the study of their books.

His saying: ﴿Or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them"﴾ is a gradual progression in the excuse, coming in accordance with what the souls of the Arabs conceal of their sense of superiority over themselves above the rest of the nations, their aspiration towards lofty matters, their confidence in their shrewdness, the eloquence of their tongues, the keenness of their minds and the speed of their understanding; and they were deserving of all of that.

In expressing this excuse of theirs there is an instruction for them and an awakening of their understanding, so that they might rejoice in the Qur'an and comprehend what returns to them from it of excellence and nobility among the nations, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your mention; will you not understand?﴾ [21:10]. Those who followed the Qur'an were better guided than the Jews and Christians by a far-reaching margin of ranks.

After this wondrous alert, the context became ready for the "fāʾ" of result (fāʾ faṣīḥah) in His saying: ﴿Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾, and its estimate is: "If you are saying that, and it stirs in your souls, then there has come to you a clarification from your Lord, meaning the Qur'an, which removes from you what you sense of falling short of the People of the Book."

[Page 182]

"Clear proof" (bayyinah) is that by which there is clarification and manifestation of the truth. The Qur'an is therefore a clear proof that it is from God, by its inimitability for the eloquent Arabs; it is guidance, by what it contains of direction to the path of good; and it is mercy, by the tolerant law it brought, in which there is no hardship, so it establishes the welfare of the community together with ease. This is among the most wondrous of legislations, and it is more indicative that it is from the command of the All-Knowing of everything.

From this excusing of them there follows the information about them that there is no one more unjust than they, because they denied and turned away. The "fāʾ" in His saying: ﴿So who is more unjust﴾ is for consequence. The interrogation is one of denial, meaning: there is no one more unjust than those who denied the signs of God.

The "min" in ﴿than one who denied the signs of God﴾ is a relative (mawṣūlah), and its antecedent is "you" addressed in His saying: "lest you should say: The Book was only sent down to two groups."

Injustice here includes the injustice to their own souls, since they dragged them to punishment in the Hereafter and to loss in this world; the injustice to the Messenger ﷺ, since they denied him, when he was not one deserving of denial; and the injustice to God, since they denied His signs and rejected His blessing. They also wronged people by barring them from Islam by word and deed.

The relative pronoun has been used so that the relative clause indicates the reason for the judgement and the basis of the construction of the predicate, because whoever has the content of that clause established for him is deserving of being the most unjust of people.

The meaning of "ṣadafa" is that he himself turned away, and it is also used in the sense of diverting another, as in the Qāmūs. Its original form is transitive to an object directly, and to a second with "ʿan", as one says: "I turned so-and-so away from such-and-such" (ṣadaftu fulānan ʿan kadhā), just as one says ṣarftuhu. It has become widely used as if intransitive, to the point that the omission of the object has become prevalent, so one says: "he turned away from such-and-such" in the sense of "he turned aside". Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿See how We variously present the signs, yet they turn away﴾ [6:46] in this surah. Al-Zamakhsharī, in the Kashshāf, estimated it here as transitive, because it is more fitting to the condition of their being the most unjust of people, in multiplying the aspects of their transgression. I have not seen this from anyone else on reflection,

[Page 183]

for His saying: ﴿We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment﴾ is more suited to the transitive sense, since the recompense is for their turning away and for their barring people from the signs. Their denial of the signs includes their turning away from them, so it is fitting that their turning away should be their diverting people.

"Dreadful punishment" (sūʾ al-ʿadhāb) is an attribution of a quality to what it qualifies. Its "sūʾ" is its most intense and strongest form. This is explained by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾ [16:88]. So His saying "punishment upon punishment" is the multiplication of the punishment, that is, its severity. It is possible that what is meant by it is the punishment of this world by killing and humiliation, and the punishment of the Hereafter. That was their recompense because they did not deny merely from a bare summons; rather, they denied after the clear signs had come to them. "What" (mā) is a verbal-source particle: that is, "for their turning away and their aversion from the signs, an aversion that is continuous and has not left any inclination towards it." Here "kāna" is for continuity, like His saying: ﴿and God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The meaning of "ṣadafa" is that he himself turned away, and it is also used in the sense of diverting another, as in the Qāmūs. Its original form is transitive to an object directly, and to a second with "ʿan", as one says: "I turned so-and-so away from such-and-such" (ṣadaftu fulānan ʿan kadhā), just as one says ṣarftuhu. It has become widely used as if intransitive, to the point that the omission of the object has become prevalent, so one says: "he turned away from such-and-such" in the sense of "he turned aside". Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿See how We variously present the signs, yet they turn away﴾ [6:46] in this surah. Al-Zamakhsharī, in the Kashshāf, estimated it here as transitive, because it is more fitting to the condition of their being the most unjust of people, in multiplying the aspects of their transgression. I have not seen this from anyone else on reflection,

[Page 183]

for His saying: ﴿We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment﴾ is more suited to the transitive sense, since the recompense is for their turning away and for their barring people from the signs. Their denial of the signs includes their turning away from them, so it is fitting that their turning away should be their diverting people.

"Dreadful punishment" (sūʾ al-ʿadhāb) is an attribution of a quality to what it qualifies. Its "sūʾ" is its most intense and strongest form. This is explained by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾ [16:88]. So His saying "punishment upon punishment" is the multiplication of the punishment, that is, its severity. It is possible that what is meant by it is the punishment of this world by killing and humiliation, and the punishment of the Hereafter. That was their recompense because they did not deny merely from a bare summons; rather, they denied after the clear signs had come to them. "What" (mā) is a verbal-source particle: that is, "for their turning away and their aversion from the signs, an aversion that is continuous and has not left any inclination towards it." Here "kāna" is for continuity, like His saying: ﴿and God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

[Page 178]

﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may be shown mercy.﴾ ﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them? We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment, for what they used to turn away.﴾

The clause ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf, coordination) to the clause ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Anʿam: 154]. The meaning is: We gave Moses the Book [6:154], and We have sent down this Book, as was mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [6:154]... and so on.

The opening of the clause with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), the construction of the verb upon it, and making the Book, whose proper place is to be the object of ﴿We have sent it down﴾, into the subject (mubtada'), all of this is for the sake of emphasising the Book and praising it. A parallel to this has already occurred: ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what is before it﴾ [6:92] in this surah.

The command to follow it, being based on its being sent down from God and on its being blessed, is clear, because whatever is of this kind is not doubted by anyone as something to be followed.

The word "following" (ittiba') has been applied, by way of metaphor, to acting upon what is in it. Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [6:50] and His saying: ﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [6:106] in this surah.

[Page 179]

The address in His saying "follow it" is to the polytheists, by the indicator of His saying: ﴿lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾.

The clause "We have sent it down" is in the place of a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a Book", and "blessed" is a second qualifier. These two are the purpose of the information, because its being a Book about which there is no doubt is not in question; rather, they doubted its being sent down from God and its being blessed. The conjunction of "blessed" to "We have sent it down" is apt, because the passive participle, by virtue of its derivation, has the force of a verb. The meaning of "be mindful" (ittaqū) is: be people characterised by taqwa, which is taking hold of the religion of truth and acting upon it. His saying "that you may be shown mercy" is a promise for following it, and an indirect threat of the punishment of this world and the next if they do not follow it.

His saying "lest you should say" is in the place of a causal clause for the verb "We have sent it down", with the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil) elided, as is well known regarding its elision with "an". The estimate is: "so that you do not say", that is, because of your saying that in the future, meaning in view of your saying and in anticipation of its occurrence. So the saying is the motive for the sending down of the Book.

The context indicates that this saying was the motive for sending down this Book. The motivating cause of something does not necessarily have to be a final cause (ʿillah ghaʾiyyah). Thus this meaning of the lam is the reverse of the meaning of the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah). The meaning comes down to this: the sending down of the Book has wisdoms in it, among them the wisdom of cutting off their excuse that no Book was sent down to them, or out of aversion to their saying that, or in order to avoid their saying it. This is by the aid of the context, out of preference for brevity; for this reason a noun is understood, such as: "out of aversion to" or "to avoid". On this estimate the grammarians of Basra proceeded. The grammarians of Kufa held that it is on the estimate of the negative particle "lā", so the estimate for them is: "lest you not say", and the outcome is one. Parallels to this in the Qur'an are numerous, such as His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [4:176], and His saying: ﴿Follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾ [39:55], ﴿lest a soul should say: "Alas for me, for what I neglected regarding God's side"﴾ [39:56].

[Page 180]

And His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains, lest it should shake with you﴾ [16:15], meaning to avoid its shaking with you. And the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm:

"We hastened the hospitality lest they insult us"

This saying may have come from them previously, for it came in the verse of Surah al-Qasas: ﴿When the truth came to them from Us they said: "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"﴾ [28:48]. It may also be that it was anticipated, and then they said it afterwards. Whichever it is, it was anticipated that they would repeat and reiterate it, a saying that accords with the reality of the matter. It was therefore anticipated that it would be uttered when blame was directed at them for their falling short of their neighbours among the Jews and Christians in respect of completing the virtues, the goodness of conduct and the perfection of religiosity; and when they would be questioned in the Hereafter about following their misguidance; and when they would witness what the people of the righteous communities attain of bliss and elevation of ranks in God's reward, so they would long for a share of that and make the excuse that they had been deprived of guidance in this world.

The Jews and Christians in the lands of the Arabs were in a condition more complete than the conditions of the people of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). Do you not see the saying of al-Nābighah, praising the family of al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Ḥārith, and they were Christians:

"Their assembly is the sanctity of God, and their religion is upright, so they hope for nothing but good ends.
They do not reckon good as having no evil after it, nor do they reckon evil as an inescapable blow."

The ṭāʾifah (group) is a large multitude of people. Its discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ [4:102] in Surah al-Nisāʾ. What is meant by the "two groups" here is the Jews and the Christians.

"The Book" is meant as a genus, confined to the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. The meaning of "the sending down of the Book upon them" is that they were addressed with the heavenly Books that were sent down to their prophets. The Arabs were not addressed with what was sent down to others. This is therefore a first excuse from them. There is another excuse, arising from their disinclination to take on the virtues and righteous deeds, and it is their saying: ﴿and we were indeed unaware of their study﴾, that is, "we were indeed unaware of following their guidance, because we were not taught", so "study" here is meant as teaching.

[Page 181]

"Study" (dirāsah) is reading with repetition for memorisation or for reflection, so the mere recitation of a book is not study. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they say: "You have studied"﴾ [6:105] has passed in this surah, and its detailed discussion has passed at His saying: ﴿and by what you used to study﴾ [3:79] in Surah Āl ʿImrān.

"Heedlessness" (ghaflah) is the forgetfulness arising from lack of attentiveness, that is, we did not concern ourselves with what their books contained, so that we might follow their guidance. Thus the coming of the Qur'an was a reminder to them of the perfect guidance, and a sufficiency that dispenses with the study of their books.

His saying: ﴿Or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them"﴾ is a gradual progression in the excuse, coming in accordance with what the souls of the Arabs conceal of their sense of superiority over themselves above the rest of the nations, their aspiration towards lofty matters, their confidence in their shrewdness, the eloquence of their tongues, the keenness of their minds and the speed of their understanding; and they were deserving of all of that.

In expressing this excuse of theirs there is an instruction for them and an awakening of their understanding, so that they might rejoice in the Qur'an and comprehend what returns to them from it of excellence and nobility among the nations, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your mention; will you not understand?﴾ [21:10]. Those who followed the Qur'an were better guided than the Jews and Christians by a far-reaching margin of ranks.

After this wondrous alert, the context became ready for the "fāʾ" of result (fāʾ faṣīḥah) in His saying: ﴿Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾, and its estimate is: "If you are saying that, and it stirs in your souls, then there has come to you a clarification from your Lord, meaning the Qur'an, which removes from you what you sense of falling short of the People of the Book."

[Page 182]

"Clear proof" (bayyinah) is that by which there is clarification and manifestation of the truth. The Qur'an is therefore a clear proof that it is from God, by its inimitability for the eloquent Arabs; it is guidance, by what it contains of direction to the path of good; and it is mercy, by the tolerant law it brought, in which there is no hardship, so it establishes the welfare of the community together with ease. This is among the most wondrous of legislations, and it is more indicative that it is from the command of the All-Knowing of everything.

From this excusing of them there follows the information about them that there is no one more unjust than they, because they denied and turned away. The "fāʾ" in His saying: ﴿So who is more unjust﴾ is for consequence. The interrogation is one of denial, meaning: there is no one more unjust than those who denied the signs of God.

The "min" in ﴿than one who denied the signs of God﴾ is a relative (mawṣūlah), and its antecedent is "you" addressed in His saying: "lest you should say: The Book was only sent down to two groups."

Injustice here includes the injustice to their own souls, since they dragged them to punishment in the Hereafter and to loss in this world; the injustice to the Messenger ﷺ, since they denied him, when he was not one deserving of denial; and the injustice to God, since they denied His signs and rejected His blessing. They also wronged people by barring them from Islam by word and deed.

The relative pronoun has been used so that the relative clause indicates the reason for the judgement and the basis of the construction of the predicate, because whoever has the content of that clause established for him is deserving of being the most unjust of people.

[Page 183]

for His saying: ﴿We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment﴾ is more suited to the transitive sense, since the recompense is for their turning away and for their barring people from the signs. Their denial of the signs includes their turning away from them, so it is fitting that their turning away should be their diverting people.
