This is explained by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾ [16:88]. So His saying "punishment upon punishment" is the multiplication of the punishment, that is, its severity. It is possible that what is meant by it is the punishment of this world by killing and humiliation, and the punishment of the Hereafter. That was their recompense because they did not deny merely from a bare summons; rather, they denied after the clear signs had come to them. "What" (mā) is a verbal-source particle: that is, "for their turning away and their aversion from the signs, an aversion that is continuous and has not left any inclination towards it." Here "kāna" is for continuity, like His saying: ﴿and God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The commentary begins here as a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question) that follows from His words: "So who does greater wrong than one who denies the signs of Allah" [al-An'am: 157]. It may carry a warning, or it may carry mockery, as will come later. If it is a warning and threat, it follows from the clause: "We shall recompense those who turn away from Our signs" [al-An'am: 157], because it raises the question of a questioner who asks: when will their recompense come? If it is mockery directed at them for turning away from the signs that came to them and for their longing for signs greater than these in their own belief, then it follows from the clause:

Page 184

"Who does greater wrong than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them" [al-An'am: 157], because it raises the question of a questioner who asks: what did they expect of signs beyond the signs that had come to them?

"Hal" (هل) is an interrogative of denial (*istifham inkari*), and it is used in this sense just as the hamza is used in this sense in its plain form. For this reason the exception (*istithna'*) comes after it.

"Yantadhirun" (ينتظرون) is the present tense of *nazara* in the sense of *intazara* (to wait). It shares with *nazara* in the sense of "to see" its past, present and verbal noun forms. It also differs from it in that it has a verbal noun of its own, *al-nazrah* with a kasra on the *za'*, and this is not used for looking with the eye.

The pronoun refers to those who turn away from the signs.

Then, if the waiting is taken to be real, meaning waiting for signs as they propose them, then the sense of restriction (*hasr*) is: they do not await anything after the signs that came to them, which they were not satisfied with, except the signs they proposed and demanded, and whose condition was that they would not believe until these were brought to them. These are what Allah relates of them in His words: "They said: We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" [al-Isra': 90], down to His words: "or you bring Allah and the angels before us as a guarantee" [al-Isra': 92], and His words: "They said: Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" [al-An'am: 8]. So some of them await some of this in earnest, as their common folk do, so the waiting is literal. And some await it in mockery of their leaders and misleaders, so the waiting is figurative in its outward form, because they displayed themselves in the aspect of those who wait, as in His words: "The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: Mock on" [al-Tawbah: 64], and so on. What is meant by "some of the signs of your Lord" is what includes what is related of them in His words: "until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" [al-Isra': 90], down to His words: "until you send down to us a book that we may read" [al-Isra': 93]. And in His words: "They said: Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" [al-An'am: 8], down to His words: "So there befell those who mocked them what they used to mock" [al-An'am: 10]. So the speech is mockery directed at them and at their beliefs.

Page 185

If the waiting is neither in earnest nor in mockery, then its meaning is that they do not look forward to any of the signs coming to them that would be greater than what has come to them. So there is no waiting for them. Rather, they have resolved upon disbelief and concealed obstinacy. If some waiting is supposed for them, then it is only the waiting for what will befall them of the punishment of the Hereafter, or the punishment of this world, or what lies between the two. In that case the exception is an emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite. The meaning is: they await nothing, but there will come to them what they do not expect, namely the coming of the angels, and so on. So the speech is a warning and threat.

The restriction, on both possibilities, is relative (*idafi*), that is, relative to what is expected of the signs. The interrogative in the form of a statement is used for mockery directed at them on both possibilities, because they do not await any sign, for they are certain in denying the Messenger (ﷺ). Yet they ask for the signs as a means of confounding him, in their own supposition. Nor do they await a reckoning, because they deny resurrection and the gathering.

The coming (*ityan*) with respect to the angels is literal, and what is meant by them is the angels of punishment, like those who descended on the day of Badr: "When your Lord revealed to the angels: I am with you, so make firm those who believe. I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them" [al-Anfal: 12]. As for what is ascribed to the Lord, it is figurative, and what is meant by it is the coming of His great punishment. Because of its great terror, He made its coming ascribed to the one who commands it with a decisive command, so that the magnitude of His greatness may be known in accordance with the great power of its agent and commander. So the attribution is figurative, of the type: "The governor built the city." This type of figurative usage occurs in the Qur'an in the same way, as in His words: "Allah came to them from where they did not expect" [al-Hashr: 2], and His words: "and he found Allah with him, and He paid him his account in full" [al-Nur: 39]. It is permissible that what is meant by His words "or" "there comes the command of your Lord" [al-Nahl: 33] is the coming of His command to the reckoning of people on the Day of Resurrection, like His words: "and your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank" [al-Fajr: 22]. That is, they await nothing but the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter.

Page 186

On all these possibilities it is permissible that the occurrence of that be on the Day of Resurrection, and it is permissible that it be in this world.

The clause "on the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith" is a resumptive explanatory clause, reminding them that waiting and delaying in faith has a grievous outcome, because they are threatened with what prevents remedy at the time of regret. Either death and reckoning will follow it, or there will follow the coming of one of the signs of Allah, which is a sign of punishment that breaks custom and is specific to them, so that they will know it is a punishment for their denial and their turning away. And when that punishment descends, there will be no room left for making up what has passed, because when Allah sends down His punishment upon the deniers, repentance does not benefit in His sight, as He said: "Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time" [Yunus: 98]. And He said: "We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be respited" [al-Hijr: 8]. And He said: "Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be given respite" [al-An'am: 8].

Among the signs of Allah are the signs that Allah made general for people, and these are the portents of the Hour, among which is the rising of the sun from its west, which signals the end of the worldly order. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will not be established until the sun rises from its west. When it rises and people see it, they will all believe, and that is the time when 'no soul will benefit from its faith if it did not believe before' [al-An'am: 158]." Then he recited this verse.

The benefit that is negated is the benefit in the Hereafter, by being saved from punishment, because the benefit of this world, by the removal of punishment at the coming of the signs, does not benefit souls, whether believing or disbelieving, according to His words: "And beware of a trial which will not strike those of you who have done wrong in particular" [al-Anfal: 25], and the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Then they will be gathered according to their intentions."

Page 187

What is meant by "soul" (*nafs*) is every soul, because it occurs in the context of negation.

The clause "who had not believed before" is a qualifying attribute of "soul", and it is a qualifier that specifies the general sense of "soul". That is: the soul which had not believed before the coming of some of the signs will not benefit from its faith when it believes at the descent of the punishment. From this it is known that the soul which had believed before the descent of the punishment will benefit from its faith in the Hereafter. The fronting of the object in His words "a soul its faith" is so that the brevity in the return of the pronoun may be completed.

His words "or had not earned good through its faith" are coordinated (*'atf*) with "had believed", meaning: or had not earned good during its faith.

The "fi" (في) is for location (*zarfiyyah*), and only the period of faith is suitable to be a location, not faith itself. That is: or had not earned good during the period of its faith.

Good (*khayr*) is righteous deeds and acts of obedience.

The "aw" (أو) is for division within the attributes of the soul. This necessitates dividing the souls specified by the two attributes into two categories: souls which were disbelieving and had not believed before, so their faith will not benefit them on the day when some of the signs of Allah come; and souls which believed but did not earn good during the period of their faith, so they are believing souls, and what they earn of good will not benefit them on the day when some of the signs of your Lord come. This second category has graded levels, because shortcoming in earning good varies: some of it is the waste of all acts of good, some of it is the waste of part of them, and some of it is neglect in increasing them. The apparent sense of the verse requires that what is meant is souls which earned nothing of good during their faith, that is, which confined themselves to faith and neglected all acts of good.

It is known from the division that these souls will not benefit from earning good after the coming of the signs, nor from what takes the place of earning good in the sight of Allah, which is what He bestowed upon this community of forgiveness of misdeeds upon repentance. So resolving upon good is repentance, that is, resolving to earn good, so an ellipsis occurs in the speech, relying on the clear indication. The estimate is: no soul which was not believing will benefit from its faith, or a soul which had not earned good in its faith before earning it. That is, or what takes the place of earning good, such as repentance, for it is part of earning good. It is not meant that a believing soul will not benefit from its faith if it has not earned good in such a way that faith occurs when earning good has not occurred, because if that were meant there would be no use in the division, and it would have sufficed to say: "no soul will benefit from its faith if it did not earn good." Rather, the conclusive proofs are firm that faith which occurred before the coming of the signs is not nullified if its holder neglects some righteous deeds. Also, even if we grant that it is so, it would only necessitate that one who did not do good but believed would not benefit from his faith, and that is creating a category that no scholar of Islam has affirmed.

By this you know that the verse is not sufficient as proof for the Mu'tazilah nor the Khawarij, who held that the grave sinner who does not repent must abide forever in the Fire, and equated him with the disbeliever. Although its apparent sense before reflection may suggest to them that it is a proof for them, and because if the matter were as they say, entering faith together with committing a single grave sin would be futile, which no sensible person would accept for himself, since he would take on the burden of many acts without benefit from them. And the easiest state for the perpetrator of a grave sin would be to strip off the bond of faith until he repents of both matters together. The absurdity of this consequence for the adherents of this doctrine is an absurdity that one of keen insight would not accept. Occupying oneself with clarifying what is derived from the structure of the verse, namely determining the limit at which benefit from attaining faith and attaining acts of good ends, is more fruitful than delving into the implications of its meanings, such as considering acts part of faith, especially given the possibility inherent in the basic meaning which invalidates the inference.

Page 189

Thus the attribute "who had not believed before" is a warning to the polytheists against delaying in faith, lest the day of the manifestation of the signs overtake them, and they are the intended subject of the context. The attribute "or had not earned good through its faith" is an incorporation (*idmaj*) within the course of the intended meaning, to warn believers against turning away from righteous deeds.

Then, the statements of the earlier exegetes concerning the depiction of these two categories diverged in a way that indicates the difficulty of extracting the intended meaning of the verse from its wording. They did not come near to a clear expression, and three statements gather these. The first: from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, that the meaning of "earned good in its faith" is: it earned righteous deeds in its affirmation, that is, with it or during its period. They both said: these are the people of the qiblah (*ahl al-qiblah*, the Muslims). If it was affirming and did not do deeds before that, that is, before the coming of some of the signs of Allah, and then did deeds after it saw the sign, it will not be accepted from it. And if it did good before the sign and then did good after the sign, it will be accepted from it.

Second point: The wording of the Qur'an follows the method of prevalence (al-taghlib), because most of those who benefit from their faith at that time are those who had earned good through their faith.

Third point: The statement is ambiguous as to one of the two matters. The meaning is: on that day, the faith of one who had not believed before that day, or who had not added to his faith the doing of good, will not benefit him. That is, the faith of those among the unbelievers who come to faith will not benefit them, nor will the obedience of those among the believers who obey (at that time). As for one who believed before, his faith will benefit him, and likewise one who obeyed before, his obedience will benefit him.

His saying ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ came after His saying ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come?﴾, restricting itself to what comes of the signs of God on the appointed day, turning away from addressing what will happen on the day when the angels come or your Lord comes. This is because the coming of the angels, and what is coupled with it, is not a possibility to be realized; its mention came only to nullify their saying:

صفحة ١٩٠
"﴿Or bring God and the angels as a group before us﴾ [al-Isra: 92]" and similar of their mockeries, whereas what they awaited was that some of the signs of God should come. That is the locus of admonition and warning. The verses of the Qur'an in this regard are many, among them His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85].

Among the signs of God are some that pertain specifically to the polytheists, namely what God threatened them with of the descent of punishment upon them in this world, as it descended upon the nations before them. Among them are signs general to all people, which are known as the portents of the Hour, that is, the major portents.

The explanation of this verse has come in the Sunnah as the rising of the sun from its west. In the two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will not come until the sun rises from its west. When people see it, whoever is on the earth will believe, and that is the time when ﴿faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before﴾." Then he recited this verse, that is, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ up to His saying ﴿good﴾.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever repents before the sun rises from its west, God will accept his repentance." In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from Safwan ibn 'Assal al-Muradi, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is a door on the side of the west, open, whose width is a forty years' journey; it remains open for repentance and will not be closed until the sun rises from its west." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a sound hadith."

Know that this verse does not contradict the verse in Surah al-Nisa': ﴿Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Nisa: 18]. This is because the intended meaning of that verse is the specifying of the time when repentance ceases to be accepted with respect to the particular circumstances of individuals. This is what was explained in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God accepts the repentance of a servant so long as he has not begun the death rattle (yughargir)." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ahmad.

The meaning of yughargir is that his soul reaches, that is, his breaths reach, the top of his throat.

The intended meaning of the verse under discussion is specifying the time when repentance ceases with respect to all people, which is the state in which all people despair of remaining.

The continuation came with His saying ﴿Say: "Wait, indeed we are waiting"﴾, as a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to threaten and warn them for their waiting, if it was actually occurring from them, or for their delay and postponement in entering Islam, which resembles waiting if the waiting is figurative. He is commanded to tell them to persist in their state, which he expressed by "waiting," as a command of threat, and to inform them that the Muslims are waiting for the victory of God and the descent of punishment upon their enemies. That is: continue in your waiting, for we too are waiting.

In the implication of the two attributes there is an indication that the soul which believed before the coming of the reckoning and had earned good in its faith, its faith and its deeds will benefit it. Thus the verse includes, in its explicit and implicit meanings, a general warning and a general promise, which the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah clarify.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 159:

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects — you, [O Muhammad], have nothing to do with them in anything. Their matter is only with Allah; then He will inform them about what they used to do.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that follows the warning, serving as a conclusion and summation (fadhlaka), because when Allah said to His Messenger ﷺ: "﴿Say, 'Wait; indeed, we are waiting.'﴾ [al-An'am: 158]," He followed that with the statement that the two groups are divergent and estranged during the period of waiting.

The relative construction (al-mawsuliyyah) is used to define the subject (ta'rif al-musnad ilayhi) to convey the certainty of the meaning of the relative clause (sila) concerning them, because it fits the aversion from associating with them. The nature of religion is that it should be one creed and one set of practices, and division in its foundations contradicts its unity. For this reason, the scholars of Islam have not ceased to exert their utmost effort to derive the intent of Allah from the Ummah, knowing that the truth is one, that Allah has charged the scholars with reaching it, and that He has granted the one who is correct two rewards, and the one who errs despite exerting full effort one reward. That reward is for the exertion in seeking it, since exerting oneself in this matter is close to reaching the goal.

As for "﴿those who divided their religion﴾", Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the polytheists, because they did not agree on one form of religion. The tribes worshipped different idols, some of the Arabs worshipped the angels, some worshipped the sun, and some worshipped the moon, and each idol had a form of worship that differed from the worship of another.

It is also possible that what is meant is that they were upon the hanifiyyah, which is the religion of monotheism common to all of them, but they divided it and made gods whose forms of worship differ. As for their being "sects" (shi'a), it is because each tribe would support its idol and claim that it would grant them victory over the worshippers of other idols, as Dirar ibn al-Khattab al-Fihri said: "Thaqif fled to their Lat, returning as the defeated, the losing one."

The meaning of "you have nothing to do with them in anything" is that there is no connection between you and them. The particle min here is for connection (ittisaliyyah), and its origin is the initial min (ibtida'iyyah).

Shay' ("anything") is a generic noun meaning "existent," so its negation indicates the negation of every kind of connection that may exist. This was discussed earlier at His saying: "﴿And whoever does that has nothing from Allah in anything﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]" in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His saying: "﴿You are not upon anything﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68]" in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Since the statement indicates disavowal of them and non-association with them, and since the discourse may prompt a questioner to ask: Is it incumbent upon the Messenger to take on their recompense for the evil of their deeds? Therefore the resumptive clause came with His saying: "﴿Their matter is only with Allah﴾". It is thus an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani). The construction of restriction (qasr) serves to reverse the belief of the one who is hesitant, meaning: their matter is only with Allah, not with the Messenger ﷺ nor with anyone else. This is a severe warning. By "their matter" is meant their deeds for which they deserve reward and punishment. "Ila" (to) is used in the figurative sense of終ending (al-intiha' al-majazi); it likens their matter to a stray animal that people have left, which wanders until it reaches its pasture, for all creation are servants of Allah and to Him they return. Allah gives them respite, then seizes them with a punishment from Him, or at the hands of the believers when He permits His Messenger ﷺ to fight them, as He, exalted, said: "﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10] ﴿covering the people; this is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11] ﴿'Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers.'﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12] ﴿How will they have the reminder when there has already come to them a clear messenger﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13] ﴿then they turned away from him and said, 'A taught, possessed man'﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14] ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15] ﴿On the day We will seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]." The greatest seizure is the seizure of the day of Badr.

His saying: "﴿then He will inform them about what they used to do﴾" — here "thumma" indicates sequence in rank (al-tartib al-rutbi) together with the implication of delay, meaning their matter remains with Allah for a period. That is from the granting of respite and extension to them; then He punishes them. The informing is applied to the punishment, because if the punishment is that of the Hereafter, it is preceded by reckoning, and in it is the informing of the transgressor about his transgression and that he is held accountable for it, so applying "informing" to it is literal, with its necessary implication intended as a kinaya. If the punishment is that of this world, then applying "informing" to it is figurative, because when punishment descends upon them after the warning, they know that it is the punishment that was promised, so the attainment of that knowledge at the time of its occurrence resembles the knowledge gained from information, and so "informing" is applied to it. Thus His saying "yunabbi'uhum" means "yu'aqibuhum bi-ma kanu yaf'aluna" (He punishes them for what they used to do).

The description of the polytheists as those who "divided their religion and became sects" indicates that it is a grave attribute, since Allah described them with it only in the context of blame. This indicates that Allah is warning the Muslims against being in their religion as the polytheists were in theirs. For this reason He, exalted, said: "﴿He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah and that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Shura: 13] up to His saying "﴿Establish the religion and do not be divided therein﴾" [al-Shura: 13].

The division of the religion of Islam is the division of its foundations after their unity, as some of the Arabs did in withholding zakat after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Abu Bakr - may Allah be pleased with him - said: "I will certainly fight whoever separates between prayer and zakat." As for the division of opinions in explanations and elucidations, there is no harm in it, and it is part of reflection upon the religion, like the disagreement over the evidences for the attributes and in verifying their meanings, while agreeing on affirming them. Likewise the elaboration of branches (furu') such as the division of the branches of jurisprudence through the disagreement among jurists, while agreeing on the nature of the act and on what validity and invalidity of actions depend upon, such as the disagreement over the reality of the obligatory (fard) and the required (wajib). The conclusion is that every division by which some sects do not declare others to be disbelievers, and which does not lead to fighting and strife, is a division of reflection, inference, and seeking the truth to the extent of one's capacity. Every division that leads its adherents to declare one another disbelievers and to fight one another over matters of religion is among what Allah has warned against. As for what occurred among the Muslims in disputes over kingship and worldly affairs, it is not a division in religion, but it is among the conditions from which communities are never free.

The Jumhur read "farraqu" with a shaddah on the ra'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "faraqu" with an alif after the fa', meaning they abandoned their religion, i.e., they abandoned what had been their religion, namely the hanifiyyah common to all the Arabs, so they discarded it and made it into numerous sects. The outcome of both readings is one.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 6, verse 160:**

﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged.﴾

It is a habit of the Qur'an that when it gives a warning, it follows the warning with (a statement addressed to) those to whom that warning does not apply, and when it gives good tidings, it follows the good tidings with (a statement addressed to) those who have the opposite of what was promised to them. The Qur'an has followed this pattern here. When it warned the believers and cautioned them against delaying in acquiring good, before some of God's overpowering signs come, with His saying:

[p. 195] ﴿No soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158], He thereby set for them a limit that is one of the manifestations of His justice. He followed that with good tidings from among the manifestations of His grace and justice, namely the recompense for a good deed with ten times its like and the recompense for an evil deed with its like. His saying ﴿Whoever brings a good deed﴾ and so on is an initial resumptive statement (istinaf ibtida'i), following the custom of the Qur'an in the Anfal (of the Qur'an) among its various themes.

So the discourse is a concluding summary (tadhyil) comprising the states of the two groups that the saying ﴿No soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and the verse that follows it, required, as was mentioned just above.

The phrase "brings a good deed" (jaa'a bil-hasanah) means "does a good deed." Its doer is likened to one who seeks gain: he goes out seeking provision by lawful means, or by gathering firewood, or by hunting, and then comes to his family with something. Similarly, the term "trade" (tijarah) is metaphorically applied to it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16].

Thus the "ba'" (bi-) is for accompaniment, and the statement is an allegory (tamthil). It is also permissible to take "coming" (majee') in its literal sense, meaning arriving at the reckoning, such that what is meant by the good deed is that he comes with its record in his book of deeds.

The "likes" of the good deed (amthal al-hasanah) means the rewards of its likes. The statement therefore contains an ellipsis of a noun (hadhf mudaf), indicated by the context of His saying ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. Alternatively, its meaning is that ten good deeds, like the one he brought, are reckoned for him, as in the hadith: "God records it with Him as ten good deeds." It is known from this that the reward follows that same manner of reckoning, as His saying ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ indicates.

"Amthal" is the plural of "mithl," which is the equal, the similar. The numeral is given in the feminine form "ten" (ashara) because "amthal" is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by "hasanah" (good deed); that is, "then he has ten good deeds, their likes." Thus the meaning of the noun that the numeral counts (its mumayyiz) is observed rather than its wording, which is "amthal." Recompense for a good deed at tenfold is a bounty from God, and it is the recompense of most good deeds. God has increased in some good deeds, multiplying them seven hundredfold, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. That is specific to spending in jihad. And in the hadith: "Whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, God records it with Him as one complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, God records it with Him as ten good deeds up to seven hundredfold, up to many multiples."

The majority of reciters read "ten likes of it" (ashru amthaliha) with "ashru" (ten) in construct with "amthaliha," which is the construction of an adjective with its noun. Ya'qub read "ashrun" with tanwin and "amthaluha" in the nominative, taking it as an adjective of "ashrun," meaning: "then he has ten good deeds similar to the good deed that he brought."

The similarity of the recompense to the good deed is entrusted to God's knowledge and His grace.

As for the saying regarding the evil deed, ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾, it uses the form of restriction (hasr) because of what its form contains of fronting the negation aspect, out of concern for it, to show God's justice. The restriction is real (haqiqi), and in real restriction there is no refutation of a belief; rather it is a report of what is in the reality of the matter. For this reason it would have been equivalent to say: "and whoever brings an evil deed, he will be recompensed with its like," were it not for the concern with the aspect of negating an increase beyond equivalence. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when Hind bint 'Utba asked him, saying: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man. Is there any blame on me if I feed his dependents from what he has?" He said to her: "No, except in a reasonable manner." He did not say to her: "Feed them in a reasonable manner." The same meaning is found in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, God records it with Him as one complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, God records it as one evil deed." He emphasized it with "one" to affirm that there is no increase in the recompense for the evil deed.

[p. 197] For this reason he followed it with His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. The pronoun refers to "whoever brings an evil deed," to manifest justice. Therefore He recorded for them that there is no wrong in this, so that they might be fair to themselves. As for counting the return of the two pronouns to the two groups, this does not suit the group of those with good deeds, because it is not appropriate to say of one who has been honored and showered with good that he is "not wronged."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 161:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion, the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (hanif), and he was not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) marking the transition from the debate with the polytheists, and what intervened in it, to a summation (fadhlaka) of what the Messenger ﷺ was commanded concerning this matter. It closes the door of debate with those who turn away, and it announces that he has taken upon himself what they were disputing with him about, so that they may take it up too, and that he is firm upon what he has brought them, and that their aversion does not shake him from the truth.

In this there is also an indication that the surah is ending. When the preacher or the debater has fully exhausted the discussion of his subject, and then begins to state what he has chosen for himself and what his settled position is, the listener knows that he has begun to fold up the scroll of argument. For this reason the style changes. So the Messenger ﷺ is commanded to say things by which he proclaims the principles of his religion, and the command to "say" is repeated three times to give prominence to what is said.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153], which He explained by His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have revealed, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 155]. So He added to that explanation with His saying "Say," ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾, to show that this religion was brought by the Messenger ﷺ with guidance from Allah, and that He made it a correct religion built on the foundations of the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, except that it exceeds it by what it includes of Allah's favour upon him, in that He guided him to that path which is the way of salvation.

The report is opened with the emphatic particle because the address is to the polytheists who deny.

The definiteness of the predicate-subject (al-musnad ilayhi) by the idafa (the "my" of "my Lord") is for pride in the Messenger's ﷺ being a servant of Allah, the Exalted, and as an allusion to the polytheists whose lords misled them; had they worshipped the true Lord who deserves worship alone, He would have guided them.

His saying: ﴿My Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾ is a metaphorical representation (tamthiliyyah): the state of guidance to the conveyed truth, which leads to salvation, is likened to the state of one who directs a traveller onto the road that reaches his destination.

The correspondence between guidance (hidayah) and path (sirat) is complete, for the real meaning of guidance is acquaintance with the way, as one says: "he is a guide who knows the desert (khirrit)," and the real meaning of sirat is the broad road. It is valid to borrow guidance for instruction and teaching, and sirat for the upright religion, so this is a compound analogy capable of being broken into its parts, and it is the most complete form of the tamthiliyyah.

The path is described as straight (mustaqim), meaning that in which there is no error or corruption, and this was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. The purpose is to complete the form of the comparison: that it is a religion that gives no entry to doubt in its benefit for its follower, just as the traveller on a broad road with no bends does not hesitate and is not confused about his course.

In His saying "a correct religion (dinan qayyiman)" there is a stripping (tajrid) of the metaphor that signals the thing compared, and "dinan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from "sirat," since it is an indefinite described noun.

Religion (din) was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], and it is the way of life that people follow.

As for "qayyim," with the qaf vowelled with fatha and the ya doubled, as read by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub, it is an intensive adjective (wasf mubalaghah) meaning upright, not crooked. The application of qiyam (standing) to uprightness and straightness is a metaphor, because when a person stands upright his stature is straight, so uprightness entails standing. The better view is to take qayyim as an intensification in the matter, synonymous with qayyum, so that standing is borrowed for sufficiency in what is needed and fulfilment of what is necessary for the wellbeing of the one who is sustained by it. Thus Islam is a qayyim over the community and its needs; one says "So-and-so is qayyim over such-and-such," meaning he manages it and sets it right, and from this Allah, the Exalted, is described as al-Qayyum. This is the better view because it adds something beyond the meaning of "straight," which took a part of the tamthiliyyah, so it is not a repetition of part of the comparison.

'Asim, Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "qiyaman" with the qaf vowelled with kasra and the ya with fatha and lightened. It is among the forms of verbal nouns (masadir) of qama, so it describes the religion with the verbal noun of standing, intended to mean sufficiency for the interest, as an intensification. This pattern is rare among verbal nouns, and the conversion of its waw into ya after a kasra is contrary to what is usual, since the usual practice for it is to keep its lam sound because it is fatha-vowelled. So whether it is light or falls upon waw or ya is equal, like 'iwad and hiwal, and this is like the irregularity of jiyad, the plural of jawad. "Qayyiman" is in the accusative as a qualifier of "dinan."

His saying: ﴿the religion of Abraham﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "dinan" or from "sirat mustaqim," or it is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) of "dinan." Milla is synonymous with din, so the use of it here is for variety of expression. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Abraham charged his sons with it, and Jacob too: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132].

"Millah" is on the pattern fi'lah in the sense of maf'ul, meaning "that which is dictated," from amlaltu al-kitab when I dictated to the scribe what he should write. Its proper form would not be joined with the feminine ta', because the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul requires masculine form, like dhibh. However, they joined it with the feminine ta' when they made it a noun for the religion. For this reason al-Raghib said: "millah is like din." Then he said: "The difference between it and din is that millah is only attributed to the prophet to whom it is ascribed, such as millat Ibrahim, millat aba'i, and it is not found attributed to Allah or to the community, and it is used only for the totality of the Law and not for its individual parts. One does not say 'prayer is the millah of Allah,' whereas one says 'prayer is the din of Allah.'" That is because in the word millah it is observed that it is dictated from Allah, so it is attributed to the one upon whom it was dictated.

The meaning of Islam being the millah of Abraham is that it came with the principles that are the Law of Abraham, namely: tawhid, conformity with the natural disposition (fitrah), gratitude, generosity, and proclaiming the truth. I have explained this earlier at His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The hanif is one who turns away from falsehood, so it means the guided one. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Say: Rather, the millah of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], in Surat al-Baqarah. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The clause ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is conjoined (atf) to the circumstantial clause concerning Abraham, peace be upon him, the one who is added to, because the annexed noun here is like the complement of the annexed-to noun, and this was discussed earlier in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 162–163:

﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my rites, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿No partner has He. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims.﴾

This is also a resumptive statement (isti'naf), which takes the place of a derivation from the first (statement), except that it has been resumed to indicate that it is an independent purpose, important in itself, even though it branches off from something else. The gist of what it contains is sincerity to Allah in worship (ikhlas), and this branches off from monotheism (tawhid). For this reason it has been said: "Showing off (riya') is minor shirk." The Messenger ﷺ was taught to say this after what had been taught to him before it, because what is mentioned here contains the meaning of thanking Allah for the blessing of being guided to the straight path. For He guided him, then inspired him to give thanks for the guidance by making all his obedience and worship belong to Allah, exalted is He. The command to speak was repeated because of what you already know.

The sentence of the speech was opened with the particle of emphasis (inna) for the sake of giving importance to the news and affirming it, or because the polytheists used to claim that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, performed his prayer for show. For "some of the polytheists said, when they saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ praying near the Ka'bah: 'Do you not see this show-off? Which of you will go to the camel of the so-and-so family, take its dung and its entrails, and when he prostrates, place them between his shoulders?'" Thus, on this basis, inna is for rejecting doubt.

The lam in lillah may be the lam of ownership, meaning: it is by Allah's facilitation; so it is an explanation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. It may also be the lam of causation (ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of Allah, He made his prayer belong to Allah alone, not to other than Him, as an allusion to the polytheists, since they used to prostrate to idols. For this reason the sentence "No partner has He" follows it.

Nusuk (rites) is fundamentally worship, and from it the worshipper is called nasik.

Al-mahya and al-mamat are used as mimi verbal nouns (masdar), and they are used as nouns of time, from hayiya and mata. Both meanings are possible. If by al-mahya and al-mamat the verbal-noun meaning is intended, the meaning is by an omitted modifier (mudaf), its estimate being: the deeds of living and the deeds of dying, i.e., the deeds which a person is characterized by with his life and at the time of his death. And if the temporal meaning is intended, the meaning is what befalls him during life and after death.

Then, the deeds of life are many and abundant, while the deeds at death are what he was upon during the period of life and his steadfastness upon it, because the state of death, or its duration, is the state or duration in which the conditions of the body change into a quality that announces the nearing end of the period of life, and that is the state of agony (ihtidar). That state may produce a change in thought or hastening toward what the living one would not hasten toward. So there may issue from its owner deeds which he would not have done during the period of health, out of caution, shame, or seeking benefit; thus it is seen that he may have despaired of what he used to observe, and so does what he did not used to do. Also, that state has particular matters which normally occur at it, such as bequest (wasiyyah). All of these are from the conditions of the end of life. But they are attributed to death because they occur near it. And with this, the mention of death is intended to encompass the entire period of life up to the time of standing on the brink of death.

It is possible that by death is meant what befalls the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, after his passing, of his spiritual attentions toward his community: supplicating for them, returning greetings to those among them who greet him, and appearing in dreams to the special ones of his community. For the Messenger, after his death, has the rulings of complete spiritual life, as is narrated in the hadith: "When anyone of my community sends greetings upon me, Allah returns my soul to me, and I return the greeting to him." Likewise are his deeds on the Day of Gathering, such as the general intercession and prostration to Allah in the plains of the Resurrection. These are deeds specific to him ﷺ, and they are all for Allah, exalted is He, because they are for the benefit of His servants or for the benefit of the followers of His religion which He has approved for them. Thus his saying "and my death" here refers to his saying in the hadith: "My life is good for you, and my death is good for you."

It is also possible that the meaning of his death being for Allah is martyrdom in the way of Allah, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was poisoned by the Jews at Khaybar in the meat of a sheep they fed him, some of which remained in his intestines. In the hadith: "The morsel of Khaybar continued to afflict me every year, until this was the time of the severing of my aorta."

By His saying "my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds," the meaning of Islam is realized, whose origin is the surrender of oneself to the One to whom one submits. This is the meaning required by His saying: ﴿So say: I have submitted my face to Allah, and whoever follows me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20], as was mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran, and it is the meaning of hanifiyyah which Allah, exalted is He, related of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131], as in Surah al-Baqarah. His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ is a description pointing to the reason for deserving that the deeds of His creatures be for Him and not for another, because there is no bounty of creation for Him over them, as His saying at the beginning of the surah indicates: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; yet those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord.﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

The sentence "﴿No partner has He﴾" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the name of majesty (Allah), explicitly stating what the combination of emphasis with the lam of ownership implied of restriction (qasr). The purpose of the description and the circumstantial clause is a refutation of the polytheists, that they did not sincerely direct their deeds to the One who created them, and that they associated with Him others in divinity.

Nafi' read "wa-mahyaya" with the second ya' vowelless, treating the connected form as if it were in pause (wasl majra al-waqf), which is rare in prose; the transmission from Nafi' established it in this verse. It is known that rarity does not detract from eloquence, and do not be troubled by what Ibn 'Atiyyah related from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi: that it is anomalous (shadhdhah) relative to analogy because it combined two sakins. For the vowellessness of an alif before a sakin letter is not something heavy in pronunciation, like 'asaya and ru'yaya. The reason for treating the connected form as pause here is the desire for lightness, because the succession of two fatha-vowelled ya's is heavy, and the alif arising from the first fatha is not regarded as a barrier, so he turned away from fathah on the second ya' to sukun. The rest read it with fathah on the ya', and this is also narrated from Warsh. Some scholars of the readings said that Nafi' returned from sukun to fathah.

The sentence "﴿And this I have been commanded﴾" is coordinated (conjoined, 'atf) upon the sentence "Indeed my prayer..." etc. So this is among what he was commanded to say, and the conjunctive particle is not part of what is said.

The reference in "And this" to what was mentioned in "﴿Indeed my prayer and my rites﴾" etc., meaning: that this was for Allah by guidance from Allah and by His command. It returns to His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 161], meaning: just as He guided him, He commanded him with what is thanks for that guidance. It was repeated here because when he attributed the prayer and what is conjoined to it to himself and made it for Allah, exalted is He, he followed it by saying that it is guidance from Allah, exalted is He. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, making religion sincerely His﴾ [al-Zumar: 11] ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for giving importance to what is referred to.

His saying "﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾," like His saying "﴿And this I have been commanded﴾," is a news statement used in its implicative (kinayi) meaning, and it is the necessary consequence of its meaning, namely accepting Islam, steadfastness upon it, and delight in it, because whoever loves something hastens toward it, so he comes first of the people. This is like the function of the verb "sabaqa" (to precede), which in their speech is used for firm establishment and preponderance, as al-Nabighah said:

You outstripped the men who strive for glory, as the swift horse outstrips, catching the prey before the pursuers.

He does not mean that he was earlier than others in lofty deeds, since among the people of glory there are those older than him in age, and some attained glory before the praised one was born; but he meant that he became capable of attaining glory, and became its possessor and steadfast upon it.

In a hadith: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in precedence) on the Day of Resurrection." This meaning is a discouragement to the polytheists from hoping for concessions to them in their religion, even the least concession. And from the use of "first" (awwal)

in such a context is His saying: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], as was mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. The intended meaning is not its explicit sense, because the news would then be of little value, since every caller to something is necessarily the first of his companions; what benefit is that to the opponents and the followers? If by "the Muslims" is meant those who followed the reality of Islam in the sense of submitting one's face to Allah, exalted is He, it does not hold, because Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a Muslim and his sons were Muslims, as Allah related of them when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132].

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read with the affirmation of the alif of "ana" when a hamzah follows it, and its madd is extended according to the rule of madd; and its omission for lightness is what the Arabs followed in the eloquent of their speech, such as: ﴿Ana Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 90]. They differed concerning it before a hamzah, such as "ana af'alu," and I reckon that the more eloquent is its affirmation with the hamzah, for the sake of the establishment of the madd.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verses 162–163:

﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my rites, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿No partner has He. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims.﴾

This is also a resumptive statement (isti'naf), which takes the place of a derivation from the first (statement), except that it has been resumed to indicate that it is an independent purpose, important in itself, even though it branches off from something else. The gist of what it contains is sincerity to Allah in worship (ikhlas), and this branches off from monotheism (tawhid). For this reason it has been said: "Showing off (riya') is minor shirk." The Messenger ﷺ was taught to say this after what had been taught to him before it, because what is mentioned here contains the meaning of thanking Allah for the blessing of being guided to the straight path. For He guided him, then inspired him to give thanks for the guidance by making all his obedience and worship belong to Allah, exalted is He. The command to speak was repeated because of what you already know.

The sentence of the speech was opened with the particle of emphasis (inna) for the sake of giving importance to the news and affirming it, or because the polytheists used to claim that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, performed his prayer for show. For "some of the polytheists said, when they saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ praying near the Ka'bah: 'Do you not see this show-off? Which of you will go to the camel of the so-and-so family, take its dung and its entrails, and when he prostrates, place them between his shoulders?'" Thus, on this basis, inna is for rejecting doubt.

The lam in lillah may be the lam of ownership, meaning: it is by Allah's facilitation; so it is an explanation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. It may also be the lam of causation (ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of Allah, He made his prayer belong to Allah alone, not to other than Him, as an allusion to the polytheists, since they used to prostrate to idols. For this reason the sentence "No partner has He" follows it.

Nusuk (rites) is fundamentally worship, and from it the worshipper is called nasik.

Al-mahya and al-mamat are used as mimi verbal nouns (masdar), and they are used as nouns of time, from hayiya and mata. Both meanings are possible. If by al-mahya and al-mamat the verbal-noun meaning is intended, the meaning is by an omitted modifier (mudaf), its estimate being: the deeds of living and the deeds of dying, i.e., the deeds which a person is characterized by with his life and at the time of his death. And if the temporal meaning is intended, the meaning is what befalls him during life and after death.

Then, the deeds of life are many and abundant, while the deeds at death are what he was upon during the period of life and his steadfastness upon it, because the state of death, or its duration, is the state or duration in which the conditions of the body change into a quality that announces the nearing end of the period of life, and that is the state of agony (ihtidar). That state may produce a change in thought or hastening toward what the living one would not hasten toward. So there may issue from its owner deeds which he would not have done during the period of health, out of caution, shame, or seeking benefit; thus it is seen that he may have despaired of what he used to observe, and so does what he did not used to do. Also, that state has particular matters which normally occur at it, such as bequest (wasiyyah). All of these are from the conditions of the end of life. But they are attributed to death because they occur near it. And with this, the mention of death is intended to encompass the entire period of life up to the time of standing on the brink of death.

It is possible that by death is meant what befalls the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, after his passing, of his spiritual attentions toward his community: supplicating for them, returning greetings to those among them who greet him, and appearing in dreams to the special ones of his community. For the Messenger, after his death, has the rulings of complete spiritual life, as is narrated in the hadith: "When anyone of my community sends greetings upon me, Allah returns my soul to me, and I return the greeting to him." Likewise are his deeds on the Day of Gathering, such as the general intercession and prostration to Allah in the plains of the Resurrection. These are deeds specific to him ﷺ, and they are all for Allah, exalted is He, because they are for the benefit of His servants or for the benefit of the followers of His religion which He has approved for them. Thus his saying "and my death" here refers to his saying in the hadith: "My life is good for you, and my death is good for you."

It is also possible that the meaning of his death being for Allah is martyrdom in the way of Allah, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was poisoned by the Jews at Khaybar in the meat of a sheep they fed him, some of which remained in his intestines. In the hadith: "The morsel of Khaybar continued to afflict me every year, until this was the time of the severing of my aorta."
