Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 6, verse 164:

﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than God, when He is the Lord of all things? No soul earns [anything] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another.﴾

This is a third resumptive sentence (istinaf), opened with the command to speak. It serves as a conclusion to what precedes it, because it has been established that God guided him to the straight path, rescued him from polytheism, and commanded him to devote his worship and obedience exclusively to his Lord, the Exalted, as thanks for the guidance. He then follows this with a denial that he should worship other than God the Exalted, because the Giver of blessings is the one deserving of thanks, and worship is the sum of the degrees of thanks. This also returns to explaining their error in having worshipped other than Him. The repetition of the command to speak has already had its reason explained.

[p. 206]

The interrogative is a denial directed at them, because they desire that he would acknowledge the lordship of their idols. They have attempted this more than once, whether they attempted it from him close to the revelation of this verse or not; they are constantly keen on getting him to agree with their religion. Ibn 'Atiyya relates from al-Naqqash that the disbelievers said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Return to our religion and worship our gods, and we will take responsibility for you for every consequence you fear in your worldly life and in the Hereafter." He said that this verse was revealed concerning that.

The object is placed before its verb because it is the focus of the denying interrogative, since the locus of the denial is that something other than God should be sought as a lord. It is also because that is the focus of the answer, if it is established that the polytheists invited the Prophet ﷺ to worship their gods. Its placement before the verb is for emphasis, for one reason or two reasons, as was mentioned in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Shall I take as a protector other than God?﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in this surah.

The clause ﴿and He is the Lord of all things﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This circumstance gives the reason for the denial, meaning that God is the Creator of all things, and they acknowledge this, because they do not claim that the idols create anything. As He, Exalted, said: ﴿They will not create a fly even if they gathered together for it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. Since God is the Creator of all things and their Lord, no one else has a right to be worshipped by the creatures. Worshipping other than Him is a great wrong and an ingratitude for His blessings, because creation is bringing into existence, and existence is better than non-existence. Mere creation necessitates worship, for the sake of servanthood.

The phrase ﴿and He is the Lord of all things﴾ was stated rather than "and He is my Lord" in order to establish that He is their Lord by way of inference, because it is the establishment of a general ruling that includes the specific ruling intended. It also serves to convey that their lords are likewise not truly worthy of lordship, belonging to God the Exalted.

His words, ﴿No soul earns [anything] except against itself﴾, are part of the commanded speech. They convey a disassociation from the polytheists and a expression of their abhorrence, in that their obstinacy cannot harm him, because what they have committed of polytheism does not reach him in any way. The earning of every soul is against itself, and they are among the souls, so their earning falls back upon them and does not pass beyond them to others. Thus the generalization in the ruling in His words "every soul" serves the same purpose as the generalization in His words: ﴿He is the Lord of all things﴾.

The word "ʿalā" (against) indicates that the object of the verb "to earn" (kasb) is omitted, and its implied object is: evil (sharran), or sin (ithman), or something similar, because the nature of those addressed is to acquire evil and sin, as in His words: ﴿You are not responsible for their account in any way﴾. You may also introduce into the sentence an ellipsis of the kind called iḥtibāk, in which the second part indicates the first and vice versa, if you proceed on the basis that "kasaba" (to earn) is predominantly used for obtaining good, and "iktasaba" (to acquire) is predominantly used for obtaining evil, whether or not both verbs appear together. I do not consider there to be a difference between the two verbs, and this was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿For it is what it earned, and against it is what it acquired﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. The meaning is that what a person acquires or earns does not pass from him to anyone else.

His words, ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, complete the meaning of His words, "No soul earns [anything] except against itself." Just as what a soul earns does not pass from it to another, likewise no soul bears on behalf of another soul anything. The meaning is: "I will not bear your burdens."

Thus the word "bearer" (wāziratun) is an attribute of an omitted noun, whose implied noun is "soul" (nafs), indicated by His words, ﴿No soul earns [anything] except against itself﴾. That is, no soul bears as a bearer the burden of another.

The word wizr means a load, which is what a person carries on his back. He, Exalted, said: ﴿But we were made to carry burdens of the people's ornaments﴾ [Taha: 87], and this was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And they carry their burdens on their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry﴾ [al-An'am: 31]. As for naming sin "wizr," it is because it is imagined to be heavy upon the soul of the believer. Thus the meaning of ﴿no bearer of burdens bears﴾ is: no one bearing a load bears [it], meaning no soul bears, when it bears the load of any other soul besides itself. The meaning is that no soul avails another soul anything by bearing its load on its behalf. That is, every soul bears only its own burden. This establishes that the burden of each person is upon himself, that he cannot have another carry any part of his burden that he has borne, and that no one is held accountable for the burden of another, whether a relative or a friend. So no soul avails another soul anything, and no soul is made to bear the sin of another. If it bears, it does not bear the load of another. This completes the meaning of non-sharing.

* * *

﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about what you used to differ over.﴾ The word "then" (thumma) indicates a sequence of rank. This statement may be part of the commanded speech, in which case it is a continuation of the disassociation with what contains a threat and warning to them. The position of "then" is for this report to be of greater importance. The address in His words ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ is addressed to the polytheists, and likewise the two pronouns in His words ﴿about what you used to differ over﴾. The meaning is: about what you used to differ over with the Muslims, because the disagreement occurs between them and the Muslims, and there is no disagreement among the polytheists themselves. Thus the threat is combined with a threat. They have made this sentence together with the preceding one a single verse in the Qur'anic codices.

It is also possible that the speech being reported ended at His words "the burden of another." In that case, His words ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ would be a resumed statement from God, the Exalted, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to those who oppose him. "Then" is suitable for resumption, because resumption is appropriate to the sequence of rank, and the statement is both a warning and a promise. This does not preclude that it may be a single verse together with the one before it.

[p. 207]

The word "tanbi'a" means informing, and what is intended by it is the manifestation of the effects of faith and disbelief clearly on the Day of Reckoning, so that they will know that they were astray. This knowledge is compared to God informing them of that on that day. Otherwise, God already informed them of what they differed over during the life of this world. Or the meaning is: He will inform you directly, without intermediary messengers, with an information that the disbeliever cannot say: "This is a lie against God," as is related in the hadith of the Gathering: "He will make the caller make them hear: there is no barrier between them and God."

[p. 210]

Apparently this is evidence for the possibility of resurrection and for its occurrence. The One who made some generations successors to those before them, so that they cultivated the earth generation after generation, is not unable to gather them all together after the end of their first life. Moreover, the One who arranged that and perfected it is not fitting to leave among them the balance of recompense for what they did in the first life, lest the transgressors and wrongdoers depart triumphant with what they committed. And if He sets up the balance of recompense for the wrongdoers, how would He leave off rewarding the good-doers? The first part is alluded to by His saying ﴿It is He who made you successors on the earth﴾, and the second part is alluded to by His saying ﴿and raised some of you above others in rank, that He may test you through what He has given you﴾. For this reason He followed it with its concluding statement: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The address is directed to the polytheists, whom the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say to: ﴿Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. This reminds them that they will come to what those (earlier people) came to.

[p. 210 continued]

The placement of this verse after His saying, "Then to your Lord is your return," is a reminder of the blessing after a warning of its removal, and an incitement to make up for what has been missed. It opens their eyes to consider the outcomes of nations, their extinction and their survival.

It is also possible that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Islamic community, and the idafa (construct) would then carry the sense of "li" (for), meaning: He made you successors of the nations that possessed the earth, so you are successors for the earth. Then the good news is that the community is the last of the nations appointed by Allah to populate the earth. What is meant by "the nations" is the nations possessing divine laws. In either case, it is a reminder of Allah's great handiwork and favour, to call forth gratitude and to warn against disbelief.

Al-khala'if (the successors) is the plural of khalifa (successor). The khalifa is a noun for that which replaces something, i.e., is made a successor in its place, meaning a substitute. It is said khalifa and khilfa. It is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and the feminine ta' appears in it because when they made it a noun they detached it from its qualified noun.

Its idafa to "the earth" carries the sense of "fi" (in) according to the first aspect, namely that the address is to the polytheists, meaning successors in it: that is, He replaced you with nations that passed before you, as the Exalted said, relating the statements of the Messengers addressing their peoples: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69]; ﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]; ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the earth, and then He will observe how you act﴾ [al-A'raf: 129]. The idafa carries the sense of "li" (for) according to the second aspect, which is that the address is to the Muslims.

In this too there is a reminder of a blessing that contains a lesson and an admonition. For when He made them successors of others, He originated and brought them into existence while He annihilated others. This is a blessing, because if He had decreed the continuation of the nations before them, these (people) would not have come into existence.

[p. 211]

The conjunction of His saying ﴿and raised some of you above others in ranks﴾ follows the two possibilities regarding the addressee in His saying ﴿made you successors of the earth﴾. It too is a lesson and an admonition, so that one does not become deluded by strength and eminence, and so that this becomes a means of thanking that blessing, striving to increase the bounty for those who fall short of it, showing kindness to the weak, and giving justice to the oppressed.

For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿that He may test you through what He has given you﴾, meaning: that He may make known to you, through the blessings He has bestowed upon you, the ranks of blessings, so that it becomes manifest to people how the possessors of blessings place themselves in their fitting positions, which are what is expressed by "ranks".

"Darajat" (ranks) is used metaphorically for the disparity of blessings. It is a metaphor built upon likening the intelligible to the perceptible in order to bring it closer.

"Al-ita'" (giving) is used metaphorically for bringing about elevation in its possessors, likening the bringing-about to a giver giving something to another.

"Al-balw" means testing. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqara: 155]. What is meant by it is the manifestation of the scales of minds in benefiting from and conferring benefit by means of Allah's gifts, and what He has facilitated for them of agreeable and supportive conditions. Allah knows the levels of people, but that is a test, because it does not become apparent to the eye except after action. That is, so that Allah may know it as knowledge of what has occurred, after He knew it as knowledge of what is decreed. This is the position of the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil). Close to this is the verse of Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i:

"I came forward while the spear swayed between us, / so that I might know which of them is the coward and which the brave."

The clause, ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the speech and an announcement that the purpose of it is action and compliance. For this reason, here He combined the attribute of swiftness in punishment with the attribute of Forgiving, so as to correspond to all that this surah contains.

[p. 212]

Swiftness is used metaphorically for the absence of hesitation and for the complete capability to punish, because the condition of one who hesitates or is incapable is to delay and to fear the consequences of the one being punished. Thus, what is meant is "swift in punishment on the Day of Punishment", and it is not meant that He is swift in it from now on, so as to be interpreted as "everything that is coming is near", since that has no place here.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is that in describing the one swift in punishment it restricts itself to a single emphasis, whereas the description of the Forgiving, the Merciful is reinforced with three emphases: "inna" (indeed), the lam of commencement, and the verbal emphasis (the repetition of the Forgiving and Merciful in a sense), since "the Merciful" reinforces the meaning of "the Forgiving". This is to reassure the people of righteous action of Allah's forgiveness and mercy, and to summon those who turn away and recoil to abandon what they are engaged in.

* * *

[p. 5]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-A'raf

This is the name by which this surah has been known since the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Nasa'i transmitted, from the hadith of Abu Malika, from Urwa ibn Zayd ibn Thabit, that he said to Marwan ibn al-Hakam: "What is it with me that I see you reciting in the Maghrib prayer short surahs, while I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting in it the longer of the two long ones?" Marwan said: "I said: 'O Abu 'Abd Allah, what are the two longer ones?'" He said: "Al-A'raf." And similarly the hadith of Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the Maghrib prayer the longest of the two long ones." What is meant by "the two long ones" is Surat al-A'raf and Surat al-An'am, for Surat al-A'raf is longer than Surat al-An'am in terms of the number of verses. This is explained by the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the Maghrib prayer Surat al-A'raf, dividing it between two rak'as."

Its naming: it is called al-A'raf because the word "al-A'raf" is mentioned in His saying, ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the A'raf are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], and the verse. It is not mentioned in any other surah of the Qur'an. And because the affair of the People of the A'raf in the Hereafter is mentioned in it, and it is not mentioned with this word in any other surah. However, it is mentioned with the word "sur" (wall) in His saying: ﴿So a wall with a gate was set up between them, its inner side containing mercy and its outer side facing torment﴾ [al-Hadid: 13], in Surat al-Hadid.

It is sometimes called by the names of the disjointed letters with which it begins, which are: "Alif - Lam - Mim - Sad." Al-Nasa'i transmitted from the hadith of Abu al-Aswad, from Urwa, from Zayd ibn Thabit, that he said to Marwan: "I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting in the Maghrib prayer the longer of the two long ones: 'Alif - Lam - Mim - Sad.'"

[p. 6]

This falls under the view that the disjointed letters found at the beginning of some surahs are names of the surahs in which they occur. This view is weak. Therefore "Al-Mas" (﴿المص﴾) [al-A'raf: 1] is not a name of the surah, and its application to it is only under the assumption of a definition by the idafa to the surah that has "Al-Mas". Likewise Shaykh Ibn Abi Zayd named it in the Risala, in the chapter on prostration in the Qur'an, and they did not count this surah among the surahs that have "Al-Mas" (﴿المص﴾) [al-A'raf: 1] among the multiple names. As for what is in the hadith of Zayd, that it is the longer of the two long ones, it is according to the intention of description, not of nicknaming. Al-Fayruzabadi mentioned in Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz that this surah is called the Surah of the Appointed Time, because it includes mention of Musa's appointed time in His saying: ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. And that it is called the Surah of the Covenant, because it includes the account of the covenant in His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. I have not found these two designations in the words of anyone else.

It is Meccan without disagreement. Then it has been said that all of it is Meccan, and this is the apparent report of Mujahid and Ata al-Khurasani from Ibn Abbas, and likewise it is reported from Ibn al-Zubayr. It has also been said that some of it was revealed in Medina. Qatada said: the verse ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 163] was revealed in Medina. Muqatil said: from His saying ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'raf: 163], to His saying ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam from their loins their descendants﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], was revealed in Medina. If this is sound, it is possible that the surah was Meccan and the two mentioned verses were later added to it, and it is possible that it was revealed in Mecca and its remainder was completed by those two verses.

I have not found anything by which the date of its revelation can be fixed. It is reported from Jabir ibn Zayd that it was revealed after Surat Sad and before Surat Qul Uhiya (Surat al-Jinn). The apparent meaning of the hadith of Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari is that Surat "Qul Uhiya" [al-Jinn: 1] was revealed at the beginning of Islam, when

[p. 7]

the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) became manifest, and that was during the days of the Hajj, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was heading with his companions to the market of Ukaz. Perhaps that was in the second year of the Prophethood. I do not think Surat al-A'raf was revealed during that period, because the long surahs apparently were not revealed at the beginning of the Prophethood.

It is among the Seven Long Surahs, which were placed at the beginning of the Qur'an because of their length. They are: al-Baqara, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'ida, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and Bara'a. The Medinan ones among them were placed first: al-Baqara, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', and al-Ma'ida; then the Meccan ones were mentioned: al-An'am and al-A'raf, according to the order of the Uthmanic Mushaf, taking into account that Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca after Surat al-A'raf, so it is closer to the Medinan surahs than the other long surahs.

It is counted as the thirty-ninth in the order of the revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed after Surat Sad and before Surat al-Jinn, as previously stated. They said: Ibn Mas'ud placed it in his Mushaf after Surat al-Baqara, and placed after it Surat al-Nisa', then Al 'Imran. In the Mushaf of Ubayy, after Al 'Imran came al-An'am, then al-A'raf. Surat al-Nisa' is the one that follows Surat al-Baqara in length, and Surat al-A'raf follows Surat al-Nisa' in length.

The count of the verses of Surat al-A'raf is two hundred and six verses according to the count of the people of Medina and Kufa, and two hundred and five according to the count of the people of Sham (Syria) and Basra. Al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan: it has been said two hundred and seven.

* * *

The opening of this surah is with an affirmation of the Qur'an and a promise of its being made easy for the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he may convey it. Its opening is a comprehensive statement

[p. 8]

corresponding to the aims that the surah contains. Thus it is an opening that comes in the best forms of expression and their most complete, as is the case with the surahs of the Qur'an.

The aims of this surah revolve around a central axis of aims. Among them:

The prohibition of taking partners besides Allah.

The warning to the polytheists of the evil consequence of polytheism in this world and in the Hereafter.

The description of what befell the polytheists and those who denied the Messengers, of the evil punishment in this world, and what will befall them in the Hereafter.

The reminder to people of the blessing of the creation of the earth, and the enabling of the human species to enjoy the good things of the earth, and of Allah's blessing upon this species by creating its origin and favouring it.

And what arose from the enmity of the kind of Satan toward the human species.

Warning people against being entangled in the remnants of Satan's deception, namely his beautifying to them the deprivation of their own selves of the good things, and against falling into what drives them into punishment in the Hereafter.

A description of the terrors of the Day of Recompense for the criminals, and of its honours for the God-fearing.

A reminder of the Resurrection and an approximation of its proof.

A prohibition against corruption on the earth, which Allah has set right for the benefit of mankind.

A reminder of the wondrous things Allah has brought into being for its reform and revival.

A reminder of what Allah has placed in the natural disposition (fitrah) of man from the time his origin was formed, that they should accept the call of Allah's messengers to piety and reform.

He expounded on the circumstances of the messengers with their polytheist peoples, and what they encountered of their obstinacy and harm, and he warned against being deceived by Allah's granting respite to people before He sends down punishment upon them, and as an excuse to them that they should desist from their disbelief and obstinacy, for the punishment will come upon them suddenly after that respite.

Page 9

He dwelt at length on the story of Musa (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh, and on the conduct of the Children of Israel towards Musa (peace be upon him).

Interwoven within his story is Allah's good tidings of the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ), a description of his community, and the excellence of his religion.

Then he turned to admonishing the polytheists: how they changed the Hanifiyyah (the pure monotheistic primordial faith) and adopted polytheism. He set for them an example of one to whom Allah gave the signs, but Satan whispered to him, so he stripped himself away from guidance.

He described the state of the people of misguidance, described their denial of what the Messenger brought, and described their deities with what contradicts divinity, and that Allah has the Most Beautiful Names, the attributes of perfection.

Then Allah commanded His Messenger (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) and the Muslims to have expansiveness of breast and to persevere in the call, and warned them against the entryways of Satan by being mindful of Allah, through remembering Him secretly and openly and turning devotedly to His worship.
